I'm going to be honest; I really like this kind of game. Turn based dungeon crawlers in the vein of Wizardry or Elminage Gothic are my favourite sort. I've even been known to break out the grid paper and do some mapping. With this in mind, it might not be an entirely objective review. If I had to make a comparison for people who don't want to read much, it's Etrian Odyssey without manual mapping and better combat.
This game is good.
Ok, so I guess I have to back that up now, because the production values are low and I must admit it looks rather like RPG-maker shovelware when you first see it. It'd be easy to discount it because of that, but that would be a mistake though, because this is obviously a labour of love from someone who's a massive fan of Etrian Odyssey and this genre.
PROS-
- Combat is really good. There's a lot of depth with plenty of different skills, strengths and weaknesses. And it's TOUGH!
- Character development is surprisingly good. Chars can be customised with skills gained from equipment as well as class and then levelled up each char level. There's quite a few different character classes to choose from as well.
- There's item levelling as well as char levelling, but it's not overpowered broken like in Class of Heroes.
- The dungeon is hazardous to explore as there's no saving in there, but an item that can teleport you out instantly is very cheap to buy.
- The price is ridiculously cheap.
CONS
- Weeaboo overload. I cringe at some of the character art, but at least it's not fan service.
- Production values are low. Like, low. Look past the 'SP_POOL' and 'alchemy_boost' code text and the basic dungeon graphics.
- It's obtuse to the point of puzzling. The manual is not a lot of help, just being 7 screenshots with some text overlaid. I've figured a lot out so far, but if you want everything explained through tool tips and tutorials, it ain't happening.
- Lacking lore and story besides 'go seek your fortune in the labyrinth'. This may well change later, I'm only up to floor 3.
If you like this sort of game, you'll probably already have it in your library. If not, what are you waiting for? A Steam sale on a game that's this low in price already?! This probably isn't the game to convert people who don't like turn based blobbers, (that might be Stranger of Sword City), but for those of us that do, this is a no-brainer.

8 hours in, and I'm not planning on stopping.
After thoroughly searching through all of the options in the game menu, I can finally change my review verdict from "Not Recommend" to "Recommend".
Lord of the Seal isn't for players who are looking for great graphics or immersive worlds.
This game is more geared towards players looking for a basic, simple, and fun RPG grind.
Pros:
- Classic dungeon-crawler (kill, farm, sleep at inn, repeat)
- Simple combat
- Fast gameplay (no flashy effects, quick animations)
- Easy to learn
- Auto-battle option ("A" on Xbox 360 controller)
- Items and skills are straight-forward (obvious and easy to understand)
- Music is basic and easy to listen to
- Job/Class system is acceptable
- Tons of control over how your characters (team members) develop and what skills they gain (reminds me to FFX-2's job system).
- Mastery/Orbs are easy to understand
- "Encounter" icon in the top-left corner makes it easy to anticipate an enemy attack
Cons:
- Sounds made from attacking or getting attacked, seem too loud compared to the rest of the sounds (selecting, confirming, encounters, purchasing, etc.)
- Shop sub-sections are inconsistent, and thus, confusing (for the item merchant, it's on the bottom-left; for the alchemist girl, it's in the top-right).
Neutral:
- The Xbox 360 controller support is non-traditional:
- It seems like "X" is the "confirm" button, although it makes more sense to bind it to "A".
- "B" opens up your party menu instead of "START".
Some of my issues prior to searching through the game's menu options have been solved and thus, removed from this review.

This was a hidden gem I only came across on accident but I think it deserves to be noticed. It is a great combination of many different ideas that come together to make a grand game. Building up your station is a fun thing to do but comes with dangers as you try to expand and find creatures living in your base. I lost many a cadet to those critters, good thing they are so expendable! Very hard to say what exactly I love the most when the whole package ended up being so fun.
The tactical combat is a welcome difference from all the extremely fast paced but boring combat of most space games. It is still very high energy as you struggle to fight against fleets stronger than you while trying to line up devastating combos that can obliterate a powerful vessle in two blows. My favorite being stunning the crew and then using suicide run to smash it to pieces. You feel strong when using your brain you defeat an enemy far stronger than you. Since this is a roguelike game expect that to be the case more often than not as they have some powerful fleets they will toss your way.
The star map is fun as it is frantic. Flying around space desperately trying to protect your stations from the aliens and deciding which ones just aren't possible to hold out any longer and evacuating them to save the crew. It is a tough decision because you will lose the resources it will generate but you get the crew of the station to build new ships and aid in defense. I had a lot of fun on my run plotting out paths that were the most efficient to pick up the resources while also obliterating any harrassing fleets trying to take out my infrastructure.
The side factions are also interesting. They seem to half want to kill you while on the other half looking to be your best pal. You'll have to discern for yourself who is truly at your side and who would love to punch a hole through your chest. My favorite being the pirates. They end up being much more than simple bandits that they first appear as you learn more about them and their internal struggles.
Couldn't recommend this game anymore than I can with just a thumbs up. It is well worth the money even in its limited early access state. Only one act out right now but for how fun it was, and that there is definitely replayability in decided who to help and who to blast into bits, its well worth the cash. Take a chance on this one, its worth it.

Deus Ex: HR is the first game where I've really felt like there were 10 different ways to achieve every objective. On my second playthrough it really hit me that you can really go the while game without an ounce of violence, without even being seen. Or by killing every single person. Or anywhere in between. It's just as satisfying blowing everyone up as it is watching your opponents through the walls, tracking their patterns, and running through them as a ghost.
But a game with so many options that it feels real has a few problems you have to justify with video game logic. Lots of air ducts with no security. The individual enemy AI seems fine, but why doesn't one guard notice when the other three have disappeared, or become suspicious of a gun lying on the ground. There is no place in the game with a stationary guard that needs to be distracted; every single one of them will eventually walk away, leaving an entrance or exit vulnerable. (At least on normal difficulty this was the case.)
There is also the problem of the big, dumb boss fights, which felt out of place with the rest of the game. I guess I just wanted more variety from them, save for the final boss which was interesting and fun.
But overall I greatly enjoyed this game. It has a somewhat open world, but without any sandbox elements. The character progression was great, allowing you to mould Adam to your specific playstyle, including options for combat, stealth, agility, hacking, even for shaping conversations,. The writing and voice-acting are both top-notch. The plot is interesting and throws a lot of surprises at you. A definite reccomend.

The story is really long and interesting, characters are well developed, gameplay is, in many ways imrpoved but the game could use a little bit of optimization. My rating is a 9.5/10. Performance issues aside, this game is amazing and you should buy it if you are a Nep fan and have played all other games before this. If you are new to this series, then play all the other games first to see if it's your type of game, then buy this.
The story is what you would expect from a Nep game, funny but it does have it's serious moments (though most of the time Neptune breaks the mood). This time, the Story is branched out into 3 arcs and is a lot longer than the previous games.
The characters introduced in this game are extremely interesting and well developed as the game progresses. I don't think there is
new character that I don't like. My favorite new characters are Uzume and C-Sha.
Some familiar tracks return like $100 and Minicar but the new ones that are introduced in this game are amazing, my favorite being More soul and Soutaisei Vision. If you have not bought the soundtrack yet, please do because this is some of the best music I have heard in my life.
If you have played the main Nep games before (Re;Birth 1, 2, 3) then the gameplay is almost the same, except there are a couple of changes. For one, there is no more Guard Points, but some enemies have parts that reduce damage, but can be broken if hit from a specific direction. EXE drives that use multiple characters now requires them to be in a certain position (circle, triangle) before you can use them. One thing that I dislike about the gameplay are the keyboard controls. In the previous games, I had no problem with them, but in this game they are horrible. If you own a controller, please, use that instead of the keyboard, will save you a lot of frustration.
While I don't have problems with performance (except for movies, which happen to a lot of people) a lot of other people do. Some people have huge lag, graphical glitches or crashes. I think this is the biggest fault of the game on PC. Idea Factory should do a lot more testing before releasing this to Steam. They do release patches which fix some problems, but it is really frustrating to have to wait for them before playing the game properly.
Hope this helped you guys, have fun Nepping!

Honestly, this is the first game I played in the Hyperdimension series, and I actually enjoyed it!
Voice actors, event CGs, and some other nitbits up to it's core gameplay, the game is well constructed and stands out from other JRPGs. The only thing that surprises me are those beef-ish system requirements to get the game running at it's best graphical fidelity considering the fact that the game is comprised mainly of cartoonish 3d worlds, models, and effects, but it shouldn't bother you too much because you the only thing you sacrifice by tuning down those video settings are battle effects, which are probably one of Neptunia's distinctive eyecandies from other JRPGs apart from their funny, memorable and relatable characters.
The gameplay itself is good for an RPG as a whole. Exploring dungeons can be fun, some are rediculously huge, some can be quite confusing to cruise around, and some are just plain awesome! Battles are turn-based, but they do have movement during those turns which can be used to strategically carry out combos and plays.  Tons of cute outfits and weapons for all characters are available (Look at kawaii little neppy -w-) with varying statistical advantages, crafting, and even investments! There are so much to list that I'm sure you'll really want to figure out for yourself at this point if you're truly interested in the game.
I think the true selling point of this game are its characters and artwork. I mean these each of the four CPU's (Neptune, Noire, Vert, and Blanc) are memorable, cute, funny,  Each 4 vary so much that many people take to liking one of them and possibly not so liking the other, but it all comes down to preference. The artworks are all well drawn, evident in the game's lively, colorful environment and CG gallery. The voice actors all did a great job of doing voice overs for each characters, too! It really helps bring out the unique flavor of each character in the game...
I'd recommend it, no doubt. Casual player or not, this game offers everything you can ask for in a traditional RPG game. Great story, well-done graphics, and memorable characters.

Just one common misconception I'd like to clear up about this game. You see, Doomguy isn't actually a badass. Being one of something implies it's possible to compare him to others and rank him in relation to them. Rather, badass is just a phrase for things that want to be Doomguy but fall short whill still managing to be awesome in their own right.
As for the game, it's as near a perfect capturing of the spirit of DOOM as is physically possible to get. It manages to capture the 1993 vibe of "to hell with the plot (pun definitely intended), let's just liquify demons with a Chainsaw", while also providing all the graphics capabilities you would expect from a modern game. In the intro, Dr. Hayden is a metaphor for the plot with Doomguy (wordlessly) expressing his distaste and indicating he's aware of how the situation is simultaneously ridiculous and deadly serious. It's painstakingly made clear that this is a game about shooting first and maybe getting around to asking the questions later, but maybe not works just fine too.
TL;DR: Two takeaways here -
1. Doomguy isn't a badass because badass is just what you call a watered down Doomguy.
2. Buy it, now.

Alright so I've used it for awhile and I had no issue giving this controller a recommendations however I will say it's based off your [Tastes]. I say this because theres afew things that's really annoying about it and you can easily come across a very intellegent player I will eventually come back and link you to who stated said things. Ok let's get started.
The Pros
-Extremely comfortable.
-Back buttons work so well I forget there are bumper buttons sometimes, and they don't hinder my ability to press other things (similar to Z button on N64 or B on Wii-mote)
-Very light and midium size for people like me with small hands and some others with bigger hands.
-Extremely responsive
-Works with any game you can utilize Non-Steam game with. Like PSO2 and PPSSPP.
-Literatel Plug'nPlay. Plug it in, let steam install files(don't be a idiot like me and go wireless midupdate), play.

-Ingame keyboard
-Config changable ingame

The Cons
-Unless you play stick I doubt you'll ever use this in a fighting game.
-Analog emulation is linier, only allowing Swipe for sensitivity instead of based off how far from center you are.
-Often reads swipes in one direction making it continue to go with right you swiped right and moves down. (I know "use a mouse emu for that is a thing but it's abit more work for games like FFXIV where it would be easier to control the camera with a touch opposed to a swipe+hold over holding click while trying to input commands for combat).
-If in wireless mode and it turns off due to power save you have to quit the game and open it back up to get it connected again. This sucks when you have to go to the bathroom or something and it decides to sleep on you. I suggest taking this power save off because of this issue as plugging it in avoids it.

- I generally don't add these things to cons but I have to mention that if you do mess up the installation you have to go to hell and back if you don't know where to look. 3: very responsive, doesn't disconnect midgame or have response lag. (Pass)

Enhancing the functions outside of Steam is something I wish they would improve. Pleasantly surprised by the controller. works better than I suspected in games like CSGO (although still inferior to KB/M) and works well as a direct replacement for an xbox style controller, but it's greatest strength is as a desktop remote. if it was possible to use the Steam big picture mode controller keyboard outside of steam, it would be unbeatable as a desktop remote.

+ It's using standard AA batteries, which means that you can have others charging or fully charged ready while playing.

(When I tested it with my index finger it didn't work properly, but it works fine with my thumb. Perhaps there might be issues if you play guitarlike instruments more than I do, or if you're a construction worker or something.)
- No headset or even a headphones port.
- The light on the button is 100% on or 100% off, no other level is actually saved even though I can select other levels. (This may be a Steam on Linux specific issue, and it seems like it's something that doesn't need a hardware fix.)
- Needs Steam Overlay to be enabled to be able to use custom setting in games (which I don't like since disabling that is the only way to not get annoyed by achievement notifications). (This can probably be fixed in the software, all that's necessary is to make it possible to not show achievement popups, but since that feature has been requested before it'll probably not happen.)
- The bumper buttons need too much force to press them. This isn't obvious immediately, but after a while they are actually painful to use, and the controller moves too much when pressing them.

For me, the negatives far outweigh the positives. Perhaps the next version will be better, but at this time I wouldn't recommend getting one.

The original Dungeons was - though interesting in its own right - quite the misser. It was clear that Kalypso was going for a spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper, but was threading the line to avoid copyright issues with Electronic Arts. Dungeons II, as a sequel, had a franchise to build on, and was bolder in where it ventured. Though also a nice game that would sooth the nerves of those who like building the perfect dungeon, the game's speed was exceptionally slow with upgrade after upgrade to be researched without too much change happening in the dungeon itself.
Dungeons III has improved upon the formula again and brought back even more elements from the infamous series. Minions have their own lairs and jobs, there is a variety of creatures to pick from, and imprisoning, torturing and sacrificing heroes is once more a thing. But even so, Kalypso has managed to take the whimsical overly satirical narrative of Dungeons II and spun it in such a way that Dungeons III can now be rightfully called its own game.
It has the good parts of Dungeon Keeper: there is a vast array of rooms and units to explore, and you can shape your army in the way you want to. It's a lot of fun watching the creatures do their own thing when left alone, and they absolutely have personality. The pacing is great: there are no dull moments, yet there is still more than enough time to slow things down if you personally feel a need to, allowing you to sit back and observe your Goblins toil away.
At the same time, the game has improved in areas Dungeon Keeper never could. We can visit the overworld. There are neutral creatures to be found underground. Players can customize their units a little bit with 'book'-type upgrades. They can fill in accidentally dug tiles. The game's got wall-based traps. There is a less linear tech tree that genuinely allows you to pick a playstyle you like. And on top of that: the "we're the bad guys this time around" mentality from the old games is there, but implemented in a fresh way - with constant over the top meta-humor. Dungeons III doesn't take itself seriously, realizes it doesn't take itself seriously, and often comments on how it isn't taking itself seriously. In this manner, the game has its own take on the satirical approach; a take which, for better or for worse, is at least unique.
+Good pacing; easy to play at your own pace by choosing to be defensive or offensive
+Characters and creatures have decent personality and the story is amusing in its own way
+Feels more like Dungeon Keeper than any spiritual successor to date, having a payload of similar rooms and mechanics
+Co-op; play the campaign with a friend and have fun together
+Accessible; you will enjoy this as both a Simcity or a StarCraft player
-Technically unstable. Had a hard time getting co-op working as the game kept giving me 'network errors' with no further clarification. The game is also prone to crashing on older systems, primarily due to the fact that...
-There are no graphics options. You can set the game to be full screen or not, that's it. Makes it incredibly hard to even try and prevent said crashes.
-The game often responds sluggishly, or with a delay. An enemy in the overworld may display a graphic for an incoming area of effect ability, and you will sometimes straight up not be able to move your units out simply because they end up moving at half speed for no apparent reason. Or because they're clipping with other units. This makes unit micro nearly impossible. Thankfully, it isn't required to beat the campaign.
All in all, I would recommend this game to anybody who liked Dungeon Keeper or is a fan of God Games or Dungeon Builders in general. Regardless of whether you are the meticulous perfectionist who wants to spend hours building the perfect dungeon, a more tactical player who wants to try various approaches to beating the campaign, or a casual player looking for something new to try: you will enjoy it.

Disclaimer: This will be very, very long. So TL;DR 10/10 Best Naruto game in existence.
For the most part I will be comparing it to Storm 3. I have Revolution, but I barely touched it as it did not continue the story.
Prior to this coming out, I binged through all of Ninja Storm 3 for the story recap, and then when I switched to this one... not only does it continue the story, but it delivers it WAAYYY better than any other Storm game. The pacing is phenomenal. They even usually save the results screens for AFTER the cutscenes, to stop from breaking pacing/immersion. As before there are a few different types of missions: Free Battles, Boss Battles, Mob Battles, etc. Many of the missions have unique mechanics, like Wall-running fights. Quick Time Events make a return, but they remain optional and reward you with a little extra back-story flavour and higher mission rankings if you do well.
There are some new mechanics that aren't just in the story! Environmental effects, and Armor Breaking. They're both fairly self-explanatory, but let me give you some examples. Kakashi has his Lightning Blade jutsu. If he charges/casts this while standing in water, the water will be electrified, and any opponents standing in it will take damage. Casting a water jutsu while tanding in water empowers it, etc. These environmental effects are only disabled for Ranked matches online. As for armor breaking, after a certain amount of damage, usually with a lot of little hits as opposed to a fewer number of stronger attacks like jutsus, the opponent's costume will take damage, and part of their outer armor/clothing will break off. This mechanic works a lot like Super Smash Bros. 4's Rage mechanic. In that game, the higher your damage, the more knock-back you'll receive on consecutive attacks. However, what's unique to SSB4, is that once you pass a certain damage threshold, your own attacks will ALSO start to deal more knockback. Storm games don't have severely important knockback mechanics like Smash, but they do have damage. When your armor is broken, you will both take and deal slightly more damage than you did before.
BUT THAT'S NOT ALL! Storm 4 is even MORE like Smash than you realize! A new feature/system are 3-round fights! We've always had 1 round fights before -- when one person's lifebar runs out, the other person wins. Now, it's like Stocks in Smash. In games like Street Fighter, the game completely resets between rounds, with only EX gauge carrying between. This is more like Smash because the survivor retains the amount of health they had when they won the first round.
That was worded weird so let me continue my Smash analogy. In SSB4, online "ranked" (For Glory, as its known), it's a 1v1 match where both players have 2 stocks (read: lives) apiece. As soon as a player loses both stocks, the other one wins. Damage persists between stocks. In Ninja Storm 4, you can see a pair of Round indicators by each player's health bar. Pretending these are like Stocks in Smash makes perfect sense.
Dodging/Defense has some new additions. Previously, you could dodge essentially by double jumping in a certain direction. The downside of this was having to actually jump first, which meant you had to do it way ahead of time due to the startup. Now you can hold the guard button and you'll immediately dodge in the direction you move, making it very much like Super Smash Bros. (Which is a very good thing)! Additionally, there is now a Counter/Parry mechanic. While you're guarding if you hit X/Square at the moment you are attacked, you'll cancel out of their attack and push your opponent far away from you, at the cost of temporarily reducing your maximum chakra. This cost is incurred whether successful or not.
Assists! "Team" matches that actually emphasize the "TEAM"! On the Character Select Screen, you can see a small icon in the top left corner of their character portrait. This icon indicates which kind of Support action that character has. In the past, all characters could be Attack, Defend, or Balance style of assists. Now, there are a bunch of kinds.
: after knock back, opponent bounces back before your feet, allows you to extend your combo or UJ.
: if you use chakra shuriken, your support will too
: Allows you to charge chakra faster
: Support assist you with combos while attacking
: Support covers you while charging chakra
: Support will take a super for you, if it would have hit you
: Support will cover you, when the opponent dashes at you
Every character with their own slot on the CSS always has just a single one of these. These Support abilities start to activate when your Storm gauge is at least halfway full.
Oh yeah, the Storm Gauge! This is like the old Team Gauge in the top left. It now sits below your Chakra gauge towards the middle. It fills up as you take damage, like a Street Fighter 4 Ultra, and as you call in your assists to attack. They also fill as you SWITCH LEADERS MID COMBO! You heard me right, folks~! Picking your 3 character team means picking THREE CHARACTERS TO PLAY AS! And NOT just a character with 2 assists!
So each assist's portrait fills up over time after you use it. In-game this is referred to as the Assist Gauge. Switching leaders consumes only HALF of the cooldown of an assist. You can switch characters mid-combo by moving the Right analog stick in the direction (Left/Right) of the assist in the corner. E.g., if I was Naruto, and Sakura was LB and Sasuke was RB, I would move the Right Analog stick to the right if I wanted to Switch to Sasuke. You can do this at any time so long as the individual assist gauge is at least halfway full.
So, as I said, switching characters can be done mid-combo, which translates to it functioning the exact same as a chakra-dash-cancel combo extender! It's amazing! You can even do it in the air!
There are a couple of other mechanics that involve your team, as well. When the Storm gauge is FULL, you can do one of two things with it. The first is Linked Awakenings. So Awakenings are just as before: it's the Naruto universe equivalent of going Super Saiyan. To enter Awakening mode is the same as it was in the past. You need to be below a certain health threshold, and then you overcharge your Chakra, and you transform. If your Storm Gauge is full when you Awaken, ALL THREE of your characters will Awaken at once!
The other way to use your Storm gauge is similar to the way team attacks worked in the past. Once full, you Chakra Load THREE times and Attack. This will send out each of your teammates one at a time at chakra dash speed to attempt to connect with the opponent. (doesn't cost anything if you miss; you can try again) One of two things can happen. In most current cases, especially with mixed teams of unrelated characters, the Attack that ensues will be identical to past Storm games where your assists would juggle your opponent and your current main character will unleash their ult. However, if you have certain team compositions, they'll actually do LINKED TEAM COMBO ULTIMATES! E.g., Naruto + Minato + Kushina will do a super-powered FAMILY RASENGAN! Or having Neji, Hinata, and Hanabi Hyuga will also bring out Lord Hiashi and all FOUR of them will go nuts with their Byakugan & Taijutsu combo!
IT'S AWESOME!

So I came into the game expecting exactly what it delivered. It's a game about disassembling and assembling guns.
However, even as free to play games go, the amount of gameplay value (if you can call it that) is incredibly minimal unless you feel like chucking in some money to unlock new guns. If you look past the theme of this game (guns) it is basically just a puzzle game with very little replayability. Disassemble and reassemble that gun! Now do it again, but do it faster! Now do it again, but without hints! To me it seems like they added the RPG element of leveling up just so that somone can't just download the F2P game and dish out all of it "gameplay" in a couple of hours. It's a lazy and pathetic way at trying to make a full length game out of 1/8th of the material. This game probably would have been a lot better off if it offered all available content at a low price, because I would imagine that would bring in a lot more money considering no one in their right mind would pay 10 dollars to click a bunch of DIFFERENT metal bits in the right order.
I can guarantee you that this will just be another F2P game that you pick up, think it's a bit nifty, then uninstall to save space on your hard drive. The only way this game can be captivating enough for you to play more than 30 minutes is if you have an extreme fascination with how you put together a firearm.

I remember at first picking this up on a whim, doing a couple guns, then putting it down for a long while and not really seeing the point. A few months later I decided to pick it up again and put some actual effort into bringing down my times and working on expanding my view of the map, and that was when I got hooked. The first time I managed to take first place on the daily leaderboards was a great feeling, and soon I started to get a feel for the general patterns of the mechanisms, like how similar the CZ-75 and Jericho pistols were internally, which helped decrease my times on both guns as I learned them. I learned that the Colt Walker is easy to take apart quickly, and whoever made the MG 34 can go to hell. Each gun had their own similarities and differences that were fun to figure out and optimize for the best times. Eventually I completed the whole map that could be done without paying (and I even got a couple of the premium guns from credits earned being the champion on different guns).
Anyway, now that I've rambled for a bit, the point I'm making is that this is a fairly satisfying F2P experience. You don't really need to put in any money to enjoy yourself, and frankly the real money options seem to not have the greatest value. Just expect to log in once every hour or so and learn every gun on the map so you can do the quizzes. You should be able to manage at least 3,000 experience every time once you learn them, and depending on how actively you want to log in and do the quizzes, can rack up enough virtual currency to unlock a gun or two every day. It'll probably take you a month or two to unlock everything, and keep in mind you can buy things that are locked behind premium guns through the catalog at an increased price. If you're good enough to earn credits to buy some of those guns, strategically pick the SVD first to maximize the amount of stuff hidden being uncovered if you want to lower the cost.
In summary, for the price of free this game is worth your attention if you like challenging the leaderboards and don't mind investing some time in the quiz system to get the currency to buy guns. It probably helps if you like guns too.
I feel it's worth noting that virtually every single gun added to the game since I originally wrote this review has required premium currency to purchase. Whereas before you could own nearly every single gun in the game without paying a cent, and good play could earn you a couple more of the paid guns for free, now such a large portion of the guns require premium currency that it's forced me to revise my assessment somewhat.
There's still a hundred or so free guns that I expect will remain free, but once you've burned through those, don't expect to be able to continue to enjoy the game as a free player. Of course, you can always go back to guns you do own to refine your times, but there will eventually come a point at which you've done about as much repetition on the same guns as you care to. My suggestion would be to play through as much as you can as a free player (which is still a fair amount of content), then decide if you want to put money into the game. If you do, wait for the
to go on sale. It'll be more economical in the long run than trying to buy each gun as they come out. You could spend $10 to get the 100 credit pack and not be able to buy all the premium guns available
. So if you can find the lifetime access on sale for 50% off or more (currently retails for $50), that's probably a good deal if you intend to put serious time into the game.

Having played the previous iterations of the Neptunia series, trying out the latest entry was something I looked forward to a good deal. The franchise returns yet again at full power. Detailed and very polished art, a pleasing and relatively varied soundtrack as well as cute and funny characters. These are things that Neptunia has always had in spades and the bar was raised even further here.
This time around some changes were made to the series' gameplay. Now the amount and type of attacks you can use in a combo will depend on your equipped weapon. There was also an even bigger emphasis placed on the difference in the attack types. Rush attacks will generate by far the most energy for your special attacks bar, while power attacks produce very little energy but inflict more damage.
Unfortunately, these differences do not play out very well in practice. Although not as quickly apparent as in previous games, the best strategy in combat is still to have one or two characters constantly use rush combos to generate energy for the remainder of the party to exhaust on special attacks. Another mechanics change that Compile Heart most likely introduced to combat this was to let the player score guaranteed critical hits on their enemies if they used combo skills in a certain order, often mixing in all three types of basic attacks. The issue is that the special attack gauge is far more important than the small amount of damage you do with combos, thus making the change largely irrelevant in important fights.
The above being said, those negatives are not necessarily very detrimental to the game. The combat is still fun, if mostly a stat check. I do however want to talk about two issues that I firmly believe are more of a problem.
Firstly, the story's way of intertwining with the gameplay is too predictable. When you complete the first part of the game, you are given a choice of which goddess' story arc you would like to play next. Eventually you must go through all four of the main characters stories before being able to proceed to the story's final stage. The first goddess' story arc, whichever one you choose based on your personal preference, will most likely be enjoyable. But it is when you must play through the other three stories that predictability hampers the enjoyment. The gameplay setup is similar each time: You play with two or three characters through a number of dungeons before fighting a different variation of the same boss that showed up in the other story arcs. You inevitably end somewhere around the same level each time.
The reason it's not particularly fun to play through is that you realize the game is asking you to do the same thing four times in a row, except with slightly different characters. If you enjoy the story this might be fine, but gameplay wise I think this is something that should be strongly avoided.
As a final negative point I want to tackle in this review I would like to mention costume variety. The game's primary characters have a number of equippable costumes. But the actual amount of different clothing designs are staggeringly few. On display are simple recolours and copies of outfits that appeared many times already previously in the series. There's very little new content in this area which is a big disappointment. The potential for wacky, cute or interesting costumes is a good fit with the Neptunia universe and it is a shame to not see that realized as well as it could be.
I understand that I have mostly focused on what I find negative as that is my tendency. However I still very much recommend the game, perhaps especially so to newcomers. In terms of graphics, soundtrack, dungeon variety and gameplay no other game in the series has managed better than this one.

Toe be completely honest, as much as I love NepNep, I can't be bothered to really appreciate what is quintessentially another Victory Re:Make.
I'll admit, I never got through the original HDN back on the PS3 because of it's myriad of both optimization issues, and will agree on at least one factoid: It's come far, in terms of technical polish.
Sure, it's better than Re;Birth 3, 2, and 1 combined and it definitely feels "polished" for what it's worth, but it still doesn't account for the fact that it's literally like looking at a photograph of it's past self, smiling a bit at the fond memories, and then watching something you used to really enjoy suddenly fill you an odd feeling of disappointment, because it didn't live up to your expectations.
But anyways, onto the game features:
What can I say: It's Nep at it's...finest?
Featuring the same combat system you've seen over...
And over...
And over...
And over... again.
Now with sparklier forms, flashier moves, same-ish meta moeshit humor, and a new cast of characters that you can add to your ever growing arsenal of Nep crew:
It's the perfect game for people who don't mind shilling out endless dollars at devs who lack any sort of creative direction, and will probably ride this series's concept to the very dirt it started from because they couldn't be bothered to try something experimentally different for their mainstay series.
We have spin-off games whose production value range from ♥♥♥♥♥♥ - Semi-♥♥♥♥♥♥, whom only die-hard fans of the series could really appreciate.
In short. Megadimension was a chance for the Devs to bring something fresh and new to the main-series table... yet they failed miserably.
My hope is that Four Goddesses Online will be willing to brave in a new direction.
I'm sorry Nep, I've failed you.
But you failed me harder.

Deus Ex: HR is the first game where I've really felt like there were 10 different ways to achieve every objective. On my second playthrough it really hit me that you can really go the while game without an ounce of violence, without even being seen. Or by killing every single person. Or anywhere in between. It's just as satisfying blowing everyone up as it is watching your opponents through the walls, tracking their patterns, and running through them as a ghost.
But a game with so many options that it feels real has a few problems you have to justify with video game logic. Lots of air ducts with no security. The individual enemy AI seems fine, but why doesn't one guard notice when the other three have disappeared, or become suspicious of a gun lying on the ground. There is no place in the game with a stationary guard that needs to be distracted; every single one of them will eventually walk away, leaving an entrance or exit vulnerable. (At least on normal difficulty this was the case.)
There is also the problem of the big, dumb boss fights, which felt out of place with the rest of the game. I guess I just wanted more variety from them, save for the final boss which was interesting and fun.
But overall I greatly enjoyed this game. It has a somewhat open world, but without any sandbox elements. The character progression was great, allowing you to mould Adam to your specific playstyle, including options for combat, stealth, agility, hacking, even for shaping conversations,. The writing and voice-acting are both top-notch. The plot is interesting and throws a lot of surprises at you. A definite reccomend.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
I've only scratched the surface with the first hour of the game, but I can already see it's my kind of thing.
With the main Earth fleet out of action, your tiny force must defend a valuable space station while also answering distress calls from civilian colonies in the area, in a sector of space teeming with hostile aliens and pirates.  Hand pick your officers and build a fleet as quickly as you can - the aliens aren't going to wait for you to come to them.
Several different races and factions are out there - you may be able to negotiate with some, but violent conflict is often inevitable.
Combat starts out pretty simple, but has the potential to blossom into a complex web of status effects, vulnerabilities, and exploitations.  Even very straightforward fights require you to pay attention and coordinate your attacks.
Already a good game and will only get better through Early Access feedback.  Give it a spin.

Short answer; no.
Is it any good? Short answer; Of course.
Here's what I have to say about this new Doom game.
The graphics and textures are just all right.
The new weapons are honestly, worse than the original ones, especially the pistol, I don't like it at all.
The shotguns are the only weapon that are good in my opinion.
But you can use original Doom first-person mode (weapon in front of you) which is way better than the normal thing but that's my opinion.

Why some of them have shields? Is it me or it takes more bullets to kill them? Music is great, that's all what I have to say about that.
Multiplayer? Honestly, I don't care about it, if it were more of a Quake III or Unreal Tournament multiplayer with bots, then I would probably love it, but it's not the case, they shouldn't have made a multiplayer gamemode, instead, they should have made more content for the single-player such as new emies, new weapons, etc...
Well, If it was just of the campaign and the multiplayer, I would honestly think that this game would not be worth the 30$+ I paid for this game but... the snapmap probably makes it the game of the year.
Wolfenstein levels? Check!
Oriignal Doom levels? Check!
Original Doom 64 levels? Check!

Doom is a great game! Definitely the best shooter I've played in the last few years.
Now, take this as a warning, if you really enjoyed the new style of Doom 3, you might be disappointed or not like this one at all.
This version of Doom drops the slow, more story driven, horror-esq gameplay of Doom 3 for a fast paced, action based one that reminds me a lot of the old school shooters. You move really fast, enemies shoot projectiles that can be dodged, and you're rewarded for your quick reflexes. You have really big maps to explore, even though your objectives are pretty simple like, "Grab the yellow and blue key cards to progress", "Kill everything to progress", "Destroy gore nests and kill enemies" with an occasional boss and mini boss fights, and some dialogue progressing the story here and there. The game combines old school mechanics with modern graphics, upgrade systems and features. It adds a "glory kill" feature, that allows you to execute a sunned enemy. You'll do this a lot as they're more likely to drop health pick ups when you do it.
"Wow that sounds boring" One might say. It does sound boring, and had it been any other game I think it would be boring. Doom stays fresh with a lot of exploration, a huge arsenal of weapons, most having two upgrades that completely changes how they function and adds a new depth to the gameplay. There's also upgrades for your power armor that you can search, some including better map tracking, shorter cooldown for grenades, switching guns quicker to make the gameplay even faster, reducing enviromental damage, among others. Each map also has challenges that award you with an upgrade point, rune trials which are also upgrades for your character, including glory kills dropping armor pick ups along with health, a better ammo auto pick up. If you upgrade those runes by using it, they can unlock new features such as dropping BFG ammo from normal demons. You can also find argent cells to upgrade your health/ammo/armor.
The exploration consists of:
* Praetor Tokens to upgrade your armor
* Argent Cells to upgrade your character
* Field Drones to buy upgrade for your weapons, most can have 2 upgrades
* Super Health/Armor (Maxes yours to 200/200 regardless of your upgrade level)
* Toy Marines (Unlocks enemy models for you to inspect)
* Classic Doom Maps on each stage. Nuff said, really cool and most of them are very well hidden.
The weapons are:
Shotgun
Heavy Rifle
Plasma Rifle
Rocket Launcher
Chain Gun
Gauss Rifle
***Special: BFG, Super Shotgun, Chainsaw, Pistol
Normal weapons can have two types of alternate fire upgrades for your right click, such as the heavy rifle firing mini missiles. The Plasma rifle overheating and shooting a blast of energy at max heat. Etc. After all upgrades for one alternate fire is completed, you get a challenge like "Kill x number of Summoners with the alternate fire" Then you unlock a super upgrade like the plasma rifle overheating on its own so you can always use the charged blast.
Special weapons have only one tree of upgrades, or none, and could use some type of special ammo. Chainsaw uses fuel charges that deplete based on how strong the enemy is, but enemies killed by the chainsaw always drops bullets for the other guns.
Doom's classic enemies are back and my god, it's so cool to see them with modern graphics. It's really awesome. The boss fights are very well done, even though they are short and the spacing between them is kinda funky (all three are closer to the end of the game).
I feel like the Multiplayer and the Snapmap features are underappreciated. The singleplayer campaign is extremely fun with a good 12 hours of content, which you'll really want to replay as soon as you're done in order to get all secrets. It is so well done that I feel the game could have been single player only, but they still added a multiplayer and a map creator on top of that.
Graphically  the game is very pretty and well optimized. I ran it at 1080p, Nightmare settings with a GTX 1060 6GB and it almost never dropped below the 60 mark. 60fps in a game like this is crucial, and it being so well optimized is an achievement. It can even run at 60fps on consoles with mediumish settings (which looks pretty good, possibly even one of the best looking 60fps titles on console). If you can run it at the Nightmare quality however, you won't be disappointed in the looks. Great textures, the spark particles, the gore, everything is gorgeous. Even when you're zipping around shooting non-stop.
The story feels like a reboot but not really. It's kinda hard to understand what they were really going for. It's not a bad story though.

With all that being said, pros and cons -
Pros:
+ Gameplay is so much fun.
+ Big maps, lots of exploring and upgrading to do.
+ The arsenal is amazing.
+ Glory Kills are a lot of fun.
+ Great Boss fights.
+ Amazing Graphics + Performance.
+ Awesome level design.
+ Snap Maps.
+ Multiplayer.
Cons:
- A couple of bugs which includes falling through the floor when executing an enemy on a specific staircase, nothing major.
- Awkward spacing towards the bosses. Would rather have one of those bosses earlier in the game.
- The game drags a little towards the end.
- Might be a bit repetitive depending on the type of player you are.
- The Download. Seriously. I had to download about 115GBs for this game, and that even on a good Brazilian internet takes an entire week.
Aside from the download simulator and those minor problems, the game is very, very good. Not only one of the best shooters of late, it's also my favorite game of 2016. I kinda feel bad now for not playing it back then. The game is an easy
for me.

So I just finally tried out this game, I loved the first and second on xbox and was very dissapointed when I saw that 3 and 4 had so much negative feedback, especially 4. While on sale I figured I would try out 3 which had better reviews and I have not been dissapointed! Tons of zombies, tons of weapons, a few gameplay modes to cater to different playstyles.
Some things are simplified in this game like combo weapons. You only need to make any combo once and you can spawn the weapon or vehicle in any safehouse, but you also get limited spawn points at every safehouse, and you need to let them recharge once you use it up. Bigger combos take up more points so you can only spawn 2 super combo weapons or 4 regular, or 8 random items to craft yourself. Personally I don't mind this, it makes it simple to arm yourself and any followers. It makes things easier but you also can't just keep spawning OP weapons indefinitely, so there is still reason to craft.
This game lets you have up to 5 permanent followers which you unlock through sidequests, once you complete a quest that rewards a follower you can then view their stats and spawn them in any safehouse. Some quests also make people follow you so you can have more then 5 at some points. It's fun watching them all cram into a van to drive off and go on a zombie rampage. It's also fun choosing what weapons you give them, they can't use some of the more OP combo weapons but you can still give them all sorts of melee and ranged goodies. My personal favorites are light sabers and flaming swords but some guns are nice too. Their weapons last longer then yours but still break eventually so you have to keep them armed. You also get 3 commands for followers, follow attack and scavenge. That makes it easy to keep them all healthy which is really nice, manually feeding them all to keep their health up would be a pain but they can heal themselves while scavenging.
I am only partway through the story so far but I have enjoyed it, watching the main guy in cutscenes with whatever outfit you give him can be hilarious. The Psycho's are also pretty challenging for the most part, though some OP weapons can make them a lot easier especially with plenty of followers and or some friends. Which brings me to the online, I have only played online a bit but it is pretty nice. People can actually randomly join your game at any point, I had a few people spawn to help me with some missions. Sometimes they go off and do their own thing other times they follow you around and help.
All in all this game has a solid amount of features, enough that it should take at least a few playthroughs to collect everything, even with the longer timed game mode. Some of the weapons are a lot of fun to use and there are huge swarms of zombies waiting to be obliterated. Leveling up can be very fast if you grind zombies with combo weapons and complete missions/ challenges, which is nice as some perks from leveling include more inventory space, better weapon durability/ damage, more XP(PP), more followers, and more HP which makes things a lot easier.

Summary: I love the thing, and own two of them. It takes some getting used to, but has allowed me to enjoy non-controller supporting games I wouldn't be able to otherwise. Great UI, great support with new features, decent build quality and reasonable ergonomics.
Full Review: Unlike my Xbox controller I don't have over 10k hours of experience so starting out is like learning to walk again (as such do not start with FPS's - wait until you've gotten partially used to the controller's ergonomics). After putting in 200 hours in a variety of games including XCOM 2, Pillars of Eternity and the Mass Effect series (via Origin) I'm starting to really enjoy it. The UI is intuitive and allows for ludicrous granularity in mapping features to the controller. Literally every input can be configured for multiple context dependent inputs in ways that can take some awkward KB controls and make them easier to execute (i.e., modifying the joystick to mimic WASD but also to recognize walk vs. run depending on how far it's pressed).  The response time is very good, with no perceptable lag in the inputs.  The controller now allows you to search for configurations of games you don't own, or at least don't own on Steam, which enables you to use a variety of starting points for your configuration.  The fact that it works with non-Steam games as well (with a little extra work) is awesome.
Ergonomically the controller feels comfortable in my hands, although the shoulder buttons are slightly too tight (more on this later).  In terms of accuracy of motion, once you get about 5-10 hours in the touch pads start to be very intuitive.  It takes a bit longer to get used to the button placement on the internal position of the controller (vs the PS4 or Xbox controllers).  For games requiring a fast response (FPS/TPS) the track pads can be set to enable rapid aiming with added precision available via the internal gyroscope. I recommend Youtube videos from Gamer Muscle and Woodsie, along with the PC gamer article for advice on how to configure the controller in a way that's best for you.
Personally, I'm way more accurate with this controller that I was on my Xbox 360, and approaching how good I ever was with a mouse. The grips are awesome - every controller should be required to have them going forward.
That being said, the build quality could use some improvement. First, as mentioned previously the shoulder buttons are a bit tight.  Initially I felt the track pad buttons were too, but either they've loosened up or I no longer perceive this as a fault.  Also, the battery compartment is REALLY tight with some battery types which can make changing them a chore. Finally, although I love the build material on the joystick (uses a similar cap on the stick to the PS4 but with a texture but with a textured edge I would prefer a slightly longer stick with a concave top (consistent with the Xbox One and PS4 tops).  The good news is that Valve published the 3D images of all the parts and I'm in the process of designing a replacement part for 3D printing.
Long story short; if you're like me and either cannot or prefer not to use a keyboard and mouse, the Steam controller is more precise than any other PC controller.

Updated review after I finally received my replacement controller after a failure of the first one.
A very good controller that delivers on close to all of its rivals strengths (with the exception of any kind of d-pad, making it a subpar controller for games that rely on it), while having a few strengths of its own that really set it appart as a superior option.
The trackpads are an excellent alternative to joysticks, and even a superior one after a time getting used to them and understanding what can be done with it. The right trackpad has been advertized heavily for its potential as a mean of controlling camera movements and aiming, but the left trackpad might be an even better option than a joystick for movements, properly configured. It's highly customizable, you got more ground to play with than with a joystick, and it's much more comfortable to use it while clicking than a regular joystick.
The rear buttons are another very nice addition. That's two extra buttons you can use without putting your thumb off the right trackpad, giving you more control and flexibility in the lot of games that rely heavily on camera control and/or aiming.
The Steam Controller also shines thanks to its software, which gives you unprecedented customization options! And you don't have to spend hours creating your perfect config for each game, as you can just download and experiment with configs from the always growing community. The impressive software is another reason why this controller shines so much over its rivals, although this asset will soon be shared with them all thanks to Valve's benevolent effort of opening its use to other popular controllers, starting with the DS4.
It is not to say that this controller is not perfectible. A D-Pad is dearly missed for some games, while the left trackpad and left joystick might be a bit redundant, as the former can do pretty much everything the latter can, and then some. Also, the carvings in the left trackpad are not doing anything for me, they might as well not exist at all as it currently is.
Overall, I highly recommend this controller, and urge players who use it not to hesitate and experiment a lot with it. Getting out of your comfort zone might be unsettling and annoying at first, but in the long run, it's for the best.

Scratches that Dungeon Keeper itch quite nicely. Give this a try if you liked the original Dungeon Keeper. It's kind of a strange cross between Warcraft 3 and DK. You build a dungeon with the goal of destroying the heroes of the land, but you can also send your monsters topside and it turns into an RTS-lite where you can go around killing creeps for EXP and a currency called "evilness". I'm about halfway through the campaign which is quite enjoyable so far and plays out a lot like Blizzard's RTS games where each map has a gimmick and you're given new units and rooms that you can use to overcome the gimmick. You can also play through the entire thing in 2 player co-op which is cool.

Those who played Dungeons 2 will be disappointed in unit variety (no more upgrades for Nagas and absence of trolls). However, this is somewhat offset with the good ol torture system seen in Dungeon Keeper games. Factions from the previous game are combined into one here (so you can go crazy with unit compositions like Demon + Undead etc).
Campaign is long and we're talking about 20 missions. Be warned though, if you're OCD like me, each mission can take 2-3 hours for about 16 or so missions. The dialogue is also nonsensical and cheesy but charming in its own way. Those who played Dungeons 2 will be pleased to know the humor is the same but ramped up to eleven.

Having come to this game as a veteran of both Dungeon Keeper and War for the Overworld, I was at first quite pleased to find a similar game.  Unfortunately my pleasure quickly ebbed when I began to play the campaign for Dungeons 3.
The storyline and humor are clearly meant for children only, which comes as a grave dissappointment to a fan who had expected the dark humor of similar games in this genre.  What's more, there is a LOT of this poor quality storyline and narration jam packed into every campaign scenario.  It quickly causes the campaign to become unplayable simply because it's not worth it to sit through all the awful jokes and crummy voice acting.
The game itself is passable.  You will find all the things you would expect from something in this genre:  workers, grunts, demons, traps, and over-zealous heroes to kill.  Unfortunately there is no option to possess your soldiers, a feature I've long considered to be a distinguishing mark for this type of game.  Control of your warriors on the overworld map is done in the more direct fashion seen in games like Starcraft and Warcraft rather than by rally flags.  Control in the underworld is managed through relocating soldiers using the hand of evil, and by assigning monsters as guards in guardrooms.  The graphics are very dated, likely intentionally reminiscent of Warcraft III.
Overall not worth the rather hefty price tag.  If we ignore the horrible campaign and just focus on the game itself, I would price it as an indie title perhaps around $15.

Bully: Scholarship Edition is a Rockstar Games production, which originally was released for the Playstation 2 in 2006, and for the PC in 2008. You play in third-person as Jimmy Hopkins, a scrappy, teenager who attends Bullworth Academy, a school of bullies. You join and fight for different groups such as; Jocks, Preppies, and Nerds, and complete missions and objectives  to help bring peace to the various factions within the school, as well as the town of Bullworth itself. The story is interesting and portrays Jimmy as a protagonist and at times antagonist as well. Bullworth is a fictional town, which is supposed to exist somewhere in the Rockstar created Grand Theft Auto Universe.
The game comes with a single player mode, competitive multiplayer, as well as various mini-games. The Scholarship Edition uses a newer game engine than the original, and feels a lot like a GTA game at times. Graphically speaking, it is a 2008 game, so it's 8-years-old right now, and it looks like it, but it is still fun to play. The PC port feels different than the original PS2 version, and seems a little off, but that could just be because of the different engine used on the port. It's still a fun game and if you enjoyed the original, you should enjoy the PC Port as well.

In rough terms, MWO is Team Fortress crossed with Arma with giant robots. There are 4 classes of mechs, light, medium, heavy, and assault. Light mechs have little armor and are like the annoying, nimble spy. Mediums and heavies are slower, have more armor and weapons, and are like the soldier. Assaults are slow, lumbering, and hightly armed like the Heavy. Basically the slower a mech moves the more armor and weapons it can have.
It plays like Arma. It's highly beneficial to move as a team and use tactics. Unless you're playing a light mech its hard to bunny hop your way out of trouble, so you must be decisive and deliberate. Mechs (other than lights) move at a slower pace than most FPS games, but I wouldn't say the game play is dull or slow. When you're in a brawl it is intense.
The progression system is grindy. To increase a mechs power you have to level up 3 variant mechs of the same chassis to master it. Then you have level up 6 more to unlock elite skills. Now you have mastered one weight class of mech and have to level up 27 more mechs. The problem is you probably don't want most of these mechs so it becomes a chore.
The payment model of the game is likely responsible for some of the lack of fun in the progression system. It should have been either a flat purchase of $60 or charge a monthly access fee. They could learn a lot from Blizzard games like Diablo III or Heroes of the Storm. There is also a purchasable in-game currency called MC which is anti-consumer because you always have to buy more of it than what you need and it obfuscates what things actually cost.
The game is stable and I don't have crash, lag, or connection issues.
The graphics are getting dated. The game needs an update to make the mechs and environments more detailed and brighter. Mechs don't feel large. The MSAA in the game is very taxing even on my NVidia 780. I just barely get 60fps when MSAA is enabled.
Despite my gripes, the game is a lot of fun. I recommend it with the caveat that you need to be willing to spend money on premium time to reduce the grind. I couldn't imagine playing it without the 50% C-Bill/XP bonus. Progression would be unacceptably slow.

I want to like this game, but I can't. The setting is lovely. The mechanics are lovely. The exploration is lovely. The levels are lovely. The controls are lovely. The first ten hours are also lovely. Wonderful stuff, very well made, please let's have more of that.
Unfortunately, it's what in between that's rotten.
After the first six or so hours, the game starts slowing down until it feels like a glorified boss rush: really long boss fights, one right after the other, each boss getting harder much faster than you can improve as a player. Worse, they're not necessarily hard because they are HARD, they are hard because every boss has eleventy bajillion hitpoints, and each subsequent boss has that much more. The difficulty curve seems to be out of control.
This is not the kind of hard that is fun -- not for me, anyway. Fun hard is nailing a really hard 10 second long level in Super Meat Boy. Tough as nails, but it's 10 seconds. "Can you execute flawlessly for even just 10 seconds? How hard can it be?", SMB taunts you. Fifty tries later, you finally deliver.
Rabi Ribi is more like "final boss on hard is 15 minutes long," quoting another commenter who no doubt knows everything about reverse wall jump ground smashed zero range double charged rainbow attacks of doom. Fifty times ten seconds later, you're probably still in your second try.
So each boss takes a bunch of tries to nail, and maybe you didn't work twelve hours today and you have the mental fortitude to go do just that. But as you go through this necessary learning process, the game grows increasingly desperate with you. "Go buy items," it suggests. "Use your invincibility orbs," it begs. "Oh my god please forgive me and take those free buffs," it cries, knowing full well what it has done.
In a way, it reminds me favourably of One Way Heroics, which also tried to cheer you on and give you helpful advice after every run, while celebrating every single thing you did right. On the other hand, it also misses the point spectacularly.
I don't know about you, but to me, personally, a fifteen minute endurance test is not fun. You can accept the buffs on your third death in a row, but that's not fun. You can drop to the lowest difficulty level, but that's not fun. You can backtrack to buy health recovery items and some timed buffs before every boss fight, but that's not fun. There are a few good spots to grind EN to afford all that, but that's not fun. It's just doesn't feel right, and it is just not fun.
You could give me a mode where I can one-shot all bosses, and guess what? It would just not be fun.
No amount of aids dispels the nagging feeling in the back of your head that there will be a time when you'll have taken all of those aids, and you still won't be able to make it, because the developer put one zero too many in a file somewhere, and that'll probably be it.
While I should be careful about what I wish for, I'd much rather be playing much harder bosses with one tenth or less of the health each.

I first found out about the game when I saw a vod of Dodger playing it and figured it seemed kinda fun. Platformers and bullet hell titles aren't usually my jam, but even despite that, it seemed like an interesting experience.
So, I've played it for around thirteen hours at this point. The game? It turned out to be not only that, but an absolutely brilliant time.
First and foremost, it's a platformer, so how's the platforming? To me, it's feels solid and responsive. I've had no issues with it what's-so-ever. Even the occasional Metroidvania thing with requiring power-ups didn't really annoy me.
The combat system feels just as tight and has a decent bit of variety of spells and the sort.
The boss fights, the ones that I've faced up until this point, despite being bad at bullet hell, I'd never felt like they were unfair or unwinnable...and, I always felt like I had the option of trying again and getting good or backing out and seeking some power-ups to assist with the fight.
Another noteworthy thing is how the game (mostly) doesn't restrict you from picking what order you do things in. You can pick what order you meet the other characters in, you can even skip things. If you want some examples, just check some of the achievements. If experiences are anything to judge by, I'm interested in playing through again once I finish just to see how things will be different.
Now, if I did have any complaints, it's worth mentioning that the story basically pants. Still, the art is fantastic, the music is enjoyable, the characters are silly and fun, and considering everything else about the game that I've already mentioned...even if story is not great, I'd still strongly recommend the title. If you're already familiar with the franchise, I'll take you through what's so different about this one that I like so much;
More characters! About 10 of them, of which all are likeable, perfectly realized, and relevant to the story. Uzume quickly became one of my favorite characters in the franchise and she's just awesome. Both new and returning characters are given lots of time to (exclusively) interact with one other and the relationships between them are clearly defined aside from ones I made up myself via Lily Rank. All characters are humanized past their stereotypes just enough and nobody takes a backseat to the main plot. Voice acting is great on everyone's part (especially Uzume), and they're all cute in their own ways,
The story takes place throughout 3 dimensions and is divided into segments with an underlying plot that ultimately connects everything together. The story also maintains a good sense of urgency whenever it's relevant and does something pretty awesome (twice) into the game where it branches out as multiple events occur at the same time, and you get to see everyone doing their own thing i.e. contributing in their own ways. It keeps things current, interesting, and doesn't allow for as much downtime as the previous games.
Another thing about the story is that it feels more personal, and I can't get into that without spoiling the underlying plot. A lot of people may disagree with me on this, but the main villain is well developed as a character (especially compared to previous games) and makes way for a few touching and appropriately hilarious moments towards the story's last act. It's still severely flawed in the way that it's cheesy with many very arbitrary plot conveniences and seemingly too crazy ideas, but
. Sue me.
Speaking of previous games, this is pretty disconnected apart from the many returning characters, but the game expects you know them already so it still doesn't really make for a good entry point to the series. There's no mention of the Ultradimension, nor the remains of both ASIC and the Seven Sages, so don't expect to see Peashy, Rei, Pururu or CFW Magic here. The game has better sprites (and backgrounds) and visual fidelity in dungeons, though I did experience framerate drops in world maps. It has better balance between random/irrelevant and contextual humor, and is still endlessly garnished with 4th wall breaking,
, and pop culture references as well as subtle commentary about the gaming industry,
Gameplay is a bit better I guess(?), I never really liked the dungeon crawling in the first place. I like the new investment system, the Sharing Field battles, formation skills, scouting system and the especially
fast-forward button for battles (and almost everything else really). Grinding in a Nep game has never been easier (still very tedious though). Anyway, they're awesome
but these mechanics feel very underutilized and I ended up not using a lot of them in the end, much like the previous games. Development is mostly unnecessary, Sharing Field is just spamming skills, disc development doesn't have enough impact, so on and so forth, and these things seem to cater to hardcore gamers--which I am not--and offers little to no incentive otherwise aside from prolonging playtime via micromanagement.
Megadimension Neptunia is a Neptunia game on every level, rest assured if you've played any of the previous ones then you know what's coming. That said, I find this one to have the most interesting story and characters, and that kept me engaged for longer in comparison. Production quality in general seems much improved but gameplay is still lacking for a filthy casual like me. Game's not revolutionary, it still cheesy, cliche'd, and very lighthearted,

Nothing has changed much. It’s still the same JRPG that got the same game systems working in the background as the Re;Birth branded titles. But there are enough changes here that seem to rebalance those systems, so much that the game as a whole resulted in being a more refined, more tactical and once again enjoyable gaming experience.
For the 4rd time you play as teenage girls having an adventure by progressing the story trough reading VN-Events, by visiting dungeons, fighting monsters and collecting items. With story being a big focus of the game again, the writers finally found the middleground between the too serious written Re;Birth2 and the over the top hilarious humour of Re;Birth3. The girls act surprisingly close to their characters this time which works in favour of story progression. Dialogs no longer sidetrack into what seemed like endlessly going on walls of texts with bad jokes.
What are the most interesting additions to the gameplay now? Stella’s Dungeon is no more. Scouts are now implemented into the maingame and can add certain bonuses to the dungeons you visit. Higher Droprate, Monster Change, more EXP, less Credits, etc. You also no longer just warp between Nations on the overworld map. Instead you have to walk along a path with random encounters between Dungeons and Points of Interest. The Investment system is a great addition too: You can upgrade each nation thus adding more items to the shops, to find additional scouts or to increase the nation’s shares.
Combat is tighter than ever! Bye bye 9999 damage! The Guard Break System got removed. Combos now consist of Standard, Power and Rush attacks that activate combo bonuses when specific criteria are met, like “didn’t used power”, “last attack was rush” and so on. Each weapon starts out with one of those three attack types and combos need to be set up according to their combo bonuses for maximum damage effect. There is also a higher priority on items now because status effects occur more frequently.
What’s not so good about the game? No NewGame+ or Endgame content! Re;Birth3 had up to 2 hours more VN-events to watch and more dungeons with worthwhile loot to offer. Victory II does not. You can level up your characters to level 999 again but with only a single mob available to you that gives 10million EXP. To reach the golden 999 the game requires you to fight this single mob over 5000 times or more. Not an elegant solution.
The character DLCs are great because they add new characters with their very own VN-Events and story. The downside is that those characters are so overpowered that they break the tight balance of the game. My advice, use them in NewGame+. Weapon and Item DLCs include even more content to break the balance while Nightwear and Bikini DLC just add cosmetic changes.
Victory II is a tight game, even more so without the use of DLCs. The characters are loveable and the humour marvelous. Expect lots of anime tropes and popculture references. Don’t regret buying if you love anime, JRPG’s or cute girls doing cute things.

Deus Ex HR is personally one of my favourite games of all time, top 10 at least. Like the original Deus Ex, it's very open world before open world games became all the rage. Although the game is still driven by quests, you are given alot of latitude in how you do them. You can be mega sneaky, or run and gun, or whatever.
I thought that the story was particuarly well done. You are Adam Jenson, an ex-cop who was brought back to life with cybernetics (ever seen this plot before? =) and now works for the people who designed the augmentations that saved him.
As with many games of this genre, your past comes back to haunt you and everything is not what it seems, etc.
The story is very long, it took me about 38 hours on easy mode (almost certainly take longer on hard mode). however, I personally loved playing it.
I've always been a big fan of the cyberpunk genre and Deus Ex HR delivers in spades, with tons of augmentations you can get (some of them rather useless imho, but I suppose it all depends on your playstyle.)
The plot is long and involved and eventually winds up with you having to decide the future of humanity (something else common in games I have noticed.. =)
I personally thought the graphics, and especially the cutscenes were great, if you have a powerful enough computer, playing it in full 1080 is beautiful.
I really can't reccommend this game highly enough, especially now that they have incorperated the DLC. My only niggle was with the inventory, which is kind of limited, but then I suppose that is sort of realistic.
There are lots of weapons in the game, some great, some useless without augs, but as I said above, because it's an open world game, you get the benefit of choice.
The characters are well written and the voice acting is really good, although you may find that the fact that Jenson has only one kind of voice (deep and husky, sort of menacing, like some action movie stars.. =) gets a bit samey after a while.
Still the only things I can fault in this game are very small things that are really just a matter of personal taste.
Overall, if you like cyberpunk and you like FPS and stealth, then grab this game.
