Buy the game if you enjoy fighting the same thing over and over and over again with the same abilities and strategies every fight.
The enemies simply get larger and gain more HP so you just have to keep doing the same thing over and over for longer as time progresses!
EDIT: You will spend the great majority of your time fighting the enemy by inflicting status effects and then using a different ability that exposes that status effect for extra damage. You then repeat this process many times until you win.
There are other aspects to the game beyond the combat, but due to the nature of the alien enemy, they will spawn endlessly from their spires (spawn points) until you reach a certain research level (tier 3 I presume, I haven't actually got there yet).
During that time in which you cannot attack their spires from which they spawn, you will have to deal with endless waves of enemies that progressively get larger and stronger as I said above. You have to progress in tech and build larger ships to combat these stronger aliens but it doesn't feel like I'm making progress, I'm constantly trailing the enemy in an attempt to keep up. I never have the advantage.
There will times when your resource colonies fall before you have a reasonable chance to save them. Mostly they don't, but I have had it happen a couple times already. This is frustrating but what's worse is that you cannot restart colonies in ruins(from what I'm able to see), so once they are gone, that's it. This would be a good thing to change if you were going to change something.
You do not get a very high pool of officers to use in the game. You can only reasonably run 1 fleet of 3 ships for most of the time you're playing. Researching later technologies and building the appropriate buildings within the station increases the amount of officers you can have, but it's very slow. As it is now, I'm struggling to use my meager one full fleet of ships trying to do everything while 2 other officers sit at the station doing nothing but short supply runs because you can't reliably combat anything without a full fleet.
Exploring the H-6 Station requires having other characters on the station doing nothing in order to deal with combat situations that arise. Sending a character to explore without Officer support is extremely risky. The "Red Shirts" that you can recruit to help you during on station combat when no other officer characters are around have the most basic abilities and die extremely quickly. They shouldn't even exist really. Most of the enemies you encounter during on station combat have AoE abilities and kill these characters in the first round. Exploring the station requires multiple officers.
The research system is fairly basic as well. You don't wait for research to occur over time, you simply purchase the technology out right. As long as you have the materials and dark matter (the game currencies), you can purchase and use any technology right away. The fact that laboratory type buildings don't exist on the station is a massive missed opportunity. Especially given the nature of the story within the game. I honestly can't believe it.

I'm another original Kickstarter backer and glad I am now playing this game.
Everything, from the start of the Kickstarter to the entry into Early Release, was communicated to backers and I feel great that I was part of this game.  The developers are clearly 'on their game' with their game; so to say and the game runs and feels great!
They've really nailed the 'rogue'like' feeling with the random events and combat to the management of precious resources, which can make or break your run.  Both ship combat as well ground combat (Blarg!) work well and really test your meddle.  A player who simply takes the easy road will NOT become victorious and it really takes quite a bit of decision to leave your first officer in a new space or collect the space algae which could overtake the entire system!  It's glorious the  possible decisions and randomness I've found so far and I love it!
I've played it now just under 6h on this  Early Release version and it's getting better every iteration.  I cannot recommend more Massive Damage and their commitment to the project.
Great job Massive Damage and can't wait to see what the future brings.  Currently riding strong on Day 139 now and fully upgraded ships (Tact & Engi) and working on my Science vessel now!
[Edit 2] I wanted to add this so no one would be mistaken on what I've been told is a 'fanboi' review.  Some of the combat, early on, is repetative.  This is because of not only being EA and they have stated they are working on mixing it up more but as well the story itself works towards this reason.  The main enemies, which people rightfully state get boring to kill, are similar to a locust plague or something that is trying to take over and consume the entire galaxy.  Because of this plotline, of course there are going to be similar battles and until you unlock higher tier ships and powers (you get more as your ships and pilots advance) you do tend to use the most resourceful 'combo' of powers/attacks.  It doesn't mean they always work as I lost a Legendary captain on day 250 on seemingly 'easy' enemies because of the RNG of getting hit, evading, dmg rolls, etc.  I carelessly thought that it was going to be the same combat and it wasn't.  Because of this I lost my highest rank captain.
Again, this isn't for everyone; nothing ever is so please do not buy this on my recommendation alone.  I backed it from the start and I like what I see and I enjoy playing it.  You may too.
[Edit] Oh boy.. Days pass > harder AI.  Just rescued a named Engineer from a planet and had to fight 3 waves of ever increasing enemies.  Made it out alive by the skin of my pants but also then got randomly attacked by Space Pirates who ended up killing my Legendary Engineer! :(
Beware that you WILL lose ships, you WILL lose pilots and you'll need several fleets to engage and manage threats while gathering resources.  So much fun!
Also, it must not track time in OFFLINE mode as it shows only 1.9h but I have played more like 6-8 hours already.  A good thing is you can play in OFFLINE mode unlike some others using Steamworks.

I'm giving a review based soley on my experience in the story mode. I have played Storm games since Storm 2, excluding revolution. First off the bad, as I remember in previous games there was an option to toggle blood on and off but it seems in Storm 4 that isn't an option. This led to a really kiddie feel to the game where it felt like a PG-13 movie which hurts the storyline for someone who read the entire manga and knew what actually happened. Just like every Storm game the storyline seems to have discrepancies from the true anime and manga. Some examples of this but not all are no blood, no impalement, no severed limbs, altering scenes and not using dialogue true to canon. A big nitpick for me has to be the the fact that they animated the game's storyline with stills from the actual anime and included partial in game cellshaded animated scenes. I have no idea why they chose that art direction but to me it came off as lazy or maybe lack of resources and time, as I remember since Storm 2 every scene was in game animated. For the good, I like to say with the utmost joy that CC2 deserves an anime art award for their game because this is the best cellshading on current generation consoles and PC to date! The beauty, vibrancy, art, shadows, bloom, effects, etc are just outstanding and they have truly surpassed themselves and of course the cut-scenes and quick time also great as usual. I also really enjoyed how the main storyline had a sort of side story that branched off of the main. The fact that it was actually tied into the canon and gave a little more insight and depth into the story on an individual basis is outstanding. Now one last note and some of the personal gripes others have been having as it seems most of their problems are system or optimization wise. The game just launched so it's expected that just like most all new games that Storm 4 was going to launch with some problems. Is it a bad thing? maybe. Can it be fixed? Yes and it will with a patch and followed by an update once CC2 addresses all of the issues. It happens to all the big titles, infact even bigger titles such as GTAV, Skyrim, COD, BF4, and most all AAA games. People just have to learn to be patient and give the constructive feedback that the devs look for and not blatantly bash the game because of day one launch issues. That won't put the money back in your pocket nor will it help make the game as great as it can be if you choose to be negative rather than positive. In conclusion I have my fan boy gripes with the game as I pay attention to detail but at the same time the game is amazing, fun and still remains most of what I expected out of a Storm 4 title so I can definitely recommend this to a anyone new or wanting to get into the series.

I cannot, honestly or willingly, recommend this controller as a worthwhile product.
Below are my main gripes:
1. The controller uses AA batteries, the USB micro on the controller is data only and cannot be used to charge rechargeable batteries (you may use rechargeables if you charge them separately)
2. By default the haptic feedback on the two touchpads is horridly annoying, this can be changed but only under Big Picture Mode.
3. Changing any settings at all on the controller must be done through Big Picture Mode, this isn't a negative but it's more a pain if you want to quickly change something and aren't using Big Picture Mode. Give us a "Tool" or "Software" under the library please.
4. The battery cover / backing tray clicks horribly when trying to hold the controller, if you apply any sort of force or grip around the handle you're greeted with a tacky, clicky, noise. (Edit: These are actual rear buttons, similar to an Xbox Elite controller, personally I don't like them and they've caused more issues than they've solved for how I hold and use a typical controller)
5. There is no space within the controller to store the receiver, why? The one thing that usually gets lost or broken is receivers, even mice these days have the ability to clip the receiver to their underside so you don't lose it. And how much are you going to charge for another receiver if we do inevitably lose it?
6. The general ergonomics of the controller's handles are poor, you have to arch your thumb across to press any of the buttons and this opposite to the tried and tested methods of the Dualshock and Xbox controller. The handles slope away from your thumb, meaning you arch your thumb over to press the touchpad or buttons, where with the DS and Xbox they slope upwards and help support your hand and thumb.
7. Lack of rumble feedback of rumble motors, or any equivalent. Haptic feedback works for the touchpads and triggers but this doesn't compare to your traditional controller.
Some very slight redeeming points:
1. If you have Steam installed, using the controller in desktop mode works nicely without any configuration or fuss.
2. The controller can work without batteries if connected via USB micro to your computer, perhaps useful to those who don't stockpile AA batteries. (Why not just sell us a wired controller instead of a cheap AA battery powered controller with proprietary receiver?)
3. Makes a great throwing weapon, it's weight being heftier than that of a wired Xbox controller. (Seriously, why is this so heavy, it doesn't even have rumble motors?)

After having much trouble using a Playstation 2 controller with usb adapter and x360ce, I figured there would only be two options for playing with a gamepad on PC:

I was wrong.

I just received this yesterday, so here is a first impressions review:
It could stand to be made a bit better on the materials side, but I understand they were taking a huge leap of faith and probably figured they should not make a super solid controller that people would not even try on account of price. Still, I wish there were an elite version, that I could get in a year or so if this end up being as amazing as it seems right now.
What makes this amazing is also what probably damns it to staying a super niche product. We have been groomed to think of controllers as ready-to-use no-brainers. We want them to be standard, intuitive, and we want to leave the dev the hassle and power of deciding mapping, sensitivity, and all that. Face it, most of us never remap stuff, apart from inverting camera and aim if the game has the opposite from what our brain can handle. Steam Controller shines in that you can not only map buttons, but decide sensitivity and behaviour with a depth I honestly never considered. The problem is that you actually... have to do it. Finding a user template that sorta works will always be possible, but I get the feeling no user-made configuration will be 100% fitting without some user tweaking, and to understand what to tweak, you need tutorials and trial and error.
So... if you are the kind of nerd that likes 3-hour tutorials on how to configure stuff, then playing a new game with keyboard and mouse for two hours to get a feel for it, then spend an hour making your own controller configuration and an afternoon or two tweaking it, then this thing is an amazing toy that might bring countless hours of joy and frustration. If you want things to work out of the box, and you prefer to adapt to controls that might never feel natural to you for the sake of ease of use, then stay away from this, or try it at a friend's first.
Lucky for me, I'm the tinkery kinda nerd =)

Every lover of the 2nd Amendment Beware! This game will absorb all of your freetime!
Just kidding! Don't worry guys, although I'm on here nearly everyday, it not too addictive.
It is however a very fun and educational program about firearms, and its FREE! However, I will admit, for extreme gun gurus, this game may be dissapointing for its somewhat watered down approach to firearms dissassembly. When I got this, I was thinking "AWESOME", finally a game that will help me figure out how to dissassemble my AR without getting shot in face the with the Action Spring! However, it turns out there is no in-depth explaination of the dissassembly process for any weapon.
Actually, the game is more about raw step-by-step memorization than anything . . . . Although you will be able to see every single firearms 100% dissassembled, and learn whice pieces need to be screwed/unscrewed first, there is no explaination about the methods of dissassembly, or the purpose of each individual part, or even groups.
In other words, the game runs as simply as this. In all of the game modes (except operation and shooting range), you have a 3D model of a weapon, you wait for the computer to 'clear' the weapon by racking the action and expelling all ammunition, and then it is your job to click the pieces that are to be dissassembeled 1st, 2nd 3rd, as the computer automatically dissassembles the parts/groups, and all the way until you have a complete 3D exploded view of the weapon, and then click the pieces in backwards order.
Although there does seem to be some inconsitencies with the ordered parts in this game (on the AK-47, you must click the 'butt screws' before dismantling the wooden stock, however on the MP-5, the lower receiver just falls off magically?), this goes does serve as a great INTRODUCTION to each weapon. The operation mode allows player to watch the weapon fire with X-Ray vision, to watch the parts interact, however, there is no further explanation.
Another word. The game is FREE, therefore there are a couple draw backs. You do not have access to all the weapons at the start of the game! You have one starter gun, the AK-47, then you must master the dissassembly of this weapon to get 'XP" before unlocking more weapons! And oh, there is no list of weapons to choose from. Although weapon progressoin is not linear (there are often a couple branches to choose from), you will have to slog through some boring weapons before getting to your all-time-favorites. I will however REDEEM the developers by saying, this does force a player to actually master a weapon, and often times GO BACK to a previous weapon to re-learn and hopefully get more XP, but it can be really tedious . . . . OR you can purchase the game for $40 and have every weapon unlocked!
However, start with the free version to make sure you can handle it ;)

I have almost eight hours in my game, but I use the modified exe on PC Gaming Wiki for this game in order to play with 60 FPS and don't use Steam overlay. The game as it comes in Steam is locked to 30FPS for no reason. However, the game WILL crash often for you. It's not a good PC port in any way, but it runs alright. Keyboard controls are worthless so I use a controller (native support with prompts).
The game itself is a masterpiece as far as I'm concerned. Amazing gameplay and an immense number of things you can do to interact with and explore the world. A solid story and funny dialogue keep me engaged with missions, and the classes are great. You can fight students, lock kids in lockers, hurl eggs and firecrackers at people, grope little girls (for real), beat up your math teacher, mow lawns, tag walls with graffiti, sneak into the girl's dorm, go to an amusement park, and learn combat from a homeless guy, and all of that in the first ten minutes of the game. The map is not too large and is absolutely packed with details and interactive bits. The cliques are clearly defined and fun to interact with. And you can customize your character with haircuts and clothes options.
The PC port is a mess, and it will crash often. I can get about an hour into the game until it crashes to desktop, and since there is no autosave, you have the potential of losing hours of progress if you forget to save. Sometimes it crashes in the first five minutes of running. On some desktops, it may not run at all without compatibility mode or a modified exe. Check the PC Gaming Wiki for help with that.
I tough through it because the game is honestly amazing, but you may not want to deal with the hassle.

Pre-note: I am a person that has a very strict standard when it comes to games. Even if I like something, I don't write reviews for it as I want to enjoy it my own way. But this... this is something that any type of media consumer should really try, gamer or otherwise.
First things first. To anyone reading this, I can't emphasize this enough:
I have ran out of 2 Steam reviews' worth of characters to review this game. My whole review can be found with pastebin ID j31a9V3E
I was curious why this game isn't even half a year old but gets so much positive reception.
I dove in and now I feel like the developers deserve more than what I paid for it.
: I am currently just in chapter 4, started playing on Hard. I haven't even finished it yet and I already feel like I got my money's worth... and from what I've read, there's STILL SO MUCH MORE TO DO. It's amazing.
-There is not enough words to describe how good the Gameplay is
-The best of Metroidvania, Bullet-Hell, Platformer elements.
-You can play it like an Action RPG with the amount of customization, or like a challenging bullet hell by giving you difficulty that scales with your progress and preference
-Definitely hard, but can't stop playing it anyway. Difficulty is mostly on the bosses, and most bosses have stories behind them that make you want to defeat them despite having to retry many times.
-So many ways to play the game. You can play casually by lowering the difficulty and experience the strangely vast but uncluttered story, hardcore by raising difficulty and/or limiting items (and there are achievements for it), completionist by blowing things up randomly, for fun by doing random things and the game actually has things to explore with it, etc.
-There's so much content and yet you're never pressured for it. Find it in your own pace, or complete everything, whatever. It's your choice how you want to finish the game!
-So many things to find, but you'll never feel lost. Even if you go deeper and deeper, you never stray from your primary objective, and the game reminds you in a non-annoying fashion. You will never feel stuck because you have no idea what to do. (if you ever feel stuck, it's because you can't beat a certain boss and you need to get better or find more items)
-You can completely skip the fanservice and art-style for the gameplay. It's never shoved in your face except in parodies sequences, which actually get used as part of the plot very well
-But there's also enough story and fanservice for those that like those kinds of things.
-Character designs are not just for fanservice despite all of them being fanservice cliches. They make sense once you get to know them. Succubi are obviously half-naked, that's an easy one, but a computer geek shut-in being in jammies and wearing nothing underneath is not actually just for fanservice and is very real when you consider people's behavior when alone in their room and tinkering with their computer.
-Story has excuse-plot elements, but the presentation makes the story in no way an excuse-plot at all. Game uses the main character's human features as a plot device instead of just for the cute-inducing effect.
-Story's pacing is very good. It's simple but mysterious. Light-toned but dark enough to really amp up the feeling of conflict.
Please, PLEASE, PLEASE give this game a chance, even the slightest chance you have. I don't care if you hate any form of the first impressions, whether it be the fanservice or the art-style or the gameplay or even it being on a PC (disclaimer: I'm a Playstation guy, and I'm super stoked this is coming to the Vita/PS4 soon), this is one of the games I may actually be bold enough to recommend to anyone who thinks that they will hate this game. Like, even if I end up losing a friend as a result of playing this game, I don't think I'd have much regrets.
There is not enough words to capture how great this game is.

The one take-home message I get from playing Rabi-Ribi, is that the director absolutely understands (and loves) the best parts of the metroidvania, brawler, and bullet hell genres, and the whole of the game is built around this.
This game does the standard
part very well, with themed areas and gated interconnections. It also has all sorts of hidden passages and a couple of hidden moves, that, if you know about them, you can finish the entire game without acquiring a single ability or item. These passages and moves let you do what the game calls "sequence breaking", by accessing areas or fighting bosses you're not meant to reach yet, at least in terms of the story, to access abilities or items early. This non-linearity is very much unique to this game.
Bosses will fill the screen with brightly-colored death, but unlike regular
, you have to obey gravity this time around, so you can't just move freely around the screen. However, it's worth pointing out that the patterns are fair. For example, if you haven't acquired air jump yet, the boss will only use patterns which you can avoid with your regular jump. Of course, it will still be difficult as you don't have any room for error in timing your regular jump, but this is very much good game design.
The regular enemies, while much more predictable, are also very much aware of where they can hit you with their projectiles from. They don't have much bite initially, but on higher difficulties or on a 0% item run, you will become painfully aware of how wickedly purposeful their placements are.
If you're familiar with
like Super Smash Bros., the moves you have here are the standard suite of air jumps, air dash, wall jumps, slides etc. You unlock them incrementally, and you will need them all, both in fights to avoid the said bullets and in exploration. For attacks, you have the standing combo, uppercuts, downcuts, slide dash, mid-air attacks, and all sorts of ranged projectile attacks from dumbfire to homing to screen-filling attacks. You cannot block, but the Bunny Amulet and certain moves gives you invincibility frames that you will want to take advantage of. Customization comes in the form of badges where you can pick and choose which perk or tradeoffs you want to have, like trading mana for more HP, or nulling contact damage against bosses if you find that to be a problem.
I think the developer has absolutely nailed the pixel
on this one. He knows when and where to put in details and contrast and when to cut back, so you can see where your character is and where all the projectiles are at all times with just your peripheral vision. I cannot emphasize enough how important this is for bullet hell and how much I appreciate this clarity. Compared to other indie games with similar graphics (e.g. Freedom Planet, Bunny Must Die), your character is practically popping out of the screen. The pixel sprites are also very well done in my opinion.
The whole
thing is a running gag and is fairly arbitrary, and the story mostly just sends you to different parts of the map to recruit different bosses. The game is very much self-aware and points out that there's always an excuse for a fight before you can recruit that boss. I also didn't get the main plot arc the first time around, but it became more clear after I played the game a second time. Basically you don't play the game for the
.
A last couple of things: The game starts off with a good spread of
casual-novice-normal-hard-hell initially, with bunny extinction (BEX) and impossible difficulty unlockable. Harder difficulties mean attack patterns of greater variety, damage, and speed, bullets are denser and may linger around more, i.e. dodging becomes much more important. Easier difficulties let you carry more consumables and give you an optional buff after successive game overs. Harder difficulties are for after you have mastered the game. The
and
are unlocked on game clear, and
is unlocked after clearing hard or above. Some
change on higher difficulties, but usually it just means the character shows more skin than usual. You do have to unlock the alternate CG first before you can see them in CG mode.
If you love any of these genres, it would be a mistake to pass this game up. It thoroughly exceeded my expectations on every level.

This game is very much unlike the first game in the series, and from what I can gather--based off videos and other people's comments--is more akin with the second game in the series. You aren't building the dungeon as a way to gather heroes in to extract "soul energy" and build prestige. It's not the focus. The focus is building up an army and conquering the locals and then building up your dungeon. The game stagnates heavily if you try to go Endless, as there just isn't enough to do with heroes, and you have a limited cap to your worker and army--in terms of both numbers, their growth, and their usefulness.
On normal in an endless map, I got to a point where each wave of heroes died on the initial setup of traps I had near their one remaining entrance. There's no customizing the dungeon or 'entertaining' the heroes to have fun with being a benevolent evildoer. You're just going to murder them, nothing more. Still a good game, but I recommend getting it during a sale rather than its full price.

If you aren't familiar with the franchise there's going to be a steep learning curve. Your upper body often faces in a different direction than your movement, and your arms can swivel even further off to the side causeing new players a fair amount of disorientation. Getting used to juggling your mech's heat burden can be tricky as well. Then there's learning the maps, figuring out how to properly kit out your own mechs (once you buy them), and sometimes even mentally reverse-engineering your enemies' mechs on the fly to figure out where their weak points are.
This is a game that takes a while to get used to, expect to get mercilessly stomped your first several matches. But if you stick it out, you may find the game rewarding. It's not for everyone, but what game is? Free to play, no pay to win, most of the community is fairly helpful... It won't cost you anything to give it a try.

Do you like giant stompy robots?
Yes? Get this game.

The Good: Great Visuals, Easy to get into gameplay, Flexibility
Visually this one of the better, if not best looking BatteTech game to date. If you're a fan of BT you'll salivate over the 'mech designs. The gameplay is pretty straightforward for a FPS.  One of the best aspects of any BT game is the ability to customize your 'mech in the mechlab; in which MWO is no different. In a lot of ways, MWO is more flexible than any previous iterations. This freedom allows you to fulfill pretty much any role imaginable.
The Bad: Steep Learning Curve
This freedom comes with a steep learning curve. Finding out what works and what doesn't, can be both frustrating and expensive. Luckily there are fan-made resources available to assist in making informed builds. Maneuvering can be a bit to get used to, as the 'mechs themselves functions like tanks; turret rotation is independent of leg movement. You also must compensate for momentum and weapon travel time. The in-game tutorial is helpful in assisting new players into this system.
The Ugly: Lack of content, Lack of depth
We have 4 game modes total, all of which are different flavors of team death match. The maps are mostly lacking and repetitive. Even with this slow development, new 'mechs tend to make regular appearances. The BT universe is an expansive one and yet MWO fails to capitalize on it. If you're familiar with BT you will know that 'mechs were rarely deployed without the support of tanks, aerial and ground troops. With so much potential MWO remains to be nothing more than an mech-only arena shooter. Drops are typically won by those that maintain close proximity and focus down targets. There is no room for carefully laid plans. The Community Warfare game mode does encourages more strategy, however it is not yet fully fleshed out. I look forward to see what it becomes.
Despite what MWO lacks it is an enjoyable game that I find myself coming back to. Finding new friends that love the BT universe is an added bonus. Being a free2play game I recommend giving it a try if you like big stompy robot combat.

Best Free to Play since Planetside 2.
PROS:
* Customization (virtually limitless build options).

* Frequent updates ( updates are released on a bi-weekly schedule).
* Tutorial ( the mechwarrior academy makes the tutorial fun rather than boring. Hands on training, personal challenges, and mini games made to test your skills, almost a game in itself.)
* Gameplay ( gameplay is fun and addictive once you get into it, a really good match can leave you shaking with adrenaline).
* Dev communication ( one of my biggest pet peeves is a silent dev team, but these guys are far from silent. With command chair posts, monthly development roadmaps, and town hall meetings on  Twitch.tv I never have to guess whats next for the game).
CONS:
* Mega groups ( units with hundreds or thousands of good players that make being competitive near impossible for the small tight knit units.)
* Cheaters ( a handfull of well known units have resorted to cheating to get their name on as many planets as possible, ruining the experience for everyone else.
Overall its an extremely fun game with the best price of all.... free.

At this moment where I write the review here, I played around 11 hours and overall I think the game is pretty good. I bought it for 14,99€ or something like that in a sale and for this price it's really good. Even 29,99€ is a decent price.
Here are some points that I liked, but also disliked:
; In my opinion the story is not great, but not bad either. Here and there a little bit confusing, but overall it's a good one.
; The game looks really appealing and runs very well. Greatly optimized game.
; Sound effects are well done. The music is great as well.
; Due to the linear gameplay the world is not the biggest one, but there are definitely some things to explore!
; Don't get me wrong, the gameplay is fast and really smooth and by itself it was fun, but it's literally the same thing over and over again. There is no real variation.

This is not a full-throated recommendation. I wouldn't advise people against picking this up becuase there is a ton of fun to be had running around killing zombies, fun weapons to craft and a decent plot to plod through, but this is a mere shadow of the far superior Dead Rising 2.
Among the number of disappointments on offer here are the washed out palette, the reduced emphasis on humour and an identity-crisis in which the game just takes itself too seriously. This also extends into a lack of imagination in regard to the Psychopath boss battles, which are not terrible, but feel forced and tired in a way that permeates the rest of the game. In addition, the world map is an infuriating mess of blocked roads and dead ends, which kills the flow of the gameplay each time you feel like you're getting into a good, brain-smashing groove.
And yet, there are also vast quality-of-life upgrades. The ability to save anywhere, the ability to recreate any previously crafted weapon, and most importantly the HUGELY relaxed time constraints make it far more appealing (and less risky) to mess about and experiment with an absolutely insane amount of unique weapons and vehicles. The memorable characters of DR2 are missing (well, mostly) but I was still compelled to see it out, although it did feel a bit more of a chore towards the end.
It's also a very good-looking game if you can run it at reasonably high settings.
Overall there's no reason not to pick this up in a sale. The PC port is mostly fine now (I'm running a GTX 960 4GB and the only thing that makes it really chug is shadows), and it's always good fun to go ploughing through a horde of zombies, but make no mistake, this Dead Rising on the way down.

While I got this game on a 70% off sale, Dead Rising 3:Apocalypse Edition is definitely worth your money (assuming you LOVE the zombie game Genre AND/OR LOVED Dead Rising 1 & 2 or simply wished for a ZOMBIE themed GTA game )
Dead Rising 3 further improves the following:
*Survivors
Unlike Dead Rising 1 & 2, survivors you encounter in Dead Rising 3 are divided into 2 kinds, Stranded Survivors and Special Survivors.
-Stranded Survivors: Survivor/Survivors that will go back on their own after you "rescue" them.
-Special Survivors: Survivor that will  join you fight zombies and psychos given you accomplish their specific tasks.
Survivors no longer have to be escorted back to "safety" and Special Survivors have a "stat sheet" to them which illustrates their individual proficiency in fighting with melee or ranged weapons, toughness, running speed and ability to break away from a zombies grab.
*Combos
Weapon Combos introduced in Dead Rising 2 is further enhanced in Dead Rising 3 by adding in VEHICLE COMBOS and SUPER COMBOS on top of having over a 100 weapon combos to discover and craft.
-Vehicle Combos: While you could combine a dirt bike , paddle and chainsaws together in Dead Rising 2, what happens when you combine an ambulance and a construction dozer? Or a sports bike and a chopper? FUN FUN FUN is what!
-Super Combos: Some weapon combos don't stop at just ONE assembly, you could add another component that will FURTHER upgrade your weapon into something EXTRA gnarly (lookin at you lightningfire staff!)
*Time-based Quests:
This aspect of the game is the deciding factor of whether you'll LOVE the game or HATE it. Either way, quests have a LONGER time span now compared to the previous entries of Dead Rising.
*New Protagonist
New guy (seems to be the youngest protagonist so far), Nick Ramos is a mechanic by trade so combining weapons and vehicles makes more sense than it did on Chuck Greene (Dead Rising 2 Protagonist).  Also, on top of being the typical NICE GUY, Nick Ramos has no recollection of his youngin days and  has an odd tattoo of the number "12" on the right side of his neck, so add MYSTERIOUS into his layer of awesomeness.
Although there's more content for me to talk about,I'm going to cut this review short because I want to go back in and play some more!

This game's story feels shorter than previous storm games, but that's because of the removal of the exploration aspect, and a lot of the stand-still dialogue that filled the gaps between fights and boss battles. All of that is now part of "Adventure" mode, which i just like it was in previous games, just without the story. The "Story" mode itself is great in a  few ways, and bad in one or two ways. Let me start with the bad.
For one, we're getting about 70% FMV cutscenes here, which explains the huge file size of the game. There are two types of these, stills from the anime (Which replace the standstill sessions and some of the less interesting story moments), and 3D FMVs that look just like past games' 3D cutscenes, albeit with a bit more expression and actual action. overall the pacing is much better thanks to these, but the quality of the 3D cutscenes is even worse than console quality, it looks identical to past games, except now with filters and compression artifacts all over it. if you can get past this, you'll experience the best storm story so far, but just don't look forward to many live cutscenes.
The second bad thing is the mob battles, which i feel still haven't really been improved on. They're more lively and action-packed than previous games- sometimes, so many will be on screen you'll feel like you're actually playing a Dynasty Warriors game or something. But these modes suffer the lack of variety in your movesets and tactics even more than those kinds of games, they feel out of place even if they are a little more tolerable now.. also, the lock-on is gone, so you'll have a tougher time hitting specific foes.
With the bad out of the way, we can move on to the good.. as you may know, previous STORM games have been quite heavy on story overall, but failed to tell it as deeply as the anime or Manga could, while also not giving the proper justice to some fights, and having repetitive battles with the same villain over and over.. this for the most part is gone. The story is paced well, you get to know every detail you need to know, and the sad moments are sad. The epic mioments are epic.
This game's story is made of mostly boss fights. Meaning every major fight has an enemy with many health bars, quicktime events, secret factors, and cool gimmicks or mechanics such as flying, running on walls, shooting or using giant summons or tailed beast / susanoo instead of a human fighter. The story is woven nicely into each fight, especially the final fight of the game, which does Naruto's ending FAR better than I expected it would, and actually jerking some really big feels out of you even if you've seen the ending before. The substance of this ame more than makes for it's story length overall, and you'll want to beat each fight again for the S-ranks, that's how fun the majority of them are. There is of course some share of repetition, but it's somewhat mitigated this time, you see...
There are some new Mechanics in Storm 4. But the biggest, most awesome mechanic in this game that's new is leader switching. No longer are you stuck for a whole fight as just the leader character you pick- tilting the R-Analog stick mid-fight allows you to PLAY as your support characters. You can do this mid-combo, while charging, or at a standstill-whenever you feel necessary except of course if you're being hit by the enemy. This helps both regular free battles AND story, because it allows for more variety, more strategy, and offers more ways to mix things up and take an opponent off guard in battle. It brings a layer of freshness even to fighting the same foe in story mode, which is done a couple of times.
Battles do still end quickly in the storm series- even more so now. But that ties in to another new mechanic.. the rounds system. In free battles, you now fight for three rounds against an oponent, in a best out of 3 to decide the victor. This means that your foe has twice the health bars compared to normal, and allos fights to go on longer. The rounds do not reset the battle at all, in fact, when your opponent is KO'd they get right back up and their health gets refilled, but your health does not. This makes the battles still feel fast and uninterrupted, but does provide a quick moment of relaxation and time to gather one's thoughts if they're getting their♥♥♥♥♥beat. overall, it just feels like a nicer system, however, single health bar battles are sill an option.
Now I guess would be the time to talk about the game's visual presentation, as well as details on the PC version itself.
Unfortunately, the game's animation engine is still tied to the framerate, meaning a 30FPS cap is in effect just like in the previous entries. However, just like in those games, it never feels choppy, because the animations are keyed to the framerate nicely, and the controls are not complicated enough that they require super-precise input. Whether this is an acceptable excuse or not is up to you, but in the end, the game runs smoothly as long as you meet the requirements, and have everything set up properly.
When it comes to PC settings, a few things need to be cleared up. The settings now get chosen within a menu in game, and they are quite limited.. SSAA is gone, replaced by FXAA. There are only two resolution options, 720p and 1080p.. and there is no vsync. However, the two latter issues can be fixed by going into the config files, wheras the former issue can be fixed by going into your GPU's control panel and forcing some MSAA or the like. People are also reporting sound issues, but this seems rare, and is easily fixed (look in the forums)
The only other major issue seems to be input lag in the menus. This needs to be fixed, though it should be noted that a PC reboot can fix it in most cases- an extreme solution, but it works.
The visuals themselves are gorgeous. The in game cutscenes, gameplay, and the overall presentation of menus and such are all a treat to look at. The FMV movies suffer from compression artifacts and aliasing sadly, but there's really nothing you can do about it. The gameplay feels fluid despite the 30FPS update, and the character models still look super nice. Facial expressions are vastly improved, and there are also great new particle effects, damage effects, destruction, and other knick knacks that make the game look great in motion. Ultimate attacks are still a visual treat, and the in game quicktime events are also just.. mmh.
If you're playing this game for the combat, it'll feel like a graphically improved version of past games. Of course, you have a large number of new characters to choose from, costumes to unlock, and all kinds of other content. You can also now customise which ninjutsu and ultimates your character uses in battle, instead of it being tied to just the costume mostly. There is also adventure mode to keep the game's length nice and long, even for solo players. I haven't yet tried the online multiplayer, but I've heard it performs just fine.
So really, aside from a few issues, this game is far better than most steam reviews will have you think. it's the best game in the STORM series by far. Sure, the game is in need of fixes, but right now, the money's worth has been met for me. I've only truly beaten story mode, and done a few things in the other modes, so I'm looking forward to playing more.
Update: I finally got around to playing the DLC characters and... eh. they're not really worth it to be honest. a little underwhelming.

Okay, here we go.
At this point in time my computer is only just slightly better than a toaster oven, but the game runs well enough for me not to tear it apart at every given moment, and that's at lowest settings without config edits. Is the game flawless? Hell no, it's in a shaky start. Does it deserve such terrible reviews, I honestly don't think so, this is no Arkham Knight. I don't know my exact specs, but my hardware is a few years old now, so it's not anywhere near top of the line. I'd give it a 7/10 in it's current state. I'll start with the Cons, to get the bad out of the way first.
Cons:
-30 FPS Lock, despite being said that this game would be optimized well on the PC.
-Slightly lower frames on menu screens. I go down 19 frames at most, usually it's around 24-27. Battles run pretty smooth.
-No option to turn off mics in online play. Seriously, why? I know how to do it, sure, but I want to be able to fight someone without hearing a tornado rip their homes apart.
-Slide show cutscenes in story mode. Seriously, this was a terrible desicion.
-Low framerate when awakening. Usually affects Susano'o characters.
-Crap keyboard support, as always. Doesn't overly matter to me since I have an Xbox controller to use, but still that should be better looked at.
I haven't experianced some of the other issues mentioned, so I can't comment on those.
Pros:
-Great story. Seriously it was nice to finally watch Naruto come to an end rather than the dub being 30 years behind and the sub being to caught up in the infinite filler to complete the story. (FYI I did read the manga, notice how I said "watch") Loved how they handled the final battle.
-Animated cutscenes were great. Seriously if we had this quality of cutscenes during Obito's backstory, or when the mask fell off it would have been amazing. They all looked so well done, it's a shame a good portion was just a slideshow.
-Better English dub acting. By far one of the highest points for me. In previous games several of the characters didn't show enough emotion in their lines. It's especially noticeable on Naruto when he shouts. This is the first time since Storm 2 that English Naruto's Rasengan actually sounds intimidating. This wasn't his actress's fault, but the people who handed her the script and told her to read it, and those who put weak sounding voices in the game rather than rerecording new ones.
-Overall smooth gameplay. Minus awakening, menus, and not being 60 FPS the gameplay is pretty smooth, and that's really what needs to be done right in the end, as that's what makes the game actually playable, you know?
-WORKING Online play. Last time I bought a Storm game (Full Burst) I regretted it immediately because the online was broken and by the time they fixed it they'd already begun hyping up Revolution. I can actually play the game with friends, rather than being disconnected partway through every match.
-Adventure Mode is pretty good, a bit bland, but about what you'd expect from an Adventure mode.
Is this game perfect? Hell no. However it's definitely better off than Full Burst was. If they fix up the issues that can be fixed with it I'd easily give it an 8.5/10, maybe even 9/10, but as it stands now, it's at a very shaky 7/10. I have a few more personal things, but overall they're not worth mentioning. I'd still recommend it to fans of the series, as everything seems fine on my end. Here's hoping they fix the issues others are having swiftly so we can all enjoy it.

The touch pad controls work wonderfully and make for the easiest typing experience on a controller out there to my knowledge. A keyboard is brought up onto the screen while you use your thumbs to point and click your way though whatever you are typing, and I think its one of those things you just have to try for yourself to understand. the paddle controllers in the back are a great touch and have come in very useful for me thus far. If a combination of buttons you need to press are hard to access at the same time you can substitute one for a back paddle, I did this in Guacamelee and it came in very useful. Being able to set your own controller layouts is something that in itself comes in very helpful in many games. I don't support ripping off game developers and studios, so if there is a game that is available for purchase and easily accessible I believe that you should do the right thing and give the developers what they have earned by creating a game that you want to play. However, if the video game is dead and hard to find in any other format I think that playing the game on an emulator is a great way to keep the spirit of that game alive, for inspiration and pure enjoyment and I am sure that I am not alone in believing that. That being said, this controller also works great for emulators and is an all around great tool for PC gaming. If you have been on the fence about grabbing yourself one, as I was,  I would urge you to buy the thing and give it a shot. It feels in your hands almost like an OG XBOX controller, but with more innovations on the game pad front than I had previously given it credit for. Its definitely just one of those things you have to experience before realizing how much you have always needed it, and I am thoroughly pleased with the experiences my Steam Controller has delivered thus far.

The steam controller is a breakthrough for power users!
This controller can accomplish anything. It requires skilled configuration for non-Steam games. I have found that Steam games will typically have profiles that are close to the mark and ranked by most used.
Game vendors are also releasing their own versions of Steam Controller configs, Warframe, for example has different configs based on what mode you are in, (melee, menu, or shooter mode) that allows you to take their customized profile and tweak it based on your preferences.
I have to mention the gyro, you have to configure this as a low speed mouse, you can supplement fast trackpad movements with a slow gyro aim for amazing results!!! CSGO and other shooters become instantly playable with this controller. I am a lifetime kb/mouse user saying this, from an Unreal Tournament background.
This is the first review I have ever written about a device, I can honestly say the Steam Controller is ground breaking, but will require days and days of playtime before you (click) with it. Old habits will be relearned, new muscle memory will be programmed, I can see a day when the steam controller and its subsequent profiles are hailed and used @ tournament level!!
Use it as a supplement, use it as a primary, I think it would be wise to learn this controller. It blows console controllers out of the water once you get over the learning curve.
I know there are people that grew up on Xbox 360 controllers, I know they swear by them. This controller is years / decades ahead of that design. Any 360 controller user that thinks shooters are in their domain, no. You will never be competitive with a gaming kb/mouse, but the Steam Controller could be once tweaking and memory are learned.

Absolutely amazing. This is, hands down, the best gaming controller I've ever used. It feels great in your hands, the mark of a well-made controller. Of course, like any change, it takes getting used to. Those who are expecting just another Xbox or PlayStation controller... go buy one of those.
However, if you're ready to take your control of your games to the next level, and are willing to customize controls (which most gamers already do to some degree) then migrating to the Steam Controller will be a breeze. I've found that the community layouts are excellent, and easy to modify if you want to make changes. Creating your own layouts is also extremely simple, with advanced options if you really want to tweak things. I have to say, though, that the standard layouts that Valve has designed work very well for most games. Games like Skyrim, however, may take a little tweaking and getting used to, depending on whether or not you previously used a mouse and keyboard, or another game pad to control the game in the past. This is probably true of most games. If you were using a mouse and keyboard to control it, you might migrate more easily than those of us who were using gamepads. This isn't to say other gamepads are better (they're not) -- just that it might take a bit more adjusting if you're used to dual sticks. The nice thing is, using the right pad as right stick gives you unbelievable accuracy once you've got the controller set up.
I've only had the controller for a day, and I already love it. Wish I could use it on my consoles!
EDIT: After owning the controller for about 6-7 months now, and having put 1200 (!) hours of Neverwinter on it (along with a 100 on Skyrim and 100s on other games) I have to say, this is still my favourite controller ever. The customizability is just amazing. The accuracy and precision of the touchpads are perfect. However, after all those hours, the right bumper button broke. It sounds like it was normal wear, as that button gets used a LOT by me in Neverwinter (I have it mapped to Tab, which on a CW is our fourth encounter power, so it has been pressed probably 5-10 thousand times easily.) I certainly don't hold this against Valve -- I'm pretty hard on this controller. But guess what? Because it was less than a year, it was still under warranty. I took it back to EB Games in Canada, where I bought it. They said they don't do warranties, and they also lied to me and said that Valve had stopped producing the Steam Link and Steam Controller. So I contacted Valve, and they immediately shipped me a new controller with a return box for the old one. Now THAT is good customer service! Just reinforces this as my favourite controller ever.

[ Introduction ]:
Blockland is a mix between Roblox (non-steam) and a bit of Garry's Mod, therefore looking and playing like a "Roblox done right".
The idea of the game is great: allowing players to build things with LEGO blocks and host their own servers with different game types.
For further customization and setting of servers, Blockland also presents a simple enough Eventing System (simplified scripting) allowing the user to affect the entities, game client or the game running in the server.
[ Positive Points ]:
- Freedom of creation: For those who like to create and host servers, there is a great deal of freedom in the game, allowing anyone to create and host an unique server.
- Easy to learn and get started.
- DIfferent gametypes, that varies from Freebuild to Kart Races (with or without guns), Team Deathmatchs, CityRPGs, Empire (Civilization-like mini-games) and more.
[ Negative Points ]:
- As expected, the worst part of the game is it's community, probably composed by many children (or brain-damaged young adults and adults). Some very annoying and immature/offensive/pornographic stuff is said on the chat in any server. Even some servers Admins/Moderators are stupid and may get into the way of the players (derping in the middle of a firefight, standing in the middle of a road during a race, etc).
- Also as expected due to the large amount of stupid members, many people don't know how to read, don't bother or are simply trolls, and dedicate themselves in annoying others. Stupid players also ruin RP games, like "Super Murder Mystery" (Blocklands' Trouble in Terrorist Town counterpart), turning most RP games into TDMs with lots of RDMing. Many mods and admins do their best to keep their servers clean, but any player will see this happening many times.
- Buggy and laggy collision physics on vehicles, make some game modes very annoying or take much fun away.
- Build mode can be very boring to work with when using a laptop without a numpad.
- Little number of players and servers (from my experience).
[ Conclusion ]:
If you can get past the annoying community, there's fun to be had in Blockland. Switching between game modes and the shared simplicity of the games is very fun. Forming up a group of friends to play on a self-made server is also a great idea.
I'm pretty sure that Garry's Mod would be a better option, but still, Blockland has it's own vibe to it to make it worth a try, so try the Demo from the official site before buying.

This was a fun game once.  It had great unique characters, it was skill based, and it had outplay.  This last feature made Paladins extremely unique for a modern FPS.  You didn't just die if someone else pressed a button, it was what separated Paladins from Overwatch for me and it was what I genuinely enjoyed about the game.  Fragging people took a little bit of effort and actually felt rewarding.
Over the last year the skill based and outplay based components were chipped away.  Old champions got their mobility nerfed into the ground.  New champions have little to no mobilty.  Weapon attacks are far more confirmable, projectiles got sped up and have even larger hitboxes, hit scan weapons fire faster and or do more damage, the list goes on.  This game became another utterly brainless modern shooter and ultimately lived up to the meme of being "Overwatch for poor people."
What finally prompted this review was Hi-Rez's actions over the last month.  Keep in mind, I am an older gamer.  I remember the days of UT2k4 and Tribes.  I can understand if the modern gaming generation doesn't enjoy those sorts of games.  It's perfectly acceptable if a company changes the direction of their game to appease the majority of their playerbase.  It's another thing to push out an extremely buggy mess of a patch that contains security vulnerabilities (don't link your twitch) whose major changes the community has been completely against during the entire month of testing.
This game is a mess.  Most aspects that made it unique have been stripped away.  What's left is a game that is almost indistguishable from any other modern shooter except for the copious amounts of bugs and a new card system that is P2W for the casual mode.  I would literally recommend Overwatch over this game and I desipse that game.

tl;dr: Worse than Dungeons 2. Starts off nice, but turns shallow quickly.
While both the underworld part where you manage your dungeon and the overworld part where you command troops RTS style are both not really deep mechanics, the fact that you need to juggle both at the same time will keep you on your toes and well entertained, at least for a while.
The graphics are candy-sweet (which some will not like), but offer a very consistent style throughout.
Audio is very well done, too and I did not encounter any bugs so far - so the tech is fine as well.
One problem is the humor:
Yes, it can be very... annoying, especially at the beginning of the campaign. But its cringiness is reduced later - or I just got immune to it by playing a while.
If you cannot deal with humor that isn't fully yours, that is full of memes and some forced puns, better skip the campaign dialogue.
The biggest problem, and the one that made me change my review from recommended to not recommended after a while, is that they removed the best part about Dungeons 2:
The different races.
Where you had three very different races in Dungeons 2, here you have them all merged into one, with each being reduced to a rather shallow sub-section of your race.
And focusing on either part doesn't make sense as that would make you skip essential building parts of your dungeon.
Want traps and doors? You need Orcs.
Want spells, mana and improving your troops? You need Demons.
Undead? The only ones not mandatory, but at the same time cannot stand on their own early on, either.
So what you will always have is a mix of all three branches.
It is a shame. I really liked Dungeons 2 and had hoped the developers would focus on its strengths. But the strange merging of the races in Dungeons 3 simply makes this entry of the series an inferior game.
Maybe this was done for the sake of balancing.
As if DK-style games were ever about competitive multiplayer balance.

One bad part, there is a glitch where the main menu music will keep playing over your game music and just absolutely deafen you, only way to stop it was to avoid using the main menu unless you need to and restart the game if it happens.

Even though I'm absolutely terrible at bullethell games, and never really got into any prior, I really enjoyed Rabi-Ribi. The artstyle is great and cute, some of the characters are adorable, the music is amazing and the dialogue is actually pretty amusing at times.
In terms of gameplay, it's a 2D platformer game, fairly open worlded, in that you can pretty much go whichever way you want, when you want, within reason that is, though there ARE achievements for doing certain "late game" things first, so it's perfectly doable to go where you want if you have the dedication and know how.
The combat is, as you might guess, bullethell style, with a heavy focus on you learning attacks, patterns and how to dodge them (or in my case, dodge enough to not die before the bosses do). Combat is very fluent, boss battles are varied and intense and there were only a couple times where I went "I have no idea how I'm even supposed to dodge that?"
Most of the attacks I personally failed at dodging, I could easily see how one could dodge, and even managed to do so, I was just not the best at it at all times, so it's very fair in the regard.
I played through on Normal difficulty, and I had my share of difficulties as I went, so it sure isn't an easy game, and losing repeatedly on bosses is something to be expected, especially if you have my level of dodging skills, or worse. The game does offer you some "help", in the way of a two buffs that reduce damage taken and heal you, if you lose too many times on a boss, though I only had to resort to accepting that on the very, very final/last boss battle (final chapter end boss) and only after having lost 9 or so times in a row, because I realized I had probably reached the limit of what I was capable of beating.
The controls are pretty good, the different types of magic you can get all have their uses, I found myself cycling between them fairly frequently, of course I had a few I prefered more than the others, but none of them I found useless.
The consumable items you can get were also all useful, there's only four of them, but they really help out in times of need (3 healing items, one damage item)
All in all, great game, very cute, very fun, easily one of the best I've played.

BEFORE YOU GET THIS GAME, know that the combat is purely cinematic; you have absolutely no control whatsoever over how your ships move, flank, target, etc. except through cards (lame I know). So don't go buying this based on the trailer (like I did), because it's depiction of the combat is extremely misleading (I knew in the back of my head that there was a reason I hadn't gotten it before, but I jumped the gun and am $8 poorer and not feeling too happy over that). That being said, however, the game does have rather extensive tech, colonisation, diplomacy, and expansion mechanics, and any fan of games like Civilization will immensely enjoy the level of strategy involved in this game. One tip, expand into nearby systems as fast as you can (You'll need to build colony ships, and the tutorial is♥♥♥♥♥♥ so that won't help), as you need tons of resources as soon as possible to get stuff built, researched, etc. Focusing on the exploration tech branch will help you expand.

This is what I consider the spiritual sucessor to Space Empires IV and V. It is a bit hard to get use to the interface and the actual gameplay itself but its totally worth it to experience diplomacy, war, science, and trade between other races in this game. It can also be modded to some extent by its players.
One of the things I like about each faction in the game though is that they have their own unique style of gameplay and some unique attributes to them. For example, the Cravers have to constantly expand and conquer other worlds because eventually their planets will be depleted of resources. Another example is the Automatons who have the ability to 'stack' industry which can make building ships or converting industry to science and/or dust much easier.
The game has random events that can be positive or negative and there are even some in which you can choose what to do and which consequences you might face such as massive plagues, anarchists, etc.
There are also multiple ways you can win the game, including expansion, wonder, research, conquest, exploration, and/or economic victories.
Graphics wise it was made using the Unity Engine but considering how beautiful everything looks in-game its hard to believe it was made with it.

Halcyon 6 has been a work in progress for some time, and it has much more to go, but don't let that discourage you from playing it.  The combat system is already fairly deep, and the simplicity of the mechanics* allows for significantly more, while the admittedly-derivative base-building system prevents it from overwhelming the player with its depth all at once.
*Attacks will both apply and exploit status effects.  This method makes combos the primary driving force during combat.  However, you control three ships at once, which decreases the inevitability of learning rote combos and, when that does occur, makes them three times as complex, as the process of setting up and knocking down enemies is no longer a simple back-and-forth repetition.
It's not perfect, though: content is slightly lacking at this point, which is to be expected from an early access game such as this; the progression and, by extension, fleet-building systems are very light; and the game can be quite frustrating.  However, the lost depth is made up through the combat system, which is likely to be a highlight of Massive Damage's entire catalog of games in the future.  I'd recommend it to most anyone I know; at least at a sale price, though it's worth full cost.

Just one common misconception I'd like to clear up about this game. You see, Doomguy isn't actually a badass. Being one of something implies it's possible to compare him to others and rank him in relation to them. Rather, badass is just a phrase for things that want to be Doomguy but fall short whill still managing to be awesome in their own right.
As for the game, it's as near a perfect capturing of the spirit of DOOM as is physically possible to get. It manages to capture the 1993 vibe of "to hell with the plot (pun definitely intended), let's just liquify demons with a Chainsaw", while also providing all the graphics capabilities you would expect from a modern game. In the intro, Dr. Hayden is a metaphor for the plot with Doomguy (wordlessly) expressing his distaste and indicating he's aware of how the situation is simultaneously ridiculous and deadly serious. It's painstakingly made clear that this is a game about shooting first and maybe getting around to asking the questions later, but maybe not works just fine too.
TL;DR: Two takeaways here -
1. Doomguy isn't a badass because badass is just what you call a watered down Doomguy.
2. Buy it, now.

I got to say that this is by far the best neptunia game i have played and i have played all of the neptunia games that have been released on steam. All the characters are lovable, Most of the villians are memorable which is a great thing, and the music is great as well. To preface, I already played through this around 50~ hours on another system, didn't reach the end but got pretty damn near close so, here goes.
This is easily the best neptunia game to date, it plays better than the previous titles, the story is better, the soundtrack is god tier, and I'd rank it above any other jrpg I've played to date. The PC port of this game is marvelous (atleast for my system, I have encountered no issues so far, Windows 10-64 bit, Nvidia GTX 860m, Intel i7-4710hq processor, 8 gb ram, using a Steam Controller with xinput.)...
So, The game itself, this is a sequel to V Generation, or
on steam. It takes place a few years after, so while it helps to have knowledge of the previous games (namely, sister generation and V generation,) it's not required and you can easily get into the game without knowledge of those. The story knows how to take itself seriously, though most of the time you're going to have comedic parody and fun moments, the soundtrack is perfect for the serious times, just as it is for the fun, and honestly the best soundtrack to any JRPG I've played so far,(seriously, recommend that digital deluxe just for the soundtrack if nothing else.) and as a visual novel I'd definitely rank it in my top 5 for story especially with how it ties in to the previous games. (order without megadimension pretty much being steins;gate>grisaia series>clannad series>tsukihime, not sure where it'd fit in, it could easily be a #2 slot after steins with the sheer amount of fun it is, the epic soundtrack and what not.)
From a gameplay perspective, you set your characters combo skills for battle (as in when they're doing their chain of attacks, which order they come up in and what moves for what type of attack, which is important as when you make a chain of abilities they can have combo traits which boost the power of the move if it meets the condition allowing you to clear enemies faster, and sometimes giving you that small edge you needed to defeat a boss), usable skills for buffs, special techniques, transformations and the like which all are required for the more difficult content, this game has a pretty decent difficulty curve and finally feels like a true jrpg game, while the other neptunia games were fun for the story, they weren't all that great for the gameplay itself; though if you liked that gameplay, you will LOVE this.(especially love how
)
The in-game cutscenes and character animations are all well done, crisp, and look great, character personalities are all varied and you have your typical cliches, but the way they're written is very well done from my view, and this game is worth multiple playthroughs, when you new game+ you keep all your previous characters and equipments and what not, so that you can hop right back in and try to get that true ending on your next playthrough or whatever floats your boat, since I think this game is good enough to play again just for the gameplay itself.
Furthermore, to add on to visuals, the visuals in the fight for an anime-style jrpg are fantastic, the special moves and combos are fun to watch and truly look devastatingly powerful, the transformation sequences look great, and I can't think of any improvements off the top of my head that I'd ask for, again, considering the art style and direction this game took I believe they fully utilized what they could to achieve the look they were hoping for.
Fanservice, as always, is plenty, and I don't just mean that typical fanservice, I mean references to nearly every major game/anime/movie you can think of done in amazing ways, the first encounter of the game is a
reference even, and while a lot are pretty subtle, they do some of the bigger mentions in amazing reveals and if you have an extensive knowledge of current and past mainstream culture(even some small ones make it in there) you'll have a great time catching and picking out all the references, and that alone affords multiple playthroughs of scrutinizing the text so that you have an Aha! moment and realize what it was referencing.
Overall, as a neptunia game, and a jrpg, I give this game a solid 10/10, for me, at least, I'd be hard pressed to find a better jrpg that's currently out, maybe later, but for now this is my top game for that genre.

Megadimension Neptunia VII (V-2, not 7) is the sequel to Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory/Re;birth3, the plot is as follows:
One day, Neptune was taking a nap, when she woke up and was heading back to the basillicom, she found a strange broken game console, upon her arrival, her and Nepgear attempted to fix up, but the power buttons opens up a portal to a new dimension, after travelling in said dimension, Neptune and Nepgear find Uzume Tennouboshi, the two then learn that like themselves, Uzume is a CPU, named Orange Heart, the two also learn that they're in the Zero dimension, and that Uzume fights against the 4 dark CPUs, giants the size of a skyscraper, Nep and Gear then swear to help Uzume while finding a way back home to their dimension.
VII follows the core Neptunia battle system with some minor variations, your weapons now affect what attacks you can pull off, in addition, some attacks have combo potential, meaning that if executed in the proper order, you will be guaraunteed to pull of serious damage rather than spamming the same buttons, the EXE bar also fills up faster but is not stored after battles, some enemies and bosses have parts that must be broken to deal more damage, when said part is broken, you gain more EXP and credits
VII also introduces random encounters on a grid-styled map system, these can be turned off after completing the game once should you decide to do a NG+
The main cast of the Neptunia franchise is still here and in full force, Uzume is a right-round blast of a character, showing off her cool side while occasionally becoming her valley girl self, there's also Umio, the most gentlemanly fish-man you will ever see, and Adult Neptune, The Neptune that didn't become a CPU in the Ultradimension, replacing the maker characters of the past games is the new "Gold Third", consisting of K-sha: a yandere soldier, C-sha, a hunter who wants to do the people good, B-sha who likes credits but also uses her Presto mask persona to fight crimes, and S-sha, who has a severe case of the "not interested"
Overall: VII is a great addition to Neptunia, but in order to understand some of the plot points, you must have some knowledge of Re;birth2 and Re;birth3, else some plot points may leave you questioning it

An interesting game that doesn't deviate from its core design concept, which is a party-based almost roguelike experience centered around defeating bosses and clearing dungeons in a sarcastic high fantasy setting filled with pop culture references. This would normally get boring after a few hours, but it's surprisingly fun to see what classes, dungeons, equipment, and spells you can unlock next. Unfortunately, some classes are just straight up better than others, and because of how the battle mechanics are designed, there isn't much of a point in using the more utility driven classes except for healers. The boss battles are extremely creative and can be quite challenging, forcing you to adapt your tactics to fit specific dungeons. You'll find yourself dying unfairly to the aforementioned bosses, but that's really the main appeal of the game - its replayability. Make sure to change your party dynamics each run to keep the game fresh. Try not running any healers and going full damage, you'd be surprised how well that can work. If you don't see the appeal, feel free to skip this one. If you are an indie game connoisseur, you should give it a try.

The game has good intentions but falls flat due a major flaw:
the combat is turn based and it alternates between one player action and one enemy action, even if you have 3 characters alive and there is only 1 enemy.
This means that reducing the number of enemy during a fight is almost allways useless, if the enemies all do the same damage it means that your team takes the same amount of damage each turn no matter how many you already killed.
This wouldn't have been a problem and could have been an intresting mechanic if the game embraced it and built around it, but unfortunatly it seems like it tries to borrow mechanics that don't work with this system. The biggest one of these is hybrid classes, classes that don't exceed in either magical or physical damage. The adventurer, for example, is an hybrid between an healer and a fighter having just dicreet damage and a sub-optimal heal, this means that both his attack and his heal doeas less than an enemy attack, so even if you have 3 characters and there is only one enemy, healing with the adventurer would be not only useless but also incovinient because the enemy team will still get 50% of the combat turns, so for each of your weak heals a monster would damage you for a greater amount, rendering the adventurer and all other hybrid classes less than useless.
The humour of the game is below average, it makes you appreciate the effort but fails to deliver.
Also for my taste the music is repetitive and forgettable, I played with it turned off.
CONCLUSIONS:
Pixel Hearos feels like a work of love but not enough effort went into it, if it was a school student his teacher would say "he's good but he doesn't apply himself". Good intentions aren't enough to deliver a good game and major flaws in the combat and the forgettable music and humour make it so it's not really worth playing.
