I have been playing this game every now and then for quite a while now, and while it has some flaws, I can really recommend it. It is a comparatively slow-paced shooter with many simulation aspects, and playing it feels like controlling huge BattleMechs unlike some other mech games. One has to be aware of the positions of friends and enemies as disengaging can be difficult especially for heavier mechs. One has to decide which part of enemy mechs to attack while trying to shield damaged parts of ones own mech, one has to take into account weapon ranges, heat dissipation, and can aim arm and torso weapons independently to an extent.
The game of course also has some weak spots: There is no single-player mode, which was a highlight of the earlier MechWarrior titles, but "MechWarrior 5: Mercanaries" is a single-player title that is currently being produced by the same developer, using the Unreal Engine 4 instead of CryEngine 3 of MW:O.
Buying mechs and cosmetic items with real money is pretty expensive, but almost all mechs are available for free ingame currency, and if you don't feel the need to own all mechs (which for me personally is totally unnecessary), that is not a problem. There are events and "challenges" where cosmetic items and reasonable amounts of premium currency are given away freely, and the mechs that are not available for free ingame currency (so called hero mechs) are most often inferior to variants that are available, so this game is certainly not pay to win. It is "pay to not grind" and "pay to have mechs a few month before others", though.
Note that the community warfare mode is some kind of endgame mode and not really suitable for beginners. There is no matchmaking in this mode, so 12 uncoordinated noobs can face a premade team of 12 veteran players that meet two times a week for training. Before entering this mode, one should at least own four mechs that have been customized to ones preferences. Also, this mode is still in development; currently, fighting over planets on a star map is nice, but every planet has the same maps, and victory is inconsequential. Better stick to Quick Play for now.
Much of the bad publicity the game had in the past were from a time where the developer PGI was influenced by another publisher, but since they bought back the game, they are doing their best to improve it, doing very good so far. The learning curve in this game is steep, but it is also very fun and unique, so give it a try.

Ok so I am an original founder, been playing since 2012.  I am also a MechWarrior/Battletech nut and have been since the 90s.
Objective review:  Big stompy robots, check.  Lazors, missiles, and huge guns, check.  ♥♥♥♥♥in' Betty voice, check.
There is a lot of polarization in the BT community over this game.  Bold promises were made as to what this game would be and I would have to agree that some things have not been delivered on.  However, forget all of that.  Forget the history of development, forget the things that coulda woulda shoulda.  If I look at this game simply as a game, and not a representation of the universe I am so passionate about, then I have to say it is a good game.  The core gameplay is solid.  It requires tactics, thoughtfulness, and skill.  It is not like your typical clicky shooty FPS game (and that is a good thing).  The experience is unique, and gratifying.  There is a learning curve (also a good thing).  You are not going to jump into this and wreck face right off the bat.  It takes a lot of practice to become a really good mechjock.  You can solo PUG and have fun, but it is much more fun playing with an organized group.  It is not pay2win as some might say, though there is some grind factor if you choose the strictly free route.  All of my best mechs are mechs you can get without spending real cash.  Anyways, it's free to play?  Why would you not at least give it a chance and see for yourself?
Now for my biased, uber passionate MechWarrior fanboy review: This game has the potential to be sooo much more than it is.  For a long time, the pace of development was mind numbingly slow.  That has improved a lot since PGI took total control over from IGP but I still feel like meaningful new content has been slow in coming.  The BT universe is massively rich in lore to draw from and I feel like PGI has done a poor job of immersing us in that universe.  Community Warfare was what I most looked forward to when I signed up for the Founders program and I feel it is pretty dissapointing in its current state.  There is no benefit to taking planets, no story, no depth, no economy.  It doesn't give you that feeling like you are accomplishing something.  I'm not going to get into individual suggestions for features/content etc.  This is not the place for that.  I just want more depth to make me feel like I am really participating in the Battletech universe.
So TLDR: My fanboy feelings are hurt, but it is a good game and you should try it.

MWO provides a unique gameplay experience unlike any other first-person shooter/vehicle games out there. It delivers the best real-time MechWarrior gameplay since MechWarrior Living Legends. If you have any interest in that and don't mind a bit of a learning curve, give it a shot. It's not perfect but it can be quite fun.
The game's content is currently a mile wide and a foot deep. The mile-wide part is the roughly 300 mechs to choose from (as of December 15th, 2015) with over 60 different chassis with multiple variants per chassis. This amount of variety ensures there's a mech or a configuration to suit just about anybody and any play style.
However, the gameplay itself is currently limited to three minor variations of Team Deathmatch called Skirmish, Assault, and Conquest, as well as an early draft of Community Warfare (CW) which still has a long way to go to provide meaning and purpose to the matches played in that mode.  That's the foot-deep part.
Right now all game modes are 12v12 and are primarily won by killing the enemy team before they can kill you. Even in CW, which is the mode with the strongest alternative win conditions, most matches will be won by eliminating the opposing team rather than playing to the alternative win condition (for better or worse).
There are also private lobbies for units to practice and they can be configured to run any amount or assortment of players up to 12v12.
The combat gameplay itself is solid, and for the most part enjoyable. The game recently went through a balance pass that slightly reduced mech maneuverability across the board and buffed armor/internal structure on a lot of chassis that needed some help to make them viable. Overall, the balance pass makes the game more newbie friendly, which is generally a good thing, though it's hard to deny the competitive edge has been dulled a little bit, as time-to-kill (TTK) has risen, resulting in a little less emphasis on pure aiming skill and positional advantage to win engagements. Overall, not a huge deal though.
The biggest fault with this game is its pricing model - if you decide to buy into it. I have, despite being of the opinion that it is over-priced. I look at it as supporting the game over the past three years to help it get here to its Steam release. I look at it as giving to support the developer and getting in-game content in return, rather than viewing it as a pure business transaction of actual value per dollar.
There are many people who have played this game for years now and have never spent a dime. And PGI, the developer, has started to incentivize weekend contests and tournaments with rewards that include free Premium Time and MC (the paid currency), which allows even free players the opportunity to acquire some paid content for 'free'. Players can also unlock Mech Bays (used to store mechs in your inventory) for free via Community Warfare faction loyalty progression.
So while the store prices are undeniably high, you can choose to skip it entirely. You will have a hell of a grind ahead of you though,
you have visions of being a mech collector and owning them all. Even purchasing every pre-order mech package to take advantage of the best price-per-mech and essentially buying the mechs instead of grinding out the c-bills for them, I still have put in hundreds of hours of gameplay just to fully unlock them all. Essentially, the choice for a collector is between an insurmountable grind with free play, or a steep grind alongside paying.
But you don't have to be a collector. Read up at /r/OutreachHPG or
and then try the Trial mechs in the game to see what sort of gameplay suits you. Once you have that figured out, just focus on grinding out the c-bills for one or two chassis you really like. You start out with four mech bays, which is enough to fully unlock an entire chassis by purchasing three variants of that chassis. So choose wisely and you can enjoy MWO with your sole investment being your time.
MWO's best community, imho, is found on the /r/OutreachHPG subreddit. You'll learn a lot there about everything MWO-related. It's a good balance between competitive and casual players and while no community is perfect, I think you'll find a helpful and welcoming lot there.
Overall, the MWO community skews a bit older than most due to a significant portion of the community being 35-and-up fans of Battletech tabletop and BT simulator play back in the '90s. You'll also find a lot of MW2/MW4 veterans. But there are plenty of younger players as well, including some of the best in the game. So regardless of your age bracket, it shouldn't be hard to find a group to slot in with.
This game is a LOT more fun when you play it in a group with friends or by joining a unit and playing with them. If you only experience the solo queue, you are missing out on the best the game has to offer, because MechWarrior combat is all about teamwork, coordination, and communication. There are MWO units that run the gammut from pure casual to top-tier competitive play and everything in between.
Leave Leeroy Jenkins thoughts behind, because trying to rush alone into the enemy will lead only to your death and frustration. Highly recommend watching some competitive MWO footage on YouTube to get an idea of the feats that are possible when a well coordinated team is on the field.
Start by playing MWO with a keyboard and mouse. Unlike previous MechWarrior games that controlled best with a flight stick and throttle setup, MWO is designed foremost for kb+m control. Can you use a joystick or a gamepad? Probably, but until there's a singleplayer experience, you'll only be doing yourself and your team a disservice to use a less accurate method of control and aim compared to the rest of the players in the match.
Want your MWO experience to be successful in the long run? Do your research before buying any mechs, start reading Outreach to get a better sense of the game, consider joining a unit as soon as you're comfortable controlling a mech on the battlefield, and use a mouse for aiming. :)
PGI has improved a lot over the past year. While they still have a ways to go with fostering a healthy community and actually heeding experienced player feedback and weeding out the chaff, they have more consistently delivered on their timelines, roadmaps, and promises than they did during the previous two years.
I'm hopeful this game continues to succeed to the extent that PGI is able to fund the creation of a quality singleplayer campaign and co-op missions, as well as the anticipated rounding out of CW next Spring. This game needs some PvE content in addition to general improvements on the "foot deep" elements of its content, such as injecting Battletech lore tie-ins and info throughout Community Warfare, really expanding on the game modes and the purpose of the missions played in CW, and making better use of the public queue maps by revamping or improving those game modes as well.

Oh gods Tribes Ascend. This would be one of the best games I've ever played if it weren't for the ridiculously high skill requirement. It isn't even a learning curve, it's a time commitment. You have to first get a feel for Skiing - the primary means of getting around a map - then you have to learn how to use at least one of the game's weapons, all of which are hard to use. Mastering one of the game's weapons is akin to earning your 5th degree black belt, both in terms of effort and timecomitted to it, as well as the effectiveness that results from your mastery. I have yet to come close to even becoming adept with one of the weapons in this game. Another thing is that the lag, even though it is miniscule and very well covered up by lag compensation, will MESS WITH YOU. A 0.2-second delay in firing your Spinfusor means the difference between scoring a direct hit and accidentally killing yourself in the explosion. Another thing is that the class balance is a bit off-kilter; Medium and Heavy classes can easily travel 9/10ths the speed of a Light class, and their weapons can one-hit Light classes with splash damage. Whereas, the Light classes have to score nothing but direct hits to even come close to leaving an engagement with their lives. It's not a huge issue; the Light's job is to run around sewing chaos, not engaging directly, but it can get under your fingernails when a misfired shell kills you instantly after you walk out of the spawn area.
Besides that the game really is deservent of the title of "The fastest FPS on the market." With practice, you can easily reach racecar speeds of 300 KPH on a regular basis; I've seen some people get up to a supersonic 600 KPH when they try. The skill-based weapons are both rewarding and aggravating at the same time; you can go an entire match without a single kill or assist because of how bad your aiming skills are, and the next match you can rack up 10 mid-air kills with grenades. It's entirely dependent on how good you are, how bad the lag is, and whether or not the gods of hilarious killshots are on your side. The team balance isn't stellar, but there is at least an algorithm that exists to balance out teams. All of the gamemodes are stupid fun, and teamwork does matter even if you hardly ever get it. This game is a proponent of the "Awesome Moment"; you know, those time where there is 1 minute left in the game, you're playing as Pathfinder, the most fragile class in the game, and you skii into the enemy's flag room, kill 3 guys in one shot, grab the flag right before the enemy team captures theirs, kill the flag carrier and return your flag, skii all the way home dodging missiles and AA fire as you deftly slide up and down ramps and hills, and just before the game ends, you cap the flag and tie the game. Much Shazbot will be heard.

It's an enjoyable Free-to-Play Hero Shooter with 3 modes; The main one being capturing the objective and then pushing it to the enemy base, the second one focusing solely on pushing the objective, and the last one being typical point-based deathmatch. It's all pretty standard.
Some time ago there was also a survival mode where everyone had just one life, but they removed it for some reason. What it already has is decent enough, but it could use some more varied ways to play and have fun.
There's no real lore or story here, unlike other popular Hero Shooter/Moba games, just some one-liners and jokes to give the colorful cast some character.
But it doesn't need any, in this type of game, it's all about characters and gameplay.
The characters are hit and miss, but that's just my opinion. They all offer something unique to the table and are fun to play with (Unique in regards to this game and its characters. You will find a lot of parallels between Paladins and Overwatch or TF2.)
There are also plenty of maps to play with and much more to come (with the being available to players for testing, which is a nice idea, involving the playerbase into some part of the creation of the game.) all of them being colorful and generally well designed.
Of course, there are still a lot of glitches and broken elements present, but it's understandable as it is still in the Open Beta, and the developers are constantly working on it, throwing in patches after patches, changes, and new content.
It's amazing to see. Especially recently, when they were introducing new Champion every single month.
But then, Cards Unbound happened...
A new patch that basically threw away the unique loadout system that differentiated it from the other Hero Shooters, allowing the player a lot of customization of Hero's abilities to suit their playstyles while still being balanced, which was easily the best part of this game...
And instead they put in a system that not only removed all the balance from the game modes where the vast majority of players are, but also turned the grind up to eleven, making it really annoying for the old players, horrible for the new ones, and more Pay-to-Win than it was ever before (and the funny thing is, they've decided it was a good idea to announce it right after the StarWars Battlefront 2 afair,) pretty much forcing the players to use what they get from lootboxes rather than building the loadout they want... so they wouldn't get destroyed all the time by players that have all their cards maxed out without any limits.
To be fair... I didn't really test those changes for myself, so it may be that I misunderstood some mechanics of it, but in any way, it's blatantly obvious what they're trying to do.
If you want to learn how to ruin a solid game with a single patch, definatelly give this game a try.
UNBALANCED

This is based off of a controller I got June 2016. Like most other hardware, the first batch was most likely poorly put together and lacked support. I expected something that would be a cool gimmick sometimes but never a main controller. The first game I loaded up was Dark Souls 3 and after about an hour of messing with settings and different recommended profiles I didn't really want to stop using it.

The obvious downside is that there isn't really a "plug and play" setting. Some default profiles for games are awful and made me say "who thought this was a good idea?". Using big picture mode also had a couple of weird issues. The menu wouldn't pop up sometimes and I had to quit out of Steam completely.
I don't normally write reviews but a lot of people hate this thing and I was pleasantly surprised with how cool it was. I would love to see them continue and add support to it or even develop an evolved version of this idea.
If you're debating getting one, ask yourself if troubleshooting, customizing settings and a bit of getting used to before playing is worth it for a really interesting controller. If it's worth it to you, then grab one and I doubt you'll be disappointed. If not, nothing quite beats an Xbox 360/Xbox One/PS4 controller. Xbox One controllers on Windows 10 are incredibly easy to set up(when the controller itself works right) and will still probably be used regularly by me. Hi there! My name is Claire, I am 26 years old and from Denmark. I have over 20 years of gaming experience. I do all achievements for the game before I review it. So my review truly reflects a 100% completion of the game.
However it is still my subjective opinion of the game, so take everything I say with a grain of salt. Hope you enjoy!
Adventure Capitalist is a very simple game. You start off on Earth with nothing but a measly lemon stand that earns you a couple bucks every time you click on it. As you click on it, you gain more and more money. This money allows you to buy the next source of income, which is a newspaper stand. You then start clicking on that aswell, until you unlock the next source of income. You get the picture.
As you unlock more and more sources of income, you also unlock managers. These managers enable your sources of income to be automatic, so you don't have to click on them anylonger.
As you earn more and more money, you start accumulating Angels. Angels serve the most pivotal mechanic in Adventure Capitalist. Every Angel increases your income by 2% (with upgrades, even more so), but in order to activate your Angels, you will have to start all over from scratch. Restarting might sound like a bad idea at first, but the angels allows you to accumulate more and more income over time.
Once you get into the game you will be restarting A LOT to keep progressing at a decent pace. The game becomes much more about restarting at efficient timings, than being an actual clicking game.
As you get further into the game you will unlock both the Moon and Mars. The Moon and Mars are seperate economies which work quite differently to Earth. These serve as a decent distraction from Earth, and while Mars didn't take me very long to max out, The Moon was actually longer to complete than Earth was.
You play as a greedy capitalist, male or female, out to conquer the entire world!
Okay, it's a free clicking game guys, there's not going to be a deep story here.
It's basically just an interface with buttons to click on. Comparing it to something like Clicker Heroes, which is also free, Adventure Capitalist is not as interesting or nice to look at.
There's basically not much going on graphically in this game.
The Moon, Mars, Earth and the occasional event has different styles to their menus, but that's about all you get for variety graphically in Adventure Capitalist.
There's a different song looping on every planet. It gets very annoying and very monotonus quickly. I turned it off after about 5 minutes.
The songs are however light-heartedly themed, and very self-aware in the sense that it's almost ironic listening to these very happy tunes, as you're raking in fantastical amounts of money.
Seeing as the game is very simple, I find that game would've been better off with no music and a bigger emphasis on making the actual game menus more attractive and interactive.
You can play the game from start to finish without spending a single penny. The game has an option to let you spend real money on the ingame currency: Goldbars.
The Goldbars allows you to buy multipliers, flux capacitors, time skippers and gear for your "character".
It basically makes you complete the game more quickly, or makes you get past wait times.
I personally spent 10 dollars on the game, mainly to support the game, but also so I could test out the shop for you guys!
It's important to notice that the game gives you daily rewards and milestone rewards in the form of gold bars, so even if you decide not to spend any money on the game, you can still get everything if you're patient.
Adventure Capitalist is a very simple clicking game with very few mechanics. You buy sources of income, you buy upgrades, you buy managers, you wait... You use your angels to reset and you do it all over, this time even quicker than the last. The game is undeniably very monotonous and simple.
With that said, I find myself with almost 100 hours played before I finished all the achievements and planets, and I can honestly say I didn't find it boring. Seeing yourself go from 1 buck to absolutely enormous amounts of money is quite addictive. The fact that you have both Mars and The Moon as little side economies helps aswell.
Ultimately, Adventure Capitalist is free and it can be played on a potato, so it makes for a good game to play when you just want to chill out, and I think that is the fundamental nature of clicking games.
I give Adventure Capitalist: 8 out of 10.

Endless space is a 4x (explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate) turn-based strategy game. As any 4x game, you have different victory conditions that you may choose to pursue in order to beat your opponents, be it technological victory,plain domination or whatever your preferred style of play is.
The Factions are balanced and nicely done, not only that, you can even create your own faction by selecting positive and negative traits. I like how they all play out differently and each of them has their own story and culture.
To make your "civilization" flourish you have to colonize new planets, balance their output of basic resources and collect the luxury resources that help your empire. You can set Taxes, decide what to build in the entire system and specialize the single planets.
Every hero has two classes and statistics that help you determine what is his best role, you can place it as a Governor on a system or to command a specific type of fleet. Heroes gain experience and you can choose various skill in a big tree, big enough so I can safely say that even if both players get the same hero (which is impossible in the same game) they might end up with completely different characters.
The combat is original. Some hate it, some love it. Me? I personally like it a lot. When two fleets encounter, they engage in a battle consistent of 5 phases (3 of them are combat phases). The Initial phase, where everyone lines up, the Long range phase, the Medium range phase, the Short range phase and the conclusion. In these phases you can give orders and play "cards" that represent tactics (which you can unlock through technology or heroes). Every tactic then has a general group that can counter or be countered by what the enemy plays. I find it a streamlined fun experience, it just gives you the good stuff to do while you watch the battle unfold.
The customization of the ships is near perfect imho, you choose the components you want to install, modules, weapons (and at what range), defenses, of course, after first choosing a "frame". After that you name your ship and you can produce it in series. Later, when your technology is better, you might want to Update your old design, you can do that simply and then update any old ship of the same class.
The learning curve is so-so, I mean, it's still a 4x game, but it's very easy to learn compared to other ones. I think it has a good balance between accessibility and complexity. You could really say it's easy to learn but hard to master, especially against human foes. The AI is good, but not the best, I would recommend playing it with friends or other people, even if it's just you and another friend with 6 bots.
All in all, I recommend this to anyone who likes space sci-fi and 4x games, buy it with the expansion, it's worth it, especially new players coming into the 4x genre. Sword of the Stars players might find this game too casual, then again, I find the SotS series, while great, very demanding, more like a chore than an actual game; that's why I prefer this one.

Endless Space is best summed up as 'Civilization in Space'. Multiple victory types, strategic gameplay, massively stupid AI. But Endless Space somehow manages to do combat even worse than Civ. Think about that for a second: Civ's combat was pretty bad. One unit per square, chunky movement, and penalties for even thinking about building a large, war-minded empire.
Endless Space's combat is even worse than that.
Every fight is rock-paper-scissors. Literally. Didn't guess the correct defense for your opponent's offense? You lose. Parity of offense and defense? Nothing at all happens. Add to this an annoying, time-consuming "card" system that adds ANOTHER layer of roshambo and you have the most annoying combat system ever encountered in gaming. Combat invariably boils down either to turtling or kamikaze attacks.
It can be a fun game and has a unique setting, but if you're looking for any kind of smooth, interesting, or even just functional combat system, you should look elsewhere.
Edit after achievement hunting: If you're the type that enjoys getting all the achievements in a game, you'll be dismayed - as I was - to find that Endless Space has many hidden achievements. They are nearly all incredibly difficult to get. Not challenging, mind you. They just take hours and hours of grind, luck, and AI decisions randomly working in your favor. Annoying and not worth the time.
Top tier UI; really impressive. And it's a time-sink. Play with caution.

As you may have heard, the Director's Cut is the definitive edition of Human Revolution. It combines all the dlc and integrates them into the game seemlessly. Additionally, the game comes with a director commentary of sorts that runs about 8 hours long total. You can leave the commentary option on,and still not hear it in the game. You simply push f when prompted to hear it. If that kind of thing interests you like it does me, you'll find dev commentary to be a very cool expirience. The boss fights have also been reworked to be a little more fair. You have the option to activate something either before the fight, or during it that pushes the odds a little more in you favor. You can't skip them, but now they suck way less.
All that being said, the game does have some kinks. First off, the commentary can be a tad annoying at times. If you checkpoint while listening to a clip, it restarts it every time you respawn, should you die. Also, the commentary freezes activatable options (like talking to people) when being played for you. You may end up standing around for a few minutes listening to the commentary before you're actually allowed to move on.
Another issue is that this edition of the game takes the entire game backwards a few patches, thus reintroducing bugs not previously seen in the base game.
But, seriously, that shouldn't stop you from giving this a try. It's fantastic, and definitely worth the money. Also, I spent around 24 hours getting through the entirety of the game, and that was skipping a couple sidequests. 9/10

I REALLY wanted to like this game.  I generally love this genre, and the game mechanics are interesting.  The three hero combat systems actually works, and the inventory system isn't too bad (awkward at first, but you learn it).
The thing that just stops me cold from keeping going with the game is that you can get into a situation in a dungeon where you lose your healer, or your DPS.  That means you have ZERO chance of finishing the dungeon, especially if you are on part 6 of 8 in a dungeon.  You can't go back, you can't get a noob to fill the spot, you can't leave the dungeon at all.  It is a one way trip to win or die.  One guy left?  So what.  Keep playing until you die.
Just allowing a party to bail on a dungeon and return to town when their bags are full to sell off stuff and get some potions would have a HUGE impact on playability of the game.  As it is right now, I don't see myself coming back and spending time on this.  It is too slow to be a real rougue game (typical game time would be < 10 mins).  But the dungeon system means investing 45 mins to just wipe with ZERO chance of doing anything about it.
Its a shame, the game has a lot of potential to go well beyond the current implementation.  But I think the dev has moved on anyway.

For users on Windows 8.1 (and possibly Windows 10) gaming laptops:
- Configure the game to use your dedicated GPU instead of Integrated Graphics.
- Run the game in compatibility mode and choose Windows 7.
As long as you meet the minimum requirements to run the game, you won't have any slowdown after taking these steps.  Solving the audio issues requires changing the audio play back sample rate to 44100 MHz in your speaker properties.

I've been a player since closed beta, and have logged over 4500 maches. This game has definitely gone through some rough patches, and periods of slow progress, but I think it's shaping into a good or even great mech game. Consider my opinion a bit colored though, I'm involved in the Battletech franchise.
I believe the main shortcoming of the game at the moment is its lack of significantly different game modes, as essentially all modes are a deathmatch with potential side objectives.
However, the game has kept me coming back for a long time, so I think any new player looking for some mech shooter action will be entertained for some time. Being able to come into the game and experience its improved state from the start is a plus, and the initial grind for new players has been significantly reduced.
As far as spending, it's a F2P, so you know what you're getting into, it can either be very cheap (spend about $20 on mech bays), or ruin your finances. Pretty much no pay to win here, just plenty of options for pay to advance. If spent wisely, a bit of cash in can largely eliminate the grind.
My biggest tip to enjoying this game is to join a merc team. Playing alone can be fun, but much of one sides success is dependant on tight teamwork, and you'll get a lot more of that in a premade group.

mechwarrior online at its core is a competant mech game that you are guaranteed to have a modicum of fun with. like many F2P games it rides that line between fun and not fun that makes you want to keep playing while at the same time grumbling about all the things that could be better. and like many F2P games it has a rabid defense force that will shoot down any criticism you have so don't even bother taking your opinions to the forums.
Gameplay-wise, MWO does what it advertises. You're in a big robot and it more or less feels like you're in a big robot shootin other robots of various sizes, and the 'time to kill' so to say is fairly high as far as shooters go (at least until clans were released), which leads to very meaty brawly blow-trading fps combat that you just don't see that often, and is the sole reason why you should at least give this game a try.
The mech customization is fairly straight forward, your mech has a tonnage capacity along with eight segments: arms legs head and body (split into center and two side torsos) and each segment has a set amount of slots for equipment along with hardpoints for the different types of weaponry you can use. however, the store and mech garage UI (and every other UI in the game) can only be described as a war crime of check boxes, drop-down menus and hidden buttons.
Character and mech progression is entirely linear, there is no skill tree(EDIT: THERE IS NOW AND ITS TERRIBLE) or path to go down you just grind the numbers and unlock all the bonuses. Mech progression is based on the mech chassis, and to fully upgrade that chassis (which is required if you want to stand a chance against the lifers who populate this game) you must grind unlocks on 3 of its variants. Character progression lets you unlock the usage of modules, which unlock special abilities such as being able to see mechs within a 100 meter radius on your radar (completely negating the use of maneuvering tactics such as flanking) or making your guns shoot faster and farther.
I mentioned before the sort of gameplay this game showcases, however when put into practice you will notice that the current mechanics allow people to do stupidly high amounts of damage with pinpoint accuracy, destroying the prospect of brawly close-quarters combat unique to the series. Also with 12 vs 12 game sizes you will find that matches quickly devolve into a numbers game of whoever has the biggest mechs and whoever is able to run around in the biggest clump of people, strategy (other than 'everyone focus fire on robot A') simply doesn't have a place in this game.
I've given this game a yes out of no because steam doesn't have time for numerical ratings. Yes, this game is worth trying out FOR FREE. No it is not worth spending money on, your dollar/euro/zog will not go very far in this game and because you are an ignorant newbie you will most likely blow all your premium currency on terrible mechs that you didn't know were terrible, consumables you don't know how to use and mech slots that you get for free via monthly events. Like many mediocre F2P game devs, these ones do not deserve your money because for the past 4 years they've managed to do the absolute minimum amount of effort require to keep this game functional because they know they can get away with it. They know this is the only show in town and everyone has to come to them to get their mechwarrior fix.

Don't worry about the negative reviews, it's just salty long time players who are struggling.
The game has a good hard learning curve, you'll need patience to gather a foundation of suitable META mechs to play with and compete well. Look up meta builds and good mechs, join a unit to play with and learn. Playing with people is better than playing alone.
Buy mech packages once you know if you want to play Innersphere or Clans.
You will get stomped in pub matches and community warfare often, learn to move around and not sit still !

Good controller, would recommend!
It does not quite replace a mouse/keyboard combination, nor can it match up to a regular controller (say Xbox One, seeing how I've been using that until now). Although, for me, it's a great means to combine both worlds. I'm particularly fond of the ease by which the controller replaces mouse functionality in some games ; something which I've been dying to find for months. (I've got a desk job and most of the times when I feel like gaming, I can't stand to sit in a desk chair to look at a computerscreen and click a mouse -- I do that for a job 8 hours a day already.) This controller basically lets me lay down in the couch and play games for which I'd ordinarily use a mouse. Brilliant!
The controller feels great while using it, it's rather easy to get used to. It even has an optional HUD-display which shows on screen the buttons which you are pushing. (For me, this was easier to learn the position of the buttons in the beginning.)
It's highly customisable, allowing several controller mappings per game which can be selected on the fly (they're just a few clicks away from inside the game you're playing)
The only cons I can name is that (A) the ABXY-buttons are in a rather strange place which takes a while to get used to ; (B) the controller feels rather cheap, as if the manufacturer skimped on some materials (I'm not saying it's flimsy or bad or anything... it just feels rather cheap, plastic-y).
I'm also not sure if it's worth the full price (€54.99 + €9 shipping = €63.99 total) if you've already got another controller around which you're used playing with (for controller-supported games) and if you, at the same time, don't mind sitting at a desk to play with mouse/keyboard for games that don't support controller. But, when on sale (which is when I got my controller), it's undoubtly worth it.
<tl;dr>
Good controller, would recommend! Consider buying it when it's on sale if you've already got a controller of sorts ; consider buying it any other time if you don't have a controller and are looking for a good buy.

This game has something of a steep learning curve and few resources to help you out, but there is a tremendous payoff if you stick with it.
I am a big fan of the Civilization series, and so there is something of a high bar set for all games that even touch on its features. Endless Space does a good job of keeping the core elements that make the genre fun, while bringing its own touch that kept me through the frustrations of initially learning the game.
Some of these frustrations are things like difficulty making sense of the technology tree (or sorting through it in a sensible and profitable way), and not quite realizing the importance of updating ship designs and fleet construction. I suspect people will find their own points where they stumble, and while the game always will reward understanding with an entertaining game, it definately took me longer to warm to this game than I normally give.
These relatively minor complaints aside, I have found this game a lot of fun to play and fresh enough to reward multiple replays and strategies. A major feature that stands out is combat system for fleets which adds this nice cinematic feel (a bit like Battlestar Galactica scenes) while adding a mechanic that is simple to use, but quite complex to master in terms of determining a best reply (moreso against human players). The game also has a gorgeous soundtrack that will accompany you as you find yourself going deeper and deeper into the night.
This recommendation can only apply to fans of turn based strategy games with a 4X feel. There are simpler introductions to the genre, and it's hard to see what's inside that would appeal to people who don't like 'that type' of game. But if you do like this sort of strategy and have not yet tried Endless Space, you'd be hard pressed to find a better alternative.

I bought this game around the time it came out on steam for a similar price to what it is at now, during the winter sale, selling much of my DotA/CS:GO inventory to make the purchase. I had played about half (I think) of the first game, watched about half of the anime series, and bought the second game but never played it. My reason for not finishing the first game was that it was too grindy. I didn't really know what I was getting into. The characters were fun, but the gameplay was repetitive, and a lot of the mechanics weren't clearly explained (elemental damage). The only thing that matters from that prior experience is the familiarity with the characters, and even then this game does a decent job of re-introducing everyone, although there will be a few jokes or references to things that I and you may not get. That doesn't really detract from the experience.
What this game did was improve greatly on the actual battles (in my opinion) and made it so that much less grinding was required to beat the bosses. If you just naturally fought any enemies that you met, you would almost always be sufficiently leveled for the big encounters. The combo mechanic for your attacks makes your choice for moves and weapons more interesting and intuitive. The story is very engaging, and you get to spend some quality time with all of the major characters. The normal end was very good, and the story built up to it very well. The "true end" achieved by doing a couple of specific things earlier in the story, which you'll probably have to look up to do properly, is an amazing conclusion. Once you beat the story, there is a seemingly unlimited amount of gameplay to be had completing quests and doing battles.
I think this game would make a good introduction to the neptunia franchise, and highly reccomend it at its winter sale price, I wouldn't have minded paying full price for it originally if I knew what I was getting.

Role Playing Game
Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic is a challenging 2D RPG with roguelike elements. In fact the word “challenging” cannot express the virtual punishment you must endure if you wish to advance the plot within this game. And that is wholeheartedly a good thing since far too many RPGs hold your hands nowadays focusing on pure grinding instead of any strategic thinking. You can’t prevail in Pixel Heroes unless you combine pacience with experience gained from  the constant rinse and repeat pattern forced upon yourself by the title’s random encounters and especially the boss fights. You know a game is serious about its old-school heritage in terms of difficulty, when you find out there’s a cemetery/memorial erected specifically for the (many) heroes you have lost during the constant battles. This approach is similar to the one used in the XCOM series and indeed the permanent death of squad members is a type of incentive, even if I dislike it. The game is more than decently priced for all that it offers in terms of Steam auxiliaries as well as replay value. Sometimes when a game is too hard, it juggles with both your frustration and your ambition to overcome any obstacle with as few rage quits as possible. Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic is just as such, a game which evokes a bygone era in which no checkpoints or adjustable difficulty could save your injured pride, except for sheer determination to press forward and readjust your tactics.

+ Randomly generated assets and locations guarantee replayability.
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards.
+ Difficult to master but thoroughly enjoyable afterwards.
+ Humorous dialogue.
- “Permadeath” as a learning process.

Been playing MW:O since Closed Beta 2+ years ago. Compared to back then, the game has GREATLY improved, despite what many other naysayers will complain about. Yes, the game still needs improvements, and after PGI dropped IGP as a partner, their rate of improving the game has increased. A few things I would like to state for the new player:
1. When you first start out, you will be a Cadet, you will have a Cadet Bonus added to your C-Bill rewards. After your 25th match, you will lose this bonus and will make the same average as any other veteran player. Your match performance influences how much per match you are rewarded, and it will seem like it is not much. This is one thing I hope PGi alters, as I feel the C-Bill grind is too grindy.
2. As a new player, you most likely WILL get killed often and quickly as you learn the game. Run through the new Tutorial in the Academy to get more familiar with the controls first. It's easy to learn, but will take a lot of time to get skilled enough to face off against the more competitive players. Many interactions with other players can be similar to who you face in other multiplayer games. You will have the elites, the trolls, players who complain just to complain, etc. Yes there may be cheaters involved as well, but PGI has already caught many previously. Don't let these kind of players discourage you. Play legit and their due may eventually come.
3. I mentioned the C-Bill grind, and it can feel long and tedious. Light mechs can cost around a couple million C-Bills, while assaults can be over 15 million at the high end. Weapons are cheap in comparison but module add-ons range from 2 mil - 6 mil a pop. Public queue matches net about 200k+ on a win and up depending on how good your match score is. Faction Warfare matches can net about 400k+ on average for a win. EXP grind also exists, as each mech will accrue EXP after each match that you can use to unlock skills (though it's the same tree for every mech, so real variety or unique customization yet until PGI finally redoes the skill tree as they plan to do).
4. I don't recommend playing Faction Warfare as a new player yet. Think of FW as the 'end game' like in most MMORPGs. This is where a lot of the skilled competitive players drop into and can be very frustrating for a new player as your best shot includes fully mastered mechs kitted out with add-on modules as well as dropping in groups with fellow pilots.
5. Units. They are similar to guilds. Look on the MWO forums for recruitment and try to join one at some point. Dropping with a group not only provides better teamwork and communication, but can make the game more enjoyable than trying to drop solo. However, the public queue does have solo players and grouped players in separate queues, so if you drop solo, at least you will fight against other solo players and will have to rely on the in game VOIP to communicate.
6. One big thing I've seen said a lot over the time of MWO is regarding the F2P side of it. It is COMPLETELY F2P as almost every mech, module, and weapon can be bought with C-Bills. The only ones that require Mech Credits (MC) are the Hero (H) and Champion (C) variants. Heros have unique loadouts and hardpoints from the standards and will have a 30% C-Bill boost. Champions are the exact same hardpoints only with a different weapon loadout from the standard version of the same variant, but will have a 30% EXP boost. MCs are purchased with real money for the larger amounts, however you may obtain smaller increments of free MCs during events. Many will claim many of the MC bought mechs and the pre-order mech packs are P2W, but this is COMPLETELY NOT TRUE and does not guarantee your success. YOUR PLAYING SKILL IS ALL THAT MATTERS. If you don't believe me, buy a hero mech as a new player and see how well you do with it and compare it to others. Sure there are some mechs better than others, but many of them can be bought with the free almighty C-Bills. Paying real money for mech heroes just gives you more options for a mech, or in the case of pre-orders, the ability to play the newer standard variant mechs before they are released for C-Bill purchase by anyone, or simply to save time from grinding out the C-Bills to buy them for free.

Tough to get into, but worth it if you're a fan of tactical mech games like Chromehounds or even tactical shooters. I'm a founder and have probably 1000hrs played off Steam. Get into a clan or get someone to help you out if you're new. IGN: Haunt Steiner - add me if you want help and you're new.
PROS and CONS
+ Lots of different mechs with different variants of each chassis and many have specific quirks that alter their playstyle a bit. The amount of mechs you can pilot is large.
+ Building an effective mech is a challenge. You will spend hours messing with every detail and tweaking a build, testing it in matches, and going back to the garage for more tweaks.
+ Situational awareness will carry you pretty far, as well as being a team player.
+ The community is really great. There are people who can be really salty about the game's management over the past few years, but most of them are just really die-hard battletech fans who want a really great modern addition to the Mechwarrior franchise.
CONS
- Recent balance patches have changed this recently, but the evolution of the meta-game has been really rocky. Mixed weapon type loadouts used to be laughably bad. Clan mechs were king. Lasers+Gauss were king. Missles were a joke. Some variants had ridiculous quirks that were the only reason they were competitive. The new balance patch seems to have shaken the meta up and things are still developing as people figure out what works or not.
- Some weapons are just plain bad. Recent balance patch has changed this a bit but flamers and MGs and sometimes AC/2s are still a waste of space.
- Some mechs need rescaling in order to be competitive. This is announced and coming soon.
- There are people with aimbots and other hacks out there, rarely. They're easy enough to spot because they always aim center mass on any mech and seem "locked" there. Just report them.
- Mech packs are expensive. Recent classic packs aren't so bad because they come with 30 days prem time and a bunch of other goodies along with 3 variants. You don't really need to buy them if you can wait for them to be released for in game currency.
It's a fun game, play it but expect a long skill curve. I think I spent my first month or two without ANY KILLS back in 2013.

High praises to the developers for bringing these stompy robots from my childhood to life. There is really nothing like this on the market. The depth of mech customization, strategic combat, and beautifully detailed mechs combines to form an exemplary strategically minded shooter.
There is really nothing like catching the gleam of the sun bounce off your shoulder mounted Autocannon20, while your mech wades through the steamy swamp lands of Viridian Bog. Hearing the heavy bass rock out through the basin as you unlease a round of AC20 into the cockpit of a unsuspecting light mech, now a steaming pile of salvage. All the while reflecting on the satisfaction of this moment, you realize this accomplishment was achieved in your own custom war machine tailored to your very own play style.
I have played this game since Closed Beta and have been with the developers through the thick and thin. And although there was a rocky start, with some questionable decisions, both the game itself and the developers of the game have grown to a level comparable with even established industry megaliths. To this day, the developers have an attitude geared towards improvement, they are very open to suggestions and player needs.
Pros:
- hundreds of beautiful stompy robots
- countless loadout customization options
- countless cosmetic options
- engaging rewarding combat
- free to play
- loyal, passionate player base. Large amounts of amazing player created fan art.
- strong engaging competitive scene. Player run teams have their own emblems, unit tags, etc.
- responsive devs. president will personally respond to your tweets and concerns/design ideas
Cons:
- high real money pricing for mechs (not an issue because they can be bought with ingame currency anyway)
- development pace is on the slower side
- development history was bad due to conflict of interest from publisher (Infinite Games Publishing) who just wanted a minimally viable product that makes money vs. game developers (Pirhana Games Inc.) who wanted to make a good game. Good thing is, PGI won out in the end, and we can see the result is a good game.
This game has kept me entertained for almost 3 years now, and I continue to eagerly watch this game grow and evolve.
But don't just take my word for it, try it out for yourself!

I have logged over 5000 matches in pug games.  God knows how many CW.  The hours I've put into this are staggaring.  My review is as follows:
FIRST, a TLDR for you:
Game balance is better than it's ever been but it's still heavily in development.  It has an extremely punishing learning curve but is immensely rewarding once you get through it.  DO NOT BUY PERFORMANCE PACKS! THEY ARE TERRIBLE!  Buy Mastery Packs or for best value the Black Knight package of Resistance 2.  Join a unit!  It makes the game much better (personally I recommend
.  And don't even think about dropping in Faction Warfare until you have 4 mechs mastered!  Think of it as end game content!
Mechwarrior Online features giant robots fighting each other.  There are two types of mechs: Clan and Inner Sphere.  Each of those have 4 weight classes: Light, Medium, Heavy and Assault.  Clan mechs in general have longer range, higher alpha and are faster.  Inner Sphere mechs are tougher and there is a far greater variety.  They also receive "quirks" which help them balance against clans.
I have to say I don't enjoy playing Clan mechs, the game feels too easy in them as they are usually more powerful than the IS counterparts.  There's a large community for both sides so it comes down to preference.

Cons:

EDIT:
Apparently, there appeared to have been some more to this controller than I thought. While I no longer have mine, a friend of mine informed me that one can adjust the settings of the controller in great detail. If I had known, my review might have had a different outcome. Original review:
Okay, so I bought a Steam Controller and got it this week. Unfortunately, it is not what I had expected. While the size of the controller is extremely pleasant and the grip buttons were actually an innovative, handy addition, the right trackpad made the controller unusable.
I tried working with it in several different games, but the trackpad simply was not accurate enough to be able to play any first person game. Aiming is undoable, especially in fast paced games. While I'm sure that there are games out there that could be played with this controller, any other controller with a second joystick instead of a trackpad would be a better choice, in my opinion. And if you really want a trackpad so that you can use it as a mouse, I would advice you to link a PS4 controller to your computer, which is what I have done now.
Something else that I noticed was that the trackpad was a strain on my thumb and the "haptic" feedback was little too powerful for my comfort.
I would advice you to buy any other controller instead and save yourself the shipping costs of returning this one.

I find the gameplay overall to be a unique, slower paced, more strategic type of shooter.  It's got some mechanics that try to be more "simulator-y" like having to lock targets, having heat buildup and dissipate, sensors and jammers and stuff.  It sound's complicated and it is a bit to learn if you're not familiar with the MechWarrior series, but it's a lot of fun.
You can totally customize your mech's loadout, from weapons to armor, sensors, heat sinks, etc.  I seriously will play with making builds for extended periods of time, just because it's a lot of fun.
They recently changed the way quickplay maps and gamemodes are chosen, where it's a voting thing where you get multipliers for not getting the map you want, making your vote stronger.  It lead to the pre-match map selection being a kind of minigame of it's own.  It's a lot of fun.
It's free!  F2P, but not P2W, can buy any of what people consider the best mechs within a few games after doing the tutorial, no grinding to unlock them like Warthunder or World of Tanks.  I enjoy the crap out of MW:O.  If you're looking for 31st century big stompy robot arena combat, you've found your game!  Okay, that's a little niche, but give it a shot.  It's a lot of fun.

I've been playing this game for quite some time.
There have been rough patches.  Ok...  Everything up until PGI started self publishing by way of buying out their publisher's rights (as I understand it) was pretty rough.  This happened roughly mid-2014.  Since then PGI has made huge leaps forwards in all of the ways we F2P gamers like.  They listen to the community, the give a rip about balance, they implement requested features, they give stuff away regularly...  A whole list more if I really sat down to think about it.
If you haven't played MechWarrior before you can look at this game like a more tactical and technical version of something like WoT.  It's the thinking man's shooter so to speak and there's a class for everyone.  In this game it's not just Small, Medium, Heavy and Assault sized mechs.  Within each Mech class you'll find multiple chassis that play quite differently as well as specialize in firly significantly different ways.  At first they will seem quite similar and I can't argue...  they are until you understand the nuances of the game play.  To understand this well you would do well to join one of the large houses or Mercenary corps (Guild/League etc...).  Only then will you begine to have a real understanding of how each mech fits into it's role on the battlefield as well as how your skills as a MechWarrior fit into a battlefield scenario.  It is tons of fun to jump in alone and blast some enemies for sure...  But when you jump into a proper 4-12 pilot group and work together on TS with a dedicated drop commander and team structure the whole thing really comes alive.
You'll have a drop commander calling tactics and sometimes targets, You'll have a scout lance scouting and relaying that info to the drop commander and in many groups you'll also have a shot caller prioritizing battlefield threats and calling their location and chassis type to the group.  I can't even explain how intense it can get but suffice to say...  I feel it's the best example of a team based tactical shooter available.  Check these out just to whet your appetite...
<---  Mild Language
As far as P2W...  Nope.
There ARE mechs in a specific chassis line that can be bought that are very slightly better than the non-pay variants of chassis in that line BUT...
Whether or not they are better depends on pilot play style and role needs.  They are never just strictly better than any other mech that can fulfil a specific role.  Not only that but there are ALWAYS choices in the free mechs (which are the vast majority of mechs) that are just as effective and in most cases better.  Also...  In this case "better" is simply defined as things like slightly better weapon placement or hardpoint loadouts that let you do specific build types that variants of that specific chassis can't do, but other mechs chassis CAN do.  So mostly it's just that someone might want to run a specific build with a specific mech so they buy the "hero" version of the mech.  If they didn't want to they will be able to find another chassis that will fulfill the role.
As far as support the developer is STILL making new maps, new game modes, new mechs, significant feature additions and updates and balance changes.  Not to mention that they have hinted at single player and coop campaign modes.
The future looks very bright for MWO :).

First thing first; let's talk about the trackpads. Left trackpad is nearly pointless for most games. It feels terrible for character movement and the analog stick is clearly superior for this task. The right trackpad is superior to an analog stick for camera movement, however. You can feel the difference in FPS games, and even in action RPG games like Dark Souls 3, camera movement can be much more responsive and faster depending on your choice of sensitivity.
Though. the trackpad is unnecessarily huge and actually becomes detrimental. At times, you will lose your sense of positioning of your finger on the pad and start to second-guess yourself: "Is my thumb touching the top-right area of the pad or is it... oh nevermind my character just moved backwards." The huge trackpad also forces the ABYX-buttons to be too far away from reach. I have to sometimes look at my controller to see if I'm hitting the X-button instead of the B-button.
The analog stick feels pretty good. It is not too slippery like the Sony Dualshock 4 sticks. However, because the controller is quite big, the analog stick placement makes it uncomfortable to use. You have to really reach out there with your thumb in order to grip it, This design works for the Dualshock 4 due to its small frame, but the Steam controller is on that McDonalds diet in comparison.
This controller is pretty good from a hardware perspective, but I see it as a beta product in its current form. The ergonomics can be improved. The trackpad can be made smaller, and in return, a higher sensitivity configuration can compesate for the loss of surface area. And we know that smaller surface area means higher awareness of your finger placement on the trackpad as well as a closer placement of the ABYX-buttons in respect to the right trackpad, allowing the player to focus on the screen instead of looking at his/her controller. I also feel that the left trackpad should either be removed, or made smaller so that it can be placed where the current analog stick resides; And in contrast, move the analog stick to where the left trackpad currently resides at. Even more, I would give the user the option to choose either a traditional d-pad or a trackpad with a modular design.
It is a good controller even with these flaws, but I would recommend waiting for a revision to address these design issues.

Came for the cute, stayed for the gameplay.
Rabi-Ribi is a fun and colourfully-designed metroidvania game that's surprisingly addicting. The background music is incredibly catchy (my personal favourite is the Winter Wonderland track), the overall art design is well done, and the controls are tight.
All in all, this game really stands out from the rest of the moe-moe game crowd, in that it delivers exceptionally well in the gameplay department.

In short, Rabi-Ribi is amongst the best games on Steam and it's certainly one of the best games released in the past few years.
That, of course, is assuming that you're into things like Super Metroid, Castlevania, Megaman or even Ikaruga/Touhou and the like. It's a beautiful mix of genres bundled in a thoroughly charming package. Don't be mistaken, though, this isn't really a waifu game at its core despite it having cute art and adorable character designs across the board. It's difficult and not for the faint of heart but if you can withstand a bit of a challenge you'll find yourself rewarded rather handsomely with what feels like a never-ending enjoyable experience.
Through increased difficulty levels and the free-form nature of the game (you can explore the world and fight bosses in whatever order you wish so long as you're capable of executing some more advanced movement techniques without the respective items) there's a ton of replayability. Some of the achievements require you to do what's seemingly nearly impossible which is fantastic for anyone seeking a challenge (true boss rush, no-damage boss runs, etc).
Notably, though, I have to mention that the combat isn't like any other platformers; it's actually very fluid and feels almost fighting game-esque in execution. Movement and pattern recognition is the key to success in Rabi-Ribi.
I could ramble on for hours about how I have absolutely no cons to point out about the game and how it's genuinely fantastic and well worth your time and money but I'll spare everyone from that.
Did I mention it has already gotten numerous free content updates/support from the devs? Yeah. It just can't be beaten. Support CreSpirit, GemaYue and Sekai Project and your need for a thoroughly enjoyable game in 2016 and pick Rabi-Ribi up. You won't regret it, I promise.

It's 2AM, and I got out of bed to write this review because I couldn't stop thinking about how GOOD this game actually is.
Protip: I don't normally do that.
For the TL;DR people: Rabi-Ribi is what you get when you combine a *true* metroidvania platformer with a deft touch of bullet hell and combo-based brawler, wrapped up in a fanservice-flavored anime shell. What makes Rabi-Ribi great is that it understands the heart of these genres, and provides the best of each experience without falling into any of their respective pitfalls.
Because I want to get back to my soft, warm bed, I’ll finish the rest of this review in list form. I hope you understand.
(+) The controls are tight and responsive. Characters somehow manage to strike an intuitive balance between floatiness and the immediate start-stop nature of older platformers, such as the original Mario or Metroid games, though it is heavily balanced toward the latter’s pinpoint accuracy.
(+) Hitstun and knockback are minor enough to avoid notice or frustration, but can still provide a challenge in the right places.
(+) A large variety of useful attacks means that combat is more dynamic and strategic than most platformers, and the main use for every attack is immediately obvious while the more nuanced applications trickle easily into the consciousness during bullet-hell bossfights.
(+) The bullet-hell segments of the game (mostly the boss fights) are unique to each enemy, but all of their attack patterns are easy to learn while being difficult to successfully dodge.
(+) The difficulty is nicely balanced, and can be adjusted to the player’s skill level. I have limited experience with true bullet-hell games, but was able to clear all of the boss segments on ‘normal’ difficulty with only a moderate number of deaths late into the game.
(+) Secrets are hidden everywhere, and while some of them are immediately available, most of them will require back-tracking once the player has gained new attacks or mobility options. The game has the same sense of exploration as Metroid’s hunt for the power-ups, but doesn’t require the same ulcer-inducing level of perfection to reach them that Metroid did.
(+) Each new area is interesting to look at, and makes you feel you’re exploring an entirely different area of the game. Part of this due to the amazing visual and aural variety, but another large (and often unnoticed) part is due to how the level design itself changes to suit every environment of the game.
(+) The character animations are all unique, beautiful and clear in their intent and purpose.
(+) The soundtrack nicely accents the game, without distracting from it.
(?) The character designs are all fanservice-based. This can be good or bad depending on your preference, but I know I spent the first five hours of the game with my door locked out of embarrassment. After having played the game though, I would say they add more to the game’s unique charm and style than the embarrassment takes away.
(?) The writing is filled with all the worst anime tropes, but it’s done intentionally and playfully. Again, it adds more to the game’s unique and cheerful style than it takes away.
(-) The game does have a few performance issues, usually in areas where there’s a lot going on in the background. I only noticed this a couple of times during gameplay though, and it never slowed the game down more than 30%, so it was easily still playable.
In closing, this game is not Metroid. Comparing this game to Metroid is like comparing Fallout: NV to Skyrim – they may have a lot of similarities in the engine, but that’s where the similarities end. It does, however, have everything that made Metroid great to begin with, and brings the difficulty down to a manageable level where a 100% run can feel like a reasonable challenge. The execution on this genre mish-mash is nearly flawless, and the developers' love for the game is apparent with every well-placed easter egg and nerdy reference. And the best part is that it takes only the cream from each genre, and blends them perfectly into its own style.

Tribes: Ascend is the long awaited sequel to the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise. In this installment, Sega have decided to scrap Sonic's anthropromorphic qualities, and instead recreate him as a human in control of a faction of warriors known as the Diamond Sword. Sonic now wears power armour, and wields weapons such as swords and guns. They tried this in Shadow the Hedgehog, and it didn't work then. Frankly I'm saddened to see Sega trying to take Sonic back down this dark and gritty route.
True to the series, the game puts a large amount of emphasis on speed. You will spend a lot of time moving around the levels at high speed, attemping to collect flags instead of the franchises classic rings. The game offers no explaination for why you're doing this, and gives you no reward other than the satisfaction of having defeated the other team. The game also gives you the choice of playing as members of Sonic's team, who are quite honestly extremely boring to play as. I mean, this is Sonic! Why Sega would add these slow, clunky characters to a game about speed is beyond me.
The story is also very unimaginative. Instead of fighting the regular antagionist, Dr. Eggm-Robotnik, you are now fighting against Sonic's former ally, Knuckles, who has assumed control of an opposing faction known as the Blood Eagles. In an interesting twist, the game has no single player story mode. The story is told entirely through multiplayer games, where the players themselves get to choose the character's dialogue. However, this is easily abused by other players, who instead opt to spam the same dialogue choices over and over. I mean, come on, this isn't a Bioware game guys. So unfortunately, you may miss out on some of the games more meaningful and rich conversations.
Overall, Tribes: Ascend is an unimpressive addition to the Sonic series. I fear we will never see a Sonic game as good as Sonic 2006 ever again.

So many EA titles are a trashy mess but this is the most polished EA release I've played since Darkest Dungeon. Potential bypass for crashes:
As it is tradition for me, I pretty much bought this game on release, as I really enjoy the series. However, I kept crashing with a familiar 'Sorry: Application has crashed.'
I waited for a possible patch to fix the crash issues, but it never came. Now, in December, I finally decided to start playing again, regardless. I fell victim to the crashes, losing a bit of progress, forcing me to spend less time enjoying and grinding dungeons, but more time trying to find a save point before I crashed again.
This review isn't so much on the game (which is really good, by the way. Best in the series.), but an awareness post for people looking to enjoy some Nep-Nep, but can't get past the crashing.
Like many others probably have (or not.), I've found a 'bypass' for the 'Sorry: Application has crashed' problem.
DO NOT click okay on the message.
Click back onto the main game tab, and you can continue playing as normal. The game will 'crash' and show the message again, but just repeat and click back into the game.
Hope this helps for those who are paranoid about crashes, and can't properly enjoy some quality time with Neptune and the gang.

This game has not been patched since shortly after release (~5 months at the time of this review) and still currently suffers from major stability isssues, frequent crashing, and other game-breaking issues:
- The game has frequent issues with many NVidia Geforce GTX-series cards, even ones far above the minimum/recommended specs, and will crash every 10-20 minutes due to memory leaks. This can even happen to some users with AMD cards, from reports on the forum.
- The game is horribly optimized and will also crash many integrated Intel GPUs that are otherwise more than capable of running the game, in particular one long dungeon very early in the game called Sakura Park.
- The game is lacking a Japanese-only balance patch that fixes glaring oversights regarding the game's combat system and scaling, namely with activated skills and EXE drives (aka. hypers) falling off into complete uselessness past the early game.
- There is frequent stuttering and delay within the menus that can lead to crashes, especially with one of the graphics cards mentioned above. One of the July patches that IFI released helped the problem and made the stuttering far less noticeable, but it still happens.
However, the abandonment of this game by the devs is particularly concerning, as IFI has done this once in the past. A previous game in the series, Neptunia Re:Birth2, saw IFI completely drop support for it while the game suffered from constant crashes, rolled back several problematic attempted fixes, and then did nothing for the rest of the game's lifespan. It still has not been patched.
Overlooking the problems, Neptunia VII is a surprisingly good RPG with a long and indepth (if silly and whimsical) storyline, decent humor, and moderately challenging fights. I have been a fan of the series for years, but VII's abandonment by its developers in spite of its balance issues and lack of stability means I can't easily recommend this to anyone looking for a complete experience, especially not with this pricetag.

--NEP REVIEW PART 2: ATTACK OF THE ROBO GE-GES--
Okay, so now I've cleared my first run of the game and can say a bit more. Even on a regular ending, the plot was quite enjoyable! I liked a lot of the jokes and references the game makes, some were unexpected.
The difficulty never ramped up, it actually got much easier, haha. If you use the scouting system strategically (AKA you put the experience booster wherever you are) you level up far above what's required through a little grinding. That said, I greatly appreciate the ability to fast forward/skip battle animations, with how easily my party of waifus obliterated foes battles would take literally a handful of seconds. Combine that with certain characters and their abilities and you're able to tank through dungeons with barely any problems as long as you pay attention.
Got to NG+ where you can literally bring everything over progress wise (including all your end game party members unlocked from the beginning!!) so I can unlock the true ending, and they hand you all sorts of bonuses to make your second run faster, I can already tell. Props that they make multi-runs accessible, now I can dig into the other systems of the game I basically ignored without having to trudge through the game again. Smart thinking!
Final-Final thoughts are it's not a particularly challenging RPG for those willing to bite down deep with its systems, but it is a particularly-outstandingly fun one. I did feel like my goddess-like (CPU humor!) power was the result of my own planning, so I was proud of my first run. Totes fun, ya'll. Oh, and it took me 34 hours to clear the game due to super-over-levelling at the end. (Hint: The colosseum is an amazing grind spot for EXP and money, I leveled 6 times in an hour)
--Original Review from 19 Hours in--
Nep's been my closet enjoyment for the last couple of years since deciding to try it from watching my friend get the first remake of Re;birth 1, and this is the one I can definitively say is what you want out of the series. I'll admit that when I played the first few in the Re;birth series I liked the concept of the world and its characters, but that the game flow (primarily being so attached to the guild quest structure) didn't feel very cohesive. Re;birth 3 started getting better, and now we've got this one on our hands. It's finally clicked!
Maybe it just took me multiple games, but now all the systems the game has in place makes sense. You'll get the hang of the attack combo system, investing in your nations, and grinding your way to (as of now!) powering a hole into those bosses. The writing is getting better with each entry too, and the VAs really give their perfomances a lot of heart for something like this (I'm a bit biased towards my lord waifu Nepgear, but ya know).
If you're someone like me, getting past the fan service hurdles can be some mental hopskotch, but there's nothing quite like mashing your way through that obligatory bath shot still screen to avoid family judgment while still trying to comprehend what's being said. Keeps you on your toes!
TL;DR the jokes are better, references are abound, and gameplay is totally up to snuff. Judgment by your friends and love ones can be healed with time and acceptance towards your strange, new hobby and you'll be all the better for it.

Overall I enjoyed this game. I would describe it as a light dungeon crawl with enough depth to be fun for a while, but not so much that it is a chore to play. This game gives you a good flavor of old-school rpgs, but without some of the long slogs that come with most of them.
Pros:
+ Huge variety of classes means you can mix and match different parties for variety
+ Getting wiped out seems to almost be encouraged, taking some of the stress out of traditional dungeon crawling
+ Good sense of humor lightens the game
+ I thought the graphics added to the whimsy of the game. They did a nice job embracing the whole retro pixelated thing.
+ A single adventure only takes a few hours (or until you die). This means the game is long enough to get attached to your party, but short enough that it doesn't get stale.
Cons:
- Character leveling system is too simple. Once you figure out what works, the creativity in how you assign skill points or choose your party evaporates.
- Although there are many character classes, a few of them are just objectively the best if you are actually playing to win.
- The dungeons are all fairly similar, and you run the same dungeons during every play through. This makes the game get repetitive from one adventure to the next. It kept my attention for long enough that I played through all three campaigns, but I feel like I played it out.
Its just a ...meh! game. Gets old really quickly.

This game is stupid. Random number generators govern everything. It's a game all about tactics, chosing when who to attack with, trying to guess what's coming next, but the lack of tactical depth is ridiculous.
- Why can you not leave a dungeon once entering?
- Why can you not reorder the position of your party?
- Why can you not use health items in combat?
- Why can the enemy attack three times in a row, but you are limited to once, and cannot use the same character twice in a row?
- Why are characters and quests randomly generated, making it impossible to predict what you will face in an upcoming dungeon?
Some may defend this as an old school roguelike, but in old school rougelikes you have to play smart, and are rewarded for doing so. Failure means something- you learn from every mistake. In this game once you enter a dungeon, you just hope for the best, and hope the randomly generated characters you picked at the start can beat the boss (whose hit-points are hidden, for some reason?) after 6 or so randomly generated fights.
Winning doesn't feel like winning, it feels like blind luck. Don't waste your time with this game.
