Back in the 90s, shooters were all the rage. They were fast and furious, with none of the slower, sneaky, stealthy, cover-based gameplay of today’s modern shooters. The days of Quake and Unreal Tournament were glorious times – but sadly, there have been very few fast-paced shooters of any real quality recently.
But one developer – called Edge of Reality – has been beavering away on a new shooter called Loadout which aims to bring back some of the twitchy shooter gameplay of the good old days. I’ll admit that this game completely slipped under my radar until a few weeks ago, and the fact that it’s free-to-play didn’t exactly get me too enthused. There’s bound to be some caveat; there always is with F2P, right?
Loadout is purely multiplayer: there’s no campaign and no♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about. It’s a good old shooter that’s played over multiple game modes that we’re all familiar with, but with a twist to their names and objectives. Blitz (control points), Death Snatch (grab points dropped by killed opponents), Extraction (gather Blutonium) and Jackhammer (CTF) are all available on the game’s four maps that released when it launched.
Loadout
Lots of leaping around is required
Oddly enough, Edge of Reality decided that Loadout would work best as a third-person shooter. When the gameplay is fast you want to see everything around you and not necessarily your own back, so I thought the view in Loadout would be a real hindrance to my less-than-excellent FPS abilities. The good news is that third-person actually works really well and it’s something you don’t even notice after playing for a while. But why third-person?
The only reason I can think of as to why this is not a first-person shooter is the game’s art style. Edge of Reality have created a game that shares visual similarities with Team Fortress 2, focusing on being cartoony and over-the-top. There are currently three (excellent drawn and animated) characters to choose from: the Sly Stallone look-alike Axl, the Mr. T-inspired T-Bone, and the rather hideous Helga. There’s been a lot of care and attention put into these characters and that’s important when you’re playing a game that uses customisation as a selling point.
Loadout
We go all Disco because it makes you a better shot. OK, that’s a lie.
But it’s not just the characters. Loadout‘s big selling point, apart from being free-to-play, is that you can heavily customise your weapons. There are four basic weapon types: the laser-like Beam, the explosive Launchers, the bullet-spewing Rifle, and the cannonball-launching Pulse. These are the base weapons players build upon to make new and interesting tools of destruction.
As there are no classes in Loadout the weapons play an integral part in how you build your characters. For example: you can be a healer by creating a Beam weapon that fires healing rays, or you could become a sniper by equipping a powerful scope on one of the base weapons. The way you customise your weapons is down to you. That’s why the game is called Loadout. Genius.
Each player can create their new weapons, give them a unique name and then create a loadout (there it is again) from their array of created weapons to take with them into matches. These loadouts are selected at the start of a match but can also be switched mid-game when you die. There’s huge scope for experimentation, and it’s trial-and-error as to whether you can actually kill stuff with your creation. What looks like a good weapon on paper could be utter crap, depending on your skill level.
Loadout
Our first attempt at weapons.
Not all the weapon enhancements are available at the beginning of the game, as most need to be unlocked by playing and levelling up your profile. The more you play, the more you’re rewarded with the game’s main currency – Blutes – which can be spent to unlock new enhancements. There’s no pay-to-win rubbish on weapon enhancements, but there is a tech tree which has to be opened up to access new weapon features. This unlocking system is a problem when you want to try a new weapon feature but you can’t because it’s further up the tree. You’ll need to keep playing to earn more Blutes and possibly spend them in areas you may not necessarily want to, just to reach your goal.
The game’s other currency is SpaceBux, and this is where real cash comes into play. The main use for this currency is character customisation such as new outfits or emotes. You can ignore this completely and just play the game, but if you want to stand out then the quickest way is to drop some cash. The problem is that it’s not cheap, which is a real shame because the items that are available look great.
As an example, £13.99 will give you 16000 SpaceBux. A helmet costs around 1499 SB, a toothpick is 999 SB and a pair of Assless pants is 8999 SB. For your £13.99 you may get one really cool outfit but not much else. If you want to look the business in-game, then you’re paying top dollar for it.
Perhaps a rethink on some of the pricing would be a good idea, as everyone would enjoy seeing more visually appealing characters playing, and not loads of players using the three standard characters and outfits. That said, anyone who sticks with Loadout will probably think it’s money well spent.
SpaceBux can also be spent on an XP boost for periods of time to help unlock stuff on the tech tree quicker or to add extra loadout slots. If you really want to start messing about with the customisation then it’s quicker to do it that way, but again, it costs more. Damn you F2P!
Character customisation and emotes in action
Loadout is new and it’s got potential but it’s too early to say whether it will be embraced by shooter fans due to the fact there are only four maps and everyone is still finding their feet. Having sunk quite a few hours into the game now (and failed miserably at topping the end-of-match leaderboards) I’ve found it pretty enjoyable for a quick fix each day.
Messing around with the weapons is fun but it can be time-consuming to find the right fit as not every addition is useful on all base weapons, and the fact you need to keep playing to unlock more weapon features up the tech tree could get tiresome. If you’re a shooter whizz then you’ll probably be racking up the kills so this won’t be an issue for you – you just need to stick at it.
Edge of Reality has created a tasty shooter with fantastic customisation but it’s going to be down to the individual as to whether they can stick with it for long enough to really make good use of the potential within. Free-to-play isn’t easy to get right and I’m not sure if Edge of Reality has completely nailed it. They have to make money somehow, but the items are overpriced and progression may be a little frustrating for less-than-stellar players who doesn’t want to part with cash. If, on the other hand, you don’t really give a toss about buying stuff, then this is still a shooter worth your time.
Monetisation aside, the game plays well, the maps are well designed, and the characters are great. The funny emotes will probably wear thin eventually and the death animations will become old hat, but with the addition of more content like maps and game modes, Loadout has a fighting chance to gather a following – even if it’s not doing anything super-original.
It’s a refreshing change to be playing a speedy shooter like the good old days, and with Loadout being free-to-play, it’s certainly worth a shot. Boom boom.

(more especifically the Director's Cut) was one of my first games on Steam. A gift, I was actually a bit hesitant on accepting as I've never been a big fan of FPS. The RPG part made me go through the download size and didn't quite prepare me for the stealth. I believe it's more accurate to call
a stealth with FPS and RPG elements, as the first is the most proeminent trait.
As Adam Jensen, you're tasked with security in Sarif Inustries, a top notch corporation specialized in augmentations. Not too long after you started, however, the matrix (located in a 2027 Detroit) is attacked by a mysterious black ops squad and a number of questions rise as you're basically resuscitated by your employer. Seems like your typical cyberpunk setting, except it feels more realistic, more relatable. The secrets you come to know during Adam's journey for answers and revenge easily get you involved while one question is answered and another one is made. And as any person asking the dangerous questions, Adam does so mostly in the shadows. Even though the game offers a large range of strategical approaches and paths, the stealth mechanic can be more rewarding and fulfilling, not to mention lore friendly. On higher difficulties keeping a low profile is actually necessary as augmentations aren't enough to withstand a bulletstorm. Fear not, though, as you can literally be a ghost by taking full advantage of the incredible level design!
Not only the story is well written and filled with branches, but the artwork and soundtrack are some of the most relatable and beautiful in recent game history. The architecture feels unique and real, while the soundtrack tries to unite a feeling of old and new by mixing classic notes with electronic beats. It's easy to dive into
's universe and get lost in its mature themes, such as transhumanism.
Even though the experience is one worth having, it's still far from perfect. The Director's Cut came with a number of performance issues and bugs that -- after almost four years of the game's first release -- haven't yet been fixed by the developers. The game performers poorly on computers above its rcommended specifications and fixing it is no easy task. Still to this day there's no definitive method for AMD users to get completely rid of stuttering and small FPS drops, not to mention a proper (official or from the community) fix for the various bugs that lurk around the corners -- one of which got me frustrated and made me leave the game aside for more than a year. This might be one of those cases where you have to ignore the performance issues to fully enjoy the game, as
is not a proper PC title/port.
If you like cyberpunk themes and stealth games,
is a safe bet. And even if you're not particularly interested in what the game has to offer, it might surprise you!

First thing first; let's talk about the trackpads. Left trackpad is nearly pointless for most games. It feels terrible for character movement and the analog stick is clearly superior for this task. The right trackpad is superior to an analog stick for camera movement, however. You can feel the difference in FPS games, and even in action RPG games like Dark Souls 3, camera movement can be much more responsive and faster depending on your choice of sensitivity.
Though. the trackpad is unnecessarily huge and actually becomes detrimental. At times, you will lose your sense of positioning of your finger on the pad and start to second-guess yourself: "Is my thumb touching the top-right area of the pad or is it... oh nevermind my character just moved backwards." The huge trackpad also forces the ABYX-buttons to be too far away from reach. I have to sometimes look at my controller to see if I'm hitting the X-button instead of the B-button.
The analog stick feels pretty good. It is not too slippery like the Sony Dualshock 4 sticks. However, because the controller is quite big, the analog stick placement makes it uncomfortable to use. You have to really reach out there with your thumb in order to grip it, This design works for the Dualshock 4 due to its small frame, but the Steam controller is on that McDonalds diet in comparison.
This controller is pretty good from a hardware perspective, but I see it as a beta product in its current form. The ergonomics can be improved. The trackpad can be made smaller, and in return, a higher sensitivity configuration can compesate for the loss of surface area. And we know that smaller surface area means higher awareness of your finger placement on the trackpad as well as a closer placement of the ABYX-buttons in respect to the right trackpad, allowing the player to focus on the screen instead of looking at his/her controller. I also feel that the left trackpad should either be removed, or made smaller so that it can be placed where the current analog stick resides; And in contrast, move the analog stick to where the left trackpad currently resides at. Even more, I would give the user the option to choose either a traditional d-pad or a trackpad with a modular design.
It is a good controller even with these flaws, but I would recommend waiting for a revision to address these design issues.

My two cents, short and sweet:
Will this replace my XB360 controller? No.
Is it an innovative, creative, and downright fun to use piece of hardware? H3LL YEAH IT IS!
Ive been using the standard dual stick style controller since the PS1 days, and after almost two decades of using this style of controller, I have essentially committed myself to only this style. It is a great product, and with plenty of practice, I am 100% positve you could be a better player than you could with your XB360 controller, After my first, practice round on Killing Floor 2, I had the basics down pretty well, and my end stats were not much lower than my usual performances. The fact of the matter is, I am just too darn set in my ways to bother learning and getting skilled with a new piece of equipment. I will say, most of my gaming is in the FPS spectrum, and I honestly think that this is where the controller shines THE LEAST. I have no doubt that other games, more specifically top-down or RTS games (which I don't play at all) like Civ, Stellaris, DOTA, etc would benefit much, much more from this type of controller, especially due to the NEAR LIMITLESS amount of flexibility and customization.
From a strictly hardware point of view, I will agree with other reviewers on the point that it does feel a bit wonky in your hands when you first grab it out of the box. Again, I surmise that this is because I've gotten so used to the dual-stick layout, so take it with a grain of salt. It is not impossible to get used to. Like i said in the first paragraph, after only one practice match on KF, I felt pretty at home with it in my hands. The extra buttons on the back and the "double tap" feature on the trackpads means less time moving your thumbs off the pad, and more time shooting sh!t in the face.
GRIPES I HAVE: They are nit picky, and minor, so don't let these put you off from trying it.
1. Because the trackpad registers every move of your thumb, fine aiming can be a little tricky. ADS seems too precice, for me, tends to wobble back and forth, registering every single movement, making headshots more difficult, but I am sure you could be a crack shot with more practice.
2. As of right now, there are no "overall" settings for the controller (That I could find). Any adjustments have to be made on a game-by-game basis.
3. Doesn't feel as sturdy as my XB360 controller. Don't take this to mean that it feels flimsy, at all, because it doesnt. It feels well constructed, but my 360 feels like a brick. I can drop it on accident and not immediately worry that it might be damaged. The Steam'troller, with its higher tech design, makes me want to baby it, and I would definitely be worried if it fell from the coffee table.
All that said, I would definitely pick it up if you have the spare cash lying around. It won't ever replace my 360 controller, but it will make a fine addition to my collection of toys.

As the name suggests, Pixel Heroes is a "retro" game with a fantasy theme. You begin the game in a tavern, where you need to hire 3 heroes out of the 8 that are available. Exit the tavern and talk to someone with an exclamation mark over their head, who will give you a quest. Your three person party then sets off on their adventure.
The quests in Pixel Heroes are random, as are the heroes you choose at the beginning. The game follows the "rogue-lite" trend by incorporating permadeath. The action is turn-based, with an encounter happening at each node on the world map, followed by a dungeon with a series of rooms and a boss at the end. After each encounter you get a random amount of gold, xp, and loot (also random to each playthrough), and your heroes level up as well. It is up to you to stat them out according to your needs and party composition, as well as give them the right gear for the dungeon you are going to. If you don't have the right gear on, certain fights are impossible and you WILL die, many times, before you either get lucky or memorize what fights require what gear.
Overall I find the game really fun so far. I finally beat the first campaign today so I consider myself a somewhat experienced player by now and I would say that if you like turn-based games, retro games, and games with any or all of the "rogue-lite" elements, then you will probably enjoy Pixel Heroes.

It only took the disappointment of Dead Rising 4 to appreciate this game. Originally I saw this game as a major departure compared to the prior games in the series, and while that's still true going back to it I've discovered this is a fun, but very flawed game.
Pros
Even for what was a 2013 Xbone launch title, it still looks really nice despite the grey brown color palette.
Movement is so much faster and smoother than it was in DR2, making combat much more enjoyable due to how satisfying the guns and weapons are to use
2 different story modes to appeal to fans who love either to be able to do everything or who love the crippling time management.
More zombie variety, and there are lots of them on screen at any one time.
Throwable items. Chucking a chainsaw at a zombie is never not satisfying.
Psychopaths unlike their botched version in DR4 are in here and there are some creative fights.
Has easily the most amount of content in the series, there are lots of sidequests, challenges, collectables, and once you're done with the main game you also have the DLCs to do (which carry your level from the main game and actually tie nicely to main story.) When it goes on sale, you get a lot of bang for your buck.
Cons
You really need a good PC to run this game at a consistent framerate, or on higher graphical settings
Lockers and car stations remove a lot of the challenge since you can easily spawn powerful weapons/combo cars which make zombies feel like cannon fodder.
The world is annoying to navigate due to the amount of roadblocks there are.
Main story doesn't go anywhere as interesting as prior titles and only really picks up by the very end. It also felt like it tried to end the story of the first two games very abruptly.
Though the it's nice there are two story mode options, the main mode gives you too much time to do everything, and Nightmare Mode gives you too little time to do everything due to how much faster time goes by. Psychopaths also feel too much like damage sponges in nightmare mode while are complete cake walks in the regular story mode.
Ultimately the changes made in this game influenced Dead Rising 4 for the worst.
I would still recommend playing the first two titles considering the amount of callbacks there are in this game and since I had more enjoyment with them, but if you want a fun zombie game and you see this on sale, definitely give it a look.

For whatever reason, they decided that the game be fixed at 30 FPS unless you do a small edit within the game's files. The devs claim that it may cause issues but from my experience, having the frame rate unlocked caused less issues in terms of gameplay and technicalities but regardless, issues remain. Aiming with anything can get stuttery, the physics for vehicles can get weird, the UI can change involuntarily, etc.
The graphics, most of the lighting, and animations are all pretty great. For most of the game though, I've had environmental textures not load properly until a few seconds later when I'm near them. I'm pretty sure that's the result of the game having the loading screens only when you load a checkpoint, quit to the main menu, and when you continue/start a game so the map transitions supposedly become seemless so to speak.
Both KB+M and a controller play very well and can even be used simultaneously so it's just left up to preference on what you want to use. Rebinding keys, however, is somehow more complicated than it should be.
The story of the game I find to be only mildly interesting, or at the very least, didn't tell it to make it interesting as everything felt forced & rushed – the same go for the side-missions and their stories. The short of it is that you're some mechanic, Nick Ramos, in not-Los-Angeles who eventually finds a plane to fix and you also happen to be "the one" that can solve the entire zombie mess. You then meet up with characters (who I disliked the most throughout this entire game) and uncover another government conspiracy so long as you keep playing hero in the story.
I disliked most of the characters and the only ones I found somewhat interesting are the psychopath bosses, who have been made to represent the seven sins. They're all very unique in character and, for the most part, how they fight as well. My personal gripe with them though is that there aren't enough metal tracks like in the previous games to go with their fights. They're still nice in their own regard.
The entire map is based on the city of Los Angeles from the "cultural" parts to the higher class areas. The addition of cars to get around is nice but as a result, the map feels a lot smaller than the previous Dead Rising maps. The few shortcuts that are even there are rarely worth going through so long as you know how to make use of the freeways.
The game's time limit now extends to 6 in-game days before bombs hit on the 7th. Missions and such are no longer tied to the time limit, but rather on the progress of the chapters. That means you have more time than you could ever need in a normal playthrough to get scattered collectibles and get to the max level before even getting close to the end-game, so the sense of urgency is practically gone despite many characters exaggerating on how you have to hurry on a lot of objectives. You'll forget that there's even multiple endings because of that.
All side missions only activate during certain parts of a chapter, but even then you don't have to answer the calls yourself anymore to accept them as it will accept automatically after a little while. They still have a time limit on them that starts as soon as you get the call, but you still have loads of time regardless.
In addition to having a lot of time throughout the entire game, you can now even go back to specific chapters with character & collectible progress saved. Survivors saved are reset though.
Survivors are, at the very least, no longer a nuisance like in the previous games. There are stranded survivors who only need zombies in their area killed and, once they are, they'll just thank you and run along to disappear from the game. Many survivors in side missions don't necessarily need saving; they usually just stay where they are once a side mission is done. Some survivors can join you like a party member and can be dismissed, as well as accessed, via a bulletin board in a safe house or increasing your distance from them. The AI is tolerable at least and I suppose they can be useful but I never found myself using them at all.
You can now save the game pretty much anywhere. If you're not doing one of the main missions, you'll always load/respawn at a garage for some reason instead of an unlocked safe house.
Garages and safe houses make the game far easier than it already is. So long as you pick up a specific item once or entered a specific vehicle once, you can immediately access the items from the weapons locker in the safe houses and vehicles in the garages a semi-infinite amount of times. The same go for all the combo-made items.
Weapons & health items are highly abundant so the survival aspect in this "survival horror", where no horror is even there to begin with, is pretty much gone.
You can combine loads of items into one another if you get the blueprints for them and can be done so anywhere. There are so many combo weapon possibilities that there's almost no point in using regular items anymore — the same go for food combos when you learn how to make those. The humor in the combo items last as long as how fast you can craft them.
The way that you level is pretty standard; kill zeds, get collectibles, it's all passive. In this game though, you can now put points into specific "attributes" like Life, Inventory, Melee, etc. The system's all pointless though if you explore because you'd level so fast from killing, collecting, and etc. that you'll max out everything before you know it. And when you DO max everything out, you pretty much turn on semi-god mode for the rest of the game as most attacks (even bare-handed) can 1-shot most zeds, vehicles no longer explode so long as you're in them, and so on. Character & collectible progress are saved for the entire game.
There's a difficulty setting for the game now sort of where you can start the game normally or head into Nightmare Mode where enemies have more health & do more damage, the time limit goes by 4x faster supposedly, and saving can only be done via safe house bathrooms & porta-potties. I played the regular mode first making me at the overpowered level so as a result, Nightmare Mode was still very easy to go through even while doing all the side missions.
There's a co-op mode available but I barely tried it. I'm sure it's fun with friends.
The co-op character that's used is this one character who keeps popping up in the main story that rarely talks and barely makes his presence known.
The DLCs included are short side stories that take place before & during the base game. They're only somewhat lengthy because they have their own collectibles. The collectibles become more tedious than the last DLC you go through with the last DLC not being so much tedious as potentially extremely glitchy. I didn't find the stories in these very interesting.
The game's fun in its own regard probably but it's pretty much become a simple-minded game about killing zombies.
The protagonist won't shut up in-game when zombies latch on to his vehicle or when he's running in a populated area, almost like they're trying to force this feeling of urgency on you when you don't even die so easily.
Some collectibles give PP and are cleverly hidden but become pointless outside of satisfying one's completionism. The same go for weapon & vehicle blueprints since you'll be likely to only use barely a 4th of what's available. Eventually, you won't even need specific items to create specific combos; for example, you'll be able to combine an RC car and shampoo to make a large flamethrower just because one's a mechanical item and the other's a chemical.
Never mind the abundance of "humor" this game has, but whatever else direction this series is heading in terms of gameplay and such isn't doing it much good.

The only controller I've owned that is worse than this one is the Ouya controller. It's incredibly plasticky, the buttons feel terrible and are super loud, and there's some weird piezo speakers in it making annoying click sounds whenever you do anything. I really love the idea of a touchpad oriented gamepad, but the execution is just so very bad. I don't blame Valve -- making hardware is incredibly difficult, and a controller is a very complex piece of machinery that needs to evoke /emotions/ from having a good feel. It's also not well configured in games by default, requiring you to fiddle with controls for a long while for each game to get it right -- in contrast to using an xbox or ps controller, where the developer will always have configured good defaults for you.
In short, an Xbox One controller is a far better user experience. This controller is a good idea, but needs a lot of work -- several hardware iterations and much much better materials and components -- before it can even start to compete with real game controllers or a really good gaming mouse/keyboard combo.

After about 3 weeks I've been using this along with a wired logitech pro device that I've had since...oh the ps2 days. I got it because I didn't want to mice and keyboard my way through Hitman. Anyway, to best describe the controller is that it's not weird, but different. Yes, this controller is different and for some that could either be a good thing, or a bad thing.
I have small hands, but generally a lot of people still say the controller is big. Yes, that is true, but I thought it was comfortable. It's thick and it does have some weight on it. The biggest complaint is finding the buttons. When I first purchased it, the store guy said that he confuses the X and A buttons with the Y and B buttons. It does happen, but that has to do with 2 reasons: 1.The size of the controller and 2. just getting used to the control scheme. It's funny, because that was the biggest complaint from the store guy the control scheme. Not the weight, or what I think is the biggest issue (I'll get to that in a moment). The more I used it, I got more comfortable with the buttons. I actually like the toggles underneath because I don't feel that they are gimmicky and in fact,  I actually see those being used in console devices. What does feel weird is the right touchpad. Taking the place of a traditional right stick, the right pad is clickable on the edges and you can add haptic feedback so it gives you a sense a touch when touching the edges. The left pad is similar so if you want to touch the controls as opposed to pressing them you can.
But, my huge issue with this pad is the fact that it's a controller with a very high learning curve. Good luck finding ways to program this thing. It's been over 6 months since it's release and I still can't find a way to properly program this thing. It's flexible, and that is a good thing, but no instructions mean that programming it to find a sweet spot is hit or miss. The community does offer settings you can download and use to serve as default controls, for most games, but it's hit or miss. And that's a shame because unless a developer submits a default control scheme you're not sure what to really expect. Sometimes the community gives you something that gives you a better, while other times you have to jump back and forth in your game trying to get comfortable finding just the feel. Most of the issues stem from the amount of feedback you want from the mouse pad regions of both the left and right pads. For some it's a matter of getting used to it, for others that need buttons or a stick, you're not going to enjoy the experience as much.
Now saying all that...I love this controller! I have yet to test this out on fighting games, but for adventure, platform, third person and fps games, this controller is great. The ability to program keyboard inputs into your controller without the use of mods or patches is a godsend. The weight of the device doesn't hamper me at all. The ability to adjust the speed of the right pad gives me the ability to line up shots easier if I want to go slow, or if I want to make it faster I can (I realize I just complained about the right pad, but the issue was the learning curve). The bumpers underneath are not gimmicky as much as they are useful. Perhaps the most exciting thing I like about it is that I'm no longer stuck using keyboard and mouse controls. I can now purchase older games that were built for kb+m controls and map them directly to a controller. It's not perfect because I can't find a control scheme that I like, but I no longer have to find alternatives.
Overall, I would recommend this controller for those that don't want to use a kb+m and don't have or want an xbox 360 or One controller. If you got one of those keep them and use them. Most games read those inputs anyway. But, if you don't want one of those controllers, and don't mind tinkering with the controls for the first 30 minutes of your game, than I think you would like this controller.

Pros:
*Huge* catalogue of 'mechs to choose from
Great loadout customization
Some good looking maps
Constant stream of weekend events, and tournaments
Visceral and engaging 'mech combat
Very active development team
Faction Play/Community Warfare
All competitive/meta grade 'Mechs are avaliable for free-player currency.
Mech art design is really quite gorgeous
Neutral:
Sound design is functional
Devs *can* have a problem listening to the community
Unlocking 'Mechbays pretty much requires paying money, or playing every weekend event
Highish investment price, about on equal footing with World of Tanks
Frequent sales on cosmetics and paid 'mechs
'Unique' XP unlock system
Steep learning curve, but an okay tutorial
Cons:
Jarring disconnect between 'old' and 'new' map design philosophies and qualities.
Some 'Mech textures can be downright ugly
Only five gamemodes and 18 maps
Cumbersome frontend UI

Nickel and diming
Poor optimization leads to a poor performance to fidelity ratio

Conclusion:

It's probably worth a download, and some free-play, but keep your wallet closed unless you find you're enjoying yourself.

Absolute masterpiece of a game. There are only five levels, but they all feel completely different from each other, and are masterfully made. The first level is there to get you used to the controls and mechanics of the game, level two has you navigating a somewhat destructible maze, level three has you dodging the landscape as it changes and tries to crush you, level four takes place inside and around a giant wheel which is constantly firing different colored bullets at you while trying to crash into you, and level five is more of a mini-boss rush until you get to the final showdown with the last boss. The uniqueness in the levels is my favorite feature of this game, as most shmups just send tougher mobs of enemies at you as you progress, making many of those games feel repetitive and boring to practice. The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful, and as a nice touch it is perfectly synced to the action of each stage adding a nice cinematic and epic feeling to every area and fight. The scoring system is simple, but difficult to keep a chain going for an insane score, basically you must constantly destroy enemies in threes, as long as those three enemies are the same color, you will constantly be building a higher score multiplier which is necessary for getting extra lives and climbing the scoreboard. You will quickly notice that the levels and enemy patterns are designed around this mechanic, and it requires a bit of strategy and restraint to destroy three same-colored enemies to keep your multiplier going, rather than just blasting everything as soon as it appears. Like any shmup this game is insanely difficult and requires many hours of practice on each stage to become good enough to beat the game without a continue, but because you can make half the bullets on screen harmless with the color change mechanic I do find this game to be a bit easier than say most Cave shmups, or the Touhou games for example, at least on the normal difficulty. Overall I give this game a 10/10, best shmup ever by quite a wide margin and it is a must play. Nothing comes close in any aspect.

Treasure have made some incredible titles over the years but Ikaruga is the one. The only problem I've noticed (in all versions) is the slight frame drop when a boss explodes, but I don't consider that a drawback because it doesn't affect play. For gameplay Ikaruga is fast, responsive and relentlessly demanding - exactly what an arcade game should be.
Ikaruga isn't a fun little game that you can explore at your own pace, it's a gauntlet thrown down to serious gamers. If you play Dark Souls you expect to be punished and that's how you have to see it here. People think that Ikaruga is inviting them in but it's not. It's calling them out. Most modern games don't demand this level of patience and focus, and the sheer purity of a 1-coin game makes this way more than just pattern learning.
1. The game itself is flawless, precision arcade gaming.
2. Replays are a really good addition.
1. The console UI (GameCube or Saturn) remains a lot better. With the Steam port you can only replay a whole chapter and not an individual stage. So you can't do 1-3 without having to go through 1-1 and 1-2 first. I don't know why this was dropped. Maybe something to do with the replay saves?
2. Having no Restart Stage option in the pause menu means that you have to quit, go back to the chapter menu and start again from there. That gets long. You are supposed to play Ikaruga over and over again, so the menu needs to support that with easier restarts.
3. The UI is a bit messy. The main menu, pause menu and new menu style (i.e. all the replays, save etc.) are all different styles, colours and fonts. What's up with just using the standard Ikaruga font and design?
4. The leaderboards show fake scores at the top. The real highest score is around 4th, and you can always tell by the number of chains, but it's pretty weak for a game that prides itself on rankings.
If you like Ikaruga then check out Mushihimesama. The hardest bullet hell game I have ever played and has a soundtrack like keygen music on crack. Total insanity but amazing fun. The YouTube vids alone make your brain bleed.
Also worth checking out rRootage, which is basically a homage to bullet hell stuff like Radiant Silvergun, Psyvariar, Gigawing and Ikaruga. Free game, with several play modes, and really good for learning the tricks of bullet hell (like the hit box of your ship being far smaller than you think)
Radiant Silvergun is a must for fans, and easily available on the online marketplaces, but real copies are nuts expensive. It's a shame because the Saturn had some amazing bullet hell games.
Not really bullet hell but Gradius is a worthy mention. NES classic which is pretty easy to finish, but requires several playthroughs, with each getting faster and harder. Stage 5 on a 3rd playthrough is still tekkers.

Let me be clear about something.
Out there somewhere, is a game designer who helped sculpt this game.  And even though you and he have never met, will never cross paths, and never have a mutual friend, I assure you...
He hates you
He hates the very idea of you
He hates your friends
He hates your parents
He hates your political stance
He hates the way you dress
He hates your favorite color
He hates your little dog, too
He hates whatever country you hail from
He hates the music you listen to
He hates the movies you watch
He hates what you did last summer
He hates the color of your hair
He hates that little knick-nack you keep on the coffee table
He hates the side of the bed you sleep on
AND he hates the other side of the bed too JUST TO SPITE YOU
And this game...*this game*, is how he releases that anger upon you.  I have never encountered such concentrated contempt in one computer program.  I was frustrated after playing for a half an hour, after an hour I was fairly sure I shamed my family's honor somehow, and after two hours I was ready to tell Vice President Cheney everything I ever knew.  If this game were translated into a real-world axiom, I would describe it as "beating a dead horse until the bones were but dust, and then chasing after each particle of dust in the wind and spitefully pounding each speck into random piles of manure just to drive home the point".
To call this game difficult insults the idea of difficult.  The game seems to be sentient and angry at ever being compiled in the first place.
I'm giving this game a recommend because apparently there is a genre for video game sadists, and this is a shining example of it.  It excels at precisely what it sets out to do.
In other notes, the rending is actually quite beautiful, the music is nice enough, and the tidbits of dialog between levels is intriguing if nothing else.  I'd still prefer Raystorm any day, however.

An excellent SHMUP by the ever-brilliant Treasure.

It sounds simple but the level designs and enemies employ this mechanic in a very sophistacated way.
This makes the game very challenging in a traditional, ''Nintendo-hard'' way.
I highly recommend this game to fans of SHMUPs, challenging / retro style games, and people wanting to explore innovative game mechanics.

First off I wanna say I'm only putting this on 'do not recommend' because I've only played about 2 hours, so I can't really recommend it based on the little I've seen so far.
THAT SAID though, here's my thoughts on it:
A lot of people say that this is a simple Overwatch clone, or Overwatch for poor people, or Hi Rez's version of Overwatch, but let me tell you, it is not really an Overwatch clone at all. Sure the gameplay is a bit similar, and fundamentally Paladins attempts the same genre as Overwatch, and yeah, maybe some of the characters are a lot like Overwatch's characters like Young Hanzo, Less-Cyber Sombra, Turtle Road-Hog and Spanish Reinhardt, but really Paladins is trying to do something way different.
You can level up heroes individually, so that they're better in matches, which means the more you play a certain character (i.e., your main) the better they'll be, so there's a good bit of progression there. There's also more cosmetic options I think, though so far I've only unlocked cosmetics for characters I don't own (yeah that's a bit of a downside I guess- there's a much bigger roster here, but you have to unlock characters or wait for them to become available on rotation, a bit like Smite). There's also like a card system thing that gives you better abilities, and you can buy items in-match a bit like your favourite MOBAs to give yourself a bit of an edge. So I think it's a bit more open than Overwatch, which, like most Blizzard games, I think is just trying really hard to be an e-sport.
The downside to Paladins comes in the OB64 update, which takes the limit of cards or something? I'm not sure. But it means if you've got level 1 cards and go against level 5 cards, you're going to get a nasty ring sting from how often you get ♥♥♥♥ed dry, though there is the option to play Classic mode, from what I saw at least, so maybe people are too trigger happy with complaints, who knows.
Best thing to do? Try it out for yourself, like I did. These first two hours I've really enjoyed, so we'll see how it goes. I probably won't play much because my SO really prefers OW, so by definition I do too.

Going into Tribes Ascend I didn't really expect much. Another bloody multiplayer only free to play shooter, they'd probably be the most overdone type of games if ♥♥♥♥ing zombies didn't exist, but I was really surprised. The movement-based play style is certainly a hell of a lot more fun than your typical cover-based fare, there's a certain thrill to nailing another player with a rocket when you're both shooting across the map at 200km/h in opposite directions and the vehicles are fairly weak, unlike in other games where the match is pretty much over once someone gets into a tank, which brings a good sense of balance to the game and means that it's always possible to win. I remember I joined a Capture the Flag match where the score was 4-0 against the team I just joined. I turned it around entirely and scored 5 caps and won the match. Why don't more games have that sort of balance? It brings a sort of tension to a game and a real sense of victory when you win, which is what makes it so balls-to-the-wall fun, and the emphasis on objective-based gametypes over just killing each other is highly applaudable. I've never seen a game where Capture the Flag is actually more enjoyable than Deathmatch. It means that the game isn't just comprised of running around trying to score kills, which adds more to the teamwork aspect.
On that topic, there's a certain sense of strategy and teamwork that you just don't get in any other game. The community is a marvelous bunch of people who are all fun to play with and the in-game chat interface means that communications are more than just some prepubescent ♥♥♥♥wit screaming in your ear. The only class based shooter I can think of that could compare is TF2 before it got♥♥♥♥♥♥ Everyone has an important role, and if your team's stupid enough to have 4 Raiders and no Technicians, you or someone else will rectify that pretty quickly to keep your chance of winning and having to play a support role doesn't make you feel any less important than the other players, which was my main problem with playing as a Medic in TF2. There's nobody screaming for you to go fix somebody else's ♥♥♥♥up every 2.8 nanoseconds and you actually feel needed because you know your team appreciates it even if they don't say it.
I've heard Tribes Ascend being described as pay-to-win, but it's really not. The default gear holds up great against endgame gear if you're not terrible at the game, and it's remarkably well balanced. This game takes time, patience and practice, but it's so fun to play you barely notice. Not only does it look good, it plays beautifully. Unless you have a horrible PC, you have no excuse to not try this game.

Well, if you're looking for a genuine NES revival, the good news is that
is nearly indistinguishable from a number of titles in the 8-Bit behemoth's library. The bad news is that those titles are far closer to the barely functioning Cheetahmen than they are any 'instant classics' as this game bewilderingly touts itself.
I was hooked in by the Mexican horror theme as there is precious little of it to be found in gaming but nothing feels particularly culture-specific about shooting down a tedious Halloween gallery of ghosts, bats, cats and, uh, monkeys for some godforsaken reason. The boss fights, although clumsily handled, are a little bit livelier, recalling the milder confrontations of the original Castlevania trilogy but out of a total of five of them, two are against the Grim Reaper and one is against an alien overlord so that really leaves you with precious little of what Abo Mando promises you.
The two biggest problems here are that every stage looks like crap on account of being one colour (whether or not that is an artistic choice becomes irrelevant the minute it starts to affect enemy and platform visibility) and the fact that enemies constantly spawn on top of you, sometimes in mid-air, of which you can either shut up and like it or quit to refund (my personal option). Trying to sell this as a 'Mega-Vania' hybrid is, frankly, insulting to both of those games and even the several generations of knock-offs that came after them.
A disappointingly lazy effort. Full review below.

When I started playing Dead Rising 3 I thought it was going to be an epic zombie adventure filled with twists and turns and a heartfelt story. What I got was a technical mess with a very small and limited open world, paper thin characters and poorly written story that isn't going anywhere. This feels more like a DLC that was stretched out to a full game due to poor quest design and padding.
Visuals look decent. There are some good animations and some characters do seem to have a nicely detailed body, the world has some good interiors and there is a vast number of zombies on screen at all times. However there are quite a lot of problems. First of all the game seems to be stuck at 30fps, there resolution does not go above 1080p (i tried it and it crashed the game), there are numerous instances when the game would not load up textures until they were right in your face and several times the lighting was just... odd (shadows flickered).
The voice acting and sound are passable but the script and story really doesn't go anywhere. Very predictable and honestly not very engaging. Without spoiling ... you're trapped in a city where everyone but you is a zombie and somehow you're special. By the end everything works out and the villain is as one note and predictable as you'd suspect.

Halcyon 6 calls back to a time when men were real men, women caused things to explode with tricorders, and uniforms were made of high quality velour. It combines a little bit of combat, a little bit of base building, a little bit of exploration, and a lot of wanting to slap the alien-of-the-week upside the head for being crazy.
It has character and captures the feel of the genre it's aiming for, and that to some extent weighs more heavily than its gameplay problems, since you can rebalance gameplay more easily than you can revamp the feel of the game.
Pros:
* Pixel graphics master race
* Aliens are hilariously insane in a manner that reflects the Star Trek style genre without being too direct a copy
* Cadets die with appropriate frequency when sent below decks to find out what that sound was
* Combat relies heavily on applying/consuming debuffs, which can make for some interesting tactical choices (do you consume a sensor disable debuff to do more damage, or leave it on to keep enemy accuracy low?)
Cons:
* Illusion of choice in ship selection - there are other ships in tier 1 other than the ones you start with for example but their ability balance leaves them subpar in actual usage
* Play is vulnerable to the "doom loop", where losing trained personnel in combat can mean being unable to continue, since it's not possible to train and equip new personnel fast enough to keep up with higher tier enemies. It is even likely to be completely unable to continue, in that attempts to harvest resources to rebuild a fleet after several ship losses and/or research higher tier ships can be stymied by your resource harvesting fleets being destroyed by pirates. The inability to retreat from combat when outmatched compounds this issue.
* Illusion of choice in deployments due to limited officers - in theory having 4 officers is good, since you can send 1 to explore levels or harvest resources, or even split up 2 groups of 2 - in practice this is a recipe for failure since you can be ambushed and there is no option for retreating if you stumble upon enemies that you might have been able to handle if you had a group of 3 officers. See "doom loop".
I am somewhat hesitant to recommend the game as it is now, but presumably the above balance issues will be addressed in future development before it escapes Early Access. If they aren't this review will have to change to a downvote.

I think Megadimension Neptunia V-II marks something of a watershed moment for the Neptunia series in that it's no longer "good, but...[insert caveat of your choice here]", it's just plain good. Actually, great, even.
Finishing my first playthrough of the game took me roughly 55 hours; that was taking it fairly leisurely, unlocking this and that that wasn't absolutely necessary for the first playthrough and goofing around now and then. After that, there's still the "true" ending, which leads to a post-game segments during which you can clean up any bits and pieces you didn't finish off first time around - Or trophy hunt.
Well, at first, I want to say that I think this is Compile Heart's finest work to date. While there are some technical issues regarding frame drops in a few places, most of them are not really all that significant. Ignoring some typos, the script and translation are both excellent, the gameplay is enjoyable, smooth and well-balanced. The first and last points there adress two of the biggest criticism the Neptunia series has had ever since its release - technical issues regarding atrocious framerates that weren't really justifiable for the kind of game they were, and balancing issues regarding inconsistent or just way too easy difficulty. MegaNep counters both of these problems: It runs at pretty consistent 60fps pretty much all of the time, only dropping in particularly busy scenes, and has a very well-paced progression with no point in the game that felt too easy or too difficult. The revamped game systems work extremly well: Skills feel neither under- nor overpowered, characters feel unique and pretty much any party combination can work perfectly fine.
Now, narrative and characterisation has never been an issue for the Neptunia series, but, pleasingly, MegaNep even improves this, making up a story that is spectaclar, dramatic and even emotional at some points in the end. Additionally, it keeps the humorful atmosphere, with Neptune being the goofy, likeable, forth-wall-breaking protagonist that we all know and love.
In other words, it's not just a great Neptunia game - It's a great RPG, period. The only thing that saddens me is the fact that so many people will write it off without even giving it a shot for themselves; still, I guess that makes it all the more special for those of us in the know who can enjoy and appreciate it, both on its own merits and as, to date, the absolute pinnacle of the series.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a surprisingly good game.
I'd been told it was a good game previously, but never had a chance to try it out. By the time I remembered about the game, it was a few years after release and the graphics looked somewhat dated and I was foolish enough to give the game a skip based on that.
Then a friend of mine offered me a spare copy of the game going free, so I thought 'Ack, why the heck not!' and installed with haste. I played it straight over the following three days, putting 25.8 hours into the game, completing it on the hardest difficulty (or at least, the hardest available. I think there might be an even harder level now available after completing the game).
Oh boy, it was good.
Problem was, I went through the entire game without killing anyone. Or so I thought. Then I remembered I shot someone in the tutorial. Whoops. Oh well, just an achievement.
The game was rather easy to play, especially if you play non-lethal ghost. I've not tried out going loud - I suspect it'd be much harder, considering the amount of damage they deal on harder difficulties. So one might want to take that into mind.
Gameplay wise the game is above average - it's not exactly a great shooter, but the stealth is decent enough. It could be improved and I hope in the new game they make the combat a little more intuitive and/or realistic. But there will always be more one can want.
Yet what makes it great is the world and the story, and how people react to your actions. It feels nice when people comment about your lack of lethal use throughout the game - and, without spoiling anything, saving certain characters also happens to have a significant impact on the game too.
Obviously in my review, however basic it may be, I'm biased to a degree because I didn't actually purchase the game - but having played it, I would've bought it (at sale price, because I'm stingy) had I know what the game was actually like to player.

While support is far from ideal, the fact that the community itself can provide suggested control profiles for games, and that you can customize your own certainly makes it a worthwhile purchase for a linux steam player like myself.
The hardware is not flawed by any means - it's really just the acceptance of controls by both the steam application and the individual games that could, at times, be a great deal better.
It would be exceptionally nice if full support for controller profiles could be supported -without- using the big picture setup.  Insofar on linux systems with limited resources, this is a real downside.

Fully customizible, built like a ♥♥♥♥ing tank, feels great for a dude with large hands, has a good wieght behind it, long battery life.
Only downside is learning curve and Big Picture Mode. Both will be resolved with time, I think.

There is no controller on the market that will allow as much customization as you will get with this thing.  And really we owe that to Steam itself.  It looks weird at first, but feels great once you learn to use the 6-axis properly.  I mean the touchpad does great at emulating a mouse, but a mouse is an extension of my arm, and I can coordinate so many more muscles together for finely tuned motion (not just my thumb).  But once you enable the accelerometer to be active while you are touching the right pad things go up many levels.  Now I can flick my thumb across the pad for large movements, spins, etc.  But now when I get my crosshairs near a bad guy, my arms nudge the controller over a bit to get the crosshairs lined up for a headshot, and pull the trigger.  It's an amazing concert of motion that only improves if you stand up.  So now I look like some n00b in the 80's playing a NES for the first time swinging the controller around, with the exception that swinging the controller around now MOVES my character.  Love it!  I bought a second one just so that I can show it off to freinds when they come over, without giving up my own.

I've been using it for the last few months. I've played witcher 3, tomb raider, fifa 16, and cities skylines mostly.
I've owned many and played every game system since about 1994, and this controller is in my top 3. It is also my preferred controller because of the versatility and precision with the right track pad. I've actually just ordered a second.

I love the idea behind the controller. Versatile touch pads? Haptic feedback? Awesome! Unfortunately, the actual product is disappointing.
To be short: the physical layout of the controller is terribly awkward.
To be a bit longer, the trackpads are too big, which makes using the left one as a dpad useless. It also makes switching from the right pad to the XYAB buttons a surprisingly difficult and lengthy process. The shape of the controller, especially the protruding handles, actively gets in the way, and this further compounds the issue. So much so that using the controller actually hurts me.
The shoulder buttons are both too big and too hard to press. Trying to press one is more likely to make the controller move than to result in a click. I have to use a light grip. If I don't, the controller's shape comes back with a vengeance to ruin wy wrists. These handles are a menace.
I'd like to say that I love the underside buttons, but one of them broke down after a couple of hours playing Hyperlight Drifter, so...
Returning the controller for a new one was mostly painless, though.
On the software side, well, things aren't exactly perfect either, but it is not unreasonable to give Valve the benefit of the doubt. Exploring the configuration options is fascinating. The descriptions of the options is very helpful most of the time, and will give you a glimpse of what goes on under the hood.
Speaking of configuration, I wish there was a way to save parts of a configuration, for the right pad in particular. Finding a way to handle the camera in third- and first-person games required quite a bit of trial and error. It would be nice to be able to reuse these particular settings quickly and easily when configuring the controller for a new game.
In conclusion, even if the actual hardware is by and large almost entirely atrocious, I hope Valve will keep at it and, like MS with the OG Duke controller, release the equivalent an S version with much needed improvements - and some seriously revamped handles.
This controller is amazing!  I've been using this controller on games that I've never been able to use a controller on.  This is the best controller I have ever used.

I bought this a while back and wanted to posted a quick pros and cons list. The controller takes a lot of what I like from other console controllers and adds quite a bit few of its own unique features. I don't use this at my desktop it is setup with the Steam Link downstairs, mostly for streaming movies and family games.
Pros:
The ability to upgrade the controller with drivers to enable new features or game profiles is REALLY nice.
Paddle shifter buttons on the bottom are new to me makes me wish more controller makers would add this.
Controlling the desktop cursor and mouse clicks while across the room or say downstairs when I want to watch a downloaded movie is awesome.
Battery life seems amazing so far...
Steering with motion control, and being able to play point and click games with a controller is cool. I don't think I prefer this to a mouse and keyboard for these style games or FPS like Dayz or Rust but it is nice for more boardgame/tabletop style games which I play a lot of.
The mini speaker for controller sounds are great.
The steam controller seems super light to me as well, which is great if you are using it for motion controls for extended time but in no way does the device feel cheap.
Cons:
Even after using this for a few months my hands don't like the kind of tear drop sides. Like my hands actually feel like they may cramp after a moderate amount of playing (45 minutes or so). For long sessions where I will use a controller for racing or platform I would rather just use a Xbox one or 360 controller.
I have also used the PS4 controller and wish for the little additions like being able to wirelessly use my headphones (plug into steam controller), this is an awesome feature...
I would still recommend this if you are looking for a wireless controller depending on the types of games you play. Hopefully they will adjust the grip a bit in the next one but that is just a personal preferance.

Having played this game on and off since it first entered Open Beta, I feel justified in saying that this game is an amazing addition to the Mechwarrior universe, though not necessarily the Battletech one.
If you're pining (like I always will be) for a strategic simulation in which you have to take care of every aspect of your mechwarrior's life, this may not scratch that itch. This isn't a full campaign simulator, but it retains the
of "Big Stompy Robots" storming across a landscape.
I've played for years, and it still makes me pleased when my 50+ ton war machine crashes into what may be a 20-30 year old tree, sending it crashing to the ground with a satisfying sound of snapping timber and falling branches. It's
to round a corner, see a smaller mech, and pummel it with the satisfying
of an autocannon. It's immensely satisfying to tear pulse lasers across the face of a mech and watch glowing pits be gouged across its armor.
For real though, this isn't the complete Battletech experience. It's a streamlined, much improved, graphically beautiful, and fairly well balanced Mech Combat Simulator. It isn't "Pay To Win", but paying real money gets you ahead of the curve. Complaining about grinding in a F2P title is kind of silly in my opinion, since devs can't work for free (and Battletech, much as I love it, is not exactly a cash crop).
In the past year, PGI has made strides in making the game a great deal more enjoyable and more fun. While the early years have embittered some players seemingly eternally, there is a strong and fun community here to be had. For Battletech loyalists and for the casual gamer who likes shiny robots and explosions, this should be a lot of fun. The game alternates through "Trial mechs" which allow you get experience different chassis, from heaviest to lightest, without actually investing in-game currency or real world currency. I can't actually find much
with the game, to be honest. It may not be
out of a Battletech game, but it's solid fun and an easy/pleasant way to burn 30 minutes to... several hours.
So really, until there's a complete HD remake of Mechwarrior 2: Mercenaries, this is the best thing out there, and I enjoy it immensely.

Ok, so unlike alot of commentaries here I'm not going to discuss the progression of this game since Closed Beta, through Open Beta to today. Today is what matters, as the game goes to STEAM.  To be up front, I have about 11,500 matches under my belt and hundreds of hours of game play so I'm not new to the game, it's background or it's challenges.
Video fx/Graphics (8): The artwork for the Mechs is fantastic imo. Even if you don't necessarily agree with the direction of the Art team or modeling of the Mechs, they still look well done and attractive. Intimidating and lethal, they look much as any fan of the intellectual property of BattleTech might imagine. I deducted points here due to some pixelated terrain that looks like a game from 2003 in places and some odd modeling/animation mistakes. Additionally, some of the mechs need a scaling overhaul, as some smaller tonnage mechs are larger than mechs in heavier weight classes. Overall tho, a great effort and all indications are this will get better.
Audio (9): Again, barring some minor aesthitic disagreements, the sound effects are well done and the game sounds good during gameplay. Autocannons have a great bang/crunch mechanic, lasers sound vicious and explosions/getting hit add to the immersion.
Immersion (6): This is where the video excellence and audio excellence fall short, in tandem with other things that are decidedly lacking. The musical backdrop is solid usually, but there are no immersive ingame sounds. While you are in the Mechlab/game join screens. If I'm in some giant bay somewhere modifying a 60-ton warmachine, shouldn't there at least be some air-wrenches screaming or the sounds of metal clanging or SOMETHING besides simple music? Missed opportunity there. Additionally, there's no tie to a back story within the game. If you're not already familiar with the IP, most of the game will mean nothing to you nor does the game give you much information in that respect.
Backstory (0): PGI makes no effort to tie the grand-lore that sets this IP apart from any other "walking-tanks" battlesim and misses out hugely there. Hiring some writers or poaching directly from the novels/game books that are associated with the IP would make sense here, but there's no real history at all. Just some forum links to community based websites (such as
that are great efforts, but in no way as reach, or as accurate as actually being source material. With the addition of "communit warfare" some of the planets have information about them, but no context really. Ultimately, you know this IP/background already or you're finding it from other sources, as PGI hasn't bothered.
Gameplay (7.5): Purely from a gameplay mechanics and fun aspect, I enjoy playing it BUT I've been playing it for years now. The initial stings of playing through the learning curve are long past for me. I can enjoy the new Mechs as they are introduced immediately for their various strengths and weaknesses. This is not the same for new players.
New Player Experience (2): I only grudgingly even give it a 2. The tutorial is a great (recent) addition to the game, but the game mechanics are not explained well anywhere, forcing new players to learn through pain or comb through dense forums. The occasional tip at the start of the match isn't enough, and usually have to do with reminding players about key-bindings to use. It has no centralized resource to explain how the Clan, Inner Sphere, Trial, Hero, or Champion mechs work differently, how certain weapons when "boated" in larger quantities cause ghost heat, etc to help people understand what the heck they are doing. The cadet bonuses to your first 25 matches are substantial but easily squandered by new players who are completely clueless on what does what. A PDF file attached to the game with all of the tips and key info, or a wesite framework with a similar design would be incredibly helpful to new players. The current website information is largely out of date.
Balance (7.5): The weapons have some balance issues that are bound to be improved upon but are not intuitive to the player. The Mechs themselves as the platforms have some glaring optimal performers and some glaringly bad Mechs, with the majority in the comfortable middle. If all Mechs had useful roles, even if those roles were not purely combat related, that would improve their value immensely. Players who live primarily Clan, or Inner Sphere tend to accuse the other side of being "OP" based on Clan mechs having significant intrinsic advantages uniformly, while Inner Sphere mechs enjoy very niche, but powerful "quirks" to bring them up to par. Overall, balance has improved much over time and continues to balance the main systems to a reasonable degree. Room to improve here, but overall it's solid.
Modes/Replayability (2): The game has three quick modes....assault, where teams can kill the enemy team or capture a objective on their opponents' side of the map, conquest where teams can the enemy team or earn points by owning up to 5 slow-ticking objectives scattered between the two teams, and skirmish which is team death match.
Community warfare, involving larger maps (but still 12 on 12 matches) with 4 spawns per pilot is the "meta" level of the game, where players are fighting over planets. As much as I'd love to say they got this right....it's incredibly tough to enjoy at the moment for a variety of reasons you can read about on the forums. I'm very hopeful that Beta 3 will introduce some options that add more to that mode and help attract more players to it.
EndGame/Why play factor (2): Once the fun wears off in playing the same three modes, you're left with grinding new Mech chassis for the sake of collecting them. Without a driving reason to fight and no value to community warfare outside of bragging rights (no politics, impact to resources, impact to your gaming experience for fighting etc), you're literally just playing because you enjoy the shootem up portion or to make your collection larger.
F2P factors: There's no penalty to P4F, as the "hero Mechs" don't represent a real leg up in any true sense, but it does cut into the grind ALOT to pay for premium time.
Grind:  This game does have a grind/leveling component that can be daunting for new players only because again, within the New Player Experience (NPE), they are likely to make mistakes in how they spend their initial funds.  Recently, PGI increased the rate of return on c-bills (ingame currency) that helps mitigate this facet of the grind, and players will learn quickly about the experience/mastery grind which really isn't something you can get around without spending MC ($ for game currency) to expedite.
In 2013, I gave this game a 5 on metacritic.
My overall opinion of the game would be to give it a 7 currently, but again I'm biased due to my love for the Battletech IP.  If you "scored" things with roughly equal weight as I laid them out above, you'd get a lower #. In the end though, the community is small but overall pretty good (ignore the toxic outliers), the game has a certain amount of fun factor that cannot be explained, the game continues to improve albeit at a slow pace AND it's F2P without any real penalty to do so.
Well worth the serious stab at it if you're at all interested in tactical shooters, especially ones that are not pure twitch.

Mechwarrior Online
One of my favourite games of all times. It has certainly been quite a ride to get from when I started in the Fall of 2013, with all of the Ups and Downs of development, but things really started to improve a lot last year, and I think the game has been improving since that day and will continue to do so as long as it has supporters.
I play from a gaming laptop, so I am not going to comment much on the graphics. If you have a good computer, you can make things look pretty I guess. But I have everything turned down to create a nice and playable game. And it is quite stable. The game rarely crashes for me which is great!
"Welcome to MW:O. The thinking mans shooter!"
I always like that title, and for me it is quite true. When you do solo-drops it can be quite frustrating when everyone on your side of the match runs around wildly and there is no coordination. Well, that is what happens when noone thinks like a team. This is what MW:O is all about. Teamplay. Without it, you might as well flip a coin to see who wins. With teamwork, you have a much greater chance at winning!
I started playing without a Unit, but as I just noted, quick play can be somewhat tiresome from time to time, so I started playing in Community Warfare CW, which is where the Units meet and slug it out against each other. Unlike the quick play option, where there is a matchmaker to make sure you are given a fair fight, CW just picks unit against unit with total disregard of your own skill. You have to be prepared and you have to work together as a team. This is where I like to play most of my time. Even when I drop solo in the CW - unit game, I know this is where things are serious!
I have played some 2450 matches in my two years in MW:O and I am not going to stop anytime soon. I think this is a great game. It is somewhat repetitive, which is why I mix and match the different play-types (quick drop and CW solo drops), and I take breaks now and then if it gets too much. But I always return for more!

I've played this a little bit over the last few years and while the general idea of it is very fun, this game suffers from three giant problems:
1. Strict adherance to the source material smothered any kind of innovation in the crib. There is nothing new here, and there never will be. Now don't get me wrong, the Battletech Universe is incredibly cool in a lot of ways, but I feel like all the current Battletech projects all just kind of stagnate in a universe where all the broad strokes are already in place. Let alone the fact that many of the coolest mechs in the series don't show up until late in the timeline means that any game that strictly adheres to the lore can't actually put all the fan favourites in the game. Want an large caliber autocannon that can fire further than 300 meters? Tough luck, it's not in the source material so it doesn't exist and never will. Don't even think about shields, repair tools, ammo boxes, or any other number of things that seem like a pretty straight forward adition to a game that's keeping with the times.
2. The game doesn't really allow you to have a giant robot power fantasy, because the only thing you ever get to shoot at is other giant robots. It's one of those games that would be absolutely brilliant if there was more stuff to shoot at, like tanks and helicopters and infantry and all sorts of things like that, but it's running on a very straight forward system that gives you one mech, as it takes damage it continuously gets weaker, and the win condition is most often simply killing the enemy team. The best you can do is often merely surviving till the end of the match. It's the same problem as World of Tanks and it's ilk have, while they are very realistic in a sense they never give you space to just enjoy being a super powerful mech or tank or whatever.
3. Progression in this game is incredibly slow, has very few meaningful rewards, and you need to drop absurd amounts of money to buy things. Basically this game has the tiniest little hint of a progression system where your pilot levels up and gets better at using certain mechs, but the way it's implemented is just awful. In order to become a master of a specific chassis for example you have to earn a large amount of XP not just with the mech you actually want to drive, but with different variants of that same chassis.That means buying the same mech multiple times and spending a lot of time playing with setups that aren't actually what you want. The only way to make that a little easier on yourself is to drop real life cash on mech packs that give you all the variants.  A lot of mechs, like the clan mechs and various premium machines are basically absurd money sinks where you can drop as much cash as you'd spend on a whole other game just to buy a single mech.
So overall: This game is extremely good looking, and it has its moments in gameplay, but it's adeherence to Battletech lore basically means nothing new and surprising will ever happen in this game, and they cannot innovate on play mechanics in any way. The overall feel of the game isn't like what you got from the old Mechwarrior titles, because there is nothing to fight in this game that you are supposed to win against. A competitive environment is fun and all, but it kind of sucks the fun out of giant robots if there is nothing you can simply step on. The monetization scheme of this game along with it's extremely grindy and shallow progression system kind of keep this from being any fun unless you are just really into the competitive aspect of it. There is little reason to just play because you want to build your ultimate mech.
Wish there were more options than "Yes" and "No" for reviewing games, because I feel like I'm giving a negative review but I still want people to check it out for themselves.

+Highly polished game with tons of content and replayability. No question.
+Great artwork, and really good music.
+Definately an accomplished MetroidVania.
+If you are really into bunny girls, this is your jam.
+Dialogue is way too thick, and is largely meaningless. It's all pretty silly and tedious, even though I understand this is a translation.
