Dead Rising 3 is exactly what you would expect from the series, no real deviation from the established formula other than a much more lenient time frame for doing missions.
The only real major changes are the much larger number of combo vehicles and the fact that basic weapons dont do much and the combo weapons are insanely good once you reach their final tier.
The game allows you to spawn weapons at weapon chests in your safe houses. You can spawn anything you've picked up before and it gives you a point value for the weapons but you always have enough points for at least four or so weapons.
The game is decent fun for what it is, worth it if you pick it up on sale but I'd not go over $30 for it as it's easily beatable in around twenty or thirty hours. I wasn't even rusing and I beat it on the hardest mode 100% on my first placethrough without a guide.
The only real weakness is since the game is so easy and the zombies aren't really a threat it gets old very quick and has little replayability once you've beaten it once. All that said it was still decently fun. If I could give it a "so so" I would, as it wasn't really good but it wasn't really bad either.

I had always been aware of this franchise and briefly played the first two but when I heard about this sequel my reaction was that it lost some of its silly charm. Now I still believe that but it's also fun enough to play as a new player and keeps some of the qualities the first two games gave us. Those qualities include the psychopaths, clothes, time factor and ridiculous weapons like the jack in the box or horse head.
However one grief I do have is that early on you're given access to powerful weapons and vehicles that are easily replaced. I find myself retreating to a safe house to replenish my weapons or spawning a new vehicle because mines went up in smoke. So I'm not relying on the weapons around me unless I'm desperate or running out of time.  What made the malls so great was dashing from store to store and finding something weird to fight with. You can still do this but it's just not as fun.
Which leads on to Zombies which are easy prey during the day (unless on the road) but they swarm the streets at night to the point they respawn within minutes of you mowing down a large group. Psychopath fights have been fun so far and they add something more to the story.
There's a lot of little things going on to help fill out the streets; safe houses, survivors, tragic moments and other collectables. It's worth playing but you might find yourself a tad lost as to why certain things are happening because they link to the previous. But I'm gaining PP like crazy and at night, with the right weapons, you can net a lot of PP- allowing you to level up quickly. But you can't grind as time is of the essence! Something Dead Rising 4 left out and even I can see that as a stupid move.
One last thing; Xbox controller for windows works perfectly well. I am using X360ce emulator but can't say if that's why; only because I hear people have issues getting it to work. Just don't use the steam controller support.
TL;DR - A lot of fun. Bit easy, Co-Op is nice. Miss the atmosphere of the Malls but vehicles are a nice touch.

This is more like Dungeon Keeper than Dungeons 1 was, and that's a good thing. The story is one big meme parade, though. In the intro mission you'll have your character dealing "over 9000" damage (9001 do be precise) and there are a lot of Lord of the Rings references. If you enjoy that kind of silly humour, then the campaign is pretty fun and slowly gives you more units to play with. The underground world and overland world split is nice; I don't think the first game had that. Underground you gather gold and mana, overland you take control of villages or landmarks to gather "evilness", a resource you use to advance your research tree beyond the basics. Heroes from the overland world will occasionally break into your dungeon, so you have to put down traps and guardposts to defend yourself. It also gives you a reason to leave some minions in the dungeon so they can work the machines in special rooms, and defend you when required. Your other minions can go into the army you use to attack objectives in the overland map. All in all, it's a nice game that has an almost sandbox like quality to it, even while you are playing the campaign missions.

As a Kickstarter Backer I just got my Beta access last week and i've spent a lot of time since then playing this game. It's great to see the game being pretty much exactly what they promised. But it's definitely still in beta. There are graphical glitches, minimal tutorials, insufficient tooltips, hotkeys aren't customizeable or even detailed anywhere I could find in the game and the ones I could figure out don't make a lot of sense to me, and game balance needs improvement. But I haven't found any genuine bugs in the mechanics of the game so far and that I'm happy about, it means they've built a solid framework for the game and just need to work out the details.
Getting through the first few story missions felt like climbing Everest...just completing the first step in the story took me more than an hour in my first game. The resources required to research and build the next tier of officer structure to unlock the 3rd officer feels extremely prohibitive, then building him/her a ship to join your fleet is another chore. I started a new game once I knew what to expect and it still took me almost 45minutes to get a 3rd officer and a ship for him, all the while fighting for my life against pirates and trying to respond to as many distress calls as I could to try to hold on to a few resource producing outposts and evacuate all the ones that were too far from the station for me to effectively protect so I could pad my crew on the station and not feel like a total failure when the Chruul eventually killed them. It took me nearly three hours to reach the target of the next stage of the storyline once I had my 3rd officer...sending a fleet of three ships to New Terra ended up feeling like a huge risk because it's so far away from the station and while the fleet is away you're defenseless. By the time they got home I had 2 enemy fleets sieging the station killing my crew in the bombardment.
It's been fun playing and I'm going to keep at it since i enjoy a challenge. The game is in a good spot for an Early Access release, but it does still need a lot of work.

Where can I start?!
Paladins is a hero shooter that is more then 2 years old and still in the "Beta" (you alredy know that something is wrong with game when it's in Early Access this long).
Paladins looks like Overwatch when you look at it but similarities end here. Paladins plays very differently from OW and has more depth into it thanks to loadout system. Maps are small and simple, good for you if you love getting in combat faster. There are 33 playable characters in game and each one feels ditincuishable. Game is deep and complex and it's very satisfying to master champion (but I can't say same about every champion)
sadly, this is where fun part ends. Paladins is 2 years old game it's full of bugs and glitches. I joined when Paladins came out on Steam (more then one year ago) and game still has same bugs and they add one or two more on every single patch. Some of those bugs are just gamebreaking and devs don't even bother to fix them. Game also suffers from poor balance (it was not in a good shape before OB64 patch but this patch just through out balance out of the window), some champions are overpowered as hell when the others are underperforming. Servers are another issue I've never seen such unstable and weak servers (expect 80+ ping in every match). Bonus point - poor optimisation. At least game was going right direction but this new OB64 patch just destroyed everything, balance is worse then it was before, also it added 100 more bugs in game and new loadout system is restrictive af.
So. Core of Paladins is really funny and it will easily hook you, but game suffers from so many problems that I can't recommend it. Go and play Overwatch or TF2 if you want hero shooter, or you can try it by yourself and see what bad game looks like.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a surprisingly good game.
I'd been told it was a good game previously, but never had a chance to try it out. By the time I remembered about the game, it was a few years after release and the graphics looked somewhat dated and I was foolish enough to give the game a skip based on that.
Then a friend of mine offered me a spare copy of the game going free, so I thought 'Ack, why the heck not!' and installed with haste. I played it straight over the following three days, putting 25.8 hours into the game, completing it on the hardest difficulty (or at least, the hardest available. I think there might be an even harder level now available after completing the game).
Oh boy, it was good.
Problem was, I went through the entire game without killing anyone. Or so I thought. Then I remembered I shot someone in the tutorial. Whoops. Oh well, just an achievement.
The game was rather easy to play, especially if you play non-lethal ghost. I've not tried out going loud - I suspect it'd be much harder, considering the amount of damage they deal on harder difficulties. So one might want to take that into mind.
Gameplay wise the game is above average - it's not exactly a great shooter, but the stealth is decent enough. It could be improved and I hope in the new game they make the combat a little more intuitive and/or realistic. But there will always be more one can want.
Yet what makes it great is the world and the story, and how people react to your actions. It feels nice when people comment about your lack of lethal use throughout the game - and, without spoiling anything, saving certain characters also happens to have a significant impact on the game too.
Obviously in my review, however basic it may be, I'm biased to a degree because I didn't actually purchase the game - but having played it, I would've bought it (at sale price, because I'm stingy) had I know what the game was actually like to player.

Don't get me wrong: there's lots to like with this package, and it was dirt cheap when it came out. However, there is no option to skip Missing Link, and no way to uninstall it. I can understand if this review sucks in your opinion, as HRDC added in new features like hacking turrets in boss fights. The boss fights in the vanilla game though were incredibly easy though, and most could be dispatched with explosives or EMP mine/ hot lead combos. I know you'll criticize me for suggesting you break a play style, but we're in this situation because the Dev's wanted you to kill the bosses in the first place. One method is as good as another, and the one I employ only requires you collect explosives, rather than unlocking hacking.
Either way, Missing Link is an unwelcome interruption--especially the parts that are masked as loading screens. Originally, you would be able to reach the end and then watch the game go downhill upon reaching the last level. Instead you play ML, groan, get to the second last level, get hyped that the game's good again, and then have your joy come crashing down upon getting to the last level. It really gets in the way of wanting to finish the game.
I'd say get the original HR in place of DC, but Steam is forcing people to get this instead, which is another reason I am not recommending this. Avoid.

Let me start out by saying that, even after only playing it for a few hours, I LOVE this game and I honestly believe it's the absolute best Storm game and Naruto game to date.  If at any time during this review you begin to lose sight of that, return to this first sentence.
If you've played any of the previous games you will definitely enjoy this one.  They've perfected the system they've been struggling with since the first game.  Battles are faster paced and much more dynamic, the boss fights are as exciting as we were promised they would be a few games ago, and the cast of characters is more plentiful than ever.  Players of the very first UNS will be delighted to find that they've brought back the option to change what jutsu characters use instead of being stuck with one.  This isn't with all characters, but it is still with quite a handful of them.
The battles run smoothly with the exception of quicktime events.  The quicktime events are great to watch and are rewarding when you succeed, but they are more frequently the most unresponsive thorns in my♥♥♥♥♥that have ever been programmed.  You have plenty of time to do the inputs, they just don't register.  Speaking of not registering, let's talk about the menus.  All of the menus in the game are slow, laggy, unresponsive, and very easily break the flow between battles as most of your time in between battles will be spent waiting for the menu to finish loading and repeatedly hitting A or the thumbstick frustradedly waiting for one of your attempts to finally work.  This can kill your mood and really take you out of the thrill of the good parts of the game.  I do want to reiterate that this is only with the menus.  The actual battles run very smoothly.
Also, I don't know if this is something everyone has been experiencing, but when my health gets low in a battle, this ungodly annoying as sh*t siren alarm noise goes off nonstop until I exit the game mode completely or go back to the start menu.  Not the main menu.  The f*cking START menu.  It is linked to the SFX setting, but I don't want to turn it all the way down to mute the siren because I want to hear the punches and justu and such.  So that's beyond irritating.
All that said, the game has only been out for a few days.  I'm hoping a patch will come out to fix the terrible bits.  But really, when the only glaring issue with a game is the menus, how bad can it really be?
As a side note, for those of you that were p*ssed at how they did Kushina in Revolution, prepare to be disappointed all over again because she remains unchanged.

I've played this a little bit over the last few years and while the general idea of it is very fun, this game suffers from three giant problems:
1. Strict adherance to the source material smothered any kind of innovation in the crib. There is nothing new here, and there never will be. Now don't get me wrong, the Battletech Universe is incredibly cool in a lot of ways, but I feel like all the current Battletech projects all just kind of stagnate in a universe where all the broad strokes are already in place. Let alone the fact that many of the coolest mechs in the series don't show up until late in the timeline means that any game that strictly adheres to the lore can't actually put all the fan favourites in the game. Want an large caliber autocannon that can fire further than 300 meters? Tough luck, it's not in the source material so it doesn't exist and never will. Don't even think about shields, repair tools, ammo boxes, or any other number of things that seem like a pretty straight forward adition to a game that's keeping with the times.
2. The game doesn't really allow you to have a giant robot power fantasy, because the only thing you ever get to shoot at is other giant robots. It's one of those games that would be absolutely brilliant if there was more stuff to shoot at, like tanks and helicopters and infantry and all sorts of things like that, but it's running on a very straight forward system that gives you one mech, as it takes damage it continuously gets weaker, and the win condition is most often simply killing the enemy team. The best you can do is often merely surviving till the end of the match. It's the same problem as World of Tanks and it's ilk have, while they are very realistic in a sense they never give you space to just enjoy being a super powerful mech or tank or whatever.
3. Progression in this game is incredibly slow, has very few meaningful rewards, and you need to drop absurd amounts of money to buy things. Basically this game has the tiniest little hint of a progression system where your pilot levels up and gets better at using certain mechs, but the way it's implemented is just awful. In order to become a master of a specific chassis for example you have to earn a large amount of XP not just with the mech you actually want to drive, but with different variants of that same chassis.That means buying the same mech multiple times and spending a lot of time playing with setups that aren't actually what you want. The only way to make that a little easier on yourself is to drop real life cash on mech packs that give you all the variants.  A lot of mechs, like the clan mechs and various premium machines are basically absurd money sinks where you can drop as much cash as you'd spend on a whole other game just to buy a single mech.
So overall: This game is extremely good looking, and it has its moments in gameplay, but it's adeherence to Battletech lore basically means nothing new and surprising will ever happen in this game, and they cannot innovate on play mechanics in any way. The overall feel of the game isn't like what you got from the old Mechwarrior titles, because there is nothing to fight in this game that you are supposed to win against. A competitive environment is fun and all, but it kind of sucks the fun out of giant robots if there is nothing you can simply step on. The monetization scheme of this game along with it's extremely grindy and shallow progression system kind of keep this from being any fun unless you are just really into the competitive aspect of it. There is little reason to just play because you want to build your ultimate mech.
Wish there were more options than "Yes" and "No" for reviewing games, because I feel like I'm giving a negative review but I still want people to check it out for themselves.

I've had this game in my library for at least 5 years now, and during that space of time I have gone on and off it. I have always think it is a brilliantly unique game, but sometimes I just get a burnout. However, I always find myself coming back to it. Tribes: Ascend is a brilliant game. It is set in a futuristic time with huge open maps, which you traverse with a combination of jetpack and "skiing" - your boots eliminate any friction beneath them so you can slide along, surprise surprise, like skiing, and this can bring you to speeds of over 300 kph. Using these and a combination of weapons, some with a high skill level, some considered noob, you can fight in a variety of game modes, the most common being CTF, TDM and Arena. With a huge array of weapons and abilities, you can tailor your loadout to any number of abilities, such as flag capping, stealth, or just pure combat.
Now the downsides...
The developers, Hi-Rez Studios (Paladins, Smite) have abandoned the game. Twice. A while back they abandoned it a first time, to focus on Smite, then began updating again, but have ditched it again. It has a very small playerbase, with only about 50-65 players online at one time across all the servers, at a maximum. However, the player count isn't nescessarily a downside. The lack of updates, maybe.
If you can get used to the different feel of this game, it will be worth your while. I would definitely recommend this.

Pretty fun game, playing this quite a lot since beta. You don't need to buy anything for real cash to enjoy MWO, well maybe except for mech bays then again quite often, almost every week there is an event during which you can win something like; mech bay, MC(cash shop currency), c-bills, gxp, cockpit items, premium time, colours, sometimes mechs, camo patterns. Except for hero mechs, every single mech is avaialble for in-game currency after some time, hero mechs are slightly different variants and come with a 30% C-Bill bonus.
We have a lot of mechs to choose from in this game(some have quite nice models I must say) there is of course nice customization too (armor/weapons/engines/equipment/modules/colours/camos/decals), I wasted so much time tweaking my mechs in the hangar, that is quite fun on its own.
It is not the easiest game for new players, it is important to find your favorite role in game, brawler or sniper etc. to enjoy it completely, get yourself mech perfect for your playstyle, join some unit especially if you want to play CW(Community Warfare) which was also called FW(Faction Warfare) and now FP(Faction Play), playing that solo may be quite painful experience, it is a team based game after all. Not to mention that in CW/FW/FP unlike in "quick play" you won't be playing only versus players of more or less similar skill.
The combat is fun, each mech is made of parts; separate legs, separate arms, two side torsos, central torso, cockpit and the back. To kill a mech you need either to destroy both legs, central torso, cockpit(which is very small so you rarely can hit it) or the back where armor is weak.If mech is using XL engine(it is lighter than standard engine) you can kill it not only by shooting the parts I mentioned earlier but by destroying side torso, that works at least with Inner Sphere mechs because you won't kill clan mechs by destroying one side torso, you need to get both side torsos to kill a clan mech(clan IIC mechs can use either std or xl engines, rest can use only xl).
If your mech will lose a leg you will move way slower, if your side torso gets destroyed then arm attached to it gets destroyed too.
Teamwork, positioning and communication are all terribly important in this game, rambos and stragglers will be easy prey so you should stick with your friends unless you are in very fast mech with ECM. You usually won't die instantly unless you get shot in the back/cockpit with some big gun or if you will be unfortunate enough to get a lot of unwanted attention from more than one enemy.
There is "heat" in the game, every weapon will give you some heat whenever fired, mech can withstand just so much of heat before shutting down for a moment, which makes you an easy target. Energy weapons give more heat(but you don't need ammo for those) than ballistic weapons but with those you have to put some ammo on your mech, which not only takes precious space but possibly can explode when you get shot at. Right now missile weapons are somewhere between energy and ballistic, heat wise, more or less.
At the end I must say that there are few things that I would like to see added to the game in future; more maps, melee combat(which sadly I doubt we will ever really see implemented), npc infantry/vehicles, changes/updates for CW/FW/FP which will make me care for my faction, also I really hope for better optimization, maybe engine change since we can already see that this is not the prettiest game around.

As much as I feel a bit mixxed with this game (and I'll explain why), it's a great, well done, creative game. Worth the price or no less than $10. Felt a hint of Paper Mario from the N64 with the badges.
The story is interesting, but I had trouble keeping track of it since most of the names aren't very easy to remember to a specific character. In fact some of the characters talk in first person and I forget who's talking at times or find myself not caring much about the story, sadly. (I would like to say I was bored of the story here and there, but everyone will assume I was in it for the breasts or whatever. Despite I have a thing for melons, that wasn't the case for this game.)
Here's the story from what I can recall:
Erina wakes up in a box in an area she doesn't recognize. She was a rabbit prior to waking up, but became human and for some unknown reason is dressed like a playboy rabbit (in terms of the clothing since the ears and tail are real). After exploring the unknown area, she wakes up back on her home island with her head on some girl's lap (who may or may not have a crush on Erina.) Erina eventually meets a frantic fairy named Ribbon, who believes she's a real bunny that eats fairies, and ends up attacking Erina in near exhaustion. After the battle, they become friends and head over to Rabi Rabi Town where they meet Erina's master (remember, Erina was an actual bunny before turning human, so think "pet owner" master). Her master, Rumi, is shocked to see her pet turned human and explains what lead up to the change, along with Bunny Lovers becoming very rampent and nearly causing an extinction of rabbits on the island, and Rumi's missing sister, Miru. From there, Erina and Ribbon set out on an adventure.
That's just the Prologue too (roughly the first hour of the game). As you progress, you'll notice some references/cameos, even from another Sekai Project game.
The gameplay just keeps me glued to the point I have to hit the panic button to summon a friend with a crowbar to pry me away from my laptop! It's that addicting and fun. Last game I played that was a metroidvania + bullet hell was Rogue Legacy (however the layouts change every death, but is a decent comparison) but that was more frustrating than this (yet both challenging).
Now this is where I start to have mix feelings. I'm fine with fan-service when it makes sense, is humorous, and/or subtle, but when it becomes abundent, even if subtle, I start to question the value of the game. Everytime I see fan-service in a game, my first thought is "Is it a poorly made game with eye candy to cover it or is the game very well made and the fan-service is just the icing to a very delicious cake?" This time, cake is no lie, but the icing does become too much that I can somewhat taste the cake and gradually become sick of the icing.
Majority of the fan-service I was comfortable with. Most of the characters, while may be sexualized, aren't TOO sexualized and feel more down-to-earth of how they appear. There's a handful that are beyond subtle, but it fits their character or the people they interact, so no real complaints. The game does recognize this that even Erina acknowledges she has no idea why she's dressed that way, with another character calling her outfit "Shameless", and another instance of one character showing boob envy of a close friend of hers. As for the fairy's clothing... well faries are faries. How they dress is really up to speculation and imagination (look at Tinker Bell) so there's really no use in throwing a fuss about that. Ribbon is about the size of an average palm anyway (with no telling how old she really is).
Sadly, no explanation was ever given for why Erina was dressed in such fashion, I say as I glare at the devs since Erina doesn't deserve to be dressed that way (she's WAY too innocent for that). Do expect innuendo jokes and context though. You be a fool to not expect them from this game.
Overall, don't let the fan-service deter you. It's 100% non-sexual/suggestive. It's just appealing and nothing more. Yes, I was skeptic at first, but I asked around to verify from other players to help ease my mind.
(However, if you get easily offended for seeing a girl in a bikini, some cleavage showing, and/or dressed in what's suppose to be sexual/suggestive but, in game context, isn't, well you're a kill-joy, paranoid person, or down right prude. Or maybe just a horny teen looking for content to get off on... you creep.)
There are at least two CG's that I just couldn't help but facepalm or groan in massive annoyance as it made two female characters look degrading than they should be. (You'll know once you see them and after you know the characters.)
The music I just LOVE.
Controls do feel odd, but will take a bit to get used to.
Now I need to mention some technical issues. My laptop surpasses the minimum system requirements, however there are isolated cases of frame dropping. I usually don't care about FPS beyond 30, but this game was programed to run smooth on 60, and if it drops to like 45 or 30 the effects clearly shows visually. Sadly there is no frame skip option, and even setting everything to the lowest settings there's still frame dropping. It's believed to be due to a certain number of sprites in one area, the background, or some unknown variable.
This is a known issue from others, not just me, and the devs are trying to find solutions for it. I'm unsure if this is recent or since release. Try not to let that deter you though as it can make boss battles easy since they're bullet hell/endurance.
Story is well made, however wonders off a bit.
Characters are each unique in their own way.
Fan-service is decent and subtle majority of the time.
Gameplay is VERY addicting and challenging.
You'll want to explore EVERYTHING and EVERYWHERE.
This is not porn.
Get it at full price or no less than $10 (any cheaper and you're hurting the devs and killing innocent rabbits.)

For starters, I bought this game at a little bit of a discount (I can't remember how much). $17.99 seems fair though. Axiom Verge was $19.99, and well worth it. I may be wrong, but Rabi seems to have more content. So, there ya go. Really fun gameplay. Dynamic. Unique. Great idea meshing the open world metroidvania style with bullet hell. It really works. Full disclosure, I'm not an anime guy. And the story, with the corresponding wall of text is grating to me. Not knocking you, if you like it. But, if you're like me, you almost definitely will not. The constant text stops really takes away from the overall fantastistic gameplay, in my opinion. I saw there is a speedrun mode which I assume is devoid of text. So, that's pretty sweet. Also, you can fast forward it pretty quickly. So, if you're here for the gameplay don't fear, it's there in abundance. I like the leveling, it's decently unique. And, the game doesn't limit what bosses you fight or what direction you go as far as I can tell. Which, is probably the single most awesome feature. Wanna get slayed by something double your level? This game says, "go right ahead". If you manage to beat that boss, and trust me, it will be a real challenge. You probably won't be hindered by some dumb incumberence, like having a certain item or ability. For the most part, you should be free to explore. Which is seriously cool. Tons of overhead with the difficulty, at least for me. Haven't tried the harder modes, but there are 5 or 6 different difficulty levels which is incredibly promising. Someone correct me if I'm wrong. I was playing in normal, and after a while, I was getting my a** kicked. I'm pretty darn accustomed to shmups and metroid, so the challenge is definitely there. On a more nitpicky note, the menus are really nice at least from what I've used. Really high level of polish in this game, and you can see it with how logically so many pieces of UI are laid out. Again, the anime style story has not been for me. The art is great especially in the stills, but how many ellipses can a single piece...of...dialogue...possibly...have...  That said, awesome game. Great buy for metroidvania people looking for a fulfilling feeling twist or bullet-hellers who like a well crafted platformerer. Definitely a fan. Definitely would suggest it to either of those types of gamer.

This is an adventure you can go through with one hand. If you like charming, undemanding turn-based fantasy games where victory over the bad guys is determined by plans and careful decisions, 'Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic' is for you.
'Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic' is all about working with what you're given. All the way from the start, at team composition: you have to hire just three heroes from a diverse group, and you have no control over their traits or specialties. Don't be alarmed though, you can find a balance of variables like strength and healing abilities because all the stats and skills are clearly laid out for comparison purposes.
At the central town, citizens will send you on quests. Each destination is found on a linear path, with no worries about getting lost or missing something during the trip. Along the way there, the game directly offers events to you, and you decide whether you'll take a chance in exchange for experience and random items, or ignore it and focus on the task at hand.
I like to think majority of the game is played on the Inventory screen, where you can heal, change equipment, compare items, and throw away the excess. With limited backpack space, two-handed heroes, and growing needs, you address questions like: 'Should I keep this 100% Venom Fillet Knife, or hold on to the Anti-Confusion Ascot?' The answers are found in the locations, and you pick the details up along the way. 'Are enemies immune to poison?' 'Do they have magic insanity spells?' 'Why is this carrot talking to me?'
Evidently, 'Byte & Magic' also succeeds because of its good sense of humor. Even in simple speech bubbles and flavor text, settings and characters are given enough personality that we give a dang about them: and this trait may be necessary in a game where your characters can get permanently killed, and the survivors have to get all the way back to town before you can revive anyone.
Of course, as Rogue-like games go, if all your characters get killed, it means having to start from the very beginning again. This was the aspect that turned me off from Rogue-likes in the past, but I was surprised how much I liked this game in spite of its format. This may be because of how simple its mechanics are under the surface. One user berated it for being too simple, 'like a mobile game,' however, as a person who loves the opportunity of light weight in mobile games, I find that an advantage. The simplicity makes it worth the effort when you sometimes have to start all over.

Let me disclose that I've played DOOM in all of its forms, from the classic from 1993, which also had its sequel Doom 2: Hell on Earth from 1994, Doom 3 both the original form and the BFG edition, and went as far as playing several Doom mods or better known as WADs in the classic game's respective community, and of course there's Brutal Doom and its further modded counterparts in Project Brutality and its lik. From a year back, I knew that I was going to expect when i finally got my hands on the DOOM Reboot which I'll always call DOOM 2016, as this is one of those games that made 2016 such an epic year not just for the FPS genre but for the whole gaming experience in general.
Also, to really appreciate this game, one must also consider the general state of First Person Shooters after DOOM's time. I bet there's a bunch of the really wise and cultured players who actually was so sick and tired of every Shooter trying to be like Call of Duty or more modern shooters simply not having enough shooting when many games that aren't Doom are filled with junk such as unskippable AND LONG cutscences, lame mechanics that stop you from shooting, reloading which stops you from firing your weapons and thus interrupting the action, samey enemies armed with guns and nothing else that rarely change the dynamics of the gameplay, and other useless fat and junk that we simply had enough of. DOOM is that game to simply raise its middle finger to all of that bullcrap. Now, for a game to carry up such a long and storied history behind it, spanning more than 2 decades as of the writing of my personal opinion about this game, it needs more than just some of the most beautiful graphics to ever grace any game system (whether it be PC or the consoles) and the namesake of DOOM to really live up to its classic counterpart. This game requires a general understanding of what people loved about Old School First person shooters back in the day and what DOOM was all about from 2 decades ago, and this game nails everything that people loved about Doom.
What was Doom all about? Simple. "Shooting Demons in Mars". That famous quote was how it was described by John Carmack, one of the original creators of DOOM. It didn't need anything else for it to be a seller. Today, SHOOTING DEMONS IN MARS is still ridiculous as it was more than 20 years ago. It didn't need that much filler or fat. It was all the meat that every gamer craved, and this game carries over the same legacy while providing some modern touches and facelifts to appeal for the younger lads and even those such as myself who have been with this franchise longer than most people have started gaming.
When it comes to what it has to offer, it downright nails it harder than impaling someone with a bloody nailgun. Upon opening the first few minutes of the game's campaign, you are greeted with a short cutscene that says these beautiful words - "RIP AND TEAR, UNTIL IT IS DONE" and from that few seconds of dialogue, you are greeted with the game simply starting and you simply shooting a bunch of zombies, walking a bit to grab your precious Praetor Suit, and proceeding to do more and more and more for the next 12-20 hours or so. There is a glorious lack of cutscenes in the game's campaign which really gives this game a tone where you know its all about, constant action with the correct amount of pacing. The game's campaign really nails it well by making sure that each level has a cleverly arranged set of action sequences and exploration sections to keep the pacing in check.
General gameplay mechanics and dynamics is splendid. Doomguy moves fast without any "lame" mechanics such as sprinting, and we all know how we have grown sick and tired of sprinting since it stops us from actually shooting, again pointing out that DOOM is not subtle when it comes to avoiding as many lame and overused FPS mechanics in the last decade or so. You also have an assortment of weapons of different strengths and weaknesses, thus you have to actually know what weapons to use to deal with the assortment of enemies you have to face. Facilitating that, your player character Doomguy switches weapons fast, and there's even an upgrade that enables you to switch weapons even faster. Being able to move and shoot at full speed is such as joy compared to other experiences in other shooters that aren't Doom and the like. If you are one of those youngins that never played the classic games, but was unfortunate enough to drown yourself in the likes of Call of Duty and Battlefield or even Halo (LUL), I won't say I'm sorry but I'll be unapologetic when I say, it feels good to wield multiple weapons at once at any given time and moving at top speed while shooting non stop until the ammunition counter says otherwise.
Now one of the game's selling points is the Glory Kill system, which are basically first person fatalities for the uninitated. Many had the impression that it would interrupt the action and was just silly overall, but they either have not played the game yet, or didn't bother understanding its essence. The thing is that Glory Killing was meant to further emphasise that this is a game that's all about moving forward, sideways, backpedalling, among directions as you massacre those demons. The glory kill animations are entertaining, and because they are such an essential part of the overall action, they are things you have to get used to seeing. But you may be thinking, these first person fatality or takedown animations may get too old rather quickly, slow down the game, or interrupt the action? --> WRONG. The Glory Kills given how fast they occur, they never interrupt the action, and they never get old at least for me. This isn't something like God of War where Kratos turns kill animations into damn cutscenes. Doomguy does them fast and clean.
I won't even limit this to how you play as your player character but I'll also describe the experience whats it like fighting your enemies, which is another important aspect of any shooting game, and a really remarkable trait found in many old school shooters In DOOM, part of the challenge is knowing what your enemies do. This isn't a game where you face guys with guns and hide behind cover like a bunch of wussies, hoping to kill you in 2 bullets or less. This is a game where you can actually tell what your enemies can do, since they fire either projectiles that you can see, or charge into melee range and hit you with rather damaging attacks. Old School shooters are known for such gameplay, and DOOM nails it well. You see, in this game, if you ever do die, unlike in more modern themed shooters, IT IS CLEARLY YOUR FAULT. You got hit with projectiles, you were not aware of your surroundings, you didn't use the correct weapon for the correct job. You stopped moving to do something or you probably had an itch. If you got killed by any of the monsters in this game, it is clearly YOUR FAULT, and you get a death animation as your reward, telling how much you suck.
As far as some of the modern facelifts go such as Upgrade Systems for your weapons, the suit, and even the runes which are found as secrets, they add so much to the game without ruining the experience. You see, most of the upgrades that you get are not direct stats for you, but are more directed to improving your handling statistics and your weapons.
Of course there are some weaknesses. Some weapon modes are not as effective as they should be, like the Micro Missles from the Heavy Assault Rifle, the last few levels feeling rushed compared to the earlier levels, I also feel that there could have been MORE LEVELS, like ACTUAL SECRET LEVELS instead of just these old school maps that was put there as fanservice, and explosive weapons lacking visual power like the Rocket Launcher and the Grenades, the plasma rifle just feeling so weak since its now an early game weapon, also there are A FEW (count 3) cutscences that can't be skipped. Steam character limit is also a CON.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution has made me a fan of the franchise.
One of the greatest things about the game is the augmentations. You can pick your route and how you want to play the game through the augmentations. It doesn't penalize you for going straight into the fray or stealthing your way through missions. There's usually more than one way to accomplish a task and with that type of freedom I felt compelled to try everything. Nothing's more fun than walking around China slums causing havoc in their gangs or flexing on unsuspecting enemies.
There's no black and white in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and the end hinges on the player's choice. Even your interactions with the NPCs is affected by the player's choice. In the first mission as a newly augmented human being, Jensen is tasked to infiltrate Sarif Industries company and rescue the hostages. The SWAT team is put on hold so that he can go in and find a resolution. David Sarif gives you two options: Lethal, or non-lethal.
In the end, it doesn't matter because Jensen comes equipped with enough moves to subdue opponents peacefully or lethally. However, your perception in the game will be determined how you handle these situations. Will you have Jensen murder all the terrorists to set an example? Will Jensen rescue the hostages or botch it up? Will you engage the terrorists leader at the end or talk him down? These choices will manifest as you play through the game and people's opinion of you will be set.
These are the type of games I love because it gives you the freedom to choose. It may be a small thing, but it was enough for me to play through the game multiple times and in different ways.
Like Deus Ex: Human Revolution, what will you choose to do after this review?

I've played the game since founders beta so on and off since 2012.
This game hasn't fixed its huge issues for years.
Mech combat is poorly balanced, favouring clans, the more expensive faction, since they were released.
The grind is rough, the first 25 matches gives you a large bonus so you can buy one IS mech and most of its upgrades. But that is only once and each new mech requires some basic upgrades like double heatsinks, a necessary update at 1.5 million for every mech, endo-steel, and new engines and weapons. After you get one mech you need to master 2 other variants of the same chassis to unlock the skills required to compete with veterans who have been playing for a long time.
The queue times are probably the biggest killer, taking 5+ minutes to find a basic match for the game's most common game mode and that's the fastest it gets. Community Warfare queues can take up to 30 minutes.
Game modes in this game are all really simplistic with the TDM and team conquest styles because really basic kill-all-enemies is fine but the community warfare mode is completely lacking on any deeper roles or meaning despite it being supposedly the final game mode for faction vs faction warfare. Factions are so empty that everyone jumps around to whatever faction has enough people and there's no meaning to planetary losses or gains.
Overall, this game has been developed poorly for years, minimal viable product being an actual term used to describe it by the developers, and this is just an attempt to gain a few more people before the game goes under. The free to play game is usually described as having whales to make money and a large amount of people to fill the game so everyone's happy. MWO is a game that only has whales left and they're desperate for the game to appeal to people who don't want to spend hundreds of dollars on this game.

I like games that are about skill and wit. I like games where you dont run out of things to get better at. I like games where you can choose how to play it. The best ones are the games where YOU are your worst enemy.
MWO has all that so yeah, got pretty hooked once i started to get the hang of it.
The gameplay is pretty deep once you start getting into it. Selection of mechs is huge and most do play out quite differently. You can also customize them extensively. Most importantly, you can really get a sense of improving your skills which is the aspect that makes me come back time after time.
The earnings do become quite modest after the first twenty games (Where you get a huge bonus) so it really might seem that the game is all pay-to win and the grind for new mechs nearly eternal unless you throw some money at it. (It really isn't such a bad idea to dop a few bucks for that mech pack you want at this point.) But rest assured: The earnings will get much better once you get better at it. After a while, you can easily  buy mechs faster than you can learn to play them.
Money really can't buy anything that skill doesn't make up. Only fasten the grind, get vanity items and ofc that newest shiniest mech they just released. What of it? By the time you run out of mechs to play, those new mechs are already on sale, for ingame currency.
Now the game does have it's flaws as do ever other game. What they are really depends on who you ask.
If you expect some true to the lore grand mmo revolving around dominating galaxies in giant stompy robots, you might be in for a disappointment. Hopefully we get some of that once the community warfare's out of beta and all that, but it's not there yet.
If you instead take it as a tactical battletech fps mortal kombat with guns and lasers in big customizable robots, your are in for a treat.

It's hard to find a game as polarizing as MWO. Some love it, some hate it, but both sides have their points.
The game is far from new, at the time of this review its a little over 2 years old and just hitting steam now. It launched in 2013 to middling reviews, many can agree the core gameplay is solid. But on launch it only had two gamemodes, and in the two years since they claim to have added 3 more. Though one is Skirmish (Deathmatch) which added nothing new gameplay wise, and Invasion/Invasion Counter Attack (Same mode mirrored).
A vast majority of games will come down to destroying the enemy team, and to do so you have a very wide selection of mechs and loadouts. The meta of which has been evolving over the life of the game. As a Legendary Founder who has played on and off since beta I've seen the rise and fall of OP Alpha-strikes, LRMgeddon, Poptarting, etc. Currently the game revolves around mid-short range brawls, generally playing peakaboo at the line of skirmish until one side finds an edge and pushes through to vitctory. Games tend to play out a little one sided.
At the core of many arguments is the pricing model of MWO. At launch they offered tiered packs with exclusive mech variants to raise support for the game. While many accepted it as a good way to kickstart the games development, few suspected it would carry on as a common occurance. In 26 months there have been 5 more drives for money including Resistance I and II, and Clan invasion 1, 2, and 3. Not counting pre-order exclusivity to new Mechs for cash only. These typically offer a range of mechs from Light all the way up to Assault in increasingly expensive packs. A common criticism is the option to buy mechs 'a la carte' being much more expensive without offering many of the benefits of the pack. Making heavier mechs arbitrarily cost more as you will either have to pay the fee or suck it up and buy the rest of the lighter mechs bundled together.
Another criticism is the exclusive variants of mechs marketed as "heroes" for cash only. While they are generally considered on par if not worse than ones available for in-game currency. Many find it distastful to lock potentially gameplay and balance effecting loadouts behind a paywall. In recent months they've began running tournaments which make it possible to earn their premium currency and time without spending money. But you'll be grinding for a long time to catch up on all the mechs they've released since.
MWO is not a pay to win game, but its definitely pay to skip the grind. It can be unfriendly to new players with a steep learning curve (Tutorial has helped somewhat), uncooperative community, and combination of unfriendly game mechanics. To master a mech you will need to own three variants of it, which means you will need to do your research if you don't want to waste your initial cadet bonus C-bills on a mech that you'll abandon down the road. It will also take a fair amount of games in each chassis to reach your maximum potential. Even just maxing out your favorite mech of each weight class will be a large undertaking without shelling out money for a mech with Cbill or Exp boosts and premium time. While not mandatory, it is a competitive PvP game and you're going to want every advantage you can get.
The developers objectively haven't handled the game very well, they are typically slow to react to the players or occasional controversy such as the backlash surrounding the infamous $500 golden mechs. Their actions, or in-action has lead to the current climate in the community where it seems to be a 50/50 split between die-hard supporters of the franchise who love the game for what it is, and those that are upset with the direction the game has taken and that it doesn't stay true to previous incarnations of the series. At least within the vocal minority, many have silently left or continued to enjoy the game. Which if you intend on playing is my recommended course of action, avoid the forums/subreddits/discussions unless you want to see the toxicity first hand.

This game has a great concept but its game play is bad. Learning about how guns work is interesting and taking apart and reassembling the guns is fun but the way the game makes you go about it is infuriating.
I really enjoy seeing how each gun comes apart and how they go back together. Its great seeing how each part in the weapon works together to fire the bullet and chamber the next round. The x ray and slow motion options are great for capturing exactly how it all interacts. This game does present this all in a very nice way. I feel like i have learned alot about the weapons that i have unlocked however, some of those weapons are of no real interest to me.
You must unlock each weapon with experiance you earn from playing the game but you dont earn enough to ensure you will unlock the next weapon from hitting the most common achiements. This mean you need to repeat each test several times and combine with the frustrating mechanics you'll end up hating the game quickly. Additional the weapons are only unlocked following a tree that might see weapons you want to learn about hidden behind dozens of guns you are not interested in.
The experiance needed to advance is earned from getting achievments such as finishing under a set time or not clicking the wrong part. This method would be fine except that you have to wait out each animation before you can start the next part and by default the camera swings around wildly when each part is moved. This all makes it almost impossible to reach the better times needed to get some of the achievements. Additionally, clicking on a part before the animation has finished will count as clicking the wrong part and shut you out of another achievement further adding to the frustration.
Finally, several achievements are require you to have a faster time then other people in the last 24 hours. These seem almost impossible to achieve as there are people who have unreasonably fast times blocking everyone from getting these achievements.
Many of these problems would be resolved by buying the game but I feel it is simply not worth the money for a collection of interactive user manuals.

Not sure why this game is getting so many negative reviews, though I do agree with some of what they're saying.  The main character isn't a hardnosed badass like you normally get in zombie games.  Nah, he comes off as a relatively normal dude put into the middle of extreme chaos and he isn't having much fun (even though we, as the players, are).  There ARE graphical glitches, but I'm able to overlook many of them.
Controls are a little slippery and delayed at times, which isn't that big of a deal unless you are doing PLATFORMING...then it sucks.  No, this isn't game of the year material here, but I also didn't expect it to be.  I'm having fun running through the streets with a shark mascot head on with a full tuxedo to match (riiiiight).  I'm having fun making ridiculous vehicle combinations and equally ridiculous weapons combos anytime I want instead of having to hit specialized areas to do so.
I'm having fun being able to recall anything I've ever held or crafted at a moment's notice in hideouts.  I'm having fun being able to call up saved survivors to join me at hideouts.  And I'm especially having fun knowing I can save wherever, whenever.  Does this make the game overly easy?  Eh, at times.  It's certainly not as hard as the original Dead Rising, but MAN is it fun.
If you're looking for a tough, tense zombie game, this probably isn't it.  If you're looking for something that is hilarious, aware of how ridiculous it is, and absolutely does not care, then this is right up your alley.

persuasion.  Know that your player-character is a bunny girl in a sexy outfit.  Still interested?  Well, I guess you got past
filter, you degenerate nerd!
Upon first glance, most people will probably take
to be some kind of
, but there isn't any nudity (
, so don't bother looking for an uncensor patch).  There is, however, tons of cartoon cheesecake, as Rabi-Ribi island is entirely populated by cute young girls -- and as you might surmise, the lesbian overtones are pretty thick.  I wouldn't play it in public or around relatives; the potential for embarrassing queries is sky-high!
On to the most important part:  the gameplay!  The framework of the game is metroidvania; you collect items, explore, fight lesser enemies on nearly every screen, and level up.  If sequence breaking is your bag (I don't care for it personally), this game encourages it outright, even spawning springs and stepping stones to help you reach "later" levels if it detects that you are purposefully doing things out of order.  The platforming is enjoyable and relaxing; I never ran into a gauntlet of pitfalls or spikes that made me cry out in wordless rage.
Sounds pretty easy, right?  Well it is, until you reach any of the game's 35+ bosses and the difficulty smashes through the roof!  Every boss fills the screen with curtains of glowing bullets, and you've got to navigate your character so that her chest (wherein lies her hitbox) stays clear while her neotenous, scantily clad fairy pal lays down return fire.  Every boss must have about a dozen different attack patterns, so any one of them may keep you retrying again, and again, and again . . . and AGAIN!  I took a masochistic pleasure in this, but I understand that there are some who don't get their kicks from having blushing manga chicks repeatedly flagellate them with strings of brightly colored plasma beads.  And yes, I did cry out in wordless rage during the boss battles, and how!
There's only one thing I didn't like about the game:  the endless dialog.  These crazy
girls don't know how to say anything short 'n' sweet, so if you are in the least interested in narrative happenings, prepare to wade through barrage after barrage of maddeningly circuitous prattle that is strangely comparable to the bullet bombardments of the merciless bosses.
is very long, and on top of that, it's polished; I don't think you'll run into any bugs no matter how long you play.  Its bosses make for the hardest "normal" mode I've ever seen, but I like it like that!  If you're in the market for bullet hell platforming punishment, and you're not bothered by a bit of (potentially uncomfortable) cartoon sexiness, I don't think you can do much better.  I will definitely pick up the inevitable sequel (but I sure hope that Crespirit learns a little about condensing dialog before then)!

I've been replaying this recently and loving it (I use the non-steam client) so I thought I'd repost this recommendation now that the character limit has gone.
======
So far the best iteration of Tribes since Tribes 2. What's more its free to play so you've got no excuse not to give it a try.
Skiing
For those who don't know the series Tribes offers team based gameplay with one of the best movement mechanics in arena style FPS called skiing.
It combines physics, jetpacks, the environment and the skill of the player to have you rocketing around the map at the speed of sound and makes for some excellent chases in capture the flag type scenarios and great combat that has you estimating trajectories of projectiles and players to produce some of the most epic trickshots you'll see in any game.
Classes
It also has a really nice class system that has subtle class differences which are exaggerated by player role choices in game. The subtlety results in a much more natural role selection basic much more on strategy rather than the "I'm playing the heavy-defender class therefore I only defend"
Map Design
One thing that also stands out to me is that I think the map design is beautiful for an arena game. While they do share some common features on the whole each map feels unique and have loads of great little details to bring them to life.
FTP
Finally for those who are nervous about free to plays being pay to win (as I was until recently) Tribes: Ascend feels like its got the right balance of paying giving you enough perks to make it worth it (which is important if you want the game to stay alive) but without being an essential element to play and kick♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rather than money opening up bigger scarier guns, it seems to open up alternative roles to play within the game, all of which are available over time when playing the game for free.
Downsides
The only thing missing from this wonderful iteration of the classic franchise is the modding that came with Tribes and Tribes 2. I remember my brother and I having a whale of a time as kids playing with a lot of mods and user generated maps that added a whole ton of content to the game. While it's obvious why this can't work in a FTP game, it's a bit of a shame. Hopefully though, if HiRez studios are successful they'll be enough interest to keep them adding official content to the game to keep us all keen.

As far as “Quality” is concerned, It is quite literally amazing how much graphical fidelity they can squeeze out of the 2.5gb of data that this game uses. The game looks really REALLY! good, not to mention that the optimization of the engine is absolutely perfect.

Other companies need to take note here, this is F2P done right!
Now the real question is, would I recommend Loadout?
Yes, just YES! Please take the time and download the 2.5gb of epic fun. How can you say no to hours and hours of free laughter?

Halcyon 6 wasn't just going for a genre, it was going for ALL the genres, and the question becomes whether it can keep gamers entertained, or confuse the sweet internet JESUS out of them.  There are a huge amount of options, menus, choices, resource gathering, and of course combat in Halcyon 6, and in this review we'll be going over what we've currently been given as an Early Access Beta.  As usual we'll be looking at three categories in particular, Gameplay, Sound, and Look.
For those that would rather listen/watch an in-depth review rather than read it:
Halcyon 6 is a game that has a clear and defined attention to detail when it comes to the various game mechanics, and believe me, there are a LOT of game mechanics.  It's one thing when a game tries to do too many things at once, but when a game succeeds at doing most or even all of those things, THAT is the real triumph.  All of the things that I mentioned Halcyon 6 does it DOES do well.  Combat is filled with a measure of strategy, including a vulnerability exploration combo style system.  Exploration is fun, but somewhat limited in scope, allowing you to visit various planets and moons in an attempt to find additional aid, enemies, or resources.
Your team is built exclusively by you choosing from three random prospects whenever an open slot appears thanks to you increasing your fleet to three officers, or one of them meeting an untimely death.  You must utilize the resources you find to improve your technology, build additional ships, or upgrade the Halcyon 6 itself.  And the game itself gives you the opportunity to make choices, like allying with Pirates for, air quotes, “mutual gain” or canceling out a 2666 year loan by participating in a trial by combat (PICK THE TRIAL BY COMBAT).
Halcyon's only weakness is that the development team is still clearly measuring how to balance the progression of the game and the strength of the enemies the player has to deal with.  Since there's no difficulty button, several players have quickly found the game can go from tutorial mode to DIE ♥♥♥♥♥ DIE rather quickly.
The sound in Halcyon is superb, when it exists, which luckily is most of the time.  I only found a few small instances where ships or weapons didn't have accompanying sound effects, but the rest of the time the retro sci-fi music and the various blips and blasts of your offensive and defensive powers were a joy to listen to.  Halycon 6 remains classy and professional, while not letting go of that 1990's arcade style soundtrack.  There are no voice overs, but I wouldn't have expected any in a game like Halcyon 6, instead it's all about having satisfying effects for the players choices.  Right behind gameplay,
Halcyon 6 is a pixel art style game, which means you're going to get your Chinese buffets worth of pixels.  If you go into the game understanding that this is the art style, you won't be disappointed.  The character designs are quite well done, and in some cases outright fantastic.  Even the effects can appear to jump off of the screen in some instances, showing Massive Damage definitely has a knack for working with this style of artwork.  Most importantly, while the game is pixel-art, you can actually see and understand what is happening.  An alien looks like an alien.  A space ship looks like a space ship, and more so, each races spaceships are different, which is a damn fine example to set, rather than cutting and pasting the same few models over and over.
You'll notice that in most scenes, such as combat scenes, the background not only varies, but is animated, which scores big points for Halcyon 6.  Even if it's just a few chunks of space rock floating to and fro, it adds so much compared to a simple, static background that remains completely stagnant.  Most importantly, the text and numbers are clear and easy to read, which has been a pet peeve of mine in some pixel-art style games.  One of the few immediate suggestions I would have is to make the health bars much more contrasted so that the overall amount of life the various combatants have is easier to see.

The main reason Paladins is getting a huge number of negative reviews recently is due to the latest OB64 Patch and how Hi-Rez Studios have responded / did not respond to the situtation with the community.
OB64 brings out a new
System, which was / is hugely unpopular among the community and this displeasure can be seen on Paladins's Youtube, Facebook, Reddit platforms (Comment Section). Previously, players had the freedom of changing levels of cards to suite their playstyle. Now it is fixed at Level 4 for the competitive mode (and classic mode?)
Customization was one feature that Paladins had that was unique of an FPS shooter compared to Overwatch for instance. A Champion named Fernando for example, he is mainly a tank but some cards of his will allow him to reduce his Fireball cooldown, making him an awesome flank in some games. Or you could reduce the cooldown of you shield, making you play role of the protector / staying on the objective.
[h2]Issue#2 Pay to Win Mechanics[/h2]
Before proceeding, know that all cards are given to players when you play the game and are again fixed at level 4 to provide a fair playing field on competitve mode.
However, their casual mode allows players to upgrade each card up to
level 10, which means that some cards would allow players to have faster cooldowns on their hero abilities (Which means they have a higher chance of killing you faster) So how do you upgrade your cards? Well, you have to use gold (which can be acquired by grinding very long hours or real $$$) to open chests.
The best part? If you want to upgrade a champion card  from level 1 - 10, you must get 10 duplicate / same cards from these chests. There are over 20 Champoins right now, so imagine the number of hours / money you have to spend to upgrade all champions cards to level 10 (Just so you can be overpowered / not die so easily in Casual Mode) Also take note that each champoin hjas around 20 - 24 unique cards of their own. Goodluck upgrading all of them in time without money.
[h3]Issue#3 Poor Community Engagement from Hi-Rez Studios[/h3]
Hi-Rez prides itself with listening to community feedback (Once Upon a Time)
But after almost a 1 month delay of OB64 due to the backclash it got, Hi-Rez decided to proceed with OB64 because they remain committed to it.
Look I understand that the Hi-Rez team put countless of weeks / months into developing the OB64 system BUT if majority of your online community have already said that they want to remain with the old customizable system and do away with OB64, the company should listen to its community no?
Plus the lack of replies / responses from Hi-Rez on social media itself was painful. The only information they shared was new skins, more competitive gameplay and that they are committed to the new system. There are rumors that OB64 was implemented to cater to the China market but I digress, I will not say more because it did not come from Hi-Rez's mouth.
[h4]How it Impacts You, the Players and the Community[/h4]
More players will play Ranked / Competitive mode because all the cards are stuck at level 4, so that is where most players will play becuase it provides an equal playing field.
More unskilled / unexperienced players will play ranked. Leading to the overall quality of players in ranked mode to decrease. Will that make it more Fun? No, more frustraing especially when you are trying to get ranked higher.
The "Fun" value of playing in Casual mode is gone. Is it fun getting killed all the time by a player who has maxed out all Champion cards to Level 10? Just thinking about it makes me frustrated. That is not how games should make you feel on a constant basis.
My motivation to play Paladins was low ever since the annoucement of OB64 but how Hi-Rez responded to the situation killed any trust / motivation in playing Paladins again. I am disgusted to say the least on how it was handled and I can personally say I am not easily disappointed.
If you are an existing player, I hope that if you are frustrated with the state of the game now, move on and try other games / genres. I have found fun and joy again in games while playing JRPG's for example haha.
For new players, nothing is stopping from trying since it is
Pay to Win
But I urge you to not support this game mainly because Hi-Rez Studios does not take care of its playerbase anymore, their engagement is terrible and are becoming Money First / Community Last.
Thanks for reading, I hope you continue finding joy in gaming.

If you had asked a couple of months ago what I thought of this game, I would have given a strong recommendation. As is right now, I can only tell you stay far, far way from this skinner box. This game used to have good mobility, high TTK, and good customisation. The game was fun to play. Even on characters with fixed loadouts, you could create different loadouts of buffs and effects on varying levels to create multiple playstyles for a single champion.
Now, that system has been thrown out the window. Hi-Rez has seemingly looked at the controversey with Battlefront 2 and decided what they were doing was a good idea. Use to be that once you unlocked a card you had it forever, and you could use in a loadout at any power level you wanted. You could decided for yourself which cards would suit your playstyle and which should be more powerful than others. Now, all cards are set to level 1 and you can only upgrade them by unlocking multiple copies of the same card. Which are of course gated behind lootboxes. And previous loadout limits are gone, which means all cards can be at max power. Instead of theorycrafting builds, now all you can do is grind to try and become more powerful. Or you can pay to do it faster of course. This game has become the very definition of P2W. There are far more problems this patch has brought, but if you're interested, it won't take much to find what else went wrong.
Stay far, far away from Paladins. And considering their track-record, it would be safer to stay away from all Hi-Rez titles in the future as a well. (Note that I have much more time on Xbox version of Paladins, so I've played for longer than it will say on my Steam profile)

Ultimately, I'm a little torn with this review.
I play this game,
day, and I
enjoy it, but a lot of the time it feels like I'm just playing out a sense of obligation - because I want to unlock all of the ridiculously time-consuming achievements, to appease my achievement hunting nature.

However the grind is
real.
This game, like most clickers, sends you in circles - progressively larger circles, but circles nevertheless. You'll start off struggling to buy anything, saving your pennies and gradually buying a few of whatever is available to you. After a while, you'll have reached a stage where you can afford to have some of everything, and you start to recieve a few extra little bonuses for reaching certain levels with every asset on the same planet.
This is where things usually start to slow to a crawl.
You'll eventually get to the point where you can "sacrifice" your progress, in exchange for "angels" which provide a small, accumulative, percentage bonus to all your incomes on that particular planet.
...And that's essentially all there is to the game.
This is where you start going in circle, constantly redoing what you've done before just to get more angels and try to get a little further.
As the game is free to play, trading cards are
incentive to play this game, as you'll have to spend
amounts to unlock card drops.
The achievements will keep you busy for, quite honestly,
. I'm not even kidding. This
is cray.
The game's art style is very nice - cartoonish and consistent - so for some that may be an extra point in its favour.
The game's additional events feel inconsequential and I've not personally bothered playing any of them since the first one I played ended.
Honestly, despite all its good parts, I'd struggle to recommend this game to anyone, except maybe an achievement hunter looking for a significant time-sink.

I said I would take a look at this again, and I honestly don't know if the game has changed a lot since I last looked at it or if the fact that I play Minecraft much less is influencing my opinion... If things have changed then the devs deserve a big round of applause for moving so far forward. If everything is the same then I really wonder what the heck I was thinking on my original review. That said here are my revised opinions.
An excellent tutorial gets you up and going in no time. An option has been added to choose whether you have a laptop or not so now controls are less confusing. Building is still a little slower going than many other block based games but it is very precise, so you don't waste time placing bricks where you do not want them. I'm getting faster at placement all the time now so I guess it is just a matter of getting used to them. The meat and potatoes of the game are the many different game modes. There is a bit of everything here: Racing, pirates, a treasure hunt and even just plain old building. I think i'm going to get some more of my friends to try this one out: I'm guessing this is a gas with some buddies around to torment.

Dungeons 3 is the latest installment in this Realmforge Studios series, heavily influenced by the original Dungeon Keeper series by Bullfrog which released in 1997. I played Dungeon Keeper on release and have a lot of fond memories of it, which probably reveals just how old I am. Dungeons was pretty awful (but I still played it!), Dungeons 2 was respectabley decent but with a lot of room for improvement, and Dungeons 3 has stepped up the game again and gets a solid really good but not quite perfect rating from me.

It follows on the trend of the previous games, with a humourous narrator and at least 5 billion jokes and puns, most of which I fully understood, which I think makes me some sort of epic nerd. It uses the same voice actor for the narrator as Dungeons 2, for which I'm grateful, as Kevan Brighting is seriously talented and has gained a lot more recognition now after being the narrator for The Stanley Parable.  Added to that, it has cartoonish, colourful graphics and doesn't take itself seriously at all. Despite it's rather frivolous overtones, the story is well written and actually has some decent character development and plot arcs if you're completing the campaign.
The gameplay is a mash up of Dungeon Keeper and Warcraft RTS. In the underworld you build a dungeon filled with traps and torture for any hero who wants to have a go at taking down the ultimate evil, whilst keeping your armies from hell well fed, entertained and happy. In the overworld you go on a quest to pit evil vs good and with army management, resources and spells. Both levels have complexity and depth and the controls have been made a lot more accessible than in Dungeons 2, which was a bit of a hot mess in places.
That being said, the UI still needs a lot of tweaking and the first priority should be setting your hot keys, because the pull from the left menu is incredibly annoying to use in the heat of battle. It's definitely an improvement; but they've not nailed it yet.
In addition to a fairly in depth campaign that should take about 20-30 hours to complete, there's an impressive skirmish mode. You can have randomly generated maps, a lot of settings and the AI seems to know what it's doing, allowing for some serious challenges. There's a multiplayer for pitting yourself vs random opponents or your friends (frenemies?), and you can also play the game in co-op mode, although I didn't personally get to try this out, having no friends. Wipe away your single tear, even playing this solo it offers plenty of fun.
Dungeons 3 will never return that feeling of nostalgia I have from the original Dungeon Keeper - but it does feel satisfying, fun and entertaining to play. Sometimes it's nice to just be evil and torture people to death, raise a few demons and control the undead whilst daddy yells at us for being naughty. Wait, do I have some underlying issues there...?

After finishing the main story I can safely give this review the thumbs up it deserves.
For the record, I have never played a older Dungeons game, have wanted too, but I never really picked them up. When I saw Dungeons 3 come out, I simply had too try it.
I'll be breif, going over the pros and cons as quick as I can.
Pros:
- Gameplay is true to an old warcraft/RTS title. Clunky at times, but works well 95% of the experience.
- Diverse ways of doing each mission. No one way set in stone. Some mission objectives are specific, but mostly you have the free will to do as you want to finish the job.
- Visuals hold to the theme of the game, and all of the art works well.
- Music fits the areas and changes well for Good/Evil side.
- Story is hilarious but with a serious backdrop. Good character arcs that I won't spoil.
- Jokes are well fitting and references all sorts of memes, pop-culture, and otherwise.
- Game ends with a hint to either DLC or a new game. Really hoping for it.
- Extremely addictive base building and upgrading. So much so that I plan to try out the skirmish modes to see how they work ever after the story.
- The $40.00 price point fits the content you get, and the devs earned it. As did the narrator, but I think he might need some more dialogue. *Ahem.* I mean, he has enough as is.
- Thalya is a hottie, the Devs better pass the word along to her.
Cons:
- Music glitches. Sometimes it would loop over one another and I'd have a battle and 'idle' theme going at once.
- Clunky movement in some areas. Sometimes my characters walk in place or lose their footing, but it hasn't been enough to harm my gameplay.
- Some of the references are lightly cringy, but it didn't really harm my experience, perhaps made it better. Only reason I put it on a con because I can imagine people seeing that as a fault.
- Audio bugs such as when I'm loading in a new level, I would hear the ambiance of the level before BURST OUT for a split second to shatter my ears. Ow.
- Loading times are a tad slow in some levels, but not enough for it to seriously harm my enjoyment of the game.
- The story ended, and I wanted more. Give me more.
Overall: This game has consumed my time fantastically away from my University and Work. I've pumped in 24.8 hours in the last two weeks because of how much I enjoyed the gameplay and story. If what you've seen so far has interested you, and this review has given you a internal 'I want this game!', pick it up. You will NOT regret it.
Looking forward to any (moderately) priced DLC, or the next addition to the Dungeons series!
