I've been around since Closed Beta, and have enjoyed the MechWarrior and Battletech franchise since the early 90's; I'm a 'hardcore' fan, but like many hardcore fans of various franchises, I have high standards for what I want to see in my favourite fictitious universe. MW:O, for the most part, does not disappoint.
If I was to explain what the game was to a total newcomer, I would describe it as a complex, tactical game that goes beyond the 'one man commando' style of most FPS'. It's more of an old-school 'combat simulator' than an FPS, and that's its strength.
MechWarrior/Battletech have been around since the early 80's, and all of its PC titles have consistetly delivered complex, 'thinking-required' gameplay. This is a game that rewards you based upon more than just how well you shoot, but upon how well you coordinate with others, manipulate the battlefield, and strategically pick your opponent apart. With having to manage everything from your 'mechs heat levels to ammunition, dynamic armour, diverse load-outs, and wildly varying chassis, each battle can feel very unique, and require different approaches and tactics to win. This is what keeps MWO fresh, and what has always kept the series compelling.
This is a game for smart, coordinated, team-oriented players. It could use more developing in how it handles old Battletech/Mechwarriror lore, and Community Warfare (the 'main game') is still a bit 'thin', but the combat is compelling, the learning curve challening but rewarding to progress through, and the community far more welcoming and mature than most.
Heartily recommended.

A thinking man's shooter, Mechwarrior Online takes the best part of tank battles and first person shooters and merges them together in Giant mechs ranging from 20-100 tons in weight and dwarfing other types of units on the battlefield.
Let me start out by saying that this game does have a steep learning curve.  If you have not played this game before, you will need to go through the Academy first.  That will give you the basic tools to play the game.  After that, you will want to play your Cadet bonus matches in a variety of mechs to get the feel of the different weight classes.  Do NOT buy a mech until you have gotten a good feel for the different weight classes.  Once you have gotten an idea of what you want to play with, go ahead and head to the in game store to buy your first mech with C-bills, the in game currency.  You should have plenty for your first mech after those cadet bonus matches for even an Assault mech.
Now that you have bought a mech of your own, you can customize it in the mechlab.  This is going to cost you more C-bills to buy the parts and weapons and upgrades that you want.  You will also find that you have various skills you need to earn experience to unlock and upgrade.
After that, if you want to play casually, have fun and enjoy stomping around in your Battlemech.  If you are more competitive, check out the forums on the main game website and see who is recruiting.
Overall, I have loved this game, is it perfect? No.  Is it a lot of fun?  You bet it is!  I'll see you out there, Mechwarriors!

Like any game, it has it's flaws, but the gameplay is fun and the devs have been working constantly to expand and improve the game.
Pros:
+ Fun and strategic multiplayer battles
+ Over 100 mechs to choose from
+ All mechs are deeply customizable
+ Tons of weapon and equipment choices
+ Fairly good game balance overall
+ Lots of community events and challenges
+ Very good and active community
+ Not Pay-to-Win
Cons:
- Steep learning curve (expect to die early and often until you get up to speed)
- No single player or AI outside of the basic tutorial
- Limited number of game modes
- Can be frustrating when playing solo
- Like most Free-to-play titles, it can take a lot of time to get some items if you don't pay real money for them.
Overall, this is a very fun and rewarding game for people who take the time to get past the learning curve.  For that reason, I'd suggest finding one of the many groups in game to play with, or playing with friends.

tl;dr
What it is : A great controller with tons of customization and rebinding options.
What it's not : A replacement for mouse+keyboard, especially in anything competitive.
I was thinking of writing a long review covering everything about the controller but I'm guessing that most people reading this, and considering buying the controller, are more interested in actually impressions rather than walls of text explaining what you can easily find in the promotional material.
So these are my impressions after using the controller for more than 150 hours.
If you're a person that hates investing a bit of personal time configuring and tweaking settings and if the Xbox controller satisfies you 100% then the Steam Controller is probably not for you.
But if you ever got frustrated at a games bindings and found no way to change them or if you fumbled with joy2key or xbox360ce to get your controller working with games that don't offer controller support then the Steam Controller is the controller for you.
It bridges the gap between controller and mouse+keyboard nicely, allowing you finer camera controls and more buttons at your disposal (through the use of "shift" key configurations that alter button bindings when held).
Don't expect to be playing CS:GO on a competitive level with your Steam Controller, it can't replace your trusty mouse, but expect to enjoy finer precision and a more "skillful" feeling when enjoying your single player FPS on the living room TV.
I actually played 40 minutes of CS:GO with bots using my Logitech RumblePad and then another 40 with the Steam Controller and the difference in aiming is plain as day.
After mere minutes of tweaking I was able to play Shadowrun Hong Kong, Homeworld Remastered, War for the Overworld and Path of Exile, PC specific games that don't even offer controller support, from my couch on the living room TV.
For me the Steam Controller is THE definitive controller. It's the gold standard by which to judge other controllers. It does more than other controllers and costs, well, about the same.
Hardware-wise it's sturdy and feels good in the hands. Button placement might take some getting used to.
Haptic feedback is great, using the touchpads doesn't feel like playing a game on your phone, you always feel when actions are triggered.
Doesn't have Rumble support exactly, though there's an option for an experimental type of Rumble emulation.
Works off of two AA batteries. You can use rechargable ones but the controller can't charge them. The plain Duracel alkaline ones, included with the SC, got me ~100hours worth of gaming.
Wireless range is good, playing from about 4 meteres away there was no lag or dropped input, while the controller still worked at about 8 meteres away (though I didnt' actually game at that distance).
If you're in the market for a controller get the Steam Controller.
If you feel that a plain controller is holding you back get the Steam Controller.
If you want to enjoy PC games in your living room without a flat surface to use a mouse+keyboard on get a Steam Controller.
If you think the Xbox controller is the best thing since sliced bread, try the Steam Controller but be sure to give it a chance.

The touchpads are terrible substitutes for analog sticks, period. The simulated track-ball is ok for using a desktop or playing turn-based games, it is terrible for clicking on or aiming at moving targets since you can only flick in a straight line. This is an inherent issue with trackballs, and no amount of software modding can fix this. There is a good reason that mice won out over trackballs as the standard input device for PCs. If you want a mouse for your link (and the Link is very good) buy a wireless Logictech or similar mouse and save yourself the annoyance.
Additionally, the face buttons are poorly located, and while the controller can be held in a way that makes them accessible, there really isn't a good position that lets you use the right side track pad and all of the face buttons on the fly. The back paddles are nice, but their large size makes stability a bit of an issue. Paddles have been done much better elsewhere, and they feel like a poorly thought out addition in this case.
The one positive thing I will say for the controller, is that buried under an awful UI, there are a lot of good customization options. It’s all polishing brass on the Titanic though, because customization doesn’t mean much when the hardware is this badly flawed.
In short: There is no reason to buy this controller, it does not perform as well as pretty much any other option that you have available to you.
This can easily replace the mouse and keyboard for me from the couch. It takes some time getting used to the controller, butI recommend this product for any console gamers who want to play PC games.

I have only played Dead Rising 2 and all it's spin offs, Off the Record, Case West, and Case Zero so I'm going to be comparing this game to that.
First of all, I do like the idea of being able to build your weapons wherever you are and not have to go looking for a workbench. However, I feel as though I'm limited to this because all the other combo weapons are locked through level ups and collectibles around the large map.
Being able to drive vehicles is a cool feature and being able to combine two different vehicles to make one super powered vehicle is also pretty neat. However, the driving is terrible in this game. From time to time, my vehicle will just slowly stop moving as I try to go over a hill or plow through some zombies. I either have to make a complete stop and continue driving or reverse and continue driving. All the vehicles also seem to go the exact same speed, no matter what it is. I feel as though I'd get to my destination quicker by running than driving there, since the vehicle can only take so many hits before it starts to explode.
I do like the map in this game, it's more open and a lot more places to explore than being stuck to one block like in Dead Rising 2. However, the game forces you to use vehicles to navigate through the map because there are hordes of zombies everywhere and going in there without a vehicle is suicide. Like I previously mentioned, the driving in this game is unbearable at times.
This game is a lot more linear than Dead Rising 2 is. Where in Dead Rising 2 you literally have to go out of your way just to get to your story mission, along with having to keep your eye on Zombrex for your child. In this game, driving to your next destination is easy. I don't like how there's no longer an arrow to guide you to where you have to go, I got myself lost through the highways and bridges in this game every now and then. Going through the story in this game is a lot more bearable than Dead Rising 2, you're still timed of when you have to get these missions done, but at least you don't have to walk around with tank controls and have to keep worrying about Zombrex.
Bare in mind, I've only played about 2 hours of this game, even with graphics on the lowest settings my computer still had a hard time keeping up with this game so I had a lot of framerate issues. Though, this would only occur during cutscenes, during actual gameplay it's fine. I would say Dead Rising 3 has a lot more replayability than Dead Rising 2, considering Dead Rising 3 has a lot of collectibles scattered throughout the whole city. Thankfully finding these collectibles won't be as hard as it sounds: If you keep an eye on your mini map on the bottom right corner, there'll be symbols that indicate a collectible, plus the game will always notify you when you're near one of these collectibles.
This is just a nit picky thing, but I for one like to play my games in Windowed mode. Just like Dead Rising 2 and Off the Record though, the game is locked in Full Screen. Not even using DXWnd forces the game to go into Windowed mode, where as the other Dead Rising games worked with it.
6/10, would recommend to a fan of the series, but I wouldn't recommend for anyone new to it. If you're new to Dead Rising and you just want to know how the gameplay is like, I recommend Dead Rising 2: Off the Record.

I've been replaying this recently and loving it (I use the non-steam client) so I thought I'd repost this recommendation now that the character limit has gone.
======
So far the best iteration of Tribes since Tribes 2. What's more its free to play so you've got no excuse not to give it a try.
Skiing
For those who don't know the series Tribes offers team based gameplay with one of the best movement mechanics in arena style FPS called skiing.
It combines physics, jetpacks, the environment and the skill of the player to have you rocketing around the map at the speed of sound and makes for some excellent chases in capture the flag type scenarios and great combat that has you estimating trajectories of projectiles and players to produce some of the most epic trickshots you'll see in any game.
Classes
It also has a really nice class system that has subtle class differences which are exaggerated by player role choices in game. The subtlety results in a much more natural role selection basic much more on strategy rather than the "I'm playing the heavy-defender class therefore I only defend"
Map Design
One thing that also stands out to me is that I think the map design is beautiful for an arena game. While they do share some common features on the whole each map feels unique and have loads of great little details to bring them to life.
FTP
Finally for those who are nervous about free to plays being pay to win (as I was until recently) Tribes: Ascend feels like its got the right balance of paying giving you enough perks to make it worth it (which is important if you want the game to stay alive) but without being an essential element to play and kick♥♥♥♥♥♥ Rather than money opening up bigger scarier guns, it seems to open up alternative roles to play within the game, all of which are available over time when playing the game for free.
Downsides
The only thing missing from this wonderful iteration of the classic franchise is the modding that came with Tribes and Tribes 2. I remember my brother and I having a whale of a time as kids playing with a lot of mods and user generated maps that added a whole ton of content to the game. While it's obvious why this can't work in a FTP game, it's a bit of a shame. Hopefully though, if HiRez studios are successful they'll be enough interest to keep them adding official content to the game to keep us all keen.

A Dreamcast era masterpiece that will certainly please fans of the shoot'em up and bullet hell genres.

This isn't so much an arcade shoot 'em up as a high intensity puzzle game. The primary aim is to survive each level by avoiding bullets of the opposite polarity to your ship - for example if your polarity is white, your ship is invulnerable to white bullets, but contact with a black bullet will kill you.
The secondary aim is to maximise your score by 'chaining' enemy kills by polarity, i.e. destroying enemies of the same polarity in groups of three. Each chain increases your score multiplier - which affects the points awarded by each individual kill - by a factor of one. The higher your score, the higher your grade at the end of each level. The highest grades can only be achieved with very high score multipliers.
Alternatively you can complete each level without firing once by avoiding bullets of the opposite polarity until the timer reaches zero. You're awarded with a special grade and ranking on a separate leaderboard.
The layout of enemies and their bullet patterns is identical each playthrough, and therefore repeated attempts are the key to success. Memorise enemy patterns, identify how to continuously chain enemy kills, and ultimately become good enough to complete the game in a single credit!
A full playthrough tales approximately 25 minutes, but it will take many hours of practice before this can be achieved with just three lives.
Ikaruga expects you to die over and over again, but persevere and you
progress. The further you go, the more you learn.
Fast reflexes and limitless patience are a good start!

This is a great game, but can be hard to get into, and is definitely not for everyone. There are a lot of habits from other action games you'll need to unlearn, and the game will throw a lot of information and tools at you all at once when you start.
If you can push through it though there's a surprisingly deep game to be found. Matches are decided by positioning and maneuvering more often than by marksmanship. You will know the best units (clans/guilds) in the game when you see them because they will appear on your flank as one, and not even stop moving as they plow through you.
The great thing about this tactical emphasis is it creates a lot of moments of tense pauses between or leading up to action.
Mech customization is huge. As you grow familiar with the game you'll quickly realize how important every seemingly trivial choice in design you make is even down to the placement of ammo. It means that even when a popular meta sets in and many mechs in the field look the same (which is good, you know what to expect from various chassis) you still have freedom to personalize to your tastes.
Be warned: game is a bit rough around the edges. The developer was relatively new when the game started out, and it's shown in the development history. But particularly in the passed year they have demonstrated that they are raising their game to a higher level. The rate of new content is still relatively slow, but there's tons already here, and as a multiplayer only game new content isn't even critical to ongoing enjoyment. It's just a matter of if the core game appeals to you or not.
(context: hundreds of hours played pre-Steam since closed beta)

Rabi-Ribi is a pretty underrated game. While at first glance it might appear to be only fanservice or semi-hentai, it's a surprisingly deep metroidvania that is actively updated - since I last played it, it has gotten a new difficulty setting, a boss rush mode, and a huge overhaul to the map system. Rabi-Ribi is very projectile-based, sort of playing like a danmaku platformer, especially during boss battles, and while 50 HP might seem much when most enemies deal damage in the single digits, rest assured that it's not.
The main draw with RR is how free it is. During the first section of the game, you pass through 6 different areas, and you are more or less free to stray off and explore any of them if you want to - and know HOW to get around - and, most of all, can handle the enemies. The game even has an achievement for beating the game without getting your main weapon in the first area, despite said area appearing impossible to leave without obtaining the hammer.
I've only played the game for 2 hours so far, but it's been 2 very enjoyable hours; the main reason I've not played more is because I realized there were some cool updates coming (in particular the map overhaul; the map was the version I played's biggest flaw by far) and I wanted to get them first. The only remaining flaw now is that there are plenty of human enemies in some areas, and they are hard to distinguish from random bystanders. Then again, you can't hurt friendly NPCs, so there's no harm in shooting them a bit just in case.
There are plenty of moves in the game: your normal hammer attacks, carrot bombs, dashing, controlling your fairy sidekick and using her for magic support fire, eating food for emergency recovery... the game is more or less unplayable without a controller due to the sheer number of inputs you need to handle. (FYI, I've played through all of Axiom Verge with a keyboard with no real issues)
If you like bullet hell games or shooters in general, you'll like Rabi-Ribi. If you like metroidvanias or Super Smash Bros., you'll like it too. In fact, I'm sure this game will make you like both bullet hells and metroidvania games, even if you didn't do it before. If you're into fanservicey anime CGs, you'll have a blast, but even if you despise it, the gameplay will make up for it. Higher difficulties don't just increase the damage you take, they radically change boss attack patterns, and bundled with the free exploration, this makes for stellar replayability.

That's what the game is about, you play as a rabbit, Erina, who suddenly finds herself in human form wearing bunny clothes in a hospital, following a mysterious voice, you end up waking up in a forest, sleeping on the lap of a girl who runs away the moment you wake up, from here on out, you are on your own, you have complete freedom, but I'll start by covering the game the way you are expected to play it
This game is a sidescrolling platformer with heavy emphasis on bullet patterns like shoot em up games like Ikaruga, Crimzon Clover, Touhou etc, I'm not big on platformers but I really like shmups and I have to say the combination works damn well, your weapons are a hammer, explosive carrots and Ribbon, a little (and scantily dressed, if this is a problem for you) fairy with 7 shot types, each comes with their own normal and charged shots and a Boost attack that will attack all enemies on screen while creating a little area that will buff you as long as you are inside it
At first, by using these weapons you earn experience that will improve them, but you will max and forget about them very early in the game, later on you will find items that give you new skills like hammer rolling or flying hammer dash, or passive skills like moving at normal speed while underwater, less damage from spikes and also consumable healing items
Your objective is to go around mercilessly destroying anything that opposes you because it seems everyone here loves to fight, as some 4th wall jokes will imply, from little animals to weirdos from an organization with an unhealthy obsession with rabbits (which are extinct in this world, you are like a godsend to them), although the bosses are supposed to be your friends, and if not, beating them into submission will fix that, after which they go back to town and will help send you into the real world to discover what's going on, there you get to beat otakus trying to get pictures of you (and if you are careful you get to fight the director of the game apparently).
As for stuff to do after you beat the game, it has you covered, when you beat the final boss, you unlock boss rush mode and in story mode there is something else that needs to be taken care of, featuring 3 more bosses, 2 of them in very intense dungeons, and then when you clear this post game you unlock another boss rush mode, speed run mode and if you go back to your save you can fight all bosses again but there are also special, lv 336 versions of 3 of them
Now then, say you don't have enough with all that, you have MAX ranked, no damage clear every boss and want more, the achievements show that you can play the game in challenging ways that after one proper playthrough might make you think it's impossible, I suggest you read this only after you have cleared the game once, or at least not attempt any of this in your first playthrough
In short, this game is an absolute blast, if you get fooled by the appearance of the game (or more specifically, the scantily dressed characters) you are missing out, but I would recommend it more because of the bullet hell aspect rather than the platforming one

Five parts metroivania, five parts bullet hell, ten parts fanservice is the simple formula for Rabi-Ribi. Possessing an almost quaint and innocent charm, Rabi-Ribi tells the story of a bunny turned into a girl in a world populated (almost) entirely by females. Explore a fairly large map, just about the size of one of the castles of Symphony of the Night, and revel in a game that allows you to do any and all things: Including beating the game without getting items!
At its core, Rabi-Ribi is a celebration of the classic Metroidvania item turned on its head. Taking many conventional platforming and exploration tropes, Rabi-Ribi is first and foremost more akin to a bullet hell then a bog standard Metroidvania. This distinction creates a very different feel then most of the genre, as it's focus is as much on dodging as it is on getting things done. Bosses are scalar, meaning that all exploring will do is reward you with a larger toolkit. This may be a mark on it, but the beauty of the game and its focus on non linear gameplay ensures that any boss can be a challenge regardless of the items at your disposal.
Character wise, the main focus is on Erina (the rabbit girl) and her companion Ribbon. Much of the characterization comes from how she and Ribbon interact with a large cast of diverse characters (granted, all scantily clad women) but slowly creates and shows the feeling of a specific character. While the story is arguably minor, it's much more appropriate to label this as a "slice of life" or "character driven" game, even though there is an overarching goal. Many NPCs have non romantic relationships with other NPCs and, barring one pair who are all but a couple (plus a succubus), there is an overall sense of celebrating a friendship. The art style of the game reinforces a large amount of the writing, with very cute and endearing chibi sprites mixed in with the very fanservice oriented portraits. Each character has a different feel simply due to their costume and interactions, along with their sprites and the writing.
In terms of replayability, the game excels. There are many differing ways to go at the game, from a speedrun driven mode to the aforementioned no item run to the throw caution to the wind and completely break the story of the game run. Assisting the freedom of exploration is the fact that many base moves are able to be done out of the box, instead requiring different tricks which reward those looking for a challenge. Because of this, and incredibly strong level design, you have a game where you can access virtually everywhere with a minimal amount of skills, truly testing your exploration skills (barring the use of a guide).
All in all, Rabi-Ribi is a delighful interpretation of a fairly beloved genre. If you prefer a more dodge focused or "dance" kind of gameplay in your Metroidvania, or just want to enjoy a cute and fun story and all the fanservice it brings, pick this game up. The DLC even allows you to do one of the modes, boss run, with other characters! Definitely worthwhile and enjoyable for fans of the genre and just as worthwhile for those looking to break into it!

If you are one of those gamers that can play Halo on an Xbox controller, this controller might work for you.  I am not.  To me, there is no substitute for a mouse and a keyboard.  However, I can see myself using this in a pinch if I was ever in a place that doesn't allow me to use a traditional mouse and keyboard, such as playing in an airport on my gaming laptop.
While the total customizability is a great addition to a gaming controller, finding that perfect configuration can be a little time consuming and frustrating.  I found myself spending long enough trying to tweak the configuration that I eventually would want to stop playing the game for which I was configuring the controller.
The haptic feedback is great and works well, but the "directional pad" is lacking.  But perhaps my largest complaint with the gamepad is the the positioning of the XABY buttons, as they are super tiny, and at the limit of where my right thumb can reach and it felt very unnatural.  This made playing any sort of fighting game nearly impossible.
All in all, I would not recommend this controller to anyone yet.  The Xbox 360 Controller and Xbox One controllers work great already.  Perhaps if the controller was two pieces, like the Vive controllers, it might feel better with all the customization.  As it is now, it is just an average designed controller with a lot of customization features.

I was in the market for a wireless controller  and I decided to get this controller because it was 10 bucks cheaper than the leading competitor for a wireless model and I already owned a handful of rechargable AA batteries on top of liking the idea of easily changing my controllers configuration for a given game. I have found this controller to be more useful to me than any other controller currently on the market would likely be, This contoller to me offers a better gaming experience with the right configurations. I really like being able to turn on my PC with a press of the home button.
the customizability as well as the ergonomics of the controller are second to none in my opinion. The touchpads are very responsive and easy to get used to. The underside buttons are pretty useful as well but probably take the longest to get used to using of all the features of the controller. I can't comment on the gyroscopic controls without using them first but it is a pretty cool idea for finer FPS controls or maybe a racing game. I use this controller sometimes just to surf the web from my futon because it is well set up for page navigation and the on screen keyboard feature works very well for occasional search terms.
I've found so far that I can hand this controller to people who don't play games with a controller and that they can use it about as quickly as any other controller without explanation past telling them what is a touchpad on it and the basic controls of the game. I was able to get someone with a learning disability and hadn't gamed since they had a gamecube to learn how to play games on it well in just a couple of hours. This leads me to suspect that a lot of bad reviews for this controller are partially just allergic to change. I fully recommend this controller to anyone who wants a top notch gaming controller, and or something to use their PC from across the room with,
P.S. I let my fiance play with this contoller and a game i figured she would like and now she wants my old gaming PC just like I was hoping she would. haha

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a first-person action RPG set in the future. The game's story in addition to the way you choose to proceed through it and the gaming style you choose to follow complement one another deftly to provide you with an exceptional experience.
The good things
* Story: It mainly revolves around the ethics of "augmentations", that is cyberntic extensions that can be attached to a human being to improve the body or/and the mind. You are Adam Jensen, one who was recently cybernetically augmented. Yes, you are the the main character but you'll quickly see that you are part of a very big story with multiple secondary characters having their own agendas. The ending is satisfactory as there is no loose plot, and everything falls nicely into one place.
* Level design: There are many ways for you to complete an objective. There generally is the main way (rambo), and many other paths. There is always a secondary path that will allow anyone to get inside a building without requiring special augmentations, while other may require you to level up a cybernetic part of your body. Being curious is a good thing. Also, being a "hacker" is great: it's a bit difficult to invest on this from the start but it pays off quickly as you are able to get to places you couldn't reach easily otherwise.
* Stealth: You can finish the game without killing anyone, except the bosses. I wish more games do that.
The less good things
* Boss battles: it's certainly the weakest point of the game. Yes, you can use the environment rather than weapons to kill them, but all boss battles (except the last one maybe) left me underwhelmed.
* Difficulty: If you go the "hacker" way, you'll find that the game gets much easier. I had only one playthrough (too many games to play to do it a second time) so maybe it's true only for the hacking part.
It's also supposed to be an action game, as you can play it "rambo" style... But you would miss a lot by doing that. I suggest anyone wanting to get the best from this game to play it in stealth mode: also, try to avoid killing anyone (Pacifist achievement) and avoid starting off alarms. And, play in on max difficulty. This combination should arguably be the best way to play the game.

Graphics: 9/10

There are new features in this game like the revamped combo system, route, and the development system has been changed. It gives this games a fresh feel that wont make you say, "This is just another Neptunia Re:Birth Remake with a different story and some added characters. Gameplay still same so boring zzz". There is also a minigame called Neplunker, based on the game spelunker, that is honestly frustrating when you never played spelunker before playing this (like me) but eventually you will get used to it (still frustrating to die jumping so high tho). Grinding in this game is WAYYYYY EASIER compared to the previous games. or maybe its beacause i forgot to turn on the level cap dlc. but hey you dont really need lvl 999 in completing the achievements. Also there is a new form called Next form. EDIT: there is a lvl 999 cap and colo battles and grinding up to that level is a challenge since the biggest xp monster only spawns once and the you can only use 30 of an item that force spawns it per run.
Sound: 9/10
The music of the story part is mostly still the same from the old Nep games but the new maps and boss themes are new. The opening soundtracks of the three series is my favorite. (fun fact: I actually heard musou katharsis before playing this game and I immediately liked it). And the monsters here have sounds when its their turn. wow.
Story:7/10
Story has never been the selling point of Neptunia games (I think). But this tries to amaze the player with the new character's coolness. The fourth wall breaker and comedy is here. My favorite thing about this is how they put the gaming puns and I just laugh when I get it. (S-sha's lines are my favorite).
End Game Content: 8/10
I guess the post game content for this is unlocking the endings, the colosseum, , , uh I guess that's it. you will probably spend most of your time finish that rng based achievement (*cough* CPU CHIPS *cough*) and with a painful hand. EDIT: There is a lvl 999 colo battles and that grind is hard. For those new to the series, there is a new game plus so dont worry if you missed something you can just try again. warning though: you scouted areas and hidden treasures will be reset.
Conclusion: 9/10
yeah maybe this score is biased but if this is your first neptunia game, you may have a hard time playing the older ones, as this I said, this is the best nep game there is currently. Post game maybe a little lacking but completing the achievements sure gives you a lot of hours to play this game. Taking Occam’s razor to the wonderful yet mechanically dense Radiant Silvergun, Treasure has achieved a small victory for design aesthetics, necessary for a game which demands perfection through repetition. Ikaruga finds elegance through simplicity, the yin and yang of the polarity system makes this perhaps the most endearing shoot-em-up to learn the song and dance to.

For long-time players of the Neptunia franchise, Megadimension Neptunia VII is a clear step in the right direction in terms of gameplay and storytelling. It also manages to strike a beautiful balance between relentless comedy routines and tearjerkers, something the Neptunia series has struggled to do until now. Framerates are mostly stable even on my integrated graphics card, but the bloom looks atrocious in certain dungeons. Overall I would certainly reccomend it, but you'll get more out of it if you have some prior experience with JRPGs.

This review is based on 3+ hours of gameplay. Code was provided by the developers free of charge. I did not play the previous games.
Dungeons 3 is a Simulation Management Fantasy RTS in the vain of old Dungeon Keeper games and apes a lite amount of mechanics from Warcraft 3. While the game is not mechanically complex like Dungeon Keeper it has its own degree of originality and polish for a thematic experience.
Gameplay:
The game basically has two segements: Underworld dungeon construction (traps, rooms, etc) and Overworld RTS battles that can be switched between seamlessly. Like Dungeon Keeper, you mine out areas of the underground to construct rooms that generate resources. You can buy units immediately instead of waiting for them like in dungeon keeper which helps speeds things up a bit. You only have to provide rooms with food and lodging to keep your soldiers happy and fighting. You will also have to pay an upkeep every few minutes in gold to your soldiers. Not doing any of these can lead your soldiers to either not fight or flat out leave your army. Gold is used to buy research for new units, units themselves as previously mentioned, traps and other items, some items requre “evil points” to research. You want to constantly mine out your dungeon for gold but also be careful as mining out too much can lead to uncovering nasty surprises such as spider nests that attack your dungeon's heart. If your heart is destroyed, you lose the game. On the Overworld side, you have a separate map that you can transition to fairly easily. You can send units to the surface to fight and complete objectives as well as capture areas to gain evil points. While the game has a good variety units and even a hero, the Overworld segments aren't the best except in the campaign when there are scripted sequences. Otherwise, there are no interesting abilities, RPG elements or items that change up your units or hero in a significant way. It's just click and attack until you kill the enemy with more guys. It can be relaxing but it's not super deep and fans of Dungeon Keeper might be better off playing War For The Overworld for their tougher strategy fix.
Sound & Visuals:
By far one of the games strongest assets. Unfortunately, the game does not have a detailed options menu but the performance is great (on an I7 4790k with an R9 390). Visuals are bright and colorful. Unfortunately, animations during battle sequences leave much to be desired as characters simply flop over when dying. The sounds can sound a bit stock and can sometimes stack a bit but the game's strength lies in its dialogue and voice acting. Like Dungeon Keeper you play the evil side and it's done differently here. It's more light-hearted rather than as dark and cynical. The narrator you will be hearing throughout the game is voiced by Kevan Brighting, the same guy responsible for the excellent The Stanley Parable naration and he is great here. You feel like your starring in a darker, cynical, children's fairy-tale book. The dialogue can be a bit overwhelming when first booting into the tutorial than the campaign itself but it grows on you fast and your hero character, Thalya, is a good stand-in and has some great dialogue of her own that mixes well with the narrator and the protagonist/antagonist that you fight.
Content:
The game has 20 missions and each takes around 20-30 minutes on average to complete. While some missions can feel like a bit of a slog they are still engaging and fun. I never got bored because the scripted sequences and voice acting was enjoyable enough. The biggest problem is the selection of maps outside of the campaign. With only a handful of maps and 3 modes (survival, endless, skirmish) there isn't a whole lot to get into outside the campaign, especially since you don't get a lot of the contextual events but you do at least still hear the narrator.
Overall, Dungeons 3 is a great, casual, thematic experience. For $39.99 it's a decent value but the variety of maps and mechanics hold it back from being something truly amazing. I can easily recommend this game on sale for anyone and I can recommend it now if you want something Dungeon Keeper adjacent with some good writing and colorful visuals with some reasonably polished mechanics. It's the type of game you can relax into without a ton of waiting or grinding, at least that's my experience so far.
Thanks for reading. You can check out a video review for some visual information:

A wonderful ride through the famously awesome game/genre we were introduced to more than two decades ago (DK), Dungeons 3 does the concept a great deal of justice.  It is a rich, strangely soothing romp fit for almost any gamer, but true fans of the OP will really appreciate it.

There is a fun game here.  Does it have it's issues?  Yes, just about every game does.  Is it as pure BattleTech as the hardcore fans will want?  No.  Some changes and exceptions have been made to make this a workable online game.  Here's the core of it... if you are a fan of BattleTech and MechWarrior games of the past, (you probably have already heard of this game ;) ) you should try MWO.
I come by MechWarrior, mostly playing in the VWE Tesla II simulator pods and MechWarrior: Firestorm - heavily based off of MechWarror 4.  NOTHING will compare with that experience, and a majority of that is due to the community of friends I have built around that, and a great deal to do with the level of control and the immersion.  But, at home, MWO offers a fun game that can played with friends and online groups.  Working together with your team to accomplish the mission is a rewarding experience and offers quite a bit of fun.  Did I mention this was because you're doing it in giant robots with big weapons? ;)
Now, important caveat: NO MONEY NEEDS TO BE SPENT TO ENJOY THIS GAME!  Anyone who calls it P2W is not paying attention to the game mechanics.  Purchases will only buy you convenience in this game.  I will recommend at least a token purchase of some MC (the real money currency for the game) among you and your friends if you wish to do fully customized private matches.  To do so requires both 'team leaders' to be running active premium time.  However, that is only if you want to do so, you'll earn no in game rewards for doing private matches.
Also, run the tutorial missions.  Never mind the fact how the Atlas got on top of the building.  Just run the missions for a good intro to the controls and feel, and also to earn a fair amount of rewards in CBills (the ingame earned currency) that will allow you to purchase your first mech(s).  Also, reach out to the other palyers if you have questions!  Aside from the normal amount of complaints you find on the MWO forums, there is quite a lot of helpful info.  Also, pleanty of videos of game play are around on YouTube, so you'll certainly be able to see both serious and some not so serious vids.
All in all, give it a try.

MWO is a simulation/shooter hybrid. You take the part of a Mechwarrior, piloting a Battlemech or an Omnimech (different build philosophies that impact customization). Mechs are giant walking tanks with discrete hit locations (arms, legs, side torsos, front/back, etc.) that each track their own health (armor and internal health) and can mount equipment (from weapons, to ammo, to sensors, and more).
Run the Tutorial before you do anything else. It'll help you get a feel for how your Mech operates, and when you finish it you'll get a chunk of c-bills (in-game currency) to help you get started. Visit the official forums and check out the New Player Help section - there are numerous veteran players who will do everything they can to help you get started.
There are two modes: Quick Play and Faction Play. Quick Play can be solo or group. You will be matched with players who are at or near you skill tier (new players start at 5, with the scale being 5 at the lowest and 1 at the highest). As you play, your Pilot Skill Rating (what the Tier level is based on) will change based on your performance, and should eventually result in you being consistently matched with and against players at or around your ability level, making for consistently challenging matches.
Group play requires being in a group, from 2 to 10 players, or a full 12-man team. This tends to be a lot more challenging, especially if you group with a player of a much higher tier, but it also is more rewarding, as nothing beats playing with a group of friends and coordinating your maneuvers and focusing your fire to defeat a superior foe.
Faction Play involves teams of 12 players attempting to sieze planets on behalf of one of the factions in the game. Each player chooses 4 mechs for their Dropship, within certain tonnage limits. You then pick which mech to drop in first, and after it is destroyed you return to your Dropship and choose the next mech to use. This can lead to some truly epic matches, including upsets and turn-arounds as a losing team picks the right combination of new mechs that allows them to roll over the enemy and take a dominant position. Game modes so far include Invasion, where one team defends an orbital defense gun and the other tries to disable it by destroying generators, and Counter Attack, where the attacking side tries to hold conquered territory against rallying defenders.
Faction Play is currently a mixed bag, as it tends to be dominated by large player groups (units), making it hard for small groups and solo players to succeed. However, there are enough tools built into the game to allow a smart team of solo players to beat a full pre-made team, though it's always an up-hill battle. The recent addition of Faction Chat and Looking-For-Group features makes it easier to create an ad hoc team, rather than relying on random matchmaking to build your team.
Faction Play is also going to be getting a major new addition soon, in the form of 4v4 Recon drops. These are supposed to allow a faction to unlock special abilities for their teams in Invasion and Counter Attack games, starting with intel on the enemy team, moving to periodic sensor sweeps, and culminating in off-map Long Tom artillery support (see the giant explosion at the end of the Steam Launch Trailer).
Quick Play and current Faction Play modes are all 12v12, which can make it difficult for a single player to feel like he's making a significant contribution to the game, and it makes positioning mistakes incredibly deadly. 4v4, when it arrives, should fix that problem, and Faction Play does have the 4-mech Dropship limited respawn function, which mitigates the cost of bad luck and minor mistakes.
Regardless of how you choose to play, remember that there is integrated VOIP. Use it to figure out tactics and call targets, but try not to abuse it by spamming music or yelling obscenities. There is an in-game mute option if you encounter an abusive player, as well as an integrated report function. VOIP, if you use it, can let a group of random solos defeat a coordinated 12-man premade team.
The in-game economy is solid. There were some recent improvements to the reward structure, meaning that a moderately good performance will earn enough c-bills to purchase a new mech after only a few hours of playing, though admittedly it will vary quite a bit depending on how well you do and how expensive your target mech is. There are ways to accelerate your earnings, ranging from 1st Win double XP bonuses, to Premium Time, to Hero and Special mechs, etc. There are also frequent mech preorder packs, which usually include significant bonus items on top of the mechs themselves.
It is entirely possible to run this game well and enjoyably without spending a dime. The bulk of the possible real-money purchases are either vanity or convenience, with the only exception being the unique hardpoints of the Hero mechs (but no Gold Armor or Gold Weapons or Gold Ammo - Hero mechs use all the same gear as everything else in the game).
The game is incredible fun as-is, and there is more and better to come. Plus, it's free. There's no appreciable downside to giving it a try, and it offers a unique approach to gameplay that no other shooter can match.

A good F2P mech-based arena shooter.  Try it.  Get yourself through the Academy and then play 50 matches or so.  You'll know if it's right for you.  And if it's not, no money wasted.
- If there's one legacy that might endure from PGI's version of MechWarrior, it's the mechs themselves.
- The game's primary function, mechs shooting mechs, looks and sounds amazing.
- Mechwarrior Academy is a great way for the completely new to get good enough to deal with a real battle.
- It's as free as you want it to be.
- Build and skin the mechs however you want.
- There are loads of people that want to be helpful, that want you to do well, and discuss a love of mechs.
- It's as expensive as you want it to be.
- This can be overwhelming at first.  Just because you CAN build it, doesn't mean it's a good build.  And it starts to get expensive to build, tear down, and rebuild mechs.  Ask around!  There is a lot of help out there.
- There are people that are overly invested in the success or failure of this game for some reason.  They have very petty wars in various venues.  Beware of both sides.
- You will need a VERY good CPU to get this running smoothly.  Any half decent GPU will be fine.
- Needs a bit of refreshment here.  Quick Play Assault mode is the worst.  Faction Play is not well populated so it can be difficult to find matches in off-peak hours.  Quick Play is always available and well populated.

Most shooting games put the players in a slow-paced environment where the desire to move quicker than 7 mph is not an option. In this game, if you're moving slower than that, it's because you're standing still.
This game requires a good aim, reflex, tracking, and anticipation. Most of your gameplay will require that you anticipate. There are enormous hills all over the place, and between the "skiing" and jetpack abilities, there's really no way you'll have to NOT anticipate before shooting.
It also features several cameos and essences I really enjoy, even one relating directly to Sonic the Hedgehog (the best video game series ever). Several voices and  statements and whatnot from prior games were dragged into this game, and better yet, you can control the exact statement you use, unlike previous games in the Tribes series.
As a First-Person Shooter game, I give it a 10/10, hands down. Most shooters I play get around 5/10. As a video game altogether, I give it 9/10, graphics and physics and originality and whatever else factors all considered. From a PERSONAL standpoint, I give it a 6/10. It's something I like to play, but not very often. Games are meant for fun, aaaaaaaaaand that's how I tend to rate games on a personal level. This game is a LOT of fun, especially to someone who hasn't played a Tribes game in 9 years or so when they find out this one is free. VGW

I've played a variety of competitive multiplayer shooters throughout my gaming life and I have to say that Tribes: Ascend is easily my favorite of them all. The main attraction is their "Capture the Flag" mode, which is the most intense game of CTF one will ever experience due to the game's unique playing style: a mix of futuritsic "skiing" or "gliding" over vast mountainous playing fields at high speeds. Combine that with precise and challenging shooting at the correct angle and direction to hit the other opponent and finally the correct tactics and timing for offense and defense between your teammates and the opposing force.
To top it all off, the game also has excellent graphics, sound, and a fairly large multiplayer community. The game is free to play and upgraded weapons and other items can be unlocked through normal play time, but you can unlock things early through their online store. If you're looking for your next great multiplayer shooter that will challenge you a little more than the average Call of Duty or something similar, then this is your game and it wont cost you a penny!

Endless Space is a 4X (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate) turn-based space strategy. I've been playing it since alpha and have to admit that it's a sort of a mixed blessing. Let me list all the pros and cons as I see it to give you a better picture.
PROS: Solid graphics with fantasticly detailed awesome planet textures, neat art style, memorable and diverse races, clean and slick UI, some of the core game systems, e.g. the FIDS concept (Food, Industry, Dust, Science), research trees are quite the beasts with many interesting techs.
MIXED: Battle system is controversial. Player has a limited input on the battles - no direct control over ships, just cards (actions), formations and targeting. I don't mind the concept as a whole and it got better with the Disharmony addon, but  there's for improvement IMO. Heroes are also in the so-so category, their ability trees are dull and not diverse enough although I like the concept. Events are cool but too few and not detailed enough to my taste.
CONS: Diplomacy is weak in its current form + you have to research even the most basic types of interactions which really hurts multiplayer, espionage is basicly non-existant. Fast early expansion aka system grabbing is still the best strategy for most races, the penalties are not strong enough to encourage alternative strategies in most cases.
Even with many negatives I consider Endless Space to be one of the better 4X strategies of the last years. It lacks depth as a single-player experience IMO, most game systems are too straightforward and multiplayer has plenty problems of its own. Still, if you dig the genre and don't expect ES to be the best 4X strategy ever you might sink couple hundred hours into it not without pleasure.

Very well made, polished, graphically pleasing 4X space strategy.
From what I gather, developers take player feedback rather seriously, there are even player-suggested achievements or whole race designed by a player (in a competition). This comes through voting (and with Emperor Edition your votes have bigger gravitas, apparently - I haven't tried it myself though). I'm pretty certain this helps with game's balance and also shows in the well designed UI which never let me down (you can easily find info you need and execute orders you want).
Well, maybe it's somewhat hard to keep track of enemy fleets and their movement, especially that even if it is turn based, the turns are simultaneous, and you can't zoom out far enough to have eagle eye view of the entire galaxy, but this is somewhat alleviated by the fact that if you do see them, it means you or they are close and the intentions of fleets are pretty clear.
As far as 4X space strategies go, this game seems pretty standard and
not complicated. This is probably another outcome of quasi-communal design, I'd have to track its history to be certain. But I don't mean this as a bad thing - if anything, this lends itself to the final polish, letting the game stay focused on what it is trying to do. It still does some things its own way obviously, especially interesting feature are heroes who improve efficiency of your colonies or fleets if assigned a post and level up increasing their abilities.
This
not complicated approach also means it is a good place to start your adventure with the genre, if you're curious. The learning curve here is not as notoriously steep as usual in such titles (doesn't mean it isn't steep at all, though). And if you already are familiar with the genre you'll feel right at home and still get kicks from figuring out how the things work this time around.

Purchased the controller on initial release.  Played FEAR2 first and was exceptionally pleased with how well the controller replaced the keyboard and mouse.  Fully programmable, the precision is fantastic.  Don't want to program the controller?  No worries.  There are controller gameplay templates available for download in Steam to suit nearly everyone for most all games.  While I don't use it for everything - it's a great addition to my gameplay arsenal.

Well, I'm going to be frank.  The firmware for this thing is sketchy.  It's desktop keyboard only pops up a white box and no keys whatsoever.  Looked for support on the subject, no cake was found.  For a mouse, however, this thing excels when configured correctly.  Ever used the gyro-sensor as a mouse input?  I recommend having that set on with a high sensitivity and setting the touchpad to a slightly lower sensitivity for more fine movements.  The gyro-sensor allows me to glide across the screen with minimal hassle.  I only recently got it and haven't done much gaming with it, but the gaming tests are good so far.  Again, it does need some configuring, but for the most part, it's pretty dang good.  The ability to change the touchpad on the right and make it act like a joystick is almost necessary.  It's kinda weird that the Steam Controller only emulates a mouse and keyboard and doesn't use Xinput much at all...  Which actually puts it at a DISADVANTAGE when a game is actually configured to handle input from an Xbox controller.  The only Xinput that I see is the joysticks.  The rest of the buttons are keyboard emulation.
Just for example, with an Xinput (Xbox) controller, the A-Button would be LITERALLY the A-button.  On the Steam Controller, the A-button emulates the keyboard E-key (or whatever is set as the OK button in-game).  The smaller issue here is that you'll be getting keyboard button hints in-game.  The bigger issue is here that it can't play Xinput games or applications (The big application that it ISN'T compatible with is Controller Companion, which would be a godsend addon for this controller if there was support for it) that aren't connected to Steam at all.  It's gonna emulate a keyboard and mouse.   And it isn't gonna be as clean for movement.  Fun fact: Skyrim has native Xinput compatibility  Tried it with the Steam Controller: not very clean turning, but again, using the gyro mouse input set at VERY high sensitivity works somewhat well, but overall the controls are pretty annoying.  So, if you have Xinput games, you're better off using an XbOne controller/Xb360 controller.
Overall, this controller is pretty neat, but it's firmware needs a whole lot of firmware refining.  Xinput support would be great, as it would work with other applications that use this type of input to operate.  Definitely work on support for controller companion.  It may be third-party software, but it's the best controller-to-desktop software I've ever seen, and would be a godsend for this controller.  Fix the keyboard emulation for desktop.  Otherwise, it's pretty dang snazzy.
Would I recommend this?  Well, not so sure yet.  At this VERY moment, not really.  But that's definitely subject to change.

This is the latest entry in the sim-PvP MechWarrior series. Based on the tabletop game BattleTech, it features Western-style mecha — "BattleMechs" — engaging in terrestrial, unit combat that combines line-of-sight armored warfare with deliberate, blow-by-blow gladiatorial pacing. You can choose from dozens of 'Mech chassis with four weight classes, half a dozen weapon-based fighting roles, and a variety of silhouettes and unique performance quirks.
At its best, MWO captures BattleTech's rock-'em-sock-'em action as forces of up to 12 'Mechs face off and pound each other with cannons, missiles, and lasers until one side, shattered and smoldering, destroys the last enemy.
Highly customizable, 'Mechs play fairly differently from one another, allowing even a small stable of chassis to provide alternating experiences. If you like the tabletop game, you’ll immediately notice the attention to visual and thematic details from BattleTech fiction. Lead devs obviously love what they’re doing.
You can jump into playing with free, community-tested ‘Mechs in a matchmade solo queue, bring friends along to a more organized and challenging matchmade group queue, or shop around and join one of many player-created contract guilds that frequently participate in ongoing interstellar campaigns. ‘Mechs can be purchased and owned after a pretty modest grind, although you’ll need to make a micro-transaction for chassis slots (“‘Mech bays”).
BattleTech is an obsessively loved franchise that's thirty years old. Its devotees are nearing middle age, enjoy high disposable income, and had been waiting nearly a decade for MechWarrior's next official release.
Piranha Games knew a captive audience when it saw one — but as a small developer with more ambition than resources or experience, soon fell short of goals negotiated with founding players, and has struggled with some expectations of a multiplayer game, from balance to persistent content to user interfaces.
Its persistent campaign, Community Warfare, is currently simplistic and generally regarded as repetitive and unfairly time-consuming. The game’s engine is monumentally CPU-bound, so you might see wild fluctuations depending on single-core power.
MWO is simmy, crunchy fun as short-session, scratch-the-itch entertainment if you’re a stompy-robot type or a BattleTech fan like me who gets a kick out of seeing the tabletop game in realtime. If want this to meet every fantasy of immersion, you won’t find it — and searching will just wear you out. Still, MWO draws from a rich brand, Piranha’s getting better with time, and, with guidance from the recent emergence of BattleTech’s creators with another project, this game has a lot of potential.
It's not for everyone, but everyone should give it a try.

Microsoft paid for the development of Dead Rising 3, so that it would be an exclusive Xbox One launch title. I would speculate that Microsoft wanted the game to have mass appeal. As a result Dead Rising 3 plays like a GTA clone, rather a dead rising game.
Dead Rising was a niche series that a lot of people would not like. The strict time limit in the first two games meant that grinding experience, by killing zombies, resulted in the player having less time to complete side missions and main quests. The strict management focus made many people think that "new game plus" mode was required to get the best ending.
Dead Rising 3 is an decent game. I got from humble bundle and it kept me entertained until the end. Do not expect much and you will not be disappointed.

Don't get me wrong, I quite enjoy the game. It has a good story which I enjoyed, as well as tons of creative, mindless, zombie killing fun. With a wide variety of unique weapons ranging from crazy awesome effectivness, and then weird and nearly pointless ones.
However, it has a fair share of bugs that really killed the experience. The controls themselves are fine, but sometimes act a bit too "touchy" and things will go off in odd directions along with the odd halt in movement. But what really did it in for me was the known issue with the game not loading your character progress (levels, attributes, recipes, and items) and then writing over said progress. This bug happend to me twice, once when I was nearing max level, then again when I was trying to build myself back up again.
I will continue to play and enjoy the Dead Rising series, but this is a "buyer beware" of the known issues one might encounter.

I am so close to recommending this game but i just can't do it. I've put in several hours and for the most part it's been a good experience but there are just a couple things that keep this game from being great.
The Good:
Replayability: There are a lot of different types of characters to choose from and each new time you play offers a unique experience.
Graphics: Fantastic pixel graphics make this game a lot of fun.
The Bad:
Balance: The game feels very unbalanced. It seems like some enemies die right off the bat and others will wipe out your entire party. Leveling up your character is a very lackluster experience. If you don't put the leveling up points in the character's primary stat than you are just nerfing your character. Really there are no choices for leveling up your characters when it all comes right down to it.
Story: There really isn't one. A lot of the NPC's just speak jibberish and if you are into character development and a good story, this game is not for you.
Loot: You get a lot of random loot that you spend a lot of time sorting through. Most of it is junk and once in a while you get a good item but it is usually not worth sorting through it all. Although an item may have a chance of doing a cool status effect like paralysis to the enemy, they will probably be immune to it. Why bother? Just sell it all.
Party Building: You are pretty much forced to make a party a certain way if you want to succeed in this game. You have to go tank, damage dealer, and healer if you want to make it through the final quest. It would be fun if you were able to try different builds and different types of heroes. But if you do, you will get clobbered. i tried
The Ugly:
My biggest gripe about this game is that it is impossible to protect your heroes from all status effects that your enemies will use. Your armor can give you immunity to certain status effects like poison or bleeding but then you will just get paralyzed every turn. Same with other status effects. With only 20 item slots you can't switch out different armor depending on what enemies you are facing, you just don't have the room with all the random loot floating in. It gives this game a false sense of difficulty but really it is just pure frustration.
Another gripe is that you can also get in endless loops in this game where your opponent will absorb all the damage you can do and you don't take any. I threw away my items and fought with my fists only to die by a infest ability that only should have done a little bit of damage but ended up blowing up my priest to kingdom come. I was on the last leg of the final quest too...grrr.......
right now i give the game a B-, if they fixed the balancing issues it would become a A- it really is a good game with a lot of potential.

First, forgive the low playtime on Steam.  I've been playing this game since Closed Beta, so Steam hasn't logged that amount of time.  I am a Legendary Founder, and a great fan of Battletech.  I've spent more money on this game than I (or my wife) would care to know.  Additionally, I am not a high-level competitive player.  I am a casual player, that has to balance work and family life with my gaming time.  So take that into consideration when reading my review.
That said, here's my review:
MWO is a fun game that has an incredibly steep learning curve.  As a new player, you will likely get frustrated as you learn the intricacies of controlling a BattleMech.  While this is not the Mech simulation game like previous Mechwarrior games, the controls are still complex enough that it will take time to get used to them.  Additionally, the Mechs feel as if they have mass to them (unless you're piloting a light Mech with a large engine).  Your Mech will not (usually) stop and turn on a dime, and it does take time for the Mech to accelerate.  The large Mechs feel as if they are cumbersome, which is a good thing.
The actual gameplay also takes time to become adequate.  There are many details and intricacies that are not readily apparent to new players, unfortunately.  You must learn to target multiple weapon systems, spread damage, manage heat, and a host of other tasks.  I remember years ago where one MWO trailer touted the game as the "thinking man's shooter".  This is definitely the case.  This is not a twitch shooter, and you will have time to line up shots.  That is not to say that aiming is unimportant; it is in fact critical, but reflex shooting is not as relevant to this game as it is to other FPS's like CS:GO.
MWO is a team-oriented game, and that is a crucial feature.  You will not survive if you try to engage the entire enemy team by yourself.  New players must get used to the fact that fighting is a group is mandatory if you wish to succeed.  This can be a challenge for some.
Long-time players will decry the balance of the game, but on a very high level, the balance is pretty good, though not perfect.  (Most) Mech chassis are viable, while all weight classes are essential.  Yes, there are some chassis that are better than others, but if you are playing at a casual level, this will not usually be detrimeental.  I am of the opinion that there are no Mech chassis that are completely obsolete; they all have their fun elements.  Weapon balance is pretty good as well; PGI has come a long way with balancing the weapons.
Perhaps the greatest issue of balance is the discrepancy between Inner Sphere technology and Clan technology.  There truly are some balance issues here, but I've found that it doesn't detract significantly from the casual game.  I do not find myself choosing Clan or Inner Sphere because of balancee reasons; my choice is solely based on whether or not I like that particular Mech.
Additionally, I am happy to report that there are no Mech "tiers" in the way that other F2P arcade shooters might implement them.  Provided that you have the funds, you can start with the biggest Mech as your first Mech.  You do not need to unlock a Locust before you can purchase a Stormcrow, for example.  The "tier" model from World of Tanks does not exist in this game.  This is a benefit because the grind in this game is minimal.  Yes, to min-max your experience, you will have to grind multiple variants of the same chassis to unlock pilot skills, but the performance boost has been reduced so this is no longer mandatory.  C-Bill (in-game currency) earnings have also been significantly boosted, so buying new Mechs is not a significant time investment either.
The Mech Lab is amazing.  If you like building Mech configurations and experimenting with that piece of Battletech loree, you will not be disappointed.  The weapon customizations are endless and there are hundreds of Mech builds.  Not all of them are super viable, and there is a "meta build", but almost all of them can be fun, especially if you don't take yourself too seriously.
There are some optimization issues with this game.  I've read where high-perfomance setups have trouble running the game at max settings.  I have a six year old desktop that has a brand new GTX 960 and but an old i5 CPU.  I do not have problems running the game at "normal" settings.  Granted, I am not shooting for a 4k resolution, nor am I trying to run all max settings.  Your mileage may vary.
The question of Play 2 Win always crops up with F2P games.  PGI has done a good job in this realm, though sometimes they've strayed towards P2W with early-adopter variants.  However, none of the MC (real money currency) Mechs (known as Hero Mechs) are overpowered or even routinely used in the competitive scene.  PGI follows the model of paying real money for early access to certain Mechs before the Mechs are released to the public.  For example, the Warhammer and Marauders were recently released/available for purchase by real money.  This gives purchases first access to these Mechs, but they will enter the in-game store for C-Bill purchase very soon.  Additionally, Hero Mechs do not convey any gameplay advantages except for increased C-Bill earnings.
MWO does have a deficit of game modes.  Currently, in the public queue, there are only Assault, Skirmish, and Conquest available.  Assault is basically team death match with the option of capturing the opponents' base, Skirmish is team death match, and Conquest is capture the points.  That's it.  In Faction Play (Community Warfare), it's limited to attack or defend.  This is certainly a big disappointment.
My biggest gripe is the matchmaker, specifically the group matchmaker.  Creating balanced teams has been a significant challenge for PGI, and they've decided to create two queues: One for solo players and the other for group players.  What this means is that if you wish to play with your friend, you will likely be matched against other groups.  This isn't a big issue except many Units (guilds or clans or whatever) will drop as a group, and so you end up playing against some very coordinated teams.  If your small group is brand new, this can be a very frustrating experience.
Finally, don't think of MWO as the "Mechwarrior 5".  It is not.  MWO is a Mechwarrior-themed shooter.  That's it.  If you're expecting Mechwarrior 5, you will be disappointed.  If you are expecting a game where you pilot a Mech and blow up other Mechs, you will be happy.
Overall, this is a fun game that has its flaws.  PGI is doing a decent job of addressing them, but there are certainly still some issues.  It's fun, it's free, you should give it a try.
Pros:
+ It's Mechwarrior!
+ Not a twich-shooter. "Thinking man's shooter."
+ Mech Lab is immersive and intricate and awesome.
+ Lots of customization.
+ No "tier"/gated system of unlocking Mechs. Play what you want to play.
+ No P2W.
+ Constant updates.
+ Great support staff.
+ Decent balance of all Mechs.
+ Heavy emphasis on team work.
Cons:
- Not Mechwarrior 5.
- Decent balance of all Mechs, but still some balance issues.
- Optimization issues.
- Sparse game modes.  Only three plus the Faction Play.
- Group queue can be discouraging to new players that wish to play with friends.
- Heavy emphasis on team work.
- VERY steep learning curve.

I'll keep it short. The game is not without faults, there is some untapped potential for sure, but it is good. It has kept me entertained for over two years now, which is unusual.
My top 5 pros:
+ Beautiful mech models
+ Perfect for people with wife and kids, one solo game lasts 5-10 minutes (CW 20-30 minutes, but this is not mandatory)

+ The core game is fun (kind of mech deathmatch, but less twitch and more positioning)
+ Constantly developing. Too slow for some critics, but it's getting there. More players, more support, faster updates.

I'm a long time battletech fan that grew up with Mechwarrior 2. I absolutely love the franchise and played Mechwarrior Online before it was ever released on steam. Played closed beta since 2012, and revisited the game after a long hiatus to see how the clan mechs were in game. Revisited the game again and logged in over 400+ combined hours with my profile. Scroll down to TL:DR if you don't want to read this long review.
If you are a new player in this game, beward of the skill tree that these devs plan to torture you in the future with. There is a SEVERE lack of commuication between the devs and the player base. While the game has a forum for suggestions, it is often overlooked in favoritism by the devs for Twitter. Yes that's right, Twitter. If you spot something that needs to be fixed in the game or a suggestion I hope you can get your point across in less than 121 words.
With this being said, they are planning to drop in something called the Civil War tech era which will introduce new mechs and new technology to try and breathe new life into the game. Sounds good right? Well, PGI has some kind of short sighted vision to make MW:O into an e-sport so "balance" takes "top priority" (as CEO Russ Bullock tends to repeat) as something akin to CS:GO. May I add that this is the only game in the mechwarrior franchise that has GAUSS RIFLE CHARGE UP TIMES. So wan't a sniper weapon platform for your mech? I hope you like holding down your firing button precisely at the right time or else it won't go off. Not to add on top of that how unlore friendly this entire concept is.
Another thing that proves how disconnected PGI is to their own game is when they start nerfing things with no logical reasoning behind them. Certain mechs got hit in the past with nerfs THAT WERE UNDERPEFORMING TO BEGIN WITH. I can speak for myself since the Executioner I have in game feels like a card board cut out than it does a war machine. And while the playerbase rose their voice about it, nothing ever came of it.
This doesn't even cover a fraction of the problems that this game has.
PGI's dependency of income now is the occasional steam player that might buy a mech pack for $20, and the nostalgic whales that still lurk in the community that are living in denial for a better Mechwarrior title. They already lost most of their founders that backed the kickstarter project for the game. PGI also has unfortunately a monopoly over the battletech franchise title. Their holding over the license won't expire until 2018 to 2020. Rumor has it that they might have been responsible for disbanding titles like Assault Tech 1: Battletech and Mechwarrior Living Legends. Now they are working on MW5:Mercs which will be an single player focused game.
Why don't you fix what you have now for more customer confidence if you want people to buy your new game?
TL:DR A game that had a lot of potential during that went to the wayside over the years.
I'll change this review to a positive one if there are any permanent positive changes. As of right now, I honestly can't recommend this game to anyone. If you wan't your mech simulation fix, I strongly suggest revisiting the older titles or checking out MW:LL for online multiplayer.
