This is the BEST online shooter. I'm one of the original backers and have played over 1000 hours, still more fun than ever. Big challenge for new players though, it's a steep learning curve - but worthwhile. This game features deep customisation, no respawns, very few one-shot kills, fast or slow mechs, it's NOT pay-to-win, and you can use great teamwork tactics etc. The game has deep lore behind it, but the main difference between this and other shooters is that your targets are damaged in different places - you actually have a reason to shoot their legs or arms in MWO.

Mechwarrior online is an unconventional firstperson shooter multiplayer only “light” vehicle sim game in the same vein as world of tanks, warships, warthunder, and armored warfare. However, unlike those games, MWO is player skill based rather than RNG based. I have been playing it since closed beta started three years ago. Being my most played game since release I quite like the game, obviously, but I cannot give an unconditional recommendation. This game is quite difficult, and has a very high learning curve, especially if you are not familiar with vehicular games, or past mechwarrior titles. Additionally the new player experience and progression is quite difficult, and will require patience, and dedication.
Where as in the other F2P vehicle games progression is based on working ones way up a tech tree of vehicles (tier 1-10, with low tiers being very easy to work through), MWO has no such model. All mechs are available from the word go, and the only limitation is the amount of currency you have (the soft currency C-bills, or MC). The problem with this model of progression is that the grind hits immediately, and can be very intimidating to a new player. MWO does have systems in place to speed a new players acquisition of Cbills however, (the inflated income from the Cadet Bonus, and money rewards for playing through tutorials, early achievements etc), but it will not last forever. There is no easing the new player in with low tier (1-4) vehicles like in World of tanks.  Additionally, there is currently no in game tutorials for using the mechlab (the area where you customize your mechs and loadouts), so you will either need to seek guides elsewhere, or work it out through trial and error.
Be sure to play though the tutorials, practice in the training grounds, and try out each of the trial mechs to get an idea of the kind of game-play you want before committing to your first purchase, as it could color your whole experience. But once you find your bearings, MWO is a very fun and challenging multiplayer arena shooter with a lot of room to expand in the future (single player content is currently under development).
It should also be noted that the developers often run special events (around 2 per moth at least) where you can earn prizes by completing various challenges. The prizes vary with the event, but can include Cbills, General experience, consumable packs, to premium content such as cockpit items, additional mech bays, paints, skins, MC, and even premium mechs. Christmas will be a good time to play is all I am saying :D

First let me start off by saying, this game will change your life. The Characters are great, the world is colorful, theres alot to do and different modes to play.  Now with that said, lets get started with this review.
The Plot
The game starts off in a mysterious place where the Main Character is in a unfamiliar place, then suddenly meets a shadow figure. Next thing she wakes up into a world full of adventure, secrets, and challenges. From there you'll eventually go to a Certain Town, which will pretty much be your HUB of the game. Think of that as your base of operations; stock up on materials from the shop, get buffs, etc etc.
The Gameplay/Mechanics
Rabi-Ribi is a bullet Hell. So expect the game to get harder and harder as you venture deeper into the game. With that being said, theres 5 modes to choose from, 3 is available on your first play-through, the other 2 are unlocked after. It's a platformer also. You control 2 people, a Bunny and a Fairy. With those two you work together to defeat enemies who are in your way. Along the way you can collect power-ups that are hidden, or you need a certain skill to get to it. Theres also hidden areas so you can explore as much as you want. Meaning, Rabi-Ribi is pretty much unlinear.
The Music
I felt as if this deserved its own little review because well, it's freaking amazing. Pretty much every Soundtrack fits it's atmosphere well. The developers nailed it big time with this. At first I was gonna just buy the game, which i did, but now I'm going to buy the OST once I get the chance. Trust me, I can tell the amount of effort put into the music and I think It's one of the best yet, especially for a bullet hell.
More Personal Opinions
I feel as if Rabi-Ribi the best Bullet Hell I ever played. It has a decent story-line, great graphics for a pixelated game, ( which btw i love) and overall a nice feel to it. Some people see this game and think it's just another Ecchi type game considering the clothing but in all honesty once you play the game and start to get into it, you'll honestly forget about it. Your mind will be on upgrades, exploring, and how to get stronger for bosses.
Rating
I find Rabi-Ribi a marvelous Bullet-Hell that should have more attention to it. I'll tell this to my friends for a fact, this game needs more love. Easily one of the best Bullet-Hells of 2016, if not One of the best in it's genre.  The Pricing is nice for the amount of content and love the developers put in.

MY RATING ON THIS GAME IS A SOLID 10/10. I can not reccommend this game enough to you guys, buy it asap, you WILL love it, thats all i have to say, just please buy it, let it change your life like it did to me and everyone else who loved this game.

This game is a fun little hybrid.  Much of the time it's a 2D Metroidvania exploration game with dozens of upgrades scattered around a big 2D-platformer game world, and a (sequence-breakable) set of mobility upgrades that help you explore said world.  Sprinkled liberally throughout are boss fights wherein the game suddenly becomes a bullet-hell dodge-and-counter action game, complete with the genre-conformant unreasonably-tiny hitbox on your character to make it possible to dodge the crazy attack patterns many of the bosses can dish out.
The plot is a bit ridiculous, but it's clearly just there for window-dressing, so I find that entirely forgivable.
If you like both Metroidvania-style action-platformer games and bullet hells, this is the game for you. Buy it, now.
If you like Metroidvania-style games but don't really feel like dodging bullet storms, you should probably buy this game anyway. Just play it on a lower difficulty setting; the main difference between difficulties is how many different attack patterns each boss gets.

An actually challenging bullet hell metroidvania game with good music, a fun art style, and bunny girls.

Simply put one of the best stealth/infiltration games of 2011 and arguably one of the best cyberpunks games ever.
As for the plus/minus of this game, here it goes:
*
: It mainly revolves around the ethics of "augmentations", that is cyberntic extensions that can be attached to a human being to improve the body or/and the mind. You are Adam Jensen, one who was recently cybernetically augmented. Yes, you are the the main character but you'll quickly see that you are part of a very big story with multiple secondary characters having their own agendas. The ending is satisfactory as there is no loose plot, and everything falls nicely into one place.
*
: There are many ways for you to complete an objective. There generally is the main way (rambo), and many other paths. There is always a secondary path that will allow anyone to get inside a building without requiring special augmentations, while other may require you to level up a cybernetic part of your body. Being curious is a good thing. Also, being a "hacker" is great: it's a bit difficult to invest on this from the start but it pays off quickly as you are able to get to places you couldn't reach easily otherwise.
*
: You can finish the game without killing anyone, except the bosses. I wish more games do that.
*
: it's certainly the weakest point of the game. Yes, you can use the environment rather than weapons to kill them, but all boss battles (except the last one maybe) left me underwhelmed.
*
: If you go the "hacker" way, you'll find that the game gets much easier. I had only one playthrough (too many games to play to do it a second time) so maybe it's true only for the hacking part.
Other than that, except good graphics (for 2011), and 40 hours of solid gaming if you want to resolve secondary missions and/or plan to play to get all achievements.
I suggest this game to anyone that likes stealth/infiltration, cyberpunk or good story. If you happen to like all three, like I do, then you'll have a blast.
: It's also supposed to be an action game, as you can play it "rambo" style... But you would miss a lot by doing that. I suggest anyone wanting to get the best from this game to play it in stealth mode: also, try to avoid killing anyone (Pacifist achievement) and avoid starting off alarms. And, play in on max difficulty. This combination should arguably be the best way to play the game.

(Based on a true story.)
This is the story of Hacky, Samira and Jamal, three legendary adventurers. Hacky, true to his name, was a dwarf who excelled at hacking at stuff. Samira was a human enchantress, and supported the party with magical expertise. And Jamal - well, he smoked pot all day. Which was good, cuz weed be good healz, mon.
They were a formidable trio. Hacky took all the hits at the frontline, while Samira melted their foes with righteous fire, and Jamal - well, he smoked pot at the back. Which was good, cuz weed be good healz, mon.
They'd been to the Stormy Peaks and took from the giant squirrel Ratatoskr his razor-sharp tooth, which Hacky would use to slice and dice. They'd gone to the Sunken Empire and defeated the geisha for her magical harp, which Samira used to curse and bless their enemies at the same time somehow. And Jamal - well, he didn't need anything beyond his own pipe. Which was good, cuz weed be good healz, mon.
---
They vanquished foe after foe, completed quest after quest, with none of them succumbing to Death's touch. Before long, they were equipped with the finest gear, and nothing at all could stun them, much less take them down. It seemed they were invincible.
But alas, on their final quest to save the world from the abysmal lord of the Cyclopean Pyramid, they got what was coming to them. It was quite impossible for the monsters they encountered to kill them, for they simply lacked the firepower. There was only one thing in the world that could stop the formidable three: themselves. An evil-eye-thing they met on the way played a most sinister tune. The gang was impervious to being stunned, but this song got them dazed and confused. Hacky and Samira turned upon each other and wound up taking themselves out, with Death sweeping in to claim their souls. And Jamal - well, he was just minding his own business, smoking pot at the back.
All he had was weed. No weapons, just weed. He had to drop some weed from one of his hands just so that he could punch the evil-eye-thing with it and somehow take it down. (Waste of good weed, I tell you.) When at last the song had been silenced, Jamal was left alone in the chamber. It was all over, it seemed. What could he do all on his own when all he'd been doing from the very beginning of the journey was smoke pot at the back? But it wasn't quite over just yet (and Jamal had nothing better to do), so he decided to stick it out to the bitter end. He grabbed Samira's old harp and marched on deeper into the Pyramid all on his own.
Death seemed certain but Samira's harp wasn't anything to laugh at, even in Jamal's intoxicated Rastafari hands. With the power of the Harp's cursed harmony (and his weed), Jamal somehow clawed his way up to the final boss. And the duel was on.
As the lord of the minions who proved to be Hacky and Samira's bane, the Giant-Evil-Eye-Thing also knew how to play the confusing tune of doom. Jamal was dazed and confused on multiple occasions - he would throw perfectly good bags of weed at the thing for no good reason. (SACRILEGE!)
But in the end, Samira's harp outplayed the Giant-Evil-Eye-Thing. Through an act of miracle, Jamal had single-handedly vanquished the Great Eye and emerged victorious!
---
Jamal made his way back to the town. The townsfolk were overjoyed to hear of the Giant-Evil-Eye-Thing's demise, and prepared a great celebratory feast in the tavern. Jamal had one thing left to do. He went to the chapel, and through the great power of RPG gold, he bought back his old companions' souls from Death and resurrected them, good as new. He returned Samira's harp back to its old owner, and then the three of them went off to the tavern to enjoy the good life.
The rest of the story is just hearsay. Hacky apparently got drunk off his head on mead. Samira played a bewitching tune and then vanished until the next morning, when she emerged silently from one of the rooms, with the local blacksmith following not too long after. And Jamal -
Well, he smoked pot all night.
10/10, cuz weed be good healz, mon.

Alright before I get started let me address the main reason there is so much hate for this game right now. The game itself isn't bad, but the optimization and graphic options are the main reason for the negativity towards Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 4.
YES, it does suck that so many people are being affected by this and;
YES, CC2 should really be doing something about this.
BUT, I'll be review the game itself, not the graphical errors. (I know that it is part of the game too. I fixed my input lag, and frame drop by restarting my PC after downloading it.)
Now, for the main review:
Overall, I give this game a 8.5/10 (Rating against all other storm games) and here's why.
STORY 9/10 - The story is awesome, simply put. It closely follows the anime and manga, though there are some things that never happened (Various fights put in the game). There was screenshots of the anime that was injected into the story cinematic scenes. This really helped with making you feel like you were watching an anime. The in-game cinematic scenes were well done as well. The animations did feel like they were 'stiff' and the facial expressions were awesome as well (some kinda' look weird at some points but only very, very rarely). My only problem with the story is there was almost too much cinematics. There were several points were I was getting restless and decided just to skip ahead.
CHARACTER ROSTER 9/10 - This is their biggest roster yet, so of course it isn't bad. With that being said, I do hope they add some other characters that the community is asking for (AKA: Toneri Ōtsutsuki, Momoshiki Ōtsutsuki, and Kinshiki Ōtsutsuki). Other than that, the roster is good enough for me. EXCEPT for Adult Naruto and Adult Sasuke being DLC. *SPOILER* They are shown off for a moment at the last cut scene. Why would you put them there and then make them DLC?
MULTIPLAYER 7/10 - Now, I haven't played too much multiplayer but I would like to. Currently I have played 10 matches (won 8 lost 2) and only 3 have them have truly been enjoyable. It seems that this game suffers the same as the other Storm games. I don't know if it's just me, but it seems everyone I face (save for 3 opponents. One of which I lost too.) is playing from the very outskirts of the country with 1 bar of Wi-Fi from a McDonald's a couple miles away. The lag is God Awful and the micro-stuttering is worse. It's hard to time out your dodges, counter-attacks and attacks when you are two seconds behind the other person.
COMBAT 9.5/10 - I find this to be the most satisfying part of this game. The combat feels fast paced and flows incredibly well. The character switch is amazing and not as 'cheesy' as I thought it was initially going to be. Yes, I'm sure some players can find ways to abuse this mechanic like everything else, but I for one love it. I also really enjoy that you can switch between various ninjutsus on some characters, as well as some Ultimates on a few. The only reason I give it a 9.5/10 instead of a 10/10 is because you can't wall run. Unless I'm completely missing something, and I hope I am, the only wall running I've seen in in Story Mode. In that, it only happened 3 separate times. Why would you put this in and not put it in multiplayer or at least free battle mode?
All-in-all, awesome edition to the Storm series and a great finish. It's a shame they have optimizations problems at launch, and hopefully they fix it (doubtful but I'm hopeful).

TL;DR - This game is a wonderful last edition to the UNS series and unless "Boruto Ultimate Ninja Storm" comes out, this is the last BIG Naruto game to come from CC2. So far I have only experienced minor FPS drops during Triple Awakenings / Combination Ultimate Jutsus, but that doesn't take away from the experience at all. There are some issues people are experiencing but a patch should be on the way as consoles get the game February 9th. The negative reviews overly exaggerate the negatives to the game and I don't think it gives the game as much justice as it deserves.
Most Edits Made will be too the Last section of the review where I suggest ideas.
Why you should get the game:
If you're a Naruto Fan
HUGE roster of characters (More coming with DLC)
Final Naruto game by CC2 (CyberConnect2)
Epic storyline battles (During the Obito / Madara / Kaguya Saga)
You've played any other UNS game and enjoyed it
You "Believe it!"
Beautiful ultimate attacks
You have a good gaming computer (specs AT LEAST on par with requirements)
Story Mode, Adventure (Free Roam), Collection, Online Battle, Free Battle (All Modes)
Lots of things to buy with Ryo (Money) for your Collection
Additional Costumes for Practically every character in the game
Split screen battles so you can invite your cousins over and battle them
Why you shouldn't get the game:
If you have a computer that the specs aren't on par with the requirements
If voices coming from just the left ear bother you (Story Mode)
If you don't like Naruto
If DLC bothers you
If 30 FPS is a major problem for you
If you'd rather not "Believe It!"
If fighting games aren't a big deal to you
If over 100 characters isn't enough to play as
If you don't have some type of controller (it REALLY helps)
My Opinion:
The game runs good and looks fantastic. The huge roster makes versus battle very entertaining. Story Mode is just amazing with the battles they've created. I guess it's ok.
I feel compelled to recommend it seeing as how i have attempted to get friends to play with me and I am still actively playing, but if you're not already into mechwarrior it's really hard.
THE REASONS:
Grind:
There are still issues with how long it takes you to really get set up with good equipment.  You're honestly lookin' at between 100m-250m to get into faction play with a decent set of robots.  Monthly contests help, but if you're not givin' them money to speed up your money gain/match, you're gonna feel like it's taking too long.
Learning Curve:
There is honestly a whole lot to learn, and if you don't have someone walking you through things you're going to make poor decisions with the money you're earning early on, which is a boost that lasts only the first 4 hours or so, which will just leave you feeling like you wasted your time trying the game out.  If you make poor choices early on, you're best bet is to start a new account and just spend the starter boost money better.
Matchmaking:
There is still a whole lot of skill gap in the lower tiers, due to there being so much to learn and not enough player base to balance matches with.  At least now that I'm in tier 1, i don't get people who make the classic mistakes, like shooting allies and not understanding game mechanics.  But when you're not in tier 1, it will feel like the games will be determined by just two to four people who know what they're doing and they will almost always determine the match for or against you.
Emergent Gaming:
You can't earn money by doing practice matches (non-premium members can't do custom games)/training/doing a campaign (which doesn't currently exist), or trying to come up with your own ways to enjoy the game in custom matches (races, paint job contests, all 1 weapon matches), so you'll feel like you're not progressing when you take actual time to break down the game mechanics you should know, test different builds, or just try to play the game in an unique way with friends.
Despite all that:
It's still a pretty fun game to play, and the game is currently more balanced than it has ever been.
All in All:
I wouldn't really try to get friends to play this game, it's easier to find other people who already play it to play it with you.   Which is really interesting in of itself.

I used to game almost exclusively on consoles in the past. When I got into PC gaming, I couldn't get into using a mouse and keyboard for games. As a result, I looked around for different controllers and ways to bind buttons to keys when needed. Before I got this controller, I had experimented with other ones. Some that only lasted for two weeks, others that required a special custom drivers that can be a pain in the rear to configure. For the most part, the Steam Controller is a pretty good one, but it still has a few things that could be worked on.
The good:
1.) The design can give it more buttons than other controllers if mapped correctly. With games that use Xinput, you can make the most of it by mapping the analog stick to the left track pad and the d-pad to the analog stick. When done, this frees up an extra button you can use for another feature, which in addition to the grips, gives you three extra ones compared to a normal Xinput one.
2.) Custom controls. This goes beyond the normal button remapping trick. You can pretty much customize controls how you feel they work best. Example, you can rig up a button to act as modifier so you shake your controller or slide your thumb back and forward on the right track pad when you are instructed to move the analog stick. Figuring out a good control scheme for some games requires trial and error, though.
3.) Multiple control schemes. If a game has a driving portion and a platforming portion, you can set different control schemes based on what's needed and then switch between them when the game mode changes.
4.) Works with Xinput and keyboard and mouse games.
5.) Button Accessability. Because of the grips, it is possible to have three of your fingers on each hand over buttons in addition to your thumbs.
6.) Can configure multiple controllers with separate control schemes. What's right for one player might not work for another, which makes this a good thing when playing with family and friends using more than one of these things.
The bad:
1.) The USB cord with the controller is a little short for it to effectively be used as an old school wired controller for people who prefer those instead.
2.) Can be little uncomfortable for use at first and can requires some getting used to before you're comfortable with it.
3.) Doesn't support DirectInput mode. Don't get me wrong, the support of a keyboard is great, but some times it is easier to configure a game to use a controller instead. Unfortunately, there are some older games that do not treat Xinput controllers like they would a DirectInput controller.
4.) Requires games to be launched through Steam or the desktop configuration to be modified and Steam running to use it. It would be nice to have a separate mapper program that can be used without starting Steam that can access your configurations. A bit of a problem for those who buy games through other distributors like GOG and want to use their clients to play online.
[/list]
Overall, I would recommend this controller to anyone who is transitioning from console to PC, but it still has a few issues that need to be worked out.

The Steam Controller is the most tailorable, precise, and proper controller I have had the pleasure to hold. It seems different, but that is because it is. It should not be compared with the Xbox or PlayStation controller, because instead of giving you something comfortable to play the game with, the Steam Controller makes you the absolute player. This rant is regarding OB64 and all of the problems it introduced such as the new card system. If by chance they scrap this system entirely in future updates, this review may not be as relevant.
OB64 is here and Hi-Rez continues to disappoint with what I think is actually the worst update Paladins has ever seen. The card system is complete trash and pay to win for casuals (most people play casual/quickplay). Getting your cards to their max level takes so many duplicates and chests that even players who spend hundreds of hours on the game will have a very hard time doing it. On top of that, the game's balance was destroyed even further with new broken legendary cards (Makoas new legendary, Kinessa's new legendary) and broken loadout cards. New Players will have a much more difficult time now than ever before against players that spend some money or those that have played for a while. Another variable will be introduced to matches outside of individual skill level, strategy or teamwork, and it’s not one that needed to be there. Your “wallet” size shouldn’t determine the outcome of a match, but it’s something you will see in quickplay/casual. With that being said, Paladins now feels even more broken, buggy and unbalanced with horrible design decisions to loadout cards and lack of testing. It baffles me that so many bugs and problems get through when new patches (and this update in particular) are implemented. It’s a complete mess to say the least.
It’s unfortunate, I really do like Paladins (at least I did before OB64) but Hi-Rez can't be trusted to make sound decisions based on what the community wants. I understand that an audience may not always know what it/they want, but there is no way that Hi-Rez didn't see the backlash and skepticism people had about this update weeks before it was released. On top of that, Hi-Rez’s only concern seems to be sh*tting out new costumes and cosmetics rather than fix their own game. Their management clearly doesn’t have their priorities straight.

This game is a fun little hybrid.  Much of the time it's a 2D Metroidvania exploration game with dozens of upgrades scattered around a big 2D-platformer game world, and a (sequence-breakable) set of mobility upgrades that help you explore said world.  Sprinkled liberally throughout are boss fights wherein the game suddenly becomes a bullet-hell dodge-and-counter action game, complete with the genre-conformant unreasonably-tiny hitbox on your character to make it possible to dodge the crazy attack patterns many of the bosses can dish out.
The plot is a bit ridiculous, but it's clearly just there for window-dressing, so I find that entirely forgivable.
If you like both Metroidvania-style action-platformer games and bullet hells, this is the game for you. Buy it, now.
If you like Metroidvania-style games but don't really feel like dodging bullet storms, you should probably buy this game anyway. Just play it on a lower difficulty setting; the main difference between difficulties is how many different attack patterns each boss gets.

An actually challenging bullet hell metroidvania game with good music, a fun art style, and bunny girls.

As a devout fan of bullet hells(Touhou, Nuclear Throne, etc.), combat-based platformers(Cave Story, Metroid, Castlevania, etc.), and non-linear/exploration based games, I highly recommend Rabi-Ribi to any player looking for a challenge.
However, and this may sound bad, this is
for a casual player.
I repeat, casual players, stay away.
My reason for saying this is simple; unless you wish to throw out any difficulty in the game and not feel any pride in your victories, you're going to want to play on Normal at the very lowest when you first play(I was debating between Normal and Hard but eventually cursed myself with Hard mode, which had me stuck on a boss for over 4 hours).
I did make an alternative save file with Casual and another with Easy, just to see how much more difficult Hard mode was, and it definitely lives up to its name.
Hard mode is difficult, and there are still two difficulties I haven't unocked yet. However, let's get off of this.
The gameplay in this title is absolutely solid. Normal enemies do get kind of boring at times(though, if you're not carefu;, they can get you), but the bosses are the absolute peak of hell. I have spent 4 hours fighting
and still enjoyed it. By the end of the game, you will have a large amount of unique techniques for fighting, my particular favorite so far being the Bunny Strike(Down+Z+C on my keyboard).
Now, the fights are not the only major part of the gameplay. Exploration is just as, if not more, important in its own way. The game is extremely non-linear, though it may not seem like that at first. For instance, there was one miniboss I accidentally skipped over just by running around and finding a secret passageway. I found a way to temporarily bypass the boss that gave me so many troubles and get more health, this only being possible due to a wall that wasn't really a wall and the Hidden Tech: Reverse Wall Jump.
Oh, yes, there are hidden moves you can discover. My personal favorite is Reverse Wall Jump, but I'll let y'all discover them on your own(or use a guide, but that's cheating).
10/10 on gameplay
The story is nothing great, especially when 90% of it seems to be skippable(not even joking. There's a legitimate achievement for skipping what sees like a major plot point). Basically, you're a bunny named Erina that get transported and turned into a human in, of course, the highly provocative bunny suit(this is even made fun of by another character later in with the phrase "I know less clothing means better armor, but..."). Later, you meet a fairy named Ribbon, blah, blah, blah...

First off, I must say I was impressed on the speed, and the quality, of the port from PS4 to PC. Megadimension Neptunia VII released in Japan last summer (2015), and international PS4 release was on the first quarter of 2016. The PC version was released in Q3 2016. Unlike some unluckier ones, I had zero problems with the game from the beginning. And boy, was I impressed how much the series has grown. While the cast has been reduced quite a bit, the new additions of Uzume Tennouboshi / Orange Heart and the four Gold Third are a welcome addition. The game runs super smooth, even with my medium-specced rig (AMD FX-4100, GeForce GTX 960 4GB, 8GB DDR3) and it looks very nice (as would be expected from PS3 / PSVita to PS4 change). The soundtrack from the deluxe pack is also a welcome addition (these deluxe packs have been released for other games too, since then) but it does not contain every song found in the game (figures, as some songs are reused from earlier games).
The story is divided into three arcs, almost episodic like an television series. The premise is nothing you haven't already seen in these games; end up in a weird place, befriend some new people by fighting them and then save the world while searching for a way back home. It's cliché, but it works in games like this.
Around midway through the story the CPUs gain a massive power upgrade (Next Form). It trivializes some of the content afterwards. Overall, the difficulty seems to lean towards easy for most of the game, save for a few fights that might throw you off until you learn to prepare for them.
Overall, the game is a wonderful addition to the Neptunia series. The music is superb, animations smooth, game mechanics refined and the story, while not deep, manages to keep you interested on what is happening next.
Pros and Cons list:
+Beautiful graphics compared to other titles in the series
+Beautiful music
+Next Form, accompanied with full transformation videos and over-the-top attacks. And the music. ABSOLUTEly the best track in the game :)
+Uzume and the Gold Third
+Umio!!
+Same good Neptunia you all love. More of it and refined to the max.
+Neplurker (Depending on your gaming skills and patience, might become a negative point)
-Scout system
-Hidden Treasures
-Lack of many characters from the earlier series such as Falcon, 5pb. and MAGES.
Overall a very solid game, and a good entry point to the series if you haven't played them before. Just beware that the earlier games aren't as pretty and refined as this.

Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic is a tedious time-waster with little to recommend it.  Which is a pity because a lot of work has gone into it; but in all the wrong places.
I was expecting a party based dungeon crawler like Death Knights of Krynn or any of the other Gold Box games in 2D.  What I got was a slow mobile port lacking any real stratgey or tactics.
In Pixel Heros you 'hire' three heros from the Tavern.  You auto-walk to the only character in the 4 building town who will give you a quest and then you click go.  The quests are instantly forgettable as they are fantasy 'paradody' quests with no hook and little humour.
On the road you will meet three random encounters which are best avoided as the loot and experience gained from them is negligible compared to the risk and cost in potions.  Actually most of the loot found is pointless and doesn't bring even incremental gains.  A 2 physical damage reduction cloak of wind immunity vs a 2 physical damage recudtion shirt of bleed immunity.  It doesn't matter.
The battles - the core gameplay - are terrible and where the tedium sets in.  Your three heros stand in line on the left, the three enemies stand in line on the right.  Only the hero and the enemy at the front of each queue can physically hit each other (with a few exceptions).  The other two heros wait at the back and cast ranged magic spells.  This doesn't make for much strategy as soon as you work out that the 'solution' is put the best armoured and highest life character in front and then max the other two heros inteligence.
The battles execute slowly with long periods of nothing as an invisible timer counts down.  There are no short cuts - only the left mouse does anything and there only two frames of animation per character.  Most of the enemies look like they were drawn by someone learning to use Deluxe Paint.
The quest / dungeon crawl is just 8 rooms in a line (without back-tracking) followed by a single boss monster.  Once you've played one you've played them all.  The only variation is the background.
Loot management is a pain.  You can carry twenty items in your party - regardless of who is alive or dead.  Every interaction is a mouse drag.  You cannot double click or right click to assign or sell loot.  You cannot get a side-by-side view of items.  You cannot leave items on the floor, you can only destroy them.
Ultimately Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic is tagged as an RPG but there are no meaningful conversations unless you are role-playing as a cringe inducing ape.  It's tagged as a rogue-like but there is no exploration.  It's tagged as an adventure but it has a trite and forgettable story.  Only two screenshots and five seconds of the video shows actual battle gameplay; and that is very, very telling.
Don't buy Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic.  You're unlikely to play if for much more than an hour and most of that will be spent waiting.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is one of my favorite games. Through my time playing it, I never got bored and I never felt like I was forcing myself to play through it.
The gameplay is amazing. There is never one way to play through this game. If you are fond of running through each building with guns blazing, than there are weapons just for you and linear paths just for you. If you like to stealth you're way past guards and silently take out enemies, than there is a set of weapons, paths, and skills for that as well. On top of this, there are different ways to get into building and out of buildings, get around guards, and to get past doors. In one place, I remember that you could either break down the wall, go through the front door and secretly sneak into the place, or go the long way around and jump through a window and stealth your way through the level. On top of this is the dialogue tree. In some places, you are able to sweet talk your way past somebody and in others you were able to earn little side quests that may help you in some way. Like I said, this game is superb in the way that it lets you go through the levels and how it lets you play the game. All in all, I would say that you should get this game just for the gameplay itself.
The Graphics are decent for the time that it was released. They still hold up to today's standards and, in my opinion, look pretty good.
The story was only interesting enough to keep me interested, in my opinion. I won't tell you the story because like I said before, you should play this game for the gameplay itself.
Taking everything into consideration, I would give this game a solid 8/10.

In it's core Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a good game.
I was pleased to see, that it can both run smooth and look good (surprisingly, at least for me, it runs better with Directx 11 enabled than with disabled), although it took some research and tweaking with game's settings.
I don't have much negative things to say about sound either. Outside of fight music is more to the subtle side, after a while I started to not notice it much anymore and got used to it being there, it became inseparable part of the surroundings.
Voice acting was mostly good too.
The time you spend in the game will be divided into exploring the level, taking care of bad guys and talking to people.
Levels are designed with different player's approaches in mind. There are many paths which you can take to get on better position or to get straight past the enemy, you just have to find them or have the augmentations to use them. There is of course always an option to go head on and shoot through the enemies.
Every level has also many hidden items scattered around, which rewards exploration.
There is also a lot of hacking to be had and hacking minigame here is one of the better you will see.
Combat is cover based and stealth oriented.
Sneaking around and taking down enemies one by one is the easiest way how to play the game. Sticking to cover will get you to 3d person mode, so you can look around corners, not to mention you have radar which shows position and facing of nearby enemies.
When the enemies don't know where exactly you are, they behave really stupid. They walk on their paths, they never notice a missing buddy, when they briefly see you they will investigate but then they will quickly return to their path, sometimes they will play with their phones/tablets paying almost no attention to what is going on and they can be easily lured out of group with noise. It's the standart stealth AI we all know, nothing new but it still works.
In direct combat their AI is sufficient. They will make use of cover, they remember your last location and will try to pin you down with fire, sometimes they throw grenades and may even divide and try to get closer to you.
The story is the usual conspiracy, which you are uncovering bit by bit. For the most part it's focused on following the trail to find kidnapped scientists with sidestories on the way. There are choices to be made here and there but only a few has an impact on the game.
There are some good characters with well written dialog, but unimportant characters can deliver few pretty terrible lines. Talking animations could use some work too, I don't talk about lips but body movement. Characters have tendency to repeat animations often and sometimes they look unsettled, almost shaking. For an RPG there is not that much talking here, but it's balanced out with persuasion minigames.
Inventory system is a tetris on checkerboard with pieces of different sizes. Some might find it too small, but with upgrades it's more than enough. You won't fit all weapons there, but you will stick to few weapons which you upgrade anyway and you don't need to loot everything you find, because most things you need you will find, not buy. Unless you have a real problem with hording consumable items, you will get over it.
Augmentations, you will unlock them using praxis kits, which you can find and also you will gains them for experience. There are just a few augmentations which I found useless, the others are usefull, more or less in dependence on your playstyle.
Experience gain is problem though. You are rewarded with more experience for using non lethal methods and even more for non lethal takedowns (your close range attack consuming energy). It makes sense, unconscious enemy can be revived and for takedown you have to get close. But if you want to maximaze your experience, you are forced to certain playstale. It's either having fun or being effective. For me it would be better if there was just no set experience for every enemy, but it's more a nitpick.
There are some things, which was bothering me though.
First of all is lack of detail. Outside of main characters, there is little to no interactivity with other npcs in the levels. There are also numerous things which breaks immersion. Just to name a few, you can walk into a shop, go right past it's owner into back room, steal whatever you find there and the npc will not even take notice of your presence. Or in Alice Garden Pods during Belltower attack, you can still see closed pods with silhouettes of people just reading a book while civilian npcs are laying around dead. I guess Belltower soldiers are just kind enough to not disturb them and will settle for killing those who stand around.
What makes it even worse is that developers had balls to put in pocket secretaries with unfinished text like the writer was interrupted by the attack.
Also, if you will steal from offices in Sarif industries Headquaters, you will get emails from personel blaming each other for your thefts. This is a nice detail, which makes the overall lack of detail even more annoying.
Also, if you have Direct's Cut version, there is dlc content integrated into the game. In practice it means, that when you get into cryopod to get yourself on a boat, which is near end of the game, you will be thrown into dlc, where they will take all your augmentations away at the beggining.
I personally really hate when game takes all your benefits away without a possibility to avoid it. When you go trough most of the game exploring every inch of the level, taking down every enemy, going for the bonus experience for completing level unnoticed to get augmentations you want, and then when you have them and you finally don't have to care about experience and you can go trough level as you want, you just don't want to suddenly do that again, because game will take it away.
That made me stop playing for few months. I'm glad I take a break, or else I would rush through that part just to get over with when actually it is a well made set of levels and dialogs with Quinn were great too.
Just a few last things to mention - unskippable intro sequence and npcs interrupting you in persuasion minigame with "You have nothing to say?". Unnecessary.
So, the game is good, just rough on the edges. It is definitely a worthy sequel, recommended.

If you enjoy playing with lego's, this is certainly a game for you
Blockland is an non-linear lego-esque sandbox game with no goals or objectives. Instead, you start in an empty world with only your imagination. Players use bricks to construct anything they desire. Houses, castles, spaceships, anything you can think of. The only real limit is the brickcount, which i believe is around 1,000,000 bricks at once. Unless you're some hardcore extreme builder, you'll never hit this limit and you'll be free to build anything you want without worrying about running out of bricks(a common problem found with real life legos).
If you don't like building alone, it's very easy to set up a server and have friends join the fun. You could even enter a public freebuild server and hangout there.Building not you're style? That's alright, this game has multiple gamemodes aka multiple ways of playing the game. Challenge some friends to a kart race, or join a deathmatch server and show off your mad MLG no-scoping skills. Team up with other players to defeat a powerful boss. Escape from prison while avoiding police brutality. Enter a city rp, empires rp, slave rp,or, everyone's favorite roleplay, the family rp. If none of that sounds interesting, you could always try to make your own gamemode and contribute to the community.
Speaking of communtity content, the blockland forums is filled with countless amounts of add ons and new content to spice up your game. Download some new weapons, get a new car, fly a stunt plane. If you're a builder, there's tons of custom bricks and tools to make building easier and more fun.
A lot of reviews here seem to warn you about the game's community to some extent. I'll be honest, there are some pretty bad people in the game, particlularly on the forums. However there are lots of cool people aswell to meet in game and on the forums, and that's not so bad.
THE VERDICT:
I spent $20 on this game before it's steam release, and probably have 500 hours on that version. Now it's only $10, so it's even more worth it. And when it goes on sale, you should have no reason not to buy this wonderful game.
So, why are you reading this review and not buying/playing this game? Get it now, you won't regret it.

TL;DR - Overall a great controller with damn near unlimited flexibility and features, but awkwardly shaped and feels somewhat cheap. 8/10 stars in my opinion
The Steam Controller innovates in so many ways and is beyond useful when compared to that of the Xbox One or Dual Shock 4 controllers. It takes some getting used to, but doesn't take long. The extra paddles on the back prove to be extremely useful for every game. While the controller unfortunately uses just AA batteries and not a rechargable pack, the batteries do last for over 100 hours! In a sense, I almost prefer it because I don't have to wait for it to charge in case I need it for gaming. The controller has a great weight; not heavy, but not too light. Connecting the controller to the PC is a breeze. The customization options for the controls are far beyond that of anything I've ever used before, allowing you to customize the haptic sensitivity, every button and joystick on the controller, and even the extremely underrated Gyro controls. The controller also has an on board sound speaker that emits low grade tones when turned on or double pressing a pad (if configured). The tones can ever be customized for each event!
While there are plenty of pros for the controller, there are still a few cons. The controller feels somewhat cheap with the way the buttons and paddles click. The shape of the controller is not my fancy, though it's not exactly uncomfortable either. Lastly, the controller has no where to put the USB dongle in case you want to travel somewhere and with the USB dongle being as small as it is, it can be easily misplaced. I hope with the next version of this controller, it will have a slot to put the USB dongle (bottom maybe?) and they slightly redesign the controller for a better shape.
In the end, I highly recommend this controller and think every PC gamer should have one available in the event they want to use a controller at some point. I actually prefer to use the controller in some games such as the Assassins Creed games, platformers, and fighting games. It even holds its own for Windows navigation!

If you are looking for an accessible 4x space game, look no further.  While not as deep as MOO2 (or Sword of the Stars), Endless Space games do not require a chunk of your life to finish either.
The technology tree seems to be well-balanced, with a tech in each none-science paths reducing the cost of a scientific victory.  The usual military victory exists, as does the diplomatic victory and economic victory.
The various built-in races are different enough and offer a varied enough play style to keep the game interesting.  You can also spin off your own custom sub-race (using one of the existing races "looks").
While the majority of the game is spent at the galaxy screen - managing colonies and directing fleets - combat is very much an active aspect of the game.  While mostly a matter of numbers, combat is played out in a more cinematic style versus the direct-control of a typical RTS game.
There are three phases to combat: long range, medium range and melee range.  Each phase is dominated by one of the three weapon types: missile weapons, beam (energy) weapons and kinetic weapons, respectively.  It is possible to design ships using missile weapons that are tailored to medium range and melee range phases, in addition to the other weapon types.  This gives the player a multitude of choices and considerations for combat ship design.
After spending a considerable amount of time with the game (approximately 10 hours), I deem this a must buy for any 4x afficiandos looking for a shorter and less complex experience to StarDrive or Sword of the Stars (and SoTS2).

Hello everybody. I write this review as a fan of Battletech, MechWarrior in particular, and as an MWO player since late closed beta. According to the stats page of the game, I have spent 205 hours in-matches. Note that this does not include Community Warfare matches which should be roughly another 30 hours and tinkering with mechs inside the mechlab or one of the many player-made mechlabs available on the web. The money invested into this F2P title is around 70 dollars which includes the Hunchback IIC package (40$) and a few other MC (MechWarrior Credits, the IRL money currency in-game) transactions for hero mechs, premium time and colors. I primarily play as a Heavy pilot, with a few choice Assault and Medium mechs. I am also a Tier 2 rating, so I like to think I have an O.K. understanding of the game and it’s Meta. All these things may have colored my perception of the game and the experience it offers.
The Good:
-Unique gameplay that seems to be underrepresented in today’s market
-Vastly improved controls over its predecessors
-Complex and meaningful customisation (MechLab)
-A mostly mature community that is supportive and enjoys explaining their passion about stompy robots
-A great selection of mechs with varied play styles. This game has so many of them, there will be one for you. During the writing of this review 12/9/2015, most mechs are in a good spot with some underpowered exceptions.  The most recent balance patch was on 12/1/2015 so the new meta has yet to solidify.
The Neutral:
-Starting Trial mechs are a mixed bag. Try all of them
-Steep learning curve
-Lacking in-depth tutorial about most important part of the game (MechLab and Mech Customisation)
-Runs on CryEngine and has performance issues on weak CPU’s. Recommend lowering “Particle” setting
-A fair selection of maps, but could use more. Maps also vary in quality
-Owning 4 mechs of each chassis allows you to “Elite” your pilot with the chassis, used to grant you considerable buffs. Those buffs were since nerfed hard, but are still noticeable. Investing in a mech chassis you enjoy is still recommended and somewhat expensive
- Mech Upgrades are expensive, required for competitive play and are NOT factored in the initial mech buy price (hidden costs). Same goes for different engines ratings or engine types. It may look like Light Mechs are the cheapest but a competitive Light Mech can run you the price of a Competitive Assault Mech (hidden costs)
-All new mechs release in a Pre-Order Pack model, where the mech becomes available for those who pre-order, a month later it releases of MC and a month later for in-game CBills
-Community Warfare technically no entry requirement, but having 4 custom mechs is highly recommended
-Performance based economy. As in any game, you probably won’t be amazing at it right away. The game can be somewhat grindy between your first and second mech. However, once you perform well consistently, the money will be flowing in.
-Controversy around developer and their practises
-Community Warfare lacks a matchmaker. It’s considered the “hard core” mode where people play with their units!
The Bad:
-Limited base game modes .Quick Play only has TDM with a base, pure TDM or Conquest. Community Warfare features an asymmetrical Attack/Defend mode with turrets and dropships that let you deploy up to 4 of you mechs (Each mech acts a as a life) as well as a TDM mode where the invader team defends the destroyed base from a counter attack. That’s it until a new “scouting” mode drops sometime next month.
-Signature game mode Community Warfare has low population on off-hours and work days (This may change with steam release)
-Somewhat slow development rate on big features. However, there are 2 patches per month and fast hot fixes (even on weekends).
-Hit or miss balance patches
-Minefield of an in-game store. Somewhat expensive too! Please research a Hero Mech before purchasing, not all of them are good!
Overall, the game is solid enough to warrant a download. Most importantly, even if I find it somewhat stale nowadays, it has a way of being FUN. Try it out, but it’s not for everybody. Look up some of the excellent player guides and resources.
I recommend visiting
it has a great player resource selection. MechWarrior has a passionate community that are willing to help out new players. It might be overwhelming at first, but this game can grow on you easily.

I've played this game off and on since 2012, starting with the Founder's beta.
We'll start with the good things: the core gameplay, is solid and actually works fairly well.  The weapon effects are nice and some of the artwork is very good.    The game has very good sound design and effects.
Now, for the bad: everything else.
It is an arena shooter with long queue times, lousy matchmaking, bad netcode, a terrible community, and terrible balance decisions.  It is extremely grindy, the cash shop packs are insanely overpriced, and development on the game has been virtually non-existent for three years now.   Oh, and the game is extremely buggy.  And I can provide examples.
Let's begin with the queue times.  My average wait to get a solo match in the 'public' arena game queue is usually about three minutes.  My average wait to get a group game (groups have an entirely different queue) in my last play session was over five minutes per match.  The average wait to get a community warfare match during peak hours is typically about fifteen minutes.  Sometimes, after waiting for fifteen minutes, you don't even get a real match, but instead you're forced to grind out turrets for minimal reward.
Let's continue with the matchmaking system, which recently ditched ELO in favor of a 'skill tier' system that is actually just a grind.  If you win a match, your skill rating will improve.  If you lose a match, but displayed more activity than a moldy potato, your skill rating will improve.  The game literally rates player skill based on the number of matches someone has played.
The netcode is bad.  You can play the game and see for yourself, if you don't believe me.  However, suffice it to say that it is entirely normal in this game for shots to simply fail to register on the target at all, or for other weird things to happen, such as taking fire from the front and noticing that the damage registered on your back.
---
The game is badly balanced, because the designers of the game do not understand their own game.  With every other game update, certain mechs and/or weapon systems will go from being completely worthless to utterly overpowered, and there is absolutely no rhyme or reason to how, when, or why this will happen.  Actually, I take that back; I do know why balance changes happen.  When the lead game designer actually deigns to wade in and play his own game, he is typically embarrassed on account of being awful and not understanding what's going on.  But rest assured, that he will nerf the hell out of whatever killed him, because clearly that must be overpowered.  For instance, look up "Goons Heart Paul" on Youtube and then consider that the mech knockdown mechanic was COMPLETELY REMOVED FROM THE GAME FOREVER in the patch immediately after that video was recorded.
Oh, and there are also two different levels of technology in the game.  Inner Sphere (IS) technology, and the more advanced Clan technology.  Clan mechs are faster, more durable, and hit harder.  They participate in the same matches as IS mechs, and there is no penalty on the player for bringing a Clan mech into battle.  You may have noticed that the Clan mech packages are more expensive than the IS mech packages.  Surprise, that's because they're better!
---
When I say the game is grindy, I mean that the game is grindy.  You get a huge cash bonus in your first 25 matches, enough that after playing 25 games, you will be able to afford a mid-sized Inner Sphere battlemech.   Then you have to buy equipment for it.  Double Heat Sinks: 1.5 million c-bills, MANDATORY on all IS mechs.  Endo-Steel structure, MANDATORY, will run you maybe another million c-bills.  That's not counting the weapons and engine you're going to have to buy when you customize your mech, assuming you actually want to run a good build on it so that you can be competitive and kill people.
Note that you have to buy three variants of each chassis (full price!) to "elite" a mech, which is ultimately necessary to be on even footing with veteran players.
---
Development on this game has been dead pretty much since release.  I don't think I need to go into fiascoes such as Transverse (when the developers decided to abandon development of MWO in order to try to kickstart a Star Citizen ripoff) or the $500.00 gold mechs (Google it), but ultimately the development of this game has been nothing but one mech pack grab deal after another, with pretty much no development at all of new gameplay features or content.
The game is buggy.  The HUD is frequently glitched or displays incorrect information (generator displays were broken for MONTHS in Community Warfare matches), but is also poorly optimized and tanks the game's framerate.  Crash to desktop remains a persistent issue.
I wish I could add more, but the character limit on Steam reviews prevents me from doing so.

Long time MWO member here.
With Infinite Games Publishing (IGP) out of the way, Piranha (PGI) seems to have actually stepped up their efforts. While the core game has remained the same and there hasn't been anything particularly new to note, the core gameplay has reached a fairly playable level and netcode is... dare I say, good.
It's worth noting that this is less about shooting an enemy than about shooting the right part of an enemy, and keeping your own important parts intact. Tactcs and maintaining team cooperation is always important.
Graphically, the game is a far cry from the Crysis 2 visuals it once had in closed beta, but things have improved recently with TXAA and wider graphical options, though some settings are still finicky (TXAA breaks object-based motion blur). That said, it still looks good in the right scenes and settings. Performance is also usually not an issue anymore.
Audio has been simultaneously a strong and weak aspect in this game - some argue it's too quiet, not enough ambient noise, reactors should have loud sounds ala the old days, etc. But then the weapons all sound wonderful - especially ballistics.
It's still expensive to be a paying player, but at least now, I can say that I recommend people to join MWO. Which is something I couldn't do before. Especially when the game reached a point of "unplayable" for me. Currently the game is in a reasonably decent state and has large bonuses to help new players get in.
It's always worth remembering that this is no hardcore MechWarrior experience, but it is also no typical first person shooter.

Do you like Shooty Stompy Robots?
Then give MWO a shot. It does Robot Arena Shooter pretty well, all things considered. Gunplay is fun, TTK is around acceptable (you won't die in 1 shot most of the time, allowing for mistakes to be made, but fun still had), although the MatchMaker is just praying to RNGeesus and hoping you get fewer TerriBads than the Red team, in both the PUG LIFE (solo) and Group Queue. Taking larger groups can prevent that issue.
If you want in depth BattleTech™ Lore?
This will not be the game for you. Aside from names, almost nothing is BattleTech.
Strangely, this hasn't allowed for better balance.
I've been playing for over 3 years now, with over 10 thousand drops over that time. This is my opinion.
Due to playing a couple thousand matches since PSR tracking has begun, I am a "Tier 1 Master Race" player, but that largely just separates the new players VS veteran players. Tiers 4 &5 will never play Tier 1, but Tier 3 will play with everyone. It's so easy to gain PSR, that when you play enough matches, you WILL reach Tier 1, as long as you aren't consistently the worst on your team.
Balance
as a whole, is probably the best it's been since the Clam (colloquial term of the Clan faction) introduction, which brought a large amount of power creep.
This was done, not by adjusting the base stats of a mech, but by adding "quirks" (generally bonuses to a specific item, whether Internal Structure and Armour (IS+A, think of them as HeathPoints), range of a weapon, heat of a weapon, etc...) to each individual variant in the Inner Sphere, and the Trash Tier Clams.
While giving certain mechs double IS, 20% less heat, 30% more range, and other extreme items; the baseline of Vanilla Inner Sphere mech VS Vanilla Clam mech isn't ideal. The Sphere (and Trash Tier Omnis/Clams) require quirks to compete, but I've always been of the mind to, you know, balance the base stats, and quirk exclusively the underperformers, not EVERY MECH in the faction.
Clams have the best weapons, the best engines and the best chassis', but also some of the worst mechs, which even their superior tech can't fix (avoid Myth Lynx and Cute Fox. Take the Ice Ferret only if you are masochistic).
With quirks, certain select IS mechs can compete, and even exceed at certain niches (longest range, coolest lasers in the game).
The highly IS+A quirked mechs can even compete for durability (using the inferior isXL engine, which dies upon 1 ST loss to 2 ST loss of the Clam XL), but again I highlight how quirks are how you should be choosing Spheroid mechs.
The balance team, has in the past, been largely referred to as...incompetent.
I tend to share that view, with how stagnant the balance in the past has been. YEAR long sessions where one weapon type was SIGNIFICANTLY superior to the others. We're kind of in one of those, but not to the extreme it was in the past.
SRMs no longer have 1.5 damage (pathetically weak, after a 40% damage nerf), although PPCs are now rubbish (previously most powerful item in the game). Lasers beat everything at every range, as a general rule (while long range lasers will lose to SRMs at short range, short range lasers won't).
For the 3 years I've been playing, there has been one weapon that has never been brought up to par: the Flamer.
For 3 years, it has remained rubbish, with no reason to logically take it (the go to Troll weapon, however).
They have mysteriously also nerfed the worst weapon in the game...multiple times. A random 20% damage nerf to the Machine Gun, for no logical reason.
"Why, Paul, Why?" is a common theme for balance changes...and I don't even know if Paul is in charge of balance anymore.
As a whole, balance is acceptable, as long as you're aware to ignore 80% of the mechs available, ignore certain weapons, and learn to frontload your armour, while keeping an eye on Quirks.
At this point in time, it's less of a Clan VS Inner Sphere debate, as which Quirked mech VS which God Tier Omni (and in 5 days, Clam BattleMech).
It only really makes a difference at the top or in competitive matches. In the Solo Queue, you can generally use whatever mech you want and still be the top performer.
New players will eventually learn what those terms mean.
Visually, I've never had complaints about MWO, as I've always had a Potato of a PC. I can run it at 30+FPS, so I'm content.
Overall, if you like Shooty Stompy Robots, give it a try.
If you want in depth story? MWO doesn't have that. It's an arena shooter, with big robots. It does that well enough.
I'd give it a 6.5/10

December 18, 2017 was the day that Paladins stopped slowly declining and started failing. Do not play this game. Let me tell you why I, and many others, have stopped playing what was once my favorite game.
The game used to be extremely fun, with a reasonable progression system for an amazing card system that affected gameplays, an in-game item shop that shaped gameplay, a unique & balanced gamemode I've never seen before, promoted teamplay, a high time-to-kill (TTK) for all characters, and a lot of mobility. It had an interesting art style, a great community, and constant updates that added more to the game. Even in a public beta, it was extremely fun and constantly expanding. Lots of unique & fun characters that, although not always perfectly balanced at first, were eventually tuned in the bimonthly patches. Every update brought new skins you could buy with an in-game currency you could get for free every week OR pay real money, although you didn't need to. You could customize your cosmetics however you wanted, and with consistently great skins approx. every 2 weeks, HiRez didn't really let us down.
One of the big things about Paladins was a card system that I want to talk about, this is important so pay attention. Every character has 4 abilities. Each of those abilities had 5 cards that affected it (lower cooldown, generate ammo, gain speed, etc.) You could randomly get these cards from radiant chests or buy your choice of card with an in-game currency. Although it sounds bad on paper, it worked pretty well in practice. Once you unlocked that card, you could do whatever you wanted with it. The cards affected gameplay but it wasn't unfair, because everyone could have these cards to affect their own gameplay. Using these 20 cards, you were able to make a custom loadout for each character. Every card had 4 levels that increased the stats of that card, and you could choose. Once you own the card, you can use whatever level you want in your custom loadout. Your loadout had a 12-point requirement, so you had to adjust the levels of thse 5 cards to fit your preferred gameplay. This made every game unique, since your loadout could be different than another player's loadout. My way of playing Mal'Damba could be different from playing an enemy Mal'Damba. Eventually, a new set of cards were added. Every champion had an additional 3 legendary cards that you picked at the start of every game. You didn't have to include them in your loadout, these were 2 seperate things. This means that everytime you see/use that legendary card, it would be the exact same. No levels that you can change. You COULD make your own personal loadout based around that specific legendary if you wanted to. Even more customization for how you can play a certain champion. Every match was different and that's one of the main things that made the game special.
The game had one rough patch where it felt extremely P2W (you needed a seperate in-game currency to unlock cards that affect game) but it was eventually changed to a way that, albeit requiring a lot of planning from new players, felt easy enough for everybody to get what they wanted. There were quite a few bugs, but that was to be expected from a game still in it's beta that was constantly changing. Most of them were eventually fixed, although new bugs emerged, then were fixed, then new bugs came, etc.
I can't tell you when, but the game started having problems. Slow and subtle, but still existing. Balancing started changing for the worse. Many patches & new champions were rushed out to meet a schedule, but didn't help the game at all. More bugs appeared than were fixed. However, the main aspects of the game were still there and people still enjoyed it. Management changed, and the TTK started dropping, mobility was hardcore nerfed, newer characters had very unoriginal and boring abilities that were extremely OP & annoying to deal with. HiRez listened to the community, made some changes that people wanted, then made more changes that people didn't want nor ask for. A new system for cosmetics and an XP boost (that doesn't affect gameplay, thank god) felt like a cashgrab and started becoming the main focus for the developers. Paladins was starting to be balanced for new & extremely casual players and started to disregard existing players and mid-to-high levels. People complained, but it wasn't mindless. Especially Reddit, the community offered detailed and extremely well-thought responses to changes & what HiRez could do better.
And then OB64 (open beta, update 64) was announced. Essence was removed and all cards were unlocked for free, everybody would (ideally) be on an even playing field [Yay!]. This sounds great, right? WRONG. Remember how there used to be 4 levels for every card, and once you owned the card, you could do whatever you want with it? That part was removed. This is no longer an option. The "customization" in deck building was removed. Now, the only way to level up these cards & make them better (affecting gameplay) was with RNG, and purely RNG. You need multiple duplicate cards that you could only obtain by chests, no more direct purchases, in order to level it up ONCE. There are 10 levels for each card that extremely affect it. Mind you, this INCLUDES legendary cards, which extremely affect gameplay. A level 10 version of a card is infintely better than a level 1 version of a card. The 12-point limit was removed since you could no longer choose the levels. Now, if you own the card at whatever loadout, you just have to use it. No limits, no real choices besides what's the highest level. Again, I want to reinforce this, you no longer get to choose what levels you want the card to be. You can't choose your playstyle. You just have to pray to the RNGesus that you get a chance for a duplicate card to come close to slowly leving it up to a viable position. Remember, this doesn't apply to just you. This applies to everybody. Your teammates and the enemy. People who own a higher level card are immediately at an advantage over people who don't own all of the level 10 cards, regardless of skill (mostly). Although you can't directly pay money for these cards (you could spend money on boosters to get more gold for more chests for more chances), the system was mostly grind-to-win. The people that spent more time farming gold to spend on chests succeed, not people who spent more time to practice and get better at the game.
This new system isn't the only part about this patch that sucks. Let's talk about HiRez and the community. Specifically Reddit, since I am accustomed to that (but this still applied to the forums, Facebook, etc.). Pre-OB64, HiRez employees and quality assurance specialists were constantly looking for what people thought & wanted and these people responded. They would report to management or the devs or whoever and the changes the playerbase wanted/needed would happen. It was great. Then OB64 came out. Everyone on Reddit started complaining immediately, but with merit and proof. Every patch would have a Public Test Server where people could comment on new changes before it officialy went live. OB64 was in the Public Test Server for weeks, and had 6 minor changes (some bug fixes, some balancing, etc.). People tested, came up with meaningful arguements, and posted it for HiRez to see. HiRez supposedly listened and made those 6 changes, but nobody was happy. HiRez refused to listen to all the #CancelOB64 comments. People started leaving the game, and if you check the steamcharts data, you'll see it for yourself. The game is dying and people have given reasons, but no real changes were happening for the better. The developers stopped listening. Or if they are listening, they aren't doing anything about it.
That is why I would not reccomend this game anymore: terrible balancing, removing the parts of the game that were fun, creating an unfair G2W/P2W system, and not listening to the community. Do not play.

Now then with that out of the way, Rabi-Ribi is a 2D bullet hell metroidvania platformer where you play as Erina; a Bunny Girl who is accompanied by Ribbon; a Fairy. Erina focuses on close range combat and Ribbon with long range.
The story essentially revolves around Erina finding her master then finding helpers to help find her Master's sister. While the story isn't too strong, the bullet hell boss battles & metroidvania aspects are definitely the biggest & best parts of the game. It's also non-linear (after prologue) so you can go and tackle the bosses in any order you want, it makes speedruns very interesting.
+ Gameplay is very smooth & combat is satisfying
+ Cute & well done pixel graphics, sprites and CGs
+ Amazing soundtrack that fits very well with areas/boss fights
+ Lots of different difficulties (from Casual to Bunny Extinction)
+ Tons of boss battles (40+)
+ Different badges to pick from which encourage different types of gameplay
+ Many different areas & locations to explore and items to find & upgrade
+ Non-linear

Its fast-paced and stupid as hell, its raunchy and ultraviolent, its low class and wild, and never takes itself seriously, and its fun. Honest to goodness fun. The gun-building is fun, the experimentation is fun, the characters are crisp and clean, the purchasable costumes are silly and well put together, the whole package is great, and I'd have a hard time finding a better free-to-play model that is as truly free if you want it to be.
The Good:
Loadout knows how to build loyalty in players. They're helpful, they're available to talk, and they know how to make Free to Play as good as it gets. Every gameplay-altering effect your character gets via leveling is unlocked ingame, over a relatively short period of play, with ingame currency. This also goes for the gun parts, which you unlock with ingame currency too.  The money you can buy with real cash is only used for some very minor benefits in terms of inventory size (I.E. the number of guns you can design in total) that have essentially no effect on actual gameplay, and cosmetics.
The gameplay modes are easy to learn and creative, and the maps are concise enough that unless you're actively avoiding people, you cannot get lost or lose your team in the map. My favorite is Drop the Hammer, which is essentially capture the flag, only the flag is a nuclear hammer that instakills whatever it hits, and you get even more points for killing people with the hammer before returning it, making for some really interesting gameplay. The controls are responsive, and the character models are chunky and powerful, and the animations are concise and read well.
The Bad:
The only real problem I have is that, while you can design a weapon with all the bells and whistles you possibly can, some sort of angular monstrosity that fires bouncing, fragmenting acid grenades that home in on players, you're only going to get one or two shots before reloading, and the damage will be mediocre. Sometimes, the best gun a player can create is the most basic bullet-spitting rifle you can, because it's a reliable weapon and will vomit death at your enemy efficiently instead of the unwieldy gun I described before.
The Ugly:
The humor is just about as crude as humor gets. This is a game where you can play as a fat woman who had her skin burned crispy by flame, massive holes punched in her torso, and her arms and legs reduced to bleeding bones, and have her twerk wildly. Its up to you if you think that's hilarious, or disgusting, or possibly both. I like the dark and nutty humor, but its probably not for everyone, so check it out before you make a decision.

One of the best comedic open world games ever made that makes you feel like your in high school all over again.
-Fully Open World to Explore
-Tons of Mini Games
-Unique Leveling System Involving Schoolwork
-Replay Value
