You play as a young man who starts out being dropped off at a new school by his newlywed mother & stepfather as they go off on their honeymoon.  The story starts off great as you get to see the characters develop nearly right away.  The young boy is angry as hell & the mother don't give no ifs ands or buts about it as she's just married some rich guy.  Anyways, after all that you go to your new school & board room.  You then get the chance to learn your new natural habitat, meet some new friends, kick some nerd or jock butts.  All the fun stuff you'd do in a normal school :P.  As you progress you meet some new friends.  One's a sociopath while the other a more timid type of kid.  These are the two main characters that will help progress most of the story.  The end result is you becoming the unofficial king of the school & eventually the entire town where everyone knows you & respects you in some way.
The gameplay is very similar to GTA type games.  You run around, can steal bikes or pick fights.  If you pick fights with adults you're gonna end up getting caught.  Adults are a lot harder to fight but can be managed if you have the skill or weapons at your disposal.  Cops are a lot harder, though.  If you get caught outside of school during early hours you will be sent to class.  Classrooms act as minigames that usually involve some sort of QTE segments but doing these are very benificial as you unlock upgrades, weapons & such from doing them.  If you finish all your schoolwork you can then explore the town freely without the fear of being arrested & sent back to class since you no longer have any classes that you're required to attend.
There are also a variety of minigames that are also fun & give ample rewards.  Arcade cabinets with high scores that are actually fairly easy are one of the required mini games to progress the main story, but you do get a new weapon from doing it as well.  Then there are bike races which are really fun & give you new bikes to choose from as well as an entire theme park with it's own set of mini games & prizes such as a motor scooter which is the best vehicle in the game.  If you're riding the scooter without a helmet cops will give chase.  There are also odd jobs you can get around the town like delivering papers or mowing lawns.  Paper delivery plays like the best version of Paper Boy you've ever played & mowing lawns plays just as you'd think it would.  Just don't mow the flowers.  There's also a punch out like boxing mini game that ends up unlocking new fighting moves to utilize in combat.
All in all everything about the gameplay is well done with very little glitches or hang ups on controls.  I never had a problem doing anything in particular myself.  Exploring the world is one of the many pleasures in this game & there are lots of things to find such as trading cards, rubber bands, or gnomes to destroy.
Overall, this game is worth every penny you spend.  It's got everything you'd want in a video game.  Open world to explore, solid progression system, mini-games, vehicles, etc.  It's all great & good fun.  If it's on a sale you should definitely pick it up.  Even if not on a sale it's worth every penny spent.  IMO this game is better than most of (if not all) the GTA games.

If you enjoy playing with lego's, this is certainly a game for you
Blockland is an non-linear lego-esque sandbox game with no goals or objectives. Instead, you start in an empty world with only your imagination. Players use bricks to construct anything they desire. Houses, castles, spaceships, anything you can think of. The only real limit is the brickcount, which i believe is around 1,000,000 bricks at once. Unless you're some hardcore extreme builder, you'll never hit this limit and you'll be free to build anything you want without worrying about running out of bricks(a common problem found with real life legos).
If you don't like building alone, it's very easy to set up a server and have friends join the fun. You could even enter a public freebuild server and hangout there.Building not you're style? That's alright, this game has multiple gamemodes aka multiple ways of playing the game. Challenge some friends to a kart race, or join a deathmatch server and show off your mad MLG no-scoping skills. Team up with other players to defeat a powerful boss. Escape from prison while avoiding police brutality. Enter a city rp, empires rp, slave rp,or, everyone's favorite roleplay, the family rp. If none of that sounds interesting, you could always try to make your own gamemode and contribute to the community.
Speaking of communtity content, the blockland forums is filled with countless amounts of add ons and new content to spice up your game. Download some new weapons, get a new car, fly a stunt plane. If you're a builder, there's tons of custom bricks and tools to make building easier and more fun.
A lot of reviews here seem to warn you about the game's community to some extent. I'll be honest, there are some pretty bad people in the game, particlularly on the forums. However there are lots of cool people aswell to meet in game and on the forums, and that's not so bad.
THE VERDICT:
I spent $20 on this game before it's steam release, and probably have 500 hours on that version. Now it's only $10, so it's even more worth it. And when it goes on sale, you should have no reason not to buy this wonderful game.
So, why are you reading this review and not buying/playing this game? Get it now, you won't regret it.

There's a lot of great ideas that went into the controller, but one massive issue keeps me from using it for most games. The top two trigger buttons (L1/R1 on Playstation controllers and Left/Right Bumper on Xbox controllers) are extremely stiff. Probably at least twice as stiff as its Playstation or Xbox controller equivalents. This is absolutely crippling for games that heavily require the use of all four shoulder buttons.
The fact that the other two shoulder buttons (L2/R2 on Playstation and Left/Right trigger on Xbox) can each function as two inputs doesn't change this, since one input needs to be activated for the second to activate. I haven't found any use for this outside of shooting games.
My second-biggest problem with the controller is its physical design. It's built so you can only grip it with your palms facing completely inward towards each-other (imagine picking up a box). I haven't got a clue why Valve thought the Xbox and Playstation controllers had this wrong, but it completely changes how you need to stretch your thumbs to push buttons or move the left joystick. I just can't seem to get used to it.
I will say that the trackpads work much better than I expected and Valve really outdid themselves with the customization options for the controller that they've integrated through steam.

Received this last Christmas and it is the most comfortable controller I've ever used. Long term use doesn't hurt my hands at all. The first indication I got of this controller's quality was when I opened the box - it came with Duracell batteries!
Software-wise, I love it. Updates only happen when you approve the prompt. Full big picture mode support is very appreciated, as I enjoy the interface. If you have a Steam controller plugged in while browsing games, it tells you before buying whether or not the controller will be supported. In the vast majority of cases, support is there.
In terms of the hardware, the trackpad is very responsive and intuitive, and you'll have mastered using it within minutes. The customisation of the controller really impressed me. Even the brightness of the on button's light can be adjusted. The option to have a wired or wireless input immediately was also much appreciated, though I'm amazed I haven't lost the wireless USB connection - thing's tiny. The only gripe I have with the controller is the directional pad. It is very awkward to use and doesn't feel like a part of the controller at all. I avoid using it where possible.
The price of the controller is very fair - you wouldn't be paying much more than the cost of an official Xbox 360 controller, and the Steam controller feels superior overall. I recommend it to everyone.

I'll make this very short: try it!
If you are interested in games like this, you probably tried any of the Wargaming titles like World of Tanks.
And here is why MWO is better than those:
- No effing techtree. You wanna play an assault mech? No problem, no one will force you through playing lights or mediums first. You wanna play an Atlas? Sure thing, no one will force you to play ten other Mechs before it's unlocked! Play around with the four trial Mechs, decide what you want to play, collect the money from the achievements for the first 25 games and buy the Mech you want.
- Still rewarding leveling. You have skilltrees for each of your Mechs (and you will need three different variants of the same Mech to master it) and a pilot skill tree with lots of options to boost your prefered playstyle!
- Versability. This is not about just upgrading whatever equipment came with your Mech. Design the loadout you want on it (obeying a few rules, of course)!
- No pay-to-win. Sure, you can buy premium time for more income and XP. You can buy Mechs and nice packs for real money instead of saving up. But even the premium Mechs won't give you any advantage in battle, there is no premium ammunition...it's just making leveling easier or cosmetic. Only exception might be Mechbays, you will have to buy those if you plan on getting a collection of Mechs. But even that isn't pay-to-win.
- Maps DO matter. It's not just like: where's the best spot for me or route to attack (this is important in MWO, too). But it's also: what's the temperature (which will affect the heat rating of your Mech when firing) or what's the G (which will affect jumping - if you have jumping jets equipped).
Well, I could go on a bit more, but if that wasn't enough for you, I guess I can't help it and I said I wanted to keep this short.
So - preparing drop!

A really interesting concept nearly ruined by poor implementation.
WOG is a neat idea. It allows someone to see how these pieces of machinery work using several different methods and has plenty of models. If you happen to own one it's probably a great way to learn how to dissassemble it. Unfortunately there are several significant problems.
First, you can't just pick the gun you want and start working on it. For some bizarre reason you have to move through a tree of guns you may have no desire whatsoever to see in order to get to one you find interesting. Then you have to 'buy' it with credits from working with other guns. Or you can take a difficult quiz and log in every day to slowly increase credits. Or you can spam your friends. Or... you can just pay money.
If they had offered this at a reasonable price from the beginning I would have been happier with it than the weird 'fee to play' model they've come up with here. There is an option but I find $50.00 too much to pay for what's here. If I had the option to dive into anything from the beginning for something more like $10-$20, I'd probably take it. As it is I'm just doing the silly quiz and slowly moving across the models. This quiz is particularly annoying as all the shotguns and revolvers look the same.
The controls are also pretty bad. It feels like you're trying to land the space shuttle when you're attempting to zoom in just right to hit the right piece (and if you don't hit it just right you lose). Still, it's a cool idea for a program and at least if you want to play with a 1911 or MP5's internal mechanics you can get those pretty quickly.

This game is really awesome, and I enjoy almost every aspect of it! There is a wide variety of characters and skins for them (and more to be coming in DLC), but CC2 manages to make them all diverse and unique! Now there is one downside to this game. the microphones. There is NO WAY to mute your microphone while online for some reason, so all I get to hear is greasy adults analyze my picks and crumble up their Doritos bags and hear heavy breathing. This is avoidable if you just mute your microphone in total and turn off sound, but then you lose some quality to the game. Another thing is the Frame Rate. At first mine was a horrible 14 FPS (I know it caps at 30 FPS), but my friends and I came to the conclusion that a few tricks can ehance your FPS (please note that these are not 100% guaranteed to be the Messiah of your FPS):
1)Lowering resolution both in-game and for your monitor itself.
2)Updating your drivers.
3)Lowering graphics in-game
4) THIS ONLY WORKS IF YOU JUST BOUGHT THE GAME, Restart your computer.
Overall, I'd say this game is a buy even for the errors that were so prominently ranted about by other Steam users.  Every game will have its flaws, and this one surely didn't deter me from playing this game!

This will be my go at a review from someone who had their steam controller since the "Pre-release" days. It will be more of a "reasons I love the steam controller" than a proper review like everyone else.
I had pre-ordered, (the very few times that I do), a steam controller and was able to get it before the actual release since Valve had a special offer for pre-ordering.
You do have to get used to the controller but it is honestly the best controller hands down. I haven't touched any other controller since I switched. If you're considering getting one, do it. You won't be disappointed.
This controller will not replace mouse and keyboard (though it can be used as one), BUT it will replace any other controller that's currently on the market, (Xbox One, Xbox 360, Dualshock, etc).
There are also a ton of great things that a lot of people didn't know you could do with the controller, such as:
- Switching between different bindings  on the controller with a click of a button. (Research Action Sets)
- Control my normal desktop with ease. (Research The Desktop Configuration)
- Play any non-steam game with the controller with ease. (Just add any .exe to your steam libary)
- This is helpful with Emulators, (PS2 emulators, Wii and Gamecube emulators, etc).
- Play MMO's casually, since anything more would just need a keyboard and mouse. (Example: no raiding, but grinding is fine)
- Use Steam's Keyboard function to type into Chrome, Skype, or any other program.
There are days where I wouldn't even touch my mouse or keyboard since I would steam my desktop (using Steam Link. *A different product*), while using the steam controller. I during those days I wouldn't even think to need a mouse or keyboard.
I tried to list a few points that made me absolutely love this controller, and hopefully make you see that the controller is a very, very good product!

Other than the build quality and crap ergonomics, this is a perfect item. Look at all the reviews by professional critics and you will see exactly what this thing does(make sure you look at recent ones, as Valve keeps adding REAL features).
That being said, I don't use it nearly as much as I thought I would. I thought this would make my couch-FPS gaming as accurate as a touchpad, and it does not. Before I got my desktop, I gamed on my laptop and had zero issues using the trackpad - most people hate them but after a ton of practice I'm pretty darn good. But, because this uses your thumb instead of your index/middle finger, there is a ton of loss in dexterity. I always thought my inadequacies gaming with a controller were because analog sticks sucked, but it turns out I am the one that sucks. My thumb is still totally incompetent trying to use the touchpad, its saving grace being the gyroscope that you can activate super intuitively while aiming. If you don't have a POS thumb like I do, this will be a godsend, and is SUPER useful as a media/couch-mouse on your desktop regardless. But, if you are like me, and you hoped this would make you stop sucking if you currently suck, you'll be disappointed. You do need a significant amount of trained dexterity specifically in your thumb, even if less so on this controller.
My favorite controller for 3rd person games, and Rocket League!

This is in my humble opinion the best shoot-em-up of all time, and while I'm not a hardcore fan of the genre, I have played enough to feel that it's a decent title for that mantle.  I've rarely played a game developed by Treasure that disappoints, and this is probably their best.
The incredible visuals (which have aged exceptionally well), the amazing musical score and sound effects already set this game apart from many shooters.  However, the unique "polarity" mechanic and simple, straightforward controls truly make this game remarkable and unique, even compared to others developed by Treasure.
The ability to absorb attacks that would otherwise destroy you, and to have control over this mechanic for every attack in the game, adds a level of depth and strategy that isn't typical of games in this genre.  The mechanic is easy to understand, but often extremely difficult to apply optimally.
This mechanic is displayed throughout the masterfully crafted stages, which is the trademark of any Treasure game.  You would be hard pressed to find a shoot-em-up developer that can create stages that seem so chaotic and tense yet are so deliberate and organized in design.
I should warn that this game isn't for the faint of heart.  It's disgustingly difficult to master and really demands a lot of concentration and pattern recognition from the player to find success.  The only payoffs are bragging rights and hi-scores, which both come with a sense of accomplishment that you've overcome such a difficult game.

There are certain games that I boot up, and instantly wish I could’ve experienced them on a console 20 years earlier. Of course, consoles then wouldn’t have had the capacity for a game like this. But that excuse doesn’t really appease me. I really feel like I missed out, on missing out on my childhood. Pixel Heroes is much deeper than it seems on the surface, with tons of great references and an amazing degree of challenge. The combat system only allows one character to move each turn which makes it quite a bit more difficult than your standard RPG, that allows you to heal and do damage in the same round. My most successful run so far was with a rather unwieldy group, it actually sounds like the start of a joke. A priest, a templar, and a ranger walk out of a bar. My templar tank mostly just soaked up damage or threw buffs to the ranger. The ranger lobbed out massive amounts of damage, especially while buffed. The priest kept them all on their feet. On their venture into the final dungeon, the priest was struck down about halfway through. The ranger and templar persevered to the boss, and were actually doing quite well. Then the ranger become confused. With one shot of his bow, he dropped the templar, and without a tank he followed shortly after.
I spent 5 hours with my unlikely band of heroes, geared them up, distributed stats. Needless to say we had become quite attached. After a short period of mourning (literally seconds), I must continue the quest for the honor of all the fallen heroes that I’ve led to an untimely death. There are so many great things about Pixel Heroes it’s hard for me to pick where to start. The retro graphics are decent, and take me back to a simpler time. While they aren’t extremely well-defined, the point usually gets across regarding what you’re looking at. The music should’ve gotten a higher score, since making my Lets Review I delved into the Goblin Fortress, and that boss fight has THE most amazing music. While some music does fall quite short, the tracks that rock are truly awesome. This is an extremely difficult game, with the settings being “Hard” “Harder” and “Insane”. You will die a lot while learning the mechanics and how to utilize your character’s abilities to the fullest. The synergy between each class feels completely different, and as you play through you will unlock even more classes to tinker with. Experimenting with the varied playstyles sends this game’s replayability skyrocketing. While there are no skill trees, the progression (mostly done via equipment) is palpable and extremely enjoyable.
Aside from the fantastic gameplay, music, and difficulty, there is a bevy of nerd-related humor that is sure to rouse at least a chuckle. In the town where you start there is a blacksmith, a casino, a church where you can purchase potions and revive heroes, as well as a couple vendors selling exclamation points to desperate citizens in need of a hero. Once you leave the comfort of town, there are overworld events that randomly unfold en route to the dungeons. Even if you’ve seen the event before, the same answer can have different (and usually quite unexpected) results. Some events will turn into a battle, others will give you equipment or exp/gold and send you on your way. This system makes me wish it was possible to just wander the overworld, but unfortunately your heroes have a quest to complete. Dilly-dallying will not be tolerated. There is no exploration within the dungeons, simply 8 rooms which will either contain a treasure chest or (more likely) a battle. With no potion usage in battle, and permadeath looming over your heroes head’s, every battle becomes a gripping struggle for survival. You will learn enemy weaknesses on the fly, or be crushed. Bosses are difficult, but not so brutal that it’s impossible to beat them the first time seeing them as long as your strategy is adaptable.
The game isn’t without its flaws. Eventually you will see the same event twice, or feel the monotony that comes with fighting your way through 7 fights and a boss battle. The thing that keeps me going is the thought of conquering the next dungeon. I’m compelled to see the next boss, and smash his giant monster face into the dirt. There are always more sweet stats to stack, more lovely gear to hoard. A heroes work truly is never done. Once you’ve completed all 9 dungeons, after so many hours of pain and hardship, you can now move on to the “harder” difficulty mode. Is it actually harder? Hahahaha. I have no idea. I’ve seen the final boss once, but I want to try and get there again. That “one-more-turn” feeling is the mark of a great game in my book. This game costs less than a movie ticket and offers so many hundreds more hours of entertainment. I am a huge fan of Pixel Heroes. The tongue-in-cheek humor about its own retro graphics, along with the sheer unholy difficulty of completion is a combination that is physically impossible for me to resist. Fans of permadeath/roguelikes will love the games unrelenting (but still fair) difficulty curve. While it isn’t the flashiest game, it has quickly risen to one of my supreme favorites. Thanks so much to The Bitfather and Headup Games for bringing this vision to life.

What can be said about Pixel Heroes that hasn't been said already? Not much, but I'll try to remain as original as possible.
If you like Rogue-like games, you will love Pixel Heroes--buy it, it's worth the $10. If you like relatively simple, classic RPGs with a retro element of nostalgia--buy it, it's worth the $10. But if you don't care for any of those things, you might want to reconsider.
As of the time of this writing, I have logged about 27 hours playing Pixel Heroes. You may not think that's a lot of time spent to justify writing a review (especially considering the ludicrous amount of time some people have invested in this game), but I honestly think 27 hours is the appropriate amount of time that it will take most people to master and fully explore this game.
After you have completed the hardest difficulty level, Pixel Heroes can start to feel like a very repetitive, tedious, and pointless experience. But I can tell you that until I
complete the hardest difficulty level, I was driven like a maniac to finish this game.
I've read a lot about some people complaining about the unforgiving cruelty of the difficulty levels--but all that I can guess is that these people have probably never played a rogue-like RPG before. Overall, I had very few problems beating the three difficulty levels in just under 24 hours.
If you pick a balanced party (1 faith hero, 1 intelligence or dexterity hero, 1 strength hero), and play intelligently yourself (properly prepare for the dungeons), you should be able to climb through the difficulty levels with relative ease.
I breezed through the initial difficulty level on my first try, lost one party on the intermediate level, and lost two parties on the hardest level before completing the game. If it sounds like I'm boasting, I'm not--I only mention this because of some of the complaints I've read about the difficulty of this game. Pixel Heroes is not a particularly hard rogue-like game; maybe challenging to pick up if you're new to the genre, but ultimate victory should not elude you for very long.
In that same vein, I rather wish there was more DLC, more challenges, more achievements, more versatility to the party creation in this game, as after you have beaten it, it can feel quite pointless. With proper care and a bit of luck, almost any party can beat the game (in theory)--but especially when playing the final difficulty level, only the standard party composition will give you what you need to complete the game with a solid chance of success.
In general, this is how I feel about Pixel Heroes: it's a great ride, if a rather short one, and it can feel a bit monotonous at times. A great ride, but once you're finished, I see no real point in continuing.

First of all, a disclaimer: If you do not like perma-death/start over sort of games, this may not be for you. The lowest difficulty setting is called "Hard". If you are not prepared to accept starting over when (not if) your party wipes, maybe look for something else. You will die, and if you are the sort to be okay with that fact, you can also have a lot of fun!
Just to restate, you will die a lot in this game. My first two parties wiped before I beat a boss. My third party, however, is on their way to their fifth dungeon now. I am prepared for their eventual death, though. Every time you restart the game, different heroes are waiting to be chosen in the tavern, and more hero choices can be unlocked by doing certain in-game achievements. Even though you have to start all over again at wipe, I find it is still fun because things are sort of randomized.
You might consider buying a different game if you are the sort of person who is going to rage in the forums because you can't beat something, had to start over, and/or do not get the "right party" every time. If you are a person who realizes that this is just a video game, that you can and will die, and just want to have some good old random adventures, I highly recommend this game.

Where to begin?  I have played this game for 3 years...
The developers ignore the community, they do not listen about balance, or any game details when suggestions are made to improve the game.  In fact, most often they summarily ignore all feedback and put up what they are going to put up.  The developers are also all pro Inner Sphere, and you can tell.
The tech:
Clans have Tier 4 tech, but it is nerfed into oblivion such as:
Clan mechs have completely locked components aside from weapon hardpoints that can be semi-swapped around
Clan mechs lose 20% of their speed when they lose a side torso and lose 20% of cooling capacity
Clan mechs cannot be upgraded for anything but a missile targeting system
Clan mechs cost roughly 40% more for inferior mechs
Clan lasers do not use full double range
Clan lasers have absurdly long DoT durations to get full damage
Clans weapons run hotter
Clan autocannons are all multi projectile
Clan weapons all have longer cooldowns
Inner Sphere has Tier 2 tech (because PGI will not give them Tier 4 tech because they ignore the community) with stupid buffs:
Inner Sphere mechs can change engines
Inner Sphere mechs can upgrade multiple things on the mech
Inner Sphere mechs can add/remove Jump Jets
Inner Sphere mechs cost half of what a similar clan mech costs
Inner Sphere weapons all run significantly cooler
Inner Sphere lasers have less than half the DoT time of clan lasers (to get full damage)
Inner Sphere weapons have full double range
Inner Sphere autocannons are single projectile pinpoint damage
Inner Sphere weapons have much shorter cool downs
Inner Sphere SRMs have much tighter patterns better focusing damage
Inner Sphere SRMs do more damage per missile than Clan SRMs
Inner Sphere mechs get standard engines, which have no penalty on loss of Side Torso
Inner Sphere mechs all have ridiculous positive quirks such as:
Less heat generation (making already cool weapons absurdly cool)
Greater range (yes, they get full double range, *and* range quirks...)
Shorter Cooldowns on their pinpoint auto cannons and better SRMs
Now...onto balance...what balance?
The group queue is an arena for 8-12 man groups to stomp small groups and trash talk, so steer clear of that.  That means dropping by yourself in the solo queue.

Mech packs are a better value, but to get the one good mech in a pack, you must either pay a $55 a la carte to get it (and forego any purchase rewards for the pack), or you must often pay upwards of $80-120 for the whole pack to get a bunch of crappy mechs and the one you wanted. This game has a long and sordid history.  First released into closed beta back in 2012, the publisher, IGP, and developer, PGI, promised the sun, and all within 90 days.  Nearly two years later and they had almost nothing to show for it.  Then The developer, PGI,  bought out it's publisher in early 2014 and came out in the open about how the publisher had been holding them back all along.  Since then the game has steadily been getting better.  We now have practically all of what was originally envisioned (even if some of it is still getting polished), some of the best balance we've seen in a while, with only a handful of weapons being below average, and developers that actually listen to the community (sometimes).
The reason you see most of the negative reviews stem from all of this drama, dating back years.  Promises were broken and the founding players of the game got upset.  PGI made mistakes, but for the past two years has generally been going in the right direction and fixing many of it's wrongs.  Give this title a shot, it's free, it's fun, it's giant stompy robots!
Speaking of free, let me expand on that.  This is not a pay to win game.  Paid content falls under three categories: Early access, easier grind, and decorations.
Early access means that there are mech packs that are bundled and pre-sold before they make it in the game.  you get a bundle of high value stuff, but typically won't see it for 3-6 months.  You then get to play these new mechs for a month or two before being released for in-game currency.  Most of the time these new mechs are at or below average.  Occasionally they end up being powerful.  But anyone can eventually earn these mechs.
Easier grind deals with purchasing hero mechs and premium time.  Premium time increases the rate of XP and in game money you earn.  Hero mechs are special variants of mechs that also have a %increase in in-game money and slightly different hardpoints.  Sometimes these hero mechs are slightly better than normal, sometimes they are slightly worse.  They are rarely the best mechs in the game.
Decorations include paint jobs, camo schemes, and cockpit items.  Similar to TF2 hats and decor, you can truly customize your mech to make it uniquely you.
All in all, if you like big stompy robots, look no farther than this game.  You will truly feel like you are piloting massive tanks on legs, and the tagline "A thinking man's shooter" it rightly deserves.  Catch me in game!
Highly recommend, truly a thinking man's shooter

Mechwarrior Online is a worthy followup to its legendary predecessors, and the best large robot tactical action game on the market. It hits the rarely achieved sweet spot between first-person twitch gameplay and methodical strategy, combining extremely deep customization of beautifully brutal war machines with intense moment-to-moment combat. The pace of battle is somewhat less than the warp speed found in most first person shooters, allowing the player's tactical awareness and strategic creativity to come to the fore, in contrast to other games where raw reaction speed is king.
This more thoughtful pacing is consistent with the game's stylistic choices as well, which hew to a more traditionally "western" aesthetic of plausible tank-like distopian death machines stomping across war torn cityscapes and dangerous alien worlds, in contrast to the glut of "Japanese" style lithe robots that dance across most videogames today.
The game's free-to-play economy has gone through various permutations before appearing here on steam, but has settled into a comfortable place, providing adequate resources to free players in normal play, along with increasingly generous special event prizes most weekends that prevent any "pay to win" problems. Additionally, they have reduced "XP" requirements to narrow the gap between old-hands and neophytes, making this the best time for a new player to enter the arena since it's original closed beta launch. While the enormous variety of potential player customization makes balance devilishly tricky, the developers have consistently improved it over time, and managed to move it to a remarkably tight band that permits significant variety of viable playstyles.
In sum, I give this game my highest endorsement, I have been playing it since closed beta and it is undoubtedly the strongest it has ever been.

Played the game since closed beta and I have to say, this is still my goto for 15 minutes of fun (or hours if you continuously drop). Like any game, there are pro's and con's.
Think Tank simulator with legs and you won't be disappointed. Customization of your owned Mechs give this game depth and replayability. Make sure you play the tutorials to learn about movement, aiming, and the general basics of controlling your Mechs. The real depth comes when you learn to control your torso, arms, leg position, and convergence of torso/arms for aim, all independently all the while trying not to overheat when firing your weapon systems. These specific features can be a sharp learning curve, but once mastered, the satisfaction of making the systems work for you cannot be matched in any other game (my opinion of course).
Customizing your owned mechs is the other half of the fun in the MWO / Battletech equation. With literally millions of possibilities, this portion of the of the game can be daunting. When you get to the point that customization becomes a priority, make sure to utilize online resources such as sarna to understand what all the different pieces mean and online mech customization simulators such as smurfy-net to allow you to play around with your mech configuration offline. There are also TONS of other resources and a general search will help you find Meta-builds if that's your thing. (meta builds are typically min-max builds that a majority of the try-hards run)
As of now, you need 3 chassis variants to fully level your Mech skills (think efficiencies) for a single Named Mech type. Make sure you get your skills to Master as it gives you a significant bump to how  the mech performs.
MWO is truly a F2P, not a P2W. No golden ammo. Pay to look pretty, or pay to get chassis faster or grind faster. Quick drops give you best bang for your buck with matches only lasting as long as 15 minutes. Community Warfare is a lop sided affair with pre-mades ruling the battlefield, but it can be fun as long as you don't hit a pre-made.
Unlike other F2P, PGI has consistently delivered new features and has a fully fledged roadmap, even recently announcing that they are exploring a single player experience (YAY!). Having been around since closed beta, there have been bumps in the road but all those have been overcome and the problems fixed and/or roadmapped.

Oh, I forgot to mention this but it's important, the game has no aimbot detection. At all.
Mechwarrior Online is a game plagued with problems. I backed and founded the game based on the strength of the franchise, but I'm going to bring up any of my personal disappointments and the only mention of the Transverse fiasco will be right here. I'm giving this game a negative review for a few reasons, but if current trends continue I may choose to recommend the game instead.
PGI, when's the Flea coming out? It's been nearly two years since you announced it and MASC exists now. To whoever has the job of moderating the negative reviews, at least pass this question along when you moderate my review into oblivion.
With this review I mostly wanted to point out that the game typically goes months without anything resembling a balance update. MWO also features a few HIDDEN mechanics specifically designed to punish new players who don't know about it. That mechanic is colloquially known 'Ghost Heat,' which causes your BattleMech to gain additional (and often excessive) amounts of heat if you fire more than an arbitrary number of one type of weapon. This is never explained anywhere in game, and while the game does have a 'heat warning' that pops up in the mechlab if you've taken too many of one type of weapon that warning is small and easy to miss.
Up until about a month ago (over a year after MWO's launch) MWO was also completely without a tutorial, and the typical 'new player experience' was 'pick a trial `Mech at random, die three or four times without really understanding why, and uninstall the game.' If you didn't have a friend to show you the ropes or warn you about Ghost Heat or several of the other 'traps' (like LRMs currently being absolutely terrible weapons due to their slow speed, scattered damage, and tendency to ram into the nearest wall) you weren't going to make it very far.
This has changed, the tutorial is actually pretty nice, and there are some bonuses to help new players buy a BattleMech quickly so they can start customizing and using actually good weapons and the latest balance patch (the first one in MONTHS) has brought back a close-range brawling playstyle that's actually quite fun, but that doesn't change the fact that all of this was done immediately before the Steam launch and that the buffs to close-range weapons will almost certainly be reverted.
The real-money cost of BattleMechs is also completely absurd. They could cost a quarter what they do now and they'd still be expensive for a free-to-play game. An Assault BattleMech in MWO costs  Coupled with the fact that new releases often aren't balance-tested and aren't available for in-game currency for months after release means that new `Mechs are often pay-to-win, and due to the high prices (often approaching the cost of a AAA game for a `Mech pack or even a single Assault-weight BattleMech) this means that players who aren't shoveling their money directly into the furnace often become the punching bags of the players who are.
You also, and this is a real killer for me, have to spend real money on Mechbays (at around $1.38 per bay) to even buy a `Mech at all. Now, the MC cost of a Mechbay ultimately isn't that high, but it's another 'hidden' cost slowly nickel-and-diming the userbase to death.
MWO is a game best played with friends, and individual matches can be enjoyable once you get a handle on things. But the learning curve is steep even with a tutorial and you'll often waste tons of in-game C-Bills just trying things out. If you do play, my only advice is to save the 'Cadet Bonus' you earn over the course of your first 25 matches and buy a 55-ton Stormcrow. It's one of the most efficient `Mechs in the game and has access to the more powerful Clan versions of all the weapons, and will probably always be a good workhorse for grinding C-Bills in since it's fast enough to get to the fight and fast enough to get itself out of trouble.
Once you've learned what 'trouble' actually looks like.

I guess I'll give my own personal review of the game as well:
The Bad -
For starters, the game isn't playable for more than 10-15 minutes as it crashes, which makes it extremely difficult to get past the Madara vs Hashirama intro for the story; it crashes somewhere inbetween Madara + Susanoo covered Kurama vs Hashirama + Wood Golem and Hashirama's usage of Sage Art: True Thousand Hands against Madara. So for story mode, I wasn't able to get any progress saved and thus I would have to keep starting at the absolute beginning each time only to get to the same points in the story mode; this frustrates me very much. I've also noticed that some of the graphics were flickering as if the game were poorly optimized for the PC. While it happened to me(or I noticed it) only once, I don't particularly enjoy it. With all of these negative reviews floating around, I'm on high alert to notice anything out of the ordinary. So as of now, I'm only able to play in free-battles or anything along those lines; my progression in the game has been slowed severely because of the constant crashing. It is not acceptable.
The Decent -
Those are really my only bad experiences; I did experience low FPS during one of the opening cutscenes(I could clearly tell because of the images being really choppy and slow) but I made sure to have nVidia play the game at maximum performance, reboot it(I'm honestly sure you could just reboot and it will fix the low FPS issue. Although I am dissapointed that the game is only playing around 30FPS but every other Storm game played at it, and this particular game has some good animated effects. The game's fighting pace seems to be at a similar rate compared to the others; the game is beautiful graphically, etc. It has a good bit of the magic the other Storm games have. I've even noticed that the game has very short load times. I've also had decent sound, I haven't ran into any of the stated sound problems or they were just so weak that I couldn't tell the difference. Pre-ordering the game did pay off for me as I did get to have some short-lived fun with Boruto and Sarada, so basically I did get some enjoyment from the game. This game clearly has potential to be something.
The Verdict -
Well, I wish we had more of a scale-based rating instead of a yes or no, because I would've given this game around a 4-6  rating because some of the game was functional albeit for short periods of time, but because of this and the many small optimization issues I will have to say I will not recommend this game right now. Yes I'm aware of a patch or two that could help the game, but for one I don't totally trust them. I also believe that this game should've been optimized before release like this. I shouldn't have to apply a 3rd party patch from someone who didn't have a hand in any part of the production of the game. I shouldn't have to waste my time googling how I can make the game run without fps issues or how to avoid crashing; this should've been given to us as a solid game from the start. I love the Naruto series and I do believe the Storm games are one of the best 3D fighting games out there, so I'm not bashing the game because of any hatred. This game still has time to be saved if the right people would listen and act. I'd also like it if there was someone to report our problems to.
P.S.

I owned the original DX:HR and loved it, and every change made by this version only improves it. Odds are you already know the original was great and that DX:HR was pretty damn good as well. When I bought it they offered discounts for people who already owned Human Revolution, and I assume they still do that now. That's a business practice I'd like to see more companies emulate.
If you liked Human Revolution, this is a refinement. If you liked the original Deus Ex, this brings HR more in line with the feel of the first game.
My only real quibble is that violence is technically discouraged, but being a free-roaming game you're obviously allowed to make your own decisions in that regard. Don't buy it if you're looking for a simple, straight-up shooter, but pretty much everyone else will find something to love.

I bought the Director's Cut for $4.99 through the loyalty discount Steam had for owning the original Human Revolution and its DLC.  It took around 46 hours to beat, which is a little faster than my combined 49 hours in HR and The Missing Link.
If you're familiar with HR, the big question you're wondering is probably "is the DC worth it?"  I'd say it is, but it's not without its hitches.  There's also the fact that you can't buy the old HR at all on Steam, though it's still sold through other retailers like Amazon or Green Man Gaming and so on.  If you've never played the original Human Revolution, CTRL+F "for those new" since I can give a review of the base game here as well.
The boss fights were noticeably improved as far as catering to people building Jensen as a stealthy hacker.  Excepting the final boss, the three other fights had additional rooms added where you can access a security system to turn turrets against your enemy or activate other defenses.  You can win these fights without firing a single shot now, but you need specific augs to do it all.
There's a New Game Plus feature, but you obviously have to finish the game to be able to use it.  And you can't use your old HR saves, which I whined about a little, but I still went through the whole DC anyway.  You don't get to keep your weapons from your last game, but you can keep your augs at least.
The DC incorporates The Missing Link where it falls in the story, when you leave Hengsha for the second time.  You're still subjected to having your augs reset and weapons taken away, and while you get everything back once you clear that part of the game, some people might find it annoying to start from square one so near the end of the entire package.  The preorder DLC for HR is here too, though it's a lot more subtle in integration.
The AUD “grenades” are a godsend for the new boss battles, even if you're a master hacker.
I'd suggest not listening to the commentary your first time through since it spoils some of the story, but it also really disrupts the flow of the game.  There's no visible marker of where you're to stand to activate the commentary, but you get a little Infolink icon and a prompt to start if you're in the right place.  They seem to stop if you move away from the area enough or get an in-game Infolink transmission, so you unfortunately are gonna have to stand around a bit if you want to listen to everything.
And there's
of it.
As for the hitches, I found the game ran a bit worse than the original HR at times for no real reason, mostly things like frames suddenly dropping or things getting stuttery.  The audio also got extremely quiet at times like there was commentary playing, except I had that feature disabled.  And there were apparently a lot of bugs added back into the game for the DC, but I only really ran into one other than above and it was minor.  Some people have had worse issues, so it's a “your mileage may vary” situation.
But yeah, in summary, if you liked HR and want an excuse to go through it again, you can generally get it for $4 when it's on sale which is ridiculous for what you get.  The additions are nice, but you're buying something you own already for just a few changes and DLC integration.  If you've never played HR, $4 is a damned good price for what you get.
----
And for those new to the game, Human Revolution is a first- and third-person stealth-based shooter-RPG.  Despite that description, you're given a pretty wide range of methods to deal with whatever situations you find yourself in.  Such as, you're hiding in a room full of armed mooks and boxes.  You could just pop up and start firing, or you could watch your radar for their patrol patterns and systematically knock out each person and hide their bodies, or you could just turn invisible and skip fighting everyone by ducking into an air vent.  There's no right way to play, but some ways are easier than others.
The story starts with an attack on Sarif Industries which results in the death of a scientist team as well as nearly killing Adam Jensen, the protagonist.  The game cuts to six months later and Jensen, now an augmented human, is called out of sick leave to deal with the thugs who have taken over a Sarif manufacturing plant.  He runs into a hacker who promptly kills himself and then Jensen has to get into the Detroit Police's morgue to retrieve the hacker's cranial datavault, and things progress from there.  Will you try to sweet-talk the desk sergeant and get unrestricted access to the police department...or just sneak in and risk being shot by the police?
You're given a lot of freedom to build Jensen in the way that suits your playstyle best.  Doing quests and dispatching enemies gives EXP which leads to Praxis points, or you can find/buy Praxis Kits in the world, and with those you're able to activate/upgrade your augmentations.  You start with a small selection which gives great room to grow.  Will you bolster your hacking aug to cut through security with ease?  Maybe invest in the jumping aug and the Icarus Landing System to safely explore areas?  Arm stabilizers to improve gun accuracy even while moving?  Or maybe you'll max out your battery and cloak to just sneak through areas.
Even though the game is largely played in first-person perspective, you can take cover and sidle along walls which shift you into third-person view.  You can then blindfire while in cover, peek out for better accuracy, or just stick to a corner to be able to see around it.  It's very hard to play this like a typical first-person shooter since Jensen is so fragile and loud guns will draw more enemies to shoot at you.  You do naturally heal and can reduce damage with augments, but you still can't stand in the open and expect great results.  Not easy, but still doable.  My first time through HR I went the loud lethal Rambo route, and I went through the DC as a stealthy non-lethal hacker.  The experiences were quite different.
You'd probably like DEHR for its near-future cyberpunk story full of conspiracy, or if you want a game with a variety of ways to dispatch enemies and handle situations, or maybe if you really like customizing a playable character in a variety of skills, or maybe you just want to explore the world and hack into computers to read everyone's emails.  You might not like it as much if you're going to play it like a typical FPS, but it works for a cover-based shooter.  It's still a bit of an RPG, so if checking a skills screen to manually increase skills and having to remember that you can now turn invisible or see through walls is a challenge, things might be a little difficult for you.  Even then, if you like the idea of a stealthy game, I'd suggest this.  It wasn't my first stealth game, but it was the first one I really got into and enjoyed.

Ikaruga is an absolute gem. It's one of the best (and hardest) shoot'em up games i've ever played.
Ikaruga consists of 5 levels which some of them are insanely hard (I'm not joking) and if you want to upload you highscores to the leaderboards of save your replay, you have to beat the whole game with 3 lives and 0 continues. But if you want, you can enable continues from the options menu to make it easier.
In addition to the usual mechanics in shoot'em up games, this game features ((Polarity)) mechanic. Your ship has two forms/colors (blue and red) and by switching between them, you can avoid being hit by the projectiles that have the same color and absorb them to unleash a powerful attack (blue form/color absorbs blue projectiles and red form/color absorbs red projectiles).
By killing 3 enemies of the same color in a row, you get one ((Chain)) bonus that resets if you kill enemies without using the said pattern. Earning chains is very important if you want to get high scores and grades (and also achievements) at the end of each level; but it can also become very hard in final levels.

The game does have some gimicks which can be quite fun to mess around with, such as the X-ray vision, which allows you to see diffrent internal layers of the gun you've chosen, there is also a slow-mo mode as well.

Rabi-ribi is a mixed bag. Combat: okay, bosses: good: story: bad.
I bought this game in the sale of 2016 for anime style games and I don't think even then that it was partiularly cheap. I went on a hunch - buyer beware. I found it wasn't for me, however let me say on the positive side that, for an indy game, it's got a good amount of polish and doesn't feel cheap, nor did I run into any major bugs.
It's a 2D Metroidvania game about a bunny girl. Was she a bunny before the start of the adventure? I think so. Does the dialogue encourage you to care? It certainly does not - in fact the story, the characters and the dialogue is the thing that really brings this game down for me. I found myself skipping dialogue boxes frequently - and I almost never do that. I like a good story!
Let's skip that part for a moment and discuss the game itself. You jump around, you hit things and you explore. Like a Metroidvania, you have options about where you go and in which order you tackle bosses. There are hidden items around and lots of places to explore. As you fight your abilities will upgrade and you will gain more powerful attacks and other upgrades. There are a variety of enemies to kill and the bosses, well, I'll talk about those shortly.
So the general part of the game, not including the bosses or the story, was alright. Decent. Maybe even pretty good at times. An okay version of ideas and concepts done better in other places. The combat is reasonably interesting and the upgrades keep you going. What upgrade is next?
The bosses are the game's high point. I had fun with those, and found myself wishing more of the game was like that. They mix a bullet hell style to jazz things up and it works well.
Someone put a lot of effort into this game, but not all of it paid off. Whoever wrote the story wants to watch less bottom of the barrel anime shows and learn how to condense 25 lines of exposition into five. And 'oh, that person looked troubled when they have to leave quickly. Doesn't that make you interested in why they left?' only works if the character is remotely interesting, and even then I wouldn't use it as your staple. It's average, bordering on good at times. A good game is in there somewhere, trying to get to the surface, but its pacing keeps getting destroyed by the 'story'.

As a veteran player, a long time Mechwarrior fan, one of the first 600 players to sign up in 2011, and a closed beta tester I will say that this game is a disappointment.
The in-game new user experience is still dire after 3 years of the game being active. As of this year a new tutorial system has finally been implemented which helps players with movement, shooting, and controls but there still no in-game tutorial on how to navigate the MechLab (where you spend a good deal of time and build/customize 'Mechs). You're at the whims of the community on this one and will need to spend time reading guides and researching player suggested builds, which may be outdated or include biases. Since the MechLab is where you spend money (in-game and real), there's a good chance as a new player that you may spend money on the wrong thing and waste your time and money.
The overall gameplay once you get past the customization is shallow. In closed beta it was quickly found that the most optimal strategy was to ball up as a team and have everyone target one enemy 'Mech at a time as this would kill them quicker. This creates a snowball where once one team suffers one or two losses it's very hard to bounce back. This is the extent of strategy and tactics years later. It becomes quite repetitive.
Even though there are several game modes they all just devolve into team deathmatch, and some people even get real mad if you decide to play to the game mode objectives instead of just fighting.
Community Warfare, which sounds like it would be the main draw to the game, is just an afterthought. It's a bland Attack/Defend gamemode that, like the other modes, devolves into a deathmatch. Objectives are usually ignored. It has such a low population that it's tough to find matches at certain hours, and the matchmaking system has pretty much been stripped out and geared towards 'hardcore' players, which means if you decide to play some matches you'll be going up against veterans with years of experience and hundreds if not thousands of dollars worth of kit.
Visually the game used to look better. There was better damage modeling, the animation was better, and much of that deteriorated or was actively removed from the game in patches for some unknown reason. Some of it I'm sure was for performance reasons, but some of the changes over the years were baffling.
Overall, it's a disappointing game when you compare it to what it used to be and what it could have been.  I wouldn't recommend it to anyone, especially with so many other great games on Steam.

Ladies & Gentlemen, boys & girls.
- This here isn't your average run of the mill game, and the amount of hatred & white-knighting is immense, when it comes to this game.
- Where does the great divide stem from?
- The Former Publisher IGP's calls of pushing PGI around. Right after IGP left the scene and PGI took over as a Publisher... everything changed.
- Within 6 months, Community Warfare Beta Phase 1 was released. By now, in around two years PGI has took the 'nigh toxic community by the horns. Cleared the air, voiced concerns & opinions. This sounds more like a company that loves its community, instead of whines for more money, like it originally was.
- Was I about to abandon ship when IGP was around? I seriously was. I would be raging here with the negative feedbacks along with the rest of 'em.
After PGI bought the publishing rights from IGP, everything changed:
PGI is fixing the game, a milestone at a time, and thus far... it has delivered. +100 mechs & variants, and they all feel different.
- This alone, is quite a feat to accomplish. The core of the game is 'nigh rock-solid. Extra content is on its way for 2016 to bring first vehicles for the game as well.
***
Everything in the game can be bought with in-game money, including basic colors.
- Events are held where you can get free Mech Bays.
- Anything that you can buy with money, won't give you an advantage.
- Grinding is a lot smaller in part in comparison to most f2p games, though getting C-Bills(in game currency) fast is mostly up to your pilot talent.
- What is in major part is the simulation, and finding the right role for your talents.
Best community in TS Servers I've thus far met. Also, the most mature & the most aged in general.
- This isn't for those energy drink whopping, twitch shooter friends who crave for their next fix.
This is for us, who require a blend of wisdom/tactical thinking, and strategy, while commandeering a role that will either make the team, or break the team.
- Teamplay is the key word, so think wisely... This game is unlike any other simulator out there. Keep a cool hat and see only after 25 matches how things go. 5-10 rounds won't get you nowhere(you just might thank me later).
There's also a lot of great youtube videos out there to help you get acquinted with various roles, weight classes & "How To Build Your Mech" kind of schematics.
And one more thing:
||| Use the Search, this is your IMDB of Mechs & Battletech history, including weaponry & what they are primarily used for.

Let's see $600+ and around 700 hours spent on this game since closed beta (before steam release). Was it worth it? No, but I'm in too deep to quit now. That's essentially what PGI is counting on when they drag you into this game, abusing your love of Battletech and MechWarrior for a bare minimum product on a bad engine, and milking you dry. Actual improvements to the core game progress at a snails pace while new mech packs and paid content always seem to be at the top of the to do list. This is probably the worst free to play game to be released by a non Asian developer.
Will it improve?
Check back in the year 3050 to find out.

This game is pretty good for the most part. The freedom in this game is substantial and the content is great only when you add 'Add-Ons' which are this game's equivalent of mods. The community is great... somewhat - only when you find the right people since there are a lot of toxic people in this game. Often you'll find people comparing IDs, stating that lower IDs are generally better at the game, which is true: they've usually had the game longer. My Steam will say I've had about 400~ hours in this game, but over the 10 years I've had this game the realistic number would be much, much higher. Beware though, this was dependent on finding people I could relate to and become friends with. Two people that I met on Blockland, maybe about 8~9 years ago, I still am in contact with to this day. This game may have been with me throughout most of my life, but that doesn't mean you'll enjoy it too. Often there aren't many servers at all (probably about 30), and a lot of them are either empty or completely lacking. If you're thinking about buying this game, please know that this game has a smaller population than a while ago, however this does not mean it is dying. A lot of the people in this game are dedicated, as am I, considering I have been coming back to this game for the past 10 years.
The building in this game is obviously the largest selling point, building with virtual LEGO was this game's base, but since the start it has been evolving and has somewhat turned into a LEGO version of Garry's Mod, however obviously not as popular but can be equally as fun. The development of this game has come to a halt pretty much, since the developer (in the game known as Badspot) has stopped updating it and has just been keeping up the master server to allow for people to still host servers. Please know that in the future should his master server shut down, I would not be surprised if a member of the community set up their own master server considering that has already been done to allow people to play older versions of this game, which brings me to the 'Shaders Update' or 'v21'.
The shaders update was an update in around 2012 (don't quote me on that) where maps and interiors were removed (classics like The Bedroom) and were instead replaced with blank slates with customisable environments and floor textures. In my opinion, this update was fine. A lot of people initially couldn't run it because of their potato PCs (as Blockland wasn't intense) so it was met with mixed reviews. As well as that, the nostalgic value of maps like Kitchen and Slopes was completely gone, and therefore a lot of older users left the game because they weren't able to access this kind of content anymore. Even though I have been playing this game for quite some time, the shaders update didn't bother me. Yes, there was a nostalgic factor in those maps, but in my opinion they were ugly and I have always had a soft spot for maps built out of actual bricks instead of ugly stretched textures (this is of course just my opinion).
Overall, this game is extremely good and extremely broad in what you can do with it, however the time of day that you go on and who you meet will be complete factors in how much you enjoy this. If you do purchase this be wary, but know that the time I have spent on this game have been some of the best hours/days/months of my life.

People take advantage of what a F2P game should be, judging it unfairly for the amount of time and effort spent on creating this F2P version of Left 4 Dead.
Sure, the game is a less stylized version of Left 4 Dead, but it's ♥♥♥♥ing free, so why should that matter? The game itself is a blast to spend your free time on, and the variety of gamemodes gives you more ways to enjoy what the game has to offer. My only complaints with the game are:
- Some achievements being unobtainable until the developer adds that feature into the game [Seriously, why create the achievement to begin with if it's not even physically possible to obtain it at the moment? It's not like you can't add achievements to it in a future update, since TF2 has been able to do so, but I digress.]
- If you're a certain level in one server, unless it's on the same network or owned by the same person from that server, your level doesn't follow you. Meaning, say you're lv. 40 on a Deathmatch server, and decide to join another server. Unless they're both owned by the same people/ person, you'll be back at lv.1 on that new server [but you'll still have your progress saved on the previous server, so nothing that impactful.]
- Servers are sometimes empty or completely full, but that's mainly due to the lack of popularity the game atm has, only a few dozen~ish or so online daily, last I check.
Despite all its' glaring flaws, for the most part, if you want a F2P version of Left4Dead~style experience, and don't mind the unusual update plans, I would easily recommend you try the game out.

I just want to start by saying, this review is not meant to focus more on the cons than the pros or vice versa.
I try not to be bias when writing reviews, and try to get the most accurate information I can.
I've had this controller for a few months now, and right at first when I opened the box, I was both excited and worried. I had read quite a few reviews that had hardly anything good to say about the controller, and of course there are an abundant amount of reviews for both sides, but quickly after using the controller I had come to realize two things: You will not truly understand the versatility, and usefulness of this controller, until you use it.; and you will either love it, or you will hate it.
When I put the controller in my hands for the first time, I found it comfortable, but also different. You may have noticed the fact that it only has one analog, and it may throw you off from time to time, especially if you are used to the traditional controllers that we see for modern consoles. But don't worry, while there are times where It would be nice to have a second analog, the lack there of is made up with the two touch pads. It's very easy to set the functions for every button, including the touch pads which also conveniently enough are also D-Pad-like buttons! All of which you can customize easily, making it an enjoyable experience when trying to think of a place for certain functions that you'd like on your controller, but don't have room for, and with the triggers now being able to do one thing while it's being held down just before the *click* and then do something else if it's pressed all the way, it just adds more versatility and fun.
The steam controller is not perfect, and while it may not be able to totally replace the mouse and keyboard all together, it still offers the functionality so if you want to use the controller without being right in front of your computer, you can at least cut down the amount you'll have to get up or reposition to use said keyboard & mouse. It gives a neat keyboard that is a little awkward to use right at first, but with the ability to use both touch pads to select letters simultaneously you could potentially become a fast enough to make some people question if you're using a controller or a keyboard.
Big Picture is annoying to have to use sometimes, especially when it is the only way to get to the configuration screen for the Steam Controller. Hopefully this is something they will change in the future but as of right now, we just have to deal with it.
I can't point out every single good and bad thing about this controller, and it's constantly being updated but these were just a few key points I felt worth mentioning. You can customize this controller to function completely different from one profile to another, and if you ask me, I feel as though this controller is completely worth purchasing.

Played it back then on the GameCube, but the truth of the matter is: you can't ever have enough copies of Ikaruga, so adding it to my Steam library some time was inevitable.
Ikaruga is the very definition of a "bullet hell" arcade shooter, with the twist of the player being able to reverse the polarity of the ship at any time to enable it to either absorb light or dark bullets in order to fill a power bar that allows to unleash a devastating attack on the rather well-fortified enemies.
Sounds like a walk in the park then? Nah, not at all. There may be even more crazy shmups than this (and all of them seem to come from asia ... I see a pattern here), but if you have nerves of steel, want to gain nerves of steel or just have masochistic tendencies in general (it has a 2 player mode, so a sorrow shared is a sorrow halved I guess), Ikaruga is a must have. Also, on a side note, the Level 1 music is so incredibly catchy that I still remembered it over all the years.
The PC port is smooth sailing, graphics are okay and aged well, music is good to superb, bullets are reasonably deadly, pacing is lightning fast. Not a game for everyone of course, but a classic when it comes to this genre.

DEEP SPACE WAIFU is an outstanding addition to the adult game genre. Sure, there isn't a ton of content, but what is there is very high quality and certainly worth more than the small asking price. The most important aspect of adult-themed games is that the game is fun, and it is not just a collection of smutty artwork. Well, DEEP SPACE WAIFU is fun.
Essentially, this is an arena shooter where the goal is to shoot all the clothes off the girl in the background. Is this the most solid shooter out there? Not by a long shot, but it definitely checks enough of the right boxes to keep me entertained for a couple of hours. It plays really well with either a controller or a mouse. There is a very good selection of options and difficulty and challenges. One minor flaw I found is that sometimes the bullets are hard to see due to blending into the background. Oh well, who cares.
I think the best aspect of this game is that the whole thing has charm. There is a ton of little details that I'm quite impressed with. Things like the animations on the loading screen, and the 'intimacy warning' before the boss battle, and that pixel art city it shows. That's some really nice artwork. Plus lets not forget that the devs have added content since release, and are planning DLC, which I will most assuredly pick up day one.
Pros:
+The patch couldn't have been easier to implement; you don't even need to download anything
+The game mechanic idea is fresh
+The artwork is great and the girls look fantastic
+Definitely a fun shooter which is super important with an adult-themed game
+Nice game to 100% the achievements
+Price is too cheap; this could have been ten bucks and I'd be fine with it
Cons:
-Bullets can blend into the background; along that same thought - the bullet patterns could use a bit of work, but this is nothing deal-breaking
-It is short, but hey, the price point reflects that
A must buy if you like adult-themed games.

As a Metroidvania fan, I do like this. The most you get out of it is character renders and the cutscene stills. Everything else is colorful, innocent fun. Haven't beaten the game yet myself, but the game is pretty plentiful in content if you like long Metroidvanias or general action platformers. It sports plenty of collectibles, great abilities that help in exploration, and challnging boss fights that always change up their attack patterns, which makes them more challenging to beat since you can't predict what they do next.I recommend to any Metroidvania fans.
Also, I don't usually recommend DLC, but if you end up enjoying this game, I also would like to recommend the artbook. Yes, it has beta and concept artwork, as well as editable character stills, which is all okay, but it also features beta/unreleased game content. Playable characters, unused/scrapped bosses, as well as two new modes of play for the base game: impossible and unknown. Impossible is pretty much what it is on the cover, with enemies doing heaps more damage than usual. I'm not sure how it effects stat growth, as I only played about 3 minutes to see what it was all about, but I imagine that you don't get much in that regard. Dead Rising 3 is a open world survival horror beat 'em up video game. It is developed by Capcom Vancouver and published by Microsoft Studios.
Graphics- The graphics are very good in this game but can be turned down so a decent computer should be able to run it. The graphics have also aged very well which is not the case for most games.
Controls- I have only played on controller and the controls are very basic and easy to learn. I looked up the controls for the keyboard and mouse and they also seem to be very simple and easy to pick up
Combat- the combat has not been changed at all from the other games in the series but don't fix what isn't broke. The combat has always been really good with Dead Rising and that is still the case for Dead Rising 3
Story- If I am being honest the story for this game is decent but when you compare it to the other games in the series it is terrible. You do not care about any of the characters and the events that happen to them. I struggled to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥throughout the whole game and only completed the story for the blueprint!
Weapons- The weapons in this game are awesome! I personally love the super crazy unrealistic combo weps and do not mind them! I love the destruction you can cause and the creativity behind the blueprints. I also love the new combo vehicles. These are once again so creative and destructive and kept me entertained even through the sleeping pill this game calls a story
Psychopaths- the psychopaths in this game are terrible. I like the idea of them being based on the seven deadly sins but the characters themselves are terrible and boring. They are just not interesting at all. Plus seven psychopaths is not enough in my opinion. There are other psychopaths in the story but like I said before the story is♥♥♥♥♥♥
Survivors and side quests- I hate how survivors work in this game. You clear zombies around them and then they run away. Done, collect your xp and go home for some toast and jam (or in my case toast and butter because I hate jam). Some special survivors get their own side quest which is revealed by the classic phone call.  These quest usually amount to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fetch quest. It is obvious that no effort was put into these missions. Some survivors will follow you but most will not. The survivors do not need to be escorted to a safe zone anymore. The survivors now work as companions and can be assigned to figh alongside you. Why anybody would use them or want them I have no clue!
Difficulty- This is one of the main problems with the game. It is just plain too easy! You can kill bosses with the amazingly overpowered weapons within seconds! I do love being powerful and playing an easy game but this is just too much. I was nearly never scared of dying due to the difficulty.
Overall, there are lots of problems with this game and it is not one too take seriously but at the end of the day it is pretty fun and I do love the series so there is some bias here. I have to give it a 5.8/10

The good:
-free!
-fun team gameplay modes
-fast team-matching. Usually in under a minute you're on the battlefield (EU servers) and you can find matches even at 6 in the morning
-you build your weapons yourself from a large collection of gun parts, so you can create weapons that fit your game style (e.g. one-shot sniper weapons with slow fire rate, or a gatling gun that rapidly sets your enemies on fire, or a rocket launcher whose rockets "crawl" along the ground, or a mine thrower to set up traps for the enemy...)
-funny over-the top violent graphics (especially the death animations), and pretty explicit taunts (fat women with half of their face off taunting your by twerking, naked guys who dangle their genitals, or a Rocky Balboa guy doing a pole dance, etc etc)
-you earn XP and in-game currency while playing, so you can unlock and buy more gun parts (e.g. healing ammo, bigger magazines, remote-controlled rockets) and equipment items (such as turrets, hand grenades, spawn points, deployable health packs) the longer you play. Mostly play-to-win (but only mostly, see below).
-It is just a hell lot of fun to play!
The bad:
-if you've been playing 1st person shooters, then this will be a bit confusing because it's 3rd person (kinda like Assassins Creed)
-if you've played serious arena shooters, you will at certain moments be annoyed by the graphics, because an overkill of effects often times makes careful aiming impossible. If one enemy uses fire ammo, and another player shoots a healing rocket in the same area, you will just have fire and green health goo all over your screen and won't see the actual players anymore.
-some completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ designer thought that it would be a good idea that players have to press the shift key to run (instead of having run be the default and pressing shift to walk slow and sneaky). This has the effect that the ENTIRE time you play the game, you have to hold down shift!!! (because you want to the running around *all* the time).
-Most items sold for money in the store are only cosmetic, plus you can buy a booster pack that increases the rate at which your earn XP and in-game currency. BUT there are some important exceptions: Your character can carry TWO GUNS AND ONE EQUIPMENT ITEM (jump boots/hand grenades/turret/...). Such a combination is called a "Loadout". Every time you respawn after dying, you can choose which loadout you want to use. After playing a while, you will have quite a number of different guns and equipment items - but free players can have only a limited number of guns, and more importantly ONLY 3 LOADOUTS (ie gun+equipment combinations). So if you do not buy additional loadout slots for real money, you are at a bit of a disadvantage, since you can't use the right gun and item combinations. For instance, if your enemy has a really good sniper and has secured the base with turrets, you will need yourself a good sniper weapon to have a chance to get close, plus maybe the disguise equipment item (so turrets won't recognize you as an enemy, allowing you to just run past unharmed). If you are a paid player, you will have the right combination (sniper, plus close-range weapon, plus disguise) in one of your loadouts. If you are a free player with only three possible combinations, chances are you won't... Having said that, skill, strategy and good teamplay (especially a good healer) are definitely more important factors for whether your team will win.
