Its a decent stompy robot game, but its got alot of problems.  the biggest is the low turnaround to fixing issues with the game.
Weapon balance has been outta whack for some time with some weapons being unusable for years.  There is generally only one major "balance pass" a year rather than iterative changes, so if the weapon is useless after the pass its probably gonna be that way for a year or more.  It dosent help things when it seems that half the balance is made with dice rolls.
The new mechlab came out 1.5 years ago and was total crap, it took them over a year to get it decently useful (at least better than the old one) and there are still features that the community wants put in, like a way to strip all the modules off all your mechs, that have been basically ignored.
There are issues with map and gamemode design.  For gamemodes, the problem is that theres only 3 modes, and most of the time theres no real difference between the 3 of them.  Map design has a tendency to funnel everyone to the same spots every game, due to a combo of defensive terrain in select areas and both teams starting spread out rather than togeather.  By the time you grouped with ur team you are under attack or about to be.  This makes most maps seem very small and cramped no matter how large they are because ur fighting in the same small defensive areas.
The time to kill (TTK) is very low as well.  There has been alot of power creep in this game to the point where a game which involves huge stompy mechs of doom that are supposed to dominate the battlefield instead plays more like COD with mechs hunkering down behind cover and popping out to fire and duck back in.  The TTK has been shinking for years  with no end or solution in sight.
There is a part of the game called "Community Warfare" (or CW) which allows you to pick one of 10 factions and fight each other for control of the galaxy.  In reality the population is too low and most of the time its the Innsershere vs the Clans which gets real old after awhile.  In addition the issues with map design and gamemodes are even worse in CW, to the point where its alot like playing a tower defence game (not even joking)
To top it all off while the game is free to play pretty much any ingame items are incredably overpriced, just look at the "Steam performace packs".  The grind is real so be prepared to either shell out alot of cash or time to get a decent mech.

As a quick introduction:  I'm a

of this game.  I have played lots of MechWarrior titles before it, and have supported the game since the very beginning.
The game has come a LONG WAYS since Closed Beta.  Back then we had 8 mechs (2 per class) and there was no such thing as "balance".  Since then we've had a lot more mechs added to the game, PGI has gotten rid of IGP (who was in a large part a source of a lot of the game's darkest moments), Factional Warfare Betas have started, and PGI has really started to get a concept of "balance" into the game.
Free Players - do not mistake "pay only" options as "pay-to-win".  Mech-wise, there are only a few hero variants (Misery/Stalker & Dragon Slayer/Victor, for example) that could be considered as the "best" for their chassis.  There are an equal number of absolutely horrible or average at best pay-only mechs available (such as The Boar's Head/Atlas).  MC only consumable modules are not generally worth money and the c-bill variants you can acquire will be more than effective enough for you in the game.  Even though there are pay-only mech variants in the game, they do not necessarily have special features that make them pay-to-win such as super armor or special guns.  Usually the only real "advantage" they will have are unique hardpoints for their chassis line and that they come pre-upgraded with weight saving features like Endo Steel or Ferro Fibrous.
This game is a FIRST PERSON Shooter but it is much slower and more tactical than a general shooter.  Target your enemy, search for weak points, evaluate your strategies and approaches - and don't be afraid of taking damage.  If you need any help, search for it in the community forums on the MWO website - we're there for you.
Pros:
- Great Art Design
- Good, solid gameplay mechanics
- Developers strive for balance with constant updates
- Free to Play
- Developers have become more transparent and open over the past two years
Cons:
- Currently limited selection of game modes, can get stale and leave you wanting more
- In-game models don't always look as good as the concept
- Developers primarily use Twitter to communicate as opposed to the forums and their main website

Soon I'm sure you'll see a flood of reviews, highlighting the best and worst MechWarrior and Pirrana Games has to offer. On one hand, you'll have people who have played this game for three years and have never had a problem with it. On the other, you'll have people who have felt burned, rightfully so, and still have residual resentment for it. I want to be a slightly more moderate voice, and try my best to review the game as I see it.
I want to start, by saying I find the game fun, and I've been playing it on and off for three years. It's a very niche game, even if it didn't have giant stompy robots which is a niche genre all itself, it's "a thinking man's shooter" which takes a more slow, methodical approach to First Person Shooters. Because of this, it offers a very unique experience which, if you like that sort of thing like I do, it's very hard to find another game that quite scratches the same itch.
The game is Free to Play in the same sort of way that Ketchup is a vegetable, it's technically accurate for some value of the term. For the most part, at it's best, the game is Pay2NotGrind and Pay4Vanity. At it's worst, however, you have things like the Stalker Hero "Misery," a $30 dollar reasonably solid 'meta' mech that is only available with cash money.
Which is actually the real bulk of the problem, the pricing for the game is very, very high for very little. You can take a look for yourself at the "DLC" on this page - each of those Performance Packs are for two mechs, which - minus a boost to the earnable in-game currency - are identical to their earnable with in-game currency counterparts. I'm sure you'll hear about the $500 gold mech packages they offered a year ago, ( technically, still are offering from a year ago ) but that really is a extreme, argueably not entirely PGIs fault since they were still under IGP at the time, and I'd like to believe everyone involved has learned their lession and will never do anything like it again ( although, like I said, the offer is still available. )  The more consistant reality of it is somewhere around $20-30 for a mech, which is still fairly high.
The good news is, for the most part, nearly all mechs become available with the earnable in-game currency some months after they're released to people who first "pre-ordered" the mechs in early access packs, and after they're released to people for cash money. ( Pay2NotWait? ) Usually this isn't a problem although sometimes the mechs are slightly to very OP and unbalance things, making the game unfun for anyone who didn't pre-order. The only real exception to this are "Hero" mechs which normally are slightly underpowered but gimmicky varriants of a mech, sometimes with ties into lore, but generally aren't the best version of any mech. Usually. There are exceptions.
A lot of the residual resentment I mentioned earlier stems from the previous tendency to remain close-lipped about the direction the game was going, to ignore any real community feedback, and a very slow development cycle. Most of these have been improved upon since PGI got out from under IGPs thumb - Development has severely picked up pace and new things besides mech packs have been added to the game fairly frequently. PGI is much more open about what they're doing / what direction they want to move the game into. Feedback from what I've seen is still somewhat spotty, although from my understanding they decided to not go through with "ghost damage," a mechanic that was nearly universally hated - where in the past they would have just gone through and added it anyway ( looking at you 3rd Person and Ghost Heat ) - so, I suppose that too is improving.
Overall, since I need to select Yes or No to "Do you recommend this game?" I have to say no.
I like the game, I find it fun, but that doens't make it a good game by default. Between shaking off the ghost of IGP past, elements from three years ago which still feel unfinished ( mostly looking at Community Warfare here, which while "still in beta" has been worked on since launch ) and a high cost of premium elements ... It's just not a good game for the everyman.
Added onto the fact that even if this game was perfect, it would still be kind of a niche game - and some people would just not be able to get into it - it makes those flaws even more hard to overlook when considering a binary "Yes or No" answer.
I would, however, suggest that if you think you might be able to get into it - to at least give it a try and find out. Don't spend any money on it until you're sure you like it, but if you do - like I said, it's a fairly unique experience and hard to find games quite like it.
Small, Edit :
Everything up until this point is aimed for potential new players, not members of the prexisting userbase. I don't need to explain what's good or bad with the game to you, you already know and have your own opinions, and that's fine, you're more then welcome to make your own review or tell me what you agree or disagree about mine - conversation is good.
But, this, and only this is specifically for the prexisting userbase - I understand you like this game, I understand being critical of things you enjoy can be hard, but be a little respectful, would you? If you're so concerned about one negative review turning people away then how do you think they're going to react when they read the comment section?

Pro's:
-One of, if not the, deepest customization systems ever developed in any franchise. Mechwarrior, and the BattleTech lore and material as a whole, is famous in no small part due to its incredible customization and variety in experiences and playstyles.
-Beautiful graphics and visual effects, especially on the larger weapons. it's extremely satisfying to see your enemy showered in giant clouds of sparks, smoke, and plasma when your shots hit home.
-Tactical, challenging, and addictive gameplay. A significant divergence from the standard shooter, this game champions teamwork and strategy over reflexes and individual skill.
-A passionate and approachable community of fans. This game shines brightest when it is played in groups, and joining a unit is as simple as checking the
forums and searching the hiring hall for a group to apply to. Many will take fresh players, too.
-Still in active development. The game will only get bigger.

A lot of people don't seem to know what this game is and I think it deserves a proper review, albeit a negative one. BrainBread 2 is basically a remake of BrainBread which was a Half-Life mod released sometime in 2004-2005, I actually played it back in the day and I had no idea BrainBread 2 even existed until now.
BrainBread 2 has not evolved from BrainBread 1 in terms of gameplay, you spawn in a base guarded by AI soldiers and you shoot zombies, back in 2005 this was somewhat impressive and fun but by 2016-17 standards its utter garbage. Just because the game is free doesn't mean it gets a free pass.
BrainBread 2 is clearly a game that is not to be taken seriously but the gameplay is just awful, there doesn't seem to be a point or objective of any kind and the the balancing is just plain horrible. The mapping is just terrible and very reminiscent of BrainBread ones mapping which was also pretty bad. The maps are very much like mazes that go on for miles and have lots of dead ends, it even has big maze like air vents just like BrainBread 1.
There are two enemy types in this game, zombies and bandits. The zombie and bandit AI is horrible and this is not down to the Source Engine since Source Engine AI can do better than this if created properly. The zombies randomly spawn in the street and never stop spawning, the AI isn't smart enough to overwhelm you so the devs made the zombies incredibly resistant to bullets...Good balancing guys. The bandits are just as bad, they're like endlessly spawning terminators who suck up bullets and 360 no scope you with shotguns. There is also a boss zombie who can randomly spawn, although he's nothing but a bullet sponge and you achieve nothing upon killing him.
I think the last thing worth mentioning is that you can get infected and become a zombie, that is if the horrendous zombie AI can actually hit you. When infected some white text appears in the center of the screen and a timer begins. When the timer is up you become a fast moving zombie who does very little damage and is overall pointless. When you're killed you'll either spawn back as a human or a zombie, I'm not sure why, I think its random.
Overall BrainBread 2 is a pointless and bad game, I played for only 20 minutes before uninstalling it and writing this review. Games like
released in 2007 and
released in 2011 have far surpassed BrainBread 2 in terms of gameplay, graphics and AI. If I was to say one good thing about BrainBread 2 it would be the reload animations, who ever did those did a really good job.
BrainBread 2 is a failure and may God have mercy on its soul.

Let me start by saying that this is not a typical style of game for me. I’ve played my share of RPGs over the years, but these days I tend to shy away from “old-school” turn-based games in favor of action RPGs and FPSs.
But Pixel Heroes is special. Seriously, I’ve played it for so many hours in just a couple weeks that I kind of wish the number wasn’t on display. The game’s off-the-wall humor and lighthearted tone balance the difficulty perfectly. And yes, it is surprisingly difficult.
Here’s a quick rundown of how the game works, for anyone who’s curious (don’t worry, no spoilers here). You start out in the Tavern, where you select 3 Heroes for your party. The assortment of Heroes available is random, with re-rolls possible (a nice touch if you aren’t happy with the selection), and each Hero has a hilarious randomly-generated biography that includes unique stat boosts (e.g. “He was conceived AND born in a chapel, +FAI”). There are 30 distinct Hero classes, many of which are unlocked through achievements. After recruiting your party, you find yourself in Town, where you can buy items and talk to NPCs. At any given time, 2 random NPCs will have quests for you, each of which will send you to a different dungeon. Accept one of the quests, gear up, and hit the road! On the way to the dungeon you will encounter 3 random events… I won’t spoil any of them, but they can be quite amusing. The dungeons themselves consist of 7 rooms (mostly battles, but sometimes treasure rooms) plus a boss.
As you’ve probably read, this game has a form of
if any member of your party dies, the rest of you have to survive the whole thing—plus the return trip—to revive him in town. If your whole party dies, they are laid to rest in the Graveyard and your game is over.
Usually, permadeath and other ‘hardcore’ RPG elements are a turn-off for me, but the way the game is designed, each play-through is totally fresh—you never feel like “F*** now I have to do all the same things again!” I find that there’s a fine line between a game being difficult and just feeling “cheap,” and I will say that Pixel Heroes stands firmly on the correct side of the line. I had 5 or 6 parties wipe out before even completing the first campaign, but each time it just showed me that I needed to improve some aspect of my party or my strategy.
On that point, the combat mechanics are dead simple, but deep at the same time: a perfect example of “easy to learn, hard to master.” There’s no tutorial, but the Help screen is always just a click away and gives you all the info you might need. It’s a very laissez-faire approach, like “here, have fun, figure it out!” which I find refreshing. Many games patronize their players, and this is not one of them.
As others have pointed out, item management is a significant part of the game. It doesn’t break the experience, though; quite the opposite. Initially, it can be a bit of a drag to spend time on the inventory screen figuring out what items are best for your needs, but the depth of the game truly shines after you start to see how you can trade off between all the possible item properties to leverage your Heroes’ abilities and take on each dungeon’s unique challenges. After a few dungeons it gets to be second nature. And when you gear up your party flawlessly and wreck a dungeon like it’s your job, the feeling of satisfaction is amazing.
I’m going to wrap this up with a quick shout-out to the hilarious writing, as well as the randomized item names, which I’m pretty sure is a tongue-in-cheek homage to Diablo 2. At any moment, you might find a “Fly Hat of Fire” or a “Tenderizing Broadsword of Greed,” or even a “Mighty Shaft of Love.” Little touches like this keep the game entertaining well after you’ve powered through the first two campaigns.
And to top it all off, the devs released new content and bug fixes just 1 week after the game’s release. It’s clear that they really care about their players, and about creating an awesome gaming experience, which is why I sat down to write this lengthy review. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have to go help a washed-up Fire Mage retrieve his “special tobacco.”

I'm not fan of pixel games, nor of nerd humor, and I tend avoid games with a gameplay based on 2D horizontal scrolling. But that game surprised me. It's a great light and fast paced Rogue-lite. It merges very well simplicity with a relative depth.
The combats are surprisingly good with some simplicity but also some depth and a fair range of tactical possibilities. The combat system seems quite close to games as Wizardry or Lords of Xulima, but it has a surprising freshness coming from few key design choices.
You start at the tavern by making a party of 3 heroes that you choose among a random subset of predefined characters.  There's no real exploration and the character building is simple. But the gameplay is focused on drops, managing inventory and equipments, combats, discover gradually the specificities of each dungeon to manage them better at next party.
Another layout is through the writing, it is also light, and it is focused on nerd humor, references and winks to old computer games. But it's also a great writing, just good humor everywhere, and it fits very well the gameplay and never feel out of topic nor displaced, it's just fun.
There's also a good effort on external details, like a nice graveyard of all previous parties dead or that won, plenty cool achievements you can check inside the game, plenty stories NPC to progress, many new heroes characters to unlock. It's just cool stuff.
So overall even if few points could be even better, it's a great light fast Rogue-lite with a nice depth and plenty good humor, it's a game surprisingly fun and interesting.

It is a fun game, the combat is very solid with challenging bosses. I will say that 2D platformer bullet hells are some of the most infuriating games seeing as gravity really wants to work against you. The challenge of the bosses can range from easy to utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, some projectiles and abilities literally cover most of the screen if it wasn't for the small hitbox I'd say it is impossible to dodge them.
I hopped into this game playing on hard because why not have a challenge. I started out just kinda running around figuring out where to go, seeing as I'm not the type to read tutorials or look at maps for details it became very fun. You quickly find a lot of off limits areas and places much too high level for you. Within the world I've found a few small areas that you can farm for cash to be able to outright buy a few upgrades if you struggle so really difficulty doesn't mean as much as you'd think unless you are going for a speedrun.
When I'd found my first boss I quickly realised that they hurt, you don't have much life to get by with and getting hit a few times means you're out. It's fun dodging about and charging magic to shoot off while edging closer to smack them in the fact. With the magic you can get a few types; such as the default blue which the charge shot is just a straight shot that deals decent damage, green which the charge send out 4 homing shots that actually heal for every 2 that hit, or even yellow which while charging deals fast but low damage in a line and the charged shot is a heavy damage shotgun. You basically have a magic or upgrade for every job you'd need
What do I think? It's a great game, if you're a fan of metroidvanias I'd suggest to buy it right away. The price isn't that high and for the quality of the game you'd expect to pay a hell of a lot more. It's a solid 9/10 game it does so much right and I really can't fault it on anything except the occasional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ability of a boss, when you get unlucky and the AI decides that it wants to spam the strongest ability because it has had enough of you winning. The characters are also enjoyable especially Ribbon the fairy and a lot of the boss/side characters.
TL;DR
-You like metroidvanias? Buy this
It is inexpensive and a quality game I'd go as far to say it would be one of my top picks.

Hmm. I'm quite torn should I give this game a thumbs up or thumbs down.
Well, let's start with categorizing the game: It's a mix of Metroidvania and Bullet Hell during bosses.
The first complaint: A good Metroidvania gives you the illusion of freedom, while actually pushing you into one direction for your next upgrade which will then unlock the next area and so on. A good Metroidvania will flow beautifully from one area to the next.
Rabi-Ribi fails at this COMPLETELY. The game is mostly open... except when it goes "NO SAMUS, you're not AUTHORIZED to use the Varia Suit in this hot area!"
Because yes, that happens on numerous occasions in this game. Instead of limiting your path with obstacles which you can't clear with your current gear, the game just goes "We can't go there!"
These are reduced a lot after Chapter 1, but a couple of such places remain even afterwards. I find this baffling. If you want to keep an area off-limits due to plot reasons, why not just put a clearly fake wall there instead? And when it is plot time, a simple cutscene can open it up. That's a lot less frustrating than walking in an empty corridor only to have the game go "Ha ha, NO! Go elsewhere!"
Anyway. The game world is also very vast, which brings forth a major issue: You can easily - and I mean EASILY - get really, REALLY frustrated at how you can't go into places or get items because of your lack of upgrades. And you have NO idea where these upgrades are. So you just keep running and running and running and you see small holes you just can't fit into over and over and clearly you're SUPPOSED to have that item by now but you don't but you still don't run out of places to explore and you keep going and going and graAAAHHHH!!
Seriously, it is really, really annoying. A good Metroidvania would "lock" you into an area until you find the upgrade you need to proceed. This game, past Chapter 1, doesn't do that. You can just keep exploring and exploring and exploring and never find what you're looking for. Hmm, actually, that endless exploration doesn't sound like a bad thing, but trust me. It is.
This is further made worse by the near-USELESS map. A good Metroidvania, when you run into something you can't access yet, will mark it on your map. Either with an icon or with a clear lack of a wall on your map. This game? You come into a room from below. You can clearly see that there's an exit to the left, but you can't clear the obstacle. Okay, fair enough. There's clearly a path upwards, but you can't reach that. Okay, fair enough. Proceed to the right. What does the map say about the previous room? NOTHING. It's JUST A SQUARE, with no indication that the room connects to left and up as well. Later, when you get a jumping upgrade for example, you go "hmm, where was that room again..." and YOU CAN'T FIND IT. Since the map DOESN'T FREAKING TELL YOU.
So yeah, the Metroidvania portion of the game is largely made out of fail. What about Bullet Hells then?
Well, the game doesn't tell you where your hitbox is. Obviously, over a long course of time, you'll get a grasp of where it is, but... WHY NOT JUST TELL THE PLAYER?! Also, the precision movement button is the same as your attack button, which has a couple of frames of attack swing animation... why not allow this to be bound to a key with no other function? And why does this precision movement not apply when you're jumping? Because you WILL need to jump a lot, this isn't a game where you have 8 directional movement available.
There is a ton of bosses and they are highly varied and unique, each with a TON of different attack patterns. That part is certainly well made.
The bosses past the first few are pretty darn difficult though, so unless you're good at Bullet Hells, you don't really have any business outside of Casual difficulty. Speaking of difficulties, the game offers Casual, Normal, Hard, Hell and Bunny Extinction. If you're the type of player who likes to challenge themselves and feels good about finally beating a boss after hours of banging your head on it, well, Rabi-Ribi certainly has you covered. I'm not part of that crowd at all though, so the bosses are just frustrating for me. Thank god for CheatEngine.
Honourable design mention about difficulty though... if you die to a boss three times, the game asks if you'd like help. If you say yes, you'll get Halo Boost, granting you -25% damage taken, faster "invulnerability" bomb regen and HP leech. Combined with your pattern experience from those failed attempts, you'll probably beat the boss with ease. The biggest problem is this buff only lasts for a couple of minutes. You'll probably end up with it expiring around 25% boss health, with you at full health (thanks to life leech)... just in time for the boss to unleash their final patterns. Obviously, that tends to be the hardest point of the fight, but at full health you might be fine. And if you're not fine? Attempts 6 and 7 will give you Halo Boost level 2 and 8+ will give you level 3. Level 3 lasts for a VERY LONG TIME and gives MASSIVE buffs, so you shouldn't have any issues with any boss in the game. I give big props to the devs for including a mechanic like this in the game - it stops players from getting stuck at a boss and let's them progress even if they're bad. Oh, and Halo Boost is not available on Hard or above so don't expect to get carried through on any difficulty.
So... after all that complaining, why am I giving the game a thumbs up? I'm... not sure. But, I do enjoy playing the game a lot (even if I need to load up CheatEngine and find the Health value every single time, I can't be arsed to die to a boss several times for clearing them). There is a couple of good things I should mention:
Once you've cleared the game and know where the items are, the Metroidvania fail aspect is greatly diminished. Even further if you've stumbled across the "secret techniques" in the first playthrough. These allow you a lot more mobility, and are required if you're going to do a 0% item run. I won't tell them here because... well, if you get used to them, you'll skip a lot. Remember how I said how a good Metroidvania locks you into an area until you find the item to progress? Well, that actually happens in Rabi-Ribi... but ONLY in certain, confined areas. If you know the secret techniques, you can completely skip these actually well designed areas and miss out on vital items. Heck, I did a 0% run and I got so used to using the secret techniques that... well. The first item I went for in a new game was the item which allows you to go into small holes. So, I cleared the area and started to progress in the game and... wait, I can't go into the small holes? But I JUST cleared that ar- oh wait. I was so used to 0% run tactics that I had entirely skipped the segment where that item is. So I had to backtrack to actually get the item I purposedly went after, but had skipped anyway. Yeah, I facepalmed pretty hard after that.
The game has received a ton of after-launch support from the devs. During the first launch week, the game was updated almost hourly. Bugfixes, new achievements, balance tweaks, performance upgrades. Even months after release, the game is still receiving frequent updates. Actual new content has been fairly sparse, but some include full 0% run (I believe original game only supported half-way 0% run, changing that required a LOT of effort for sure) and three post-game bosses (who absolutely ridiculously hard).
The soundtrack of the game is pretty damn amazing.
tl;dr; version: A game which is certainly more oriented to the type of people who like Dark Souls types of challenging games, but can be really fun for others as well. The game has some glaring design issues (Metroidvania segments not leading you towards your next required item, massively flawed map, not being able to turn off items after you collect them) but... it can still be a fun.

For some reason, this game is officially capped at 30 fps. There is a way to uncap it.
1. Open your DR3 main folder. (With .exe)
2. Create a new text document.
3. Paste: "gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate = true" into the text document. (Without the "")
4. Save the text document as "user.ini" (Without the "")
5. You now should be able to see the user config file in your main folder.
6. Delete text document.

I've been playing MWO for nearly three years, since it was in Open Beta. I won't lie, the game has had its history (well documented) of problems in the past. I will say, though, that it has been on a steadily improving track over the past year, culminating in its Steam release.
Is it a grind? Yes, at times.
Is it overpriced for content? Yes, it is.
Does it get repetitive? Yes, it does.
Does it have a steep learning curve? Yes, most certainly
But...
Is it "pay to win"? Nope.
Is it fun? YES!
The only real money purchases are for Champion (30% XP boost...not needed) and Hero (30% C-Bill boost) 'Mechs. Hero 'Mechs are only worth the purchase for a unique hardpoint layout, skin, and geometry. Hero 'Mechs are not the best variants within a chassis, and certainly not the best in a weight class. Not "pay to win". Even the MC consumables are only marginally better than their C-Bill versions. And, in pug matches, consumables are often a waste.
It is tough to learn and get a feel for the game, but with the introduction of Player Tier ratings, things have gotten a lot better. Players will start in the lowest Tier, grouped with like pilots, and probably not die in seconds, as I did over my first few hundred matches.
Lots of older players are salty and burnt out on the game...but they've played and grinded for far to long. As a solid casual player, with over 4,500 matches in nearly three years (not a heavy load, by any stretch), I still find the game fun and love playing around with my 'Mechs.
It's free, so it doesn't hurt to check it out. Lots of new player help can be found on reddit in /r/OutreachHPG.
Don't let the more vocal of the community scare you off. Try it for yourself, master a 'Mech or two, and then decide.
Stick together, focus fire, and glhf!

Theres many people here recomending the game who has been players for years, just like me, who's purpose is to scare off the newer player base on Steam. A word of recomendation: Dont let them scare you off. This game isnt as half as bad as they claim it to be.
So for the ones that already know Battletech/Mechwarrior games, this is exactly what you expect. The return of your favorite mech game in arena-type multiplayer form (as in like World of Tanks). There are faction battles as well (we call them Community Warfare, or CW for short), you sign a contract with one of the 6 Inner Sphere factions you like, or 4 Clan factions (or if you so desire you can even go as a solo factionless Mercenary as well), and battle in different game modes for your faction in thousands of planets to conquer the Inner Sphere. However the developers have sacrificed the cannonity of the game lore for the game purpose, wich is alright, and im sure you will understand that decision as well. :)
For the new players, beware, this game is not arcadish, its HARD, and will require TRUE skill to manage. So if you want to test your skills and be able to survive the battlefields, you need to learn your mech like the palm of your hand. :P You need to pick up a mech and built it as your own, chose your weapons, the amount of armor, the ammo, the engine, the equipment and consumables, and so on and so forth... There are inumerous combinations you can make to your mechs, and this is what makes this game addictive... Not only you have to manage your mech's heat in environment, you also have to manage your damage, your ammo, and make the right decisions in battle with your team. Its not a matter of just shooting the mech in front of you, its survival, where team work does matter!
In a general analysis to the game, PGI is constantly improving the game, adding new mechs, adding new maps, fixing bugs (creating others), improving performance, balancing, adding new features, etc... So just like so many other games, it has its flaws, but that shouldnt turn you down. The devs do listen to the community, unlike some claim, but they are rather a small team and they are only human, but they still provide us with a patch every 2 weeks or so. The weekly events are fun and rewarding, so stay tunned for those as well. :P

It may not be for everyone, but it definitely has a type of player it attracts. If thinking-based tactical shooters are your cup of tea, then this will be a game for you. I won't lie, MechWarrior Online has had it's rough moments. There was a time where I left for a while because I felt the game back in 2013 was a bit too grindy and was missing some key elements. I returned a few months back and there have been MASSIVE improvements to this game. It's no where near grindy as it was and it actually has one of the best free to play models out there. This is by no means a pay to win game. In the hundreds of hours I have logged into this game, I have spent a grand total of $20. It wasn't necessary but I felt like getting a set of Mechs early. In reality, some of my best Mechs were purchased via the in-game currency. As a new player, you will have a cadet bonus for your first 25 matches and completing the tutorial along with that will net you quite a substantial amount of C-bills (the in game currency). You can choose to pay for premium time if you want, but it isn't necessary by any means. Plus, there are a lot of in game events that take place every once in a while that give players a wide array of bonuses. Bottom line, you can be competitive and have fun without spending any money.
The developers have been listening to the community more and the game has a good roadmap for future improvements. This game is in good hands and there is a huge community behind it. There are tons of resources to help you along the way. A short list of these resources include:
The MWO official forums, specifically the guides/new player sections
The Outreach HPG subreddit
I highly recommend that you give this game a shot and do your best to find a unit or community that has a TS server or it's equivalent! Being part of a unit has several bonuses and it's a total gamechanger in terms of finding reliable teamwork and assistance. This game punishes the lonewolf types. Trust me, in order to get the best experience you should try to find a unit/open to the public teamspeak. This is not to say you can't have fun just dropping in public groups queue or just going solo, you certainly can, it's just that being part of a community can enhance the experience of this game tenfold.  There are tons of units recruiting on the steam forums and the MWO forums. Go check it out!

The core gameplay is sort of a mix between a Tank game and a Shooter. The game is slower paced than a number of other shooters, but this does not mean that it is easier. In fact, the learning curve for a brand new player can be relatively steep. The gameplay itself can be deep and rewarding though, which keeps many players playing despite the other issues they have with the game.
For one thing, the game is very much a team-dependant game closer to a MoBA than a typical FPS in that regard. With no respawns (or limited respawns in faction warfare) it s essential for players to stay and fight cohesively. Players that run off attempting to grab kills for themselves can be quickly focused down by many other mechs and accomplish very ittle.
The game features pretty in-depth customization of mechs that goes beyond just switching out weapons. You are able to adjust armor, change engines, replace parts, and add and remove weapons and equipment depending on the sometimes complex Mechlab rules. When you start you will be using a Trial mech at first, but you gain in-game currency fast enough to be able to buy your own custom mech within a few hours at most.
There is also no tier system in regards to the mechs. There is no unlocking of better mech chassis as you play. The choice for what you want to buy is open to you from the start.
Despite the sometimes high real-world prices of items in the game and the fact that it is F2P, the game does a very good job of not being Pay to Win. All of the best mechs (determined by the community) in the game are either available for in-game currency or are timed exclusives for those who buy them (the closest thing to P2W that the game has). There are Hero mechs that are available for purchase only but they tend to not be good, but rather unique. Paid consumables are 100% identical to in-game currency consumables once the in-game currency consumables are upgraded with XP.
The most useful things in the game available for real-money purchase are mech bays to store more mechs in, but they are given out in Faction Play and in relatively frequent events.
There are certainly some hiccups with the game. It is not particularly well-optimized and the developers have not always consistently been on top of things. Some actions have generated quite a bit of animosity among past players. They have been getting better about it though and in my impression few of the issues come from anything approaching malice but rather from inexperience. They are at least still actively working on and adding to the game in significant ways (although maybe slower than many like).
In the end though I find the game quite fun which has kept me coming back to it.

This game is simply brilliant.
The story starts out with Adam Jenson, a security officer, doing tours around his company's labs. Mercenaries strike without notice and steal some key technology regarding augments for the human body. Worst of all, a doctor that was leading the research is either dead or has disapeared with the attack. The story begins to get a lot more interesting and offers some serious ethical and moral issues behind merging the body with machines. I finished the game and from start to end there is no shortage interesting dialogue.
The game play is simply stunning on this one. What I liked about this Deus Ex having played previous versions, is that they didn’t decide to completely forget what the old games looked like. Rather, they put in place a modernized version of what used to be without too much of the shiny glitter you see in newly developped games. What I absolutely love about this game is that the environment is able to be manipulated. There is always a direct course of action, but there will be options available to go around conflict VIA vents or ladders. Some quests will require the player to stack some barrels in order to climb them to jump over a fence. Some quests there will be enemies in your way and you’ll be comtemplating about throwing the dumpster you’re taking cover behind. To throw heavy objects such as the latter object mentioned, the player needs to upgrade Adam’s arms to be able to pick up such weight.
Praxis points are upgrade points that allow this to happen. Not only can Adam’s arms be upgraded, his eyes for example can be upgraded to see enemies through walls or see where they are looking. His strength can be further upgraded to punch through walls (that are slightly cracked) to hurt an opponent on the other side. Other body parts can be upgraded but not simply for more strength, attack abilities can be added or movement abilities. Some upgrades require 1 point while some take 2. To fall from any height requires two points, but is a great ability to have when jumping off a ledge running from multiple enemies (or if your just impatient and would rather jump down ladders). That is only the start of what can be upgraded, and it is only the start of adding a new depth to the game. The one minor complaint I have is that there is a limited ability to melee. The player requires certain energy cells to be at full power before Adam can use his special abilities (such as punching through a wall, a silent kill or knockout, or an explosive ability). The same applies to a melee scenario. Unless you want to use all your upgrade points on power cells, stealth speed is definitely limited. It is a good idea but when it comes to having the option of a melee button, it isn't there which sucks when your under pressure. The game is a beautiful in it’s FPS/RPG elements, but they’ve added a third person element when it comes to taking cover. Pressing LT will put the camera over the shoulder of Adam and allow for a Gears of War shooting style.
This is greatly appreciated as the player can quickly get overrun by enemies. If that’s not enough depth, they’ve added hacking features. This isn’t limited to hacking simple computers, camera’s, turret’s, heck even giant mechs can be hacked. It isn’t any boring hacking game either, the count-down timer and the art styles they chose to display the hacks can really make a player nervous when it comes to cut-throat last seconds. When not in a mission, the player is allowed to free roam and explore the area. Area’s can be tampered with and civilians or thugs (or even police) can be knocked out or killed. Once you do this though, that is it, you’ve made your bed and if anyone caught you, they may hate you for the rest of the game. There definitely is no shortage of game play here. Be careful in choosing when to use a gun as the game watches how you act morally (whether you kill or knock out opponents). The AI enemies also are quite brilliantly done. They will not go one dimension on you and attack from one spot, they will move around and often will try to ambush you from all sides. Really well done here.
The player can choose to follow the main story line missions or choose to do side missions.
The sounds are appropriate and the visuals are quite stunning. The setting the put the game is absolutely suits it. One minute you feel like your walking through a rich neighborhood and the next your looking at a gloomy sky from some sort of ghetto projects. The dialogue is excellent and the voice acting is far from cheap.
The saving scheme was done absolutely right for this game. There is an auto save feature but there exists a saving feature where if you save it, that’s exactly where you’ll be loaded. If your in the midst of being shot, and like saving in a heated situation, by all means go for it. Even if you forget to save the auto save has your back ! I wish every game had this. Infamous Ikaruga, if you haven't seen some videos online, do so. Quite obviously this is a game for people who have the tendency to be perfectionists, who love to grind every last bit out of levels and don't mind starting over quite often.
There are many games which are difficult because they are poorly designed, have stupid controls, weird hitboxes, are unfair, have too much random elements, distracting visuals... not the case here!
Controls, Gameplay, Hitboxes, Visuals, everything is perfect. The hitboxes are very well done, so it really has to hit your ship for you to die, so no frustration in that regard, just as it should be.
While being white you can absorb blue enemy fire to charge your special attack and red fire will instantly kill you (the other way around when you are black). You can switch back and forth as you wish. But here the twist: If your "polarity" (the game uses this term) is different from your enemy, you do twice the damage. So being black shooting white (or the other way around) does twice the damage to your enemy, but dodging enemy fire then can be really tricky (as a single shot of the opposite polarity will instantly kill you), this also means you can't charge your special attack by absorbing enemy fire while being of a different polarity.
And another nice feature: Changing polarity is very quick, but not instant. So if you are white and want to change since there is some red fire incoming you can't possibly dodge, you have to anticipate that slightly before.
So the mechanic is quite simplistic, but also somewhat brilliant. You have to concentrate quite seriously at times and there are various strategies how to approach different enemy formations.
Especially if you are striving for a highscore the game immensely rewards playing well, and punishes mistakes brutally. So it doesn't matter how long you are able to survive, 20 seconds of good play will trump 2 minutes of dodging everything. And that's how it should be. Having chains of streaks (shooting 3 enemies of same polarity in a row) will boost your score immensely and the goal is to keep this up as consistently as possible (and the enemy formations allow you to keep this up if you play perfectly).
The first chapter is quite alright on hard, but the progression from there on is brutal.

After vesting 23 hours into Pixel Heroes I have beat the game fully through. Nothing left for me to do now until more quests are added and diffulty is ramped up some?
What's that? You think the game is hard? Well, then you obviously aren't good at these kind of games.
People complained about debuffs, but the game does provide ways around it. Simply equip items that block the debuffs.
You don't really need the stat boosts they provide, while they're helpful, they're not needed.
The game is a breeze if you keep to having two specific characters and one of your choice.
Recruit a fighter putting all of his experience towards strength, recruit a priest putting all of his experience towards faith and give him a vita tome and a redemption tome (heal and remove debuffs from all players), and recruit another of your choice. The third one I played with a bit, choosing different styles each time and could use whoever I wanted provded I used the other two as I described above.
Simply in battle, attack one turn, the heal the next and remve debuffs in the process if needed, then repeat. Ony break the process if you dont need to be healed, by attacking with your other character.
Receiving chests is easy as well, by placing all your experience to a specific stat you're guarenteed to open it.
What about the one's that require INT? Just smash it open, and then heal afterwards.
Potions, they're everywhere, too many in my opinion as I end up with almost if not over 30 of each in my inventory at the end of the game.
So my suggestions to the developer would be to add more quests, ramp up the difficulty as I found it too easy, make a use for all the gold I've aquired, and more bosses.
My suggestion is to buy the game, it's fairly priced and worth the money.

Pixel Heroes: Byte & Magic is probably best described as a party-based dungeon crawler with roguelike elements. I myself prefer to call it the "Send-Innocent-People-To-Their-Dooms-Over-And-Over-Again"-Simulator, though. That's also more accurate!
Pixel Heroes is hard. You hire your first heroes, buy some potions, accept a quest and head off into the wilderness. On your way to the dungeon you fight some relatively easy enemies (unless you decided to attack Death, or pet the puppy). You see the dungeon on the horizon and your party charges through the front door. Two turns later your heroes are all dead. Killed by a sickly infestation some foul-smelling zombie cast upon them a round earlier. Now you either cut your losses, call it unfair and never touch Pixel Heroes again...
...Or you stick with it, learn and grow from your mistakes. Next time you will prepare better and equip your heroes with items that make them immune to the sickness and proceed to clear out that dungeon with barely any trouble. It's easy to blame all your previous deaths on the RNG, but if you bother to look there are quite a few nuances to the game and I can guarantee you that the game is not as RNG-heavy as you might want to think. If you learn from your mistakes and pay attention to the monsters in the different dungeons your heroes will gradually survive longer and longer, until one day they might even make it!
Feature list:
+ 3 Difficulty modes
+ Lots of heroes (including additional ones that unlock during gameplay) with different, randomly generated stats and zany background stories
+ Tons of loot (probably a bit *too* much loot, inventory management can become a little tedious)
+ A world map with semi-random events that you use to travel to and from dungeons, the outcomes are random as well
+ Roguelike elements: While dungeon habitants follow a fixed theme their group composition is semi-random, no two runs through the same dungeon are actually the same
+ Geeky humour (that at times might be slightly over-the-top or feel out of place)
If you like party-based dungeon crawlers (or simply enjoy sending innocent pixel-people to their deaths) be sure to check this game out!

The core gameplay is sort of a mix between a Tank game and a Shooter. The game is slower paced than a number of other shooters, but this does not mean that it is easier. In fact, the learning curve for a brand new player can be relatively steep. The gameplay itself can be deep and rewarding though, which keeps many players playing despite the other issues they have with the game.
For one thing, the game is very much a team-dependant game closer to a MoBA than a typical FPS in that regard. With no respawns (or limited respawns in faction warfare) it s essential for players to stay and fight cohesively. Players that run off attempting to grab kills for themselves can be quickly focused down by many other mechs and accomplish very ittle.
The game features pretty in-depth customization of mechs that goes beyond just switching out weapons. You are able to adjust armor, change engines, replace parts, and add and remove weapons and equipment depending on the sometimes complex Mechlab rules. When you start you will be using a Trial mech at first, but you gain in-game currency fast enough to be able to buy your own custom mech within a few hours at most.
There is also no tier system in regards to the mechs. There is no unlocking of better mech chassis as you play. The choice for what you want to buy is open to you from the start.
Despite the sometimes high real-world prices of items in the game and the fact that it is F2P, the game does a very good job of not being Pay to Win. All of the best mechs (determined by the community) in the game are either available for in-game currency or are timed exclusives for those who buy them (the closest thing to P2W that the game has). There are Hero mechs that are available for purchase only but they tend to not be good, but rather unique. Paid consumables are 100% identical to in-game currency consumables once the in-game currency consumables are upgraded with XP.
The most useful things in the game available for real-money purchase are mech bays to store more mechs in, but they are given out in Faction Play and in relatively frequent events.
There are certainly some hiccups with the game. It is not particularly well-optimized and the developers have not always consistently been on top of things. Some actions have generated quite a bit of animosity among past players. They have been getting better about it though and in my impression few of the issues come from anything approaching malice but rather from inexperience. They are at least still actively working on and adding to the game in significant ways (although maybe slower than many like).
In the end though I find the game quite fun which has kept me coming back to it.

A little background on my MechWarrior Online (MWO) experience:
Joined MWO community on November 3, 2011.
Closed Beta Tester starting in late May 2012.
Broadcasting MWO exclusively on Twitch since October 2012.
I know this sounds like bragging, but I want to be clear on how much I love this game. Is it perfect? Nope. Does it have a steep learning curve? Kind of, but it really depends on your previous experience with MechWarrior/Tank games. But it is very fun to play once you get the hang of things.
The graphics are good. Especially if you have a good processor and graphics card. The sounds are well done and help with the immersion. The game maps are fun for the most part (PGI is in the process of rebuilding older maps) and everyone has their favorites and most hated maps (Caustic Valley is my least favorite).
The Quick Match game modes are OK and currently don't have a lot of variation in how they are played due to people being stuck in their ways, but there is enough variation to keep things interesting. Usually. I suggest you stick with the Solo Queue until you are more comfortable with the game as the Group Queue tends to be a little more competitive.
Faction play (aka Community Warfare (CW)) is still in development and can be fun, but right now it is really only a game mode where you get four lives instead of one. I highly suggest a new player avoid CW until they are more experienced because it is considered to be "hardcore mode" and you will be put up against some of the better players and their friends.
The community can be very helpful and I strongly encourage you to check out the Twitch streams as the broadcasters and viewers are usually very knowledgeable and eager to help new players.
If you love big stompy robots blowing up other big stompy robots, give it a try, visit the Twitch streams, and ask questions.
Good luck and send me a friend invite ingame. I'd be more than happy to help you out.

It may not look like it, as it's new on Steam - but after hundreds of hours in this game I can safely say it's one I heartily recommend.
Not recommend without reservation, mind, but heartily reccomend.
The game is difficult.  Screamingly difficult.  The learning curve is steep, mostly because it's unlike any other shooter out there.  It moves like World of Tanks, but plays slower, and with near infinite customizeability.  When you die, you're out of the round - no respawns in quick play, and a new mech in Community Warfare.  Ammo matters - you can't resupply, there are no 'pickups' or in-game mods that matter.  Taking damage matters - you don't repair in a match, can can lose entire sections of your mech or just a gun here and there as you are beaten by enemy fire.
Your environment matters - how hot is the world you're on?  Can you stand in water to help disssapate heat? Can you see your enemies, or will the ground clutter make targetting difficult?
Your teamwork matters.  No one's rambo here - your mech has hard limitations that mean you simply cannot win a game by yourself.
You can customize every mech - mechs can suit your playstyle and loadouts are up to you, from engines to capabilities, with no real 'best'.
It's fantastic.  A "thinking man's shooter" indeed, where every decision has consequences that can be extremely far-reaching for a match.  Signal intelligence matters.  Knowledge matters.  Skill matters.  Make the learning curve and you'll have near infinite permutations to experiment with.  Hell, put on a different weight class and learn how to play an entirely different game with the same parameters.
The downside?  There are two solid gamemodes, with only a handful of objectives.  While this will expand (and it's going to take a while for them to feel stale), it's currently somewhat limited.  The initial learning curve is a cliff - it's not an easy entry, though the new tutorial helps a great deal.
All in all, though?  It's a fantastic experience, one that gives a great deal of reward to those that can get over the initial learning curve.

When I first discovered this game, I saw it as as simplified version of Minecraft with Legos. However, upon watching videos, reading articles, browsing the forum, and ultimately purchasing and playing the game, I discovered there was much more than meets the eye. The simple, yet intuitive tutorial introduces you to the basics of the game without overloading you with information and walls of text. It gives you the freedom to learn many of the amazing things available in the world of Blockland by yourself, furthering the satisfaction value of this game. There are so many things to discover in the 50 or so megabytes of initial download, and endless possibilities to further expand gameplay with scores of user-created addons and mods. Can't recommend it enough. I've played this on and off since 2008. Aside from building, there is always something new.
The modding community is huge. Hell, the game practically revolves around it. Vanilla is nice, but any server you join is going to have lots of mods. From Team Deathmatches, to racing, to prison escapes, to building with some friends, there are many things to keep you busy.
Development is always active, and with the new launcher introduced in Version 19, they're applied automatically and more frequently. There are always new content updates and bug fixes every once and a while. It's been like this for years, and doesn't seem to be slowing down.
The graphics are good for a sandbox building game, but what more could you want right? Shadows and shaders have been a nice addition in Version 21, and anyone with a non-intergrated graphics card can at least run them on minimum. The game isn't very demanding at all. Aside from the studs, the bricks looks and act like your classic Lego blocks, and the minifigures have a nice, original design to them.
In a nuthshell, this game is practically G-Mod in the style of Legos. And it can't get any better than that. If you're still unsure, there's a demo you can download to try out the game and mechanics yourself - aside from multiplayer. For an indie game that only costs twenty-dollars, you get a lot more than your money's worth.

A perfect PC port of the classic (and hard as balls) shmup Ikaruga on Dreamcast. Supports higher native resolutions and X-Input controllers. So, basically, everything this port ever needed.
It's good. If you like shmups or are a fan of the original Arcade, Dreamcast or Gamecube releases, get this port. You won't regret it.

Ikaruga's biggest strength is the fact that it plays like a puzzle game despite it being a shump. Unlike Radiant Silvergun, there are only two weapons (standard shot, and a series of lasers), and enemies have two color schemes (black and white) as suppose to three (red, blue, and yellow). Ikaruga has several improvements over Silvergun: The game is more fast-paced than its predecessor, as well as greatly reducing the clutter on the controls (you no longer need to press multiple buttons Simultaneously to initiate a special move). It does have its flaws: the game is rather short and can be beaten within 25 to 50 minutes, the visibility between enemies and obstacles can be hard to tell at times, as well as the lack of proper power-ups (as enemy chains only effect the score and rank). Nonetheless, Ikaruga is a fantastic title in its own right and if you're a fan of bullet hell games, or various Treasure games like Dynamite Headdy or Mischief Makers, this game is for you!

I can't speak at all to the multiplayer, but from a single-player perspective Doom (2016) has one of the best-realized visions of any game i've ever played. Every single mechanic, and every single reward, encourages the same style of gameplay: being aggressive and being complete. There's no conflicting goals ever-- you never have to weigh avoidance against engagement or taking your time against beating your time-- the game will always reward you for diving into fights head-on, killing every enemies, and searching the map. There's no reloading your weapons, you can't hide from your enemies, and your best chance of healing or getting more ammo is to kill the enemies before they kill you.
The aesthetic is also wonderfully-realized, but perhaps pushing the boundaries of good taste. The gore is excessive, if the foes were human this game would probably be illegal in australia, and I wouldn't feel comfortable buying this for somebody elses teenager or kid. That being said, that excessively-brutal aesthetic is a lot of fun, partially because it doesn't take itself too seriously. Some of the glory-kills are just plain rediculous. Two of my favorites are: tearing off a demon's leg and curb-stomping him with his own foot, and tearing out a demon's heart and feeding it to him.
And the sound track is great. If you're a big fan of the heavy prog-rock of bands like tool you'll hear a lot of nods to riffs you recognize. The soundtrack really contributes to the feeling of balls-to-the-walls aggression, works great in the atmosphere, and is well-timed to help you "feel" what the game wants you to do.
The game also scales down pretty well for the lower end of supported systems, while still looking gorgeous on high end systems.
I'd say the only big downside to this game is that sometimes the level design can be confusing. It's linear, but sometimes it can be damn hard to tell where you're supposed to be going.
Doom isn't the game to end all games. It doesn't fill any niches except its own, or even try to. It has an unapologetically simple plot and doesn't espouse any perspective on life, but it fills its niche as perfectly as any game i've ever played and is a darn tootin good time.

Before playing this Game, I had never been interested or even a follower of the Deus Ex series. This game changed that. Deus Ex Human Revolution is by far one of my favorite games of all time. The pure aspect of the game being a game almost without a genre is appealing to me. The reason I say a game without a genre, is because the game is open, and literally can be played anyway you want. The progression is stellar, both gameplay and storyline wise. The other thing I like about this game is just how open it is. For example, I had to get into a bar to talk to one of the contacts helping me with a mission, there unfortunately was a bouncer outside who wouldn't let me in. I looked for other entrances, and found one but I had to move a dumpster, and my strength wasn't high enough to move it to let me in, hence I pick up another side mission promising me more piraxis points to level up so then I can revisit the club and continue with my story mission. This is the reason why this game is great, there are literally so many different ways and possibilities of completing your mission it warrant multiple play throughs. On top of all of this, the storyline is fantastic, personally I love the voice acting of Adam Jensen (Elias Toufexious) and his grizzled demenour, and the stroyline is just so thick and rich filled with twists and turns and questions, its a very well put together game. Gameplay, Storyline, and Pacing are some of the things that make this great. I can't wait to see what they'll do in the sequel. The only cons I would list, are that the game isn't the prettiest, I understand this was made a couple years ago, but for example Adam Jensen's hair in game just looks atrocious. Only improvement I would request in the sequel.

Pixelated roguelikes are a dime a dozen lately, but Pixel Heroes is really something special. It's charming, with biting humor and just the right amount of strategic depth. First off, this is the best promo video I've seen.
The actual game is also quite good.  Graphics are well done in the 'classic' style with enough modern touches to not be distracting.  Game runs well and controls easily with just the mouse.  I had watched quite a bit of gameplay before buying but still consider this a 'first impressions' review.
Gameplay consists of running from town to dungeons and beating progressively tougher monsters and bosses.  You have a small inventory and must manage the loot, using pieces to upgrade your heroes various equipment.  As you progress you unlock additional classes and achievements.  A party focused turn-based dungeon crawler of the old school.  Along the way to/from the dungeons you encounter random events which as others have said are the highlights of the game and full of fun references.
Unfortunately this is also the games biggest stumbling block.  Some of these events are simply show-stoppers - you may encounter a monster that simply 1-shots your entire party and resists all attacks/magic.  This effectively ends the game and you have to start over.  Not really an issue in a regular rogue-like game, but given the focus on loot management and stat improving that is the core of this game it can be very frustrating.   Spending hours building up your party and pouring over the numerous (sometimes overwhelimgly) statistics of the gear to decide what to keep and then having it not matter as you are insta-gibbed on the way to the next dungeon isn't much fun.  Makes it quite hard to get back on the treadmill again.  The carrot is trying new classes and new strategies, but clearly there are some balance issues that need addressed.
All in all a fun little game and well made.   Worth a shot if you like loot focused crawlers or rogue-likes (that word again...) and have a high tolerance for frustrating wipes.
That video though...perfect.  Thumbs up for that alone.

Pixel Heroes claims to be a return to the old school RPGs from the NES era, and in some ways this is true. Maybe its the many many years that have gone by since I played a NES but I don't get that feeling from this game. Its a roguelike, linear RPG with some humor and a ton of "nerdy" jokes thrown in. Its fun, for awhile.
Beyond what you may see from the out set of this game, there is a odd challenge lying under the colorful pixels. Combat can become...tiresome after a few hours playing. I've read a lot of people not enjoying the limited inventory but I only ran into a issue with not wanting to toss something a few times. Like most games that throw loot at you, this one isnt giving you great stuff after every fight. A lot of it is junk and you will spend times trying to figure out which new item is best only to find in the next fight the new DooDaad is worthless.
My main complaint, and I don't google wikis for answers to games my first time playing it, is that each dungeon is random in what type of weapons do the type of damage you need. This is that odd challenge I mentioned. I went through one dungeon with shiney new weapons only to have them do very little damage, dispite the large amount of damage listed. Have a new 60 magical damge sword? May not work for f$%k in the next dungeon, or in the dungeon your in. This gets VERY annoying VERY quickly. You can't run away, you can't access your inventory during a fight and you cant use the crap load of healing potions you pick up till AFTER the fight. (Which if I am wrong, please comment and point out how to do that.) Spending a crap ton of time in a fight because your weapon only does 1 damage to an enemy is my biggest issue. There are no descriptions of the monsters you fight so you can't really tell what will work against them with out trial and error, and since you can't open your inventory to switch out a weapon till after the fight is over, can be tedious and annoying.
Regardless of the above, the game is fun and quirky. I enjoyed it when the combat wasnt needlessly tedious. If there was a "Meh" button for recommend, I'd have used that instead of "Yes" but I don't dislike it enough to say "No".
Buy at your own risk.

I think we all believed that Re;birth3 was the perfect game for Neptunia series, but I’ve to admit it, this Victory-II has proven that there were still room for improvements.
To start let’s make a beautiful
:
Pros:
+ Big Neptune
+ Finally we have graphical assets for PC (but still frame drops while entering dungeons)
+ More variety of dungeons (still feeling a bit repetitive though)
+ The added a little more difficulty and the new combo system makes the game feel more tactic along with the new way of travelling the world map
+ No more GP, we are free of the classic spam breaker/spam power system
+ Going HDD now uses Exe Gauge instead SP, yay!
+ All the CPUs have their moment to shine in their own Story Arc
+ No more Lily Max/100M credits achievements
+ They nerfed the ridiculously OP Exe Drive
Cons:
- They nerfed Exe Drive too much (above lvl40 is better to use normal combos except for AOE)
- Next forms are cool, but they don’t have a major role in the game and feel like a bit waste of potential
- The new trio (Neptune, Nepgear, Uzume) can’t beat the one made by Neptune, Plutia and UD Noire in comedy and chemistry
- Lots and lots of unnecessary fanservice like no other Neptunia main game has had (yep, for me this is bad)
- Little end game content compared to Victory
Megadimension Neptunia Victory-II is the fourth main game of the Neptunia franchise.
Taking place some time after the events of the original Victory (V Generation in Steam) , we find Neptune being, once again, transferred to another dimension were, along with Nepgear, she’ll met Uzume, a mysterious girl fighting against a giant monster called Dark CPU.
Here will start the story, which would take us in a long journey into three “sub-games” inside the game with their own OP, ED and plots making them a “trilogy within a single game” because nep is nep guys.
Regarding the
, which is one of the most important concerns from Japanese games, we have for the first time in the franchise access to a variety of graphic assets, but still a problem with frame drops at the moment the monsters in a dungeon charges. Out of it the only “problem” is the charge time between battles and world exploration.
In the gameplay, we face a classical Neptunia system with some elements added, more centred in a new balance. In this game we don’t have full access to each combo class, instead we’ll have the slots each weapon has (and no, the best weapons don’t have all the slots unlocked). This, along with the new combo traits, makes more important to chain attacks in order to activate the combo trait (100% accuracy/chance of critical hit) making a better work for the gameplay than the classic “spam breaker until you can spam power”.
There’s no longer GP, instead some monsters (and nearly all the bosses) have some kind of part that can be broken to show a weak spot, but the necessity of guard breaking has disappeared and this is a total improvement, also the Exe Drives now have been nerfed to the extreme, making them only a bit more powerful than a common skill and (in higher levels) weaker than a good chain of combo attacks.
The world map has also been redesigned into a one with a real feel of travel. Now we have to make roads to reach the dungeons with money, cities play a new and more realistic role since our characters can only recover HP/SP without items going to them, items development/scouts are also only accessible from those cities and there are random encounters while travelling between dungeons/cities.
The scout system has changed once more and, for me, to worst. The new scout system features lots of the classical Gamipics now working for us. In this system we don’t explore an external dungeon like in Stella’s one, now we explore the same dungeons that we have in the game, and each scouts has its own effect to make it easier or harder. They also find monster drops, money and clues to make the hidden treasure appear, but only work with the game running, not like in Victory.
Next Forms make their debut in this game, but they are nothing more than testimonial since their appearances in the main story are more than limited (in this game fighting a story boss with HDD from the start is rare) and, although being awesome, it feels that we need more time with them (hopes for the next game).
In conclusion, this is overall a must have for every Neptunia fan and, of course, JRPG fan.

It hurts to do this, but Megadimension Neptunia VII is hands down Idea Factory's worst Neptunia PC port to date. Even with a state of the art rig like mine crashes are a constant thing, and there are no fixes on the way. IF has made it very clear from their complete lack of any updates since the release that this version is what we're going to get, and we'll have to deal with whatever problems arise ourselves. The Rebirth Series had a lot of bugs and issues with RAM, but Megadimension is a game that will run fine for random intervals of time and crash for no apparent reason. During cutscenes, fights, it even crashes in the menus. What kind of game crashes in the Main Menu? Astonishingly, despite being a PS4 port, this version does not properly support a PS4 controller. Even when the game is running normally, graphics will flicker and get choppy just navigating the game map between areas. Sometimes the sound will begin to reverberate like the characters are talking in a tunnel or a cave. Having played the PS4 version prior to this, it's shocking how poorly this runs by comparison.
The game itself is really great, but for a lot of people it's completely unplayable on PC in it's current state. I would advise caution if you intend to purchase this. It may or may not work for you, regardless of the system you're using. It seems to be hit or miss with hardware.

I enjoyed Megadimension Neptunia VII a lot. I am writting this after having unlocked all the achievements in the game (It was tough, I tell you), this shows how much I love this game. And you might like it too!
This was my first Neptunia game, and it is definitly not the last!
The thing with Megadimension Neptunia VII, is that it has some really good points but also some rather "meh" ones about it. I will try to list them, for any of you, who would like to buy this game.
Very good points:
-The story is really good, I really loved it, it has some very powerful moments that made me love the Neptunia Universe!
-Some pieces of music in the soundtrack are amazing, I don't have any other words to describe them. If you were to listen to one I will recommend "Mousou Katharsis".
-The characters have distinct and intresting personnalities, which make them stand out in my opinion from other JRPGs' characters.
-And they are also very funny, especially Nep.
Good points:
-The game is long enough to keep you entertained for easely 80 hours.
-The New Game+ feature is really nice and make less painful the grinding for achievements
-There are many "mini-mechanics" in the game that are very nice (I will not spoil them, it is up to you to discover them! ;))
-The help messages is very clear and not invasive
-The quest system is nice
"Meh" points:
-The enemies and certain dungeons can be kind of repetitive
-The graphics for the dungeons are not that great for a 2015 PS4 game (But people say there is a massive improvement from the previous Neptunia games, so it might not be that relevent)
-The controls for a PC are not that great, I recommend playing with a controller (Xbox or PS4)
That's it for me, even if there are some rather "Meh" points, this game is really nice, I enjoyed playing it a lot! So give it a try.
I'm sure that Idea Factory International and Compile Heart are willing to improve their games, and I hope that this review helped, and that those issues will get fixed in the next main series games.
