I can't speak at all to the multiplayer, but from a single-player perspective Doom (2016) has one of the best-realized visions of any game i've ever played. Every single mechanic, and every single reward, encourages the same style of gameplay: being aggressive and being complete. There's no conflicting goals ever-- you never have to weigh avoidance against engagement or taking your time against beating your time-- the game will always reward you for diving into fights head-on, killing every enemies, and searching the map. There's no reloading your weapons, you can't hide from your enemies, and your best chance of healing or getting more ammo is to kill the enemies before they kill you.
The aesthetic is also wonderfully-realized, but perhaps pushing the boundaries of good taste. The gore is excessive, if the foes were human this game would probably be illegal in australia, and I wouldn't feel comfortable buying this for somebody elses teenager or kid. That being said, that excessively-brutal aesthetic is a lot of fun, partially because it doesn't take itself too seriously. Some of the glory-kills are just plain rediculous. Two of my favorites are: tearing off a demon's leg and curb-stomping him with his own foot, and tearing out a demon's heart and feeding it to him.
And the sound track is great. If you're a big fan of the heavy prog-rock of bands like tool you'll hear a lot of nods to riffs you recognize. The soundtrack really contributes to the feeling of balls-to-the-walls aggression, works great in the atmosphere, and is well-timed to help you "feel" what the game wants you to do.
The game also scales down pretty well for the lower end of supported systems, while still looking gorgeous on high end systems.
I'd say the only big downside to this game is that sometimes the level design can be confusing. It's linear, but sometimes it can be damn hard to tell where you're supposed to be going.
Doom isn't the game to end all games. It doesn't fill any niches except its own, or even try to. It has an unapologetically simple plot and doesn't espouse any perspective on life, but it fills its niche as perfectly as any game i've ever played and is a darn tootin good time.

Going to leave a quick review here. Personally I think MWO is a great game. I have spent, and will continue to spend, many hours playing it. I've been a player for over 2 years now. It takes a little bit of getting used to it because of the learning curve, but if you want a first person, big, stompy 'mech battle with different types of weapons, then you should try out this game.
You can drop in quick play for a 12v12 match or go into community warefare with longer matches and more 'mechs. Teamwork is a top priority. Take time to outfit your 'mechs with the right equipment for your playstyle as you go, and unlock skills with your experience points, to improve as a pilot.
Pros:
-Big stompy 'mechs
-Good graphics and sound
-Dedicated playerbase from before the Steam launch, but even more players with it
-Free to play and not pay to win
Cons:
-Steep learning curve (I stongly recommend completing the tutorial)
-Technical loadouts for 'mechs can be time consuming to research or build, including the grind to get enough in-game money to purchase equipment and unlock skills (though you don't have to go too hardcore)
Overall I say if you're unsure give it a try as it is free, and see if you like it yourself, because everyone is different. The community will give advice if you ask for it.

I have been playing this game for over 3 years and decided to write this short review to warn people who are not into Battletech about this game.
Before you start playing, mind the following:
- the game is still in a beta stage in some ways (bugs, unfinished features, core features missing or badly implemented)
- PGI (the developer) is more interested in your money than in delivering a good game (although the permanently claim the opposite)
- PGI does not do much against cheaters and even does not react when they are presented proof (and there are too many cheaters)
- the overall frustration level in MWO is quite high, especially if you are new to the game
- since the player base is quite small for an MMO, the match-finding times can be very high (> 15min) for the main game mode
- balance in match-making and concerning the BattleMechs and their weapons is not nearly as good as it could be
So why am I still playing this game and why did I give it a positive rating?
- I am a Battletech fan and there simply is no other recent MechWarrior game
- It's a good team-based game that favors working together over playing as a lone-wolf
- It's NOT pay-to-win and to be an outstanding player, you need many skills (being a good shot is not enough!)
Long story short: play if you are a Battletech fan, try if you like team-based games with substance, ignore it if you're expecting a mainstream game à la Call of Duty or Star Wars Battlefront.

First of all, the Negative Reviews at Release are due to PC port performances, not the game itself. The PC port is poorly optimized, not as "unplayable" as Arkham Knight, but the game definitely has issues like input delays, FPS lock, frame rate drop... As someone pointed out, a quick potential fix could be changing the NDIVIA setting for the game in the NVIDIA Control Panel from "Integrated" to "High-performance"
About the game itself, it's a big BIG improvement from the last games. More characters, more combos, flashy animations, interesting fights... The game mechanics remain relatively simple for a fighting game, yet you can still do more "advanced" techniques like juggling, air combo,chain jutsu, mid-combo swap characters...
The animation in this game is gorgeous, but NOT all of the story is animated. Some less important scenes are still images with moving backgrounds and audio. For the ones that are fully animated (mostly fight scenes), they are breath-taking, and I even prefer this art style to the Anime.
Voice acting is decent, even in English, if you don't mind the bad lip-syncing in some cut scenes.
The game provides a better challenge than the last games, bosses are relatively harder and smarter. The fights can get very intense and you have to try hard a little bit (depends on how good you are) to get all achievements in story battles. The main story features dual story branches, which last for about 6 - 8 hours. Then you have Adventure Mode (basically a Free Mode) to explore the events after the main game.
Did I mention the roster for this game is HUGE? It even includes characters from "The Last: Naruto Movie" and the 2nd generation: Boruto, Salada... The list of playable characters is just amazing, and there are even more to come! Your favorite character will sure be featured in the game. Huge roster also have negatives though, there are characters that feels like clones of other characters, and obviously some will have superior move sets. Thankfully, the game manages to keep the power-level of each character relatively close enough, and each of them plays differently from each other. The format is a 3-people team, so find out what work best for you to chain for combos.
The customization is also great, you can buy alternate costume, "online ID" by the Gold (Ryo) acquired in game. The only matches are mic-supported, server ping is actually pretty good. I can enjoy the online matches without issues.

Dead Rising 3 Review Raymond KT
Summary: Available exclusively for Xbox One, Dead Rising 3 marks the return of one of the most popular zombie video game franchises. Set 10 years after the events of Fortune City in Dead Rising 2, players are introduced to Nick Ramos, a young mechanic with a strange tattoo and a mysterious past, who must find a way to escape a city full of zombies before an impending military strike wipes the city of Los Perdidos, California, and everyone in it, off the map. Nick cant do it alone - he must join up with other survivors to stay alive. They must fight their way out before its too late.
With an immersive open-world experience, intense action, and unmatched level of weapon and character customization, a new generation of zombie-slaying fun has arrived with Dead Rising 3.
Dead Rising for me, I think will always be my favoite game. I was a little disappointed with Dead Rising 2 with no Frank; and now no Frank in Dead Rising 3.
Having played Dead Rising 2 on PC, I knew what to expect from this title. Being stuck in a chaotic environment chock-full of flesh eating zombies with nothing but your wits and will to survive is just what one needs to kick the gear in motion. Speaking of gears, the protagonist this time is a bona-fide mechanic with experience in “fixing stuff.” Nick Ramos worked with his boss in a garage when the disaster struck, and with his practical experience and a bit of help from conveniently scattered blueprints, he can combine any two seemingly mundane and inoffensive objects into a deadly arsenal worthy of any action hero; yes, it’s time to bring back all those sweet weapon combos. But what sets this guy apart from Frank West and Chuck Greene? Why, vehicle combos!
In Dead Rising 3, players can expect every mechanic from the previous games to return. Some of them, in my opinion, have improved. The newest and best addition is the ability to combine two vehicles into a new mass-murdering gas-guzzling hunk-‘o-junk. Is your motorcycling around Los Perdidos lack that magical amount of oomph? No more! Welding torch in hand, trusty ‘ol Nick will attach a tremendous looking steam roller to your bike, and even give it a sweet patriotic paint job to boot. Did you ever wish to have fire exhausts in front of your bike too? He’ll tack ‘em on too! Now get going, sweet flaming gore doesn’t make itself.
I liked how simplified this iteration of the franchise turned out to be. Nick, having tools on hand and the experience, can produce weapon combinations on the spot without the aid of a work bench, provided he isn’t killed by the rampant crowds of enemies while doing so. He can also clean out Safe Houses which can later be visited to organize his crusades around Lost Perdidos with a lot less running around the clock. Each Safe House provides you with a Clothes Locker that lets you customize your appearance instantly (even keeping track of completed outfits!), Weapon Lockers that contain every kind of weapon you’ve picked up at least once (including combos!), and a bulletin board that lets you manage your survivor passé! Gone are the days of painstakingly watching over a ticking clock while carefully managing the resources to make your favorite weapons and test them against the horde. By unlocking a single Safe House, the hours of fun will not be cut short because you spent too many hours scrounging around for that pair of gloves that simply refuses to appear.
Further on, leveling up is now directly controlled by the player. Attribute points are acquired per PP level (with bigger earnings as you reach certain milestones) and by clearing chapters. They can be applied to any one of the character attributes or combo proficiency. To elaborate further, not only are you personally involved in the growth of your character, but you can also purchase proficiencies for certain types of combos (like slash weapons, firearms, or even food combos), allowing you to use more types of materials to create the same combos in the proficiency sheet. This still requires you to know the blueprints to make it work, but with enough proficiency, you can literally combine anything with everything.
Great fun.

Deus EX: Human Revolution is an enjoyable and compelling game with an interesting story and decent gameplay. There is content for quite a while and situations can be approached in different ways.
Condensed list of the good and the bad, mostly arranged by personal experience:
The game is enjoyable, but has some noticable flaws in the gameplay.
is the major offender with
sprint, poor strafing capabilities, fiddly jumping mechanic and needlessly prompted actions (such as moving from cover to cover, around a cover and climbing) accompanied by awkward cutscenes (Icarus Landing System).
is enjoyable and as stated earlier, the multiple approaches available offer a commendable value to the gameplay. Direct, long range and hidden assaults are all viable options with each having a lethal and non-lethal variety.

One downside in Deus Ex: HR's combat is the melee system. Unlike the previous game(s), HR does not have melee weapons that can be equipped like other equipment, but instead you are given prompts every time you are near an enemy. This activates a cutscene where you use your arms to knock the target(s) unconscious or kill them.
Activating the prompt uses an energy cell, which limits the melee use further.
is one of the few things that feel just spot on with variety of large and small weapons, each offering their own characteristics.
[Edit] There are also minor bugs to be expected.
In comparison to the first game in the franchise (Deus Ex), the freedom of movement is much more limited. Certain cutscenes, Icarus Landing System for example tug you right out of the game. The greatest strengths of Deus Ex: HR are its story and dialogue in addition to combat and gunplay.
HR could be described as a good B-movie; an enjoyable experience with its own flaws.

I've always wanted a Civilization in space, and Endless Space was able to fill that itch very very well.  Custom factions, expansive maps, a detailed tech tree, and freedome to progress how you see fit makes for a great empire-building experience that feels both famililar and unique in its own ways.

You play as Adam Jensen, the head of security at Sarif industries, a company that focusses on developing human augmentations, such as bionic prosthetics.
Due to an attack, Jensen once fully human, has most of him replaced with augments.
After six months of recovery, Adam once again goes into the fray to stop another attack from terrorists attacking Sarif industries and uncovers a conspiracy which is bigger than he could have ever dream off.
The game mostly focusses on an action based style soft rpg and there are a lot of choices to be made, some offer direct results, others indirect.  Don't kill a terrorist and he might reward you later on in the game, help a co-worker and he might reveal some info later on.
Adam can unlock more augmentations by leveling up or collecting praxis points and some of these are things like looking through walls or turn invisible, one of the augments lets you scan humans in a conversation to more easily manipulate them.
Gunplay itself is solid and intense, even though Adam is augmented he is most definitely not invincible and even with the armor upgrades, enemies are tough, you can only carry so much with you (the game uses a trunk inventory system, so expect a lot of puzzling trying to get one energy bar in your inventory) and cover and tactics are essential, making gunfights incredibly dynamic, enemies aren't the brightest, but they can be incredibly stubborn.
The world itself is really well formed, it is futuristic and most obviously a torn one, with augs on one side and purists on the other and with diverse themes, you are just a man that had no choice in getting augmented, yet some look at you in disgust, do you accept those terms or not and what truly makes us human?
The graphics are dated, it looks good, but compared to some of the newer games, it falls a bit flat. The main characters are obviously detailed, than some of the secondary characters and there isn't that much diversity in goons except for types.
All in all this an incredible game and a must if you haven't played it yet.

What's important is this: Combat consists of spaceships of increasingly large size and fleet compositions shooting the hell out of eachother with laser guns, full-auto railguns and missile barrages, and it is friggin' cool. Great stuff all around. Doom 2016 is not a pure return to form - while original games had open mazelike levels with pre-placed monsters, this sequel presents most combat encounters arena-FPS style: player is locked in an area until everybody else is dead. This does not hamper the exploration though, and there's a lot of nifty little secrets to find. So, SP campaign is great and is decently long(took me around 14 hours to beat). It also sports a surprisingly developed story and lore, which are also really easy to ignore if you don't care. Soundtrack is praised all over the Internet, and for good reason. Combat is fast and brutal with a very heavy emphasis on mobility, and has a refreshing amount of verticality to it. Progression systems are in there and provide a healthy amount of variety and empowerment creep. Even checkpoint placement feels right.
Game also looks good, runs great, and is also very scalable to boot, providing a generous amount of settings. I'm having trouble thinking of any technical faults, except maybe that some settings make very little visual difference going even from low to Ultra, while still causing a performance hit(Setting shadows from ultra to nightmare leads to a huge FPS drop, but the difference is barely visible even on screenshots). But at any rate, it's reasonably easy to run on 60+ FPS on most modenr hardware configurations.
So is there anything wrong with it? Yes. Multiplayer is meh. It does have a lot of content: multiple game modes, lots of maps, tons of customization options, vast array of stuff to unlock. And maybe it is the problem - from the get go a lot of stuff is locked and has to be unlocked by achieving levels and completing challenges. Loadout system and two-weapon limit does not help either. It's not that those systems are inherently wrong, but they just feel out of place in this title.
So overall? If you are an FPS fan with any amount of self-respect, go and get it. It is really, really good.

SKIPCHASER has all the tools to be a great rogue-lite experience down the line.
The game follows general rogue-lite rulesets where you clear enemies throughout a level, then move on to the next one. After you clear a level you are returned to the hub world where you can research new abilities, upgrades and weapons.
The gameplay feels responsive, tight and fast paced. While I enjoy most of it, at the current state there seems to be a lack of enemy variety. More polish needs to be put on some of the enemies currently included as well, such as the sapce rats animations.
Since the game is so fast paced your character can sometimes be blindsided by enemies as soon as you load into a level, which can instantly take away a lot of your health and put you at a disadvantage. It feels cheap and I would love to see a small safe room at the start of each level to avoid that.
The artstyle is a highlight in this game. I really enjoy the minimalism and cartoon style. In many ways it reminds me of shows such as Samurai Jack. I mean that in the best way.
The upgrade system is interesting as well. You have blueprints for your weapons but you can mix and match attachments as long as they are similar in size to the blueprint you are working with. It lets you customize your weapons in interesting ways to suit your playstyle.
Overall, SKIPCHASER has a lot of potential and you should look into it once it leaves Early Access.

So, I guess it's time to actually DO a review, instead of just saying one sentence that is supposed to make you buy the game.
The simple question here that you're most likely asking when you read a review, is "Do you reccomend the game."
Do I? Well, I DID, at one point.
This game was once a great game, infact, had you asked me a few years back while it was still alive and kicking, hell, I'd tell you to get the game and enjoy it. The game itself was a nice building game, and still is, but what made it the best, at least to me, was the absolutely large playerbase, and multiplayer.
Large sums of people playing on multiple servers, all of which had players BUILD the maps, guns, and gamemodes themselves(most of which took alot of time). It was an amazing experience back then. It truly was a creative game that even in it's prime could rival that of Minecraft. Hell, even allowing a simple and easy coding system, where you could script blocks to do certain movements, or certain commands after certain perameters were met. It was GREAT, and It truly sparked a large sum of creativity for a slightly more mature audience, and it really showed. The fame of this game back in it's prime was amazing, and back then, just typing in "block" into youtubes search bar would give it's name as the first result.
But surly, a game like this that could rival such a TITAN of a sandbox game, and with such a following, plus great features... surly it couldn't have died...right...? *sigh*
Well, It did. Unfortunately, the game itself has a lack of players, most of which used to support the absolute hell out of this game and used to back it without second guessing. Back when the developer actually made updates, and tried to actually improve off what he left broken from previous updates. But unfortunately, that was lost when he decided it would be better to treat the playerbase like an absolute @ss, and expect nobody to have been upset by it. How he came to act like "I dont NEED to update the game, I'll do whatever I want." even though people simply asked for updates.
It's no suprise to what the end result of this mentality was, he abandoned the game, and left the players stranded with it. A game like this is unique, and in itself was a title that I personally will not forget, and sometimes will even reinstall just to have that nostalgic feel, just for a few minutes, before realizing that this game, and it's fame, died all too long ago.  Truly, I am saddened that such a community was left at the hands of such a♥♥♥♥♥♥ a man who couldn't even bring himself to actually do right by the people that INVESTED in his game, and then had the gull to insult them, and treat them as if they did nothing for him.
So, the question remains, do I recommend this game? No. I just cant bear to try and say "buy this game" without being reminded that all the cash you spend on this game, goes straight to a no-good dev, the same dev that not only abandoned the game, but abandoned the still-living playerbase WITH IT.
Sorry if this was a long review, I didnt want to drag this out, but after writing all of this, I feel removing any of this would sorta do the game an injustice. Thanks for reading.

Personal Rating: 7/10
Ah Bully. This games getting a sequel in 2016 so hopefully people can get hyped for that after they've stopped ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ themselves about Fallout 4. However let's take a look at the first game.
Bully is an open world game set in a school. You play as Jimmy Hopkins who is arguabley the biggest♥♥♥♥♥♥on earth at the beginning of the game. Much like Rockstar's other games, you do quests located around the map to advance the story. Very GTA IV like but without any of those silly cars or mass genocides, carried out by helicopters and bowling.
Gameplay wise, it's honestly nothing special to be honest. I can't feel connected to Hopkins because he's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I can't feel any sympathy for him or any bullies for that matter. I mean, I'm a nerd, in this game you're basically asking me to steal my own lunch money. But the jokes on him, I make my own lunch and bring it with me *pushes glasses up nose*. But nah, it's not fresh. There's nothing convincing me to do any of these actions apart from to advance the story.
One new thing they added into this game is classes. No, not Call of Duty classes. As in, actual learning classes like Art, English and Science. You might be thinking "Well what's the point in going to classes? I live the thug life". Well, these classes can eventually give you upgrades and weapons such as stinkbombs, clothing and even a bike (which I never got, apparently my lack of skills in production and art carried over into this game). Each class revolves around a minigame, like in English for example, you have to make as many possible words out of a jumble of letters, or in Art where you have to avoid pencils and stuff to draw a picture? I don't know what they were thinking but it works I suppose.
Obviously a big part of the game is combat. But it lacks a certain something. Beat 'em ups and Fighting games have never appealed to me, and Bully is basically a beat 'em up with a couple of minigames slapped on the top, with an unrelatable character and numerous little cracks in this game.
However, it's still great. As much as I've complained about this game, it really is a very good game. Graphically wise it might not stand up to today's standards, however they were good for it's time. Some of the characters like the Principal and the Homeless Bloke are well made and I enjoyed the parts of the game they were in. Now obviously I haven't played all of this game, I finished it on my Xbox 360 though so that can sort of give you an idea.
The one big problem with the Steam version is that if you try and change the options, such as the size of the screen, the game will crash. Well, it did in my case, so I'm playing the game in a 4:3 window. The game's options are full of bugs that may crash the game, so be careful.

Okay, I've put a decent amount of time into the game already with intents on pouring countless more hours into it as it grows and gets tweaked.
Thus far however, as with any game I've noticed some good things and some bad.  It is possible I missed the ability to do certain things, feel free to correct me.
For one, the game is streamlined more with the monsters and whatnot and so it makes the evolving of creatures such as Orcs into Ironhides and Goblins in Gob-Bots pretty simplistic and rewarding for your army and it helps out a lot.  The fact you can host a smaller army cap just because it is so much easier to make stronger and more buff units is nice and the tweaking of the beasties to give them more defined roles and capabilities is quite nice even if it a bit simple. (Which I like.)
The UI is.. nice, it has some small issues that I personally do not enjoy and yet it is a very nice and clean UI that has little to no issues except for one thing that I have noticed.  Sometimes you can get locked in place while doing something like refilling or digging and can't click anything until you hit esc a thousand times (Small Correction, this locking which is still on-going is more easily fixed by right clicking once or twice.  I recommend trying that if it happens to you.)  The other UI thing I do not like is the Menu on the left.  I'd personally love an option to make it there permanently just for my own screen.  Waiting for it to pop up is obnoxious, fortunately we can avoid Some of the hassle by Hotkeying the options in this menu.  Which I use ` through 5 and it makes it very simplistic and yet I still want the ability to pull and keep it up.
The difficulty isn't too over the top and you can increase it higher if you are inclined with the added bonus objectives for achievements being present, the humor from Thalya and the narrator in place make it enjoyable and a proper laugh even as you get into some intense fights and traps.
The traps by the way might be the biggest improvement, as someone whom admittedly plays far too defensively.  I play aggressive defense, and as such properly take too long to complete maps and yet I love a solid defense.  This defensive play was crippled in the second one by three or four Bards at once coming in and crapping all over my defenses and now if you aren't paying attention they can sorta stroll through and yet with one or two clicks you can obliterate the enemy and it is rewarding.
It feels like a new Dungeon Keeper (without being it.. cause.. y'know.. don't sue me.)  So overall, I find it pretty damn impressive and if you enjoyed the old Dungeon Keeper, or Dungeons 2 you should get this game and no-life it 100%.
PS:  Who the hell doesn't open with buying a Naga first?  Seems a given.

Not a bad addition to the series, but I think it takes as many steps back as it does forward.
The UI is less intuitive, and things are hidden behind pages when they should be accessible from the main screen. This is mainly an issue of spells being too clumsy to use. The game could greatly benefit from a "Hot Bar", akin to WoW.
Monster collection is just a pain in the rear, and the version in dungeons 2 is far superior as a way to collect critters. The new UI is too busy being pretty to be useful. It is entirely too damned large.
The game style is a bit of a departure from previous titles. (to include dungeon keeper). There is now a resource which you must collect from the over-world, so the days of hiding behind a wall of traps is gone. Also, your units are a lot less micro-intensive, freely using their skills without having to be "activated". I think this is an over-all positive.
The game is worth between 30-40 dollars, but if you have NOT played any of the previous titles, get dungeons2 instead. It is a slightly (ever so slightly) better game, for 1/4 of the price. Once done with that, if you want more, get this game.

What a mess! There appears to be far too many things wrong with this game. My experience: At some point in the game my workers started sleeping day and night and not coming out of their hut. I think they must have had sleeping sickness! This was concurrent with the appearance of white, yellow and green glowing sprites randomly appearing and growing and then disappearing. Later, my character became vegetarian and would only eat fruit and veg. Also, the giant glowing yellow & black worm started crawling around everywhere and eating the screen and then randomly disappearing. Things started getting worse when my workers refused to go anywhere near the market and who could blame them. Instead they delivered the good to the wrong places and lost them (and the money). Finally, my character shaved her head, refused to eat anything and soon after she became ill and died. On her death, her husband stood over her. I thought he acted a bit shifty. What bizzare stuff!
Other issues with the structure of the game are:
1- The main screen is not really useful and the overview screen is the one used most. But the character shows ups as a small grey radiating dot on a very grey overview screen. Finding the tiny grey character on a grey screen? Really clever and hard on the eyes too!
2- There is hardly any time for character chatting and socialising etc when all that the character is doing night and day, is shifting goods between places to flog them. Otherwise, will go bankrupt.
3- Having nights is pointless. It just time wasted making the game longer/slower and is very annoying. There is nothing to be done or achieved, except for the character to shift goods to the market.
4- When you upgrade anything (workplace, shelves, carts etc) often the money disappears but there is no upgrade made to the item.
5- Once you have a particular shop there is no point in producing all the goods available. The best strategy is to make the most expensive one, and sell it to the market which pays highest. For example, the farm produces many goods but producing carcases produces the best profit. Also, by not making certain goods it is possible to push others like the bakery out of business, and take them over.
6- Camera view direction randomly jumps on changing between overview and main screen. Also annoying.
Overall, I think the idea/structure of the game is poorly planned, there is far too many things wrong with the game-plan, and from my experience, too many bugs in the programming of this game.

I have never been a big console fan, and so I have never been a master of the venerable 360 controller (or any other). I feel like at the end of the day it is nice to have each control and command exactly where you want them. I love that the dpad  could be a mouse, joystick, scroll wheel, menu system, 4 buttons, 8 buttons, or even a collection of macro keys. You can even have the controller switch modes gracefully during game play so that you can use the ideal setup for roaming the world, and then easily switch to the ideal setup for combat, or building or whatever other mode seems relevant to you.
Over all the hardware feels solid, updates come regularly, and the controller provides all the individuality and customizability that sit at the core of pc gaming and makes it district from its consol breathen. If you are a pc gamer looking for a controler get this! If you are a console gamer looking to play pc games you will probably be disappointed.

What can I say?  I'm in love with this game.  I've only had this game for two weeks and I'm already losing track of how many times I've played though it.  Meanwhile my $60 AAA titles are collecting dust on the shelf and I couldn't care less.  Moar bunnies plz.
What I thought at first glance was just a fanservice title has impressed me at every turn and quickly became one of my all time favorite games.  In my eyes its success is owed to its focus on just a couple simple, but fun, concepts: you explore, collect items, and fight bosses.  This is no second-rate knockoff however -- this is a true Metroidvania/Touhou experience and I daresay even better than its predecessors from which it derives its inspiration.
The exploration is clearly in the spirit of Metroidvania, and the game's non-linear story grants you a lot of freedom to tackle events in just about any order you wish.  I myself had such a blast exploring that I ended up clearing most of the game while still in the first chapter.  Boss encounters take after the Bullet Hell genre; if you are a fan of Touhou and the like you are in for a real treat.  Bullet patterns are original and fun to learn, and with the number of difficulties available to the player both novices and veterans alike will find a suitable challenge.
The graphics are simple, but colorful and pleasant.  The soundtrack is incredible and does a stellar job of capturing whatever setting you may find yourself in -- it is more than worth the extra $5 or $6.  I found myself streaming it off YouTube whenever I wasn't playing the game and soon realized it was a must-buy.
It's also worth noting that the developers are very active in the forums and are continuing to patch in new, free content.  Just recently they added 3 new bosses, how great is that?  It's obvious they love their game.
And I love playing it.  Get this game!!!

The difficulty is extreme, even on easy mode, which I can't bring myself to play (always normal mode because damn, hard mode is nearly impossible), but well worth your time to learn the patterns and slowly progress a little further on each run.

TL:DR - Get this game. Ikaruga is a harsh mistress, but will reward you in kind.

- Dungeons 3 has, compared to Dungeons 2, less features, as others have already mentioned. This however has not affected the fun I had playing it.
- The voice acting of the narrator is great, but that of the main protagonist a bit weak, compared to Barthas of part 2.
- Apparently the tech-tree has to be re-researched from scratch  every single mission, which sucks a bit.
- Kalypso (the publisher, not the developer) has massive issues with responding to technical issues about the game. I have yet to receive anything more than a "ticket received" message following my bug report to them. (Edit from 20th October 2017: I received a standard Copy&Paste Text saying that I have the wrong Linux version. This despite me having explained them why it is not the case)
The good:
- Everything else pretty much: This game has of course lots of elements from Dungeon Keeper, but also quite a strong RPG and Tactical/RTS edge to it. You cannot just sit in your dungeon, you have to send out teams on the surface to reach your objectives. At most you can have 20 creatures (not counting workers and heroes/titans) at the same time, so the scale is not yet grand-strategy and closer to an RPG with a really large adventuring party.
- Snots now move faster compared to D2, though they are still not gaining any XP
- Improved graphics compared to D2
The really great:
- The way the developers react to bad ratings (such as this one was in the past) and to bugs. Despite Kalypso's (the publisher) best effort to keep them isolated from complains and bugs, within only 2 days of me describing the crash issues I had on Linux they had prepared a patch. Before that (see the comments below) they had already responded to my criticism and promised a quick fix. I did not feel ignored as I sometimes do when complaining to developers of AAA-games.
- Available on Linux from the start.
See below for my original negative rating:
Massive crash-issues under Linux. Game crashes again and again, without any error messages, forcing me to spam the quicksave function.

I hadn't played any of the earlier games in the series, given their age, and thought that this prequel looked interesting, but hadn't played it until it was included in a recent Humble Bundle (cheap games- hoorah!). Right off the bat, the game's gameplay gave me a vibe similar to that of one of my absolute favorite games, Dishonored. Much like Dishonored, which I quickly found to have taken inspiration from the Deus Ex series, the game revolves around player choice. Levels are littered with multiple paths to take, with many secret passages, documents, and goodies for those willing to take the time to search for them. Need to get into the police headquarters? Convince your buddy from your days as a cop to let you in! Don't want to take the time to do that? Have no heart? Waltz in guns blazing! Prefer to be an unseen ghost? Sneak in from the sewers! You don't even have to kill people, the game gives you multiple options for non-lethal playstyles by equipping the character with a tranquilizer rifle or a stun gun. Personally, I prefer the 'ghost' route, while the most challenging, it's surely the most rewarding! The game takes the player on an adventure all across the world in the amazingly detailed future of 2027, with an intriguing plot filled with corporate espionage, conspiracy, political scandal, and a surprising look at possible issues of our future. One of the core issues discussed in the game is human augmentation, and it's morality. Some argue that augmenting oneself will lead them to become more than human, losing their moral compass in the process, leading to devastating chaos and war. Others see it as progress, moving toward a better, safer future. Although this takes place a fictional future, it does serve as a vehicle to question transhumanism, is it just for mankind to try to outmatch the forces that created us? One sad flaw with this great game is the main character, Adam Jensen. Jensen is an ex-cop, dark past, blahblahblahblah, blah, blah. He has little emotion for a sizable portion of the game, and his character doesn't actually show until the latter quarter of the plot. For most of the game, Jensen is just another cookie-cutter hero, and arguably, for the entire game. I would guess Jensen was written this way so that the player could better fit into his shoes, still, he comes off as a badly written character. The world Deus Ex: Human Revolution is set in is hands down, the most in-depth sci-fi world I have ever experienced. The game touches everything from future food, to future politics. The player experiences the expansion of a city in China, Hengsha, as it has run out of room, the city has built an entire new level ONTOP of the old, truly making use of its space. Up in the artic, among choice locations in the world's other oceans, is a massive structure being built in order to counter global warming by use of iron-seeding. The player visits the world's largest news station, now corrupt and fully aware of how much power is granted to them by controlling the media. Further adding to the depth of this world are little things, such as future fashion, and vehicles. All in all, this mystery thriller was thoroughly enjoyable, and had a well-written plot that kept me wondering what would happen next, and left me with several questions to ask about the way the world works. I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who isn't scared by a lengthy playtime (it took me 26 hours, spread over the course of a month), and likes stories that make them think.

Although I was a moderate Doom fan in the early years I was not expecting to like this release very much.  I have generally fallen out of love with most shooters.  I was very very pleasantly surprised to find that this incarnation of Doom is fantastic!  The soundtrack and sound design is top-notch.  The only beef I had was a few times I loaded it up and the sound cut in and out as I was playing.  I have no idea what caused it and it made me miss some audio-only storylines in the campaign for my first playthrough on some missions.  I will have to play those missions again to find out what I missed.  The graphics are great and I had no issues at all with FPS or dropouts/freezes - it played perfectly smoothly even when the audio was stuttering and dropping out some.  In any case, I suspect it was something going on on my PC so I don't blame the game - it seemed to handle being played very well.  The campaign seemed relatively short to me.  I stink at games - even on the easy settings - but I felt like it didn't take long to get through.  Luckily, there are loads of secrets and goals to go back and replay - and the levels are great so it is nice to have new things to go back and do.  In all, I was expecting a solid 6/10 but this easily ranks a 9/10.  Now excuse me while I go buy the soundtrack!

Rabi-Ribi is a metroidvania style game with the added insanity of bullet hell mechanics during boss fights. You play as a psychopathic amnesiac, 5% bunny 95% girl with Stockholm’s syndrome named Erina. You join her on a murderous rampage through a forest filled with peaceful woodland creatures with Shadow of the Colossus like efficiency. The “artful” character models used during the lengthily dialogue sequences are almost enough to distract you form a plot so thin, it could win America’s next top model. Besides ridiculous dialogue sequences that substitute brevity for intrigue, the game has tons of upgrades that will no doubt have you backtracking through the basic and boring zones in search of that one HP+ upgrade you missed because you didn’t have the “Super Triple Mega Lightning Double Wall Carrot Jump ™ © 2016”.
All that being said, it is a fun and simple game. Rabi-Ribi tries to cram in upgrades as a substitute for complexity and just winds up feeling more like a distraction than a truly engaging experience. You can tell there is something going on in the story but the character’s unwillingness to discuss important topics leaves you reading tons of “filler” dialogue that make you wonder “ Why the hell am I reading all of this?”. Ultimately Rabi-Ribi is a metaphor for life itself, the enjoyment you get out of it is equal to what you put in, with a ton of boredom, frustration, pantsless girls and masculin fairies in the middle.

I simply can't be bothered to learn to chain since it's just not much fun. I tried it on the first stage, since it's quite easy there, but on stage 2 it's already way harder — and not just to properly chain while staying alive, but even more so to just figure out a route.
That really is the heart of Ikaruga: figuring out the best route to chain all the enemies and then of course also pull it off. I don't really care for that tough and especially not when I'm playing a shooting game.
Compared to other games with bad scoring systems like Dodonpachi, Ikaruga is way more designed around its scoring system — to such a point really that when you play for survival, the flow of the game (and the logic of the game world) is totally ♥♥♥♥ed up. There are long parts where all you do is change polarity every couple seconds and that's it. Enemies that don't even shoot at you are commonplace in Ikaruga, sections where you don't have to do almost anything in order to survive, plentiful.
Dodonpachi is at least still fun to play when you ignore scoring, Ikaruga is just depressing when you play it that way.

Let me first say I have played like 8 hours atm. The first thing to mention is, that the game still has a few bugs in gameplay. One of them gamebreaking, and had to start the mission over again. Furthermore music tends to sometimes mix up on places where it shouldn't (switching between dungeon and overworld uncorrupted land for instance)
So let's start for real now.
For those that are unfamiliar with this genre of game: dungeons is a so called 'dungeon master'. You play a evil lord that creates a dungeon for the heroes to storm in, and die in.
Now in comparison to dungeons 2, so far I can tell the dungeon functionalities have greatly improved. You have more dungeon rooms to experiment with, and healing has become available pretty soon from start. Furthermore has research become more organized in a handy menu.
The downside I so far have exprienced is only the micromanagement. Many traps are no longer automatic, and have to be manually activated, increasing the level of micromanagement. In combination with the time presure focused missions, this can pose a bit of a problem.
Overall I quite enjoyed the game so far, though it sometimes lacks the humor of the previous game. Giving this game a 6.5/10

This game is my first foray into the Dungeon Keeper style games.  I've played plenty management sims, but the closest game I've played to this is Evil Genius.
Overall?  9/10  The game is a lot of fun.  There is a wide variety of traps, research oppotrunities, and unit combinations you can try and explore.  While you are very restricted in the first few campaign missions, after a while, you are able to attack problems in a variety of manners.
My only real problem with the game is that the game doesn't teach you (or doesn't have) some valuable interface options when designing your dungeon.  For example, I don't know how to rotate traps that go on walls--I have to simply mouse over the same corner over and over until, by luck, the wall trap aligns with the wall I want.  My current solution is to avoid wall-based traps.  This alignment problem comes up in the context of structures that you place in rooms as well--I have to jiggle my mouse and hope to get lucky.  This seems like something that can be easily fixed in an upcoming patch.
There is another issue.  The game doesn't do a very good job of explaning things.  Perhaps the Alamanc could be updated with more information?

As a fan of both The Sims and all things Medieval, this game has been enjoyable for me. It's casual and low stress for when I'm not in the mood to play something fast-paced or combat heavy. There are some bumps and gaps that need to be smoothed out, but that's exactly why it's called early access. Overall, I think it has a lot of promise, and I look forward to seeing how it develops from here. I have thought of a couple of things that would streamline playability and prolonging my interest in a single character that also might interest other players:
A more developed objective system. It by no means needs to be story heavy, but a little more direction might keep it from getting aimless a couple hours in. Maybe errands or tasks on the side from NPCs to affect relationships, that sort of thing.
One of the more consistent frustrations I experienced was trying to click on people. As they move around, you have a very, very small window to click on them and access the available interactions. Most of the time I miss and end up telling my character to walk to a new location. I think refining that mechanic would make gameplay much smoother.
I'm sure the developers have a lot of ideas and plans as this game grows, and I'm excited to see what they are. I think my main interest would be to see more options for customization of the towns, characters, etc., but I also understand the time and effort required to make those sorts of changes. All of these things aside, I think this game is entertaining and enjoyable, and the replay value will only increase as it gets more refined.

All the fun of playing video games with a trackpad. Gave me nostalgia for all those inexplicable purchases I\'ve made in the past and don\'t tend to make anymore.
Technically, you can get it to work with any game that doesn\'t have controller support since it can emulate a mouse. The deep customization you can do is both a positive and a negative because it\'s pretty much required. People do upload their own profiles and Steam will detect the game you\'re in and show the relevant ones. In my limited experience these profiles tend to be half-baked and require further work. Having fun yet?
Big Picture Mode is required. Aside from being terrible in general, it also crashed once, whiping out progress on a profile I was working on at the time. Good feature.
It works fine for a game that only requires some buttons and a single stick, although the ergonomics of the controller and placement of the stick caused pain in my hand after only a short time using it. If it\'s an active game that requires camera movement with the mouse then forget it. Imagine controlling the camera with finger swipes. The rest of the controls can be summed up with being awkward in general. Mainly the layout and shape of things. The buttons on the inside of the handles I actually do like though. Probably because they\'re as easy to activate as squeezing the handles you\'re already holding, requiring no additional hand movement. My idea of a great controller is one that has the maximum amount of inputs with the minimum amount of effort required. The designers of this must have had a different philosophy.
It has rumble under the trackpads. This is somehow supposed to make it feel like you\'re using a trackball. I was also once told that it\'s meant to let you know when your finger is getting too close to the edge. Both of these statements are rubbish. Your finger is always going to be too close to the edge when using it and the rumble itself feels completely flat. Like it\'s not trying to tell you anything and is only serving to distract you from the game. It\'s also extremely loud and I thought my controller was broken when I first tried it. When I realized that it wasn\'t actually broken and that this was a feature I was very confused as to the point of it. Are games supposed to specifically support it? I feel that with a feature like this the point of it should be immediately apparent. Rumble in controllers in general is good. The rumble triggers on the Xbox One Controller are good. This? I'm left with no clue.
What would have made it better? Maybe put an actual trackball on it? Can\'t be any worse than trackpads, which have always been a compromise of design instead of an ideal method of controlling a mouse. It\'s the same here. It\'s a compromise.
In general I wouldn\'t recommend it. It only works acceptably for simple or slow games despite its deep customization options and vast key mapping possibilities. You would have a very bad experience playing Half Life 2: Episode 3 on one for example.

Oooh boy. Wow. Unbelievable. And not in a good way, either.
This controller was advertised as the bridge that would cross the gap between console gaming and PC gaming. The device that would bring power and convenience together in a big happy family. It was made to be as precise as a gaming mouse, but as easy to use as a controller. In reality though, it is neither.
The claim of ease of use assures that anyone can pick it up and use it. Assuming that the game its used for doesn\'t depend on things like accuracy or fast reaction times or the ability to hit the right button, they nailed that part. I can\'t begin to express the alien nature of this thing\'s design. First off, the right trackpad - the equivalent to the right joystick - is ABOVE the ABYX buttons. For anyone that has ever used a Playstation or Xbox, this is an obvious mistake. Most people that want to use this thing probably come from those two consoles and can\'t stand to play without a decent controller. And when they come from a world where the buttons are above the joystick, this is going to take A LOT of getting used to.
Beyond that, the trackpads are absolute garbage. I did a test in three different games; BO3, Bioshock Infinite, and Skyrim. I made two marks on the trackpad with a sharpie and while in game I dragged my finger from one mark to the other and back again. There was not a single time that the camera returned to it\'s original position, like it should\'ve. So when you\'re playing an intense game and wondering why your thumb is on the edge of the trackpad when you\'re still facing the same direction you were a minute ago, thats why.
Speaking of trackpads, they\'re awful to use. Even if they were as precise as advertised, they would still be impossible. They\'re in such an awkward position on the controller that you have to strain your thumbs to reach them. A controller is meant to feel ergonomic, but this feels more like a torture device straight out of the Spanish Inquisition.
And another thing, the buttons. Ooooh the buttons. It seems in every gaming session I have the buttons don\'t work like they should. Most commonly, it\'s a double press issue, as in, every time I press a button, the signal gets sent twice. This makes navigating menus an absolute nightmare, and the impact on gameplay is even worse. And there\'s no fix for it in sight. The only solution is to turn off and on the controller, but doing that five times per match gets frustrating. But more that that, the buttons are inconsistent in their softness, as in, a stray hair could pull a trigger but Dwayne Johnson would have trouble pressing the shoulder buttons.
At least we can make our own custom control schemes to try and compensate for the buttons. Or can we? The freaking controller configurations menus are terrifying to navigate. I\'ve lost more configurations than I can count to these ungodly menus. And every time steam updates, the configurations reset to default, and it\'s like navigating Medusa\'s Labyrinth trying to find the right one.
Possibly the worst aspect of this customization feature is the mandatory waiting period ofter an edit. When you make a new configuration, you want to be able to immediately fix and hiccups when you see them in game. But it takes almost a minute to save the stupid configurations. This wouldn\'t be bad except for \"perfectionists\" like me who want their controllers to work they way they\'re supposed to. So when you flip back and forth between the game and the controller customization menu, be prepared to spend more time on the loading screen than anywhere else.
A few other complaints that I can\'t really write an entire section on; The haptic feedback feels like death spasms of an autistic chihuahua, the plastic feels about as sturdy as a cardboard cereal box, the grips curve toward the user which pushes your hands away from the controller, the noise it makes when turning on and off make me want to fill my ear canals with rubber cement, and it looks like something my cat would hack up.
All in all, this controller sucks. I hate every aspect of it. Save yourself some money and a headache and buy a Playstation or Xbox controller from Amazon instead.

List of Pro's/Con's so far:
+ The best Neptunia release in the series for many reasons as below
+ More serious/upbeat OST along with the old ones
+ More characters introduced
+ More interaction with cities like investing etc
+ Scouts work similar to Fairies from Fairy Fencer F
+ Has that Next-Gen feel to it with wider areas with more detail
+ Reworked, Redrawn characters during dialogue scenes
+ Tweaked system from Fairy Fencer F
+ Well matched voice actors
+ New win, level-up-a-des poses
+++ Tsunako. I want to marry her art
- Old OST from previous games feels over used and shouldn't have been added
- Some characters taken out like Plutia for e.g, should have been added as DLC character
- Some areas can leave you feeling a little lost especially when in a rush to save
- EXE bars fill too fast
- No difficulty option
- No 4K support (mod workaround)
- Nepgya not worth as DLC character. I get the humor in it but should really be unlockable accessory for Nepgear

I've you've even partially enjoyed any of the previous Neptunia games then you need to play this one.
The story is their best yet, the music is better than ever, Formation and Coupling skills now actually feel like a part of the game rather than simply tacked on, and the DLC characters actually feel like a part of the world.
Add to that several story elements that are either rare in this series if not straight up unheard of and you've got a recipe for a solid experience all around.
The main story has many twists and turns that I simply did not see coming as well as several moments that reminded me why I keep playing these games time and again.
One thing that I really loved is that after your first run through you get items to make it much faster to get back to the parts you want to play through again without getting stuck with all the drudge work of the first run through.
The music, as I said before, is better than ever. Getting to a serious moment and having the perfect music kick in with flawless timing makes those great moments feel even cooler. Add in the ability to rewatch literally any scene you've seen allows for easier access to those great moments without having to trudge through an entire nother run just to see it.
Seriously, play this game. If you're here reading this then you will probably enjoy it.

TLDR
A fairly bland yet well paced game with minimal grinding needed and lots of dialog.
A hyperdimension game that exceeds all of the other RPG hyperdimension games. But still disappoints, they do not aspire to give the game the dimensions needed to win awards, or impress me. It had a few good moments but many of these fell flat. A game not worth it's 50$ price (I think it's 35$-45$).
It's still in my perspective a mediocre (but improving) JRPG that relies on it's "cutesy" characters and laid back story to sell, this game certainly ain't bad, but compared to other games this game isn't that good. Buy this game if you want a mediocre japanese RPG with cutesy characters and tons of dialog of which only 50% is voiced. (and soft porn)
---------------------STORY
Beginning with story/world, I believed it to be ok, but with a touch of anime "logic" in that in the "dimensions" there are certain rules that if one thinks can predict what is to come, and better foreshadowing; when the mysterious voice talks to some of the characters in the "better off" dimension in a certain way, indeed there is a "guessing game" in the story that is functional and somewhat captivating.
The hyperdimension drivel is still here of course, but this time is injected into scenarios even more out of place than the previous games, almost as if a checklist; whenever there is a big boss battle there is a segment of drivel dialog to lighten things up bafflingly, you can compare with minimal error it to soldiers in a "military shooter" talking about their country's superstars in the seconds prior to combat; literally about an 1 or 2 sentences are committed to it, now I like my drivel, and the overall lightheartedness of the story but there are better ways of transmitting it.
About 95% of the story is done through this animated 2d artwork that is nice and definitely cheap and effective but it leaves me craving, indeed this is a restricting thing that the developers chose to do that does not permit many cinematographic techniques; you will be seeing these 2d artworks doing the talking with little added to make it impactful, I felt they neglected to use other modes of communicating story, probably since it was cheaper this way. The cut-scenes in this game are used mainly to show transitions, and are what I feel is a neglected idea when it comes to varying how the story will be expressed and would be better if these happened more often during the middle of the game, where small cut-scenes would be played to better entertain me, but the current direction of their use is rare when used for story, and is more often as an enhancement to combat as a short improvised cutscene during it, I suspect most of their "cut-scene budget" was spent on the "cut-scene attacks" that you can make your character use.
I recall what I thought was a waste of 3d assets in a fight between the witch and the purple-haired character, where they had an opportunity to have the camera pan on the character's faces as the fight ground down and dialog ensues, instead it quickly reverts back to the 2d stuff.
About 80% of the humor and humor deriving from 4th wall breaking is coming from the dialog with comments like "switching out the protag; Really?" or "here comes a source of EXP and credits" or "UGH, annoying", and incidents with the story dialog, some of it was funny though much of it constrained in the 2d artwork. I really woulda wanted a greater "Range" of topics that can be expressed in the story, like mayhap more depth into some of the sociological impacts of games or I dare say it, something bad about video games (though I  don't think the developers are brave and/or creative enough to bring up a topic in a way that doesn't clash to harshly with the lighthearted story). Minimally there is also a wish of something more significant in this story, to reduce it's "simple/lightheartedness" and to provide more substantial metaphors, such that when I saw one of the baddies and her "delusion power" I thought we had here an opportunity to hint towards the insanity of our modern situation, but to some disappointment it was largely a baddy power, and not really a metaphor for anything. A part of me also wanted more environmental or absurdist humor in it, the kind that "goat simulator" specializes in; like making a level that is a parody of some trope or some "rule" in gaming and then have the characters comment on it, rather than having nearly all of the humor coming from character dialog, of which indeed would have been expensive but I think would expand and improve the humor. However a point against me is that likely, much of the humor is too japanese-specific to be registered by me so thus some of my points are weakened.
Midway through the game they chose to to split up the the 4 main characters up into their own smaller adventure which was nice, since it that let more of their dialog and personalities show through instead of having it to compete with all of the others, though I felt that the good guys were largely the same bunch that one experienced in the last couple of games. Often it felt that there was some absurd luck as if from a cartoon came to twist the fate of the good guys inexplicably, like when another "Goodie" fell from the sky and helped them, or when the witch suddenly is saved by the ninja, or the gullibility of the main character, or the many times the goodies or the baddies get away from danger, all of this reinforces the cartoonly narrative, but I still feel something lacking. This could all be seen as refreshing if you had not played another Jrpg or have been isolated to your own culture, but they became boring to me about 60% into the game, then I preferred to read and rush through the goodie's dialog instead of hearing it, and the only the bad guys (specifically the robots) I listen to (since I wanted to see how they would trash the goodies).
Some of the fun in that midway section came from the peculiar nature of the new rulers of the nations, they didn't really care that much about ruling and weren't about gaining power yet they still had it, and most saw it as on opportunity to live their lives closer to their dreams, indeed 3 of them weren't really in charge of their own societies, content to live in their own ideal life, and the 4th was so relaxed in exercising her powers as to be well "cool" but unfit for ruling. I personally like these kinds of reversals and the "good guys" interacting with them to get back their nations.
Towards the end (optimal ending), I felt the game was inflating it's gameplay a bit, with additional content that didn't feel timely, since clearly the "core reactor" was destroyed and the "ship" was collapsing and yet the characters stayed for an inordinate amount of time fighting bosses and enemies for what felt like 4 dungeons, the story was properly climactic at that time, but I would have preferred that once "core reactor" was destroyed the story dramatically sped up to hurry along to it's end, which I thought would have been an improvement.

After looking into the gameplay of Rabi Ribi, I found that it had some of my favorite game genres mixed together:

I like HoGs. I can mindleslly click through not-so-hard puzzles and the plot is usually easy to follow and mildly engaging.
Well, so what's wrong with this one?
Where to start? I'll leave one almost game-breaking thing for the end because it's caused only by translation. But besides that, there's nothing particulary GOOD about this game. The puzzles are decent, the graphics are decent too. The plot makes me scratch my head because I have no idea what I'm actually doing. I started with a mission to save parents and their secret order (haha, k, why not)... but then suddenly I travel to
and do weird things like crafting amulets or torches, which may sound cool on paper, but in game was a mundane task and I basically was going to the places that the map was telling me to go and was doing things with no understanding. It should make at least a little sense, but when the puzzle ends at "you need to touch this, and craft that and use this stone and set this on fire because I'm just telling you to do so" it's just... frustrating? I don't know, it simply feels like I'm no longer an active part of the story and more just a pawn to move around. It really disconnected me from the whole story and I no longer happily progressed through adventure - it felt more like dusting and old, unfamiliar place. Though someone would possibly pay me for dusting.
Voice acting... Oh gee. This is the first HoG I played with muted sound :D Normally I don't care what my flatmate thinks about the games I play, but in this case... Well, you can imagine.
GOING BACK AND FORTH. This should be banned from games in general. Half through this title I switched to moving by clicking on map, because to do one thing you have to go through ~5 locations. And when you do this thing you have to go back the ~5 locations you just passed to progress. But then the game suddenly wants you back at the location you just left... This should be banned, smh.
Btw. it didn't help with being disconnected from game. The moment you start jump around totally different locations makes it (the game, the story, the puzzles) even less approachable.
Last but not least, but it's about Polish translation, so I'll put my concerns in Polish (it's funny though how game made by Polish studio has the translation so ♥♥♥♥ed up):
Więc rzecz w tym - nazwy nie zgadzają się, z tym, co trzeba znaleźć, polecenia nie zgadzają się z tym, co trzeba zrobić, to co mówi bohaterka, ma się nijak do tego, co próbujemy osiągnąć. Nie wynotowałam wszystkich przykładów, ale:
- w jednej z hidden object scen jednym z przedmiotów do znalezienia jest RURA. No spędziłam chyba z dobre pięć minut wgapiając się w monitor jak w święty obrazek, aż w końcu machnęłam ręką i sięgnęłam po walkthrough. Otóż co się okazało: to czego szukałam to FAJKA. Zarówno 'fajka' jak i 'rura' to po angielsku 'pipe', ale rozumiecie, że różnica kolosalna. Tak samo z inną sceną, w której szukamy WIEŻY (figury w szachach). Po angielsku to ROOK, co znaczy też GAWRON. No więc gra każe mi szukać gawrona i ja klikam po raz siedemdziesiąty drugi na jakieś koślawe ptaszysko i niE DZIAŁA, GRR.
Ale to jeszcze mogę sobie jakoś wytłumaczyć - tłumacz nie widział kontekstu, przełożył jak mu się wydawało - fakap ze strony studia, ale mogę być wyrozumiała i przymknąć oko. Tylko że jest jeszcze drugi problem, który nie wiem, czy bierze się z tłumaczenia czy z czegoś innego i znów na poparcie moich żalów i pretensji wynotowałam sobie dwa przykłady:
- bohaterka mówi "potrzebuję czegoś ostrego, żeby pociąć kłody na mniejsze kawałki" (dosłownie, to cytat), po czym rozwiązaniem tego problemu okazuje się zebranie czterech klinów i wbicie je w kłody. SERIO?
- "ten kran tu nie pasuje", podczas gdy staram się zakręcić kurkiem wodę. LASKA CZY TY WIDZIAŁAŚ KIEDYŚ JAK WYGLĄDA KRAN?
Swoją drogą ^ to jest moment, podczas którego rage quittowałam i na razie nie zamierzam wracać, bo znów mam wrażenie, że pomimo tego, że "muszę zakręcić wodę" tak naprawdę gra oczekuje ode mnie czegoś innego i bez solucji nigdy nie odkryję o co tak naprawdę chodzi.
The end of rant. Not recommended, the story is too meh, if you play with Polish translation you need a solution at hand, if you want a lot of clicking... just go for one of these clickers that are free to play. It will be more appealing, that's for sure.

Reading the reviews made me nervous to play this (I got it with a pack of other, higher-rated games) but I think going in with low expectations helped. The plot isn't /so/ bad considering it's a point-and-click, but the first act moves bizarrely fast. Rather than build plot and info you start off knowing pretty much everything and go from there. Once you get past that it's not /so/ bad; it's not the best, I rolled my eyes at times, but it's not terrible. The voice-acting, though, is absolutely godawful. Click to continue when you can, and if cinematics don't matter to you (they don't reveal anything at all this go) just go beyond them. The graphics are good, but that doesn't really make up for it all. The number of clicks is low, there isn't much to find or use or puzzle out. I would NOT reccomend buying this on its own, not even necessarily if it's on a good sale. if you end up with it, though, you won't want to slit your throat or anything. It's just not great. Artifex does good games on their own, but this was just of their production, not their creation. Replayability is basically null as well.
tl;dnr - Eh. Even if you like point-and-clicks like me, just... eh. I love these things in general, but I won't be buying the prequels or the sequels.

The Order of the Griffins is facing a new danger, as a new member in the order turned traitor and murder one of the Secret Five. The assassin is about to join the order, and become a powerful member.
Sarah has to unmask the traitor, and to do so, she embarks the player in a time travel journey to retrieve an object of tremendous power!
is the direct sequel to
, although the first game is not available on Steam. It's actually a shame because the first game despise being old, could interest players who don't like to be lost in the plot. This second game doesn't tell much about the previous installment, but a short resume is available.
The quest to save the Order is indeed a lifetime voyage, following your father steps until you embark on a ship to change the past and preserve the future of the Order of the Griffins!
With fantastic visuals,
nailed with superb colorful areas and mysterious events that will make any adventure fans enjoy their time. With a beautiful design and incredible attention to detail,  the animations are the quality
approvals on their published games, so you know it's good. The same goes for dialogues, and overall quality.
The team went with a full 2D design, and some pretty neat effects to give some 3D illusions, but overall they are  artistically very common with other releases by the same publisher.
The puzzles are for every player's taste, easy and also slightly difficult providing a challenge. Even without a story background to place on the back of your mind, the game is fluid enough to make you believe this is actually the first game, and for those wondering, yes, Masked Intent is much superior to the first chapter.
Hidden Object areas can be also played as a fun, yet simple mahjong game. Adds great value for the last item you can't find, although with the design quality, it's relatively easy to pick up objects at a fast pace!
Traveling across a vast map of cities, hidden territories, and also exploring the biggest threat to the Order of the Griffins, can be pretty exciting, and you'll never feel like you're in the same place twice. In fact, traveling to such different areas, will make you feel into a new complete game, but in a good way!
Big Fish Games is selling the Collector's Edition, with one bonus chapter, concept art, wallpapers and soundtrack. As far as I know, Steam version includes this extra chapter, which is fantastic because it's an extra area in the game map, and perfectly matches within the story. This bonus content also presents the player with the hardest puzzles in the entire game.
is another great adventure HO game released by one of the most popular publishers of the moment, and of course it's a shame we don't have the original adventure as a bonus, as can still enjoy it's sucessor and save the world.

What would happen if, in the future, the prosthetics industry made such huge advances that prosthetic body parts were better than the original ones? So much better in fact that people would take out bank loans to have their (perfectly healthy) limbs cut away and replaced with robotic equivalents? It’s a scary concept, but Deus Ex crafts an absorbing and detailed world around it. A great deal of care has gone into making it all very believable – Incidental things like newspaper headlines, adverts and conversations you overhear in the street give a feel for how that world would function and the pressure to ‘augment’ that the people are under. This aspect of the game is probably the most enjoyable part of the whole experience, as pretty much every implication of the augmented society is hinted at somewhere, and you get plenty to mull over while working through the story.
In gameplay terms this is a polished version of the first game. This time the augments are a bit more balanced but the standard tactics of breaking into everything, knocking everyone out and stealing anything that isn’t nailed down still gives you the easiest route through.  Just like the original Deus Ex, you could approach things different ways though - Guns blazing, hacking, sneaking, diplomacy and exploratory approaches are all catered for, but this causes its own problems. If you like action games you can play most of it like a cover shooter, but you’ll be frustrated at the segments that impose stealth or lengthy conversations with dialogue choices similar to an adventure game. If you like stealth you’ll get annoyed when your sneaky but weak character gets cut down in a Boss fight that you can’t avoid and didn’t ask for. The inclusion of those arcade style Bosses also takes away some of the depth of atmosphere from the game, which is annoying if that’s what you like about it.
In trying to be ‘all games to all people’ Deus Ex ends up being a good game for the most part, but with some incredible elements that you’ll wish you could get more of. The competing styles of gameplay will seem a little off at times– Philosophical outpourings about ‘What it means to be Human’ don’t mesh perfectly with the cheesy cut scenes and the sections where you’re emptying every last clip into a spongy Boss, but on the whole things work most of the time. It still has the same epic scale as the first game too, with around 40hrs of story mode, so there’s still that sense that you’ve covered a lot of ground when the credits roll.

On an average. I don't like to be negative about a game that I have played for only two hours, but for Saelig I make an exception. In the current state, the game is unplayable. Why I am able to make that judgment within two hours? Because the game is too dark and has an interface, which bucks like a bronco.
Darkness. The Dark Ages were dark. I get it. It's supposed to be dark. Then again, I truly wonder why I have to explain to a programmer, that players have an individual affinity towards the darkness of their games. Is it even remotely possible, that there is a reason that I cannot adjust the darkness at night an in the shadows to my liking - I mean, other than shocking oversight? I am not just asking for a gamma correction, which on its own does little to alleviate the problem. And please, pretty please with sugar on top don't tell me to use a torch.
Which brings us to the interface. I haven't seen an interface this catastrophic in decades. It's as if the game doesn't want to be played. Let's put aside, that I actually have to learn a key command to open the map. First problem is, like every command in this game it may not work on the first attempt, which makes learning to play sheer pain. Now, that the map opened, it turns out, it matches the darkness of the daytime. I guess, in the Dark Ages maps did that. Of course, the map is not centered on the character. Of course, the house I own looks like every other house on the map. It turns out, I have a better chance to find myself and the way home in the tea leaves of my Earl Grey than in-game on the map. I can click a button and the screen centers on my home? Cool. I just learned I don't need a map... I guess. So let's not stray far from the abode and begin with something simple. Talking to people comes to mind. Then again, just because the option is offered doesn't mean, that a conversation starts. Is it that the target character was busy just showing the option for kicks and grins, or did the command not work? Who knows. What I do know is that it is unacceptable when I have to go through ten different targets to find someone who stops running away from me or simply ignoring me. Imgine all the possibilities, when my own character is no longer the one I command - not that the interface informs me or, alternatively, I figured out that it does. In the tutorial the bakehouse comes with a cart. The last time I had this much fun learning a functionality, I listened to a drunken brain surgeon at a New Year's party explaining a cat scan of a giraffe.
Aren't you happy now, that I only played this game for two hours? I wonder what all wouldn't have worked for me if I had stayed for a third.
Make the darkness adjustable, and for crying out loud completely redo the interface. Yes, I see the potential this game has, but potential means buttkus, if the game is unplayable.

I'd be lying if I said this wasn't worth watching, but there are a few shortcomings.  It's basically just about a single e-sports team, and it left me wondering whether other such teams work in a similar manner or otherwise.  Another thing is that you could argue that it's outdated.  A lot has changed with the game since this movie was made, so it's not exactly an up-to-date perspective.
That being said, it was still nice to see the history of Evil Geniuses and how things went down 'back in the day'. Nevertheless, I suspect that EG itself has changed at least somewhat since the making of this movie, and that's another question that came to mind while watching: does EG still really work in this way today?
All in all, I guess we should be glad that any movie at all is being made about an e-sports team, especially a Starcraft 2 one. So if you're an avid fan of Starcraft 2 like I am, this is definitely worth watching.  Otherwise, it might only appeal to those curious about how an e-sports team functions, and even then you might be slightly let down.
