Ikaruga is a Danmaku(bullet-hell) shooter made by Treasure. What makes Ikaruga stand out compared to other Danmaku shooters is that it has a polarity system that allows the player to change their ship to black and white. When you are in white polarity the player can absorb white bullets and deal more damage to black polarity enemies. If you're ship is black polarity you can absorb black bullets and deal more damage to white polarity enemies. The game also features a complex scoring system called chaining. To get a chain you must shoot 3 enemies of the same polairty, if at any point you shoot a different colored enemy without completing a chain it will be broken and the chain multiplier will reset. While this isn't important for survival breaking your chain is detrimental to achieving high scores.
Ikaruga as it is an arcade game isn't very story driven. However, the player assumes the role of a Tenkaku Pilot name Shinra who is nearly killed when his ship is shot down by an enemy force called the Horai. Shinra's plane crashes near a small village named Ikaruga. Being the sole survivor of his squadron he is pulled from the wreckage and nursed back to health. After Shinra was nursed back to health Shinra pledged to defeat the Horai, and the villagers entrusted him with a top-secret fighter plane that they had constructed called the Ikaruga. The Ikaruga was no ordinary ship, it was the only ship of it's kind to integrate both energy polarities and being capable to interchangably change polarities of the Horai ships.
Having over 100 hours of experience with this game spanning across the Dreamcast, Gamecube, and Xbox 360 versions the PC Ikaruga port is without a doubt the definitive version of the game. The game has never looked soo clean with HD visuals and Anti-Aliasing, It has also fixed the issues the Xbox 360 version of the game had as well. If you've never played this game before and want something challenging that has high-replay value this is the game for you. If you're someone who likes to credit feed a game and once they're done never go back to it then I can't recommend this game as it is only 5 stages long and if you credit feed through the game it can easily be beaten in 30 minutes.

Ikaruga, developed by a core team of five people at Treasure with some outside help from G.rev, took the setting and foundations of Radiant Silvergun and mixed in the polarity mechanic from Silhouette Mirage thus creating one of the most marvelous shooters in recent times. Words simply cannot express why this game is such a masterpiece, but I guess I can try.
Ikaruga is a bullet hell shoot 'em up coloquially known as "danmaku", you may be familiar with the genre by other popular series like Touhou but this is more among the lines of CAVE's DoDonPachi or Mushihimesama. Your ship has two polarities and can switch at will, only bullets of the opposite polarity can kill you while same polarity bullets can be absorbed to charge up your homing laser. This simple polarity mechanic adds a whole new layer of depth to a game where you would usually shoot everything and try not to die as the "Dot Eater" strategy becomes viable in where you just absorb same polarity bullets and retaliate with your homing laser. Not only that but stages make deliberate use of this mechanic in their design adding a puzzle element to it, where switching polarities according to the hazards becomes a necessity. There's also the chaining mechanic in which killing three enemies of the same polarity awards a "Chain" and keeping the chain up nets you BIG scores. Shmuppers and 1CCers will have a grand old time looking how to score high in here while some may pull their hairs hearing "1 CHAIN, 2 CHAIN, 3 CH- 1 CHAIN, 1 CHAIN". Reminder: this IS a Treasure game after all so expect the difficulty to be close to masochist levels at times, mostly seen in later stages. The Steam version follows the NESICAxLive version so it's up to date and fixed most of the bugs present in the XBLA version, not to mention that Treasure has been doing a good job in keeping the game updated so far with a Gallery Mode having been recently added at the time of this edit.
Graphically, the game isn't all that impressive but it looks damn good despite it's low technical level of graphic quality. The artwork, on the other hand looks absolutely fantastic with illustrations by Yasushi Suzuki's beautiful choice of coloring and hand painted style. These illustrations are ones I'd love to have hanging as posters on my wall. The real winner here is the soundtrack though, although with limited instrumentation and reusing the same melody motif in most songs composer and director Hiroshi Iuchi has managed to make each song convey a different feeling that is coreographed to match the situation of every stage and it's absolutely glorious. You might already be familiar with "Butsutekkai", the boss theme if you've played I Wanna Be The Guy.
Oh yeah, there IS a rather cryptic plot explained in manuals and extra material. It's a bit good but mostly nonsensical and has strong ties with Radiant Silvergun's plot since the final enemy is the same as it is heavily implied that Ikaruga and Radiant Silvergun universes are one and the same.
In the end, Ikaruga is simply a MUST PLAY for anyone. Even if you're not a fan of the genre it should become pretty clear that this game is truly one of the best games ever conceived. I eagerly await more Treasure games in Steam (so how about that PC-exclusive sidescroller you mentioned Treasure?)

tl;dr: The mechanical switch choices for the SC are not great and that makes the controller feel much worse than you'd expect. A HW-revision is planned, which hopefully addresses the issues.
I bought this pretty much on release and it has been collecting dust on my desk ever since.
I've tried using it numerous times in various games and ended up frustrated more than anything. You'd expect a learning curve with the trackpads, but surprisingly, that's the easy part. If you've ever used a laptop with a trackpad, it's the same thing but way better. The software is OK --- You're forced to use Steam Big Picture, so you lose good regular-Steam features like FPS counter, Recent Players and more. The possibilities the software allows you are AMAZING -- Nearly anything can be modified to your liking, but you'll soon find this is as much a curse as it is a blessing (tinkering with settings for days instead of actually playing your damn games).
But... the real issue lies in the hardware, specifically each of the buttons/switches. It seems like Valve completely ignored decades of experience we've gained from manufacturers like Sony and Microsoft and ended up using very weird components that don't work well with each other. While controllers like the Sony DS3, DS4, or Microsoft XB360 and XB1 have a very balanced feel, the Steam Controller feels like they chose components almost randomly:
Bumpers are too tight
Grips are WAY too tight
Trackpad touch sensitivity is very soft
Trackpad button clicks are WAY too tight
Triggers are too soft (not on their own but in comparison to how tight most other buttons are)
What happens most of the time is that your hands are forced into unintuitive battles of strength and grip, sometimes struggling to push one of the tight buttons without accidentally also pushing the soft buttons. For example when you need to apply X amount of force to actuate the Triggers, but X+500% to actuate the Bumpers, it doesn't feel great.
I am 100% sure that with practice and muscle-memory this can be overcome but at the same time, this isn't something you had to do with other input devices. Imagine if half the keys on your keyboard were randomly tighter than others, that's how the controller makes me feel.
There's a video where one of the lead designers of this controller mentioned they are planning a design upgrade and I expect that modifying the mechanical switches is among their main goals. I would suggest waiting for that. Here's the video, around 42min:

I bought this on a whim while deciding on what to get as a new controller since my old one was broken, and on the first day I started to doubt my purchase after I tried it with a few games. The Steam controller feels a little big for my hands, but after getting used to it in a few hours of usage, it feels really nice to use. The design of the controller really fits your hands, even if it's a lil too big. You could customize several elements in the software side of the controller outside of gaming, like naming it, choosing a startup and shutdown tune for the controller, and the brightness of the Steam button on the controller.
The touchpads has a really nice feel to it, the haptic feedback on the left touchpad adjusts to your configuration of the controller. Outside of games, I'm using it for desktop navigation, and it's not that bad. Typing with the steam controller would take a bit more time, but predictive text somewhat speeds up the typing speed.
Every game I tried it with, whether it's a Steam game or not, works well with the Steam controller. With games that are on Steam, you could import some of the community presets, use a generic controller layout, or you could configure it by yourself. With games that aren't, you could use a generic controller layout or set it by yourself. It works well with most of the games I tried it on, like visual novels, RPGs, racing games, etc.
While I don't recommend it as a permanent replacement for a keyboard and a mouse, I would recommend this controller. It takes a little bit time to get used to when you're used to a 360 controller. It's also nice as an alternative for your keyboard and mouse when you're not feeling like moving out of your couch or bed to use your computer.

Let me say first off that I am not the most skilled gamer... Now with that said, I have to say that I really like this product. For some reason it seems to be getting a lot of flack as people are saying that it doesn't function like a mouse or keyboard, and it can't perform like a gamepad... I do agree with both these statements, as it seems to function more as  a middle-man between the three widely-used peripherals.
With that said, this controller has a ton going for it, in my opinion. First off, this controller has a lot of buttons on it. Every single button can be custom mapped to a function that you commonly use, and even the two touchpads can be swapped between a mouse/trackball/scroll and 4-button function. Secondly, like previously stated, you can customize this thing to your heart's content, mapping every single button to whatever keyboard/mouse/gamepad function you like or prefer to use, meaning that you can also set up the controller so that you don't have to memorize strange layouts if you don't want, as you personally get to set up everything. It's also a very comfortable controller, and it doesn't really feel at times like you're holding a controller. It takes a lot of getting used to, though, and when you first start out with it, you're probably going to have a lot of frustration with using it, but it does get easier to use if you just stay with it.
Pros:
- Ability to completely customize the mappings of the controller.
- Can download pre-mapped layouts made by other users to work on the controller.
- Can be used on games that aren't made for a gamepad.
- Can be used outside of Steam, where it acts as a mouse with very basic  keyboard functions.
- Can even customize layouts on non-Steam games.
- Comfortable to use.
- Very good for couch-gaming if you're not the type who likes to be stuck in front of a computer screen.
Cons:
- A steep learning curve for a peripheral device.
- "Mouse" can get lost from you, especially if you have it set as Trackball.
- I don't recommend using it as  a gamepad, as the mouse does not function well as a right joystick, making it hard to control some games (for example: You can't charge the Thief's arrow in Trine when it's mapped as a "mouse joystick".)
I can kind of understand why some people are giving this such negative reviews, but I feel that personally this is a "try for yourself" product (which may seem a little crazy, as it is $50 you're putting up to try it.) But this is one of those products where each individual will have a completely different experience, so you can only take other people's opinions so far. That said, I think it's definitely worth trying if you like couch-gaming or are more used to a controller. It can be used successfully, but it takes some patience and some practice. When you get the feel of it down, though, it's extremely fun and convenient to use.
Closing help/hints:
Some people complain you can't use it on games outside of Steam, but this is easily solved by linking the game in Steam as a non-steam game. This will allow you to customize the controller's layout for the game, regardless where you acquired said game from.
When playing some more intense games like Shooters, you may want to turn the Trackball option off on the mouse section of the controller. As keeping it on can cause you to accidentally swipe the mouse too far, causing your character to look in a totally  unwanted direction.
In closing, I love the controller. It took me some time to get used to it, and I still wouldn't confidently play shooters with it at this point in time, but I'm having fun with it. Definitely give it a try if you're at all interested, you may find you really love this thing.

I don't know if to love this game or to hate it. It has a pretty badass concept of having to fight legendary monsters from Greek mythology in eerie dark dungeons, but it's just executed so badly that I am only left disappointed.
The levels seem to be randomly generated, and your main goal is to slay 7 legendary creatures so that you can unlock a weapon that will let you defeat the final challenge - the Minotaur. The atmosphere is great. It really is spooky and keeps you on the edge of your seat. But it's also ridiculously dark and you can barely see anything, even with your torch fully lit. Switch off the torch and you might as well play with your eyes closed, because there won't be any difference.
The creatures are all crazy overpowered. They all seem to have tonnes of health, some get backup from lesser creatures, and some can even 1-hit kill you. To add salt to the wound, even if you try to be stealthy and hide in the shadows, the creatures still spot you a lot of the time, from behind walls or far corners of the map. You can't hide from them and you can't beat them. You just keep dying over and over.
There are some weapons you can buy before going into the dungeon areas, but those cost a lot of gold, and gold can only be found in the dungeon areas themselves, and you can't backtrack to the shop once you're in the dungeon. The only way out is to either complete the level or to die, and when you die, you lose all the gold you've found in that level. So you just end up having to face impossible odds with weak weapons over and over.
The game also seems to lag a fair bit. I put all the settings to low and switched off camera fx, and the best I can do is to run it at a stable 12 FPS. I guess that makes those hard battles even harder.
Overall, I kind of wish this game was streamlined a bit better, to let the player get better and be able to challenge stronger creatures with time and persistence. From the almost 2 hours I've played of this game, I've gotten nowhere. I did gain some fun out of getting killed in funny ways and recording it, but that eventually gets old and you just wish to be able to actually play the game as it was intended. Not a bad game, but try at your own risk. Unfortunately I can't recommend it in its current state.

Now that I've played the game more extensively, I can make an actual review. This is going to be a long one.
Now, I know that this game is supposed to be a complete overhaul of all the mechanics and elements that made the franchise brilliant. And believe me, it's an overhaul alright. The graphics are nicer, the level design is ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant compared to the Re;Birth trilogy (which is what I'm comparing it to), and the main characters are even more fleshed out than ever before, which I like. The soundtrack is nice as well; some of these tracks are actually pretty amazing.
That said, there is one major problem with this game. I... didn't have as much fun with it as I did with the Re;Birth series. I'll go through the major issues, which combined, make this game a bit lacklustre, at least to me.
- The first is the difficulty. It ♥♥♥♥ing slides about like a wet turd on a teflon floor. The first two areas of the game are nice and easy, then the enemies suddenly gain stats that are about three times as high as the ones just before. This is a ridiculous difficulty spike and it really threw me off when I first got to that third area (and I've finished the entire Re;Birth trilogy so I should be pretty good). Unfortunately, this trend continues throughout the game. Some bosses are easy, some are challenging, but then others are downright cheating (I'm looking at you, K-Sha, you multi-turn, million shots per attack ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). The difficulty of the game flipflops like crazy throughout the whole game and it's not really fun to work around.
- The storyline is not nearly immersive or expansive enough for the story it's trying to tell. Two of the antagonists you see throughout the second part of the game, they're pretty big and important in that bit. Then at the beginning of the third chapter you just defeat them. That's it. THAT'S IT. THEY ARE SOME OF THE BEST AND MOST INTERESTING CHARACTERS AND YOU JUST... DEFEAT THEM. Yeah there's a bit of unnecessary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with the whole 'NEXT' thing, but seriously? The way they portray the whole third chapter, it's like they were never threats at all. This is just one example. Blanc's route during the second chapter is 70% EXPOSITION. The remainder is just bosses and the worst areas in the entire game. There are so many issues with the story that it's barely even worth ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on, and that's a shame, because it could have been REALLY good.
- After literally more than a dozen games, some of which are spinoffs, you'd think, you'd just THINK, that they'd bother to put more effort into their cutscenes than they do. They're identical to the cutscenes from the old games, which I find is just plain laziness more than anything else. I don't quite understand why these games take over a dozen gigabytes when the cutscenes, which take up about a third of the game in total, are just slighty animated portraits with some facial movement... and text. Just text. Admittedly there is a higher percentage of voice-acting in this one, which is great because I love the voices of the characters. It's just that they're still recycling exactly the same style and sprites for these scenes without any innovation.
- And the bosses. The ♥♥♥♥ing combat in general is a near-perfect carbon copy of any other Neptunia game, which is REALLY DISAPPOINTING. The only new mechaninc are the giant fights, of which I experienced two of them, and both of which were in the first chapter, and are never brought up again. BOOOOORIIIING. I want at least some innovation, please, is that too much to ask? But I digress. One new mechanic in the boss battles is the multiple health bars thing. BUT IT'S POINTLESS. They only exist to give a false sense of progression through a boss battle, and nothing EVER makes use of them. WHY HAVE THEM AT ALL? Some major bosses also have some quote they'll utter when they hit half health, but nothing else ever happens, so why bother? The difficulty problem also applies - some bosses are♥♥♥♥♥♥easy and do barely anything, while others ♥♥♥♥ING NUKE YOUR ASSES OFF THE PLANET. Why have bosses with nukes? That's just cheap. And don't even get me started on K-Sha.
I got the bad ending on the first run, which is good, because if I get the bad one then I like that it's because I didn't fulfil the requirements for the good one. The problem with the  bad ending is that the already short story just... stops. Abruptly, and with the whole 'we're all going to die' vibe. That whole bad end just sums up the game really. It's just that in comparison to the Re;Birth games, this is just a bit on the disappointing side.
That all being said, I still had SOME fun with it, just not as much as the old games. I can still recommend it, especially if you've not played the Re;Birth trilogy, but if you want something better, just get those.

After playing for around 4 hours, here's some first impressions:
-Solid platforming and controls. They're pretty tight enough so that you have to be just precise enough to properly move around and dodge the projectiles and other attacks. You're also not super-slow, so not a lot of tedium in traversing.
-Combat. Aside from the dodging and stuff, fighting is pretty cool. Button mashing won't get you anywhere since there's both a stamina meter and a mana meter which you definitely need to control properly to optimize damage and spacing against bosses and other foes. Also, there's a lot of different magic types to switch around for different situations, such as straight-line, AoE, etc.
-Soundtrack. Seriously. When it's cutesy and lighthearted, it fits. When it's a kick-hindquarters bossfight, it fits. And it does change depending on the area.
-The Metroidvania Feel. Large, explorable areas with some places you can't reach until you get a certain upgrade. Finding secrets is also pretty fun and rewarding. There's also Warps, so you don't necessarily have to waste a ton of time backtracking. However, some warps can only be found if you look around closely enough.
-Bossfights. Pretty much like a Touhou boss. Instead of shoot, dodge, and graze, it's shoot, melee, dodge and it feels more dynamic than just watching pretty bullets fly around and hope you don't get hit and die. Also, the bosses have "spellcards" and their movesets change depending on how much HP they have. Pretty cool.
-Artstyle. Some people may not like the cutesy, pixelated, animu, fanservicey look of it all, but it's not too bad and overboard. Game doesn't exactly take itself seriously, either.
-Story. At this point, it's not super-engaging to me, but I guess curiosity did get to me since there is a lot of mystery going around in the background. Not sure if I like it or not, though.
-Difficulty. Well, it's a bullet hell-ish game. I've heard from others that Novice is too easy so I went with Normal. It's a nice blend of difficulty, but it's a bit frustrating. I guess I just have to "git gud?"
-Unexpected Bosses. To be honest, there -are- savepoints nearby which kind of indicate when a boss is going to happen, but sometimes there isn't and the closest warp is pretty far so you can't prepare very well. Kinda sucks, especially when you just want to progress through an area. I do like it to an extent since it changes up the walk through path, dodge and kill enemies formula a bit.
Solid platformer, with that good tinge of difficulty that makes you frustrated but ends up being a thing that makes you try harder and keep going. Price seems to be a little steep, but I didn't find it to be too much for the enjoyment I'm getting.
Still, try getting it on a sale.
Very fun, definitely a recommendation in my book.

+The game offers a variety of difficulties

+ You have the ability to play most missions stealthy or loud.
+/- The stealth system is nothing too unique and combat can be repetitive
+/- The game is set in an open world environment but sometimes you feel it’s a bit linear after all.
Cons:

- Ending is anti-climactic and lacking.
Verdict:
9

The best thing in Deus Ex is that your choices matter, the way the objectives are approached is rewarded differently as you complete both the main story and the side-missions. Use brute force or stealth, it's all up to you.

Not quite my definition of a "Game". More an educational simulator. It is a "Free-to-play" game in the sense that it comes with the nowadays standard (as much as it makes me want to stab someone with a rusty butterknife realising that) psychological warfare that is "microtransactions". For advance unlocks, "Credits", "Experience Boosters", etc.
And the game is not without its problems:
Some components you have to arbitrarily disassemble yourself, even when others do so automatically, which is an "inconsistency of the rules" I consider a crime.
Additionally, some components that you'd assume could be removed or (dis)assembled without interference from other components (example, taking off a muzzle/compensator/suppressor thinking the front sight won't be a holdup), THINK AGAIN, you're doing it their way or not at all! Which is a rather irksome issue. Common sense says that such steps should be performable interchangeably. This is plainly evident with the AK-47's accessory case in the stock, were that step a requirement to proceed, I might think differently, but you can dissassemble everything BUT the stock without any restriction, not only implying that you already have tools on hand, but that the restriction has ZERO reason to be there! And that's from the *first* gun you work on.
Each gun comes with its own array of "Achievements" you unlock towards a massive XP (which is used to unlock more guns) stipend at the end. However there are no less than two such achievements that rely on leaderboard placement. Which is equal parts skill, luck, and psychosis. (Guys, AXE THOSE ACHIEVEMENTS!)
This issue is exasperated by the fact that some components take half-an-iceage to extricate or disassemble themselves.
And lastly there is a small "quiz" minigame you can take every hour that tests your ability to identify certain firearms. Problems being that you only get the thumbnail from the gun "map" to go off of, so similar looking models are easily mistaken for eachother (I'm looking at YOU, Walther PP and Makarov PM!). And on top of that, when you get ONE wrong answer, all the experience you've built up (and it builds up quickly, which is nice, and sort of alleviates some of the aforementioned psych-warfare) is GONE. And the only way to get a question wrong and make off with the points is to let the 30 second timer run down.
When you make a wrong answer, it tells you what the right answer was (after a short delay, which may confuse some), but when the timer runs out (whether by choice or simple lack of time), you leave with all accumulated points. Which may be interpreted as a tradeoff, you make a wrong response, you lose all points, but are told what the correct answer was, you let the timer run down, you keep all your points, but you are left in the dark on the last model. Which is especially frustrating when it (again) looks extremely similar to one or two other models. So, in short, make a judgement call: are you willing to lose all those points you've earned on a guess, or did you just start and have (almost) none to lose?
Overall, I think this game can do a whole lot more in terms of educating (Example: What the hell is a sear? I've never heard of one until now!), it is nothing short of fascinating to see the internal workings of quality, classic, and iconic firearms. If you like guns, learning about them [not only do you get to (dis)assemble them, but each one has a comprehensive encyclopedia interface, complete with wiki links!], or are just curious about the internal workings of said guns, I give this game a (tentative) recommendation.

I absolutely adore AdVenture Capitalist. Most clicker games will bore me after 30 minutes to an hour. AdVenture Capitalist is not most clicker games. Instead of just consisting grinding and upgrading, AdVenture Capitalist has depth. Not enough depth to make your head hurt, but enough depth to keep you playing and having fun. You start out with lemon stands. You just click them and get money to upgrade the lemon stand and make more money. Soon you can buy a car wash, so you buy it. You keep upgrading them, and you're making a lot of money. You figure out that getting a certain number of upgrades will boost a certain aspect of the investment. Eventually you start buying things in the Upgrades tab. And then you discover Angel Invenstors, and have to choose when to restart and what investments to put your money it. You're getting money like a pro, and then you launch to the moon and mars. Alas, more sections of the game! You start trying to get your extra planets to where you are on Earth. You keep playing and playing, going to events, restarting, using mega boosts, etc. This game gets you hooked. And it's free, so what do you have to lose? Beware, though, there are purchases with real money, and you might be enticed to buy them. I don't suggest it though. You can play the game just fine without them.

After a few months of using this, I keep running into the same issue.  Anything meant for a gamepad is simply better played with a traditional two-stick gamepad, and anything meant for mouse and keyboard is simply better played with a mouse and keyboard.  It also can't be used effectively outside of Steam, and requires a lot of per-game customization.
My understanding is this is a good product if you are trying to replace mouse and keyboard with a gamepad.  I just haven't found myself in a situation where I would want to do that.  Even streaming to my TV I'm more apt to use a USB mouse and keyboard for shooters and strategy games, and anything console-like suffers heavily not having the twin sticks it expects - the touchpad simply isn't a functional replacement.
If you're at your PC directly, there's no real use case for this product.  If you're streaming to your living room, it boils down to a question of if you prefer to use a USB mouse/keyboard or not.  The steam controller is, strangely, -not- a controller replacement, it's a mouse/keyboard replacement.  A lot of users are not going to fall into the narrow conditions that make this a choice over alternatives.

Wow where do I start? I haven't really used a game pad before, but this thing feels so right to use in the right situation. A lot of that has to do with the fact that basically EVERYTHING on it can be configured on the fly. It literally just requires pressing the steam button and clicking configuration and you can quickly change settings to your liking in seconds, and ho boy are there a lot of settings you can change, even going so far as to emulate an analog pad input by pulsing keypresses so you can get that smooth movement even where controller support doesn't exist. I assure you that the controller will soon become a natural extension of yourself once you get used to it, I find myself just using the right trackpad instead of dropping it to grab my mouse. I could just go on for an hour about how much fun it is to tinker with it till you are one with it but there's more to it than that.
The design, visually appealing, the ergonomics are very well done (it's made to be held by HUMAN hands) and I find it very comfortable to use for extended periods even though it is of average weight,that load is much more comfortably distributed. Another great quirk is that if you really do want to lower the weight you can remove the duracell alkaline batteries it comes with and just run it wired. Yes it can run wireless or wired with equal ease for those who either prefer being unattached or those who prefer, but honestly I can't detect any input lag but it does seem to be able to recharge the batteries and function while plugged in, or as I said go without.
Did I mention the haptic feedback is so well done with it's linear actuators that instead of just dull rumbling, it tells you when you cross the thresholds on the triggers, the trackpads can vibrate based on how fast you move, which direction you move it in, and even will keep going like a scroll ball would, emulated friction included. The fine tuned vibrations are like a 6th sense and will be very satisfying for both the average person and those who only use mechanical keyboards for that "tactile sensation" will love it.
TL:DR
It's just a great product that obviously has had a great deal of thought put into it, I think it was definitely worth the money and I plan to use it more and more as I re learn what it's like to use a controller. 10/10 deserves product of the year in gaming category.

I was never a big fan of SHMUPS back in the day. I didn't even know Ikaruga existed until I played a Mega Man online flash game that featured the same polarity system. Afterwards I found out what was the origin of the polarity system that was in this flash game, and thats when I discovered Ikaruga.
To this day, I still don't know what makes Ikaruga such a awesome hidden gem that everyone should play at least once in their life. Is it the polarity system that gives a unique twist to the genre? Is it the challenging "Bullet Hell" difficulty that frustrates (in a good way) even the most hardcore of gamers? What is it about this game that makes players want to double play (One person controlling both player ships) until they can S-rank it with ease? Is it the music? The speed? The fact that it's made by Treasure whose past works include "Gunstar Heroes" and "Alien Soldier?"
I probably will never know the answer as to why I keep replaying the first level to try to improve my chain bonus and better my high score before I move on and repeat the process for level 2. What I do know is this: This is a game that requires (a lot of) time and devotion from players before they can truly appriciate it. Ikaruga's fast pace and increasingly hard level design may lose the interest of gamers, but somehow it motivates them to keep pressing onward towards beating all 5 levels (yes, 5 levels may seem small, but it is a matter of quality over quantity that makes it worth the money.) And when you got a friend playing alongside you, it is just as challenging as if you were going at it alone.
I am very happy to see Treasure listening to its fans and porting Ikaruga on Steam with all kinds of features and giving it the HD treatment. The game looks good and runs very smooth. I have no problems in reccomending Ikaruga over other arcade SHMUPs. The combination of solid gameplay, challenging difficulty and well thought out level design make this masterpiece an unforgettable experience.

This game is insane. I will probably never beat it but even attempting the first 2 levels over and over again has been more fun than you'd expect.
It's a bullet hell (meaning there is a ton of bullets on screen and you're expected to dodge them all) but mixed with a polarity-swapping technique. Enemies are of 2 colors, and you have the ability to be 1 of the 2 colors at a time. You absorb bullets of the same polarity and die to bullets of the opposite. You shoot the same color as your polarity, and shooting enemies with matching polarity does double damage. Shooting the correct polarity across multiple enemies rewards you with a chain, which leads to a higher score (which is the point of this game).
It's one of the hardest games I've played, and this is supposedly not even nearly as hard as other games in the genre. If you like a challenge you will certainly find it in this game. I don't think anyone with any amount of gaming experience can just pick up this game and get to level 5 even within a few days. It takes lots of practice and memorization and on top of all that perfect execution to proceed through the entirety of the game.
The level design is basically art. It's amazing how they've used the polarity technique to actually generate level obstacles that, in tandem with the spawning enemies, create an entire level that you're expected to dodge and blow up while maintaining a combo and getting the highest score possible. You can tell a lot of work went into the precise timings and enemy types of enemy spawns. The bosses are very unique and well designed as well. You almost never feel like they've repeated anything in the game. Every 5 seconds you're facing something new.
This game is easily a 9/10, more or less depending on your individual taste for bullet hells.

I got this game during a sale, played it a bit and genuinely had fun playing it and think that the stealth portion of the game has a bit of tension buildup on the player going for it. However, I still can't entirely recommend this game for a few reasons. (See very bottom of review for explanation on why I actually do recommend this)
-Bad animations:
A lot of the enemies when performing certain animations look either robotic and unlife like or just flat out don't sync up with the actions they're doing (Walking animation not matching movespeed while moving and not even moving in the same direction as they're animated to be).
-Stealth not all that important to gameplay:
This is a horror themed game and as such encourages stealth instead of just loudly rushing through each level. The stealth mechanic isn't all that great in the game, however, The only way the monster's A.I can even find you is if you either get to close to them or have your torch lit, running or breaking objects such as pots attracts no attention to you at all. Even if you do get seen by one of the boss monsters they're relatively easy to lose by just putting out your torch and hiding for a few seconds or you can just run from them since only two of the boss monsters have ranged attacks and you outrun them.
-Bare bones monster A.I:
The boss monsters in the labyrinth portions have a set patrol path that they appear to never stray from unless they spot you. If you choose to fight the boss monster, with a good range melee weapon such as the axe or trident, they're pretty easy to kill with a "poke and back off" method. If you do manage to kill the boss monter they eventually respawn but there's also a chance when they do respawn that they can get stuck at their respawn point and practically stop being a threat at that point (This has happened quite often when I kill the boss monsters).
So in short, I thought the game was fun despite it's problems, but, objectively,
due to how unpolished it is. If the game's on sale and you have some interest in buying it go ahead, but for it's full price? To get a better idea of what the game is like see my video on it.
Edit: Even though I've already stated the problems with this game, in a way I still recommend it on the grounds that it seriously does have some heart put into it.

Basically like an old B horror movie: a bit rough around the edges and basic, but a lot of fun and providing some good scares. It's a stealth game taking place almost entirely in the dark where you have to navigate the different levels of the labyrinth while avoiding monsters, zombies, giant bugs, and demons. This game truly surprised me. The production values are very basic, but have a certain charm that just grows you. The game itself can be seriously chilling. There's nothing likethe experience of wandering around in the dark only to be confronted by a satyr. it lets out a chilling bellow, calling for help from its demonic buddies and starts giving chase. Until you manage to outrun it (which is no easy task given the various dead ends in the levels) and find a dark spot to crouch down in and hide, you won't be safe. Even then you're not truly safe. Sometimes, when you're in the dark, the enemies can inch near you and (possibly) detect you if they get close enough. It's pretty tense.
Overall, a very solid stealth horror game and a good way to train for the big leagues of tense, stealth horror: Alien Isolation.
Pros:

Enemies are threatening enough
B movie charm
Doesn't rely on cheap jump scares

This review is more of a focus on what issues I have with the controller. There are a lot of reviews praising the controller, but didnt hit what issues I had. If you need a new controller that can work with a steam machine or just sitting back on your couch, i  think that its not a bad choice if you get it with a bundle, like i did with the dark souls 3 deal. However, I have some issues that make me still opt for a 360 controller, like its size and it being overshadowed by the kb&m just as much as the 360 controller.
TLDR; Most of the issues I have are due to the controller being too small for my hands. the rest are due to it being beaten by both the 360 controller and kb&m.
-The review-
The size of the controller and the fit to the hand is great, if you dont have big hands. I have larger than normal hands, and it doesnt sit quite right in them. To have the controller rest comfortably in my hands, my thumbs hover over the top part of both of the pads. Not where they need to be. If my hands were smaller, it would work perfectly, as many others have said
Button layout is ok. With my larger hands, i often mishit one of the buttons when i try to hit the A button. While it took some getting used to, the two buttons on the back of the controller work quite well. The triggers seem to be placed too high, especially the rb and lb. Once again, due to large hand size. the stick works fine, and the two pads, while clunky and awkward at first, do work well. (I still have an issue moving my thumb down to the bottom right and left on the right and left pad respectively, since my thumbs are nearly touching my palm when i try to move my thumb there.
Button layout and pads work well overall. I had a hard time trying to get used to it when i played Dark souls, mostly due to the bindings being awkward.
My other main issue with the controller is that it sits in an awkward place between controller and kb&m. If i want to use a controller for a game, i have zero reason to opt for the steam controller. The 360 nails the controller format, and the tweaks that the steam controller made hold it back. If the game doesnt support controller, like XCOM 2, using the pads just doesnt match the effectiveness of the mouse, and the hotkeys like the keyboard. It tried to be the best of both worlds, but ends up being the negative of both of the 2.
I guess if you dont have a controller or a keyboard and mouse, this is an option. or really need buttons on the back of the controller

Juanito Arcade Mayhem:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is a call to all gamers! The Clonocells have started their invasion and have infected our classic arcade games. It can’t be happening, we need to do something! Can someone help . . . Anybody? You, what’s your name, young man? Juanito! Well get on with it before it’s too late. This is going to be Juanito Arcade Mayhem!
Juanito Arcade mayhem is an action / 2D arcade game where you control Juanito and his Alien friend, Gluk (in local Co-op), and your goal is to save eights classic arcade games (parody) which have been infected by the Clonocells Mutants.
I have to tell you up front, this game is a gem. It’s fun, fast, addictive and bloody hard! As I mentioned above, you have to save eight arcade classics by being teleported within the arcade machine. All world names are parodies of famous and classic games. Pillman, for example is the almighty Pacman and Arkadroid is one of my favourite games of all time, Arkanoid.   Each of the worlds have ten stages to clear, including a boss fight. That will give you eighty levels to beat and plenty of replay-ability. You must collect as many points as possible and avoid losing any health (hearts) so you can score three golden stars at the end of each level. These stars are extremely important as you will need to have a certain number of stars to unlock the next world.
There are different types of Clonocells. The basic ones are green balls, and they can be small (easy to destroy), medium or large. The other ones shoot projectiles from different directions; the yellow one shoots one projectile downward, the blue shoots two projectiles diagonally and the purple is a combination of the first two. You can imagine having six of these at once on the screen and it is absolute Mayhem for our poor Juanito! Speaking of him, what does he use to fight these aliens? A tiny laser which can shoot one shot at the time. However, our dear friend can dash his way around the screen shooting like a madman until a power up comes down. Well, you’ll have to shoot at one of these big balls and manage a combo to hopefully get one power up. He can gain hearts too, and boy, he needs them! Depending on which difficulty you’re playing, death can come quickly as you have only four hearts available at the start of each stage. Quite simply, Juanito will lose a heart when he is hit. That’s right - four hits and your dead, so grab these hearts as soon as you can!

The 2D graphics are fabulous and well-polished. Soundtracks are from the original arcade games. Control-wise, they are extremely responsive, either with the keyboard or a gamepad.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great, polished 2D graphics
-	Super fun, superfast and super addictive
-	8 Worlds with 80 levels to beat
-	Original Soundtrack
-	Great controls
-	Stack of achievements
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can be frustrating if you get stuck on the same level for a while

I figure after owning this controller since November 10th, I should probably chip in.
I'll keep this short, since anyone who is looking at the reviews before buying this is only wondering one thing: "Is it better than an Xbox 360 controller?"
Yes.
Here's why:
-Touchpads with haptics are great for FPS or third person games where precision is required
-Surprisingly good gyroscope (which many people use for quick camera movements in shooters)
-Dual stage triggers
-FULLY PROGRAMMABLE BUTTONS (I cannot emphasize enough how nice it is to rebind all the buttons on your controller on a game to game basis)
-Nice build quality and comfortable ergonomics
-Custom power on and off sounds (you can play a midi tune from Portal or TF2 if you want)
-Wireless and wired modes
-Great price for what you get
You shouldn't buy a Steam Controller if:
-You want to play competitive shooters like CS:GO
-You want something familiar
-You dislike Big Picture mode (it's required to use many of the features)
-You hate fun
Great customisability, and +1 for linux support

Full disclosure time. The ENTIRITY of my positive review relies on the question "Do you recommend this hardware?" Including the software in that decision disqualifies it from a positive recommendation. I had a difficult time deciding if I would or would not recommend this controller. I LIKE the controller quite a bit and when it works it's really amazing, but the software ruins more experiences with this controller than it makes possible. I only recommend the hardware, and I would recommend abstaining so long as the steam controller requires Big Picture mode to set controls or utilize the controls you already set. Very few games allow me to open the game before I turn on the controller (so Big Picture doesn't open with the game) while still retaining the controls set up in Big Picture previously.
Big Picture (BP) mode is clumsy and slow to navigate, uses a different steam overlay when in games while running from BP mode which makes responding to chats, even chats already started and opened, require you to go through menus to get to through BP. You can't see what's happening in your game through the BP overlay and generally makes gaming at the desk with the controller an unpleasant experience for anyone who might talk to friends while they play or have to Alt+Tab for any reason. BP is often a background resource hog that glitches or stops responding.
The Controller is sleek, fast, and strangely comfortable to hold.
-Bumpers and inner handle buttons click like tactile switches in a loud way but they're not unpleasant to use.
-Triggers seem shallow but are sensetive and feel nice.
-Trackpads are accurate and customizable but not great when emulating a D pad or analog stick.
-The grips are strange in that they bulge out into the hand. Weird compared to traditional controllers of all kinds but satisfyingly fills up the hand.
-The battery cover also acts as the inner handle buttons. It's easy to remove though some slightly-thicker long lasting AAs are not as easy to remove as a standard AA.
-Wired or wireless use with an included USB extension cord/base for the included wireless adapter. Never played wired so far with no connectivity issues on wireless.
Setting up controls is fairly easy and highly customizable. I haven't had other's experience of my set controls changing, only problems with them not working outside of BP, which is just the worst ever. All the cons of the controller have to do with requiring BP, opening BP, forcing use of the BP overlay, and everything with how BP makes gaming a far less enjoyable experience.

I got this controller as a birthday gift to replace my aging wired Xbox 360 controller. Did it replace my Xbox 360 controller? Yeah.
It's hard to describe what using the Steam Controller is like in text. Basically, it feels like a traditional controller, but it's not. The analog stick and face buttons are shifted to the bottom in favor of giant trackpads, there are dual-stage triggers along with traditional L and R buttons that have been a mainstay of controllers since the SNES in 1990 (1991 here in the States) and then there are two additional buttons on the grips, then a Steam button in the center flanked by two arrow buttons that serve as Start and Select. As far as face buttons go, there are the usual subjects, ABXY. They're arranged exactly like they are on the Xbox 360/One controller, colors and all. Not sure if that's intentional, but it really helped with adjusting to the controller.
But of course, there's the elephant in the room, the two giant trackpads. If it weren't for the haptic feedback, they would feel as imprecise as a normal laptop trackpad. Thankfully they don't, and I greatly prefer them over the traditional analog stick now. It definitely takes some getting used to, but when you do you'll be firing shots in GTA or just simply moving the camera with precision you just can't get on any other controller. Speaking of which, there is still one, which is typically used for movement in games. It feels exactly like how an analog stick would. Would I recommend using the Steam Controller competitively? No, definitely not. Even with the extra precision over a normal analog stick, the touchpads cannot truly replace a traditional mouse. You will still be worse off compared to other players in the match. Well, except for Rocket League, of course, but in something like CS:GO? No.
But would it replace a controller? Depends. If your other controller is aging and nowhere near as responsive as it was years ago, like my Xbox 360 controller was, and you want a new, different, experience, it definitely will. But that isn't to say that the controller is everyone's thing. Everyone has different ideas of what a controller should be (just look at Nintendo, they've been trying to reinvent the wheel since the Nintendo 64 with various results), and maybe someone prefers the normal analog sticks over two giant touchpads and you know what? That's fine. But would I recommend the Steam Controller as an Xbox 360 controller replacement? Yes. Otherwise, if you want a more traditional controller, the Xbox One controller is a viable choice. So is the DualShock 4.
Oh, and as an added bonus, the Steam Controller is fully configurable. You can rebind every single button on the controller to do something else, and you can make the touchpads emulate a mouse, d-pad, joystick or a mouse-like joystick. This allows you to customize the controller to fit your needs in a game. That's actually a really neat feature, and probably one of the more defining aspects of the controller. If you want the same functionality out of a more traditional controller, you'd need to spend an extra $100 on an Xbox One Elite controller, but why would you do that when the Steam Controller is $100 less? If you really want to, you can make the Steam Controller function like an Xbox 360/One controller; some games' default configs, like GTA V, even do that. If you want, you can make it act as the entire keyboard and mouse in one device. If you want, you can make it a mixture of the two. The possibilities are endless.
Overall, would I recommend getting a Steam Controller? If you want a unique experience that you can't get with anything else, absolutely. If you want something more traditional, no. But I encourage you to at least give it a try. After some quality time with the Steam Controller, it has replaced my Xbox 360 controller, and I highly recommend it.

You may get weapons to fight these monsters, but you must explore and find enough gold in order to buy them. Weapons include, but are not limited to: a wooden club, a spiked club, a trident, a bow & arrows, etc.
Like I stated, each time you enter a Labyrinth it is procedurally generated. You are never ever playing the same game twice, let alone the same floor twice. It is truly refreshing.
Highly recommended, especially for how underrated it is.
PERSONAL RATING: 8.5/10 - A very challenging, yet rewarding, rogue-like "labyrinth" crawler.

Juanito is basically a modernised version of the Pang/ Buster Bros formula. In this series you control a character who has only 3 real abilities move left, move right and shoot upwards. Your character is shooting upwards at balls (or bubbles) that split into 2 smaller balls when hit and will disappear if shot when small enough.
What have the Game ever team added? Awesome music, nice side effects, great atmosphere, power ups and more gaming in jokes then you can count!
The Game dev has taken a the original formula, changed the shooting a little bit to feel like contra or Metal slug with just he upward shooting (no more harpoons) and added game elements from a few titles like Pacman, adventure Island, Snobros, Tetris and Donkey kong just to name a few.
I’m grateful that the developers also remembered to throw away and update some of the mechanics. For example you can skip levels and return to them later. Also they’ve being nice enough to add unlockables which aren’t just cosmetic or badges on your profile but are actually quite USEFUL.  This game not only pushes the nostalgia button hard but is a lot of fun to play. I have not played a game in a long time that makes my hands sore yet addicts me so much.
This is the part where I find something to constructively criticise the game and not the game developers themselves.
Um…
I feel like there are a lot of times when you have a lot of projectiles flying around and you are forced to take damage and the dodge/ dash feels a bit useless. However I feel like that's an intentional part of the design as well. Also the Adventure Island kid is punishing but thankfully predictable in his hammer throws.
Also it can get a bit confusing and maddening when you are CERTAIN you did well in a stage but you only get 1 star or when you think you did poorly and it gives you three. The star system appears to be score based but...it feels a little random at times.
Apart from that more language support please. I’m fortunate enough to be an English speaker but have German, Japanese and Chinese speaking friends who I’m certain would enjoy this title. I fully understand that language localisation is expensive and difficult and therefore it is impossible to make everybody happy in this. Having the 4 langauges chosen is already a good set of choices.
If what I’ve written already can’t convince you now It’s on 10% sale right now.
Give it a shot.

We fired as quick as we could, but my friend was shot through the face by a fascist bullet. I, now alone, took down the remaining Germans as my friend's Nagant was still smoking. More Germans came down the tunnel picking through the weaponry of their fallen comrades. I opened fire adding more weapons to the stockpile. As the last one was still falling, I heard footsteps behind me, before I could turn around I was stepped on, a appearantly blind German was running forward through the tunnel only to find a bullet in his back. Capsule is a narrative-driven game about a stranded astronaut trying to get home. The gameplay is delivered through a radar screen. It is ostensibly a first person game: you play as the astronaut, who is sealed inside the cramped capsule, and navigates with the radar screen to pick up reserves of air and fuel while evading enemies, always trying to reach a space station.
Pros:
Spooky atmosphere. Feels like I am driving an escape pod from the Nostromo.
Tight controls.
No tutorial level. The game is simple enough to pick up as one goes along.
Increased complexity as game goes forward.
Great gameplay balance. Go fast when low on air, poke along slowly and methodically when low on fuel.
Blow up pursuing drones by luring them into mines.
Cons:
Lame nemesis. You meet a malevolent organism in the end game who gives you a devils choice, but he has a stupid voice-over and there is no choice but to accept his offer.
Expensive. I got the game for $0.99 during a sale but the full MSRP of $5 isn't worth it. No replay value and about a 1 hour experience.
Confusing enemy and pickup names. I thought nitrox would replenish my breathing air, since air is actually mostly nitrogen with some oxygen, but it didn't replenish my air reserves.
No introduction. After beating the game, I started a new campaign, and it really isn't clear why the protagonist is in space, in the dire straits he finds himself in.
Overall, this game would be a cool introduction to start a narrative, but it's too short to justify the $5 price. Buy on a sale though.

Capsule is a very short (1 to 2 hours at most) immersive game that comes with quite a few warnings, and I can understand why. The developers warn anyone with claustrophobia, misophonia, or other similar phobias not to play the game. And why? Because this is truly one game best played in the dark.
If I had to put it in a category, I’d say Capsule has a slight feel of a minimalist puzzle game; but the truth is, there’s really no puzzle to it – at least not gameplay wise. The story, however, does make you wonder even though it is at its core an immersive survival game.
The story goes as follows: You wake up trapped in a capsule, only able to experience the outside world through the radar on it. You don’t know what’s happened, but you have an idea of where to go to start the journey into finding out…
Although you’re thrown into the game with barely an idea of what to do, for this particular case the lack of a proper tutorial beyond how to move is actually not hindering, because controls and story are so minimal you really can’t go quite wrong… even if it did take me a while at first to get my bearings.
You have oxygen and power to worry about, a radar burst, a bearing, and a distance to your target. Each level you reach a destination, where you have more of the story develop in the form of messages which often give you a new direction in which to go. You have to be mindful of the hostile environment while making your way to the next destination, but watch out for your power and oxygen! You might fall short and die of asphyxiation!
The look of the game is ultimately minimalistic. You can only see the radar of your capsule, a pixelated screen through which you move with the arrows and send a sonar wave with the space bar. The blueish color is very pleasant to look at, and the flicker of the screen manages to make it quite immersive, particularly if you do play with headphones and in the dark!
The sound effects, though simple as well, help further the atmosphere of it all, and the feeling of immersion. The breathing, the static, the beeping… Even when on my first round I played it with the lights on and during daytime, I could easily forget that I wasn’t actually in the Capsule.
I have to say that because of its immersive aspect, it adds a whole level of ‘horror’ to the game that you shouldn’t overlook. Dying the first time was truly terrifying.
However… and there is a small con: it’s that the game becomes a little bit boring once you get a hold of the whole bearings/distance and when to restock oxygen and power not to die. So basically, once you get the hang of it. But the game is so very short that, honestly? You won’t even mind.
I think this a very nice, atmospheric game – simple and minimalist, if you’re into psychological type of horror you will definitely enjoy the hour of play. If you like jump scares in your horror, steer clear. This is real horror right here.
Most negative reviews are from people who obviously didn't take the time to experiment, and figure out how unique and clever interactions with later mechanics function! sucks to suck.

CAPSULE is a fairly unconventional game. Alien and hostile instead of fun. But worth every minute, despite being very short.
You're inside a vessel of some kind (I assume a submarine, but the details aren't too important). You try to get from base to base, investigating what's happening around you and trying to reach home.
As I said, it's not "fun". From the screenshots, you can see there's very little that the game gives you. You're isolated inside a capsule, and the radar is your only contact with the outside world. To get from base to base, you'll have to balance your oxygen and power levels. If you run out of oxygen, you die. If you run out of power... well, you'll then be stuck in place, slowly running out of oxygen... until you die.
You'll have to use your active radar to check what the points on your map are. These may be enemy creatures, mines, fuel, air tanks, and others. The important thing to note is that using your active radar enables your enemies to detect the signal and know where you are. If you get too close to some of them, you'll also be detected.
Each mission is essentially the same, trying to get from A to B without running out of oxygen. The difficulty increases, of course. And by the last few missions, you'll have to dive (heh) into the deeper mechanics to survive, as supplies are very rare.
So far, although the mechanics are all very coherent and purposeful, the game doesn't seem all that enticing, right? Well, yes, and no.
The atmosphere and sound design tie it all together very, very nicely! Not only does it nail the isolation, it also leaves something for you to imagine. For example, there are areas with many crates around... Maybe a shipwreck?
There are also different types of "creatures", each with a different behaviour.
And finally, although I don't want to spoil it (please don't read if you're planning on playing the game)
... And then there's something else going on with the story that may also intrigue you.
But anyway. If you like the feeling on isolation, this game is very well worth a play.
Everything from the (simple, but effective) mechanics to the visual and audio design pushed the game toward a specific objective and nailed it. Really enjoyed it!
P.S.: Forgot this before. One negative (or at least dubious) aspect of the game was the discovery element, in a sense. When you use the radar, you get the name of the "points" on the map. These are like labels, but you don't know what the label does. Unless it says "mine", its meaning may be up in the air, to you. Well, I usually abstain from running into things when I don't know what they do, or their names are the least bit ominous.
The price for being conservative is death by asphyxiation. Oops.
The point is that you will have to risk it and try all of the different labels to know what they do. The dubious part is that you will probably die a couple of times as a result (not as an insta-death type of thing, just for the lack of information, or misinformation -- I didn't pick up some fuel cells because I didn't understand what they were, from their name). It feels a bit strange, since, in that situation, the person would simply die. And it's a bit immersion breaking to have use a "respawn" as a planned strategy.
It's not too important, but it's a thought I wanted to leave here.

The Steam Controller is a very good controller.  I needed a controller to play steam games, so I bought this one.  It took me a little time to get used to it, but now I really like it for all of the games that I use it with.  It seems to work great on everything I've tried, even for FPS games. But to be honest, you need a mouse and keyboard to really play well against other humans in FPS.
There are regular firmware updates, and you can customize the controller's sounds and LED brightness (which is perfect for those who want to play in the dark without this strobe-like LED shining up from their hands). The controller customizability and community bindings are a huge bonus, because games that have a lot of keyboard commands can be mapped right on to the controller.  Also, it's nice that you can plug in the wire if your batteries die, and it works without a hitch.  Battery drain is is very low IMHO, and I used the batteries that came with it for several months.
On the down side, some of the buttons can make a loud "CLICK" when fully pressed, which can get kind of annoying (I hope it wears down over time).  Also, the thumbstick and ABXY buttons could have been placed a bit further apart, but for most people it will be good enough.
I plan on continuing to use this as my gaming controller as it stands, but if the controller thumbstick develops an un-fixable drift (ala xb360 controllers), I'll be back to update!

I first played Ikaruga for the GameCube and instantly fell in love with it. At first I treated it like any other shooter before I even started learning how to chain combos properly. The combo system is where this game really shines, it turns from a "shut your brain off and shoot enemies", to a fast paced twitch puzzle game. I've spent countless hours on the GameCube version of the game and the PC port holds up well. When you get into the groove of the polarity switching and memorize enemy patterns there really is no limit to what you can do next to improve your score.
What kept me playing is i never felt like I’ve hit a plateau in what kind of score i could achieve, there is always positive reinforcement to keep playing because you can see what the guy ahead of you on the leaderboard has done... don't go way above your means and watch the number 1 player and think I’ll never be able to do that... watch the guy who's only 2 million points ahead of you and mimic the style he's using... you'll quickly learn that the game that's touted as "impossibly hard", is actually very doable to get a high score.
I recommend giving it a fair chance turn the BGM off and play some of your own chillout tunes and enter the meditation that is Ikaruga.
Pros
-very forgiving hitbox often times you feel like "how did i just survive that?!", rather than "oh man how did i die there!?"
-mesmerizingly intelligent level scripting.
-addictive
-intuitive design
-perfect integration of the Microsoft controller,  and also very good response when linking a ps3 controller via 3rd party apps.
Cons
-no longer has slow mo, and training that was included in the GameCube release.

I got this game for free and I had a good feeling about this game as it looked like it had potential. I was right about it having potential but I was wrong about it being a good and entertaining game. I can't recommend this game because it was just bad. For 2014, the graphics are♥♥♥♥♥♥poor and noticeably so. The textures look pixelated and easily it could have been done better as well as the graphical bugs that are plentiful but not game breaking. The environments are fitting for the game and  with the randomly generated floors, it does make it fresh each time. Although, this can greatly work against you as the stealth system in this game does not work well at all since the AI is random and most of the time unfair. Even when hidden in the shadows, the monsters will see you if the game decides they can. Then the AI as a whole is just broken. A lot of times you will notice the floor boss is not around then you will find out they are stuck somewhere which is usually where you need to go to finish the level. Also, something that seems unfair is not an enemy can be found on the floor besides the boss monster before you are detected. Once detected, monsters will continue to spawn regardless of how many you kill. The common monsters are not necessarily unfair when you compare them to the boss monsters though. The Medusa is probably the worst until the Minotaur. The Medusa has a bow that has very good accuracy but her gaze is the thing to be wary of. With out the crossbow, she is impossible since she speeds towards you and if you are even looking at any part of her when she is close enough, you are stone. Now, the Minotaur is invincible until the final stage and has one of the previous bosses with him on the floor. Usually the other bosses will not give you trouble but with the Minotaur, he can charge you and hit you with his axe. The axe will rarely hit you because the game has bad hit detection but his charge can make him go in circles to hit you and it makes him go extremely fast. Not to mention, you die in one hit by it. Now that I have talked about the really frustrating AI, it is time to talk about the other aspects of the game that makes it so much worse. The music is forgettable and probably more annoying than intense since it sounds like it belongs in a game from the Playstation or something like it. The controls are functional and work well but the things that would be nice is a health bar and stamina bar. The story is nothing special because it basically does not exist. The whole story can be summarized to Theseus (you) are cast down into the Labyrinth to save the daughter of King Minos (the lord of the Labyrinth). Lastly, I think getting this game for free is not bad since it is free but I would not pay money for this unless you are a die hard mythology fan but still I would think you to be disappointed as it would not be what you would expect. So, there is better things to spend your money on than this game.

I actually came for the cute anime girls but the game goes way beyond that.
I'll get right down to the battle mechanics since that is the bulk of the gameplay.
Fighting mechanics are amazing, the sound effects and movements when you combo the enemies really make it seem you're doing something right. I also melt inside each time Erina does a basic attack; her eyes squint ><.
The different moves you can execute with the direction pad and the attack button allows you to throw enemies into the air with aerial attacks, throw bombs and various other abilities that makes the fighting enjoyable. The controls are extremely intuitive, the devs did a great job by having a quick popup with simple instructions that appears whenever you learn new skills. If you happen to forget certain combos, it is the first thing you see when you open up the menu screen with ESC.
The various moves are actually necessary, for example you would find air attacks useful against air enemies or enemies on platforms above you.
Once you get the faerie helper, it feels like obtaining a bit device in R-Type except you can control its ranged firing direction and even charged attacks (good for aiming at enemies in the air while you're busy standing aside to dodge lasers).
Hell, you can even level up your faerie by attacking with it and that unlocks even more stuff.
I started on Novice, but I believe the Hard modes would really allow you to utilize the full extent of your weaponry and skills. If you're a decent gamer, I would recommend starting on a higher difficulty (above novice) and work your way up or down.
The game is good at rewarding the player. In the first 15 minutes of gameplay the interactivity level is extremely high: killing enemies with different attacks; picking up objects; blowing holes through the ground; talking to npcs. Every little thing you do feels rewarding (e.g. killing an enemy literally throws it off the screen; obtaining an item is like getting the Master's Sword from Link to the Past.)
For fans of stories and anime character portraits, there are lots of little scenes here and there where you can enjoy the myriad expressions of the characters. If you're not a story fan, that's still fine, you can easily skip cutscenes and continue on (although the game does encourage you to watch them so that you can 'collect' the CG artwork in the gallery section). It's moe, but the characters all have their own personalities.
Can't say much for the story yet since I'm an hour into the game, but it's definitely not a mindless 'be the hero / save blah blah' - the characters hint there's definitely various things going on behind the scenes. The story is pretty quick pace, things just keep popping outta no where. There is humour in the dialogue, but mostly for the anime audience.
The world seems pretty vast. As many reviewers have already pointed out that you can just level up, explore and have fun instead of continuing with the story, which gives some freedom.
Music is diverse, themes fit the location you're in.
Graphics is what you see in the trailer above. There are windowed and full screen options.
Little references here and there from various games. At some point I swear I saw a springboard that looked like it was from Super Mario Bros to allow me to reach higher places.
It is clear that the developers put a ton of love into this game from all the minute details mentioned above. There seems to be many little gems to be discovered. I would have to say this game is very well polished. This is definitely one of those games that would amass a cult following.

I reviewed this for Two Credits. You can find the full review, the score I gave it, and some cool screenshots from my time playing here:
Summary:
Juanito Arcade Mayhem is a fun modern arcade-style game that manages to fairly seamlessly blend the most iconic mechanics of several classic arcade games into its own while offering beautiful cartoon-styled renditions of many of their characters and locales. There are some issues with the difficulty curve and the level of randomness that is present, which lead to some rage-inducing deaths, but they don’t sour the overall experience. Its parodies are close enough to the games that they are parodying that they will induce nostalgia, but it stands well enough on its own that familiarity with the source material is not necessary. It’s a game that I never expected to exist, but one that I’m quite glad does.

If you like Bubble Trouble... you will LOVE Juanito Arcade Mayhem !!
You play as Juanito (obviously) who gets "teleported" into different games.. games that are infected. Your job is to get rid of the infection.
If you (not juanito.. YOU..) are not too young.. you will immediately recognize some.. if not all of juanito's games.
The main goal is the same, but each world (every world has 10 levels) has it's own set of gimmicks.
In Pillman you eat yellow power-ups which will scare the clonocells.
In Snow Sises you will face a horde of frozen clonocells.
In Blockits you must find and eliminate the infection while avoiding some familiar looking shapes that are trying to squish you.. for no apparent reason.
Sure.. you can't complete this tasks witouth some help. You have different power-ups at your disposal.. but sadly.. you can't use them whenever you want.. they are.. dropped (randomly) after killing clonocells. You will unlock different power-ups as you progress further into the game. I find the number of power-ups.. just the right amount.. not to many.. not to few. However.. which power-up you get and when... is totally random.. so you will not always get what you want.. or need :))
I don't wanna drag this to much. So what I liked and what I didn't.
+ The worlds themselves. (Brings back old memories)
+ Each "world" gimmicks. (Maybe.. Wonderworld.. not so much.. I hate that kid :D)
+ The pace of the game. (Quick and funny.. and frustrating at times IF and only IF you wanna get 3 stars all the time)
+ Level X. There are like boss fights but not really..
+ Survival Co-Op (You even have the option to "revive" your brother in arms by standing enough time near him)
+ Power-ups
- No really a BAD thing.. but it would have been nice to have a Co-Op campaign as well.
- Maybe if you had the option to store one or two power-ups in order to use them at the right time.
Well.. that's about it. Cheers !! :)

This game, despite being 2 years old at the time of this review, holds it's own against the games of this new generation, and well.  It is still worth the retail price, and at $19.99 now, it certainly worth it for any gamer worth their mettle.  Deux Ex is a action RPG that takes place in a cyber punk dystopian-ish future.  There are plenty of choice to be made in this game, all of which will affect how the game progresses, and many different ways to handle each situation that is thrown at you.  You can actually go through the entire game without actually killing a single person aside from the boss battles.  You can play the entire game stealthily, or you can play the entire game like a human tank, capable of withstanding direct contact with a nuclear warhead launched point blank by large mechs.  You can upgrade your characters abilities at your will to tailor the playstyle to the way you want. It also retains a original Resident Evil-esque method of inventory management, having a certain amount of "squares" to store things in, some items taking up more square than others.  The story line is very likeable for RPG lovers and action/FPS lovers alike.  This is a must play for anyone worth their salt in the gaming world, you have to experience this game to completion and learn why it is given so much praise.
