Capcom is widely known for making poor pc ports so I tried this before I bought it and it ran fine so I bought it. It has crashed only maybe twice no more than three times in the single player on two playthroughs. For Capcom, that is really good. The main problem with the game though is in co op. My friends have constant disconnects or crashes, putting a serious damper on co op fun. The same happened to me when I joined their games. The crashes are not frequent, and I was able to play for long periods comfortably with one friend, but the point is that there should be zero crashes. That is a pipe dream when you are talking about Capcom games though.
Even though I hate DR2, this is one of the most fun games I have played in a long time. I hated DR2 because you are on a constant timer to bring zombrex to your mentally challenged daughter. This game has a countdown too but it isn't a huge bother like in 2: you have 7 days of game time to finish the game before the city gets nuked which equals around 25-30 hours of gameplay as opposed to only around 7 in DR1 and defintely not 25 hours in DR2. I also hated 2 because it felt like a cheesy "Sega Arcade" game like Crazy Taxi. This one is just as wild as that game but has a actual AAA feel to it and the graphics are outstanding. It is a darker more serious game, although obviously not that serious when you can build a d-ldo firing gun, among many other crazy items. The seriousness comes from the story and cut scenes, then it turns you loose to your own devices to be as creative as you want. The graphics and effects are some of the best I've seen in a long time and the music and sound are also very good. The story is great and the gameplay is smooth. The game is not very challenging though because it gives you such powerful weapons. On the second playthrough on nightmare mode it was still not a challenge because it let me keep my level, stats, and weapon blueprints. Not one single boss battle in the game is a challenge at all. I never died on any boss and never came close to dying, other than when I first started the game and the monk in the gardens killed me once because the battle comes so quickly and I was still getting used to the game. But compared to the other DR games which have imo some of the worst, most awkward and clunky boss battles I've ever seen, this game's boss battles are a godsend.
Being a Capcom port of a open-world console game, there are of course going to be performance issues. In the hands of a more capable company, probably not. There are certain areas of the game that give huge graphical lag spikes for no reason whatsoever because they are no different than other areas of the game. Besides that, the game runs pretty smoothly on max settings for me so considering that this is a huge achievement for Capcom I am pretty damn happy.
I completely understand why this game got mixed reviews because of all the people crashing and having performance issues. Capcom is among several other companies when it comes to not being able to port games very well, including Ubisoft and the kings of bad ports, Square. I am fortunate enough to enjoy the game relatively unhindered at a smooth 60 fps.

Lemme just have y'all know that I could have easily just whipped out the PS4 version of Nep VII and simply played the game on that. But no. I bought this game again, along with all it's character DLC, on the PC, just to show Compile Heart and Idea Factory that the Neptunia series is one of the best thing that they have ever created.
The game itself is pretty good, and serves as a great entry point for newcomers to the series. The only thing you'll be missing for not playing the previous games will be a few random references relating to them. They added a ton of fancy new gameplay elements, but it's still the same Nep formula, so those who have actually played the other Nep games won't feel alienated in the slightest. In fact, almost all of the additions are vast improvements from the other Nep games, making this game probably the best Nep game in the series thus far.
This game is actually crazy complex, so I'm not going to delve too deep into things. If you want to know more about this game, then go read some other review, or actually buy the game. The game comes with tutorials. Read them. Seriously though, it's a good game. Everything you need to know is explained as you play along, from the combat to the storyline. The only noteworthy flaw is that on lower end PCs, don't expect this game to peak at more than 20 FPS at any point. IF and Compile Heart really decided to jack up the graphics, given that this is a PS4 game, and all the previous Nep games were either PS3 or PSVITA games. Seriously though, having a GTX 960 as a reccommended requirement is pretty intense for a JRPG, even if it's a PS4 game. Other than that, the gameplay is solid, and I would recommend this to anyone who is a Nep fan, or really just likes JRPGs in general. The art is drawn by Tsunako, and it looks fantastic The gameplay and story are also both amazing. Also, the guy who voiced Umio also voiced Aizen from Bleach, which I find to be absolutely hilarious and amazing.

The thing about this game was that it has so much potential! The detail, the fun and everything. Only 1 thing brought it all the way down. It is that it will take ages (by ages, I mean AGES) for you to actually unlock a new gun.
Getting XP to unlock a gun will take a long time. You can reassemble and disassemble guns again and again, but it won't give you that much of XP. So if you count the daily rewards that you can get in a week, that tallys up to 6800, which at first seems like a lot. But eventually, you have to unlock guns that cost almost twice that amount. So... you just have two weeks of opening and closing the game before you can get to any action.
When I play, I always ask myself, what's the point of having so many guns if you can't even use them? The price to unlock all the guns is ridiculous too. 50 dollars?? You might as well just add 10 bucks to it and get Battlefield 4 or something.
In conclusion, this game could have worked out brilliantly. Only a flawed daily reward system and the crazy amount of time needed to progress brings it down all the way. 3/10 stars

I usually wait for a few more hours of gamepaly to write a more in depth review but, since I'm uninstalling it, I don't think my opinion will change any time soon.
First of all, this is not a horrible game at all. It's got a lot of good ideas under its belt. It is extremely amateurish-looking, from graphics and sound to the implementation, but these things are easily overlooked when the game as a whole works well. However that is not the case, nothing really clicks they way it should (I'm assuming). The stealth mechanics doesn't work well, I never know when I'm really hidden, making the indicator completely useless. The game tries to set a mood of fear and tension but it never really succeeds. I tried using a few weapons to see if the game shines more from the action perspective but so far I haven't got much luck there too.
As much as I like the general idea of non linear challenges, mixture of stealth and survival, greek mythology etc, the game is not fun.

Update:
The reason we're returning to it is the fact that the game got patched shortly after we released our initial review, and found that they'd fixed the hiding mechanic! This, naturally, means that the game now functions as intended, so we decided to revisit our review.
A few things did get borked in the process, but they're fairly minor, so we're bumping up our initial 6.5 to a much more respectable 7.5/10.

Original Review:
A first person survival game, you play the role of someone who gets thrown into the
ancient labyrinth of the Minotaur. There, the basic idea is supposedly to be ended by
the minotaur, but annoyingly, you try to survive and kill the damned thing.
As you traverse the labyrinth, a lot of interesting features make themselves known.
For one, the labyrinth is randomly generated, so every time you enter a section, you have
a new area to explore. This does appear to be the cause of some wonky pathfinding, but in
general, the idea's quite nice. Also, the graphics, whilst not excessively good, set the theme
quite well, and they do a fair bit to enhance the gameplay.
However, issues do occur. Alongside the wonky pathfinding, we found a problem with the stealth
mechanics of the game. You're told to extinguish your torch and hide in the shadows to avoid
having the Satyr slice your head off, but something went broke in patching, and it just makes
a beeline for you regardless of your opinion on the matter. That, coupled with the fact that
you can occasionally smack enemies out of the world, and some other issues, and the game is
not precisely flawless.
Our opinion on the matter is that, despite the bugs, the game is quite compelling, so we're
hoping for some patch-work on it. If that happens, the game deserves a higher score than we're
currently giving it, but in it's current state, the game is worth a 6.5/10. Passable, but not
brilliant.
Still, keep an eye on this!

What can I say about this game? It's one of the many examples on how to revive old-school first person shooters and bring them into modern day gaming. This game (along with other games like the Shadow Warrior reboot and Wolfenstein: The New Order) shows how that can happen. It's a nice break from a genre saturated with Call of Duty and it's various games.
Plot: You are the Doom Slayer, a badass from another world who went to Hell and back but got placed in a tomb. You are freed from your tomb and go into a base in Mars where a corporation (mega corporations never learn about unleashing terrors and the negative impact it has) opens a portal to Hell and uses their energy for a new energy resource. Unfortunately, a greedy scientist makes a pact with demons for power in exchange for slaughter. Pick up a shotgun and go to Hell and back!
It defintely goes back to old school first person shooter style with health and armor counters along with non-reloadbale weapons (with the exception of the double barreled Super Shotgun) and shooting demons up. The soundtrack for this game is perfect as you rip demons apart with gory kills and heavy metal to accompany it. There are plenty of nods to the old Doom games like finding a lever which unlocks part of the level to see the old levels from the first Doom as well as other cool easter eggs.
The only thing I could find negative about it is it's graphics heavy and sometimes the game will freeze but the music will stay play so you'll have to reboot on occasion.
Overall, it was a blast playing this game. If you're sick of FPS games like Call of Duty, give this one a try.

TL;DR This game is about strategy, skill, and practice. Very challenging and very rewarding.
This game is actually pretty brilliant. This game is less shmup and more *strategy*. To be able to score enough for an extra life (and you likely WILL lose your others) you basically HAVE to build your score chain up by shooting colored enemies 3 at a time. This game is hugely replayable because it's not a game where simply surviving and killing everything in sight will cut it. It turns out to be very advantageous to plan out every portion of every mission. I can almost guarantee that on your first run you will NOT get past level 3. Playing this game well is a skill. And it's rewarding to beat your high score. Because there is almost NOTHING about this game that is dumb luck. The level design is brilliant: The enemies flying on the screen are absolutely chaotic but there is ALWAYS a way to systematically eliminate them to build your chain.
One GREAT feature here is that the online leaderboards include a REPLAY of the run made to reach that score. So you can go to the top of the leaderboards, download the highest score replay, and watch it to see how he/she did it. It does the same for everyone's replays.
10+ years old and this game is pretty stellar. I find that it's just challenging enough to keep me engaged but not so much that I get worked up about it. Fun way to wind down at the end of the day.

Greetings everybody my name is tommy the game master and welcome to my channel. Well this is the first review I plan on doing with the web cam I just bought hopefully it looks ok. But since Im not quite sure what I am doing with this let me review a type of game that I am not sure if I have any business reviewing, let’s talk about Blaz (make sure to mispronounce it)Blue… oh wait I think that’s supposed to Blaze Blue umm there should be an E at the end of that.. Im not exactly into fighting games, I enjoy them from time to time. But don’t come to me asking me about things like balancing, strategy, or how to be really good at them. I play on easy or begininer mode most of the time, because if I don’t the games AI just going to wipe the floor with me. And don’t get me started about online because I usually get thrashed. Anyways lets get started talking about the steam version of Blaze Blue.
Story
When it comes too the story I hope you’re a heavy drinker because it’s one of those games were I think you have to be intoxicated to understand the plot, and while that can be true of most fighting games, Blaze Blue here takes it to the extreme throwing in alternate realities, different timelines, and time loops into the mix. Basically though it boils down are main character Ragna is out to destroy something called the Cauldron for reasons never explained although it has to do with this psycho girl that looks like his sister. He usually looses the fight gets sent back in time where they merge and become a monster that destroys everything. Character’s are either trying to stop him either do to a personal beef, or because they exist outside of the loop and just are tired of seeing history repeat itself.  While the plot is confusing and makes no sense I quickly fell in love with a lot of the charecters, while Ragna isen’t the most heroic character in fighting game history I did find myself enjoying the charecters of the good nature but bumbling idiot of Taokaka, the wilting flower Noel, and the kind hearted ogre tank Tager. It has some good points and some bad points. I would recommend you check out the story out first through arcade mode for two reasons. Number 1 it’s actually easier to ingest through story mode and number 2 your unlock your prize finishers if you beat the arcade mode.
Story mode in itself isen’t much fun however. A whole lot of text and story book scenes too shift through. And even though it has more dialogue it dosen’t make the narrative any eaiser or more enjoyable then arcade mode. I’ll give it this though the choose your own path way through each charecters mode does have more replayability. Heres the problem though getting game over sets you back too the load screen where you have to load up the file again, and then sit through the wall of text you encounter before the next fight. Yeah there is a fast forward button but it’s still an extra several second wait before getting into the next encounter. And considering how difficult some of the final scenerios are this is an unnecessary pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Gameplay
I’ll give Blaze Blue one thing it knows how to be a good 2d fighting game, I wonder who developed this, I bet you if I reviewed another one of there products I gave it a rave review. (show double dragon 4) arrgghh arrggghh argghh. Ok well even Nintendo has wii music and Urban Champions too embarrass themselves we will go with the fact that Double Dragon 4 was an outlayer, because this game is really good. It knows how to be it’s own 2d fighting game, taking the best of Street Fighter and mixing in with some clever elements of it’s own.
Ok first off lets get started with the charecters while we do have some fighting game tropes when it comes to the charecters, we have the super fast but kind of weak character, we have the kind that changes abilities has the fight progresses character, and we have the boss character that is so freaking OP that he’s almost a nightmare to face everytime you get to an end of an arcade or story mode. Yeah I hate Hakuman. But there are a few unique charecters like this boy who fights with a mechanized doll that you can contril with the A button, leaving with two fighters too control on the screen and while he’s not the easiest character too use in the game it’s defintley more unique then you get in a lot of fighting games.
Anyways the game like most 2d fighting games usually involves 2 fighters going at it until one of them is on the ground. The game specializes the attacks using just 4 buttons. A light, medium, and heavy attack, plus one that in some cases allows for special moves. Typical of most 2d fighting games there are combos too use to do special moves. And when your meter gets filled up even more compolex moves and finishes can be pulled off. The game does try to simplify things using the 2nd analog stick has short cuts for some of these moves, however your not allowed to detmine things like strength of move, and not all special moves can be mapped too a character 2nd analog. But still it comes in handy when pulling off these really dazzling hyper combos.
For the most part I had fun with the combos and using most of the charecters in combat. So what bad can I say about the game. The story mode sucks and I don’t mean just narratively. It gets points by  giving me a choose your own adventure way through the story but there’s not much too the story or the ending, again it’s just a confusing mess. But the worst part is rather then a continue screen too let you restart that fight you just lost you get a game over and taken back to the main menu. Sure there are save screens everywhere so you never start too far back, in fact most times you start right before your last fight, but you still got to go through that fricking wall of text I mention earlier.
Also the steam version has no online gameplay. While it is several years old there really was no excuse when it was released not to have that feature included in it.
Anyways the game is wroth trying out for the gameplay. The action is smooth, it’s solid, and while it does take notes from other 2d fighters like Street Fighter 2 it improves upon them rather then just copying them and it feels really fun.
Graphics
Blaze Blue being a 2d fighter takes notes from arcade games of the late 90’s for it’s look and does them really well. Think like the Street Fighter Alpha series only a lot more modern. The backgrounds are CGI and look really good cgi but the fighters and the people who populate the streets are all hand drawn animation and it look fabulous this does look like a 2d anime fighting and it’s just gorgeous.

Pure excellence is how I'd describe Ikaruga. A game that is both simple and unrelenting in difficulty, like Go. Using a polarity mechanic, Ikaruga allows you to switch the color of your ship and absorb fire of the same color thus breaking the formula of "bullet hell" shooters where you simply avoid all fire. Ikaruga brings with it a sort of challenge that beckons the player to keep trying because while the game is incredibly difficult, it is also fair and always follows its own rules. It is a pleasure to play.
Since its original arcade debut, Ikaruga has seen release on the Dreamcast in Japan, Gamecube worldwide (which still commands a high price today), and XBLA. Now that Treasure has graced us with a PC release, it's a good time to try this real "treasure" of a shooter.

Ikaruga is not for the feint of heart!  If you like punishingly hard games that demand time and dedication to master then you might like ikaruga.  Ikaruga is a bog standard space shoot-em-up with minor puzzle elements using the polarity mechanic to make you immune to bullets of same color (white = white bullet immunity).  It's a game who's sole purpose is a test of skill for who can play the game the longest and shoot enemies in the correct order to get highest rank/score.  If that is not your thing you would be probably better served elsewhere.  Note that Ikaruga doesn't have to be played this way, but the game is designed around it. my energy at clicking those lemon stands and newspaper routes, getting to the point where I could afford managers and upgrades... Not anymore...
Now? Now, it seems to be devolving, developing down to the despicable industry standard for mobile game apps. Innovativeness, gameplay, creativity all take a backseat to psychological manipulation. So, the in-app purchases have been there for a while, and, yes, I have spent a pretty dollar. Those made me uneasy, at first, but I grew accustomed, I became habituated to the shop and I got over it. What I cannot stand is the blatantly addictive features. Features such as 'daily gifts' that get better the more days of the week you check in, the brand new wheel spins to collect a prize for purchasing an upgrade, in-app purchases that unlock the next level of spending (Oh, you're wiling to put down $1 on a 3x multiplier? Lemme just have y'all know that I could have easily just whipped out the PS4 version of Nep VII and simply played the game on that. But no. I bought this game again, along with all it's character DLC, on the PC, just to show Compile Heart and Idea Factory that the Neptunia series is one of the best thing that they have ever created.
The game itself is pretty good, and serves as a great entry point for newcomers to the series. The only thing you'll be missing for not playing the previous games will be a few random references relating to them. They added a ton of fancy new gameplay elements, but it's still the same Nep formula, so those who have actually played the other Nep games won't feel alienated in the slightest. In fact, almost all of the additions are vast improvements from the other Nep games, making this game probably the best Nep game in the series thus far.
This game is actually crazy complex, so I'm not going to delve too deep into things. If you want to know more about this game, then go read some other review, or actually buy the game. The game comes with tutorials. Read them. Seriously though, it's a good game. Everything you need to know is explained as you play along, from the combat to the storyline. The only noteworthy flaw is that on lower end PCs, don't expect this game to peak at more than 20 FPS at any point. IF and Compile Heart really decided to jack up the graphics, given that this is a PS4 game, and all the previous Nep games were either PS3 or PSVITA games. Seriously though, having a GTX 960 as a reccommended requirement is pretty intense for a JRPG, even if it's a PS4 game. Other than that, the gameplay is solid, and I would recommend this to anyone who is a Nep fan, or really just likes JRPGs in general. The art is drawn by Tsunako, and it looks fantastic The gameplay and story are also both amazing. Also, the guy who voiced Umio also voiced Aizen from Bleach, which I find to be absolutely hilarious and amazing.

Since HiRez *FINALLY* released a patch for this game, after two whole years, I figured it was time to patch my review.  While everyone figured they abandoned the game (which, they pretty much did for a while there), they came out of no where with this new patch.  And it puts the feel of the old school Tribes games back in.  Gone are the individual classes, back with just the light/medium/heavy sets and customizable loadouts.  There's been a slew of quality improvements as well as a couple new maps.  I definitely feel like I'm playing a graphically and mechanically updated version of the beloved Starsiege Tribes from the late 90s, which is fantastic.  A lot of F2P games get you with their IAPs and P2W, but even HiRez has admitted they're not going to make money off this patch.  They've basically given the old players everything in the game completely unlocked.  You shouldn't spend more than $10 on the game unless you're just impatient, as it appears everything (except armor skins and voice packs) are unlockable via XP.  I can't not recommend this game to fans of the FPS genre, because the bottom line is it's just that good.

I DO NOT recommend this game, based on the most recent OB64 changes to card system.
I've been playing Paladins on and off since CB, about 300 hours, I've spent $150 on gems, another $20 on founders pack, I still have over 6000 gems on the account, with most of the cards currently available unlocked.
I would probably enjoy quite some advantage over new players/non-payers in the new system, but I cannot recommend the direction this game is going.
The new cards unbound system is tilting heavily towards pay-to-win.
Yes, Paladins like most other f2p games, has this kind of pay-to-gain advantages in the past, and I'll admit I've bought into it, benefit from it in the past, but with the most recent changes it drastically :
1) Increase the difference between max level cards loadout and starter loadout.
Previously, all players are bound in a 12 points system. Newer players will have 12 points, just like veterans, but with limited choices which cards (what TYPE of benefits). They may have sub-optimal card build, and less builds to choose from, but if a veteran uses the same build, the card level( LEVEL of benefits) will be at the same level.
With the new system, this is no longer the case, you can level up cards to provide DOUBLE, if not higher benefits than a new player.
2) Grind
As before, you can still acquire the cards through in-game currency/progression.
However, unlike before where you can use a in-game currency to craft a specific card you desire (and obtain the full benefits) you can only obtain cards RANDOMLY, through chests in the new system.
Not to mention to level up the card you need to gain duplicates of the card you want.
The time/luck, or the real-money, to obtain a maximum benefits card you desire in the old system, and the new system is incomparable.

Let's try to summarize everything nicely, shall we ?
Paladins is an open beta that was imo almost perfect, it had somethings that were better then even it's biggest competitor Overwatch.
At the heart of it was the card system, you bought cards with in game money and with a 12 point limit that you could re-distribute as you wish, you only needed to have exact 12 points and 5 cards, always.
It was imo simple but very neatly put together and the comunity flourished by trying out different layouts of the cards, that's what made people comeback again and again and again.
Now with the newest update, Open Beta 64, Paladins wishes to take a step back, ignoring the obvious heavy in-game changed mechanics in a product that is already in beta and shouldn't have those, Paladins has, in a nutshell, abandoned the old scheme, and basically went with a grind-until-you-drop-dead aproach, basically you have all the cards, but their effectiveness/power is upgradable, this on paper might actually sound like the start of a good idea, but believe it's not.
The problems lies in HOW you upgrade them, basically you have to open chests for that, and even then it's not guaranteed your favorites will drop, RNG will take care of that for you. If this souns familiar, then I guess that was the idea :p
Anyways, I could have explained it better but this was supposed to be a short review.
At least it's their goal, right ? "Make receiving cards FUN AGAIN and give a nearly ENDLESS progression path in the game" - HiRez president/CEO whateve

Endless Space is a sci-fi, turn-based strategy game with semi-real-time elements to it (yes, I know. You’re wondering what I mean by semi-real-time but I’ll get to that later). It features eight playable races where, like many other turn-based strategy game, where victory is achieved by one of several ways.
Starting the game up I had to choose the type of universe I would play in by going through the different options provided (for both single player and multiplayer). I was able to choose the shape of the galaxy, the universe’s age, how many opponents I would compete against, and the size of the galaxy. There was even an advanced option menu where I could tweak other factors such as wormholes, resources, number of planets in a solar system, and a few other details. So many options meant that I would be unable to become very familiar with any particular map since it is all randomized.
From there I had eight different races to choose from, the United Empire, Sowers, Sophons, Pilgrims, Horatio, Hissho, Cravers, and Amoebas: each race with their own sets of strengths and weaknesses and their own story. For example, the United Empire is great at making money and has a strong military whereas the Sophons are great at researching technology but produce feeble warriors. Suffice to say that there is a race to match various types of playstyles.

Blaz Blue, the spiritual successor of Guilty Gear, a fighting game series most well known for it's high resolution animation and complex fighting system. As a mostly Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter player, I've wanted to try out some of these games, Calamity Trigger being a great entry point for newcommers. This version does not feature online multiplayer and has a more limited line up of characters, but for a lower price title (which I got for a irresistible discount), it still features quite a lot of content. Visually and sonically, it's a very proficient title, combining hand drawn 2D animation with 3D backgrounds and a rocking soundtrack. There are a fair amount of modes there, from the standard "versus" and "arcade" modes to the "story" mode where we can watch animation and play along. As someone who is not exactly into Anime, I can still commend this title to any fighting game fan who wants a entry point into the Blaz Blue series. And if you aim higher, I would suggest some of the later titles that also feature online play and a lot more characters and content.

Ikaruga is one of the greatest games I'll ever get to play. Ever since the first time I played it I knew that it was not just a game, but a rival; Something I will look to and say "One more try!" for the rest of my gaming days. The newbie's goal will be survival through bullet hell, but the expert's goal will be an almost puzzle game-esque attempt to score as many points through chaining combos, and it is when one gets to that point that they realize the level of perfection this game is. It was perfectly crafted to be played a specific way. What you thought was chaos is actually perfectly arranged. What you thought you could never do has become so obvious it's like second nature.
However, you will not get that far unless you're willing to lose and lose and lose and lose. Ikaruga rewards determination and practice with complete satisfaction. Some people aren't willing to try like that for any game. They won't know the feeling of accomplishment from becoming skillful at this game.

Mastering a level could be compared, at least superficially, to learning a song – at the very least, the game’s constant forward crawl and emphasis on perfect timing on a succession of coloured marks shares a lot with the typical rhythm game.
But this only really explains the long tail of the experience. For all the zen-like, dot-eating mastery that you’ll strive for in the long term, Ikaruga’s early appeal is sustained remarkably effectively by the base elements of gaming that we’re often so quick to dismiss. Developed for the now antique hardware shared by the Dreamcast and Naomi arcade board, Ikaruga isn’t exactly pumping polygons, but it still looks fantastic.
This world of elaborate black and white mecha – always accented by reds and blues respectively – is an alluring invention. The art design gives us a unique science fiction world that is more inventive and arresting than the worlds spun out of a long list of triple-A miscellany. The music is rousing, building to some strangely affecting moments near the tail end of the game. The sound effects are pitch perfect, whether digitally screaming at you on a boss approach or punctuating your deft control with explosions and that impossibly unrepetitious chorus of ‘MAX CHAIN, MAX CHAIN, MAX CHAIN’.
[...]
Don’t disqualify yourself from playing this game. You’re probably never going to be someone who can complete
, but there’s so much more fun to be had at the shallow end of play than you’d think at first glance. 50 to 5,000 hours of fun, in fact.

Depths of Fear: Knossos is quite an interesting game. Certainly worth the two dollars I spent buying it on sale. The game is quite flawed though having been developed by only one person I believe. In fact before the recent patch it was literally unplayable, crashing to desktop often. The patch did squash many bugs and I was able to finish the game yesterday.
The graphics are rough, the animation janky. The ambiance is very good though. Gameplay is serviceable but nothing special. However, the sound design is perhaps one of the best things about the game. The sounds of the various monsters are frightening and atmospheric. The music is great, reminiscent of 80's cult horror movies at least that is what it made me think of. It actually reminded me a bit of the Hotline Miami soundtrack. The developer is quite skilled at sound work I thought.
Depths of Fear: Knossos is a rogue-like dungeon crawler. Or perhaps rogue-lite is a better term for it. You are the legendary Theseus thrown into the pits of Knossos and you must defeat the Minotaur and escape. There are several mythical monsters you must defeat including the Hydra, Medusa, and Cerebus. Each monster you defeat gives you a gold coin and when you have enough coins it unlocks a sword and you can then face the Minotaur.
Before you can defeat the monsters you must first go through the randomly generated dungeons trying to find a key to escape. You find money you can use to buy various weapons and books used to by spells by worshiping at shrines of various gods. The monsters are stalking you and cannot be defeated. You can kill them but they just respawn. You must hide or run for you life. This is quite tense and enjoyable adding a bit of survival horror to the game. There are zombies and skeletons roaming around sometimes too. Escape from four of these levels and you move onto an arena level where you face the monster. It can then be defeated and you can retrieve the coin.
I have a passion for greek mythology and this game really did the myths justice. Quite a unique game that I was glad to experience.

Learn valuable survival skills, such as ignoring all the enemies, running blindly into initially perceived danger until you find a key, then hoofing it to the exit, all while trying to avoid detection of the fearsome Guardians, and inevitably failing at that most of the time, continuing to ignore all the enemies and still make it out okay anyways!

You'll writhe in fear as you sit on a pillar too tall for them to reach while slowly rising lava eventually consumes then, trivializing the boss fight in a matter of seconds! Then again, do you dare challenge the beasts head on? Well in that case you'll probably be the one getting consumed by the rising lava, so more power to you. I didn't think it was really worth it when I could just watch them be helplessly melted by rising lava.
So? Do you think you can survive the DEPTHS of FEEEEEEEEEAR?

You are a greek man name Thesius.  You wake up in a jailcell in an undisclosed location and are immeadiatly brought to King Minos by two guards. Minos chuckles a little and tells them to push you into the gaping hole you're standing in front of. You fall what I can assume is the equivalent of two stories into a giant pool of water. You climb out as a feeling of dread slaps you in the face. You're in the ♥♥♥♥ing Labyrinth. (Not the film starring David Bowie, which would be immensely scarier.) Your attention is brought towards the existence of the Minotaur, which is Minos' son, who can and will murder the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you once you have killed every other creature from greek mythology.
Try reading that all in one breath.
Anyway, the game plays like a dated fps game, but not in a bad way. It feels natural, given the gameplay isn't full of assault rifles and other ridiculous gadgets. Instead, the game encourages stealth as you traverse the many dungeons filled with satyrs and chimeras. Overall, the entire feel of the game is entirely B-movie based. The film grain effect should catch your eye right away, as will the synth powered soundtrack. (Anyone who watched the original Clash of the Titans will know what I mean.)

I grew up using game controllers for many systems. I have used controllers for the NES, Sega Genesis, SNES, Nintendo 64, Dreamcast, Playstations 1-3, GameCube, Xbox, and Xbox 360.  I have also played several handheld consoles, starting with the original Game Boy up through the DS.  It seems to me that the basic trend has been to learn lessons and to improve controller design.
The Steam Controller is a painful, frustrating rejection of this knowledge.  It is the worst controller design of all the ones I have ever used.
First, the controller's shape and layout is uncomfortable.  The wings where your palms are meant to grip are elevated above the surface of the control, rotating the hands into an unfamiliar position that makes it a stretch for your thumbs to reach the thumbstick and buttons.  It is in fact so far that I frequently hit the "B" button when I'm reaching for the "A" button.  This is not because my hands are small.  In fact, the Dreamcast controller literally gave me blisters on the tops of my fingers because they did not have enough space inside, and the original Xbox controller was one of the first controllers that felt designed with me in mind.
Perhaps the wing arrangment would not be so bad if the thumbstick and action buttons were in the usual positions.  Unfortunately, instead of familiar, well-understood, and easy-to-use control mechanisms, we find two digital trackpads.  Thumbsticks, D-pads, action buttons, bumpers, and triggers are fantastic controls because they provide an easy sense of orientation and successful use.  Trackpads do not.  Whenever I have tried to use the trackpads (especially the right one when it's in "mouse" mode), I am badly surprised by what input is registered.  Trying to use the right trackpad as either a mouse or a joystick has not worked properly in any of the control schemes for any of the games I have tried.  Even trying to use the left trackpad as a D-pad usually does not work well.
This leads into the main problem of the controller: its unfamiliar design and emphasis on digital trackpads makes configuration of the controller's mappings very important.  Too important, in fact; I have spent somewhere between 30-40% of my time trying to use this controller switching to the home screen to try tweaking the layout or finding one that will maybe work for me.  Perhaps if I waited a year or two for the community to work all the kinks out of their profiles I would find some that work for me.  But why should I wait that long?  Why should I have to spend several hours trying to figure out how I can map buttons and quirky digital controls in the hopes that I get something that will feel natural?
The last issue with the controller are the underside buttons.  I understand how the designers thought they were a good idea, just as I understand that they thought highly programmable trackpads were preferrable to more limited and specific controls.  But here they made another mistake.  I, at least, get tense when I am absorbed in a good game.  When I start getting into the game, I start to squeeze the controller harder.  This is not a problem on most controllers.  On the Steam controller, this means that I am now pressing two action buttons that I probably did not mean to press.  Sure, I can spend more time customizing my control scheme to turn those buttons off, but they had intended these buttons to be used so that I would not have to take my thumbs off the trackpads.  Instead, I need to design a control scheme that forces me to do just that, and the rest of the controller's layout makes that difficult to use.
I allow that other people seem to love this controller.  When I wrote this, there was 82% positive feedback.  It could be that I am just not Valve's intended audience.  I do not see the appeal, and I am sorry I spent the money and time trying to see if it could work out.  Now I am going to spend my time seeing if GameStop will let me return it.

text: Jesus this game is a glorified power point on japan

In
you play as a young man from an unnamed Western country (presumably the United States) who is on vacation on his first ever trip to Japan. As part of his trip, he is meeting and staying with some friends he met over the Internet, named Makoto and Akira, whom he expects to be guys like him. But when he arrives at the airport he finds out they are actually sisters and he will be staying at their house during his week in Japan. Plus, their parents are not home! For the week, Makoto and Akira will show you around some of Japan's sights and explain some of the culture and history of the country.
I remember first hearing about this game a couple years ago via some clips on YouTube long before I even played my first visual novel in 2016 and I thought it was a rather silly concept.
certainly stands out as one of the more well-known visual novels available on Steam, but I hesitated to check it out until I finally bought it during the summer sale. I had certainly seen it parodied enough and was curious enough to check it out for myself. So the question is: Is it really that bad?
As a note for this review, I am aware that there are two DLC expansions available for this game, however, I only played the base game without these additions. My review is entirely based on just that.
As said previously, this game is a visual novel, so most of the gameplay is just reading text with some visuals to go along with it. Unlike other visual novels, this game is not heavily story-based but rather focused on the more educational aspects. Indeed, in the world Japanese-made visual novels,
is rather rare in that it is intended for a foreign audience. Playing it feels like a miniature guidebook on what to expect during a real visit to Japan. There are a few decision points in the game, most notably in deciding which destinations around Tokyo to tour. There are only two different endings to achieve.
The art in the game looks pretty good. The background art is probably the main attraction considering the game is about seeing different sights in Japan and the characters and CGs are well done as well, even if the character sprites are rather limited in their poses. However, there is an issue with the art. Even though the art that is present in the game is good, playing this really leaves one desiring more. Especially considering the point of the game, I really expected more visuals at times. There are many scenes where it just shows a shot of the sky while the text describes what is being seen. Too many parts of the game simply violate the old rule of "show, don't tell."
The writing is where this game runs into some real problems. As many other reviewers have noted, the player-character is insufferable. Despite somehow being able to speak near-fluent Japanese, it seems that his only knowledge of Japan comes from manga and anime. This quickly becomes annoying as he goes around and expresses amazement at the most banal things, even if what he encounters in Japan might be unusual by Western standards. A prominent example would be how the game explains something called a SUICA card, which in practice functions very similarly to a debit or credit card, but his amazement hardly abates. Really, this character often feels like the worst stereotype of a weeaboo.
The writing also fails in another important aspect. Even though the express purpose of the game is to educate foreigners about Japan, there was still an apparent need to put in some kind of story. The plot in the game is paper-thin and very poorly written. I think I can accept that the entire premise of the game is pretty contrived, but the lengths the game goes to in order to pander to a Western otaku audience is annoying. As the game progresses and the player-character spends more time around Akira and Makoto, they start to develop feelings for him. This eventually culminates with one of them declaring her love for him by the end of the game. Keep in mind that the entire story takes place over a mere seven days. The entire attempt to put in a light romance plot or even to try to develop the characters feels extremely ham-fisted and just distracts from what the game should have focused on.
When it comes to trying to educate the player about Japan, it is mostly hit and miss. As I said, the poor plot gets in the way, but I suppose it is possible to learn some interesting tidbits about Japan in the game. I believe it would have been more effective if they just focused on the cultural or historical aspects. Too much dialogue is spent on explaining things like how the train system works or the use of public restrooms. Since I am no expert in Japanese history or culture, I cannot speak for the accuracy of the information present in the game. However, I did note that one fact was doubly wrong. At one point, Akira states that Admiral Perry was responsible for the opening of Japan in 1863. This event actually happened in 1853 and Perry was a commodore, not admiral. When coming across this information that I knew to be wrong, I wondered what else might be incorrect that I just did not know about.
The music in the game is fairly generic sounding, though certainly not bad. It does get a little repetitive, but I still felt it was a pleasant addition.
Overall, I went into this game with fairly low expectations and saw them met. What could have been an educational game about Japan instead fails. As I said earlier in this review, I only played the base game so I have no idea if these issues were rectified in the DLC releases. As it stands, I feel like I cannot recommend this game. This might be of interest to people who want to learn about Japan, but there are much better sources out there.

Many reviewers seem to dislike DOOM's multiplayer. When playing multiplayer, your experience is shaped by ping, other people's skill levels, the community, game mode, team (if applicable) and gameplay mechanics. I could go into this a lot more but I'm not focusing this review on the multiplayer, but I am just giving an explanation why many reviews are less than positive of this amazing singleplayer experience.
It is my belief that reviews should not try to combine singleplayer and multiplayer into one rating, as the mechanics and fundamental experiences a player has are completely different and should not be treated as such.
Now that the disclaimer's out of the way, lets get into the review of DOOM 2016 Singleplayer.
DOOM is a masterpiece of a FPS.
It's atmospheric. There's a real sense of tension in between lulls of combat when you're scavenging the bloodied mars base. The ambient effects are brilliant at giving you a real sense of horror. Early on when you're fighting imps you'll notice they are very adept at crawling around on railings and scaling walls. After you smash in their skull and find your way into a supposed "safe" zone, you will still occasionally hear scuttling of claws among railings in the room above you, or something walking through the ventilation. You don't know if its an actual enemy or just the game messing with you. You're rewarded for exploring levels by gaining more upgrade points for exploration, but not enough to make it feel mandatory to be strong enough. That's a very good thing. If you want nonstop combat you can just rush into demons without worrying, but if you want the demon, scientist, artifact, weapon, lore / experiment reports, you're able to feel like you're really learning and benefitting from the insane twisted research.
There's also a real sense of progression. Finding new weapons gives you a feeling of relief and awe, every single time. It's quite impressive how the game keeps one-upping itself in this regard. It's an experience I don't wish to spoil, but upon obtaining the last weapon I squealed in joy and stopped for 10 seconds in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic awe after firing it for the first time. This sense of progression is also mirrored in armor and weapon upgrades being obtained through completing specific badass challenges and time trials. You didn't buy those upgrades. You earnt them.
That said though, the enemies also progress at the same rate so you don't become an overpowered god of death. You are powerful, yes, and can destroy the enemies that were giving you trouble at the start of the game easily, but you're always threatened by bigger and more powerful demons with more crazy powers. It eventually becomes an art where you don't even need to think about situations like:
six rockets and a shotgun blast will stagger a mancubus
and let you rush to it and tear out it's heart and shove it down it's own throat to get some health back
and then you'll be able to turn and charge a gauss rifle precision shot
and one shot a cacodemon in the eye to turn it into a fine red mist.
Combat becomes second nature and you become intimately aware of your weapon's capabilities and the enemy demon's weaknesses.
Speaking of combat, it's f**king great. None of the weapons are bad, except for the starting pistol but that's more of an ammo conserve tool, and each have their own strengths and weaknesses. Movement is fluid, enemies are scary, you're surrounded very often and have to carve your way out yet you rarely feel cornered or trapped. Glory kills are a great tool to cover distance and function similarly to something like Bloodborne's blood rally system where they encourage you to keep fighting after you take damage, instead of playing passive and running away.
However, I believe the most important aspect of doom, my personal favourite aspect of the game, the thing that influenced my gameplay and made me feel the most emotion, was the SOUNDTRACK.
THE SOUNDTRACK IS ABSOLUTELY AMAZING. THIS IS A MASTERPIECE.
The soundtrack fits the game so well. It adds tension. It adds ambience. It sounds like it's "alongside" you during combat. It mimics your movements and shots. It crescendos upon the largest spawn of demons when the firefight is most intense. It really gets your heart pumping and adrenaline flowing. It gets extra metal during your gory Glory Kills. This game utilizes it's soundtrack to the fullest extent and should be best enjoyed with headphones at max volume. It also pays homage to some older doom songs as well, which older fans might pick up on, yet they're different enough to not be copies or covers. If I could stress one point about this review it is this. If you like game soundtracks, and especially enjoy when they mirror the events happening on screen, please check out this game.
Here's just a quick list of neat features that I liked in game that are not major, but neat nonetheless
-in game map is incredibly detailed. It's actually more like a 3D architect model than a map. It is also easy to navigate, rotate, and pan.
-quickswapping weapon mods
-level challenges
-customization with weapons / armor paths
-environment design is awesome
Here's one concern I have regarding the game
-can be too exciting
Seriously. I'd be honestly worried if you had a heart condition and were playing this game. This isn't a joke or trying to belittle anyone who gets scared. I'd really suggest seeing a doctor or something about this sort of stuff. You definitely get a surge of heartrate and adrenaline while playing this game, and that could be dangerous.
Here's some things I didn't like about the game, and think it could have done better.
-rune trials are a bit hit or miss. Some are good. Some are not so good. They are also a little bit hidden / require some exploring but provide your Doom Marine suit with a rune slot, which is a decent power boost.
-runes. The runes you can put into the suit are not balanced at all. Some are great and some are meh. You need to complete 7 runes trials to unlock all three slots, which means you can't get progress towards the rank two version. I think you should be able to put runes in the slots and gain progress towards their rank two version, but not get the benefit until the slot is activated in your armor.
-stuck. I got stuck five times in game over about 12 hours. One time I had to die to get out and lost 30 seconds of progress. The other 4 I fired a Gauss rifle and that pushed me out, but I'm gonna assume that someone without the Gauss rifle would have to die. This is super minor. Also one time I jumped and my camera clipped through the world for half a second. Even more minor.
-title screen was super slow, updated my graphics card drivers and that fixed it. That isn't really a negative, I should keep them up to date, but if your graphics drivers are out of date then you might have to wait 5 minutes on starting up or something.
-bosses. I wish there were more. However, that's purely personal opinion because I love fighting bosses, and making them more common would diminish the rarity that the few bossfights had.
-bethesda. Bethesda's an awful gaming company and they didn't make this game. They gave money to ID to make this game. However, by purchasing this game, you are giving Bethesda money. That's always a negative.
-keys. I get why you need key cards in a facility, but why do they have yellow and blue skulls to open demon doors. That's a little silly in my opinion. Could have been something cooler like a demon with a matching pentagram on his torso or something. I guess it keeps it simple.
-Glory kills. They're awesome, but it's not completely clear how many variations of them there are. It would be nice if there were some glory kill manual, they could be vague enough to promote experimentation, but I don't really feel like the information provided in game gives you enough info to get you experimenting yourself.
That's my review of DOOM 2016.

The best single player FPS experience I have had in easily more than a decade.  The combat and health system is brilliant, and finally puts the trash cover based, "wait for shields to recharge" garbage to rest.  Need health?  Better run headlong into enemies cause they are your only source of health... genius.  This simple game play mechanic defines the experience.  You are never stationary in combat, no taking cover or stopping to regenerate health.
The need for health, ammo, and the requirement of dodging forces you out into the dangerous open.  you are constantly running around huge and varied combat areas, stylishly decimating enemies, and narrowly dodging fireballs in the process.  It's so incredibly satisfying, and those who try to play the game with soem type of hide and shoot approach will get splattered.  You have to face your fears and get right in there mixing it up with the demon hordes, it feels so incredible.  The style of running and gunning makes every combat encounter feel like you are narrowly escaping death and ripping endless waves of demons to shreds by the skin of your teeth.  It's bar non the most exhilarating single palyer FPS campaign I have ever played from a pure gunplay standpoint... and I really am finding a hard time putting it's badassery into words.
It's such a fkin breath fo fresh air after the last 15+ years of the same boring, cover based, recharging health, 2 weapon FPS crap campaigns that last 4 hours.  Thank god for DOOM 2016!  It's the 90's FPS love letter I've been waiting for.

Remember when you bought that game at release on PS4 because "heck i'll be done with it when it eventually releases on PC?"... yeah I remember too...
The port works quite fine, runs at constant 60fps except for minor stuttering when transitioning scenes in general in my case, not really bothersome since these transitions usually occur with a fade to black or fade to white, eg: in-game to VN mode, or back to game, or when you press the Enter dungeon button you'll notice a slight pause before the game goes to load the level.
The Soundtrack is really good, with all known BGMs from other games and really cool additions ("Encounter of Destiny" so OP).
Regarding the game, it's more Nep! So I have no objections with that, without spoiling the story too much (already beaten it a few times in PS4) I'll say it manages to strike a better balance between comedy and drama than ReBirth 2, it knows exactly when to stop taking itself seriously, that's a good thing.
Giant boss battles are entertaining, though one might say there are few of them, they come at the right moments to make them meaningful.
They also brought back CPU transformation cutscenes, when you activate HDD form, you're treated to a short cutscene of waifu's transformation into CPU, never skipping those, they're so damn cool!
Combat is a bit more streamlined, the basics are there, you have up to 5 hits per turn, but there's no more Guard Break mechanic so the Break attacks are now named "Standard" and fill a middle ground between Power attacks damage and Rush attacks EXE drive fill. Combo length is now affected by the weapon the character is holding, each weapon has a first attack of one fixed type (Rush, Power or Standard) and then it has one or more combo slots in each type of hit (eg: you can have a weapon with 1 fixed Rush slot, and following it 1 more Rush, and in parallel 2 Power and 4 Standard slots).
In addition many attacks have a "combo trait", which gives your next hit additional damage when you fulfil the combo trait condition for it.
Sort of replacing the Guard Break mechanic, you now have some monters which have breakable body parts, these are usually located and can only be attacked from a specific side of the monster (ie: back, left side, right side, etc), this gives a somewhat tactical approach to combat, since breaking parts can help by reducing one monster's defense, as well as negating the use of certain skills on some others, sadly once you start overleveling the dungeon monters by a tiny bit this is no longer really needed, but it's an interesting system to develop further in sequels (yes please give me MOAR NEP)
There are also leveling and lily rank system changes, regarding leveling, only your front row characters will get experience from fights, this can look like downer compared to previous games, rest assured though, again trying to not spoil too much, you'll hardly have a party of more than 4 characters during your first playthrough, and by the time you have a full roster, you can easily create game discs with the Racing idea chip, which allows characters to gain exp when not in the front line (gives the "Learning" ability).
Lily rank has also seen some changes, like exp, lily rank is now increased between all members of the front row once you finish a battle, as opposed to the previous front+back row pair system.
Previous lily rank increasing actions between characters still work though, such as buffing, healing one ally or allies, using items on allies, and also switching the front row character with the back row coupled one will increase lily rank between them.
Last but not least, this is the first Neptunia game I felt like being "harder" than the others, midway through the game you'll notice you are tossed into the world being underleveled for the mobs you have to fight, so it will require some grinding and good use of combo traits, skills and whatnot, it's not something that will take a huge amount of time though, it lasts long enough to make it challenging and not boring, suffice to say, if you got the DLC weapons this does not apply at all to your playthrough.
Wasn't expecting to write this wall of text, but I guess you can see I really DO recommend this game, it's a good step forward for the series, although it might not be trying to do a lot of new stuff, it's still refreshing enough to go back Nep'n around Hyperdimension and its companion universes :P

TL;DR - I love it enough that I kinda want to play games just to have a reason to use it
So, let me preface this review by saying that I was definitely one of the many people who were skeptical about this hardware, but I decided to take a chance on it, and was really happy with how it paid off. I've been using the controller for a little over 4 months now, and I've really enjoyed my experience with it. I understand that some early adopters had issues, but having come in a few months into its public life, a lot of the community configs turned out to be great for the games I play, so really, I've had very little to complain about.
PROS:
- It feels really good in hand (I have fairly large hands, so it doesn't feel small like a lot of other controllers do)
- Buttons, sticks and pads offer responsivity and feel at least comprable to modern console controllers
- It emulates a regular controller fairly well
- Custiomization is easy and robust, so in many ways, you can really make it your own, and it's great having different configs for different games
- Hybrid control with both a mouse-like trackpad and the joysticks is really nice in a lot of action games (and works reasonably well for shooters too, though the latter takes some getting used to)
- Desktop mode means I can configure and use the controller with non-steam games too (like things on Origin), which is really nice
CONS:
- Touch-based controls can be a bit weird, so it might require some calibration or creative set-ups for a smooth experience
- The gyro assisted mouse is nice in theory, but I often find that it takes away more than it offers with fine control.
- Other apps/games don't recognize it as a controller (which I guess is expected), but it's unfortunate that it doesn't get recognized as one even when configured to behave as a traditional controller. I was hoping to be able to use it on a few hobby projects, but guess that's not gonna be possibel for a while
- Usability can be disabled with some non-steam games (eg. SWTOR), which reject even the desktop configuration for some reason.
I'll end this review by saying that, though the learning curve can be a bit steep, I honestly feel it was worth it. The controller delivers as a controller and more, and being able to configure controls however you want (literally) in the palm of your hands is more even amazing than I expected it to be.

Up until I got this game (and I use that term loosely in this case) I stayed away from the manga visual novel...things (not sure what to call them exactly. Interactive manga?). I caved and got this particular example because I was under the impression that it would be educational since it basically sells itself as a virtual guide to Japan. I thought that I'd be getting a Japanese history and culture lesson, maybe learn a bit of the language.
Nope, learned only one word in just over an hour. There's japanese subtitles for everything the girls say but no attempt to teach how to even read it.
I also immediately noticed right off that the protagonist, and whose headspace you share for this experience, is pretty much a living otaku stereotype complete with cringe inducing dialogue and monologue. Oh my beloved Japan! Then it also becomes apparent that a ham fisted romance angle is just around the corner not even an hour into it when otaku!boy realizes that he staying with the two girls (one of whom may or may not be jail bait) with the parents gone for the duration.
Lastly, for a visual novel, there's more telling then there is showing. I was expecting illistrations for everything, but so far just a few set pieces and the expectation that you use your imagination for everything. Which goes against the point of this VN I think. Guess most of the budget and time in this regard went into animating the girls.
Also, the art for the main menu didn't exactly fill me with confidence for this. Just more Big Sis emphasising that, yes, she has big fun bags. And a Not!PantyShot from Sis the Younger.
Last thing, for reals this time, I thought that there would be more decision making from myself in this game. Like branching paths to the overall story and, if any, sub-plots since you are going on a guided tour for over a week. But so far apart from deciding how much yen a USD is worth, Otaku!Boy is firmly in the drivers seat when it comes to actions and dialogue. Which is a shame because the protagonist doesn't feel like a actual person and it shows.
This review may change if I can be bothered to pick up the game again later, to give it a second chance with the thought that it'll get better, but I doubt it to be honest. Too many red flags and stumbles before you even through the door.

Doom is a very fun game, more then it probably should be. The whole campaign has a very good narritive when compared to most other fps tiltes currently on the market. The characters are written well for the dialoge that is in the story. But the gameplay is what takes center stage. Doom returns to the fps genres roots with health packs, extra armor, and WAY more then 2 weapons. It 100% works as well, the enimes are challenging and the gameplay feels so unrestricted. I don't want to go to in detail with it because 1. I hope that you'll play it yourself and 2. Its simplictity is the hook of the gameplay. If you were making the first fps ever with current day graphics engines and you made it well, you would get this game. The multiplayer is also fun it's nothing groundbreaking but it definetly has some replayability. Doom's gamplay I personally think is best suited for it's story rather then it's multiplayer. There's nothing particularly wrong with it but it's nothing that hasn't been done by every othe sci-fi shooter out there. It doesn't have that unique feeling the campaign has. Double jump, advanced mobilty, symmetrical maps, somewhat unbalanced weapons. It is a fun time despite this though with solid sound design, very good moment to moment encounters, and maps that at the very least work around Doom's movement style. But agian it has been done better elsewhere. Doom is roughly around a 8/10 for me personally.

Its was around 20 years after the original doom came out that this game was released. The orginal currently runs on my phone and with head phones is still as impactful now as it was then.
Which is why the fact that I played this remake for twenty minutes and was disappointed about how muted and meh it felt.
Ignoring the fact that the orginal doom basically ran on anything and this version is unoptimised and strangly has high hardware demands,  my main complaint is it doesn't feel like doom.
It's hard to explain as it is missing visceral part that makes it feel impactful.
Maybe comparing and contrasting the start of doom, with the start of the remake.
In the orginal it starts with you in an empty room, straight away high enemy heavy metal starts to play. You have complete control from the start, movement is fast. as you leave the room you hear the moans and groans of the monsters before you you see them, you enter a room with a path going through a pool of lava, across the pool is a hairy ape creature throwing fire balls, you fire at it. The pistol has slight recoil which has slight push back and clear impactful sounds. Following this you enter a room which is completely dark, accept for one area lit up in the centre. Starting there is another human. when you get close to the human you realise it is a zombie.
Again the shots feel impactful, something which is highlighted by the monster moaning and reacting to the shots.
This entire sequence happens in the first four minutes of the game. The music, the controls and how reactive they are, the monsters from the fore shadowing, to how they act, etc all give a high energy, high control impactful experience.
Now in this remake, it starts instead with your character restrained,  a monster approaches and with out any real player control the main character crushes it's skull. The music is either amospheric or non exist depending on how charitible your feeling. The you are provided a gun and the room how four lubbering zombies who moan slowly and are no threat and can be shot to piece with the pistol with no real struggle. The gun in question does not have a significant recoil and the sound rather than the alarming bang of a gun, is basically pew-pew, making it feel like a pea shooter despite destroying the initial zombies. Rather than making the gun feel powerful it makes the zombies feel weak.
Moving is slow and feel like gliding through taffy.
This is the first 5 minutes of the remake.
As you might notice there is a significant disconnect from the high energy, high agency feel of the orginal, while the remake has none of it, down to flat out removing player agency for the first few minutes of the game completely.
The point of this comparison is to highlight the feeling that was missing from the game, so you could say that you get more impactful weapons later or maybe the music gets good later, I dont know how ever that isn't the point here, the point is how they interact and the feeling it inspires.
An example of a remake that I believe does a fanastic job of capturing the orginal feel, while modernizing the game play is wolfenstein: the new order.
Yes they changed things from the orginal but the kept the underlying feeling and theme athentic to the orginal.

As someone who had never played any Deus Ex title, I was hesitant to get into this. And to be honest, the first hour or so of playing I wasn't yet sure if I like it or not. But as I got familiar with the wonderful mechanics, I'd say the Deus Ex franchise has a new fan.
The stealth mechanics are indeed very well honed. Just the balance between the approaches to a mission creates a sense of freedom I've not experienced in a game in a long while.
The other strenght of the game is the story - or rather how it is told. It is not anything special really, but I still felt engaged and never skipped any cutscene or a line of dialogue.
The negatives are mostly visual. Some of the textures (especially some of the facial textures in a dialogue) are quite badly rendered. But I feel that pointing out the things I found distracting would be nitpicking - there really aren't any major problems I could point out (or maybe there is, I just can't remember any).
So yeah, great experience, I want more of this!

I really enjoyed the commentary track on this and definitely worth it for fans of the game.
As for the game itself:
The Good: Really solid update to the Augmentions, with most of them being really useful with a good experience system to back it up. If you like sc-fi RPGs or if you loved the first game, this is definitely a must play. There are so many things to love about this game, from the setting, art style, dialogue system, a lot of pluses. The story for the most part is engaging and flows pretty well.
I love the hacking in this game, but then, I have enjoyed the hacking in all the Deus Ex games.
The Bad: The first level is very misleading and not representative of the kind of game you are in for (it seems to be a really standard FPS game). At least, it isn't too hard to quickly get through this if you have any familiariy with these types of games. The other major gripe I have is the last level, which, while pretty to look at, is just utter crap to really have fun in. This is the last chance to use your abilities and just have fun with it, yet the tone shifts entirely and all you have to fight are the lamest enemies.
If you look at the original Deus Ex, the final level, Area 51, has a lot of layers, a lot of different bad guys, large open areas with many layered sections and more confined areas. Dishonored, also, has a great final level that just lets you have as much fun as you want using all your various abilities however you want.
The bosses don't have a multitude of ways to beat them, but they aren't super tough, either, so I didn't mind so much.
The story seems like it will be bigger and richer than it ends up being. Hopefully, future games with play more on the consperiecy aspects, since that played an integral part to the original game.
A couple of the augmentations are really useless.
OVERALL: Good game that could have been great if more time and care had been given to the first and final levels to be more faithful to the rest of the game. Still, well worth playing!
