Ikaruga is a bullethell-style shmup with a special polarity mechanic. You can absorb bullets that are the same polarity as your ship and do double damage to enemies that are of the opposite polarity. This game is not for the faint of heart - the volume of bullets rivals that of CAVE's shooters or even Fraxy or Touhou Danmakufu (the latter two being shmups built around player-made bosses).
Graphics: Beautiful but dated. The game was original made for arcade units back in 2001, as well as the SEGA dreamcast, and while the polygon count and texture resolution has increased with subsequent releases the lighting quality has not. Also, this game is hard.
Soundtrack: One of the best. Epic and driving at the same time. Also, this game is hard.
Gameplay: Simplicity is a good thing when it comes to shmups - you want to make the game mechanics as easy to memorize as possible so the player can concentrate on what's on screen. Ikaruga definately delivers in this category. Also, this game is hard.
Story: Kinda hard to describe. Think of it as a semi-sequel of Radient Silvergun, in a time loop that deviated from previous loops. Also, this game is hard.
Notes: This game has had reports of crashing on startup, however in most cases simply restarting Steam fixes the problem. This game has been previously released on multiple platforms. Also, this game is hard.
Breakdown:
Graphics: 6/10
Soundtrack: 9/10
Gameplay: 10/10
Story: 6/10
Recommended for: People who enjoy very hard games, fans of bullethell games.
Not recommended for: People who can't handle losing.
Bottom line: An iconic game that is a must-have for any shmup fan. Also, this game is hard.

One of the most beautifully made bullet-eater games I've ever played..  The game-play is incredibly unique just as it is challenging, and to master this game requires tons of practice and skill.
In Ikaruga, you pilot your ship which has the ability to swap between two polarities of energy.  There are also enemies that can be either of the two types (or both), that you must kill and avoid their bullets and path.  Within a polarity, you are able to collect (eat) bullets of the same polarity/energy type from a matching enemy, and use that gathered energy to unleash homing missiles.  Keep in mind though, that to shoot an enemy with an opposing energy/polarity color does Twice as much damage to them, but will often leave you having to dodge heavier fire as the sacrifice.
Aside from purely awesome gamplay both the graphics and the soundtrack are gorgeous as well, and will definitely leave you remembering the visuals, animations and experience.
If you're looking for a shooter that will push you to your limits.. this is for sure the game to get!  NOW!

Let me preface this by saying that if you haven't played this game yet, you most definitely should. If you like FPS, if you like RPG, if you like (psuedo) open world, if you like good story, or if you just want something kinda different then you should definitely get this game.
Now, to my actual review. I know on my Steam account it says I only have a couple hours on record at the time of this review but I owned this game on 360 and have played through it multiple times there. That being said, I originally bought this game again on Steam because I saw that it was supposed to have extra content (being a Director's Cut and all) and I couldn't resist. I have yet to get to this content so I will just focus on the things that I do know about this game.
First of all, this game has one of the better stories for a video game out there. The story arc is compelling and the conflicts inside of it ring with hints of things going on in the real world. You are presented with moral dilemmas that are extremely thought compelling and you are apt to find yourself thinking about them for hours. Throughout the game you make choices that ultimately have consequences, or rewards if you don't take the easy way. Should you help the hacker and lose time and/or resources or will you leave him hanging out to dry? Either way, you will certainly find out later if he was the vindictive type.
Secondly, the weapons and augmentations. the weapons you are given are a fairly standard array of FPS weaponry. You got your assault rifle, pistol, revolver, sniper, shotgun, etc. These are all fairly standard weapons, what isn't usually standard though is the weapon upgrades. Do you want your shotgun to fire two round bursts? How about a laser sight so you don't need to ADS for good accuracy? Or even just a flat damage boost? I even remember being able to get explosive rounds if I'm not mistaken. My only complaint about weapons is the non-lethal weapons. You have a tranq rifle and a stun gun. Now, these weapons are not terrible but I never found a way to upgrade them so they never get better. The stun gun is actually fairly decent but the tranq rifle is kinda meh. The trade off with non-lethals though is you get slightly more xp.
Now the augs. The augs are where the RPG elements start to come in. You gain xp and you 'level up' from doing various things. Exploring, taking down enemies, hacking, etc. and you get skill points in the form of Praxis Kits (which you can also buy one per area you go to at your friendly LIMB Clinic). You assign the Praxis Kits to various abilities you have. Such as being better in social situations where you have to persuade someone, being able to takedown more enemies, or becoming a better hacker. You can make youself jump higher, run faster, go invisible, see through walls, shoot ballistic ball bearings out of your body, lessen recoil, increase damage resistance, etc, etc, etc.
And finally, atmosphere. This game has a wonderful atmosphere. The soundtrack is gorgeous and the art direction was fantastic. The NPC's have their own fashion sense, and while I think that it can be odd, it is definitely unique and not your run of the mill clothes you see in every other game. The cities have people walking around, not a whole lot of people, but enough to make the city feel like it's alive. What's important about the people walking around is that you can see the various districts of a city. You can walk from an area that's pretty nice and then take a wrong turn and your in back alleys with gangsters who will shoot you for being in their turf. You'll see hobos arguing with cops and digging through trash cans looking for food. Civilians begging cops for protection and talking to each other about what's going on. The biggest thing though, is when you return to areas and see how much things have changed, for better or worse.
To sum up, this is a wonderful game. It's not perfect, but nothing is. I give it a conservative 8.7/10.

Please mind my clocked game-time, I have beaten this game 3 times on the (Se)xbox 360. I'm going to tell you this: The Director's Cut is sometimes a buggy mess, but I've fixed most of my problems by messing around in regedit.
The story itself is amazing, you play as Adam Jensen, an augmented ex-cop with a sexy voice. You work as chief of security of for a company that deals with augmentations and enhancing the human body past its limitations. When a project they're working on is revealed, mercenaries attack the company HQ, and it's your job to find out why.
The level designs are beautiful, and I LOVE the neon yellow tint to the world. There are many areas to explore and many missions to complete.  There are countless ways you can complete your tasks.
1. Open assault. If you have the firepower, you can kill all of the enemies in your path (just be sure to have plenty of ammo). This option awards you the least amount of experience points.
2. Stealth-combat. Sneaking around and quietly eliminating enemies, non-lethal if you can. This awards you the most amount of experience if you can kill a good amount of guards.
3. Pure stealth. This option leaves you with the second most amount of XP possible. Going through areas without being detected leaves you with a ghost experience bonus, which when earned, will give you a sense of accomplishment (and a lot of XP). This bonus is possible with stealth-combat, just make sure you're not seen.
As you can see there are many ways you can complete a level. Most of them will have hidden pathways, which can help you skip past a lot of guards, or go some where that can award you with fine loot. For instance, I once crawled my way into a vent and found a nice stash of weapons, even found a praxis kit one time (devices that unlock augmentations without having to level up). Some of these areas can only be accessed if you certain abilities, such as hacking.
Hacking is  (in my opinion) the most important ability in the game. Having a level 5 hacking skill early game will help you in more ways than one. Unlocking safes, doors, overriding security hubs and personal computers is key. Computers will give you passwords and even reveal some cool references from other games. Security hubs will let you bypass doors, cameras, turrets, and even combat robots to fight on YOUR side! Hacking is also important for finding alternate paths in the game (which I mentioned earlier).
Unforunately, this game comes with some pretty hefty boss fights. Going through the WHOLE game with only a stun gun and my bare hands, I had to face these over-powered enemies without anything but a stick and a rock. I think there needs to be away around these boss fights, or they shouldn't be implemented at all. After my first encounter (which was pretty easy) I had started upgrading a combat rifle on the side and stockpiling ammo for the next boss, which I didn't really want to do.
What I've noticed about this game, is that most of the characters you interact with have a random dialogue chance. That means you can't go into your guide to try and convice them to win something, or someone over. Which is a cool addition, but it rendered the guide I bought with my Xbox game useless (at some points). I don't know if this is really true, but it's happened to me a lot.
Overall, I think it's a very good game. I strongly recommend anyone who's new or familiar with the Deux Ex series to try it out.  The developers need to come back and iron out some bugs and fix the FPS problems, but once you go into regedit and tinker with some settings you should be good to go. I hope for another Deus Ex game like this to come out in the near future. I've had so much fun playing this title, that I'm currently on my fourth playthrough.
Thank you for reading.

I played this game all the way through when it first came out on the xbox 360.
This is my favorite puzzle FPG game.
The map is very primitive but the gameplay makes up for it. The monsters slowly increase in difficulty but you never feel like a battle is impossible. Unlike other puzzle games that restrict the board layout or prevent invalid moves, this does neither. If you perform valid moves  in a row your multiplier goes up. If you get stuck you can do an invalid move to set up for more plays. The only penalty is a reduction in the multiplier.
There is a lot of variety to your roster and the effects are nice as well.
The only downsides are that the audio is choppy and there is no native controller support. I was able to create a controller mapping in Pinnacle Game Profiler in about 10 minutes that matched how it played on the xbox.

Not sure why i've decided to buy this game after i have tried a demo many years ago. Maybe i thought it would have more things later in the game. But the game is more of the same stuff and it gets too repetitive and boring fast. Also the vague story telling doesn't help to improve impressions. Dialogs are often weird, story twists are silly and confusing. Hero controls on the global map are annoying. Connecting 3 items (or more) in a row by rotating a square of 4 items clockwise is a bit of too much. One has to have a very good spacial imagination to quickly see combinations. Enemies don't have to do that, so this is a bit unfare. They use your combinations for resources for their attacks. Also you don't  just have to make your attacks, but proactively remove enemies attacks from the board. It quickly becomes very frustrating as game starts to introduce more blocks (locking certain items, making enemies' attacks to trigger faster, punishing for idle rotating of items, etc.). And the attacks your monsters have don't matter much. Yes, some trigger faster and do less damage, but you still just connect lines of items all the time without keeping much attention to them and the attacks trigger automatically. Puzzle Quest is way better in this regard, where you have to select what attacks to equip, when to trigger them and it actually matters what colors you connect. This game also has steep difficulty curve. You run easily through one stage and then stumble on another because monsters are much harder. Some challenges are based on simple luck (you have to make a cascade of 7 subsequent combinations, and you can't really prepare the board for that, because the board is too small and you have to rotate 4 items at a time, so you just sit their and mindlessly rotate them hoping to get that challenge..).
There are better and more interesting games in that genre (both mechanically and story wise). Gyromancer is a bland and boring clone, which can't offer much strategy. You have to repeat samish battles over and over again, slowly grinding levels to beat stronger monsters. And the story told is boring and not rewarding.

Square Enix AND PopCap?  Oh yeah, I figured this game would be awesome!  Boy was I wrong.
The graphics are OK.  I don't expect puzzle games to be winning awards for revolutionary graphics.  What I saw was acceptable and fit with the game just fine.  If I wanted a theatrical production with my game I'd be playing Final Fantasy 23 or whatever it is up to now.
The plot I didn't pay much attention to as I skipped later cut scenes after the first one.  I don't see how anyone can come up with an engrossing plot for a matching game.   What of it I did pay attention to was adequate.  You are the Good Guy on a Quest to stop the Bad Guy who has done Bad Things.  You meet someone I assume will be your Companion and a possible Love Interest.  You choose three monsters from a pool at your disposal to battle mobs on various maps.  Now go match stuff and beat the Bad Guy. There is your plot.  Ta-daa.
I did not find the tutorial very helpful.  It seems that it was trying to explain too much while you are playing the tutorial, making you pause between each move so you don't really get a feel for the flow of the game or a concept of the rules.  I went through the thing twice and left it thinking it was a turn-based game when, in fact, you are the only one making moves.  If you match colors that correspond with your opponent, you give them the 'energy.'  I prefer written tutorials followed by a short video support.  This one was like watching a movie while someone was talking and hitting the pause button.  Annoying, to say the least.
Music in games is not generally a factor for me.  I tend to decrease the sound (I use a headset) so I can hear what is going on around me.  Sometimes I leave it on higher than normal for me if it is really good, but in this case, I found the background music absolutely awful.  I could not mute the music on this game fast enough.  I removed my headset so I did not have to suffer it further while I desparetely searched for the Options menu to silence what sounded like a large bag of cats.
I also greatly dislike the one-way twist mechanic about this game.  I would prefer that it at least allowed you to rotate either clockwise or counterclockwise.  When I play standard Match 3 games, I can move the objects to be matched in more than one direction, so why not here?  For me, the twisting is already bad enough but I am restricted to just one direction?  Ugh.
Shame on me for not doing more research on Gyromancer before I purchased it, but at least it was on sale so I am not out the full price for something I will be uninstalling from my machine and trying to repress in my personal memory.

Go! Go! Nippon! is a very casual Visual Novel that really has no plot. Basically, the game is a tour of certain places, traditions, and customs of Japan in a Visual Novel form. Of course, you are accompanied by two girls who you are living with for the time during your visit to Japan.
As mentioned before, there really is no story, other than touring around and stuff as well as your trip to Japan. In fact, the main character you play seems rather out of the loop if he get excited from purchasing a metrocard equilvalent... It's not like Japan is the only place with public transportation where you can buy a card for. Other than that, the game does provide a nice bit of background information for the places you visit, but I'd rather go visit Japan in person than spend too many hours in this game.
The art is pretty nice acutally and the two girls are drawn pretty crisp. However, they raelly only seem to have 2 different poses, even if they change outfits. Even when they change outfits, the poses are still exactly the same pretty much. The game feels shallow in that aspect. In the end, this game does start to bore you if you were seeking a game in the genre of dating sims and the sort, but if you want to play a game that gives you information about Japan, by all means go for it. However, for me this game got pretty boring too fast.
Rating: 7.1/10

Welcome to my review of Megadimension Neptunia Victory II the 4th main instalment in the series taking place years after the events of Victory/Re;Birth 3. The game takes place across a total of three dimensions (Zero, Hyper, and Heart) with lots of gloomy and hilarious moments from Gold Third, AffimaX, and the main cast.
One day Neptune happens to stumble upon a console one day and decides to bring it back home. While she and Nepgear inspect it, they get sucked in a warp and end up in the Zero Dimension, a barren wasteland of a nation. They meet Uzume Tennouboshi and her fish companion with a human face Umio who both have been struggling to bring down the “Dark CPU”
Gameplay is what you would expect from other Neptunia titles with some slight changes. For starters, weapons play a slightly more prominent role as in the most powerful weapons usually won’t cut it anymore.  Weapons now excel and lack in either of the 3 combo types (ex. Long rush combo/short power combo). The EXE Drive Gauge also resets after every battle but fills up quicker compared to past titles. Next-Gen forms are also a new thing where the Goddesses’ go beyond their HDD form.
One thing that might annoy everyone is the revamped World Map. Gone are the days of just simply picking a dungeon and entering immediately. Now the World Map is more akin to that of a platformer (ie- Super Mario World) where characters will walk slowly towards a dungeon or nation only to have a chance of random encounters occurring. The remake system and Stella’s Dungeon from the Re;Birth trilogy are not present here with the game using an improved Scout system from Hyperdimension Neptunia Victory.
Scouts provide bonuses (or handicaps) when placed in dungeons and they’ll usually discover other fellow scouts, items, credits or hidden dungeons. It works in the real time the same as Stella’s dungeon except numerous scouts can be placed all over and it plays a more important role.

As bullet hell shooters go, there isn't one as excellently realized as Ikaruga is. In this one, you are able to freely change the polarity of your ship between light and dark. Doing so allows you to absorb enemy attacks of the same color as you, and do additional damage to enemies of the opposite color. Destroying an enemy of the same color as you will produce suicide bullets (which you will either need to avoid or absorb). Absorbing shots charges a special attack, which once activated, sends a volley of polarized missiles across the screen.
This polarity mechanic takes a shooter that would have been excellent on its own, and makes it so much more.
If you're at all a fan of this particular genre of shooter, and haven't played Ikaruga, this is an excellent version of the game to play it for the first time. It lacks the online multiplayer which was found in the Xbox Live Arcade version, but is 5 bucks cheaper (and seeing how the XBL coop was a laggy mess, it isn't a huge deal for it to be missing here.)
What's added in this version is the ability to solo man two ships (if you think the game is a cakewalk as it is or something), local multiplayer support, as well as numerous screen rotation options.
It's a great version of what is quite possibly one of the best video games ever made! What're you waiting for?!

I'll start with the fact that everyone should know and understand with everyone in the community: Paladins is one of the greater alternatives to other games like Overwatch, and has become one of my favorite games since I began playing it around late Spring of '17. Complain all you want, but I began as a Viktor main, Fernando main, and for some time, a Damba main. Not much for playing Flank classes, mind you. Everything was going very swell for the game, although they rarely addressed the crappy hitboxes, nerfing champions that didn't need nerfs, though some of the noobies complained that "oh i can't hit this drogoz" or "this willo always flies so fast i can't hit her", the game felt alright with me, I've already invested nearly $200 in cosmetic items from the chests, new and redistributed chests.
I'm sorry to say Hi-Rez, but I made a mistake on that part.
With me exchanging my hard-earned real life currency on the game, we all would expect that the developers of this game would be working their hardest to become better at their jobs... but, by this point in time, they are really focused down on this new, absurd card system they've put in place. Cards Unbound is one of the major reasons for why OB64 will be much, much more worse than any other update this game has received, perhaps much worse than the addition of the Essence system. From what I have experienced in the PTS, the new card system acts rather similar or almost exactly as the Clash Royale grinding system. Although it won't be the situation now, there will probably be a future option of having you purchase individual Champion Chests/Radiant Chests with Crystals, the only currency in the game which requires you to pay Steam cash for, which you purchase a gift card with your own real life currency. Or you can just use your credit/debit card instead. If they never add the separate option to purchase those chests with Crystals, there's always those Legendary and Class-Specific keys available for purchase when opening a Radiant Chest.
There is the separate option to pay for Champion Chests and Radiant Chests with Gold, which is mostly achieved with completing quests, playing in matches entirely and earning Gold based on your performance, or you can earn your Champion Chests by playing in the Unbound Mode... which is a really bad idea. But the biggest problem with purchasing the chests with Gold is a huge problem. See, way back before this ♥♥♥♥ing mess started, there was the Wins of the Day rewards that gave you about 500 extra Gold for winning a game, which racked your rewards up to 1500 Gold per day. Hi-Rez stripped those away, unfortunately, so that means the only way to get more and more gold is through Daily Rewards and completing Quests, which to me is very frusturating. Winning or losing matches in the game gives you very little Gold, which is actually rather similar to what EA rewarded players in Battlefront II (2017) for just... playing in a match. Performance mattered very little, so regardless of how many kills you got in one life, or how many control points you've gotten, it isn't enough for even one "Loot Crate". It's sort of the same in this Cards Unbound mode, which all individual Champion Chests are currently worth 7500 per chest in the PTS. I really hope that Hi-Rez can patch this issue by at least increasing the Gold grind in matches or by lowering the price of Champion Chests, because paying for a Damage key in a Radiant Chest rarely ever gives me Viktor cards - always just Vivian, Tyra, Bomb King, and the sort.
Okay, so it's pretty clear that I ♥♥♥♥ing
this new card system. I don't care if it's directed towards an audience who would go all carefree with their money (China), but I will not spend even a cent on this game from this point on. Not even for cosmetics. And I can already bet that the playerbase will slowly decay into nothing but dust particles, the number's been decreasing massively on the Charts. The usual peak of players before this update was around 24K-25K, but it's gotten as low as to 11K in the time I have been writing this review. I cannot wait to get myself a better computer soon, so I can start on playing other games than this. It's sad to see something so young get destroyed by greed, but I suppose it's just the cycle of Hi-Rez wanting to kill another game so they can get to work on another project.

Red Orchestra is a really Good tactical WW2 FPS featuring good class based gameplay, nice open ended maps, and above all..... THE BEST gunplay I have ever seen in an FPS. Shooting a gun in this game feels almost real. Iron sights look realistic and automatic weapon recoil is just monstrous. My favorite feature is the ability to rest your weapon on any object in the game world for more accuracy and stability. I find it a lot better than some ridiculous sticky cover. Everything You do influences Your weapons accuracy: Your stance, Your character`s fatigue, Your health, etc. If you try to shoot when your hands are wounded, you`re tired from sprinting and you`re in an upright stance, then you`ll probably miss because of huge weapon sway.
Red Orchestra is generally pretty awesome but the WW2 theme starts to get tiresome after some time. I wish there was a modern day combat mod for this :(
Important note: This game is not very popular, and sometimes it`s hard to find servers with people on them. The game also enforces some serious restrictions when choosing a class ( for example: There can be only 1 or 2 snipers in each team ) so be prepared to fight as a bolt action rifleman when joining a server with many people on it.

My eyes flutter as the sun peeks over the clouds and makes a blue sky. Second Impression (update to my first impression) :
I've been looking for another good "Puzzle Quest" style game. Up to this point, the only types of those games that I did like were the actual Puzzle Quest series. Puzzle Kingdoms, Dungeon Hearts, and Legend of Fae were almost good, but not good enough in comparison to the quality of the PQ series. I loved Runespell: Overture, but that involves cards instead of gems. I've been looking forward to Gyromancer for a while and had it held up in my backlog for even longer. I definitely enjoyed it at first, though the latter half of the game may turn off some people. And like PQ, it does feel good to earn you wins through a bit a strategy, but I found alot of "close calls" came out in my favor purely due to the luck of the way gems dropped on the board.
Instead of swapping adjacent gems horizontally or vertically, you swap them with a rotation tool of sorts. While unique, it does feel rather annoying when you have an easy match, but can match gems because they are in a odd corner, to the left of your cursor, or stuck near locked gems that can't be moved. This is part of the game design of course, but in the later levels especially, you often feel like you may not have what you need to match gems to prevent damage to you or attack the enemy. Only the player gets to make the gem swaps, but over time and also depending on which gems you swap, the enemy's ability meter will increase until they activate and morph a gem into a timed attack gem on the board or cause a status effect to one or both monsters. You then have a limited amount of turns to use that morphed gem in a match and remove it before it causes damage to your monster. This generally requires strategy and a bit of luck. My other complaint is that the game does appear to want you to potentially replay completed levels, as some paths of a stage are not cleared until after you beat it, which also mean you can't complete all the stage challenges in one run.
One annoyance in gameplay I have is that you don't get enough items. In the start of the game, you get a few, but I never felt like I needed them. Once I got into the 3rd part of the world map, rounds were harder and there were so many situations where I could have used a Magic Mirror to rotate gems counter-clockwise or a Magick Key to unlock a locked gem, but couldn't because I only had one left that I wanted to save or had none at all. Items are found in chests and not in any store, but it almost feel like luck to get them because chests are found on certain parts of the level trail and you can't see the entire trail to know where to go.  You have to assume where your route will take you.
Another irritant is that it seems like you will probably need to grind to play the later half of the game succesfully. When my monsters were around level 20+, I started seeing monsters at level 50 plus. Thankfully, some older levels will have paths you couldn't get to before, but can now, but it also feels like a pretty articial way of extending the game more than it needed to be.
Gyromancer seems pretty good from the few hours I played. It doesn't keep my interest long enough which each sitting for me to have long play sessions like I did with PQ. The need to grind and backtrack put me off a bit - I don't mind it in certain games, but I don't really care for it here. That could be part of the reason it isn't well known, since this can get fairly difficult for casuals. This is probably the next best thing to the Puzzle Quest series from what I played, outside of Runespell: Overture.

TLDR: The last reason to buy a console has just died.
Even though the Steam Controller looks unusual and takes a few minutes to get used to, I've yet to see something that didn't make sense after thinking about it.
It feels well built and has a nice weight to it, while not being too heavy to hold for hours on end.
The wireless pairing with the included dongle is very quick and easily works from the other side of the room with no noticable latency.
Each trackpad has haptic feedback that, although sometimes slightly annoying, helps you to figure out what you are doing on a completely flat surface without looking.
The back buttons are really useful too, allowing you to quickly access certain functions while you are using both thumbs on the stick and trackpads.
When first starting a title you can either choose a config that makes it behave like a standard controller or choose a community config that is specifically tailored for that game.
Or, in true PC style, you can go into the easy to use config menu yourself and remap every last button on a per game basis. Just how much you ask?
There are more than half a dozen modes for each trackpad, each with with a few options including what to do when you press down on or get to the edge of the pad. Some of these modes let you use the trackpad like a joystick, some like a laptop trackpad or a trackball while another mode actually emulates a mouse in games that only have joystick support.
And all of these modes actually feel really nice.
In conclusion: the Steam Controller enables you to control any game in a reasonable way from your couch. So if you need a really nice gamepad or just don't want to sit directly infront of your PC all the time, this is indeed the controller you were looking for.

(Scroll to the bottom for the quick tl;dr list.)
I do like this controller. It's great to use, even outside Steam, to control desktop applications, including my web browser. It's difficult to beat it for, say, watching online movies in bed. That having been said, though, this controller and my Mac still do not grok each other fully. Whether this is an issue with Apple or Valve, I cannot say, but one of the primary issues is that the keyboard layout in Steam does not match the Mac OS X layout, and certain function keys simply do not… well… function. The device is not recognized as a controller at all by some applications, even though the applications in question do support controllers.
This device is similar to the standard XBOX and PlayStation controllers, and can emulate those just fine. There are two extra buttons in the grips, however, similar to gear shift paddles in racing cars. In addition, the "D-Pad" is really a touchpad that can be used for a variety of functions, including a standard d-pad. Ditto with the "right stick". The drawback to this increased functionality is that the actual control stick and the ABXY buttons have been shifted inward to a degree where I imagine it might be uncomfortable to use for some people. Their positions are not too far off from the analog sticks of a PlayStation controller, but I find that the positions of the X and A buttons in particular do not match the angle of my thumb particularly well. I have to stretch my thumb almost to the middle of the controller to use them properly. The best thing is that all these buttons, sticks, and pads can be programmed to do pretty much whatever you want, and this programming can differ from application to application.
Get this controller; however, if you have Mac OS X, carefully weigh the awesomeness of the controller when it does work against the overwhelming urge to throw it through the nearest wall when it does not.

things I like about this game that I'm not sure are good or bad:
~ The duel MP412 Rex reload animation (you'd have to carry six spare revolvers to be able to do that)
~ The sawed-off's reload animation (antigravity shotgun shells)
~ Zombies randomly collapse sometimes (presumably from tiredness, it's tough being undead)
~ Some dialogue sounds like it's straight out of Battle For The Sun (especially the voice for 'Charlie', who sounds just like General Briggs)
~ Some dialogue sounds like it's straight out of Fistful of Frags (the security guy sounds pretty hillbilly)
~ One of the models for the bandits looks like bootleg Francis from L4D
~ All of the NPC's seem to have learned Kung-Fu by watching The Matrix a few times
~ The brick is OP (1 hit kill when thrown, gibs zombies into oblivion)
~ Military NPC's all have AKs that seem to fire pure unobtainium
~ Your character's reaction to being infected is pretty chilled out
~ Extremely relaxing Moonlight Sonata main menu music is good at preparing you for the surprise buttsecks the game throws you into
Overall, I get the feeling that this game has succumb to what is known as 'The Amazing Bulk' effect, wherein the devs wanted to make a serious game, but looked back on it and thought 'eh, might as well make it silly'. The difference is, here it worked pretty well. This game is pretty fun. Sure it have a few glitches and the dialogue might be terrible in places, but that's what gives it it's charm. I recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a fun zombie survival game to play and have a good laugh with.

In all brutal honesty, I wasn't enthused about making yet another trip to Gamindustri.
was a pleasant surprise due to its colorful cast and amusing storyline. The second Re;Birth game was a solid improvement. The third game was even better, but it was also more of the same. At the time, I thought that this RPG series was long overdue for a fresh take, but I started to worry that it would never happen. I envisioned that Compile Heart had grown complacent. They would continue to hammer these Neptunia RPGs out, all with slightly different storylines, five or twenty additional characters, and memes more "dank" than ever thought possible. With the release of
, Compile Heart has put my worries to rest. This is, without a doubt, the best entry in the series thus far.
Despite having "V2" in the title, this entry in the saga has very little in common with "V1" aka Re;Birth 3. In fact, if you have at least some familiarity with the CPUs and the Candidates, then you could probably approach V2 as its own self-contained story. Without giving too much away, this game is divided into three separate acts. Each act focuses on a handful of characters, and their efforts to protect Gamindustri from a mysterious threat. The storyline is darker than in previous games, but it never becomes overbearing, or gritty just for the sake of it. The truly serious moments feel earned. Even accounting for the franchise's penchant for farce, the villains are well-written, and the heroines deal with the problems facing them in a convincing fashion.
Alongside the improved story-telling is a very strong cast. With Re;Birth 2 and especially 3, CPU Candidate Nepgear went from mediocre to almost unsalvageable. This is her best role yet. Big sister Neptune has also improved. Well, she's still as ridiculous as ever, but at least she's not completely irritating. Noire, Blanc, Vert, and Uni also have more involved roles in the storyline, which is a huge plus. As far as new characters go, Uzume is exceptional. Her story is well thought-out, and her quirks are endearing rather than grating. The Golden Third represents the "developer" characters that are common in Neptunia games (Cave, Red, Mages, etc). Again, I have nothing but praise for them. Rather than being a mere excuse to include several references and in-jokes, each of these four characters has their own arc.
While it would have been nice to see a few characters from the previous Neptunia trilogy make an appearance, I believe that sticking with just the main heroines and the handful of newcomers, was a very wise decision. There aren't as many meaningless skits, and conversations don't get buried by dozens of people voicing their thoughts at once. The three-act storyline neatly ties everything together.
Compile Heart has made changes to nearly every element of its bread & butter RPG. The dungeons are slightly larger, house more secrets, and can involve a little platforming. This provides another incentive for players to jump around, aside from the stat-boosting challenges and the ability to loudly exclaim "I'm a kangaroo!" The structure of this game has also undergone a massive overhaul. In the previous games, it was easy to unlock optional dungeons, defeat the side-bosses, and enter a cycle of constant level-ups that removed any semblance of challenge from the main story. There's still more than enough side-content in V2, but unless you're really determined, you won't reach a "kill-all-bosses-in-one-hit" level of experience... At least until new game+.
The remake system has been removed from Gamindustri. While you can still gather monster materials to craft some items or enhance gear, you won't need
the entire time you're playing. Most gear acquisitions are handled the old fashioned way; via store purchases, or finding them in dungeons. Other unlockables, like the "cheat" abilities (higher jump, faster run speed, etc) are discovered simply by playing through the game. Furthermore, by employing scouts, you can discover additional treasures and new dungeons. So, if you disliked Stella as much as any normal person, you'll be happy to know that she was kicked to the curb. While these changes might disappoint some Re;Birth fans, overall they improve the pacing and atmosphere. Your play-through of the game isn't under constant risk of being halted, just so you can look up how to find a "old dragon ball", an "old dragon horn", or the all-important "old dragon's ?!?!?"
However, some of the other changes & additions are a little undercooked. The overworld no longer functions as a "click on the location to instantly travel" map. Now you have to selection your destination, and the protagonist will run to wherever that is. The reason I don't like this setup is because there are random encounters. While they aren't too annoying, I really have to wonder why they exist. Random encounters can be turned off after beating the game. This is equal parts welcome and perplexing. A number of other unlockables such as scouts, clothes, and weapon modifications are awarded by investing in all of the major lands (Planeptune, Lastation, etc). It's a neat idea, but you're liable to spend most of the game dirt-poor. In fact, by the time you have the opportunity to do any serious investing, your first play-through is about to end.
The battle system has also undergone some slight modifications. The EXE meter resets after every battle, and overall isn't nearly the "win" button it was in the past. To balance this out, all of the playable characters have recieved more moves and abilities. The combo system has also been revamped. Certain combination attacks can result in longer waits, which effects the heroine's turn order. Combo attacks can also do more damage if certain conditions are satisfied (such as performing a rush attack just before a power attack). The differences aren't dramatic, but if you're attempting to play through the game at low levels of experience, they can be pretty important. Positioning is also more tactical than ever, since enemies (and playable characters!) take more damage, when attacked from the sides or back.
While this game is harder than its predecessors, most of the challenge is going to come from early on. The first half of the game is spent with less than four party-members. These limitations alongside a lack of primo grinding points make for a decently balanced level of difficulty. Once you recruit everyone, the battles devolve into the typical attack/special move/sometimes heal doldrums that plague most RPGs. Still, it's nice while it lasts, and players can opt out of carrying over their experience levels and equipment in new game+.
With
, Compile Heart has proven that they aren't averse to taking risks with an established series. Taking these risks not only requires a lot of confidence in the game-designers, but also the writers. Yes, there are still times where Neptune acts the fool, or Vert jokes about Blanc's lack of "plot" development. These moments are what keep the adventure grounded. More importantly, the writing goes above and beyond to give everyone a purpose beyond the cheap laughs, and this leads to a more compelling story. While I've enjoyed all of the previous Neptunia games, V2 is a necessary evolution. The improvements to both the combat systems and exploration help round out this superb RPG.

A little history before we start, Dead Rising is franchise that started on 360 as an exclusive. The guy in charge was Keiji Inafune aka "ConMan", the person who's supposedly the creator of  MegaMan and later worked on Lost Planet (tasked with the same role than in the Dead Rising developement). Mighty No.9 aka Mediocre No5.9 shed some light on his character and the fact that he's basically there as a lamp post and collects the shekels and glory when the game's out.
Capcom is home to really talented people, so even if Inafune just stood in the coffee break room all day the games would still came out good, he was just there to give pointers and pitch the gist of the game.
For Dead Rising, Inafune as a good'ol westaboo wanted to do an homage to Zombie movies (more precisely Dawn of the Dead) and a game basked in the culture of the land of the free and home of the brave. The end result was a game that was very American in its setting but also very Japanese in its design. The gameplay involved managing time, planning routes, learning item spawn locations. Replayability was encouraged. There was alternate costumes and special weapons for the most dedicated just like almost every old Capcom games. You weren't punished for enjoying the game as you saw fit, sure you might've gotten one of the numerous non-canon endings but that was part of the experience.
The gameplay in itself wasn't something elaborate but it was efficient and came from a single idea : if you could use everything in a mall, what would you do ? This resulted in unexperienced players being forced to use CD boxes, dishes, plastic swords, benches, ... as weapons.  You could also wear stupid crap too because who the hell cares ? This clashed with the serious tone of the game, psychopaths and what the characters went through, but it was never a focus like "LOOK HOW WHACKY OUR GAME IS XDDDD".
The game was a Made in Japan product through and through up to the character design, Frank West is an average looking guy, he's selfish but the more you play and discover what's behind the zombie outbreak you learn that he has heart. He's not depicted in cutscenes as a fearless guy who knows it all, he's outstandingly average and that is perhaps what makes him such a great character. He's earnest, clumsy sometimes but wants to help and figure out what the hell's going on. The game is Japanese up to the UI which is very barebones and borderline ugly like most of Jap games (the only thing Mr Choke on It was right about).
However, in gen 7 (360/PS3/Wii) there was in a huge shift. That shift was that while in Gen 6 (PS2/Xbox/Gamecube) and before Japan dominated the gaming industry, the country started lagging behind Western productions in general, resulting in less sales and thus less profit. Like a good money-hungry Westaboo, our friend Keiji "Lost Planet 2 was too Japanese" Inafune saw this as a good opportunity to push for outsourcing Capcom IPs to the Western world. This resulted in the worst Devil May Cry game ever made, the worse Lost Planet game ever made and ... Dead Rising 2, outsourced to a Canadian studio. Surprisingly, Dead Rising 2 was alright. Gameplay wise it was more or less preserved (time and resource management, route planning, improvised weaponry...). Something was starting to feel off though, focus on dumb weapons, cheesy one liners... Whatever, I thought.
Then came Dead Rising 3. Announced as an exclusive to the biggest sh*tshow of a console, the Xbox One, there was red flags during all the announcement presentation : dull color palette, semi-open world just because they could, dude playing mostly using firearms, unmemorable main character, companion phone app... The game completely missed the point of the series.
It got undemanding on the time constraints, making the game easy as sh*t zombie killing. It made the game semi open world, making each zone less interesting and less content packed. It removed escorting survivors, making not only the game feel artificial but also added to the pile of dumbed down elements of the first two games. This last one is one of the many example proving the Canadians missed the point of the series, Dead Rising 1 wasn't a simple game because people were inexperienced with the formula. You were running everywhere fighting against time and struggling, escorting survivors and seeing them fill the safehouse, getting special rebellion events was part of the experience. Dead Rising 3 feels hollow, the boss fights are p*ss easy, the game in general is p*ss easy, the story of the first two games is thrown out the window. It's like my mom watched me playing Dead Rising 1, said "so you just kill zombies with stupid weapons ?" and got appointed Dead Rising 3 director. It's surface level "LE WHACKY ZOMBIE KILLING GAME XDDD" from the promo trailers up to the game design. There's nothing to challenge you, there's nothing to keep you interested and it's a bad departure from the first two ones.
The cherry on the sh*t sandwich is that the port is pretty bad performance wise. It's the worst Dead Rising game by a long shot and I wouldn't recommend it whether you're a fan of the series or not.

I bought this game for €15 with 4 DLC's included and for that price I really recommend it.
It only took me 20 hours to complete the main story, but like I read in other reviews: I really wasn't bothered by the deadlines like I was in previous DR games. The main character in this game is more likeable than in the other games and the story and cutscenes are well enough. The city is bigger and you can use (combo)vehicles to drive all around the map. The map is filled with barricades though, but I feel this makes the game balanced, because otherwise you would only drive everywhere.
The combo weapons are cool en finding them and other collectibles is fun. Since the main story is only 20 hours (with a lot of sidetracking in the meantime). Most fun after that comes from getting everything and killing the most zombies in the most effective, fun, gory, or unique way. Since I think that is the main goal of every DR game, I recommend this game.
As far as the port goes, I bought this game late August 2016 and I manage to run it without any problems (now). (But PC is pretty strong though so I don't know how other machines would run it).
If I had to list downsides to this game I can only think of the fairly short first run through and the fact that controls are sometimes irritating when several aspects come together (for instance when you are up against a wall and a climb-able object, while surrounded by zombies and wielding a weapon that wants to pick it's own targets). At these points the console port side of the game comes through. on the whole the controls work fine though.
Also survivors with melee weapons are idiots when you are also wielding a melee weapon. As long as you have a ranged weapon to give them, this is OK.
Summary: Good (the best?) DR game. Fun, it runs, looks nice, bought it at a good price. It's not the next huge step in gaming, but it's the next step in zombiekilling. I recommend.

Originally I was very sceptical about the Steam Controller... But in the end it's not that bad at all.
- What needs to be said though is that the Xbox controller is still the prototype for most of in-development testing and in some games you feel that very hard. Especially the obvious console ported games.
- The replacement of of the 2nd Joystick we all know and love on both the Xbox and PlayStation Controllers for a Touchpad is a lame attempt at progress. While in some games it does it's job exelently in other games you really miss the accuracy that I feel the touchpad lacks sometimes.
- 2 Extra Buttons on the back. (A gamer can't have enough buttons on his controller!)
- It's a very sturdy Controller that can be used for hours on end once you get the touch for it in your hands.
- The Controller is perfectly adjusted for all Steam use and you'll find yourself using "The Big Picture" more and more as it really enhances that navigation.
- While the Touchpad is not on my personal list of amazing innovations it's ability to function as a mouse trackpad in some games is an obvious boon.
If you have an Xbox controller and are happy with it stick with your Xbox controller. If on the other hand it's worn down or you're just looking for a 1st time PC controller (and play most if not all of your games through Steam) then I would recommend getting this one instead.
I do hope that game developers who are selling their games though Steam and are making them controller supported would keep this controller in mind a bit more in the future but I don't think that will be a big problem Valve will probably be working on that a little bit with the developers otherwise the Technical and Commercial Departments aren't doing their jobs.

It took about 20 minutes for me to really get used to the thumbpads and the other buttons (there are so many!). It's worth mentioning that I've only ever played with a controller a handful of times in my life, so if you haven't used them much it's not too bad to get used to.
When you do configure it, it is extremely in depth and there are tons of options and configuration screens if you want to get really nitty gritty. I suppose the downside to configuring it yourself is the time it takes to put it all of the options you want, but the fact is that there will never be the same amount of options as a keyboard, so sometimes I find myself sacrificing less used commands for more important ones. But then again, it forces you to get a bit creative and come up with ideas on how best for you to control your game. You can even just choose a community one and configure theirs if you just want to change a few things.
All in all, I really love the steam controller and think that it's a cool gadget. If you don't mind taking the time to learn it, then it's an awesome purchase!

Gyromancer started out well enough. Sure, it's cribbing on the whole Puzzle Quest phenomenon but the game was fun at least. Then a few missions into the game, they added a new rule where you can't switch jewels without causing a match without getting penalized. That, combined with an enemy ability that locks certain jewels into place makes this game too hard and too unrewarding. If you really want to play Gytomancer, just get one of the Puzzle Quest games instead.

With a slightly different twist on the typical puzzle game, Gyromancer could have been a little better, but was still fairly satisfying.
The gameplay is about what you would expect of another 'Puzzle Quest' type game, just with a few different rules concerning the switching of gems. If you liked 'Puzzle Quest' then you'll probably like this one too. The story was actually interesting, but was unfortunately very short, could have been flushed out better, and at a few points left me a bit confused due to seemingly random plot points.
That having been said, Gyromancer's one true failing is that it is far too short. You'll likely only get about 10 to 15 hours out of story mode assuming you poke around a bit. Despite that, if you're in the mood for a decent puzzle game, or if it's on sale and you'd like to have something to pass the time other than Solitaire, then by all means buy Gyromancer!

Go! Go! Nippon! is a short Visual Novel based on the idea of someone visiting Japan for the first time.
Of course you as the main character speak really good Japanese, and is also an Otaku.
The story is mostly centered around you exploring Japan in the company of two girls who take turns going with you depending on where you decide to visit. The nudity tag doesn't really belong on this game but whatever.
Personally the story felt as if it was a bit lacking because of the nature of the premise: visiting Japan for the first time. There are few choices that you can make that make any difference and only two endings.
Overall it can be an entertaining game if you're in the right mood, just don't expect much from it. If you want to visit Japan though, it has cool features like being able to hit a button and see what that specific location looks like on google maps from a street view. I found this to be interesting as I wouldn't know exactly where to look for those specific attractions.
Though it's not amazing, it's still worth the playthrough twice if you get it at a discount on the base price.
If you're  VN lover, you'd probably rate it higher than my 5/10.

This game is my first visual novel, so I can't compare it to others.  As a standalone experience, it's interesting.  You play a tourist coming to Japan for the first time, staying with a couple of brothers you met on the Internet.  The brothers turn out to be sisters - shocking! and also, you forgot to ask and apparently never shared a pronoun - and in among the inevitable progress to seduction (you only get to fall for one of them per game) there's a lot of first-time tourist information about visiting Tokyo and the environs, along with light language lessons and some good practical advice about tourist mistakes to avoid.  Which is actually pretty cool. I've never been, but now I'm quite curious.
There's no nudity; the Steam game tag is wrong on this score.  You manage to catch each sister minus some clothing by forgetting to knock and then forgetting to look away or close the door, but the pictures are PG-13 in nature, if not intent.  Apart from that it's all about True Love, and in fact the game gets embarrassed pretty easily, like if anything ever even remotely suggests that people might be physically attracted to each other.  The number of awkward-pause ellipse screens to click past [...] is staggering.
There are two endings (one each for matching with each of the sisters), and if you check a game guide, as I did after my first play-through, a couple of judicious saves and liberal use of the "Skip" button will let you play quickly to the other ending and give you the couple of scenes you missed by choosing this restaurant instead of that one, and so forth.  Acing one or two of these alternatives unlocks extras that will let you look at the pictures of your times with Makoto and Akira, replay scenes, and give you an index of information about the sites you visited - you can also click through in-game to Googlemaps pictures of the places you go.
The game definitely wants you to end up with one sister rather than the other, or so it seemed to me.  They will both fall for you if they're called on to do so, but one harbors a quiet crush and the other is all "Hi, I'm the hot one but don't let me near the kitchen."  Goofy, but absorbing.

Oh boy it's DOOM. Honestly, considering it's success i doubt this game even needs a review anymore but why the hell not? Doom 2016 is a reboot of the legendary Doom from 1993 from the kings of FPS, ID Software. It's concept and design borrows heavily from the famously successful mod known as "Brutal Doom". Does it hold up to the original? Well, that depends on what's more important to you, Multiplayer or Singleplayer? Doom's Singleplayer experience can only be defined as sublime. As you rip and tear demons' faces off faster than a katana wielding ninja in a toilet paper factory, you will experience a variety of ways to forcefully relieve your stress onto the unaware denizens of Hell. Punching, Squashing, Ripping, Sawing, Blasting, Burning and slapping them in the face with your massive space marine♥♥♥♥♥♥are only a few of the things you can do in this singleplayer adventure. The plot? OH NO GUYS THERE ARE DEMONS IN THE BASE! I MUST KILL THE DEMONS! And then he did. If you enjoy completely obliterating helplesss AI goons while headbanging your face through your monitor you've come to the right place, because DOOM 2016's soundtrack is arguably one of the best soundtracks to listen to while TAKING THE LIVES OF YOUR ENEMIES! YEAH, EAT THAT SUCKER. POW, RIGHT IN THE BALLS. I'M DOOMGUY BABY, WOOHOO! Oh and it has an even faster paced classic-style "Arcade Mode" that's honestly even more fun than the campaign! It's a great time all around.
PROS
+ Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥it's fun killing things!
+ Holy flap jacks it's fun killing things!
+ Holy chicken sandwich it's fun killing things!
+ Holy hell it's fun killing things!
CONS
+ I personally can't stand snapmap compared to the quality material the modding/mapping community for the classic games has to offer. There's simply no contest!
+ The environments can all start to look a little stale after binging the campaign.
+ Spamming 'glory kills' get old after doing it 20 times to a revenant's face.
BOTTOM LINE
If you love fast paced brutal FPS action, look no further than Doom 2016, truly an amazing feat of gaming development considering it's troubled history. Well done developers, let's see what you do for Doom II now!
--------------------------------
DOOM MULTIPLAYER
... The multiplayer on the other hand is an unusual creature. Caught between the trends of 90s gaming and modern gaming, this multiplayer experience is... confused, to say the least. They got some things right, like no regenerating health, no reloading animations, nice arena sized maps and it's real fun to blow people up with a rocket launcher, when you actually can that is. However most of the time you'll just be frustrated. At least i was. Be it the often terrible netcode, wonky matchmaking, infuriating bulletsponge health (That completely negates any fun, with any weapon) and a buttload of other crap, for me it often just doesn't feel as fun as it could be if they weren't trying so hard to appeal to Halo fans for some reason. Not to mention, it's really colorful. Like, it's so bright and hyperactive it kind of doesn't feel like doom at all. You could just slap another name on the multiplayer and boom, nobody cares. Granted they did try to rectify this this with a pickup that let's you turn into a demon during combat for a short period of time, but you usually end up dying so quickly after you obtain it, that it usually makes it's purpose seem unnecessary. But hey, at least Free-for-all (Mixed team modes) and Deathmatch (Last man standing) can be genuinely entertaining and fun at times with the right opponents.
PROS
+ Character Customization can be fun
+ No stupid reloading (Thank god)
+ No regenerating health
+ Weapons are satisfying to use
+ Maps are varied and interesting
CONS
+ Looks/Feels way too similar to Halo
+ Bulletsponge health is unfathomably annoying
+ Repetitive announcer who never shuts up (Can thankfully be muted)
+ Runes/Perks were an awful idea, and you should be ashamed
+ No custom mod/map support or usermade content
+ They tried way too hard to cater to the casual crowd
+ Character Progression/Leveling is pointless
BOTTOM LINE

Please mind my clocked game-time, I have beaten this game 3 times on the (Se)xbox 360. I'm going to tell you this: The Director's Cut is sometimes a buggy mess, but I've fixed most of my problems by messing around in regedit.
The story itself is amazing, you play as Adam Jensen, an augmented ex-cop with a sexy voice. You work as chief of security of for a company that deals with augmentations and enhancing the human body past its limitations. When a project they're working on is revealed, mercenaries attack the company HQ, and it's your job to find out why.
The level designs are beautiful, and I LOVE the neon yellow tint to the world. There are many areas to explore and many missions to complete.  There are countless ways you can complete your tasks.
1. Open assault. If you have the firepower, you can kill all of the enemies in your path (just be sure to have plenty of ammo). This option awards you the least amount of experience points.
2. Stealth-combat. Sneaking around and quietly eliminating enemies, non-lethal if you can. This awards you the most amount of experience if you can kill a good amount of guards.
3. Pure stealth. This option leaves you with the second most amount of XP possible. Going through areas without being detected leaves you with a ghost experience bonus, which when earned, will give you a sense of accomplishment (and a lot of XP). This bonus is possible with stealth-combat, just make sure you're not seen.
As you can see there are many ways you can complete a level. Most of them will have hidden pathways, which can help you skip past a lot of guards, or go some where that can award you with fine loot. For instance, I once crawled my way into a vent and found a nice stash of weapons, even found a praxis kit one time (devices that unlock augmentations without having to level up). Some of these areas can only be accessed if you certain abilities, such as hacking.
Hacking is  (in my opinion) the most important ability in the game. Having a level 5 hacking skill early game will help you in more ways than one. Unlocking safes, doors, overriding security hubs and personal computers is key. Computers will give you passwords and even reveal some cool references from other games. Security hubs will let you bypass doors, cameras, turrets, and even combat robots to fight on YOUR side! Hacking is also important for finding alternate paths in the game (which I mentioned earlier).
Unforunately, this game comes with some pretty hefty boss fights. Going through the WHOLE game with only a stun gun and my bare hands, I had to face these over-powered enemies without anything but a stick and a rock. I think there needs to be away around these boss fights, or they shouldn't be implemented at all. After my first encounter (which was pretty easy) I had started upgrading a combat rifle on the side and stockpiling ammo for the next boss, which I didn't really want to do.
What I've noticed about this game, is that most of the characters you interact with have a random dialogue chance. That means you can't go into your guide to try and convice them to win something, or someone over. Which is a cool addition, but it rendered the guide I bought with my Xbox game useless (at some points). I don't know if this is really true, but it's happened to me a lot.
Overall, I think it's a very good game. I strongly recommend anyone who's new or familiar with the Deux Ex series to try it out.  The developers need to come back and iron out some bugs and fix the FPS problems, but once you go into regedit and tinker with some settings you should be good to go. I hope for another Deus Ex game like this to come out in the near future. I've had so much fun playing this title, that I'm currently on my fourth playthrough.
Thank you for reading.

June 22, 1941. Breaking his nonaggression pact with Josef Stalin, Adolf Hitler launches Operation Barbarossa, the invasion of the Soviet Union and begins one of the longest and most brutal campaigns in modern military history. Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 masterfully captures this front of the second world war like no other game to date. Red Orchestra is a realistic, team based, multiplayer first person shooter. It is not a simulator like the ARMA series, but is still a game that must played with the upmost seriousness. The game places you into the boots of a soldier in the Soviet Red Army or in the German Ostheer and allows you to assume the different roles of infantry or armored vehicle crewmen. Players can assume a variety of roles from riflemen, assault troopers, and tank crewman to snipers, sappers, tank hunters and tank commanders. Some roles are leadership roles, with the purpose of guiding and ordering your teammates to victory like squad leaders and tank commanders, with the ability to call in support, like devastating artillery strikes. Combat is realistic, tough, and gruesome. Every mistake is punished by death. Infantry must work together, take cover, and use real world tactics, with different roles coordinating with each other to achieve victory. Vehicle crews must also communicate and coordinate if they are to survive, let alone win, whether it's in an APC transporting troops to the frontlines or engaging enemy tanks as a gunner in your own tank. Fight several battles in historical locations all over the eastern front from the earlier days of the onslaught with the victories of the Germans to the final days of the Third Reich, with the Soviets in the heart of Berlin, with several weapons fully realized and vehicles with realistic handling and mechanics. Red Orchestra: Ostfront 41-45 is one of the most terrifying, realistic, authentic, and greatest multiplayer shooters of all time. A complete masterpiece.

Got my Steam Controller bundled with Dark Souls 3, and while I was waiting for it to arrive I played through the entire game (twice!) on my friend's 360 Controller. My Steam Controller arrived recently and I've been testing it out on various games.
I've come to the conclusion that it's pretty terrible when it comes to needing to react quickly to things. As this concept seems to apply to the vast majority of games on Steam, I cannot in good faith recommend the Steam Controller to people. I could imagine the controller being particularly good with slower-paced games, however. I'm looking forward to testing it out on Factorio later on in the week. Games that require more precision and choices rather than speed and adaptability are likely significantly better suited for the Steam Controller than otherwise.
The Steam Controller attempts to do too much with too much. The two trackpads are massive and overly-touchy at their centers but incredibly difficult to work with as you near their edges. The left trackpad is also the highly-sensitive D-Pad of the controller, and both trackpads can be pushed down and function as buttons themselves. You've also got the standard ABXY buttons, though they're placed slightly off-center of the controller rather than further out, meaning the highly-ergonomic thumb-angle familiar to 360/PSX controllers does not apply here. For games that sparsely use the ABXY buttons, this isn't so much an issue, but for others that are centered around those buttons (Dark Souls), expect mass-frustration. Swapping the location of these buttons and the rightmost trackpad would go a long way to improving cross-controller familiarity and general ease-of-use. As it stands, the thumb is inclined to hover over the trackpad rather than the set of buttons.
And let's talk about buttons, shall we? Alongside the ABXY buttons, you have a SELECT/START pair of buttons as well as a central 'Steam' button. You've also got R1/R2 and L1/L2...but also R3 and L3, found on the back of the controller over the batteries. I hit these mostly by accident, and frankly would prefer that they were simply not there. You also have the 3 'buttons' from pressing in the trackpads/joystick. Ignoring the Steam button, that's a whopping 15 things for you to press while also finagling with two trackpads and a joystick. And one of those trackpads is actually four minitrackpads (the DPAD). Sound daunting? It is.
In short, and as I said before, the Steam Controller attempts to do too much with too much. It attempts to replace typical controllers and keyboard/mouse alike, but ultimately falls short on both fronts due to too much complexity and illogical default mappings (Yes, I've changed the mappings for my various games as some users have suggested. No, it doesn't help.) For $50, I cannot recommend this product. I've already ordered a $30 XBox 360 controller and if I wanted to I could buy a keyboard/mouse combo for <$20 and be vastly more satisfied with the usability of the products than I am with the Steam Controller.

If you like puzzle games, you should play Gyromancer. Period.
Entertaining puzzle game; some of the enemies can be quite frustrating depending on if you luck out with the puzzle gems.

By opting for an asymmetric style of puzzle play (as opposed to Puzzle Quest et al's symmetric style of you move, AI moves), Gyromancer more consistently rewards mastery, making for a much more satisfying play experience. If you enjoyed PQ but felt frustrated by its high variance, Gyromancer is for you.
If you enjoy playing the Puzzle Quest franchise of games developed by Infinite Interactive, this purchase is simply a no-brainer!   Match 3 meets Role-Playing Game.  A marriage made in heaven.  :)
Fun little Bejeweld style puzzler, but with the twist that you're clearing gems to power your monster (or prevent the enemy monster from being powered up) and to use skills.

It may not be the best example of story-telling you've ever seen, but by jove, the gameplay more than makes up for it.
If you haven't seen PopCap's 'twist' on the Match-3 genre of casual games, this will come as a total surprise.  If you have, then you may appreciate the further strategic bent this lends to the original design.
Instead of swapping turns with an omniscient and overly-planning AI opponent (Puzzle Quest), the outcome of each match can be determined almost solely by the player.  Moves must be selected carefully to prevent opponent's skill gems from counting down, while also trying to detonate your own.  Features originally introduced as chains and locks make a comeback, but are used as skill results, not just randomly mixed in.
Overall, don't miss this.  It's a fantastic example of how to blend two genres of gameplay into a masterful whole.

Human life is not as fragile as ‘Cahors Sunset’ makes it out to be. At least that’s something of a lasting impression that was left on me, for what it’s worth.
I was left with little choice but to put aside the fact that the developers intended for us to play the role of an old man. Quite simply, even though I make his decisions, I don't feel as though I
him. Decisions made by the player and random events can affect the old man's attributes by increasing or decreasing their values. An example of this is an event in which a pigeon defecates on the old man's head.
Now, we’re led to believe that this sort of event is supposed to worsen someone's mood. I don't know about you, but if I was an old man and this happened to me I would probably laugh it off after cleaning myself up. It's not the end of the world, but in ‘Cahors Sunset’, these sorts of insignificant events are supposed to have lasting effects. That is, unless they're mitigated by some other decision and its corresponding effects. One must also keep in mind that if an attribute’s value is less than 25, there is a chance that the old man will book a one-way trip to rigor mortis.  Numerous situations like this are likely to leave one thinking throughout this experience, ‘If it were me, I just wouldn’t have this kind of overblown reaction’. There is a strange sense of disconnection as a result.
Given the frequency in which I encountered events involving faeces, one has to wonder if the developers were just having a laugh. In fact, it was the repeated defecation on the old man's head and his inability to avoid stepping on dog doo-doo that led to his unfortunate demise at the relatively young age of 71. I guess that after all of that poop, he just really didn’t want to live, quietly and tearfully doing away with himself in solitude. I must say that the animals of France must really have it in for this old man.
In between making decisions, I enjoyed reading about the old man’s past, which I believe may be part of the developers’ plan to make some sort of emotional impact on the audience. However, as a whole, ‘Cahors Sunset’ is more of a ‘numbers game’ than anything else. A numbers game where the odds may very well be stacked against you and before you know it, it’s death by poo.

A game that feeds you story day by day. It goes from story segment to stat-raising decision to random stat-changing event and then repeats as long as you keep your stats high enough to live another day. You celebrate every birthday by losing stats and getting closer to death.
The story was pretty interesting but depressing. From as far as I got in my playthroughs, it's a depressing story that highlights the bad things that happen when you live long enough to experience them.
The gameplay was disappointing to me because the choices were only about the stats.
In my first playthrough I hoped that the choices mattered beyond juggling stats. I picked choices that felt good to me (stats were important but I also factored in how I felt about the actual action). But eventually it felt like the options were randomly generated and didn't affect anything beyond the stat gains/losses. There were times when two options had the same stat changes but the action was seeing a different movie/show. I hoped that meant there was something special about the choice but I never saw the difference. Nothing special happens if you skip your meds, smoke or quit, pay back debts, or keep in touch with family. If I recall correctly, at another time I got the option to sell my old car which I declined, then two months later bought a new car, and then again, two months later I bought another new car. That was silly enough to break my immersion.
I got to the 'end game' in my second playthrough by ignoring the action flavor text and picking choices that had the best overall net gains (there are choices that give you a net loss) and prioritizing stats that were getting low.
Maybe worth a try if you want to see a depressing story. The gameplay itself is just filler that limits how much story you can see.
