Do you love trains? Do you love elevator music? Do you love simulated paper? This game has all three. Proceed with decision to purchase as necessary.
But seriously. Screaming at my PC while my life ticks away has never been so entertaining.

Paper Train Traffic is a second Steam game ported from smartphones and made by isTom Games (Nyan Cat: Lost in Space). This time memes turned into something more serious, trains!
Whole gameplay is based on right timing for every situation - you are in control of traffic lights and rail-switches, and your task is to keep the railroad going without any crash. It might sound easy, but the levels push you with higher difficulty to need for getting more and more patient.
What's worth mentioning is the fact that remembering the train sequences for repeating of levels won't help you - the number of wagons for trains is randomly generated, so after every restart you have to patiently check how many wagons trains on the railroad has (and how fast they are). Prepare for often crashes and keeping determination, as the game can make you tilt pretty easily.
Visuals of this game are really nice, the pen and paper style looks great! Every level looks and feels different (and there are 300 levels!), that shows up the great work developers made.
But let's mention also the cons - I can't get rid of the feeling that the smartphone version was made by a full team with proper graphics designer, but the PC version required a new menu and popup windows, which in the end look like to be done in a rush by a programmer who done the port. It looks ugly, with regular font you might use in a document and without any thought of style worthy the pen and paper in-game visuals. It's no wonder that the menu and popups are nowhere to be seen in trailer and screenshots. Also, the game's text would deserve a proofread for few small mistakes.
Paper Train Traffic is a nice game for 4 euros, considering the drawn graphics style and big amount of content that can provide you hours of fun... or frustration, it depends on your patience and acceptance of challenges.
My copy of Paper Train Traffic was obtained for free for reviewing purposes. This fact hasn't changed my opinion about the game (and the review) in any way.

EDIT: Having passed Level 100, I can only say PT:T continues to exceed expectations; constantly challenging w/o becoming tedious. I do not hesitate to call the overall design and concept "brilliant", and far exceeding the average.
Paper Train: Traffic is a very special game. Special in its simplicity, in its design and concept, in its wonderful anything-but-simply graphics (though simple to understand), and special in the joy of playing such a FUN game. (Oh, yes, VERY special in its wonderfully low price.)
The premise to Paper Train: Traffic is nothing new, so the learning curve isn't even an issue (except for helping to develop skills.) You have a number of trains crossing the screen. Pretty much all the player can do is stop, then start traffic on specific tracks to avoid collisions (which are quite fun, and not necessarily rage-inducing), or switch tracks on some levels. (Perhaps other things later on.) There are variables to consider, such as trains are of different lengths and travel at varying speeds, f'rinstance. (And did I mention that the trains aren't always the same in every attempt.....) Some of the tracks are very convoluted, and involve many crossings. You are also able to "boost" the speed of the entire screen in order to increase points generated, but then aren't close to the "stop/start" buttons. Any collisions results in a "Retry", while a level completion results in a grade of 1 - 3 stars. As in most games of this type, cummulative star count opens features, and each of 300(!!!) levels must be accessed through completion of prior levels. There is also at least one leaderboard with the option to compare to friends only (and perhaps other choices.)
I haven't played Paper Train: Traffic very long, but I really don't need to to recommend it at this price. My suggestion? Buy it, play it, decide for yourself within the "refund" period. I suspect there will be few refunds requested.
(Hopefully more as I have more to report.)
Thank you.

Well, I really don’t know what to think about this thing. Cahors Sunset is not really bad.
Basically, it has a very neat idea. Manoeuvre through the life of an old, depressed man by making very basic choices that affect more or less the basic conditions of his life. All that with a great look and horrible music. It could be a great thing if you are in this kind of games, as I am usually.
I find the Narration most of all good: While the life goes on and you learn, what month after month in France, the home country of the old man, you learn also all his biography until the point of departure of the game. That is interesting in terms of storytelling as well as in terms of telling history.
But what bothers me extremely is that the game looks and feels over all unfinished. After half an hour (half the time it took me to finish it with the age of 73 years) it feels very repetitive. Your possible choices as well as the random events repeat again and again. Also, I felt disappointed, because I think, the devs missed the opportunity to combine the historical events with the actions of the old man. Surely, this can be seen as part of the story: The world goes on and changes, and the old man’s life remains always the same depressing course down in the direction of depression and death. But I think, there could have been made a lot more.
At the end, Cahors Sunset is a pretty little game that can be played, if you like to experience this kind of games. And I am not left with anger or any negative feelings. I really really like the story telling and gameplay ideas and the minimalistic style. But I wouldn’t recommend it to a broader public.

I have a review for this game, but I'm going to type a wall of text here in hopes that you can't see my review. Because I think there's a major point to this game that you can't ever have someone tell you about. I think you have to experience it.. I think you have to feel it.  If you can come to that point on your own, it's a beautiful and amazingly well designed game for a very low price.
The problem is, in my review I'm going to spoil what I believe the "secret" point of this game is. I know some of you will click it anyways and miss out. But I'm challenging you. Is $2 really so much to pay to believe in another human being? Just please. Trust me. Don't read the rest of this review until after you've at least played through the game once on your own.
For those of you that insist on seeing it now, or for those of you who have played through once and are back now to read this, here is my review:
This game is magnificent. It's not amazing as far as gameplay, sound, graphics.. No. It's clearly not meant to be that type of game, but is any visual novel really about the visuals? They're just an accentuation for the story you're being immersed in.
The point of the game is the reason why I love it. I played the game for about 45 minutes. Just one play through. The first ten to fifteen minutes, I was treating it like another silly game I didn't care about.. Halfway through I started really getting interested in the story. It hooks you in and goes from using third person references to saying "You did this. You remember this. You were sad because." ... without you noticing, the game goes from telling you a story about someone else to engaging you in a story about yourself.
At some point, I think year seven or so. The stories stop. The family history goes no further. You learn about your parents, how they met. You learn about yourself. You learn about your brothers, and how you struggled. You learn about your first love and how she was your pillar when times got hard. When times became harder she was only there for you more. And then suddenly the history stops. The GAMEPLAY stops.  And you're asked.. there really a reason to balance your life? To prolong your suffering and loneliness? To keep thinking about things. To keep hoping for another love as deep and fulfilling as the one you lived.
And at that point I realized. This game lies to you. The game tells you the point is to keep yourself alive as long as possible. And yes, you can do that for the leaderboards if you like. You can be a robot and experience life in the most optimal way for survival. Or you can do what you feel is  right as you come to terms with death.
In my own final days, I visited many loved relatives and friends. Put aside money for my children, even when I didn't have any. Went out to theatre and surrounded myself with people I cared for. People stole from me and silly things would bother me.. And one day the money ran out and I died. I cried a little bit but.. I died living to the fullest.
And that. That is what I think this game is truly about. It's not a grind to live as long as you can. It's only a grind for as long as it takes for you to realize that grinding your life away is NOT the life you should want to live. At that point the game teaches you something deep about yourself and allows you to come to terms with human mortality.
For that reason I believe this game is magnificent.  But who knows. I might be seeing magic where there is nothing. Perhaps it wasn't their intention. Regardless, I'm very glad for what I got out of this game.. I'm kind of sad I would have missed it if it wasn't so cheap.

Bully:Scholarship Edition is a third person game that takes place in a VERY stereotypical american high-school, if you're looking to do a Columbine this isn't for you unless you want to substitute with a slingshot or spud gun.
In one mission you break into the girls dorm and steal panties.
The game is full of fun minigames, hell some of the classes are minigames in themselves. (I don't count Maths and English as minigames, ok.)
You can basically do whatever you want in a school-themed game and not have any real life consequences, go ahead and shoot that fat nerd with the spud gun.
You've got the Nerds, the Preppies, the Greasers and i'm pretty sure everyone would know there would be Jocks in this kind of game, each with their own theme whenever you're fighting someone a part of their faction, speaking of themes, when you get the game you get the soundtrack too for free, some of the soundtrack (like the theme that plays when a prefect chases you down) sounds like 80s cop music and it's just so memorable it's no surprise that it may get stuck in your head quickly.
Let's just get to the most fun parts, you can beat people up of course, you could throw itching powder at people and watch them thoughtlessly scratch themselves, you can throw stinkbombs and firecrackers, shoot a slingshot, bottle rocket launcher (kinda like fireworks), and spud gun, make out with several different girls (Or guys, don't talk about that seriously.).
The game offers at least 15 hours of gameplay unless you just speedrun it and have no fun at all outside of the main storyline.
Conclusion: 8.5/10, I absolutely wish for a sequel, and a sequel with many more hours of gameplay, Happy nerd hunting, gamers!

A little late to be writing about this, but still wanted to as I really enjoyed this game. Surprise as this is coming from someone who didn't really enjoy or have any interest in the genre outside of Super Smash Brothers (if you even want to count that, I consider it more of a beat-em-up) and a couple oddball games like Soul Caliber and Virtua Fighter 5 as well as even a Street Fighter game, none really caught my attention until I bought this on a whim. Just like with Skyrim, I wanted to give it another chance, maybe I'd find something enjoyable here that I didn't with the other games and did I ever.
The first thing that I loved most about this game was the art style, the main reason why it was high on my list. That annnd it was on sale...heh. After playing a bit of the Arcade and Story, I immediately fell in love with the game and all it's characters who really shine in their own unique way. Each one plays vastly different from the other, though there are a couple who play kind of similarly. BlazBlue is a game worth picking up if you're are wanting some gameplay with some excitement, a low-ish skill floor but a very, very high skill ceiling compared to some other titles.
While playing through, you notice you have all your attacks plus a special? Yes, this ability, called the Drive, allows your character to do neat attacks such as regain health, control a puppet or chain some gunplay. Along with the amazing roster of characters you can play, there's also a mode to go through each of their tales to figure out the overaching story (as of me writing this, I have not finished it, but am about ~70% the way through).  I believe that this is where the game shines brightest alongside the amazing characters. As you go through, they become memorable because of their personality as well as movesets. I'm really loving the story, though it might not be for everyone as it makes you try to put together all the pieces which may seem more of a chore than fun.
There's also a vast gallery where you can unlock art and movies, all of which are really well-designed. Again, I really love the art and aesthetics of this game, the music is alright, nothing too special although some are relaxing yet give a nice tone when you do listen. Surely there's nothing wrong with such an amazing title. Well, there is and probably the greatest downfall, a lack of an online multiplayer and a tutorial. You're pretty much left to either play single player or get a friend with another controller/keyboard. From what I've read around, it's because it is a port from the original XBox launch. Still, it's a nice game worth the time I've put into it. I highly recommend using an Xbox controller or an arcade stick if you want to play.
You probably noticed I said
That's the greatest thing I've found out about this game, a lot of the characters you can pretty much mash buttons and still do damage. However, with practice you can do some pretty amazing things. I'm pretty sure that this goes for a lot of fighters, though I think it's a lot more noticeable in here. If you're looking for a nice entry into fighting games, I highly suggest giving this a try, the replayability, while little, is really worth it for those who are looking for something nicely competitve.

Ok, about Blazblue. It is, probably, one of the new hits of the fighting games, and well deserved. Created by the same guys who make the Guilty Gear Series, and the Persona Arena series, both good ones, this is a game that really serves well its purposes.
The commands can be a bit clunky and hard to use at first, for those that are new to the game. This is one of those games that requires a bit of you to get into it. But the idea here is to use well your 'X'(PS)/'A'(Xbox) button, since it helps to make the combos and also make the special moves. This is a game where you have to understand your character, and it is hard to pick any fighter and have some fun (you can still button smash though, that helps a lot)
The problem of this game itself is the lack of any online multiplayer mode. It is understandable, since this game is really old and there is a newer game of the series here in the Steam (go look for it, Continuum Shift). But, the thing is that the story and arcade mode is good and can get yourself into the game somewhat easy, so, I only recommend it if you want to play it for the story mode. Also, if you buy it, it is nice for you to understand the mechanics of the series, or even if you play a lot with any local friend.
This game gets a nice discount in sales, so I recommend that you don't buy it full price. And if you like it, go look for the Continuum Shift. It is really better.

After reading through reviews, comments, and having my own experiances with this simulation, there are several things I wish to point out.
First, this is a simulation. It doesn't have to meet standards of a game. It can be as boring as possible to get its point across or provide the education it is designed to give. World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a simulation that is meant to teach you the innerworkings of several guns. That is its objective, nothing incredibly fancy. Too me, it accomplishes this. The developers of this program provide a large quantity of guns, more than any other simulator that focuses on disassembly and reassembly does, and more models are being developed. Negative reviews that state their main point as being "This game is boring" don't understand this game is not supposed to be fun. It can be fun if you are interested in weaponry, but if you wish to shoot other people or targets, this is not made for that. I think you should experience this to see if you have any interest in models or guns in general.
Second, people point out the grinding for a new weapon. There are ways around this. One being an option on the main interface with the weapon trees. It is at the very bottom and is the "Catalog". This allows you to purchase a weapon without having an adjacent weapon on the tree unlocked. This does require more xp than purchasing it when it is able to be normally unlocked. A second way to reduce grinding is the "Quiz" tab at the top of the interface. This opens a 30 second quiz where you have to name a weapon being given only it's silhouette. To succeed, you must name the weapons with no mistakes. One mistake will forfeit your xp gained from the quiz. You can do this quiz once every 2 hours. A third way of gaining xp is to log on once every day. Each day logged on gives you xp, which increases each day. I believe that the xp needed to unlock a weapon should be decreased a little, which it most likely will be decreased in an update due to public opinion.
Third, dlc costs are high. This simulation is still growing. The developers are offering you the chance to purchase every existing model, and have access to every new model that is developed. That is extremely generous so I believe that the price should stay relatively high to moderate. I for one will not purchase the dlc because I am dedicated enough to earn every weapon because for me, this simulation is pretty high quality.
Fourth, now that I have mentioned the quality of the simulation, I'll talk about graphics and overall structure. The simulation has graphics that work. They are not high resolution, and that shouldn't really matter for this. I would like to see better graphics, but for what the simulation wants to accomplish, it is perfectly fine as is. The graphics are simpler which makes it easier to show contrast between parts which is important when trying to disassemble something. The graphics themselves should not make or break this download. Now the simulation progresses by having the player do certain tasks, staring with a field strip of the selected weapon. Once the field strip section is complete, you move on by performing a disassembly and reassembly. Then you move on to the operation of a weapon, which introduces you with how the weapon works while firing, reloading, unloading, using a safety, different rates of fire, and add-ons to the weapon such as a grip or flashlight. Once complete, you move on to the game, super game, and hardcore game which are all about learning which parts can be removed in which orders, and how fast you can do so. After xp is gained from each exercise, you can purchase a new weapon, and the cycle repeats. This may seem boring, but this is how disassembly of a weapon works, you break it down and build it back up again.
Finally, people complain about bugs. This simulation is new to Steam. Bugs will happen. One common bug is the "LOGIN_BY_CLIENT" bug. Several people have fixed this bug by deleting and reinstalling the program. People have also complained about having their save data "vanishing". Your data will come back. This happend to me and my data came back within the hour. These bugs will eventually be ironed out, but for now are not major problems since the simulation is new.
I realize that this review has been long and has jumped around, and for that I am sorry, but this simulation has had ridicule for not appealing to some audiences, and I know that some people are going to see those reviews and be turned away. I feel as though this is a simulation that has already achieved a lot, and still has great potential given the variety of weapons humanity has created. I for one love this simulation. I recommend it for people who enjoy complexities, machines, construction, and guns. This simulation can be quite taxing on the mind so be wary of that, but the innerworkings of guns are extremely specific and thus are difficult to disassemble in reality, and this simulation replicates that extremely well. I hope you give this simulation a shot and that people can learn about weapons in a cheap, and safe manner thanks to this simulation.

I've played the other Dead Rising games, and I found this to be a distant 3rd place. The problem, largely, is the setting. On paper, the environment sounds like it offers good variety - there's an outdoor amphetheatre, a school, a museum, police station, and various shops. TL;DR: The game is a random number generator dependent upon RNG. So long as you keep attributes at a stable level (sometimes dependent upon a lot of luck) you'll survive. The payoff is unrewarding. The game has potential to be more than what it is.
Purchase reason: Game appeared in the new releases of Steam. The description piqued my interest. There aren't many games on the platform that appear to have this type of background. Further, my partner adores French culture and history so that helped the purchase decision.
Install note: Be forewarned that the game will attempt to install Adobe Air when you try and start the game for the first time.
Initial reaction: The concept plays out a little too simply - You make a single choice for the month (they can be very simple things that would be a common occurrence in everyday life such as attending a sports contest). There doesn't appear to be nearly as much substance in the game as what there could be.
In game music: It's pleasant enough to listen to at first. However, I must admit to turning the sound down/off before completing my first game as it became grating.
A possible subtle point of the game: Each month the game provides a description of what is happening in the world beyond your control. This effects your own life minimalistically. As such I can see that this is one of the points that Locomotivah may be attempting to make with the game. That we as individuals believe that what happens in the greater scheme of life may not impact us nearly as much as we may believe it does.
At the beginning of each birth year you make a fresh resolution. This resolution provides a positive and a negative effect each month. One option is to take up smoking which increases your anxiety while decreasing your physical health. Another thing that happens each birth year is that you lose a point in each attribute for each year that you've survived. For example, after your first year you lose one in each category and so on.
Post-first game reaction: My initial reaction stands. The game has potential for deeper gameplay than it currently provides. At this current point in time it's essentially a random number generator with different categories that you can't drop beneath.  So long as the RNG is in your favor and you select the most appropriate choice each month you will continue to survive.
Unfortunately, I don't believe that the reward/payoff is rewarding enough for spending much time with the game. Unless, of course, your goal is to get into the top of the leaderboards. That's about all you can hope for as the game has no achievements nor does it have trading cards (yet).
My Recommendation: It's one of those games that deserves an inbetween recommendation. I wouldn't recommend purchasing it by itself - even though at $2 or $1.69 with its 15% launch promotion it's certainly priced correctly - but it is something that's worth a playthrough if the setting and the mini-storyline piques your interest. I'd recommend holding off for an inevitable indie bundle.

If you remember Golden Axe, then it is enough to say that Dungeons: The Eye of Draconus is a clone of that game with over the top violence and hit&miss humor.
If you have not haerd of Golden Axe, Dungeons: The Eye of Draconus is a 2D fantasy brawler in which you control a character and slaughter waves of enemies before moving on to next stage and repeating this activity. It can be played in single player or local co-op (not sure if online co-op is available), up to three players, which is probably the most enjoyable way.
What this game has, and Golden Axe did not, is lots and lots of blood and nerdy humour type jokes (wacky voice acting / fighter named Bolax / mage's special attack summons a giant fire-breathing chicken mount / orc frat boys / gay zombies / etc.), which may or may not work for you.
The game is quite challenging, although you get unlimited continues (at least on normal difficulty), so the challenge lies mostly in getting the achievements. I died a lot, and only got 2 of 12 in the end. Curiously, the first boss was the hardest for me.
Note that The Eye of Draconus game is approximately 1 hour in length, so getting it at a discount or in a bundle is about the only way to get your money's worth. Might be worth a playthrough, if you enjoy slaughtering kobold children.

So I've had the steam controller for nearly 2 weeks. I went through and tested several different games.
Killing Floor 2 - 10 hours

Pay Day 2 - 5 hours

If you happen to be looking for a new controller I highly suggest it.(just keep in mind it does have a learning curve)

When I was gifted Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ for Christmas, my immediate reaction was "oh jeeze did I never take that off my wishlist", followed by "well I guess it'll be interesting research material". My ~4 hours of playtime represents a complete 100%-ing of the game - there's no cheevos to obtain, so you'll have to take my word for it.
Here are some thoughts on the game and its content:
- The game is a pretty simple visual novel, in that there aren't really any branching trees - your choices across the game (of which there are three "big" ones, being your sight-seeing for the first three days) will culminate in one of four endings, each of which represents one of two outcomes with your waifu of choice. The waifus, while limited in number, are fun enough, but I have to question their general decision making capabilities considering they are two young adult women who welcomed a weeb from the internet into their home, and after a few days together fall in love with him.
- The protagonist, while not given a specific country of origin (you enter your own currency to better immerse yourself), is a pale blonde dude with no eyes, which I guess is meant to reflect the generic Japanese dude with no eyes in most VNs??? He is also a dude who can apparently speak pretty high-level Japanese but has never heard of/experienced: convenience stores, yukata, ramen, and many other things that any good weeb is well-versed in.
- While I like that the game simultaneously displays Japanese and another language, this system is troubled by the lack of furigana (complicating any language-learning that could take place), and a narrative weirdness involving one sister not speaking Japanese - there is never any indication (from what I could see) of when the characters are speaking Japanese or English, though both are referenced. Sometimes one of the sisters speaks in phonetic English (rendered in katakana), so there's clearly meant to be a differentiation, but it's a weird thing to not have in there.
- There is no onsen scene, which would normally be an automatic 'no' review, but you do peep on one of the waifus after taking a bath, so it scrapes by on the anime cliche checklist.
- The emotive animations for the waifus are pretty neat, and I would likely play more VNs that include such a system.
Overall: I recommend this game if you want to experience a VN that puts you in the perspective of the simultaneously best-educated and most oblivious gaijin weeb possible. It's a quick ride, but fun for what it is.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a very good game for killing time, and learning about the guns and other things (Such as Skeletons and other goodies) that the game has to offer. While people complain about grinding, you can test your gun knowledge with a Quiz, that shows you images of guns by their silhouettes and asks you to identify the model. At a decent rate of 300 XP per correct answer, it's a good way to get experience.
There are undoubtedly microtransactions in the game, though they're really quite unobtrusive. Credits, Experience, and other little packs can be bought to help the developers and get yourself a few new things as well. People in their reviews are complaining about the need to reassemble and disassemble the same gun to progress, however at this point in time I've not had to do that. The game itself offers login bonuses, in addition to the hourly test, that helps progression.
Overall, it's an interesting little program that lets you assemble, disassemble, and operate weapons as slow or fast as you want to, with new weapon models being added every couple months. For a free game, it's really quite a bargain, as there's a way to get mostly everything without needing to buy so-and-so microtrasnaction. I enjoy it, and would recommend it to anyone who has a passion for guns.

Really disappointed honestly, it's a concept with a lot of pontential but poor implementation. The controller has a light, low-quality plastic feel to it, but it's comfortable to hold. What isn't comfortable is the angle at which you have to move your thumb to access the single joystick and ABXY buttons, which can be blamed on the size of the trackpads. The buttons are super stiff like Cherry Blue switches and the throw on the triggers is way too short.
The trackpad surfaces are no substitute for actual joysticks; you won't get the level of sensistivity you would expect from touch surfaces on smart phones for example. My advice is turn on smoothing filters to the maximum setting (especially in Dark Souls 3), otherwise the trackpad movement micro-stutters rather than gliding into position. Also increase the dead zone a small amount, so you don't move your thumb back to what you thought was the dead zone only to move the camera again.
To compensate for the lack of physical feedback from the trackpads there is a clicking sound from the internal speaker when you move your finger, which was a nice idea but it annoys more than it helps. It's particularly bad in games where the micro-stuttering is really obvious, so it's the first thing I turn off in any default binding.
Big Picture Mode is required in order to make changes to controller bindings, but navigating the menus with this controller is not very intuitive and feels sluggish. You will likely find yourself spending upwards of 15 minutes trying to get the bindings and trackpad settings right, so it gets annoying. The level of configuration is amazing though, and the bindings are associated with your controller so if you happen use your controller somewhere other than your own home Steam will download your bindings. You can also use the controller for games that don't have controller support.
If Valve made a few more changes I think it would be a great controller, so I will be keen to see what they do in the future. Higher sensitivity on the trackpads, perhaps a different texture on the dead zone of the trackpads to help new users get adjusted to them.

In 2004, I seen an artical in a PS Mag which displayed a early concept for a game about a teenaged "Bully" attending a rough school. Thats all that was said, also displaying early screenshots of the alpha build. It had no name at the time and I did not realise that Rockstar was making it (I was 8 at the time so did not notice). I would just look at this artical over and over, fantasizing how good a game would be where you play as the 'c,0,ck' of the school. (In England/Liverpool, if you are the c,0,ck of the school this means you are the hardest/toughest kid in school)
Years went by and I had forgot about the this artical, as games like MGS3: Snake Eater and GTA: SA and God of War had released, which occupied my little brain for a while. Then in early 2006, a video appeared on GameSpots PS2 page. An eight minute clip of a game called Canis Canem Edit surfaced. MY MIND WAS BLOWN! I rewatched that 8 minute video more than 50 times before it came out in October 2006. I had to wait till Christmas to get my hands on it. I even opened it 2 weeks early as I could not wait to play it (Thug life chose me brah). And when I lowered my TV volume to 4 and stealthy put the disc into my dying PS2, my childhood was complete. My expectations where met ten fold. The gameplay was fantastic. The characters were fantastic! The story was fantastic! Basically the game over all was fantastic. I had never enjoyed a game as much as Canis Canem Edit. Playing that game in the time period I played it has a very special place in my heart, as it was honestly that important to me at the time.
Ok, lets face it. This is not a review about Bully: Scholarship Edition, its just me reminiscing about a game I played. But I can't help writing about how special this game was to me. And how much of a effect it had on my life. Which must make a statement on how great this game was overall back in the day.
If you have never played this game before and pick it up and feel underwhelmed. Thats because the gaming industry has expanded and progress so much in the past 10 years. But when this game first came out, trust me! This was something special.
10/10

I didn't expect much since I got this in a bundle of games but it has knocked my socks off.
The art is totally like a comic book you'd read in the late 80s and the environments are so well designed, they almost look like illustrations from the "Heavy Metal" magazine, though the character designs are a bit more modern, and did I mention the music rocks♥♥♥♥♥and kicks your ears in the face?
This is a game made for older gamers or people who like older things.  The sense of humor is adult, hilarious, and full of references, with more than one to Monty Python and and a load of jabs at the games that inspired Eye of Draconus, the wit is just so great.  The voice acting is good too and the actors have great timing, they made me bust a gut.
The gameplay itself is your standard beat'em-up from the 80s and 90s, but leaning more toward Golden Axe.  You move all directions, have an attack move, a jump, and jump attack of course, a grab button to pick up food and power-ups, and you have a special ability button that does cool attack varying by character, the Wizard's special ability is especially funny but I don't want to spoil it.  You also come across enemies with mounts which you can steal and use for a while.  You even get the sword sign that says when to "GO", and the controls are sooo smooth.  Did I mention the music?
You get to pick from three characters:  The Barbarian, the Wizard, and the Thief.  Each character, of course, has unique abilities and their special moves are all varied and fun.  The characters themselves(and voice actors) as I said before are great, absolutely spectacular. The jokes are top notch, and did I mention the awesome music?
The game also boasts smooth local play but apparently the online COOP is waiting for a patch and isn't very functional at this point.  Like most beat'em-ups from the old days it get's pretty mindless and repetitive, but that's part of the fun.  The music is awesome too.
The game is pretty short but it makes for a lot of play throughs with all your friends, so it's kind of a good thing and kind of a bad thing, but the gameplay is well paced though and the difficulty dosen't jump from stage to stage.  Plus the awesome music helps to keep you in that mind setting of destroying everything on screen.
So, I would definitely recommend getting this game if you like the sound of what I described, and if you grew up in the 80s/90s you will definitely not be disappointed by the amazing nostalgia factor.
9/10 (1 extra point for nostalgia)

Dungeons: The Eye of Draconus (or D:TED for short) is a retro-inspired hack & slash that draws inspiration from Golden Axe, 90s Konami beatemups, and even a little Battletoads (at least the most infamous part). Boasting three playable characters, a multitude of adversaries to slay, and a lot of humor, does D:TED deliver?
Well.....You saw the big fat thumbs down didn't you?
First off let me start by saying I become a real jerk when it comes to reviewing beatemups, hack & slashers, and similar belt-scrolling games. Some children were raised by wolves, I was raised by arcade machines. I know what to expect out of the genre and I hate it when certain essential elements aren't properly handled.
D:TED clocks in at less than an hour, potentially less than 45 minutes if cut-scenes are skipped. This is a good length for an arcade-styled beatemup. This isn't supposed to be Castle Crashers where there are dozens of stages, experience points, and tons of weapons that are +1 here and -1 there. A fair number of bosses have to be contended with, and they require different strategies in order for the player to succeed. Enemy variety is also pretty solid, which is rare for the genre and always welcome.
The three playable characters consist of a barely-clothed drunk who angers easily, a thief(harlot?) who swings daggers, and the cleric that throws fireballs and summons a fire-breathing chicken. I didn't know clerics could do that, but I guess it depends on what God they're trying to convince everyone to worship. Whatever the case, this line-up is diverse enough to satisfy any play-style.
But now we have to get to the main failing of D:TED. The complete lack of proper mechanics. The life-blood of the beatemup (or any game for that matter) is in the mechanics. It's a catch-all term that accounts for all the rules the game has to follow. Mechanics could be what constitutes the player doing or taking damage, the height and arc of the jump, or determining whether a sword that is swung at two monsters registers a hit on one or both.  When the mechanics are faulty, the entire game suffers, and all the good decisions and intriguing game-design in the world can't save it.
Basically, all deadly objects don't even have to touch the player to do damage. I've been hit by everything from flying kobold toddlers to rainbow hearts, even though on-screen they weren't even close. I've killed orks despite the blades of my daggers missing them by several feet. A flying boss takes far longer than it should due to constant misses. These occurences add up and the game ceases to be enjoyable. If you're going to play this game I recommend the Cleric. Thanks to his projectiles I don't have to deal with the crapshoot that is the melee-based combat.
D:TED has promise, good ideas, and its own unique story and characters, but the execution simply isn't there. I couldn't get any enjoyment out of the game. YMMV

This game is awesome. It takes some time to get used to some unique aspects of the game, but when you do, it's fun 4 dayz (see what I did there?). Here's a few things to help anyone who doesnt understand certain parts of this game.
-The double barreled shotgun is unique in how it fires (left click to fire left barrel, right click to fire right barrel). The reload is faster when you reload 2 bullets, rather than 1, since for 2 shells you just open the gun and flick 2 shells into the barrels super quickly, as opposed to one shell, which involves opening the gun carefully to avoid having the other unused shell fly out.
-All mag-fed guns (like in most fps games) have a slightly longer reload when all ammo in the clip is used up. However the beretta has an even longer reload time with a reload animation that takes up some of the screen. When using the beretta, avoid using all the ammo in a clip for faster reloads. @Husky Love pls check out this review, see if it helps.
-Armor only REDUCES dmg taken. It's possible to run out of health while having armor leftover, so keep an eye out for that.
And now, I'm gonna say this once, and only once: GRAPHICS AREN'T EVERYTHING!!! So please, disregard any negative review that involves disliking purely for bad graphics. It's all about the gameplay, which, in this case, is pretty damn good. Fast-paced gameplay lets you finish games pretty quickly, at least in my perspective.

After what I believe to be 100% completion of the VN w/o the DLC, I can definitely recommend Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~. It appears at first to be a fairly standard dating sim and while that aspect is present in a way, it serves the purpose of educating about the various districts of Tokyo and beyond much more than it sates the dating aspect.
Pros:
+Informative- A majority of the places you can see are really fleshed out and given detail, which is very nice. They provide both cultural and historical insight into places that are seen a lot in anime but not explored. It has a good balance of entertaining and informing to maintain the casual atmosphere it generally succeeds in having.
+Beautiful- Honestly a lot of the art was just very, very well made and made the experience all the more enjoyable.
+Implementation of "Archetype" Characters- While Makoto and Akira do fall under fairly common stereotypes of characters, the manner in which they operate in the story is unique and responded to their situations really consistently according to their personality. They are endowed with qualities that make them both enjoyable to be with and depending on the route you take, find satisfaction in their endings.
+Endings- I thought the endings of Makoto's route was really sweet and Akira's as well in their own different ways that felt really appropriate for how they were characterized.
Cons:
+Few choices- Other than where you went, there were few choices that made it feel much less linear than the VN is. The first readthrough took much longer than my second because a lot of interactions up until the last couple of days stay the same.
+Derpy Protagonist- At times, it was rather annoying to find the protagonist get excited over literally the smallest details but honestly, as long as you keep an open mind, it's not a deal breaker.
+Not Enough Art- There are crucial transition points like on the train when getting an idea of the surrounding is important to learning but alas, they revert to the same shot of the sky as filler for that scene. Again, not a dealbreaker, but just another thing that I felt could have benefitted the VN.
+Epilogues- Makoto's was too short and Akira's ending was just a bit too melodramatic for me at first.
Conclusion:
If it's on sale (or even not to be honest), definitely check out Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ and its DLC which I have yet to try. Really informative and entertaining, and while with a few drawbacks, still well worth my time and money!

A great skill-based team shooter. It is far different from traditional shooters, as there are very few hitscan weapons. This means that almost all weapons fire projectiles that must travel through the air before it hits your target, whether the projectile be bullet or explosive. You are equipped with a jetpack and jet boots that allow you to slide down surfaces and fly up them, allowing to reach speeds of up to 300 km/h. Combining this with projectile weapons (especially the ones which explode on impact) make for great duels, with great shots. The main gamemode is CTF, which is far more complicated than most shooters.
Graphics are very good, but nothing to brag about.
You can do one of the following: 1) You build up speed, pick up their flag as you fly past, and zoom back to your base without getting blasted to pieces. 2) You stand on you flag so that when someone tries to grab it, they slam into your body and lose their speed. 3) You chase down people who grab your flag. 4) You destroy the enemy's base defenses and their power supply, or just weaken their anti-capper defenses in general. 5) You protect your base from the above people.
Unfortunately pretty much all support has been dropped for this game. Don't expect any new content.

I find myself playing this more than I probably should.
This is one of those games that lets you get strong through practice, very strong through luck, and then snatch it all away in just a few seconds. You try fighting 5 orcs at once as a chicken and you'll understand.
Why did I buy this game?
It was on sale at the time. I never expected to put so many hours into this with friends, or for my friends to kill me so much.
Is it good?
-You notice an enemy's pattern, react to it, and kick them into the nearest wall.
-Several classes to choose from, with pros and cons to each.
-Simple combat system with a few combos. Easy to pick up, but the difficult decisions about items, weapons, and whether or not to go just one more run bring this game extra replayability.
Some people will get bored with this game very quickly. Others will find a gem. I'd say go for it if you like old school beat'em ups. The variety of things that will go horribly wrong to your character on any particular run might keep you hooked for longer than expected, and when it's on sale it's absolutely worth trying.

I've enjoyed Rockstar Games' 'Grand Theft Auto' series ever since the release of 'Grand Theft Auto: Vice City'. I thought they did a great job technically with their game engines and stylistically with the visual designs. Plus, 'Grand Theft Auto' games are great satire of the crime film/game genre and of contemporary society for the most part. While aware of the negative impact the games can have on society and the younger generation of gamers, I still defend the merits of 'Grand Theft Auto' games.
I was pretty stoked when I first read about 'Bully' back in 2005/2006, but was disappointed that the first iteration would not come to the PC platform. About a decade later, I finally got my hands on the remastered version of the game, thinking that Rockstar had injected similar type of technical and stylistic mastery, and social acuity into crafting this game as they did with 'Grand Theft Auto'. Was I wrong. True, in the year 2015, the game engine that runs 'Bully' will definitely show its age; I can accept that. However, 'Bully: Scholarship Edition' looks and sounds very uneven in spite of the remastering. The keyboard and mouse controls for the PC also feel unoptimized.
The truth is, I just can't recommend 'Bully: Scholarship Edition'. It simply lacks the energy, fire and humour that I enjoy in 'Grand Theft Auto' games. The setting of Bullworth Academy, while well-designed, just doesn't seem to allow for much exploration. It feels too confined and claustrophobic even when compared to 'Grand Theft Auto: Vice City', which was released in 2002. Most importantly, 'Bully' doesn't play or feel like a satire. It is pretty much a straight-up (private) school simulator full of cliques and stereotypes with uninspired early missions.
While you may approach 'Bully' and complete missions with good intentions, and that your character implicitly dislikes being bullied, you ironically need to be a bully to accomplish your goals. The unsatirical tone of 'Bully' actually makes me feel horrible for my heinous actions in the game. While I can find some reason to justify my undertaking of violent acts in 'Grand Theft Auto', I find my actions and bullying in 'Bully' to be distasteful.
In the end, I guess where 'Bully' fails is that it is too real. Whereas the action sequences, violence and set pieces in 'Grand Theft Auto' were designed to be cinematic, grandiose and hyperbolic -- making the games rather hyper-realistic, all the bullying and hijinx in 'Bully' are mostly possible and hit too close to home for comfort. Given the well documented negative impacts of bullying on people of all ages, I cannot in good conscience recommend 'Bully: Scholarship Edition'.

Your poor hit detection and unsatisfying combat left me bored and frustrated, your looks shuffled between blurry sprites to clashing art styles, and your dialog...I can barely begin to describe what an atrocity it is.

But back to the writing, I have to wonder if you ever made it out of fifth grade. I had a rocky start with Dungeons: Eye of Draconus. First the game's activation key didn't work right, then I went to seek help on the Steam page, and it didn't exist. When, a few days later, I finally got the game installed and booted up, I played for about 30 minutes before the game crashed during the second stage boss battle.
Needless to say, I was not smitten with my first interactions with Eye of Draconus. I'll tell you my first impressions before I go any further. It immediately felt repetitive, the comedy felt forced, and playing as a single player in a game meant for three was *terrible*. The only saving grace is that you can keep continuing when you run out of lives, akin to the old arcade games like Golden Axe and TMNT (which is what this game reminds me so much of). It can be very challenging at times, which isn't a bad thing.
The game doesn't list online coop as available on its page currently, but it is clearly available as an option in the menus. I gave this game another try later on as a local coop (Two controllers) and it was a far less painful experience. It still wasn't great. The game plays better with more players, as I'm sure was intended. I also had problems with the sound in the game. It needs normalization... it was too loud when I booted up the game so I lowered it to about 40%. At that mark, the player's speech was a 2/10, music a 4/10, sound effects 6/10 and cutscenes 8/10 (Sound level). I definitely think some adjustment to the sound is in order.
I really tried to like Dungeons: Eye of Draconus. I was a big fan of the games that it pays homage to, but I felt it just wasn't what it could have been. As mentioned previously, I feel like it really tried too hard on the humor, the graphics had some strange discrepancies (Rose was skinny in the hand-drawn images and a muscular amazon woman when you play her in-game?!), the music was alright when you could hear it, the gameplay was extremely repetitive (and I *love* Dynasty Warriors), and in general I just don't feel like it brings anything original (gameplay-wise) to the table. Except a chubby Barbarian in a speedo. That's genuinely terrifying.
I know that developers go through alot of work to create games for us, and I'm not discounting that. As a friend told me, not every game is for every person. Unfortunately, as bad as I feel for submitting a negative review, this one just wasn't for me. Sorry SuckerFree.

TL;DR Don't make a track pad based controller a combo deal for Dark Souls 3. I'm sure it's fine for other games.
Alright. This is an interesting controller, sure. I love the idea of being able to fully customize each button and every aspect of the controller. In theory this sounds absolutely perfect to play any steam game I could possibly imagine.
However--Now maybe it's just me--but this device (Which I specifically got for Dark Souls 3) is terrible to use. The D-pad is some sort of touch screen, along with the camera controls which flick around awkwardly more than mario in an ice level. There are two buttons on the back which I disabled, because on default they simply were shortcuts for buttons that I couldn't figure out exactly where they were in the controller unless I looked down.
For Dark Souls, this is the most unwieldy controller I've ever used. I was using an XBOX 360 controller to play the first two games, and just for a moment, lets compare the two:
The D-pad on the 360 is a physical button, so you know what you're pushing without having to look down. The steam controller is touch activated with the ability to turn that off in settings. But when I turned that setting off, it's just a disk that my thumbs can't tell the difference between up and right because the disk is a lot larger that it's suppose to be because you're supposed to be able to type with it as the left half of a keyboard.
The other disk on the right is where the rest of the keyboard is used to type things out with. That's cool if you want to, say, text your friends in between turns of a Civilization like game or something you can pause in. Dark Souls is not a game you want to have text chat in. It's too fast past to open up the menu and type, "Thanks!" when the game itself already has an emote system and wooden carvings that say, "Thank you," when you use them. The only time you need a keyboard in the game is naming your character. And you can use a keyboard for that or maybe say, an analog stick.
Lets talk about the touch pad... disk... thing on the right. In place of a camera control analog stick, it's essentially a touch pad pulled off of a laptop and it controls the mouse. I'm not sure why Steam thinks this is a good combination for Dark Souls considering the past two games have had TERRIBLE keyboard and mouse control unless you get a patch to fix up a couple essential features.
The buttons on the controller feel weirdly placed. Maybe it's because every controller I've ever used had them on the top right where the new touch pad... disk... thing is currently. There are also two extra buttons on the back for the grips. I don't mind those but the default control was drink an estus/use item on the right grip, and dodge-roll on the left. This was a little weird considering (X) is use item and is on the left and dodge is on right on the (B) button. This was easily changed in the controller menu, which I found as I played, there wasn't a good way to lock on to anything since there wasn't a camera control stick I could press down on. You can press down on the track pad... disk... thing on the right to open up a hotkey menu to do a bunch of things that looks handy but got me killed more than anything as I tried to lock on to an enemy and strafe around him when I realized I had selected to use my estus and run into a wall with my shield lowered.
Maybe they'll release a new controller chassis that has the option for track pad replacement and analog stick customization options. I really
to like this controller and I hope there are other games it works well with, but in my honest opinion... It's not good for Dark Souls.

So the PC port has it's issues, probably the same amount issues I have with my social anxiety. The capped 30FPS is a problem, but you can fix that, so that's not so bad. For a Dead Rising game, the free roaming aspect is my favorite, no load times in between areas, lots of different stores to go into much like DR1 and DR2. The main character, Nick, is a chumpy chump in the beginning, but he becomes a lot more fearless as you progress through the game, mostly due to the fact he's aching to get laid. And why wouldn't you become fearless for that reason, right? Kill a few thousand zombies here, so you can score some poon for your achievement.
The crafting system is better, you can make weapons on the go with some duct tape and Elmer's glue compared to DR2 where you have to find a workbench each time.
Saving the Survivors is about the same, but their wonky AI is still a problem, just don't bring them along as companions. They just weigh you down in your quest to get laid. Their constant complaining when you sprint too far away and the fact they need to be healed every few minutes because they didn't take Zombie Defense classes.
Psychopaths are all made after the seven deadly sins, pride, covetousness, lust, anger, gluttony, envy, and sloth. The Pride fight being my favorite because it's the only fight that has a heavy metal song. Was never big fan of the electrionic music that was introduced in DR2. I want to fight the mentally ill to edgy thrashy guitar goodness.
All in all, I would recommend it if you can get over some issues the PC port has. Free roam zombie slaying for your quest to claim your manhood.

I, like many Steam users, have more games in my library than I will ever play, but I still keep coming back to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I've played through it twice, and even now I'm contemplating another play-through, this time attempting a perfect, no fatalities run. I find the game has a thoughtful depth and open ended-ness that, now that I've experienced it, I miss in other games. I won't say DE:HR is perfect, but for me, it's as close as a first or third person game has ever come. After my last play-through, I installed and played through Bioshock Infinite. I found Bioshock, as much fun as it is, clumsy and lacking nuance compared to DE:HR. Now that's one gamer's opinion, so take it with a grain of salt, but yes, for me, DE:HR is that good.
If you like straight-up shooters and don't care about plot in video games, then this might not be your cup of tea, but for everyone else, I'd really recommend giving it a try.
A note about the Director's Cut: I'm a big fan of it. I like the way it integrates the DLC flawlessly, and I've never encountered any of the bugs that others on here note. It also ameliorates the biggest problem DE:HR had - the boss fights. The boss fights are still there, but you can now use whatever play style you want to take them out, and instead of a colossal annoyance, they've become an intriguing puzzle.
At the current prices (especially when it's on sale), I really can't recommend DE:HR highly enough. If you like non-traditional shooters, you will like this game.
I want to spend more time in this world. I'm waiting with bated breath for a sequel, and if/when it comes, it will be a first day purchase.

For quite some years I've been thinking that what we really need is half a controller in one hand (with a joystick, most importantly) and a mouse in the other, for whenever I've played with my controller I've missed the mouse and whenever I've played with keyboard and mouse I've missed the handy buttons and the joystick on the controller. With the steam controller that problem can finally be solved as it has both a joystick and not only one but TWO touchpads!
Now, most games are not optimised for simulatanous controller and mouse input even if they control it, but with its (mostly) excellent driver and configuration software, the Steam controller is
usable, even in games that only take kb&m input, and I always prefer it to other controllers. I also suppose (and hope) that many future games will be better optimised for this combined gamepad and mouse input.
You can
. Want more fine control near the center with the joystick? Want the joystick or a trigger to make a soft "click" when you cross the deadzone? Maybe there's an annoying in-game deadzone, you'd like to counter? Wish you could turn the gyro control on only by holding a button? Too few buttons and you wish one touchpad could act like a d-pad or a scroll wheel or a 7 button menu when you press the right grip? Well, you can, and it's super easy. That and much more, you name it.
With regards to
:
I've found nothing to complain about. It lies perfectly in your hands. I was happy about my xbox 360 controller, and it still is a good one, but after trying a steam controller, you will realise that you've been awkwardly grabbing every other controller while this one just lies in your hands. The weight is well placed and balanced and I can't stress this enough: You don't hold on to it, it just fits in your relaxed hands. And it fits with your index and middle fingers resting nicely on the triggers and bumpers, something I've had trouble with on other controllers.
The vibrators are very well placed and they can do everything from single big TICKs to a fast series of the subtlest of shakes - and there are some even under the touchpads. This makes the controller able to simulate a trackball in a very believable manner, and it works well. Both the gyro and the touchpads are sensitive enough for fps shooters, no problem at all.
Nothing bad to say about the buttons either. Easily reached, easy to tell when they're pressed and released, comfortable enough that I can use the controller hours on end every day without getting as much as one sore finger from it.
Is that you need the entire steam client to run in order to use the controller. I see no good reason it must be so, and it is slightly annoying to have to start up steam and watch their ads when I wanna watch a movie from the bed and find the controller easier to use from there than my mouse. I can live with it, especially since it's the only bad point I've found and so far I haven't heard of any other gamepad with touchpads. Once I get the choice, though, I'm prolly going for a controller that doesn't require an entire client for advertising, selling, installing, and running games as well as a bunch of social stuff. Those things are not what I buy a gamepad for.

I absolutely LOVE this controller. It's taken a bit of getting used to, but it's very ergonomic and if you're used to a playstation or xbox controller, it's not too big of an adjustment.
The main thing I had trouble with was getting used to the mouse touchpad instead of a second joystick. That said, it's extremely responsive and within an hour of gaming I was totally used to it. I'm almost afraid to try playing anything on my playstation now, I've gotten so comfortable with this controller.
One of the biggest boons about this controller is it's ability to essentially replace your mouse and keyboard. With the use of the big valve-logo button in the middle of it, you can call up a virtual keyboard on your screen, which you can control with the dual touch-pads. The right-hand touchpad serves as your mouse most of the time, while the left and right trigger buttons serve as right and left mouse buttons, respectively.
There are a few glitches here and there, mostly on my end. Customizing the controls can be tricky, and I've killed myself ingame more than twice because I hadn't set the controller up correctly.
Thankfully that's only happened to me on games where the Steam community hadn't already done the hard work for me and I was able to download a custom-made configuration for a specific game.
So far, I've tested this controller with Dragon Age: Origins(I've been playing that a LOT actually...), The Witcher, Orion: Prelude, The Elder Scrolls Oblivion, Path of Exile, and Sanctuary RPG. So far, the only game that flat out refused to acknowledge the controller's existance was Sanctuary RPG, which is an ascii-based rpg that apparently says "No." to anything that isn't a keyboard's input. It took me some time to configure the controller to my comfort for both Orion: Prelude and Path of Exile, neither of which had no pre-configured setup available. The others all were quite easy to set up with a quick selection of a community-created pre-configuration for the controller.
Overall, I am extremely happy with the controller, and even more happy with all the community support for it out there. (The very solid and reusable storage box was a nice touch as well.) I highly recommend this controller for any gamer looking to add a sofa to his or her arsenal of comfortable things to use while gaming.

Its simple as that. You want to costumize your buttons, go ahead! add more, add actions to your triggers' extra option. Not satisfied? Add two more buttons! (back paddles, x2)
Other functionalities: You can use your controller on your desktop!  Yes and even type. Atmosphere, challenge and excitement — three words to describe this game.
First of all, let me designate the borders by telling that I'm totally not a man of such games. Even the almighty and all-favored Isaac did not catch my interest for a single bit (even though it took my time while I was persuading myself into playing it). But hey, enough for the self-introduction.
The first thing to pick me up in Prisoner was definitely the game menu. With no doubt and lies it is one of the most atmospheric and intriguing pictures I've ever seen. Those shimmering light, blood stamps on the walls and mysterious music — it was enough to take my breath straight away, and I'm not exaggerating! And along with pressing the 'Start' button and walking through the entry location towards the first level, I was already turned on something exciting...
...Aaaaand the game did it! It not only didn't ruin the expectations, but in fact brought my interest to the whole new level: all those tricky traps, ROK timings (no racism intended), deaths, shifting rooms, deaths, game restarts and deaths (btw, did I mention deaths already?) — are what truly grabbed my testicles and did not released 'em until I finished the game for the first time. Can't say that it took my blood, sweat and tears (and who in their clear mind would say anything like that 'bout the video game, huh?), but the whole process was quite challenging, as I've been ought to be learning from my own mistakes, getting better step by step and studying the game mechanics in order to deal with Complex and pass through the so-long-desired Exit.
Nevertheless, it was a truly enjoyable experience and I can't wait to play it once again with a higher difficulty (as well taking trials) and also am looking forward to see DLC's and of course the new products. Thank you for your attention.

It is important to ask yourself first: what exactly do you expect from a game like this? Because you know how hard it is – to objectively analyse an indie game developed by one person that has no experience but needs an opportunity of sharing his work. Fortunately, Steam provides such opportunity, and that’s why we’re here. We’re choosing the lesser of two… hundred or even thousand evils. These games may be simple but yet enjoyable and with potential, If you’re looking with right perspective.
Steam Direct (Steam Greenlight until recently) has a lot of garbage and finding worthy games became nearly impossible. But this one is a good example. There is no plot, no puzzles, no battle or inventory system with further interaction with objects. The point is defined by challenge and replayability, which will test and improve your timing skills.
There are really a big variety of traps, each with it’s own sound effect. Even though it’s evading comes to jumping over and running through with a proper timing, it’s pretty much addictive and makes you wanna replay it over and over again without even mentioning it.
By the third playthrough the game becomes more fair, varied and engaging, as extra levels occur more often, mixed with other levels, which change its appearance and has a pack of two points of health by the end of it. It’ll make you prepared for the next big level (2-1 – 2-7, for instance).  Despite the fact that I started getting tired of the game by the end of third playthrough, recently opened trials in some way has gifted me a second breath, and Prisoner became interesting to play once again. It really affects your playstyle and changes the pace of the game. Especially, if all five trials is activated.  However, fairness ends right here.
There is something that worth mentioning before you start playing. You can consider everything said below as the cons of the game:
One of such things is damage mechanics. The blinking is literally shows you that you got hit and does not provide you temporarily invisibility. Because if you messed up a jump or missed timing, you might want quickly escape the epicenter of the problem, but it doesn’t work like that, and sometimes it can cost all 4 health points at a single mistake.
I don’t know how to explain the situation with the mood of the game. The soundtrack itself is gorgeous, but sometimes you foget that it exists in the game, probably because of concentration on traps, as each mistake may be fatal for you.
The price is a bit too high. Not because the game is not good enough, but because there isn’t much of content here.
As the first attempt to create your own video game without any help, it came out quiet decent. It shows that developer has potential to create something good, but with right guidance and passion to learn more about gaming. This is definitely not the game that should be criticized because of it simplicity.

I, like many Steam users, have more games in my library than I will ever play, but I still keep coming back to Deus Ex: Human Revolution. I've played through it twice, and even now I'm contemplating another play-through, this time attempting a perfect, no fatalities run. I find the game has a thoughtful depth and open ended-ness that, now that I've experienced it, I miss in other games. I won't say DE:HR is perfect, but for me, it's as close as a first or third person game has ever come. After my last play-through, I installed and played through Bioshock Infinite. I found Bioshock, as much fun as it is, clumsy and lacking nuance compared to DE:HR. Now that's one gamer's opinion, so take it with a grain of salt, but yes, for me, DE:HR is that good.
If you like straight-up shooters and don't care about plot in video games, then this might not be your cup of tea, but for everyone else, I'd really recommend giving it a try.
A note about the Director's Cut: I'm a big fan of it. I like the way it integrates the DLC flawlessly, and I've never encountered any of the bugs that others on here note. It also ameliorates the biggest problem DE:HR had - the boss fights. The boss fights are still there, but you can now use whatever play style you want to take them out, and instead of a colossal annoyance, they've become an intriguing puzzle.
At the current prices (especially when it's on sale), I really can't recommend DE:HR highly enough. If you like non-traditional shooters, you will like this game.
I want to spend more time in this world. I'm waiting with bated breath for a sequel, and if/when it comes, it will be a first day purchase.

This is a very good interactive simulation of how guns are broken down through all their screws, pins, springs, barrel, trigers, etc. It has nice smooth animations that illustrate how everything is taken apart or put together, and it shows how complicated guns can really be. Since I only know how to field strip guns, and would be afraid I wouldn't be able to put the gun back together properly if I dissasembled a real gun, this is a welcome alternative.
The visuals are decent, but for something released in 2014, If you want me to drop money on this, you're going to need to do A LOT better: it should have high resolution textures, and high polygon models. These visuals look like something from the year 2000.
It has some neat features like x-ray and cutaway that let you look at how the gun operates while you watch it fire in slow motion. Really interesting.
Now to the reason I will not recommend this. In order to disasemble specific guns, you need to accumulate experience points to unlock them. It gives you experience points by  learning how to field strip and completely dissasemble, then gives you more experience points through timed tests, and tests that fail you if you select the wrong order of parts. This might be interesting for the first few weapons, but becomes annoying after you have to go over the same thing over and over until you finally get to the gun you're interested in. I was really only interested in the Springfield Armory XD(m), which requires 18, 000 experience points to unlock, and each gun doesn't reward you much, so that would require a lot of xp grinding until I finally got to it. Either a whole lot of grinding, or you pay to buy experience point to unlock guns. That's why I don't recommend this. It has some great features, but while this crap still exists, I can't recommend it to anyone. Oh well, too bad, Noble Empire Corp.

A rare example of a reboot that manages to maintain the essence of the original games whilst appealing to more modern FPS sensibilities. The guns are meaty, there's a great variety of monsters and parts of the level design are spectacular, both visually and in terms of gameplay. Thankfully narrative takes a backseat to the action, but there's just enough of a story to keep you going. The first half of the game is definitely better than the second as certain battle scenarios start to become a little repetitive. The whole campaign could do with more dynamic sections akin to the Argent Tower level. Boss battles are a big disappointment as they just throw you in to a single-atrium arena and make you fight a bullet sponge. There are occasional flashes of creativty in the boss monsters attacks, but they would definitely benefit from some more interesting level design.
Don't bother with multiplayer or snapmap. The former was shopped out to a different development team who took all of the soul out of the game, and snapmap is an incredibly limited tool that just comes across as a lazy apeasement to the modding community. It might be exciting to console gamers, but PC gamers have come to expect more versatility from modding tools.
All said and done, this is the most fun single-player FPS since HL2, Wolfenstein coming in a close 2nd.

The game mixes solving Rube Goldberg machines with environmental puzzles. Instead of giving you loose pieces like in the Incredible Machine, you're given complete tile sets each with several start and finish points that you have to piece together. It's a bit like the game 'the Mouse Trap'. The graphics are really well done and I genuinly like the look of the Whodos. You can also talk to the Whodos who will give you a tiny bit of back story about the mansion. You can pick up a limited number of items and use them to solve puzzles in the various rooms of the mansion. This gives the game some variety and prevents it from being just a string of puzzles.
However the story about what happened at the mansion as is promised on the storepage is merely mentioned once or twice instead of actually told. I still don't know what an automatician is, why Emma wants to be one, where the Whodos came from and what happened to the previous automatician. The game is also limited to the ground floor of the mansion and just as the puzzles where becoming slightly more difficult, I had solved them all. I had expected to do more puzzles in the rest of the mansion so hopefuly that will be added in DLC. The Rube Goldberg puzzles are fun but in the end I discovered they were actually easier than I thought. You're given a limited number of "puzzle pieces" at the start of the level. And you have to use those puzzle pieces to connect the start and end tile. In the beginning you need to use all puzzle pieces just to get from start to finish. But I managed to solve the final puzzle using only three of the five available pieces. I thought you were supposed to use all of them, so I spent a relative long time solving the previous three puzzles trying to fit all available pieces between start and finish. I probably could have solved them quicker by leaving out one or two pieces.
The game is played using keyboard and mouse and even though you can move Emma around using the gamepad, it's impossible to interact with anything. So gamepad isn't really supported and probably only responds because it's part of the Unity engine they've used. Also you can press the Tab key to open up your inventory and notes. I thought I'd mention it here since you won't find that piece of information in the game itself.
Cons:
Pros:
While it doesn't feel like an early access game, since it runs smoothly and I've found no bugs or glitches, it feels incomplete. The game doesn't deliver on the promises done on the store page. The story is only partly told and there is no big reveal at the end.
I hope they end up adding more puzzles to the rest of the mansion and actually tell the whole story.

Middle-of-the-road budget pinball game, part of a series which also includes football- and fantasy-themed sets. The problem is not so much that it offers three tables - that's already more than the likes of Worms Pinball offer - but that the tables on offer are really not very good. Hitting ramps - the most basic thrill of a game of pinball - is so rare as to be a happening, and most of the rest of the time, the ball just flounces around not hitting a whole lot of stuff. The physics don't help matters, as the ball and flippers feel heavy and wooden, rather than smooth, as should be the case in a computerised pinball simulation.
The rest of the game is equally as unremarkable - the soundtrack is limited to a single, Z-tier Playboy Channel soundalike, while table graphics revolve around the sort of imagery no one over the age of 15 will really be enticed by. What a mature gamer is left with is an extremely pedestrian, if competent, pinball simulation - good to kill 10 minutes, but instantly discardable the minute something better is available. Much like Playboy magazine itself, actually...
Not a hearty disrecommendation, but a thumbs-down nonetheless. If you're after a solid, budget pinball title, seek out Dream Pinball 3D instead.
Best table: Car Wash
Worst table: Moulin Rouge (good luck getting more than 2.5 million or so on that one, even if you're a veteran PC pinball player!)

Some games even feel better doing a kb+m setup than doing a controller setup, you have just an obscene amount of buttons you can use. ABXY, start & select, 4 triggers (which can have partial presses mean a button and a full click mean another), 2 butons on the back, d pad buttons while using as a joystick also, clicking in each pad and the joystick, 19 buttons right there instead of the standard 12. Add on the ability to set modifiers like you can have select switch you over to a different control setup. I'm not even using some of the crazier features cause I can barely wrap my head around the standard stuff at this point.
