Dead Rising 3 may have serious flaws, but it does what we want and it does it GOOD. What do we want?
1. To kill zombies.
2. To kill entire crowds of zombies.
3. To drive through zombies.
4. To kill zombies with @#$%ed up combo weapons.
5. To drive through zombies with even more @#$%ed up combo VEHICLES.
6. To kill all the weird psychopaths that went insane from the previous 5 options.
And it DELIVERS. Unlike previous games, this isn't a race against the clock scavenger hunt survival horror. This is a zombie butchering game, one that brings a new level of whacky to your murderfest.
Pros and cons compared to original game:
Pros:
More zombies, more special zombies, weirder bosses!
You thought Dead Rising 2's weapons were wacky? THINK AGAIN.
New abilities allow Nick to use junk items in place of the default crafting ingredients, thereby allowing more flexibility.
WEAPON. LOCKER. No more frantically scavenging for a rare item whenever you're near a safe house!
Allies are competent this time; they know the difference between fight and run, and some abilities will make them tanks that will never die on you.
Cons:
Game world feels small.
This game NEEDED A CROSSHAIR. Players will be forced into a pick-up-sticks game when dealing with multiple contextual items.
HORRIBLE FRAMERATE: YOU MUST LOWER THE GRAPHICS TO LOW OR THE GAME WILL BEGIN LAGGING AT AROUND THE 30-MINUTE MARK.
Very few combo vehicles, horrible standard for a core element.
Roads are severely restricted (to prevent vehicle dumping at critical areas, but COME ON), preventing seamless transition of every vehicle from one sector to the next.
Overall, get this when it's on sale, find a combo weapon that is synonymous with FIRIN MAH LAZOR, and have fun.

Chances are, if you've played Deus Ex: Human Revolution before, this Director's Cut version will feel like more of a sightseeing tour, with developer commentary added into the game - however, there are some bits and pieces that have been changed/improved, with the addition of DLC content (The Missing Link, Explosive Mission & Tactical Enhancement Packs).
As of right now, there are no issues to report of with this port, but should there be any, I'll edit this review to include them - that is, if I actually remember to do so.

Human Revolution takes us back into the conspiracy filled world of Deus Ex, but before the first two games are set. The conspiracy doesn't run as deep as it did in the first game, but the writing is still great. The new augments are fun to play around with, and the gunplay is good. The stealth system has issues, but it's playable.
The Director's Cut expands on the base Human Revolution experience slightly, but it's worth getting it instead. The Missing Link expansion is bundled with it, and tied into the story rather than being a separate game. It also has minor improvements to the boss fights, but it's just little tweaks to help players who went for stealth or hacking augments.
illuminati confirmed? No.
Truly epic game ... great story, engaging characters and play as you will.

After Invisible War, vast swathes of people who enjoyed the original Deus Ex clung to the common hope that Human Revolution would be a return to form. While the initial release of DX:HR in 2011 went some way to accomplishing this feat, it didn't emerge from its development completely untainted by the effects of the modern day.
The story and the world were certainly much closer to the original game than its predecessor, allowing multiple methods of accomplishing the game's objectives and a near-future setting depicting the burgeoning transhumanism that the original game - set 25 years later - would have embraced.
However, the main gripe that the fans had with the DX:HR of 2011 was the boss battles; the unavoidable fights into which the story shoved you which could only be done a single way: utilising brute force. This simply wasn't the Deus Ex way and, as expected, the outcry was quick to begin.
Thankfully, with the advent of the Director's Cut edition, this gripe has very much been ironed out. While the fights themselves are still present - due to the adversaries being somewhat pivotal to the storyline - the arenas in which they take place have had themselves an overhaul, allowing a player to finally use their Jensen's strengths to dispatch the enemy.
Now, the "brute force" approach is just one option of many as opposed to the mandatory route of progression. While it's not possible to simply sneak out the door and bypass the fights, those players who went for the stealthy hacker route will finally have a way to use those strengths directly, whether by controlling turrets, awakening mechs or opening up lockers full of additional supplies.
The Director's Cut edition also comes with the Missing Link DLC fully integrated, meaning that instead of having to load up the DLC separately as required previously (the original editions of both come up as separate "games" on Steam), the Director's Cut will simply transition into the Missing Link content at the appropriate point in the base game's story, making the complete game a more cohesive whole as well as more convenient to play than the original release.
And, at only £12.99, it's definitely worth it if you're into the Deus Ex series. While many will argue that the original Deus Ex, coupled with mods such as New Vision, is the better game, the Director's Cut version of DX:HR is by no means a bad entry in the series. If you were holding off on account of the boss battles or the DLC being separate from the base games, now's probably the time to jump in. It often ends up getting discounted in Steam Sales too, so there's that.

"Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~" is a "choice adventure game" in which the protagonist, which is a foreigner admiring Japan, experiences the life in Japan and tours famous tourist attractions during his homestay with the older sister Makoto and the younger sister Akira (tsundere) that he met online.
It is originally made for foreigner otaku who have an interest in Japan, the UI is in English, but the speech lines can be displayed in Japanese and English at the same time, which lets people learn the language at the same time too.
The amount of CG is small, it doesn't stop at only being a guide to Japan's tourist attractions, it also introduces manners like saying "itadakimasu" before meals, how to eat Japanese food, how to use SUICE and PASMO, the toilet seats with functions, and even small details like the obviousness of how Japanese people are used to vending machines and konbini operating 24-hours per day in Japan. But there is too much info that I found it boring.
The protagonist heads off for a week’s stay in Japan with two friends he met online, who show him around the sights. one playthrough you get to choose 3 destinations to visit out of a total of 6 options, plus you have a trip to Kyoto, and a trip outside of Tokyo on your last day with whichever girl whose route you’ve ended up on. Then after the credits you get a cute bonus scene with your return to Japan.

This is my experience with the Steam controller.
I'm using this on my personal desktop from a small two-seat couch. I bought the steam controller as an alternative to mouse/keyboard and foremost for local co-op games.
I have my main desktop running a variation of the Linux OS that is not the steam one and a laptop running a windows OS. I use both machines on the same monitor wired with a HDMI cable
I decided to just go ahead and buy two controllers from the get-go, since in my opinion a console system is made for local co-op on a couch and mouse/keyboard for FPS and online multiplayer. Maybe because the online games I play are rather competitive and a mouse still offers better precision and faster reactions than the trackpad on the controllers.
The idea of the track-pads used for navigation is really what pulled me toward these controllers and not the xbox or playstation designs. Also I liked the idea of having a three-finger-system below the controller creating a quite different experience than the other designs. I would like to add, that the last console I had was the glorious N64 so I Haven't been using a controller on a regular basis for many many years.
In the box I found.
There are two options when connecting the controller, wired and wireless. I'm not a fan of wireless or batteries in general, so I started out using wired option for both controllers. The included USB cable is only 150 cm so I had to extend the cables for the desired reach. Needless to say this was really not ideal having cable running over the floor.
Now I'm running both controllers on the wireless bluetooth connection, the batteries last very well and I have not experienced no input lag whatsoever(I have so far not had the need to use the Dongle extension dock). Both wireless and wired setup connected instantly on both my machines and worked from the very same moment.
The trackpad could move my mouse around really well and was able to left/right clicking and easily navigate my system, folders, files and even third-party-programs. Once I started Steam big-picture it prompted me to update the firmware, takes a few minutes and you can't disconnect the controller meanwhile, worked flawlessly for both though. Also it asks you to customize turn-on sound for each controller so you can distinguish them from one another, a real nice feature, you can also modify the turn-off sound which I didn't care for. You can set when the controller turns off when left idle, a feature I really like using batteries but also if wired.
So after the easy setup that went super smooth I wanted to test a few games. I have decided to make a few comments on my personal exsperience running games from diffrent genres.
Before I begin a few things about the controller setup pre-game. The controller configuration can be customized, not just what buttons do, but how hard you pressure them before a reaction and multiple functions for one button based on how hard they are pushed. Also the trackpads can be configured for all sort of customized uses. I've used the most popular controller configuration for all the games listed, just to keep it simple. keep in mind that the customization of the controllers is very in-depth and can be modified for very specific needs.
If nothing else is mentioned, the games are marked as full controller supported on Steam. I will rate each game from 1 to 10 based on how enjoyable I found them to be playing with the controller and not how good games they are. (take into consideration that this is based on my personal opinions and experience, you might not agree)
So that's some of the games I've been using these bad boys for, and many more, over the past 6month.
Nice stuff to do:
Browsing my media center(kodi) movie, tv-shows and music.
I'm able type pretty quickly using the Steam on screen keyboard that you can navigate with the trackpads(Far as I know no other controller can type as quickly).
Playing old-skool games through an emulator.
I can see how some people attached to their old controllers and making it really hard to adjust to a completely new layout. For me this was not an issue and I have grown really fond of my controllers over the past 6 month. Be ready for something a little different.
Overall, I recommend this piece of hardware. maybe like I, you will become fond of it.

Great game, Bad start, But it's all good now.

Firstly, the game now takes place in one 'large' open world city of approximately 1 squared mile with no loading zones between the various areas (woohoo). The size may sound small but it's actually very impressive considering you're able to enter most building in Dead Rising 3, with many being multi-storied.
Secondly, you have 6 in game days now instead of 3 before the game ends, although the amount of content isn't much higher than the other Dead Rising games so you won't really be under any time pressure for this one. The story missions actually have no tmers anymore & can be completed entirely at your leisure.
Lastly, the scavenging elements of the first, & to a lesser extent, second game, are now almost entirely gone. In Dead Rising 3, you'll find yourself armed to the teeth throughout the game, with good equipment always being only a few metres away. Blueprints for combo weapons are marked on your map, they will almost always come with the necessary components too, & any weapon you pick up or create in the game is saved & can be retrieved from weapon lockers at safe zones.
The result of the latter 2 changes is a more casual, laid-back, action-focused approach to the game. While I'm a huge fan of the original Dead Rising's gameplay style, the new approach definitely works really well with the world Capcom has created in 3. It reminds be alot of the direction Volition took Saints Row in with the third instalment. A game mode called 'Nightmare Mode', which makes things a bit closer to the original style of play exists however.
Zombie slaughter is as fun as ever in Dead Rising 3. Both the shooting & melee are very fluid, although using context sensitive commands is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ Driving also isn't the best, but it could be worse. DIsmemberment was done very well, & the dead zombies will stay on the ground for a very impressive length of time. In short, Dead Rising 3 knows how killing zombies is done.
The controversial 30fps lock may annoy people with higher-end hardware. I personally can only get 30fps at high settings on mine so I don't really mind. It can be removed by editing an ini file anyway. I'm personally more annoyed about the texture pop-ins. They happen way too frequently & way too noticeably. It's also worth noting that using the in-game V-sync option made things a little choppy so I opted for the option in the Nvidia control panel.
This version includes 4 DLC missions where you play as various other characters. The main missions alone add a sizeable chunk of content, although in 3/4, there are simply way too many collectibles littered around the world. They seem to be included only for the sake of there being collectibles to pick up that do absolutely nothing.
Dead Rising 3 may not be the best Dead Rising, but it's still a pretty good game & well worth the $20 I paid for it.

This is a simulation of an actual golf career. You can either choose to simulate everything or play the tournaments yourself.
When just simulating the career it feels a bit to passive. All you really do then is assuring you get a good balance between practice, tournament and resting and once in a while check if better caddies and coaches are available. That's about it really.
If you do decide to play, be aware that you just watch the holes from above without even the possibility to zoom in in any useable fashion. You can choose to either use a traditional 3-click swing or you can choose not to hit and let it be hit by the computer for you (so called 1-click).
If you choose to 3-click it was very easy to win the tournaments by a dozen or more shots. But for some reason there seem to be a bug in the gauge speed so if you log in another time to play the gauge speed might be 5 times faster than before making it impossible to play with 3-click. That is obviously annoying. Another annoying aspect is the putting. As mentioned you can only view the game from above and the slopes on the greens are only indicated by some vague arrows (that doesn't really seem to be accurate) or by listening to the caddy advice (which usually doesn't say anything useful). Chip shots around the green sometime hit at 45 degree angle from where you where actually aiming without the game telling you why it did it.
The putting is so flawed and uncontrollable it almost alone ruin the entire game. It is one thing to have putting being hard (most golf sims suffer from putting being to easy), I in fact like when putting is hard. But in this game it's hard for the wrong reason. It's hard simply because you have no clue how the green actually look like. They should probably had been better off to make the putting 100% automated as the interface doesn't allow for any useable way of assasing a putt.
Another annoying aspect is that you cannot cancel your shot selection or for that matter change club or aim (when you press either normal swing, over swing or soft swing). That makes no sense at all as you haven't even started the actual swing when doing that.
The 1-click format is probably the most natural solution for this game as the game simply doesn't have the mechanics or interface to make 3-click logical. 1-click can be very interesting in theory as it makes the game all about course management and reading the holes. But when you are not really well introduced to what can go wrong, when it can go wrong and why it can go wrong, it sort of feels like you are not in control anyway and it often seems like you miss fairways more when hitting with a Hybrid or iron then when hitting a driver, which makes the risk/reward aspect skewed.
This again makes you want to simply simulate the rounds, but that as earlier mentioned makes the game to simple and passive...
It's OK to not be in total control of every outcome if you are being told why, but this game doesn't do that. In fact most golf games suffer from the problem of making the game to predictable and to dependant on simply good timing the swing making them more of a "timing skill based" game which is an insult to the game of golf. But this game had the potential to change that , but I cannot recommend anyone spending money on this game at the moment, even if you are a vivid golf fan that likes the course managemant (like I do).

I enjoy playing golf. I enjoy various golf variants, from "Calvin ball golf" to "Improvised course golf" to simple and pitching around the yard. I enjoy computer golf, dating back to old Dos games with polygons so sharp you could cut yourself on them all the way up to various iterations of PGA games and even an old NES Mario golf game that I had back in the day.
I also enjoy management games, because I'm boring like that. I've played various manager games from stock market sims to football, hand egg, and baseball managers.
I do not enjoy this game, however. It's clunky, local coop is even clunkier, there's no feedback on what impact the items/employees/housing/car/training/what-have-you actually makes on your character and their play style (I'd like to pretend they matter, but after 2 hours I'm still not seeing any consistent changes anywhere), and the golf "minigame", such as it is, is a joke without a punchline.
The minigame first off suffers from the fact that it's so forgettable that you can actually skip over it without realizing it. Just click the 'sim the day' button one too many times and you've skipped right over it. Next up, local multiplayer is a pain in the tuckus. The game makes no effort to help you find your characters, so you'll be sifting through a million names to find the ones that you actually made. Once you're actually into the game it becomes a bit of a buggy and poorly made affair. The game seems to pick your default club based on random chance rather than what would actually be useful for an approach, if you don't designate where the ball is supposed to go then it's pot luck whether you even shoot it in the right direction (regardless of your stats(!) and even with the wind turned off), and the 'triclick' function (the bit where you could have any real skill involved) is completely unusable on my computer. It zips along at a million miles per hour, and there's no way to click it accurately because of that. I think this game was made for much older computers than my fairly dated and lack luster gaming rig.
The game suffers from a few other bugs as well, most notably in having some items incorrectly priced. Save your game before you go shopping, because there's no undo button and it will happily let you go tens of thousands of dollars into debt.
In summary, if this were a $2 game or even a $5 game I'd recommend it only for management fans. At $20, I recommend not buying it unless it's in a bundle. Even then, there's better games that work better, look better, and are infinitely more enjoyable. If the minigame looks fun then I'd recommend looking for some freeware golf games, as there's several out there that look the same and play better.

This is a review for the vanilla version, without the 2015 DLC.
"Go! Go! Nippon! ~My First Trip to Japan~ is a simple VN from Overdrive and MangaGamer that's part romance game and part travelogue. You play an unassuming and rather naive weeaboo visiting Japan for the first time. On your arrival you find out that A. the two guys you had befriended online and arranged to stay with are actually cute teenage girls and B. their parents are out of town for the duration of your stay (of course!). This brings about a surprising but not unwelcome predicament as you're suddenly sharing a roof with two very attractive women.
The two girls have distinct but frankly rather unremarkable personalities. Makoto, the elder, is nicer and more cheerful and generally just a bit moe, and can speak pretty good English.  She's good at housekeeping with the awful exception of cooking. She also has a much nicer- ahem- physique, compared to her sister. Akira, the younger, is your basic tsundere, though perhaps more mellow and reasonable than some. She can barely speak any English at all, which doesn't really affect the plot that much since your character is mostly bilingual. She is also a great cook, to balance out for her lackluster housekeeping skills and attitude. I would say she's also the more fleshed out of the two, with a slightly more satisfying arc.
The romance of the game is simple, and who you end up with in the end is based purely on who you spend more time with, determined by where in Tokyo you go explore. See, throughout your week long stay, the girls will take it upon themselves to give you tours of the city, giving you lots of great information about the places, people, and customs. This is also the area where the game shines, as the presentation is both interesting and informative, and basically gives you a lot of pointers if you ever actually want to visit the country in real life.
As for the aesthetics, well, I actually quite like the character design. It fits very well with the nature of the story and theme, and is pretty memorable. The backgrounds can also be pretty gorgeous, which is unsurprising since it's basically giving you a tour of famous sites. The music was pretty forgettable for me, though (as in, I honestly don't remember much about it).
This is a good game to pick up if you're interested in Japanese culture and/or visitng Japan. If you're just looking for a general VN, it's okay, but there are lots of better ones around. I would recommend buying this, but only when it's on sale.

A great controller, and i highly recommend it!
Steam controller is a gamepad for the PC, which, the concept of it, is that in one controller you’ll be able to play all of your Steam and other PC games, controlling Steam, and it gives you also somewhat of controlling your operation system. All of this with a comfortable and precise controller. This is also great when you are far from the keyboard/mouse. So, it have to be a multirole controller that can do all the types of the control forms there are: Keyboard, Mouse, Joystick, Gamepad etc..
Who this controller for? for PC gamers who plays from a couch/bed, but also for those who like to play with gamepad at the desktop, or any other place to play.
You can highly customize everything about this controller. But, also, you can choose a community made Steam controller configs, or use one of the default ones, and then refine these configs, or leave it as it is. So, it’s good for those who want a quick and easy use, but also, for those who want to spend some time and config it deeply. The controller also gives you somewhat of controlling your operation system. The controller works the best in Steam, so, for non Steam games you can add these games to steam.
The general layout of the controller will reminds you any other gamepads, buttons, triggers, thumbstick etc.. but, the major difference is the 2 touchpads, and as what these are config. Each of these touchpads can be mouse, virtual joystick, D-pad, keyboard keys, touch menu, scroll wheel, and more..To simulate the feel of these different control types Valve added an Haptic feedback to the Steam controller, which, gives you a feeling indication of the controls. Also, the touchpads are concave and have a noticeable edges for you to know where is your thumb is on the touchpad. Also, the haptic Feedback used as a rumble force.
The Touchpads are much more intuitive and precise than thumbstick, especially in aiming tasks.
The Steam controller also have a built-in motion sensor, which is great for using it as an steering wheel, plane yoke and whatever you want. Some peoples also using it as a refined tool for aiming.
Personally, i don’t use the motion sensor for aiming, for more refined aiming, i prefer to putting the thumb on a certain spot on the touchpad and tilt the rest of the hand, which will give a nice refined control.
The design and built quality is very nice.
The software is intuitive, pressing the Steam button will bring Steam up, second press will enter to Steam Big Picture mode. While playing a game, pressing the Steam button will bring you to config menus, quit game etc..long press will bring you the general Steam menu. For those who play on consoles the experience will be similar. But it also possible to config the controller in regular desktop Steam mode. The software and firmware continuing to evolve, so, new features and fixes will continue to come.
In my country the Steam controller is still in a “coming soon” state, so, i had to buy it from Valve on Amazon, the delivery was nice and fast.
I'll be happy if the controlling of the operation system with the Steam controller will be more advenced, and i'll be happy if "Controller Companion" will work with the Steam controller.
For summery, it’s a brilliant controller. A lot of thought was put into it, and it’s still continue to evolve and get more features.

I' am a huge fan of the Dead Rising games, and when this game was announced for a PC launch, I was estatic! Finally, a crummy Xbox One "exclusive" game on the PC.  So when I first played the game, what did I think? Umm... ok, I suppose.
Don't get me wrong, this game is a pile of fun. But, there is a lot of choices the developers put into the game that makes a Dead Rising veteran like me scratch my head and wonder why they did such things. Here is a list of pros and cons of what I think about the game;
+Pros
>The custom weapons are back. And bloody hell, they are fun! From a giant Grim Reaper's scythe and machine gun gloves to motorised boxing gloves and an effin' staff made from a battery and traffic lights!
>The custom vehicles are pretty fun. But later on, quite necessary.
>The zombies on-screen is incredible, up to a thousand on-screen at one time.
>Lots of references to the previous two games and tons of returns of old favourites!
+Cons
>The performance of this game, even on my PC with an AMD FX-6100 Six-Core processor and AMD Radeon R9 200 graphics card, is average at best. One minute it runs faultlessly, then it lags and is almost unplayable.
>The graphics are poorly optimised and look rather muddy, even on high settings of 1920x1080p.
>The map design is awful. Just filled with clutter. Potential and useful shortcuts to evade the undead hordes are cut off with loads of crap.
>The story is schizophrenic. One miniute, it is all bleak and hopeless, then the next minute, it is straight up comical. Bear in mind, it is a Capcom game, so the story is not really important.
>The bosses are just... bizzare. And surreal is the word I used quite a lot to describe the boss fights. I won't spoil whom you may fight.
>The challenge which made the first two games brilliant, is all but gone. No survivors to rescue and escort back to safety, any weapon you pick up or create (including custom weapons) can be obtained in a locker and there is now multiple safe houses instead of the tradtional one. There is a Nightmare Mode, but it only shortens the game to three days and only saves at bathrooms. This game does have balancing issues and lacks challenge.
>The DLCs are just five long "fetch quests" with different characters.
>And finally,the main character, Nick Ramos, is just not likable in my opinion. Frankie, will always be my favourite!
Overall, this game is fun, no doubt; fun ways to kill the undead with custom weaponsa and vehicles. But what made the game extremely appealing in the previous two games is now missing and the performance can be a real pain. Get this game at a discount, and play the previous two games if you want a better Dead Rising experience. Lets hope the announced Dead Rising 4 for the PC has learnt their lessons from this port of Dead Rising 3.

August 2017 update:  Game has been dead for a year or two. Don't spend your money.
Original review:  I love this old-school style FPS, with its new-style progression rewards.
Sometimes I just want to shoot things and spend less time strategizing. I've been playing FPS games since Doom II, and the original Unreal Tournment and TimeSplitters: Future Perfect hold special places in my heart, and form the foundation of my views of the genre. Loadout really goes a long way fulfilling that old school FPS scratch that I can't seem to get fixed.
Loadout does a nice job of balancing quick FPS gameplay with progression rewards to keep you coming back. At first, you might find yourself just playing occasionally, as a refresher between more complicated shooters like Titanfall or COD, but the more you play of Loadout, the more you will recognize its complex foundation of old school FPS gameplay and modern reward systems. The maps are wel designed and full of a distinct personality while not being cluttered. Controls are tight whether you are using a gamepad or a keyboard/mouse.
I found myself going back to this game so much, I even threw some cash at them via the Steam Starter Bundle, and I consider it money well spent. I thoroughly recommend this game, especially if you are an older gamer who has been around the block a couple of times and knows exactly what you want.
A very fun FPS game. It has a simple feel which will keep you playing. I'm looking forward to future updates like more maps.

First of all, I would consider this more of a niche type of game. If it isn't your style, or if you aren't into fast-paced, gory, Source engine games, then don't play it.
Now, if it is your style, then this is perfect for what you're looking for.
Positives:
-No price tag
-fast-paced gameplay (in and out of a match within 15 mins)
-easy-to-use development kit
-development team works hard and quick on delivering bug fixes, patches, etc.
-action-rpg-esque feel, level up and fine tune your character to your playing style
-zombies have that classic feel to them, while also having variety between the runners and walkers
Negatives:
-it is a Source-engine game, which can be a good or a bad thing
-more content needs to be added to give the game more flavor/variety
-zombies are a little too weak in the current build, they need to be buffed just ever so slightly
Overall, I would recommend it for the very fact that it is free-to-play, and if it is your style, you'll likely enjoy it.

A really good WW2 game with a slant towards realism, but still remaining accessable and easy to pick up and play.
There is a large selection of maps by default, with great mod support with new theatres other than the Eastern Front, like Crete and North Africa in Mare Nostrum or Normandy, the Ardennes and France in Darkest Hour.
The graphics are now rather dated and the standard Multiplayer is dead as disco. However the game has bots and LAN games, just dont expect 64 people per server, and what few servers are left seem to be in Europe.
One the biggest advantages of this game compared to others is due to it's dated look it can run rather well on lower-end PC's, and the game stands out as one of the few realistic/ semi-realistic games that have in-built Mac support.
There is a large selection of weapons depending on the date of the map you are playing on, ranging from bolt action rifles like the Kar-98 and Mosin Nagant, to rare protype weapons such as the G41 semi-automatic rifle (Replaced by the G43 in later maps.) The weapons are directed more towards the realistics side of play, with bullet drop and breathing, with you being able to mount or brace a weapon against walls to increase stability, or mount machineguns or anti-Tank rifles.
The tanks have multiple round types, and sloped front or turret armor can cause tank rounds to ricochet, so plenty of practice is needed to command a tank and its crew. Many tank/transport models appear in the game like the German Panzer IV, Tiger, SDKFZ 250/1 Half track, as well as Soviet tanks like the KV1 and T34/75.

It's actually a really great port of a port of a game on the PS2. I have fond memories of spending hundreds of hours playing this game as a kid on my PS2 when it was released. Even though I beat the game, it's still always tons of fun running around being a dumbass and bullying students and adults, and doing other random♥♥♥♥♥♥
The controls aren't that bad, but not perfect. But its definitely manageable. The updated graphics are also REALLY nice, as well. It made me tear a bit seeing the game I spent so much time on as a kid look almost completely different. It's no GTA 5, or even GTA 4, but still.
The storyline is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. I don't want to spoil any of it, but the game progression and how new things are unlocked all the time as you progress always make it a treat. The characters are also really loveable and somewhat relateable, if you remember High School being this ♥♥♥♥ed up. Eventually, you'll know all the names of every single student and will know them by heart, as every character in the game also has their own personality. You'll eventually grow attatched to one or two of the characters in the game, and definitely the main character, Jimmy Hopkins. They're also all hilarious, as are most of the missions.
The customization is really great, too. It might not be as detailed or anything as GTA 4 and 5, since it came out before those games, but it's still really great. Now, the BEST part of this game would have to be the soundtrack. The soundtrack, composed by Shawn Lee, is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. Sad to see a game with great potential going down the way of corporate greed.
The game was basically finished, the players were happy, only thing left to do was bug fixes/balancing and the occasional new content (Skins etc). But since a couple of weeks, Hi-Rez has started to change the very core of the game. The thing that set Paladins apart from other games (like Overwatch for example) was the way you could have your custom playstyle.
It used a loadout system where every player could play different, each champion could be played in a number of ways. This feature helped me overlook some major flaws (mostly bugs) and not play Overwatch, cause i find it boring if every champion is exactly the same.
Then they started some questionable champion reworks and tweaks, which resulted overall in a lower time to kill (TTK), which took away a lot of the fun. Now every team had the same champions, and it was more like a generic shooter than a champion based, objective focused game. The very nail in the coffin however was the announcement of OB64.
They decided to throw the 12 point loadout system overboard and replace it with the abomination that is "Cards Unbound". Basically, there is now less customization and a noticeable difference between a new player and a veteran, before taking into account skill level. The longer you play the game (or the more money you invest), the better your chances of winning the game are. This is play 2 win at its very core and the community was outraged. Absolutely no one wants this system to go through, but Hi-Rez doesn't even acknowledge the player concerns. In Q&A or Livechats during their streams, question as to why they are intent on pushing this through are simply ignored.
It is sad to see a favorite game of mine vanish from my library, but I simply do not feel fun anymore when I play Paladins, which is what I am looking for in a game. I cannot recommend this game or this company, at all.
Rumor has it it has to do with a chinese company named Tencent and Paladins is being prepared for the Chinese market, which is heavily geared towards microtransactions. Hi-Rez itself doesn't say anything about that matter, which is no surprise.

Rampage Knights by Rake in Grass is a cartoon-fantasy throwback to sidescrolling arcade brawlers of old. Its taken a few ideas from other games along the way and dared to try something a bit different; what we ended up with is a game that not only challenges the player, but tempts and taunts them with treasures to risk it all for. Simply put Rampage Knights is the Roguelite RPG equivalent of a beat-em-up. Gone are the rather bland stat placements of some recent ventures into the brawling genre, and in their place the game simply brings a huge variety of weapons, items, magic, afflictions, curses, and characters to play with.
Rampage Knights takes a page out of the old roguelike genre and introduces something of a permadeath mechanic. You do have the opportunity to have multiple lives depending on how you play the game, but once you run out its done, there are no continues, you cant insert another coin and proceed on your merry skeleton-bashing way. Plentiful upgrades and restorative items exist to help mitigate the inevitable damage you'll take along the way, but not everything you find will always be of help to you in your current situation. You may just learn that the shiny new item you got has a few drawbacks and is going to alter how you approach each new situation for awhile.
The difficulty ranges from easy-ish to pretty unfair. Unlockable permanent upgrades like stat boosts will help you along the way and with a bit of effort you can even unlock a few new characters which will change how you play slightly. The game offers plenty of mini achievements to complete during your adventure to achieve these upgrades, from racking up a number of kills or killing monsters in specific ways, to having certain combinations of items, and even to beating the game without dying, if you're skilled enough for the task. The unlockable modes in the game include a wave-based arena, an infinite adventure, a couple of different challenge modes, and even hard and impossible difficulties which really ask you to not only perform your best, but sometimes to also get a little lucky as well.
Rampage Knights is going to kill you over and over again, but thats okay because each game is just a little bit different. The layout of the world tends to be pretty straight forward and linear, but it has a few optional loot rooms, shops, and challenges along the way, and what keeps it fresh and interesting is that most of it changes between each game. Additionally, online and local co-op modes means that you can bring a friend to share in the experience with. And do not fear if you die, your less-dead companion can always bring you back by performing well, collecting souls, and sending some of those demons back to hell. Whats more is that while you're having an out-of-body experience your ghost can even help out in some small ways as well, from scouting ahead to knocking down enemies to even breaking destructible items and setting off some traps.
At the end of the day if you're even a mild fan of some of the old 90's arcade brawlers you're almost certain to enjoy Rampage Knights, its got the variety and challenge to keep you coming back to find new items, complete the mini-achievements and unlock new modes, upgrades, and characters, and get further along than you did in your previous game by learning from your mistakes. Its just different enough each time that you don't feel like you're doing the exact same thing over and over again, and its a very easy game to just pick up and play when you've got a bit of time to kill. Rake in Grass hit it out of the park with this excellent indie game.
The Good:
- Secrets to uncover.
- Fair but difficult challenge.
- Local and online multiplayer.
- Risk versus reward gameplay.
- Lots of items, weapons, and magic to discover.
- Randomization of levels, enemy encounters, and powerups.
- Permanent upgrades / characters / modes / difficulties to unlock.
The Bad:
- You can only see what the last item you picked up does.
- Randomization means that some runs may come down to luck.
- The character and mode unlocks might not be paced for everyone.
- Breaking objects on the level to earn gold / health can slow the pacing.
- Friendly fire: Not everyone will like that your attacks can interrupt your partner.
- Permanent upgrades can create a bit of a player/skill gap in multiplayer with newbies.

As a fan of visual novels and someone with a mild interest in Japanese culture, I was intrigued by the idea of a guidebook to Japan that could be experienced in a video game format. I bought Go! Go! Nippon! as part of a bundle and was eager to try it out in hopes of seeing a unique mix of story, characters, and culture. Unfortunately, I was disappointed.
The characters were shallow and unneccesarily awkward, with juvenile writing and dialogue that seemed like it was built for an almost illiterate teenage audience. The plot (outside of sightseeing in Japan) was nonexistent. The only decisions the player gets to make revolve around which sights to go see and the relationship aspect of the game seems contrived and more than a little bit forced.
If you're looking for something to give you a hint of Japan's culture you might enjoy this. (I definitely learned a couple of things about Japan that I didn't know, despite only playing for around thirty minutes.) If you're looking for a more in depth experience than a Wikipedia page with a smiling anime girl on it, though, look eslewhere.

This was easily my game of the year 2017. I recommend
to play this at least to the first ending, and then if you really like the game to continue on from there. From the beginning of the game to the credit roll is about 7-10 hours depending on how fast you speed through the content, but you are rewarded if you show dedication by the story continuing further if you play the game after that.
This year was certainly a good year for gaming, even if it only came up at the very tail end. I've played so many amazing knock out indie games and AAA games this year that it was honestly hard to decide what would even top out the list for me. So why did Nier:Automata take the spot?
Simply put, this game is pure expression and love put on a playable format. Nier:Automata is more than just a game (sorry for being cliche), it is both an experience and one of the craziest passion projects I've ever played.
Have I played games this year with better graphics? Yes- Resident Evil 7 is probably one of the graphically gorgeous games i've seen, and Mario Odyssey is admittedly very pretty with the stylization mixing with graphical fidelity.
Have I played games this year with better gameplay? Probably- While Nier:Automata's control scheme is very unique at times and plays like a standard good platinum game, it sometimes gets overconvoluted and bogged down. The simplicity and grace of Breath of the Wild's exploration and combat took my heart for that this year.
But it's not about these individual elements of gameplay, graphics, even story, that make Nier:Automata special. It's the way they mend together. Each of these elements in the game mix and mingle both with Yoko Taro's personality and the other parts at play. The way you can remove parts of your HUD and display to make room for more upgrades, the way that getting hit by an EMP causes your vision to mess up, the way the music changes whenever you zoom into a hacking minigame..... It just gives the game
good game feel and flow, and makes you feel extremely invested in what would otherwise be "just another platinum game". There's even examples with the story getting hooked in to all of this, but they're huge spoilers and I'd rather just let people experience it for themselves.
And personality... boy, this game oozes it. Yoko Taro's tone of voice and vision for this game persist from moment one you pop it in all the way to the ending credits and even past that. As I said earlier, this really does feel like a passion project. It feels like somebody had a dream for a game they'd love to make one day and then got a team with hundreds of thousands of dollars to back them. On top of all this, Nier:Automata is also well put metacommentary on people who dedicate themselves to gaming as a hobby. But instead of degrading this group and putting them down like others who have made similar statements, it instead celebrates both them and the type of gamer who just wants a casual playthrough. The fact that there's two main endings, both giving what each respective player type might want out of a game, highlights this. If you just want a casual runthrough of the game, you might get a conclusion you seek. But if you want to dig deeper into the game and really get into it, you also might get a completely different conclusion tailored to you instead. It's really quite brilliant.
In short, Nier:Automata is a passion project, a love letter to gaming, and on top of all that, just fun to play. I recommend it to everyone whose interest is piqued. The only person this might seriously disappoint is people expecting it to be similar to other platinum titles- this one has more story and is less reliant on the gameplay beat-'ems. More games need to be made like this. That, and Yoko Taro needs to never stop making games.

A lot of people say this is an excellent RPG game. Many reviews (on steam or otherwise) praise it for allowing the player to choose multiple pathways through missions. I'm telling you: neither of those are true.
Despite what everyone says, you don't really get any options when it comes to objectives. The game is clearly designed to be a pure stealth game because even on the easiest difficulty the combat is too hard. The game doesn't give you enough ammo. You can't get enough from shopkeepers because they only sell very limited amounts, and enemies only drop 1 bullet at a time. You are vastly outnumbered and die in 1 or 2 shots. The enemies have rockets and awesome grenades while you pretty much get basic  weapons. In summary, you pretty have to stealth through missions or you're just going to die over and over. I've played many fps games so I can assure you, it has nothing to do with my skill level.
At least the stealth mechanics are good right? Not really. You have to be absolutely perfect. If you get seen once, the whole map aggroes on you instantly and you die because like I said, combat is to hard.
Also hacking is a must have. There are many quests I found in which that is the only way through.
So essentially you're forced to be a stealthy hacker. It's not an RPG then, just a stealthy hacking game. I bought this game because I thought it was an RPG. I though could play the way I want and not the way I'm forced to. I was wrong.
If I knew all this before I bought it I would have passed. This game is very misleading.

Before the review I have to tell you that I played the original Deus Ex:HR, not the Director's Cut (which probably won't be that of a problem because most of the content is still the same). Also, I don't want to write the whole story-thingy here because you can LOOK IT UP under "About this game" right above the review section - which leads me directly to the PROs and CONs of the game.
PROs:
+There are many augmentation-upgrades, which can give you the possibility to lift heavy things, such as vending machines. Others make that you don't take any fall-damage, or let you jump higher and much more.
+The graphics are really good looking and are mostly very detailed.
+You can choose how you want to play the level: Stealthy, avoiding or just gunning everything down.
+Through the hacking you can unlock special areas of the map, where you can find extra missions.
+You have to make sometimes quite tricky choices in order to reach your goal (mostly through talking with the main person in the mission) which also affect your later gameplay.
+The story is quite long, even if you dont do any side-missions.
Sadly there are also some really annoying CONs:
-The faces of the randomly generated people you meet on the street not only look bad (and by bad I mean the faces look as if they were photoshopped out of a potato by someone who doesn't have any skills in doing that) AND it feels as if there are only 5 differnet faces per gender in the game - I mean it really ruins the feeling if you are running around and suddenly you walk past 2 people with EXACTLY THE SAME FACE AND HAIRCUT!
-The boss fights. I mean I feel genuinly sorry for people who invested all their augmentation-upgradepoints into hacking because in most bossfights THERE ARE NO ALTERNATIVES but GUNNING THE BOSS DOWN!
But all in all I'd say it's one of the best games I've played so far and if you don't mide the CONs you should really start playing RIGHT NOW!

Truthfully as of now, I can't recommend this controller to anyone. It's riddled with bugs with the latest patch. Most notably, the issue with the controller not functioning in games when Steam Overlay is enabled. This can easily be remedied by disabling Steam Overlay, but there's a catch. Your Steam controller will map the keys to the default Keyboard buttons, meaning some actions will not function the same as they would on a gamepad. There is no way to configure the keys or download templates customizing your controls for a game if you are not able to utilize the Steam Overlay. I loved this controller to death when it came out, but now, it's practically unusable. Maybe in a few patches the functionality will be restored and I'll be able to use the controller again, but until then, let this post be a warning to all future buyers that you may experience some issues by buying this controller.

I'm giving this a positive review just for the fact the hardware itself is great. I love the feel of it, I love the features it has, how easy it is to use. The button layout is definitely something to get used to, but it's not super foreign. It took me a bit to get a feel for the buttons and where everything was, but I managed to adapt fast. It's definitely different than a traditional gamepad.
The software though... it has good intentions but... how should I say this... it's primitive. Very early on in development, and it shows. It has a bunch of really cool features. I can manage to navigate my entire web browser using just this controller. I can go on Netflix and watch shows. The on screen keyboard is extremely unique, but I instantly fell in love with it. Playing games is weird at first, but as somebody who could never get used to thumbsticks, it was perfect. Again, it was kinda weird getting used to the abxy buttons, but after a while I got used to it. Some complaints are that the build quality is lacking, and I noticed a few of the buttons (namely RB and LB along with the plastics they used on the triggers feels low quality) but for the most part, it does feel pretty solid. It could be made with better material, but it could also be made with much worse. I personally think it feels fine, but I do see the complaints.The games that are supported have pretty great layouts from what I've experienced and add some pretty unique features to the mix that no other gamepad has (like pressing the left touchpad might activate a small on the fly menu with quick options, the back buttons are quick access buttons for other buttons that just make everything way easier so you don't have to move your fingers away from the action, etc) and if you don't like those button layouts, the button customization and profiling system is EXTREMELY simple and easy to use.
That being said though... there are issues. A big one I've noticed, sometimes your settings won't stay saved. I'll make a button profile and they'll work, then in mid game go back to default settings. On desktop mode some of the buttons won't work 100% of the time. Sometimes I'll make a search and hit enter (the A button) and... nothing happens. I'll check profiles and all is fine, but it still doesn't work. The biggest issue I have though, and this is a killer, you have to launch big picture mode to load your settings. I'm not sure if this is accurate 100% of the time, but to play games or launch custom profiles, they don't just load when your pc boots. In fact they won't load at all unless you launch steam in big picture mode. No, not just normal steam (in my experience), but big picture mode. Load it, exit it, and all's fine (until something crashes as mentioned above). There are very few games that actually support this controller. There is a fair selection, but a lot of games do not support this even here on steam. Also games off steam won't play using the controller at all... for the most part. Only a select few games will play with the controller, even with custom control mapping. There are a few exceptions to non steam games as I've found out via google searches, but to play them you MUST (according to forum discussion threads, I've never done this myself) launch through big picture mode. The controller needs big picture mode to load the button layouts and settings in order to apply them in game. I think that's a major flaw that could very easily be fixed, and very well might be one day.
At the end of the day though, despite the flaws, I've fallen in love with this thing. All the issues I've found were purely software related, and simple updates over time I'm sure will fix most of these issues. There's a couple settings that are currently unavailable at the time of this review, so it's clear they have plans to add more features to these already great devices. I would definitely reccomend this only if you're curious about new hardware. It's unique and intuitive and full of experimentation, but if you're looking for an every day use gamepad, I would definitely look elsewhere... at least for the time being until they push a few more updates out and fix some of the issues I mentioned above.

Super Puzzle Sisters is quite the puzzling game. The presentation is good, the music is servicable and the controls are responsive however for a puzzle game it just isn't good enough.
For one thing the game has 5 buttons...FOR WHAT PURPOSE?!
Let me explain, this game is seemingly a reimagining of the old SNK puzzle games, Magical Drop series. I imagine it was at the very least inspired by them because it copies the basic puzzle forumla but manages to ruin it.
Typically you line blocks up and when you get 3 or more in a row you get a 'line' and score points. If you break a line that forms another line you make a combo and that scores even more points. This game takes the combo scoring aspect and attempts to base the whole game around it. This isn't a terrible idea in itself but where this game falls apart is that you have to manually break the blocks by punching them, with button B.
But only the first stack, if it makes a combo then it automatically breaks the rest, which is confusing in its inconsistancy. There is also a bug or feature where by you can break blocks on opposite ends of the grid by punching them but as long as you do it fast enough then that also counts as a combo.
You want to perform combos so you can build your super meter faster, which comes in offensive and defensive flavor so if you are in a pinch you can defend yourself or you can attack your opponent if they are in trouble and make it worse. Except some of the characters have attacks that are pointless (hiding the AI screen isn't going to have any effect) or broken like the little caveman that makes rocks that cannot be moved.
When talking about the games systems it sounds like a very deep and engaging game but the usage of 5 buttons wears thin on your patience as a beginner and even when you are an intermediate player, this game has no online. So good luck finding someone local to play against and then explaining all the convoluted systems too!
Even then, assume you do tick all of the above boxes by some miracle, the game itself offers little challenge if you pick the caveman and feels like rng dice rolls if you pick any other character.
Also why is the block speed so high? This isn't an issue when you get used to it but remember tetris? remember how it starts slowly before getting faster and faster? This is to ease you into the game. My first few runs were a nightmare trying to figure it all out and then after I did I had to convince other people to play this game and they got bulldozed by the fast movement speed. Yes I checked the options, no there is no way to slow it down!
My final thoughts are this, adjust the speed so the game starts slow then speeds up and reduce the number of buttons required! Make special powers activate as soon as you charge the meter (there is literally no benefit to holding onto the super meter!) and perform both defensive and offensive actions simultaniously. Make blocks break automatically (remove punching) and finally add online.
IF this game ever gets a sequel and addresses the above issues then I am sure it will do better than this game did. I like puzzle games but Bedjewelled really set the standard and I apprechiate this game didn't try to be a copy of that one but it was too clunkly.

A fun little Japanese-style Arcade Puzzle game with super charming, vibrant art and delightful tunes. Not a lot for a solo player to dive into though; just a timed mode (2 or 3 minutes or something; come to think of it, I haven't been paying attention :P ), an Endless Mode, and a Wide Mode that reformats the playfield into something that fits in widescreen, which seems like an impossible thing to keep up with. But it all plays well, which is great news. Especially if you've got some friends around to dive into multiplayer with.
Its that puzzle design where there are colored blocks on the playfield, and you remove some, then plop them back down on other like-colored blocks to clear them (though you have to activate the clear manually - called "Punching" here). All the while, blocks slowy creep towards the top of the playfield threatening to crush you when they reach you if you can't clear them fast enough. If you have ever played Capybara's "Critter Crunch", or Teyon's "Ball Fighter", its pretty similar except flipped around (grabbing/shooting blocks from the TOP of the playfield instead of shooting them up from the BOTTOM). Its a good design, and one most arcade puzzle fans should definitely check out if they haven't. Super Puzzle Sisters executes it well and also does the right thing by adding its own twist here in the form of special moves, which change depending on your adorable SD anime girl avatar.
The only real problem I have are the color choices for the blocks. Most are fine - yellow, green, blue, red, purple and violet. Out of those, most stand out from each other. HOWEVER,the red and the violet look way too similar imho, and there's already a purple (which DOESN'T look like the red). That makes the violet a redundant color choice, and I don't like how much it resembles red. Even the designs are too close - a 4-sided polygon (a diamond) on the red and a 5-sided Pentagon on the violet? C'mon now.
It throws your brain off a bit while you're scrambling around grabbing blocks. There's no punishment for trying to pick up a different colored block when you're already holding some, it just won't let you pick it up. Your brain will take a quick beat to adjust and you'll move on. Still, its a little annoyance that seems like it could be easily fixed with a quick asset swap. Merely changing it out for a different color/design - what about a white block? With 5 DOTS on it (like dice)? None of the other pieces have dots on them. That would stand out a whole lot more.
If the violet block color is an issue for me, I imagine people who are color-blind will hate it. But mostly, the lack of content is what gets me. Puyo Puyo games have cute, simple little story modes. Puzzle Quest and Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes have psuedo-RPG modes; I'd love to see something like that here. Granted, this is like $7 - little for the solo player is no deal breaker; I just want more to do :) Its great for a quick little pickup game though, which is EXACTLY why you'd want an Arcade Puzzler like this in your Steam Library. And there's lots more fun to be had if you plan on playing multiplayer stuff.
Overall, its really well done. Not flawless, but definitely very enjoyable, and perfect for quick pick-up-and-play sessions. Besides Magical Drop V and Raining Blobs, and Doctor Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine in the Sega Genesis Classics Collection (which is Puyo Puyo in Japan - you can pick up the mod to play that version in the Classics Collection Steam Workshop if you're not a fan of Robotnik's aesthetic, remember), there's just not enough of these types of games on Steam. If you enjoy games like this, or think you might enjoy arcadey puzzlers, feel free to pick it up :)

If you are interested in Paladins, be warned that you could easily be sucked into the same pain train as long time Paladins fans.
